The hollow circle marks the pole each chart \emph{omits}: $\sigma_N$ is undefined at $N$, since the line through $N$ and $N$ is not determined, and as $P$ climbs towards $N$ the image $\sigma_N(P)$ runs off to $\pm\infty$. Every other point is hit exactly once, so $\sigma_N$ is a bijection onto all of $\mathbb{R}$.

The vertical ray is the case $P = S$: the line through $N$ and $S$ meets the axis at the origin, so $\sigma_N(S) = 0/(1-(-1)) = 0$, and by symmetry $\sigma_S(N) = 0$. The two charts are mirror images in this respect --- $\sigma_N$ compresses the \emph{lower} half-circle into $(-1,1)$ and throws the upper half outside it, while $\sigma_S$ does the reverse. On the overlap $S^1 \setminus \{N,S\}$ this exchange of inside and outside is exactly the transition function $u \mapsto 1/u$.


\begin{propbox}[Chart Domains on the Circle]\thmlabel{prop:circle-chart-domains}
A connected open subset $V \subseteq S^1$ is the domain of a chart if and only if $V \ne S^1$. Every such $V$ is an open arc, homeomorphic to an open interval.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} There are two implications to prove, and the description of $V$.

\emph{If $V \ne S^1$, then $V$ is a chart domain.} Pick $q \notin V$, say $q = (\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$, and a rotation $\rho$ of $S^1$ with $\rho(q) = N$: the rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by the angle $\pi/2 - \alpha$, restricted to $S^1$, which sends $(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$ to $(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}) = N$. A rotation preserves lengths, so it maps $S^1$ into $S^1$; it is linear, hence continuous, and its inverse is the rotation by $\alpha - \pi/2$, also continuous. So $\rho$ is a homeomorphism of $S^1$. Since $q \notin V$ and $\rho$ is injective, $N = \rho(q) \notin \rho(V)$, so $\rho(V) \subseteq S^1 \setminus \{N\}$; and $\rho(V)$ is open in $S^1$ ($\rho$ is a homeomorphism), hence open in $S^1 \setminus \{N\}$. The stereographic projection $\sigma_N : S^1 \setminus \{N\} \to \mathbb{R}$ of Example~\ref{ex:circle-stereo} above is a homeomorphism, so $\sigma_N \circ \rho$ maps $V$ homeomorphically onto $\sigma_N(\rho(V))$, which is open in $\mathbb{R}$ (the image of an open set under a homeomorphism onto $\mathbb{R}$). This image is connected, as the continuous image of the connected set $V$; and a connected open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is an open interval (the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are the intervals, and an open one is an open interval, possibly unbounded). So $\sigma_N \circ \rho$ maps $V$ homeomorphically onto a connected open subset of $\mathbb{R}$, which is an open interval; this is a chart, by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-chart}.

\emph{$V$ is an open arc.} The same map shows that $V$ is homeomorphic to the open interval $I = \sigma_N(\rho(V))$, and $V = \rho^{-1}\big(\sigma_N^{-1}(I)\big)$ is the image of $I$ under the continuous injection $\rho^{-1} \circ \sigma_N^{-1}$, an open arc of the circle.

\emph{Conversely}, $S^1$ is not a chart domain, by Proposition~\ref{prop:circle-no-global-chart}: a chart with domain $S^1$ would by itself be a one-chart atlas.
\end{proof}
\begin{exbox}[Angle Atlas on the Circle]\exlabel{ex:circle-angle}
Parametrize by angle, which cannot be done globally --- the same meta-principle --- so use two overlapping ranges:
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_a &= S^1 \setminus \{(1,0)\}, & \varphi_a(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) &= \theta \in (0, 2\pi); \\
U_b &= S^1 \setminus \{(-1,0)\}, & \varphi_b(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) &= \theta \in (\pi, 3\pi).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here $U_a \cap U_b$ is the union of the open upper and lower half-circles, $\varphi_a(U_a \cap U_b) = (0,\pi) \cup (\pi, 2\pi)$, and
\[
\varphi_b \circ \varphi_a^{-1}(\theta) = \begin{cases} \theta + 2\pi, & \theta \in (0,\pi), \\ \theta, & \theta \in (\pi, 2\pi), \end{cases}
\]
a translation on each component of its domain, hence a diffeomorphism. A parametrization is just the inverse of a chart --- ``putting labels on points'' --- so the two descriptions carry the same information.
\end{exbox}

\begin{rembox}[Three Atlases and One Structure]\label{rem:three-atlases-one-structure}
$S^1$ thus carries at least three different atlases. They are not competing structures: every chart of one is compatible with every chart of another, so they determine the \emph{same} smooth structure. This is proved in Proposition~\ref{prop:circle-atlases-same}, once regular level sets are available. For instance, on the arc where $U_2$ (upper half, coordinate $x$) meets $U_a$ the transition is $\theta \mapsto \cos\theta$ with inverse $x \mapsto \arccos x$, and $\sigma_N \circ \varphi_2^{-1}(x) = x/(1 - \sqrt{1-x^2})$ is smooth on $(-1,0) \cup (0,1)$. ``Which atlas you write down is a matter of convenience'' --- what is intrinsic is the maximal atlas they all generate.
\end{rembox}

The circle through the course: the circle group $\Ugp(1)$ in Example~\ref{ex:1-circle}; the homogeneous space $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ in Example~\ref{ex:circle-RZ}; three atlases --- four charts, stereographic and angle --- in Examples~\ref{ex:circle-four}, \ref{ex:circle-stereo} and~\ref{ex:circle-angle}, with the remark \emph{Three Atlases and One Structure} in \ref{sec:smooth-structures}; $\mathbb{RP}^1$ homeomorphic to it in Proposition~\ref{prop:rpn-topologies}; its external, graph and internal descriptions, and the one smooth structure of its three atlases, in Section~\ref{sec:ex-circle}; and covered by a line, a local diffeomorphism that is not injective, in Example~\ref{ex:line-circle}.

\subsection{Maximal Atlases and Smooth Structures}

\begin{defbox}[Compatible Atlases]\deflabel{def:compatible-atlases}
Two atlases $\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{A}'$ on $M$ are \textbf{$C^\infty$-compatible} if every chart of $\mathcal{A}$ is $C^\infty$-compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}'$; equivalently, if $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{A}'$ is again an atlas.
\leeref{Proposition 1.17(b)}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Maximal Atlas]\deflabel{def:maximal-atlas}
An atlas $\mathcal{A}$ is \textbf{maximal} if every chart compatible with all the charts of $\mathcal{A}$ already belongs to $\mathcal{A}$. Equivalently, $\mathcal{A}$ is contained in no strictly larger atlas.
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Smooth Structures}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{thmbox}[Every Atlas Lies in a Unique Maximal Atlas]\thmlabel{thm:maximal-atlas}
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an atlas on $M$ and let
\[
\overline{\mathcal{A}} = \{\, (V, \psi) \text{ a chart on } M \mid (V,\psi) \text{ is compatible with every chart of } \mathcal{A} \,\}.
\]
Then $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ is the unique maximal atlas containing $\mathcal{A}$. Consequently two atlases are compatible if and only if they are contained in the same maximal atlas.
\leeref{Proposition 1.17(a)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{$\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ is an atlas.} \textit{(Lecture~6's sketch, completed.)} By Definition~\ref{def:atlas} two things are needed: the domains of the charts of $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ cover $M$, and any two charts of $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ are compatible.

\emph{Cover.} It contains $\mathcal{A}$ (whose charts are pairwise compatible), so its domains cover $M$. Indeed, a chart $(U,\varphi) \in \mathcal{A}$ is compatible with every other chart of $\mathcal{A}$ because $\mathcal{A}$ is an atlas, and with itself because compatibility is reflexive (Proposition~\ref{prop:compat-not-transitive}); so $(U,\varphi) \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$. The domains of $\mathcal{A}$ already cover $M$.

\emph{Pairwise compatible.} The content is that any two of its charts are compatible with \emph{each other} --- which does not follow formally, compatibility not being transitive (Proposition~\ref{prop:compat-not-transitive}). Let $(V,\psi), (W,\chi) \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$. If $V \cap W = \emptyset$ they are compatible by Definition~\ref{def:compatible}. Otherwise $\chi \circ \psi^{-1} : \psi(V \cap W) \to \chi(V \cap W)$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $\psi \circ \chi^{-1}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:transition-homeo}), so by Definitions~\ref{def:compatible} and~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean} it remains to show that both $\chi \circ \psi^{-1}$ and $\psi \circ \chi^{-1}$ are smooth.

We show $\chi \circ \psi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\psi(V \cap W)$. Smoothness is a local property --- a map on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is smooth as soon as every point has an open neighbourhood on which it is smooth, since partial derivatives at a point involve only values near it --- so it suffices to prove it near each point $\psi(p)$, $p \in V \cap W$. Choose $(U,\varphi) \in \mathcal{A}$ with $p \in U$, possible since $\mathcal{A}$ covers $M$. The set $O = U \cap V \cap W$ is open and contains $p$, so $\psi(O)$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ containing $\psi(p)$. For $b \in \psi(O)$ the point $\psi^{-1}(b)$ lies in $U$, so $\varphi^{-1}\big(\varphi(\psi^{-1}(b))\big) = \psi^{-1}(b)$ and
\[
(\chi \circ \psi^{-1})(b) = \chi\Big(\varphi^{-1}\big(\varphi(\psi^{-1}(b))\big)\Big) = \big((\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1})\big)(b).
\]
That is, on the open set $\psi(U \cap V \cap W) \ni \psi(p)$,
\[
\chi \circ \psi^{-1} = (\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}),
\]
where $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ maps $\psi(O)$ into $\varphi(O) \subseteq \varphi(U \cap W)$, the domain of $\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}$. Both factors are smooth because $(U,\varphi)$ is compatible with each of $(W,\chi)$ and $(V,\psi)$ --- this factorization is the ``little bit of diagram chasing'' of the lecture. In detail: $(V,\psi) \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$ is compatible with $(U,\varphi) \in \mathcal{A}$, so by symmetry of compatibility (Proposition~\ref{prop:compat-not-transitive}) the transition $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1} : \psi(U \cap V) \to \varphi(U \cap V)$ is a diffeomorphism, in particular smooth; and $(W,\chi) \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$ is compatible with $(U,\varphi)$, so the transition $\chi \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U \cap W) \to \chi(U \cap W)$ is smooth. A composite of smooth maps is smooth (chain rule). Hence $\chi \circ \psi^{-1}$ is smooth near $\psi(p)$. As $p$ was arbitrary it is smooth on all of $\psi(V\cap W)$, and exchanging the roles of the two charts gives smoothness of the inverse: the same argument with $(V,\psi)$ and $(W,\chi)$ renamed into each other shows that $\psi \circ \chi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\chi(V \cap W)$. So $(V,\psi)$ and $(W,\chi)$ are compatible, and $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ is an atlas.

\emph{$\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ is maximal.} If a chart $(V,\psi)$ is compatible with every chart of $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$, then in particular with every chart of $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}$, so $(V,\psi) \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$ by definition. This is the condition of Definition~\ref{def:maximal-atlas}.

\emph{Uniqueness.} Let $\mathcal{M}$ be any maximal atlas with $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{M}$. If $(V,\psi) \in \mathcal{M}$ then it is compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{M}$ (with the others because $\mathcal{M}$ is an atlas, with itself by reflexivity), hence with every chart of $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{M}$, so $(V,\psi) \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$; thus $\mathcal{M} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}$. Since $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ is an atlas containing $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}$ is maximal (contained in no strictly larger atlas, Definition~\ref{def:maximal-atlas}), $\mathcal{M} = \overline{\mathcal{A}}$.

\emph{Compatible atlases.} Let $\mathcal{A}'$ be a second atlas. If $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{A}'$ are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible-atlases}), every chart of $\mathcal{A}'$ is compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}$, so $\mathcal{A}' \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}$; as also $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \overline{\mathcal{A}}$, both lie in the maximal atlas $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$. Conversely, if $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{A}'$ both lie in one maximal atlas $\mathcal{M}$, then a chart of $\mathcal{A}$ and a chart of $\mathcal{A}'$ are two charts of the atlas $\mathcal{M}$, hence compatible (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}); so $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{A}'$ are compatible.
\end{proof}

Lecture~5 argued uniqueness only (``anything in one is contained in the other, so they are equal''), taking for granted that the collection of all compatible charts is an atlas. Lecture~6 returned to the lemma: Uribe defined $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ as above, called maximality ``not that hard'' and the atlas property ``more substantial'', and sketched it --- a point of the overlap lies in some chart of $\mathcal{A}$, compatible with both charts, ``and then you have to do a little bit of diagram chasing'' --- skipping the details for time. The proof above completes that sketch. That step is the one with content, and the remark on non-transitivity above shows it really needs the mediating chart $(U,\varphi) \in \mathcal{A}$: without an atlas to pass through, pairwise compatibility with a single chart proves nothing. Compare Lee, Proposition 1.17.

\begin{defbox}[Smooth Manifold Structure]\deflabel{def:smooth-structure}
A \textbf{differentiable (smooth) structure} on a topological manifold $M$ is a maximal atlas $\mathcal{A}$ on $M$. A \textbf{smooth manifold} is a pair $\mathcal{M} = (M, \mathcal{A})$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}, specifying any atlas specifies a smooth structure, and two atlases specify the same structure exactly when they are compatible.
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Smooth Structures}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Restricting and Recomposing Smooth Charts]\thmlabel{lem:smooth-chart-modify}
Let $(M, \mathcal{A})$ be a smooth $n$-manifold and $(U, \varphi) \in \mathcal{A}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $U' \subseteq U$ is open, then $(U', \varphi|_{U'})$ belongs to $\mathcal{A}$.
    \item If $h : W \to h(W)$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}) of an open set $W \supseteq \varphi(U)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ onto an open set $h(W) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, then $(U, h \circ \varphi)$ belongs to $\mathcal{A}$.
\end{enumerate}
So a chart of the smooth structure may be shrunk to any smaller open domain, and recomposed with any diffeomorphism of Euclidean open sets (a translation, a permutation of the coordinates, an invertible linear map), without leaving the smooth structure. This is the smooth version of Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-modify}.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. It is used, often tacitly, wherever a chart is shrunk or its coordinates are rearranged.)} In both parts the new pair is a chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-modify}; what has to be shown is that it is compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}$ (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}), because then it belongs to $\mathcal{A}$ by maximality (Definition~\ref{def:maximal-atlas}). So fix $(V, \chi) \in \mathcal{A}$. Since $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \chi)$ are two charts of the atlas $\mathcal{A}$, they are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}): the transition functions
\[
\chi \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U \cap V) \to \chi(U \cap V), \qquad \varphi \circ \chi^{-1} : \chi(U \cap V) \to \varphi(U \cap V)
\]
are smooth (Definitions~\ref{def:compatible} and~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}). Two facts from calculus are used: the restriction of a smooth map to an open subset of its domain is smooth, since partial derivatives at a point involve only values near it; and a composite of smooth maps is smooth (chain rule).

\emph{(1)} $(U', \varphi|_{U'})$ is a chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-modify}(1). If $U' \cap V = \emptyset$, it is compatible with $(V, \chi)$ by Definition~\ref{def:compatible}. Otherwise the overlap is $U' \cap V$, an open subset of $U \cap V$, and since $(\varphi|_{U'})^{-1}$ is $\varphi^{-1}$ restricted to $\varphi(U')$, and $\varphi|_{U'}$ agrees with $\varphi$ on $U' \cap V$, the two transition functions are
\[
\chi \circ (\varphi|_{U'})^{-1} = \big(\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}\big)\big|_{\varphi(U' \cap V)}, \qquad \varphi|_{U'} \circ \chi^{-1} = \big(\varphi \circ \chi^{-1}\big)\big|_{\chi(U' \cap V)} .
\]
The sets $\varphi(U' \cap V)$ and $\chi(U' \cap V)$ are open in $\mathbb{R}^n$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-modify}(1), applied to the open subset $U' \cap V$ of $U$ and of $V$, the restrictions of $\varphi$ and $\chi$ to it are charts, whose images are open by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-chart}. So both transition functions are restrictions of smooth maps to open subsets of their domains, hence smooth. They are mutually inverse bijections (Proposition~\ref{prop:transition-homeo}, for the charts $(U', \varphi|_{U'})$ and $(V, \chi)$), so $\chi \circ (\varphi|_{U'})^{-1}$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}) and the two charts are compatible.

\emph{(2)} A diffeomorphism is a homeomorphism (it is continuous, and so is its inverse, being smooth), so $(U, h \circ \varphi)$ is a chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-modify}(2). If $U \cap V = \emptyset$ there is nothing to show. Otherwise the overlap is $U \cap V$, and $(h \circ \varphi)(U \cap V) = h\big(\varphi(U \cap V)\big)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$, as the image of the open set $\varphi(U \cap V) \subseteq W$ under the homeomorphism $h$ onto the open set $h(W)$. On $h(\varphi(U))$ we have $(h \circ \varphi)^{-1} = \varphi^{-1} \circ h^{-1}$, so for $b \in h(\varphi(U \cap V))$ and $a \in \chi(U \cap V)$
\[
\chi \circ (h \circ \varphi)^{-1}(b) = \big(\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}\big)\big(h^{-1}(b)\big), \qquad (h \circ \varphi) \circ \chi^{-1}(a) = h\big((\varphi \circ \chi^{-1})(a)\big) .
\]
In the first, $h^{-1}$ is smooth on the open set $h(\varphi(U \cap V)) \subseteq h(W)$ and maps it onto $\varphi(U \cap V)$, the domain of the smooth map $\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}$. In the second, $\varphi \circ \chi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\chi(U \cap V)$ with values in $\varphi(U \cap V) \subseteq \varphi(U) \subseteq W$, where $h$ is smooth. So both transition functions are composites of smooth maps, hence smooth, and they are mutually inverse bijections (Proposition~\ref{prop:transition-homeo}); so the charts are compatible (Definitions~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean} and~\ref{def:compatible}).

\emph{Conclusion.} In both parts the new chart is compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}$, so it belongs to $\mathcal{A}$, by Definition~\ref{def:maximal-atlas}.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Open Subsets of a Smooth Manifold Are Smooth Manifolds]\thmlabel{prop:open-smooth}
Let $M$ be a smooth $m$-manifold and $S \subseteq M$ an open subset, with the subspace topology.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$, the restriction $(U \cap S, \varphi|_{U \cap S})$ is a chart on $S$, and these restricted charts form a smooth atlas on $S$.
    \item The smooth structure on $S$ generated by this atlas consists exactly of the smooth charts of $M$ whose domain is contained in $S$.
\end{enumerate}
So $S$ is a smooth $m$-manifold, whose charts are the charts of $M$ that live inside $S$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. The argument was first needed for $\SO(n) \subseteq \Ogp(n)$ in Corollary~\ref{cor:On-consequences}.)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:open-submanifold}, $S$ is a topological $m$-manifold.

\emph{(1) The restricted charts.} Let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart of $M$. The set $U \cap S$ is open in $M$, so $(U \cap S, \varphi|_{U \cap S})$ is a chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-modify}(1), and even a smooth chart of $M$ --- a chart of the maximal atlas of $M$ --- by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), applied to the open subset $U \cap S$ of $U$; its domain lies in $S$ and is open there. These domains cover $S$, because the domains $U$ cover $M$. For two smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(U', \varphi')$ of $M$, the transition function of the restrictions is
\[
\varphi'|_{U' \cap S} \circ \big(\varphi|_{U \cap S}\big)^{-1} = \big(\varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1}\big)\big|_{\varphi(U \cap U' \cap S)} ,
\]
the restriction of the transition function $\varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1}$ to the open subset $\varphi(U \cap U' \cap S)$ of $\varphi(U \cap U')$ (open because $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$). It is a diffeomorphism, with inverse the restriction of $\varphi \circ \varphi'^{-1}$: the two restricted charts both belong to the maximal atlas of $M$, as just shown, and any two charts of an atlas are compatible (Definitions~\ref{def:atlas} and~\ref{def:compatible}). So the restricted charts are pairwise compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}) and form an atlas $\mathcal{A}_S$ on $S$ (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}); it determines a smooth structure $\overline{\mathcal{A}_S}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}).

\emph{(2) The charts of $\overline{\mathcal{A}_S}$.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}, $\overline{\mathcal{A}_S}$ consists of the charts on $S$ compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}_S$, and the smooth structure of $M$ of the charts on $M$ compatible with every smooth chart of $M$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{A smooth chart $(V, \psi)$ of $M$ with $V \subseteq S$ lies in $\overline{\mathcal{A}_S}$.} $V$ is open in $M$ and contained in $S$, hence open in $S$, so $(V, \psi)$ is a chart on $S$. For a restricted chart $(U \cap S, \varphi|_{U \cap S})$, the overlap is $U \cap S \cap V = U \cap V$, since $V \subseteq S$, and the transition maps are $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ on $\varphi(U \cap V)$ and $\psi(U \cap V)$, smooth because $(V, \psi)$ and $(U, \varphi)$ are compatible in $M$.
    \item \emph{A chart $(V, \psi) \in \overline{\mathcal{A}_S}$ is a smooth chart of $M$.} $V$ is open in $S$, and $S$ is open in $M$, so $V$ is open in $M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}); thus $(V, \psi)$ is a chart on $M$. For a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$, the overlap is $U \cap V = (U \cap S) \cap V$, and the transition maps $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \psi \circ (\varphi|_{U \cap S})^{-1}$ and $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ on $\varphi(U \cap V)$ and $\psi(U \cap V)$ are smooth, because $(V, \psi)$ is compatible with the restricted chart $(U \cap S, \varphi|_{U \cap S}) \in \mathcal{A}_S$. So $(V, \psi)$ is compatible with every smooth chart of $M$, and belongs to the smooth structure of $M$.
\end{itemize}
Every chart in $\overline{\mathcal{A}_S}$ takes values in $\mathbb{R}^m$, so $S$ is a smooth $m$-manifold.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[On the Connectedness Assumption]\label{rem:connectedness-assumption}
The board wrote ``let $M$ be a topological manifold (connected).'' Nothing in this section uses connectedness, and the definitions above are stated without it. It is a harmless convenience --- with $n$ fixed in advance (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}) the dimension is already constant --- and it can be dropped. It does matter under the convention where $n$ is allowed to vary with the point (Corollary~\ref{cor:dim-loc-const}).
\end{rembox}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: PROJECTIVE SPACES AS SMOOTH MANIFOLDS
% ============================================================================

\section{Projective Spaces as Smooth Manifolds}\label{sec:projective-smooth}\label{sub:projective-atlas}

\roadmark{Stage: foundations}{The quotient-built manifolds get their smooth structures from atlases written down by hand: $\mathbb{CP}^n$, with holomorphic transition functions.}

The projections $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ and $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$ through the course: the second is the quotient map that defines $\mathbb{CP}^n$ in Section~\ref{sec:ex-cpn}, an orbit map in Example~\ref{ex:cpn-orbit}; the first is the quotient map of Proposition~\ref{prop:rpn-topologies}, and both are read in the standard atlases of Section~\ref{sec:projective-smooth}; Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf} shows the first is a two-to-one local diffeomorphism and the second a submersion and a fibration, the Hopf fibration, with local but no global sections; and for $n = 3$ the first returns as $S^3 = \mathrm{SU}(2) \to \SO(3) \cong \mathbb{RP}^3$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:double-cover}.


\textit{Assignment 2, Problem 2(b)--(c). This completes the construction begun in \ref{sub:cpn}: there $\mathbb{CP}^n$ was shown to be compact, Hausdorff and second countable; here it acquires charts, and the charts turn out to be smoothly --- indeed holomorphically --- compatible.}

\begin{defbox}[Homogeneous Coordinates]\deflabel{def:homogeneous-coords}
For $\vec z = (z_0, \ldots, z_n) \in \mathbb{C}^{n+1} \setminus \{0\}$, write $[z_0 : z_1 : \cdots : z_n] \in \mathbb{CP}^n$ for the complex line through $\vec z$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-lines}). The $z_i$ are \textbf{homogeneous coordinates} of that point; they are determined only up to a common nonzero factor, $[\vec z] = [\lambda\vec z]$ for every $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}^\times$.
\leeref{Problem 1-9}
\end{defbox}

Let $\pi : \mathbb{C}^{n+1} \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$ be the projection $\vec z \mapsto [\vec z]$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-lines}. Throughout, $\mathbb{C}^m \cong \mathbb{R}^{2m}$ by Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}.

\begin{defbox}[The Standard Charts on $\mathbb{CP}^n$]\deflabel{def:cpn-charts}
For $i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$ let
\[
U_i = \{\, [\vec z] \in \mathbb{CP}^n \mid z_i \neq 0 \,\},
\qquad
\varphi_i : U_i \to \mathbb{C}^n, \quad \varphi_i\big([z_0 : \cdots : z_n]\big) = \Big( \frac{z_k}{z_i} \Big)_{k \neq i}.
\]
It is convenient to index the $n$ entries of a point of the target by $\{0,\ldots,n\} \setminus \{i\}$ rather than by $\{1,\ldots,n\}$; this only relabels the slots. Equivalently $U_i = \{\ell \mid \ell \cap \{z_i = 0\} = \{0\}\}$: the lines not lying in the $i$-th coordinate hyperplane.
\leeref{Problem 1-9}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Each $\varphi_i$ Is a Chart]\thmlabel{prop:cpn-chart}
$U_i$ is open in $\mathbb{CP}^n$, and $\varphi_i$ is a well-defined homeomorphism of $U_i$ onto $\mathbb{C}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n}$, with inverse
\[
\varphi_i^{-1}(\vec w) = [\, w_0 : \cdots : w_{i-1} : 1 : w_{i+1} : \cdots : w_n \,] \qquad \text{($1$ in slot $i$).}
\]
\leeref{Problem 1-9}
\end{propbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=4em, column sep=6em]
\pi^{-1}(U_i) \arrow[r, shift left=0.8ex, "\tilde\varphi_i"] \arrow[d, "p"'] & \mathbb{C}^n \arrow[l, shift left=0.8ex, "s_i"] \arrow[dl, shift left=1.1ex, "\psi_i", pos=0.45] \\
U_i \arrow[ur, shift left=1.1ex, "\varphi_i", pos=0.45] &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Here $p = \pi|_{\pi^{-1}(U_i)}$, the map $\tilde\varphi_i(\vec z) = (z_k/z_i)_{k\neq i}$ divides by the $i$-th coordinate, and $s_i$ inserts a $1$ in slot $i$. The pattern of Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-lines} recurs: upstairs $\tilde\varphi_i \circ s_i = \mathrm{id}$ but $s_i \circ \tilde\varphi_i$ rescales $\vec z$ to $\vec z/z_i$; downstairs $\varphi_i$ and $\psi_i = p \circ s_i$ are mutually inverse. The triangle $\varphi_i \circ p = \tilde\varphi_i$ is where the universal property is applied --- to $p$, not to $\pi$, which is the job of Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-restrict}.


\begin{proof}
\emph{$U_i$ is well defined and open.} Every nonzero vector on a line $\ell$ is a scalar multiple $\lambda\vec z$, $\lambda \neq 0$, of any one of them, and $(\lambda\vec z)_i = \lambda z_i$, which is nonzero exactly when $z_i$ is (as $\lambda \neq 0$); so ``$z_i \neq 0$'' holds for one representative iff for all. Hence
\[
\pi^{-1}(U_i) = \{\, \vec z \in \mathbb{C}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\} \mid z_i \neq 0 \,\},
\]
whose complement in $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$ is $H_i \setminus \{0\}$ with $H_i = \{z_i = 0\}$ a linear subspace, hence closed. ($H_i$ is the preimage of the closed set $\{0\}$ under the continuous coordinate $\vec z \mapsto z_i$, and $H_i \setminus \{0\} = H_i \cap (\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})$ is then closed in the subspace $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$.) So $\pi^{-1}(U_i)$ is open and, by the definition of the quotient topology ($\pi$ is a quotient map, Definition~\ref{def:quotient-map}: a set is open iff its preimage is), $U_i$ is open.

\emph{$\varphi_i$ is well defined.} The value $\varphi_i(\ell)$ must not depend on the representative. Two representatives of $\ell = [\vec z]$ differ by a factor $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ (Definition~\ref{def:homogeneous-coords}), and for $k \neq i$, $(\lambda z_k)/(\lambda z_i) = z_k/z_i$. The quotients are defined because $z_i \neq 0$ on $U_i$.

\emph{Bijectivity.} Let $s_i : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$ insert $1$ in slot $i$, and $\psi_i = \pi \circ s_i$. The vector $s_i(\vec w)$ is nonzero with $i$-th entry $1 \neq 0$, so $\psi_i(\vec w) \in U_i$. Then $\varphi_i(\psi_i(\vec w)) = \vec w$, since the representative $s_i(\vec w)$ has $i$-th entry $1$:
\[
\varphi_i\big([s_i(\vec w)]\big) = \Big( \frac{s_i(\vec w)_k}{1} \Big)_{k \neq i} = (w_k)_{k \neq i} = \vec w .
\]
Conversely, for $\ell = [\vec z] \in U_i$ the vector $\vec z/z_i$ represents $\ell$ (take $\lambda = 1/z_i$), has $i$-th entry $z_i/z_i = 1$, and has remaining entries $z_k/z_i$, which are the entries of $\varphi_i(\ell)$; that is, $\vec z/z_i = s_i(\varphi_i(\ell))$, so
\[
\psi_i(\varphi_i(\ell)) = \big[s_i(\varphi_i(\ell))\big] = [\vec z/z_i] = [\vec z] = \ell .
\]
Thus $\varphi_i : U_i \to \mathbb{C}^n$ is a bijection and $\psi_i = \varphi_i^{-1}$, which is the displayed formula.

\emph{$\varphi_i$ is continuous.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-restrict}, since $\pi$ is a quotient map and $U_i$ is open, the restriction $p = \pi|_{\pi^{-1}(U_i)} : \pi^{-1}(U_i) \to U_i$ is a quotient map. The map $\tilde\varphi_i(\vec z) = (z_k/z_i)_{k\neq i}$ on $\pi^{-1}(U_i)$ is continuous (each component is a quotient of continuous functions with nonvanishing denominator) and constant on the fibres of $p$ by well-definedness: the fibre through $\vec z$ is $\{\lambda \vec z \mid \lambda \in \mathbb{C}^\times\}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-lines}), and $\tilde\varphi_i(\lambda\vec z) = \tilde\varphi_i(\vec z)$ by the computation above. By the universal property (Theorem~\ref{thm:univ-quotient-full}) it descends to a continuous map on $U_i$, which is $\varphi_i$. In detail: the theorem gives a unique $f : U_i \to \mathbb{C}^n$ with $f \circ p = \tilde\varphi_i$, continuous because $\tilde\varphi_i$ is (its part (1)); and $\varphi_i$ satisfies $\varphi_i \circ p = \tilde\varphi_i$, since $\varphi_i([\vec z]) = (z_k/z_i)_{k \neq i} = \tilde\varphi_i(\vec z)$ by Definition~\ref{def:cpn-charts}; by uniqueness $f = \varphi_i$.

\emph{$\varphi_i^{-1}$ is continuous.} $\psi_i = \pi \circ s_i$, and $s_i$ is continuous (its components are coordinates or the constant $1$), as is $\pi$. So $\psi_i$ is continuous into $\mathbb{CP}^n$, and since its values lie in $U_i$ it is continuous as a map into the subspace $U_i$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:univ-subspace}). Hence $\varphi_i$ is a homeomorphism of $U_i$ onto $\mathbb{C}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-5}
This is where Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-restrict} earns its place. The map $\tilde\varphi_i$ is defined only on the open piece $\pi^{-1}(U_i)$ --- it divides by $z_i$ --- so the universal property cannot be applied to $\pi$ itself; it is applied to $\pi$ restricted over $U_i$, which the lemma guarantees is still a quotient map. Every chart on a quotient space is built by this two-step move.
\end{rembox}

\begin{thmbox}[The Standard Atlas Is Smooth]\thmlabel{thm:cpn-atlas}
$\{(U_i, \varphi_i)\}_{i=0}^n$ is a $C^\infty$ atlas on $\mathbb{CP}^n$. For $i \neq j$,
\[
\varphi_j(U_i \cap U_j) = \{\, \vec w \in \mathbb{C}^n \mid w_i \neq 0 \,\},
\qquad
\big(\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}\big)(\vec w) = \Big( \frac{w_k}{w_i} \Big)_{k \neq i},
\]
with the convention $w_j := 1$.
Consequently $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is a compact smooth manifold of (real) dimension $2n$.
\leeref{Problem 1-9}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=1.4em]
& U_i \cap U_j \arrow[dl, "\varphi_j"'] \arrow[dr, "\varphi_i"] & \\
\{\vec w \mid w_i \neq 0\} \arrow[rr, "\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}"'] & & \{\vec w \mid w_j \neq 0\}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The compatibility triangle of \S\ref{sub:compatibility} for two standard charts. The overlap lives upstairs in $\mathbb{CP}^n$; its two images downstairs are open subsets of $\mathbb{C}^n$, each cut out by one nonvanishing coordinate, and the bottom arrow is the transition function computed below.


\begin{proof}
\emph{Cover.} Every point of $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is $[\vec z]$ for some $\vec z \neq 0$ (Definition~\ref{def:homogeneous-coords}). If $\vec z \neq 0$ some $z_i \neq 0$, so $[\vec z] \in U_i$. Hence $\bigcup_i U_i = \mathbb{CP}^n$.

\emph{Domains.} Fix $i \neq j$. Since $\varphi_j : U_j \to \mathbb{C}^n$ is a bijection (Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-chart}), $\vec w \in \varphi_j(U_i \cap U_j)$ iff $\varphi_j^{-1}(\vec w) \in U_i$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-chart}, $\varphi_j^{-1}(\vec w)$ is represented by $s_j(\vec w)$, whose $j$-th entry is $1$ and whose $k$-th entry is $w_k$ for $k \neq j$. It lies in $U_i$ iff its $i$-th entry is nonzero, i.e.\ (as $i \neq j$, that entry is $w_i$) iff $w_i \neq 0$. This set is open, being the preimage of $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ under the continuous coordinate $\vec w \mapsto w_i$.

\emph{Transition functions.} Applying $\varphi_i$ to the representative $s_j(\vec w)$ divides every entry by its $i$-th entry $w_i$ and deletes slot $i$, giving the displayed formula; in particular the entry in slot $j$ is $1/w_i$. Explicitly, for $w_i \neq 0$, by Definition~\ref{def:cpn-charts},
\[
\big(\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}\big)(\vec w) = \varphi_i\big([s_j(\vec w)]\big) = \Big( \frac{s_j(\vec w)_k}{s_j(\vec w)_i} \Big)_{k \neq i} = \Big( \frac{s_j(\vec w)_k}{w_i} \Big)_{k \neq i} = \Big( \frac{w_k}{w_i} \Big)_{k \neq i},
\]
where in the last step $s_j(\vec w)_k = w_k$ for $k \neq j$, and $s_j(\vec w)_j = 1 = w_j$ under the convention $w_j := 1$. Each entry $w_k/w_i$ is a quotient of polynomials with denominator nonvanishing on the domain. In real coordinates, writing $w_k = a_k + \mathrm{i}\,b_k$ (with $\mathrm{i}$ the imaginary unit, to distinguish it from the index $i$),
\[
\frac{w_k}{w_i} = \frac{w_k\,\overline{w_i}}{|w_i|^2} = \frac{a_k a_i + b_k b_i}{a_i^2 + b_i^2} + \mathrm{i}\,\frac{b_k a_i - a_k b_i}{a_i^2 + b_i^2},
\]
so both real components are rational functions with nonvanishing denominator $|w_i|^2$, hence $C^\infty$. (For the slot-$j$ entry $1/w_i$ take $a_k = 1$, $b_k = 0$.) A map into $\mathbb{C}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is smooth iff each of its $2n$ real components is, so $\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$. Exchanging $i$ and $j$ gives the inverse transition, also $C^\infty$: the same computation with the letters $i$ and $j$ swapped shows that $\varphi_j \circ \varphi_i^{-1} : \{w_j \neq 0\} \to \{w_i \neq 0\}$ is $\vec w \mapsto (w_k/w_j)_{k \neq j}$ with $w_i := 1$. So $\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}$ is a bijection (Proposition~\ref{prop:transition-homeo}) which is smooth with smooth inverse, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}); for $i = j$ the transition is the identity. So any two charts are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}).

\emph{Conclusion.} The $U_i$ are open and cover, the $\varphi_i$ are homeomorphisms onto the open set $\mathbb{C}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n}$, and all transitions are diffeomorphisms: this is a smooth atlas (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}), determining a smooth structure by Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}. Hausdorffness, second countability and compactness are Propositions~\ref{prop:cpn} and \ref{prop:cpn-compact} (proved for $S^{2n+1}/S^1$, which carries the same topology as $(\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{C}^\times$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-lines}). Together with the charts onto open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, which make $\mathbb{CP}^n$ locally Euclidean of dimension $2n$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-charts}), these make $\mathbb{CP}^n$ a topological manifold of dimension $2n$ (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}), and with the atlas a compact smooth manifold of real dimension $2n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[$\mathbb{CP}^n$ Is a Complex Manifold]\thmlabel{cor:cpn-complex}
The transition functions of the standard atlas are holomorphic. Hence $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$, in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:regularity-classes}.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} By Definition~\ref{def:regularity-classes}, two things are required: charts with values in open subsets of $\mathbb{C}^n$, which the standard charts $\varphi_i : U_i \to \mathbb{C}^n$ are (Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-chart}); and transition functions that are holomorphic with holomorphic inverses. Fix $i \neq j$ (for $i = j$ the transition is the identity). Each component $\vec w \mapsto w_k/w_i$ of a transition function $\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cpn-atlas}) --- including the slot-$j$ component $1/w_i$, by the convention $w_j := 1$ --- is a quotient of complex polynomials with denominator nonvanishing on the domain $\{w_i \neq 0\}$, hence holomorphic. A map into $\mathbb{C}^n$ is holomorphic iff each component is, so $\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}$ is holomorphic. Its inverse is $\varphi_j \circ \varphi_i^{-1}$, given by the same formula with $i$ and $j$ interchanged, hence holomorphic by the same reasoning. So the standard atlas is a holomorphic atlas with values in $\mathbb{C}^n$, and $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[$\mathbb{CP}^1$ Is the Riemann Sphere]\thmlabel{prop:cp1-sphere}
$\mathbb{CP}^1$ is homeomorphic to $S^2$.
\leeref{Problem 4-5(b)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Points of $\mathbb{CP}^1$ are written $[z_0 : z_1]$ (Definition~\ref{def:homogeneous-coords}), and $N = (0,0,1)$ is the north pole. The plan: define $\Phi : S^2 \to \mathbb{CP}^1$, show it is continuous and bijective, and conclude by compactness.

\emph{The two formulas agree.} For $(x,y,z) \in S^2$ the identity $(x+iy)(x-iy) = x^2 + y^2 = (1-z)(1+z)$, which holds because $x^2 + y^2 = 1 - z^2$ on $S^2$, shows that $[x+iy : 1-z]$, defined when $z \ne 1$, and $[1+z : x-iy]$, defined when $z \ne -1$, are the same point of $\mathbb{CP}^1$ wherever both are defined. (The first is defined when $z \neq 1$ because then $(x+iy, 1-z) \neq 0$, and the second when $z \neq -1$ likewise.) In detail: if $z \neq \pm 1$, then $x^2 + y^2 = 1 - z^2 > 0$, so $x - iy \neq 0$, and $\lambda = (x-iy)/(1-z) \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ satisfies, by the identity,
\[
\lambda\,(x+iy) = \frac{x^2+y^2}{1-z} = \frac{(1-z)(1+z)}{1-z} = 1+z, \qquad \lambda\,(1-z) = x - iy .
\]
So $(1+z, x-iy) = \lambda\,(x+iy, 1-z)$, and the two classes are equal.

\emph{$\Phi$ is well defined and continuous.} So there is a well-defined map $\Phi : S^2 \to \mathbb{CP}^1$, given by the first formula on $O_+ = \{z \ne 1\}$ and by the second on $O_- = \{z \ne -1\}$. On $O_+$ it is the composite of the continuous map $(x,y,z) \mapsto (x+iy, 1-z)$ into $\mathbb{C}^2 \setminus \{0\}$ with the continuous projection $\pi$, and similarly on $O_-$; so $\Phi$ is continuous on each of the two open sets $\{z \ne 1\}$ and $\{z \ne -1\}$ covering $S^2$, hence continuous. (For $W \subseteq \mathbb{CP}^1$ open, $\Phi^{-1}(W) = (\Phi|_{O_+})^{-1}(W) \cup (\Phi|_{O_-})^{-1}(W)$, and each piece is open in an open subset of $S^2$, hence open in $S^2$.)

\emph{$\Phi$ on $S^2 \setminus \{N\}$.} The point of $S^2$ with $z = 1$ is $N$ (then $x^2 + y^2 = 0$), so $O_+ = S^2 \setminus \{N\}$. On $S^2 \setminus \{N\}$ it is $p \mapsto [\sigma(p) : 1]$, where $\sigma(x,y,z) = (x+iy)/(1-z)$ is the stereographic projection: multiply the representative $(x+iy, 1-z)$ by $1/(1-z)$. This is a bijection onto $\mathbb{C}$, with inverse $w \mapsto \big(2\operatorname{Re} w,\, 2\operatorname{Im} w,\, |w|^2 - 1\big)/(|w|^2+1)$. To check both composites: for $p = (x,y,z) \in S^2 \setminus \{N\}$ and $w = \sigma(p)$,
\[
|w|^2 = \frac{x^2+y^2}{(1-z)^2} = \frac{1+z}{1-z}, \qquad |w|^2 + 1 = \frac{2}{1-z}, \qquad |w|^2 - 1 = \frac{2z}{1-z},
\]
so $\big(2\operatorname{Re} w, 2\operatorname{Im} w, |w|^2 - 1\big)/(|w|^2+1) = \big(\tfrac{2x}{1-z}, \tfrac{2y}{1-z}, \tfrac{2z}{1-z}\big) \cdot \tfrac{1-z}{2} = (x,y,z)$. Conversely, for $w \in \mathbb{C}$ the point $q = \big(2\operatorname{Re} w, 2\operatorname{Im} w, |w|^2 - 1\big)/(|w|^2+1)$ satisfies
\[
|q|^2 = \frac{4|w|^2 + (|w|^2-1)^2}{(|w|^2+1)^2} = \frac{(|w|^2+1)^2}{(|w|^2+1)^2} = 1,
\]
its third coordinate is $<1$, so $q \in S^2 \setminus \{N\}$; and $1 - q_3 = 2/(|w|^2+1)$, so $\sigma(q) = \dfrac{2w/(|w|^2+1)}{2/(|w|^2+1)} = w$. So $\Phi$ maps $S^2 \setminus \{N\}$ bijectively onto $U_1 = \{[w : 1]\}$: there $\Phi = \varphi_1^{-1} \circ \sigma$, where $\varphi_1^{-1}(w) = [w : 1]$ is the inverse of the standard chart $\varphi_1$, a bijection $\mathbb{C} \to U_1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-chart} with $n = 1$, $i = 1$).

\emph{$\Phi$ at $N$.} Since $N \in O_-$, the second formula gives $\Phi(N) = [2 : 0] = [1:0]$, and this is the one point outside $U_1$: every point outside $U_1$ has the form $[z_0 : 0]$ with $z_0 \neq 0$, which equals $[1 : 0]$. Hence $\Phi$ is a bijection $S^2 \to \mathbb{CP}^1$.

\emph{Conclusion.} Thus $\Phi$ is a continuous bijection from the compact $S^2$ (closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}^3$, Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(1)) onto the Hausdorff $\mathbb{CP}^1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn}), hence a homeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(6)).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:smooth-structures-6}
For $n = 1$ there are two standard charts and a single transition function, $w \mapsto 1/w$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$ --- the complex counterpart of the stereographic transition $u \mapsto 1/u$ of Example~\ref{ex:circle-stereo}.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[Real Projective Space]\thmlabel{cor:rpn-atlas}
Let $\mathbb{RP}^n = S^n/\{\pm 1\} \cong (\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{R}^\times$, the space of real lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. With $U_i = \{[\vec x] \mid x_i \neq 0\}$ and $\varphi_i([\vec x]) = (x_k/x_i)_{k \neq i}$, the family $\{(U_i, \varphi_i)\}_{i=0}^n$ is a smooth atlas, and $\mathbb{RP}^n$ is a compact smooth manifold of dimension $n$.
\leeref{Example 1.33}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Every argument of \ref{sec:ex-cpn} and of this section goes through verbatim with $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{R}^\times$, $\{\pm1\}$ and $S^n$ in place of $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{C}^\times$, $S^1$ and $S^{2n+1}$: the group $\{\pm 1\}$ is finite, hence compact, and acts on $S^n$ by isometries; the transition maps are the real rational functions $x_k/x_i$. Hausdorffness can alternatively be read off from Corollary~\ref{cor:orbit-T2}. Step by step:

\emph{The two descriptions.} Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-lines} with this renaming: the orbit of $\vec x \neq 0$ under $\mathbb{R}^\times$ is the punctured line $\mathbb{R}\vec x \setminus \{0\}$, and $\mathbb{R}^\times \vec x \mapsto \{\pm \vec x/|\vec x|\}$ is a homeomorphism $(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{R}^\times \to S^n/\{\pm1\}$; the proof is the same chase, with $g(\vec x) = \vec x/|\vec x|$ satisfying $g(\lambda\vec x) = (\lambda/|\lambda|)\,g(\vec x)$ and $\lambda/|\lambda| = \pm 1$ for $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^\times$. So the two descriptions of $\mathbb{RP}^n$ carry the same topology. Write $\pi : \mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\} \to \mathbb{RP}^n$, $\vec x \mapsto [\vec x]$, for the quotient map.

\emph{Hausdorff, second countable, compact.} The group $\{\pm 1\}$ acts on $S^n$ by $(\varepsilon, \vec x) \mapsto \varepsilon\vec x$, continuously (a restriction of scalar multiplication), and is finite, hence compact; $S^n$ is compact (closed and bounded, Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(1)) and Hausdorff (a metric space, Proposition~\ref{fact:metric}(1)). So $S^n/\{\pm1\}$ is Hausdorff by Corollary~\ref{cor:orbit-T2}; the direct argument for $\mathbb{CP}^n$ of Assignment 2 also applies, since it uses only that the group is compact and acts by isometries. The orbit relation is open (Lemma~\ref{lem:orbit-open}) and $S^n$ is second countable (Proposition~\ref{fact:metric}(3)), so $S^n/\{\pm1\}$ is second countable by Theorem~\ref{thm:2c-quotient}. It is compact as the continuous image of $S^n$ under the projection (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(2)).

\emph{Charts.} As in Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-chart} with $\mathbb{R}$ for $\mathbb{C}$. $U_i$ is well defined, since $\lambda x_i \neq 0 \iff x_i \neq 0$ for $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^\times$, and open, since $\pi^{-1}(U_i) = \{\vec x \neq 0 \mid x_i \neq 0\}$ is the complement of the closed set $H_i \setminus \{0\}$, $H_i = \{x_i = 0\}$. $\varphi_i$ is well defined, since $(\lambda x_k)/(\lambda x_i) = x_k/x_i$. It is a bijection $U_i \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with inverse $\vec w \mapsto [w_0 : \cdots : w_{i-1} : 1 : w_{i+1} : \cdots : w_n]$ ($1$ in slot $i$): applying $\varphi_i$ to this point returns $\vec w$, and for $[\vec x] \in U_i$ the vector $\vec x/x_i$ represents $[\vec x]$ and is $\vec w = \varphi_i([\vec x])$ with $1$ inserted in slot $i$. $\varphi_i$ is continuous by Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient-restrict} and Theorem~\ref{thm:univ-quotient-full}, applied to the continuous map $\vec x \mapsto (x_k/x_i)_{k \neq i}$ on $\pi^{-1}(U_i)$, which is constant on the fibres; and its inverse is $\pi$ composed with the continuous map inserting $1$ in slot $i$. So each $\varphi_i$ is a homeomorphism of $U_i$ onto $\mathbb{R}^n$.

\emph{Atlas.} Every $\vec x \neq 0$ has some $x_i \neq 0$, so the $U_i$ cover. For $i \neq j$ the computation of Theorem~\ref{thm:cpn-atlas} gives $\varphi_j(U_i \cap U_j) = \{\vec w \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid w_i \neq 0\}$, an open set, and
\[
\big(\varphi_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}\big)(\vec w) = \Big( \frac{w_k}{w_i} \Big)_{k \neq i}, \qquad w_j := 1 .
\]
Each component is a rational function of real variables with denominator $w_i \neq 0$ on the domain, hence $C^\infty$ --- no splitting into real and imaginary parts is needed; and the inverse $\varphi_j \circ \varphi_i^{-1}$ is the same formula with $i$ and $j$ interchanged, also $C^\infty$. So all transitions are diffeomorphisms, the charts are pairwise compatible, and $\{(U_i, \varphi_i)\}_{i=0}^n$ is a smooth atlas (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}), determining a smooth structure (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}). The charts take values in $\mathbb{R}^n$, so $\mathbb{RP}^n$ is locally Euclidean of dimension $n$; with the two point-set conditions above it is a topological $n$-manifold (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}), and with this atlas a compact smooth manifold of dimension $n$.
\end{proof}

The chart $U_0$ of $\mathbb{RP}^1$, drawn in the plane of homogeneous coordinates. A point of $\mathbb{RP}^1$ is a line through the origin. A line $L$ with $x_0 \ne 0$ meets the affine line $x_0 = 1$ in exactly one point, $(1, x_1/x_0)$, and the chart $\varphi_0(L) = x_1/x_0$ records where. The one line with $x_0 = 0$ --- the $x_1$-axis, the point $[0:1]$ --- is parallel to $x_0 = 1$ and never meets it: it is the point at infinity that $U_0$ misses, and the second chart $U_1$ covers it. On the right, $\mathbb{RP}^1$ drawn as a circle, with $U_0$ everything except the top point. In $\mathbb{RP}^n$ the same picture holds with the affine hyperplane $x_0 = 1$ in place of the line.

\begin{propbox}[The Two Topologies on $\mathbb{RP}^n$ Agree]\thmlabel{prop:rpn-topologies}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Under $[\vec x] \mapsto \mathbb{R}\vec x$, the quotient topology on $\mathbb{RP}^n = S^n/\{\pm1\}$ agrees with the topology of $\Gr_1(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ transported from the coset space $\Ogp(n+1)/(\Ogp(1)\times\Ogp(n))$ in \ref{sec:homogeneous}.
    \item $\mathbb{RP}^1$ is homeomorphic to $S^1$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Examples 1.5 and 1.33}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} (1) Write $\pi : S^n \to S^n/\{\pm1\}$, $\vec x \mapsto [\vec x] = \{\vec x, -\vec x\}$, and $\beta : S^n/\{\pm1\} \to \Gr_1(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$, $[\vec x] \mapsto \mathbb{R}\vec x$, a bijection because each line through $0$ meets $S^n$ in exactly one antipodal pair (the remark \emph{On the Index} in \ref{sec:GH-topology}). The claim is that $\beta$ is a homeomorphism when $\Gr_1(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ carries the topology of Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}.

\emph{The action.} $\Ogp(n+1)$ acts on $S^n/\{\pm1\}$ by $g \cdot [\vec x] = [g\vec x]$, continuously: the map $\mathrm{id} \times \pi : \Ogp(n+1) \times S^n \to \Ogp(n+1) \times S^n/\{\pm1\}$ is an open continuous surjection, hence a quotient map, and the action descends along it by the universal property. In detail: for $g \in \Ogp(n+1)$, $|g\vec x| = |\vec x| = 1$ and $g(-\vec x) = -g\vec x$, so $[g\vec x] \in S^n/\{\pm1\}$ depends only on $[\vec x]$; and $I \cdot [\vec x] = [\vec x]$, $g \cdot (g' \cdot [\vec x]) = [gg'\vec x] = (gg') \cdot [\vec x]$, so this is an action. The map $\mathrm{id} \times \pi$ is continuous by Theorem~\ref{thm:univ-product} (its components $\mathrm{id} \circ \pi_1$ and $\pi \circ \pi_2$ are continuous), surjective because $\pi$ is, and open: $\pi$ is open by Lemma~\ref{lem:orbit-open} (it is the projection of the orbit relation of the continuous action $(\varepsilon, \vec x) \mapsto \varepsilon\vec x$ of $\{\pm1\}$), so the image $A \times \pi(B)$ of a basic open box $A \times B$ is open, and the image of a union of boxes is the union of their images. So it is a quotient map by Proposition~\ref{prop:open-surj-quotient}. The map $(g, \vec x) \mapsto \pi(g\vec x)$ on $\Ogp(n+1) \times S^n$ is continuous (matrix multiplication followed by $\pi$) and constant on the fibres $\{(g, \vec x), (g, -\vec x)\}$ of $\mathrm{id} \times \pi$, since $\pi(g(-\vec x)) = \pi(-g\vec x) = \pi(g\vec x)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:univ-quotient-full} it descends to a continuous map $\Ogp(n+1) \times S^n/\{\pm1\} \to S^n/\{\pm1\}$, $(g, [\vec x]) \mapsto [g\vec x]$, which is the action; so the action is continuous (Definition~\ref{def:continuous-action}).

\emph{Transitive, with the Grassmannian's isotropy group.} The action is transitive: given $[\vec x], [\vec y]$, Proposition~\ref{prop:On-transitive} (with $k = 1$ and $n+1$ in place of $n$) gives $g \in \Ogp(n+1)$ with $g(\mathbb{R}\vec x) = \mathbb{R}\vec y$, so $g\vec x = c\,\vec y$ with $|c| = |g\vec x| = 1$, i.e.\ $c = \pm 1$, and $g \cdot [\vec x] = [\pm\vec y] = [\vec y]$. Let $e_1$ be the first standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ and $V_0 = \mathbb{R}e_1$. Then $g \cdot [e_1] = [e_1]$ iff $ge_1 = \pm e_1$ iff $g V_0 = V_0$ (as $|ge_1| = 1$), so the isotropy group $H$ of $[e_1]$ equals that of $V_0$ in $\Gr_1(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$, which is $\Ogp(1) \times \Ogp(n)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:grassmann-isotropy}.

\emph{The homeomorphism.} The action is transitive, the coset space is compact, and $S^n/\{\pm1\}$ is Hausdorff, so Theorem~\ref{thm:GH-homeo} identifies $S^n/\{\pm1\}$ homeomorphically with the coset space --- which is precisely the transported topology. In detail: $\Ogp(n+1)/H$ is compact as the image of the compact group $\Ogp(n+1)$ (shown in the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}) under the continuous projection (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(2)), and $S^n/\{\pm1\}$ is Hausdorff by Corollary~\ref{cor:orbit-T2}. So Theorem~\ref{thm:GH-homeo}(2) makes $\Phi_1 : \Ogp(n+1)/H \to S^n/\{\pm1\}$, $gH \mapsto g \cdot [e_1] = [ge_1]$, a homeomorphism. On the other side, $\Phi_2 : \Ogp(n+1)/H \to \Gr_1(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$, $gH \mapsto gV_0$, is a homeomorphism by the definition of the transported topology (Definition~\ref{def:homogeneous-topology}, Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}). Since $\beta([ge_1]) = \mathbb{R}\,ge_1 = gV_0$, we have $\beta \circ \Phi_1 = \Phi_2$, so $\beta = \Phi_2 \circ \Phi_1^{-1}$ is a composite of homeomorphisms. That is, a set $W \subseteq \mathbb{RP}^n$ is open in the quotient topology iff $\beta(W)$ is open in the transported topology.

(2) Let $\sigma_N, \sigma_S$ be the stereographic charts of Example~\ref{ex:circle-stereo}, and $\varphi_0, \varphi_1$ the standard charts of $\mathbb{RP}^1$, $\varphi_0([x_0 : x_1]) = x_1/x_0$ on $U_0 = \{x_0 \neq 0\}$ and $\varphi_1([x_0 : x_1]) = x_0/x_1$ on $U_1 = \{x_1 \neq 0\}$. Define $F = \sigma_N^{-1} \circ \varphi_0$ on $U_0$ and $F = \sigma_S^{-1} \circ \varphi_1$ on $U_1$.

\emph{Well defined and continuous.} On $U_0 \cap U_1$ we have $\varphi_1 = 1/\varphi_0$, since $x_0/x_1 = 1/(x_1/x_0)$, with $\varphi_0 \neq 0$ there; and $\sigma_S \circ \sigma_N^{-1}(u) = 1/u$ for $u \neq 0$ gives, applying $\sigma_S^{-1}$, $\sigma_N^{-1}(u) = \sigma_S^{-1}(1/u)$. So for $\ell \in U_0 \cap U_1$, with $u = \varphi_0(\ell)$,
\[
\sigma_S^{-1}\big(\varphi_1(\ell)\big) = \sigma_S^{-1}(1/u) = \sigma_N^{-1}(u) = \sigma_N^{-1}\big(\varphi_0(\ell)\big):
\]
the two formulas agree and $F$ is well defined. It is continuous on each of the open sets $U_0$, $U_1$ (a composite of homeomorphisms), which cover $\mathbb{RP}^1$, so it is continuous.

\emph{Bijective.} It maps $U_0$ bijectively onto $S^1 \setminus \{N\}$, as the composite of the bijections $\varphi_0 : U_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma_N^{-1} : \mathbb{R} \to S^1 \setminus \{N\}$. The one point outside $U_0$ is $[0:1]$ (a point $[0 : x_1]$ has $x_1 \neq 0$ and equals $[0:1]$), and $F([0:1]) = \sigma_S^{-1}(\varphi_1([0:1])) = \sigma_S^{-1}(0) = N$, since $\sigma_S(N) = 0/(1+1) = 0$. So $F$ is a bijection onto $S^1$. So $F$ is a continuous bijection from the compact $\mathbb{RP}^1$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:rpn-atlas}) onto the Hausdorff $S^1$ (a metric space, Proposition~\ref{fact:metric}(1)), hence a homeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(6)).

\emph{Diffeomorphism.} Both transition functions are $u \mapsto 1/u$, and in the charts used $F$ has coordinate representation the identity; so it is even a diffeomorphism, in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism} below. Explicitly, with $S^1$ carrying the stereographic atlas: $F(U_0) = S^1 \setminus \{N\}$ and $\sigma_N \circ F \circ \varphi_0^{-1} = \sigma_N \circ \sigma_N^{-1} \circ \varphi_0 \circ \varphi_0^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}}$; likewise $\sigma_S \circ F \circ \varphi_1^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}}$; and $F^{-1}$ is $\varphi_0^{-1} \circ \sigma_N$ on $S^1 \setminus \{N\}$ and $\varphi_1^{-1} \circ \sigma_S$ on $S^1 \setminus \{S\}$, with coordinate representations $\varphi_0 \circ F^{-1} \circ \sigma_N^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}}$ and $\varphi_1 \circ F^{-1} \circ \sigma_S^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}}$, all smooth.
\end{proof}

The quotient $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:rpn-topologies}, drawn for $n = 2$. A line through the origin meets the sphere in two antipodal points $p$ and $-p$, which $\pi$ identifies. Every line meets the closed upper hemisphere: once if it is not horizontal, and in a pair of antipodal points $q$, $-q$ of the equator if it is. So $\mathbb{RP}^2$ can be pictured as a closed disc with antipodal boundary points glued, as the arrows indicate. For $n = 1$ the same gluing closes a half-circle into a circle, which is $\mathbb{RP}^1 \cong S^1$.
