% Lecture 7 (Wed Sep 16, 2026), last part
% SECTION 8: TANGENT SPACES
% ============================================================================
\subsection{The Unitary Group as a Smooth Manifold}\label{sub:un-smooth}

\textit{Assignment 2, Problem 4. The argument is that of \ref{sub:on-smooth} with one change that is easy to get wrong: the spaces involved are complex, but the map is not complex-linear, so everything must be done over $\mathbb{R}$.}

Write $A^* = \bar A^{\mathsf T}$ for the conjugate transpose, so that $\Ugp(n) = \{g \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \mid g^* g = I\}$. Throughout, $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ is regarded as a \emph{real} vector space of dimension $2n^2$ (Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}).

\begin{defbox}[Hermitian Matrices as a Real Vector Space]\deflabel{def:herm}
Let $\Herm(n) = \{A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \mid A^* = A\}$. It is closed under addition and under multiplication by \emph{real} scalars, so it is a real vector space; it is \emph{not} a complex subspace, since $(iA)^* = -iA$. A Hermitian matrix has real diagonal entries ($a_{jj} = \overline{a_{jj}}$), arbitrary complex entries above the diagonal, and entries below the diagonal determined by $a_{kj} = \overline{a_{jk}}$. Written out,
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix}
a_{11} & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1n} \\
\overline{a_{12}} & a_{22} & \cdots & a_{2n} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\overline{a_{1n}} & \overline{a_{2n}} & \cdots & a_{nn}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad a_{11}, \ldots, a_{nn} \in \mathbb{R}.
\] Hence
\[
\dim_{\mathbb{R}} \Herm(n) = n + 2\binom{n}{2} = n^2 ,
\]
and reading off the real diagonal entries and the real and imaginary parts of the entries above the diagonal gives a linear isomorphism $\Herm(n) \cong \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[A One-Sided Inverse Suffices]\thmlabel{lem:one-sided-unitary}
If $g \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ satisfies $gg^* = I$, then also $g^*g = I$. Consequently $\Ugp(n) = \{g \mid gg^* = I\}$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
Let $gg^* = I$.

\emph{$g$ is invertible.} Taking determinants and using that $\det$ is multiplicative, $\det(g)\det(g^*) = \det(gg^*) = \det(I) = 1$, so $\det g \neq 0$ and $g$ is invertible.

\emph{$g^*g = I$.} Multiplying $gg^* = I$ on the left by $g^{-1}$ gives $g^* = g^{-1}$:
\[
g^* = g^{-1}(gg^*) = g^{-1} I = g^{-1}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad g^*g = g^{-1}g = I .
\]

\emph{The description of $\Ugp(n)$.} By Definition~\ref{def:unitary-group}, $\Ugp(n) = \{g \in \GL(n,\mathbb{C}) \mid g^{-1} = g^*\}$. If $g \in \Ugp(n)$, then $gg^* = gg^{-1} = I$. Conversely, if $gg^* = I$, the two steps above show that $g$ is invertible with $g^{-1} = g^*$, so $g \in \Ugp(n)$. Hence $\Ugp(n) = \{g \mid gg^* = I\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[$\Ugp(n)$ Is a Smooth Manifold of Dimension $n^2$]\exlabel{ex:Un-smooth}
Define
\[
F : \Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \longrightarrow \Herm(n), \qquad F(g) = g g^*,
\]
both regarded as real vector spaces. Then $\Ugp(n) = F^{-1}(I)$, the identity is a regular value, and $\Ugp(n)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $2n^2 - n^2 = n^2$.
\leeref{Example 7.29}
\end{exbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.6em, column sep=3em]
\Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\cong"'] & \Herm(n) \arrow[d, "\cong"] \\
\mathbb{R}^{2n^2} \arrow[r, "\widehat F"'] & \mathbb{R}^{n^2}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The vertical arrows are the real-linear identifications of Definitions~\ref{def:complex-groups} and \ref{def:herm}. This is the square of \ref{sub:vs-differential} with $X = \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ and $Y = \Herm(n)$ regarded as real vector spaces: $F$ is smooth, and $I$ is a regular value, exactly when the same holds for $\widehat F$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vs-smooth-indep}, Corollary~\ref{cor:vs-regular}). Nothing is computed in the bottom row; it only certifies that the top row may be used.


\begin{proof}
As for $\Ogp(n)$ in Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth}, four things have to be shown: $F$ is a smooth map into $\Herm(n)$; $F^{-1}(I) = \Ugp(n)$; $dF_g$ is surjective at every $g \in F^{-1}(I)$; and this makes $\Ugp(n)$ a smooth manifold of dimension $n^2$. All vector spaces are real, and ``linear'' means real-linear.

\emph{$F$ is well defined and smooth.} Using $(PQ)^* = Q^*P^*$ (conjugation is multiplicative and transposition reverses products) and $g^{**} = g$ (conjugating and transposing twice),
\[
(gg^*)^* = g^{**}g^* = gg^*,
\]
so $F$ lands in $\Herm(n)$. For smoothness, take the linear coordinates $L$ on $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ of Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups} and $K$ on $\Herm(n)$ of Definition~\ref{def:herm}. The components of $K \circ F \circ L^{-1}$ are real and imaginary parts of entries of $gg^*$, and each entry is
\[
(gg^*)_{jk} = \sum_{m=1}^n g_{jm}\,(g^*)_{mk} = \sum_{m=1}^n g_{jm}\overline{g_{km}} .
\]
Writing $g_{jm} = a_{jm} + i\,b_{jm}$ with $a_{jm}, b_{jm}$ the real coordinates of $g$, each summand is $g_{jm}\overline{g_{km}} = (a_{jm}a_{km} + b_{jm}b_{km}) + i\,(b_{jm}a_{km} - a_{jm}b_{km})$. So each entry $(gg^*)_{jk} = \sum_m g_{jm}\overline{g_{km}}$ has real and imaginary parts that are quadratic polynomials in the real coordinates of $g$, so $F$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:vs-smooth}).

\emph{$\Ugp(n) = F^{-1}(I)$.} Lemma~\ref{lem:one-sided-unitary}: $g \in \Ugp(n) \iff gg^* = I \iff F(g) = I$.

\emph{The differential.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves}, applied with $X = \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ and $Y = \Herm(n)$ as real vector spaces, for $g \in F^{-1}(I)$ and $h \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$, $dF_g(h) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} F(g+th)$ with $t$ \emph{real} --- the line $g + th$ is formed with the real scalars of $X$. Since $(th)^* = \bar t\, h^* = t h^*$ for real $t$, and $^*$ is additive, $(g + th)^* = g^* + th^*$. Multiplying out,
\[
F(g+th) = (g+th)(g^* + th^*) = gg^* + t\big(hg^* + gh^*\big) + t^2\, hh^*,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
dF_g(h) = hg^* + gh^* ,
\]
the derivative at $t = 0$ of this polynomial in $t$ being its coefficient of $t$ (the constant term contributes $0$, and $\frac{d}{dt}(t^2 hh^*) = 2t\,hh^*$ vanishes at $t = 0$). It is Hermitian, as it must be: $(hg^* + gh^*)^* = g^{**}h^* + h^{**}g^* = gh^* + hg^*$.

\emph{$dF_g$ is surjective.} Fix $g \in F^{-1}(I) = \Ugp(n)$; we must show every $A \in \Herm(n)$ is $dF_g(h)$ for some $h$. Put $X = hg^*$; then $gh^* = (hg^*)^* = X^*$, since $(hg^*)^* = g^{**}h^* = gh^*$, so $dF_g(h) = X + X^*$. As $g$ is invertible, $h \mapsto hg^*$ is a real-linear bijection of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$, with inverse $X \mapsto Xg$: indeed $(hg^*)g = h(g^*g) = h$ and $(Xg)g^* = X(gg^*) = X$, using $g^*g = gg^* = I$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:one-sided-unitary}). So as $h$ runs over $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$, $X$ runs over all of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$. Hence $\operatorname{im} dF_g = \{X + X^* \mid X \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})\} = \Herm(n)$: the inclusion $\subseteq$ because $(X + X^*)^* = X^* + X$, and $\supseteq$ since any Hermitian $A$ arises from $X = \tfrac12 A$, as $\tfrac12 A + (\tfrac12 A)^* = \tfrac12 A + \tfrac12 A^* = \tfrac12 A + \tfrac12 A = A$ (the scalar $\tfrac12$ is real, so it passes through $^*$ unchanged). Explicitly $h = \tfrac12 Ag$, by $X \mapsto Xg$:
\[
hg^* = \tfrac12 A gg^* = \tfrac12 A, \qquad gh^* = g\big(\tfrac12 Ag\big)^* = \tfrac12\, g g^* A^* = \tfrac12 A ,
\]
using $(Ag)^* = g^*A^*$, $gg^* = I$ and $A^* = A$; adding gives $dF_g(h) = A$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.8em, column sep=2.2em]
\Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \arrow[rr, "dF_g"] \arrow[dr, "h \,\mapsto\, hg^*"', "\cong"] & & \Herm(n) \\
& \Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \arrow[ur, "X \,\mapsto\, X + X^*"'] &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The surjectivity argument as a diagram: $dF_g$ factors as a bijection followed by $X \mapsto X + X^*$, and the second map is onto $\Herm(n)$, hitting $A$ at $X = \tfrac12 A$. Hence $dF_g$ is onto.

\emph{Conclusion.} $\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) = 2n^2 \ge n^2 = \dim_{\mathbb{R}}\Herm(n)$ (Definitions~\ref{def:complex-groups} and \ref{def:herm}), so by Corollary~\ref{cor:vs-regular} surjectivity of $dF_g$ at every $g \in F^{-1}(I)$ is exactly the statement that $I$ is a regular value. In the coordinates of the square above, this says: $\widehat F = K \circ F \circ L^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^{2n^2} \to \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ is smooth, its Jacobian at $L(g)$ has maximal rank $n^2$ for every $g \in F^{-1}(I)$, and, $K$ being injective, $\widehat F(L(g)) = K(F(g)) = K(I) \iff F(g) = I$, so $\widehat F^{-1}(K(I)) = L(\Ugp(n))$; thus $K(I)$ is a regular value of $\widehat F$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}). Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}, with $W = \mathbb{R}^{2n^2}$, $n + k = 2n^2$ and $k = n^2$, makes $L(\Ugp(n))$ a smooth manifold of dimension $2n^2 - n^2 = n^2$. The topology of $\Ugp(n)$ is the subspace topology of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$, defined by $L$ (Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}), so $L$ restricts to a homeomorphism $\Ugp(n) \to L(\Ugp(n))$, and transporting along it (Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}) makes $\Ugp(n)$ a smooth manifold of dimension $2n^2 - n^2 = n^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:vector-spaces-7}
\textbf{Why over $\mathbb{R}$.} The derivative $h \mapsto hg^* + gh^*$ is real-linear but not complex-linear: $dF_g(ih) = i\,hg^* - i\,gh^*$, which differs from $i\,dF_g(h)$ unless $gh^* = 0$. This is the conjugation in $g^*$ at work, and it is why Problem~4 insists that both spaces be regarded as real vector spaces. It is also why the holomorphic regular value theorem of \S\ref{sub:holomorphic-level-sets} does not apply, and why $\dim \Ugp(n) = n^2$ can be odd, which no holomorphic level set can.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[The Kernel of the Differential]\thmlabel{prop:Un-kernel}
For $g \in \Ugp(n)$,
\[
\ker dF_g = \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g = g \cdot \mathfrak{u}(n), \qquad \mathfrak{u}(n) = \{X \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \mid X^* = -X\},
\]
the skew-Hermitian matrices, and $\dim_{\mathbb{R}} \mathfrak{u}(n) = n^2$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{$\ker dF_g = \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g$.} By the proof of Example~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}, $dF_g(h) = hg^* + gh^*$, and $h \mapsto hg^*$ is a bijection of $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ with inverse $X \mapsto Xg$. So every $h$ can be written uniquely as $h = Xg$ with $X = hg^*$ (uniquely, because $Xg = h$ forces $X = hg^{-1} = hg^*$). Then, using $(Xg)^* = g^*X^*$ and $gg^* = I$,
\[
dF_g(Xg) = (Xg)g^* + g(Xg)^* = X\,gg^* + gg^*\,X^* = X + X^*,
\]
which vanishes iff $X^* = -X$, i.e.\ iff $X \in \mathfrak{u}(n)$. So $\ker dF_g = \{Xg \mid X \in \mathfrak{u}(n)\} = \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g$.

\emph{$g\cdot\mathfrak{u}(n) = \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g$.} Conjugation by $g$ preserves $\mathfrak{u}(n)$: if $X^* = -X$ then $(gXg^*)^* = g^{**}X^*g^* = gX^*g^* = -gXg^*$; so $g \cdot \mathfrak{u}(n) = (g\,\mathfrak{u}(n)\,g^{-1})\cdot g = \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g$. In detail, both inclusions, using $g^{-1} = g^*$ and $g^*g = gg^* = I$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:one-sided-unitary}): for $Y \in \mathfrak{u}(n)$,
\[
gY = (gYg^*)\,g, \qquad gYg^* \in \mathfrak{u}(n),
\]
so $g\cdot\mathfrak{u}(n) \subseteq \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g$; and for $X \in \mathfrak{u}(n)$, $Xg = g\,(g^*Xg)$, where $g^*Xg \in \mathfrak{u}(n)$ by the same computation with $g^*$ in place of $g$: $(g^*Xg)^* = g^*X^*g^{**} = g^*X^*g = -g^*Xg$. So $\mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g \subseteq g\cdot\mathfrak{u}(n)$.

\emph{Dimension.} A skew-Hermitian matrix has purely imaginary diagonal ($n$ real parameters) and arbitrary complex entries above the diagonal ($2\binom n2$ real parameters), so $\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\mathfrak{u}(n) = n^2$ --- agreeing with $\dim \Ugp(n)$ by rank--nullity, $2n^2 - n^2$. In detail: $X^* = -X$ says $\overline{x_{kj}} = -x_{jk}$ for all $j, k$. For $j = k$ this is $\overline{x_{jj}} = -x_{jj}$, i.e.\ $\operatorname{Re} x_{jj} = 0$, so each diagonal entry is $i$ times a free real number; for $j < k$ the entry $x_{jk}$ is an arbitrary complex number (two real parameters), and the entry below the diagonal is then determined, $x_{kj} = -\overline{x_{jk}}$. Written out, with $x_{jj} = i\,t_j$, $t_j \in \mathbb{R}$,
\[
X = \begin{pmatrix}
i\,t_1 & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1n} \\
-\overline{x_{12}} & i\,t_2 & \cdots & x_{2n} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
-\overline{x_{1n}} & -\overline{x_{2n}} & \cdots & i\,t_n
\end{pmatrix}.
\] Hence
\[
\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\mathfrak{u}(n) = n + 2\binom n2 = n + n(n-1) = n^2 .
\]
The real-linear isomorphism $X \mapsto Xg$ maps $\mathfrak{u}(n)$ onto $\ker dF_g$, so $\dim_{\mathbb{R}} \ker dF_g = n^2$ as well. Rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) gives the same number from the other side: $dF_g$ is surjective onto $\Herm(n)$, of real dimension $n^2$, so $\dim_{\mathbb{R}} \ker dF_g = 2n^2 - n^2 = n^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[$\Ugp(n)$ Is Compact]\thmlabel{cor:Un-compact}
$\Ugp(n)$ is a compact smooth manifold of dimension $n^2$.
\leeref{Example 7.29}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
By Example~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}, $\Ugp(n)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $n^2$; it remains to show it is compact. By Heine--Borel (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(1)) it suffices that $\Ugp(n)$ be closed and bounded in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n^2}$ (Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}).

\emph{Closed.} It is closed in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n^2}$ as $F^{-1}(I)$ with $F$ continuous: $F$ is smooth (Example~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}), hence continuous, and the point $\{I\}$ is closed in $\Herm(n)$.

\emph{Bounded.} It is bounded because the columns of a unitary matrix are unit vectors of $\mathbb{C}^n$, so every entry has modulus at most $1$. Indeed, $g^*g = I$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:one-sided-unitary}), and its $(j,j)$ entry is
\[
1 = (g^*g)_{jj} = \sum_{i=1}^n \overline{g_{ij}}\, g_{ij} = \sum_{i=1}^n |g_{ij}|^2 ,
\]
so the $j$-th column is a unit vector and $|g_{ij}| \le 1$ for all $i, j$. In the real coordinates of Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups} the squared Euclidean norm of $g$ is $\sum_{i,j}\big((\operatorname{Re} g_{ij})^2 + (\operatorname{Im} g_{ij})^2\big) = \sum_{i,j} |g_{ij}|^2 = n$, so $\Ugp(n)$ lies in the closed ball of radius $\sqrt n$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2n^2}$.

Apply Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(1).
\end{proof}

\section{The Circle}\label{sec:ex-circle}

\roadmark{Thread: examples}{The circle in one place: its external, graph and internal descriptions, and the one smooth structure defined by its three atlases.}

The circle through the course: the circle group $\Ugp(1)$ in Example~\ref{ex:1-circle}; the homogeneous space $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ in Example~\ref{ex:circle-RZ}; three atlases --- four charts, stereographic and angle --- in Examples~\ref{ex:circle-four}, \ref{ex:circle-stereo} and~\ref{ex:circle-angle}, with the remark \emph{Three Atlases and One Structure} in \ref{sec:smooth-structures}; $\mathbb{RP}^1$ homeomorphic to it in Proposition~\ref{prop:rpn-topologies}; its external, graph and internal descriptions, and the one smooth structure of its three atlases, in Section~\ref{sec:ex-circle}; and covered by a line, a local diffeomorphism that is not injective, in Example~\ref{ex:line-circle}.

\begin{exbox}[The Circle in Three Descriptions]\exlabel{ex:circle-three-ways}
Near the point $p = (0,1)$ of $S^1 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ (here $n = k = 1$):
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{External:} $F(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 - 1$, with $\nabla F = (2x, 2y) \neq 0$ on $S^1$, so $0$ is a regular value and $S^1 = F^{-1}(0)$.
    \item \textbf{Graph:} on $(-1,1) \times (0,\infty)$, $S^1$ is the graph of $h(x) = \sqrt{1-x^2}$ --- which is the chart $\varphi_2$ of Example~\ref{ex:circle-four}, read backwards.
    \item \textbf{Internal:} $\alpha(\theta) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ on $\theta \in (0,\pi)$, with $\alpha'(\theta) = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta) \neq 0$ --- the angle chart of Example~\ref{ex:circle-angle}, read backwards. As the Jacobian of Definition~\ref{def:internal-description}, the $2 \times 1$ matrix
\[
D\alpha_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} -\sin\theta \\ \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}
\]
has rank $1 = n$.
\end{itemize}
The three are related exactly as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int}: $h$ comes from $F$ by the implicit function theorem, and $\alpha$ comes from $h$ by $x \mapsto (x, h(x))$ followed by the reparametrization $x = \cos\theta$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Three Circle Atlases Define One Smooth Structure]\thmlabel{prop:circle-atlases-same}
The four-chart atlas (Example~\ref{ex:circle-four}), the angle atlas (Example~\ref{ex:circle-angle}) and the stereographic atlas (Example~\ref{ex:circle-stereo}) on $S^1$ are pairwise compatible. All three generate the smooth structure that Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} gives $S^1 = F^{-1}(1)$, $F(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The graph charts are the four projection charts.} Here $F(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$, $c = 1$, $n = k = 1$, and $F'(x,y) = (2x \ \ 2y)$. At a point of $S^1$ with $y \neq 0$ the column $\partial F/\partial y = 2y$ is nonzero, and one solves for $y$ in terms of $x$; at a point with $x \neq 0$, for $x$ in terms of $y$. What the construction before Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} needs of the box is that the equation be equivalent to the graph of a smooth function there, and the boxes may be taken as large as that allows: on $(-1,1) \times (0,\infty)$,
\[
x^2 + y^2 = 1 \iff y = \sqrt{1 - x^2}
\]
(the positive root, as $y > 0$), with $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ smooth because $1 - x^2 > 0$; likewise $y = -\sqrt{1-x^2}$ on $(-1,1) \times (-\infty,0)$, and $x = \pm\sqrt{1-y^2}$ on $(0,\infty) \times (-1,1)$ and $(-\infty,0) \times (-1,1)$. The corresponding graph charts are the projections $(x,y) \mapsto x$ on the upper and lower half-circles and $(x,y) \mapsto y$ on the right and left ones, i.e.\ $\varphi_2, \varphi_4, \varphi_1, \varphi_3$ of Example~\ref{ex:circle-four}; every point of $S^1$ has $x \neq 0$ or $y \neq 0$, so they cover. So for $S^1$ the graph charts of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} are the four projection charts, so that atlas $\mathcal{A}$ is the four-chart atlas, and the smooth structure in question is the maximal atlas $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ it generates (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}).

\emph{What has to be shown.} It suffices to show that every chart $(V, \chi)$ of the other two atlases is compatible with every chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $\mathcal{A}$. All such charts then lie in the maximal atlas $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}, which describes $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ as exactly the charts compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}$), and any two charts of an atlas are compatible --- which is how Proposition~\ref{prop:compat-not-transitive} is circumvented. Both claims then follow. \emph{Pairwise compatible:} a chart of one of the three atlases and a chart of another both belong to the atlas $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$, hence are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}); so any two of the three atlases are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible-atlases}). \emph{One structure:} each of the three atlases $\mathcal{B}$ is contained in $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$, which is a maximal atlas; by the uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}, $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ is the maximal atlas containing $\mathcal{B}$, i.e.\ the structure $\mathcal{B}$ generates (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-structure}).

The charts $(V, \chi)$ to be checked are $\sigma_N$ on $S^1 \setminus \{N\}$ and $\sigma_S$ on $S^1 \setminus \{S\}$ (Example~\ref{ex:circle-stereo}), and $\varphi_a$ on $U_a = S^1 \setminus \{(1,0)\}$ and $\varphi_b$ on $U_b = S^1 \setminus \{(-1,0)\}$ (Example~\ref{ex:circle-angle}). Each such $\chi$ has two properties.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(a)] $\chi^{-1}$ is smooth as a map into $\mathbb{R}^2$: it is $\theta \mapsto (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ for the angle charts, $u \mapsto \big(2u,\, u^2 - 1\big)/(u^2+1)$ for $\sigma_N$, and similarly for $\sigma_S$. Explicitly, $\sigma_S(x,y) = \sigma_N(x,-y)$, so $\sigma_S^{-1}$ is $\sigma_N^{-1}$ followed by the reflection $(x,y) \mapsto (x,-y)$:
    \[
    \sigma_S^{-1}(u) = \Big( \frac{2u}{u^2+1},\, \frac{1-u^2}{u^2+1} \Big);
    \]
    one checks that this point lies on $S^1$, as $(2u)^2 + (1-u^2)^2 = (1+u^2)^2$, and that $\sigma_S$ of it is $\frac{2u/(u^2+1)}{1 + (1-u^2)/(u^2+1)} = \frac{2u/(u^2+1)}{2/(u^2+1)} = u$. The components of $\sigma_N^{-1}$ and $\sigma_S^{-1}$ are rational functions whose denominator $u^2 + 1 \ge 1$ never vanishes, and $\cos$, $\sin$ are smooth; so each $\chi^{-1}$ is smooth.
    \item[(b)] $\chi$ is the restriction to $V$ of a smooth function $\hat\chi$ on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ containing $V$. For $\sigma_N = x/(1-y)$ take $\{y < 1\}$, and for $\sigma_S = x/(1+y)$ take $\{y > -1\}$. (On these open sets the denominators do not vanish, so the quotients are smooth; and they contain the domains, since on $S^1$ we have $y^2 \le x^2 + y^2 = 1$, with $y = 1$ only at $N$ and $y = -1$ only at $S$.) For an angle chart take a smooth branch of the argument on the plane minus a closed ray: for values in $(-\pi, \pi)$, $\theta = 2\arctan\big(y/(x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2})\big)$, and other ranges follow by rotating and adding a constant. In detail, let
    \[
    \Theta(x,y) = 2\arctan\frac{y}{x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \qquad \text{on } \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(x,0) \mid x \le 0\}.
    \]
    It is smooth there: $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is smooth away from the origin, and the denominator is positive --- if $y \neq 0$ then $\sqrt{x^2+y^2} > |x| \ge -x$, and if $y = 0$ then $x > 0$ and the denominator is $2x$. At $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ with $\theta \in (-\pi,\pi)$, the half-angle formulas $1 + \cos\theta = 2\cos^2(\theta/2)$ and $\sin\theta = 2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$ give $y/(x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}) = \sin\theta/(1 + \cos\theta) = \tan(\theta/2)$, and $\theta/2 \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$, the range of $\arctan$; so $\Theta(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) = \theta$. \emph{For $\varphi_b$} (values in $(\pi, 3\pi)$): if $\theta \in (\pi,3\pi)$ then $\theta - 2\pi \in (-\pi,\pi)$ has the same cosine and sine, so $\varphi_b = \Theta + 2\pi$ on $U_b$; take $\hat\chi = \Theta + 2\pi$, smooth on $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(x,0) \mid x \le 0\}$, which contains $U_b$ because that ray meets $S^1$ only at $(-1,0)$. \emph{For $\varphi_a$} (values in $(0, 2\pi)$): if $\theta \in (0,2\pi)$ then $(-\cos\theta, -\sin\theta) = (\cos(\theta-\pi), \sin(\theta-\pi))$ with $\theta - \pi \in (-\pi,\pi)$, so $\Theta(-x,-y) = \theta - \pi$; take $\hat\chi(x,y) = \Theta(-x,-y) + \pi$ (rotation by $\pi$, then the constant $\pi$), smooth on $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(x,0) \mid x \ge 0\}$, which contains $U_a$ because that ray meets $S^1$ only at $(1,0)$.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Compatibility.} Fix such a $(V, \chi)$ and a chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $\mathcal{A}$; if $U \cap V = \emptyset$ there is nothing to check (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}). Here $\varphi = \pi|_U$, where $\pi : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is the linear projection $(x,y) \mapsto x$ or $(x,y) \mapsto y$, and $\varphi^{-1}$ is one of $t \mapsto (t, \pm\sqrt{1-t^2})$, $t \mapsto (\pm\sqrt{1-t^2}, t)$ on $(-1,1)$ --- a smooth parametrization (observation (1) in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}), smooth because $1 - t^2 > 0$. We must show that the transition function $\varphi \circ \chi^{-1} : \chi(U \cap V) \to \varphi(U \cap V)$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}). It is a bijection, being the composite of the bijections $\chi^{-1} : \chi(U \cap V) \to U \cap V$ and $\varphi : U \cap V \to \varphi(U \cap V)$, with inverse $\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}$; so it remains to see that both are smooth. On the overlap, $\varphi \circ \chi^{-1} = \pi \circ \chi^{-1}$ with $\pi$ a linear projection, which is smooth by (a): $\chi^{-1}$ takes values in $U \cap V$, where $\varphi = \pi$, and a composite of the smooth $\chi^{-1}$ with the linear $\pi$ is smooth. And $\chi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \hat\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth by (b), $\varphi^{-1}$ being a smooth parametrization: $\varphi^{-1}$ takes values in $U \cap V \subseteq V$, where $\hat\chi = \chi$, and these values lie in the open domain of $\hat\chi$, so $\hat\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is a composite of smooth maps between open subsets of Euclidean spaces. Hence $(V, \chi)$ and $(U, \varphi)$ are compatible, which is what had to be shown.
\end{proof}

\chapter{Tangent and Cotangent Spaces}

\section{The Geometric Tangent Space}\label{sec:tangent}

\roadmark{Stage: geometric}{Tangent vectors as velocities inside the ambient space, $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$ --- available only for manifolds presented by equations.}

\textit{Reference: Lee Ch.\ 3, ``Tangent Vectors.'' Begun at the end of Lecture 7; the abstract definition is promised for Friday. Logistics: a grader (a doctoral student) has been assigned; HW3 Problem 1 is the diffeomorphism $\mathbb{R} \cong \widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$ of Example~\ref{ex:two-structures-R}.}

\begin{rembox}[Why This Section]\label{rem:why-this-section-7}
The goal is to attach to each point $p$ of a smooth manifold $M$ a vector space $T_pM$, the \emph{abstract tangent space}, so that maps between manifolds acquire differentials $dF_p : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ as in \ref{sub:vs-differential}. The obstacle is that the familiar picture --- a plane resting on a surface --- lives in an ambient space: ``if you have a sphere you can think of the tangent plane, but that is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$. If you do not have $\mathbb{R}^3$, then what do you do? You do not have room to put your vectors.'' An abstract manifold has no ambient space, so the construction ``is going to take a little while.'' This section therefore treats the case where an ambient space \emph{is} available, and defines there the \emph{geometric tangent space} $T^{\geo}_pM$ --- as motivation, and because it covers all the matrix groups. The abstract $T_pM$ is built in \ref{sec:abstract-tangent}, and the cotangent space in \ref{sec:cotangent}. (Uribe noted that it is in some ways more natural to define the dual space first --- the cotangent space --- but follows Lee in not doing so.)
\end{rembox}

\subsection{The Geometric Tangent Space of a Regular Level Set}\label{sub:geometric-tangent}

Throughout this subsection $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ is open, $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is smooth, $c \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is a regular value, and $M = F^{-1}(c)$, a smooth $n$-manifold by Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}. Fix $p \in M$.

\begin{defbox}[Geometric Tangent Space]\deflabel{def:geometric-tangent}
The \textbf{geometric} (or \textbf{ambient}) \textbf{tangent space} to $M$ at $p$ is
\[
\begin{aligned}
T^{\geo}_pM \;=\; \Big\{\, \gamma'(0) \;\Big|\;& \gamma : (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \text{ smooth},\ \varepsilon > 0, \\
& \gamma\big((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\big) \subseteq M,\ \gamma(0) = p \,\Big\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k},
\end{aligned}
\]
where $\gamma'(0) = \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\big|_{t=0}$ is the ordinary derivative of a curve in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$. In words: $T^{\geo}_pM$ is the set of velocities at $p$ of smooth curves that pass through $p$ while staying on $M$. The same definition applies verbatim with $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ replaced by any finite-dimensional real vector space containing $M$, such as $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, with $\gamma'(0)$ computed in that space.
\leeref{Ch.~3 (geometric tangent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$) and Proposition 5.37}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent}
\textbf{Notation.} Two different objects in this section are called ``the tangent space at $p$'', and the notes keep them apart throughout. The \emph{geometric} tangent space of Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent} is written $T^{\geo}_pM$: it is a linear subspace of the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ in which $M$ sits, and it exists only for manifolds presented inside a Euclidean space (here, regular level sets; also open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^N$ and of finite-dimensional vector spaces). The \emph{abstract} tangent space of Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}, built from derivations in \ref{sub:derivations}, is written plain $T_pM$: it exists for every smooth manifold, and is not a subset of anything. The phrase ``tangent space'' is always qualified by one of the two adjectives. The two are identified, for regular level sets, by Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract} --- but the identification is a theorem, not a definition. On the board they appeared as $(T_pM)^{\mathrm{ambient}}$ and $(T_pM)^{\mathrm{abstract}}$.
\end{rembox}

``Smooth'' for $\gamma$ means smooth as a map into the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$; the constraint that it take values in $M$ is a separate condition. The derivative $\gamma'(0)$ is computed with the vector space structure of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, which is exactly what an abstract manifold lacks. The figure shows the definition: a curve $\gamma$ drawn on $M$ through $p$, its velocity $v$ at $t=0$ (a vector of the ambient space, drawn from $p$), and the plane these velocities sweep out as $\gamma$ ranges over all such curves --- which Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} identifies as $\ker F'(p)$, and which is therefore orthogonal to the gradient $\nabla F(p)$, shown in grey for contrast. Note that $T^{\geo}_pM$ is drawn as a plane through $p$ only as an aid: as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ it passes through the origin, and it is the \emph{translate} to $p$ that is tangent to $M$.

It is not obvious from Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent} that $T^{\geo}_pM$ is closed under addition: given two curves through $p$ with velocities $v$ and $w$, there is no evident curve with velocity $v + w$. ``How do I add two curves?'' Both this and the dimension follow from an algebraic description.

\begin{lembox}[Locality of the Geometric Tangent Space]\thmlabel{lem:tangent-local}
If $M' \subseteq M$ is open in $M$ and $p \in M'$, then $T^{\geo}_pM' = T^{\geo}_pM$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
Both sides are subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, so the claim is two inclusions; each is checked on a single velocity.

$\subseteq$: let $v \in T^{\geo}_pM'$, so $v = \gamma'(0)$ for a smooth $\gamma : (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ with $\gamma\big((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\big) \subseteq M'$ and $\gamma(0) = p$ (Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent}). Since $M' \subseteq M$, the same $\gamma$ satisfies $\gamma\big((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\big) \subseteq M$ and $\gamma(0) = p$: a curve in $M'$ is a curve in $M$. So $v \in T^{\geo}_pM$.

$\supseteq$: let $v = \gamma'(0)$ with $\gamma : (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ smooth, $\gamma\big((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\big) \subseteq M$ and $\gamma(0) = p$. Since $M'$ is open in $M$ (subspace topology), $M' = M \cap O$ for some open $O \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$. As $\gamma$ is continuous (being smooth) and takes values in $M$, its preimage
\[
\gamma^{-1}(M') = \gamma^{-1}(M \cap O) = \gamma^{-1}(O)
\]
is open in $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$, and it contains $0$ because $\gamma(0) = p \in M'$. An open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ containing $0$ contains an interval $(-\delta,\delta)$ with $0 < \delta \le \varepsilon$. The restriction $\gamma|_{(-\delta,\delta)}$ is smooth, takes values in $M'$, and sends $0$ to $p$. Its velocity at $0$ is the limit of the difference quotients $\big(\gamma(t) - \gamma(0)\big)/t$ as $t \to 0$, which for $0 < |t| < \delta$ are the same as those of $\gamma$; so it equals $\gamma'(0) = v$. Hence $v \in T^{\geo}_pM'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[The Geometric Tangent Space of a Graph]\thmlabel{lem:tangent-graph}
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $G : A \to \mathbb{R}^k$ smooth, and
\[
M = \{\, (x, G(x)) \mid x \in A \,\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}
\]
its graph. For $p = (x_0, G(x_0))$ with $x_0 \in A$,
\[
T^{\geo}_pM \;=\; \{\, (u,\; G'(x_0)\,u) \mid u \in \mathbb{R}^n \,\},
\]
the graph of the linear map $G'(x_0) : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k$. In particular $T^{\geo}_pM$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ of dimension $n$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Set in Lecture~8 as an exercise --- ``not a trivial exercise''; filled in.)} Write $L = G'(x_0) : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k$ and $\Gamma = \{(u, Lu) \mid u \in \mathbb{R}^n\}$ for its graph. The claim is $T^{\geo}_pM = \Gamma$, proved as two inclusions, followed by the dimension count.

$\subseteq$: let $\gamma : (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) \to M$ be smooth with $\gamma(0) = p$, and write $\gamma = (\gamma_1, \gamma_2)$ with $\gamma_1$ into $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\gamma_2$ into $\mathbb{R}^k$. Both components are smooth, since their coordinates are coordinates of $\gamma$. For each $t$, $\gamma(t) \in M$ means $\gamma(t) = (x, G(x))$ for some $x \in A$; comparing first components, $x = \gamma_1(t)$, so
\[
\gamma_1(t) \in A \qquad\text{and}\qquad \gamma_2(t) = G\big(\gamma_1(t)\big) \qquad \text{for every } t,
\]
that is, $\gamma_2 = G \circ \gamma_1$. At $t = 0$, $(\gamma_1(0), \gamma_2(0)) = p = (x_0, G(x_0))$, so $\gamma_1(0) = x_0$. By the chain rule for the curve $\gamma_1$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}),
\[
\gamma_2'(0) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} G\big(\gamma_1(t)\big) = G'\big(\gamma_1(0)\big)\,\gamma_1'(0) = G'(x_0)\,\gamma_1'(0) .
\]
So, with $u = \gamma_1'(0)$,
\[
\gamma'(0) = \big(\gamma_1'(0),\; \gamma_2'(0)\big) = \big(u,\; G'(x_0)\,u\big) \in \Gamma .
\]

$\supseteq$: given $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we must produce a curve in $M$ through $p$ with velocity $(u, G'(x_0)u)$. Since $A$ is open, some ball $B(x_0, r)$ lies in $A$; put $\varepsilon = r/(|u| + 1)$, so that $|tu| < r$, hence $x_0 + tu \in A$, for $|t| < \varepsilon$. Set
\[
\gamma(t) = \big(x_0 + tu,\; G(x_0 + tu)\big), \qquad |t| < \varepsilon .
\]
This is smooth into $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$: the first component is affine in $t$, and the second is the composite of the smooth $G$ with that affine map. It takes values in $M$, since $\gamma(t) = (x, G(x))$ with $x = x_0 + tu \in A$. It has $\gamma(0) = (x_0, G(x_0)) = p$. And by the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} G(x_0 + tu) = G'(x_0)\,u$, so $\gamma'(0) = (u, G'(x_0)u)$. Hence $\Gamma \subseteq T^{\geo}_pM$.

\emph{Dimension.} The map $\iota : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, $\iota(u) = (u, Lu)$, is linear because $L$ is: $\iota(au + bu') = (au + bu', aLu + bLu') = a\,\iota(u) + b\,\iota(u')$. In matrix form, $\iota$ is multiplication by the $(n+k) \times n$ matrix with the identity stacked on top of the $k \times n$ Jacobian $L = G'(x_0)$:
\[
\iota(u) = \left(\begin{array}{c} I_n \\ \hline L \end{array}\right) u = \begin{pmatrix} u \\ Lu \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\left(\begin{array}{c} I_n \\ \hline L \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \cdots & 1 \\ \hline
\dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1}(x_0) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_n}(x_0) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial G_k}{\partial x_1}(x_0) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G_k}{\partial x_n}(x_0)
\end{array}\right),
\]
where $G = (G_1, \ldots, G_k)$. The top block $I_n$ is what makes $\iota$ injective below. Its image is $\Gamma$, so $\Gamma$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$. It is injective, because $\iota(u) = 0$ forces the first component $u$ to be $0$. By rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)), $\dim \Gamma = \dim \operatorname{im}\iota = n - \dim\ker\iota = n - 0 = n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent-2}
Uribe stated this lemma and left it as an exercise, calling it ``not a trivial exercise''; the proof above is short but both inclusions are needed, and the $\supseteq$ half --- lifting a straight line from the chart --- is the construction that reappears in \S\ref{sub:derivations-motivation} as the curve defining $D_v$. In words: \emph{the geometric tangent space to a graph is the graph of the differential.}
\end{rembox}

\begin{thmbox}[The Geometric Tangent Space Is the Kernel of the Jacobian]\thmlabel{thm:tangent-kernel}
$T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$, where $F'(p) : \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is the Jacobian at $p$. Written out, with $F = (F_1, \ldots, F_k)$ and coordinates $x_1, \ldots, x_{n+k}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, it is the $k \times (n+k)$ matrix (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian})
\[
F'(p) = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_{n+k}}(p) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial F_k}{\partial x_1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F_k}{\partial x_{n+k}}(p)
\end{pmatrix},
\]
with one row per equation and one column per ambient coordinate. In particular $T^{\geo}_pM$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ of dimension $n = \dim M$.
\leeref{Proposition 5.38}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
The order is Lecture~8's sketch, which built on an inclusion proved in Lecture~7. The plan: prove $T^{\geo}_pM \subseteq \ker F'(p)$ directly, show both sides have dimension $n$, and conclude equality.

\emph{1. The inclusion (Lecture~7: ``last time we saw this inclusion'').} $T^{\geo}_pM \subseteq \ker F'(p)$. Let $v \in T^{\geo}_pM$ with $\gamma$ as in Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent}, so $v = \gamma'(0)$, $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma(t) \in M \subseteq W$ for all $t$. The composite $F \circ \gamma : (-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is smooth, being a composite of smooth maps between Euclidean spaces, and since $\gamma(t) \in M = F^{-1}(c)$ for every $t$ it is the constant $c$; a constant curve has velocity $\vec 0$. Differentiating at $t = 0$ and applying the chain rule for curves (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}),
\[
\vec 0 = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} F(\gamma(t)) = F'(\gamma(0))\,\gamma'(0) = F'(p)\, v ,
\]
so $v \in \ker F'(p)$.

\emph{2. Everything is local near $p$, so WLOG $M$ is a graph.} ``Since everything is local near $p$ \ldots\ these regular level sets are locally graphs of functions, for various choices of variables.'' \textit{(Completion.)} The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value}, in the form of Corollary~\ref{cor:rvt-open} (open domain $W$, value $c$), gives the following. There is a permutation of coordinates $\rho : \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ (Step~1 there), an open box $V \times V' \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^k$ containing $\rho(p)$, and a smooth $G : V \to V'$ (Steps~2--3 there) with
\[
\rho(M) \cap (V \times V') = \{(x, G(x)) \mid x \in V\} .
\]
The permutation does not change dimensions of geometric tangent spaces. Indeed $\rho$ is a linear isomorphism, so if $\gamma$ is a curve in $M$ through $p$, then $\rho \circ \gamma$ is a smooth curve in $\rho(M)$ through $\rho(p)$ with $(\rho\circ\gamma)'(0) = \rho(\gamma'(0))$ (the derivative of a linear map is itself); and conversely with $\rho^{-1}$ in place of $\rho$. Hence
\[
T^{\geo}_{\rho(p)}\rho(M) = \rho\big(T^{\geo}_pM\big), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad T^{\geo}_pM = \rho^{-1}\big(T^{\geo}_{\rho(p)}\rho(M)\big) .
\]
Next, $M' = \rho(M) \cap (V \times V')$ is open in $\rho(M)$, because $V \times V'$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, and contains $\rho(p)$; so by Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-local} the geometric tangent space is unchanged on passing to this open piece: $T^{\geo}_{\rho(p)}\rho(M) = T^{\geo}_{\rho(p)}M'$.

\emph{3. The claim: the tangent space to a graph is the graph of the derivative.} Write $\rho(p) = (x_0, G(x_0))$ with $x_0 \in V$. Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-graph}, applied to the graph $M'$ of $G$ over the open set $A = V$ --- set in lecture as ``not a trivial exercise'' --- gives $T^{\geo}_{\rho(p)}M' = \{(u, G'(x_0)u) \mid u \in \mathbb{R}^n\}$, a linear subspace of dimension $n$. By Step~2, $T^{\geo}_pM = \rho^{-1}\big(T^{\geo}_{\rho(p)}M'\big)$ is the image of this subspace under the linear isomorphism $\rho^{-1}$; so $T^{\geo}_pM$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ of dimension $n$.

\emph{4. The kernel has dimension $n$, by rank--nullity.} Since $c$ is a regular value and $p \in F^{-1}(c)$, the Jacobian $F'(p) : \mathbb{R}^{n+k} \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is surjective, i.e.\ has rank $k$ (Definitions~\ref{def:regular-value} and~\ref{def:regular-point}). Rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) gives
\[
\dim \ker F'(p) = \dim \mathbb{R}^{n+k} - \operatorname{rank} F'(p) = (n+k) - k = n .
\]

\emph{5. ``We must have equality.''} By Steps 1, 3 and 4, $T^{\geo}_pM$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace contained in the $n$-dimensional subspace $\ker F'(p)$. A basis of $T^{\geo}_pM$ consists of $n$ linearly independent vectors of $\ker F'(p)$, and $n$ independent vectors in an $n$-dimensional space form a basis of it; so they span $\ker F'(p)$, and $\ker F'(p) \subseteq T^{\geo}_pM$. The two are equal.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent-3}
The structure is worth noticing, because it is not the obvious one. Only the \emph{easy} inclusion is proved directly; the reverse inclusion is never constructed, but forced by a dimension count. Uribe: ``it's best actually to prove something else'' --- namely the graph lemma, from which both the vector space structure and the dimension of $T^{\geo}_pM$ are immediate, after which ``we must have equality.''
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[Three Descriptions of the Geometric Tangent Space]\thmlabel{cor:tangent-three}
In the notation of the proof, with $\alpha : V \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, $\alpha(x) = (x, h(x))$ the parametrization inverse to the graph chart,
\[
T^{\geo}_pM \;=\; \{\text{velocities of curves in } M \text{ through } p\} \;=\; \ker F'(p) \;=\; \operatorname{im} D\alpha_a ,
\]
and $D\alpha_a : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$, $u \mapsto (u, Dh_a u)$, is an isomorphism onto $T^{\geo}_pM$.
\leeref{Propositions 5.37 and 5.38}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
As in the statement, the coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ are numbered as in Step~2 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} after the permutation there, so that near $p$ the manifold is the graph $\{(x, h(x)) \mid x \in V\}$ of a smooth $h : V \to V'$ (the map called $G$ in that proof), and $p = (a, h(a))$ with $a \in V$ (the point called $x_0$ there). Then $\alpha(x) = (x, h(x))$ takes values in $M$, and $\alpha(a) = p$. There are three equalities to prove, and then the isomorphism.

\emph{First equality.} $T^{\geo}_pM$ is by definition the set of velocities at $p$ of smooth curves in $M$ through $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent}).

\emph{Second equality.} $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}.

\emph{The derivative of $\alpha$.} The components of $\alpha$ are $x \mapsto x$ and $x \mapsto h(x)$, whose derivatives at $a$ are the identity and $Dh_a$; so
\[
D\alpha_a(u) = \big(u,\; Dh_a u\big) \qquad (u \in \mathbb{R}^n) .
\]

\emph{Third equality, $\ker F'(p) \subseteq \operatorname{im} D\alpha_a$.} Let $v \in \ker F'(p)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}, $v \in T^{\geo}_pM$; by Steps~2--3 of its proof (Lemmas~\ref{lem:tangent-local} and~\ref{lem:tangent-graph} applied to the graph of $h$), $T^{\geo}_pM = \{(u, Dh_a u) \mid u \in \mathbb{R}^n\}$. So $v$ has the form $(v_1, Dh_a v_1) = D\alpha_a(v_1)$, with $v_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ its first $n$ components.

\emph{Third equality, $\operatorname{im} D\alpha_a \subseteq \ker F'(p)$.} Since $\alpha$ takes values in $M = F^{-1}(c)$, the composite $F \circ \alpha$ is the constant map $c$ on $V$, so its derivative at $a$ is $0$. By the chain rule, and $\alpha(a) = p$,
\[
0 = D(F \circ \alpha)_a = F'(\alpha(a)) \circ D\alpha_a = F'(p) \circ D\alpha_a ,
\]
so $F'(p)\big(D\alpha_a(u)\big) = 0$ for every $u$, that is, $\operatorname{im} D\alpha_a \subseteq \ker F'(p)$.

\emph{The isomorphism.} $D\alpha_a$ is linear, and injective because its first $n$ components are the identity: $D\alpha_a(u) = 0$ gives $u = 0$. So $D\alpha_a$ is a linear bijection of $\mathbb{R}^n$ onto its image, which by the three equalities is $T^{\geo}_pM$. Consistently, both spaces have dimension $n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent-4}
The corollary is the infinitesimal form of \S\ref{sub:ext-int}: the geometric tangent space can be read off from the \emph{external} description as the kernel of the constraint map, or from the \emph{internal} description as the image of the derivative of a parametrization, and the two agree. The geometric definition, via curves, is the one that makes no reference to either presentation --- which is why it is the one that will generalize.
\end{rembox}

\subsection{Examples}

\begin{exbox}[The Sphere]\exlabel{ex:tangent-sphere}
For $S^n = F^{-1}(1)$ with $F(x) = |x|^2 = \sum x_i^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, the Jacobian at $p$ is the row vector $F'(p) = 2p^{\mathsf T}$, written out
\[
F'(p) = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x_1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x_{n+1}}(p) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2p_1 & 2p_2 & \cdots & 2p_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad p = (p_1, \ldots, p_{n+1}),
\] and $1$ is a regular value since $p \neq 0$ on $S^n$. Hence
\[
T^{\geo}_pS^n = \ker\big(2p^{\mathsf T}\big) = \{\, v \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} \mid p \cdot v = 0 \,\} = p^{\perp},
\]
the hyperplane orthogonal to the position vector --- the tangent plane of calculus, now as a theorem. Directly from the definition: any curve $\gamma$ on the sphere satisfies $\gamma(t)\cdot\gamma(t) = 1$, so $2\,\gamma(t)\cdot\gamma'(t) = 0$, and at $t = 0$ this is $p \cdot v = 0$.
\end{exbox}

The sphere through the course: a topological manifold with hemisphere charts in Section~\ref{sec:ex-spheres}; the homogeneous space $\SO(3)/\SO(2)$ in Example~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}; the Riemann sphere $\mathbb{CP}^1$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:cp1-sphere}; its geometric tangent spaces in Example~\ref{ex:tangent-sphere} and its transverse intersection with a plane in Example~\ref{ex:sphere-plane-transverse}; the double cover $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ and the Hopf fibration $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$ in Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf}; and $S^3 = \mathrm{SU}(2)$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-su2}.


\begin{exbox}[The Orthogonal Group]\exlabel{ex:tangent-On}
For $\Ogp(n) = F^{-1}(I)$ with $F : \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \to \Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$, $F(g) = gg^{\mathsf T}$, Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} applies after identifying both spaces with Euclidean spaces by linear coordinates, under which the Jacobian corresponds to the differential $dF_g$ of Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential}. Proposition~\ref{prop:On-kernel} then gives
\[
T^{\geo}_g\Ogp(n) = \ker dF_g = g \cdot \Skew(n,\mathbb{R}), \qquad T^{\geo}_I \Ogp(n) = \Skew(n,\mathbb{R}),
\]
of dimension $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, as it must be. Directly from the definition, at $g = I$: if $\gamma$ is a curve of orthogonal matrices with $\gamma(0) = I$, then $\gamma(t)\gamma(t)^{\mathsf T} = I$ for all $t$; differentiating at $0$ gives $\gamma'(0) + \gamma'(0)^{\mathsf T} = 0$, so the velocity is skew-symmetric. This geometric tangent space at the identity is the object that will later be called the \emph{Lie algebra} $\mathfrak{so}(n)$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent-5}
For $\Ogp(n)$ the ambient space is $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ rather than $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$; Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent} is used in its vector-space form, and Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} transfers across the linear isomorphism of Proposition~\ref{prop:vs-manifold}. The description $T^{\geo}_g\Ogp(n) = g \cdot T^{\geo}_I\Ogp(n)$ --- every geometric tangent space is a translate of the one at the identity --- is the first sign that a group structure simplifies the tangent bundle; it will be a general fact about Lie groups.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[The Unitary Group]\exlabel{ex:tangent-Un}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:Un-kernel} and Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} (transferred to the real vector space $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ as in the note above),
\[
T^{\geo}_g\Ugp(n) = \ker dF_g = \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g = g\cdot\mathfrak{u}(n), \qquad T^{\geo}_I\Ugp(n) = \mathfrak{u}(n).
\]
Directly from the definition at $g = I$: a curve of unitary matrices with $\gamma(0) = I$ satisfies $\gamma(t)\gamma(t)^* = I$, and differentiating at $0$ gives $\gamma'(0) + \gamma'(0)^* = 0$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{thmbox}[The Classical Groups]\thmlabel{thm:classical-summary}
Each classical group of Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-manifolds} is a smooth manifold, of the dimension and with the geometric tangent space at the identity given below. Moreover, for $G = \SL(n,\mathbb{R}), \Ogp(n), \SO(n), \Ugp(n)$ and every $g \in G$,
\[
T^{\geo}_g G \;=\; g \cdot T^{\geo}_I G \;=\; T^{\geo}_I G \cdot g .
\]
\leeref{Examples 7.27--7.30}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
\begin{tabular}{l l c l}
\hline
Group $G$ & Presentation & $\dim G$ & $T^{\geo}_I G$ \\
\hline
$\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ & open in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ & $n^2$ & $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ \\
$\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$ & open in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ & $2n^2$ & $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ \\
$\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$ & $\det^{-1}(1)$ & $n^2 - 1$ & $\mathfrak{sl}(n) = \{A \mid \tr A = 0\}$ \\
$\Ogp(n)$ & $F^{-1}(I)$, $F(g) = gg^{\mathsf T} \in \Sym(n,\mathbb{R})$ & $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ & $\mathfrak{so}(n) = \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$ \\
$\SO(n)$ & open in $\Ogp(n)$ & $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ & $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ \\
$\Ugp(n)$ & $F^{-1}(I)$, $F(g) = gg^* \in \Herm(n)$ & $n^2$ & $\mathfrak{u}(n) = \{X \mid X^* = -X\}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{proof}
For each group we need its smooth structure and dimension (the table), its geometric tangent space at $I$, and, for the last four, the two translate formulas. Throughout, Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent} and Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} are used in their vector-space form, with the differential in place of the Jacobian, as in Example~\ref{ex:tangent-On} and the remark after it.

\emph{The general linear groups.} An open subset $U$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $\dim V$ (one chart, the restriction of a linear chart): $V$ is a smooth manifold with a linear chart $L : V \to \mathbb{R}^m$, $m = \dim V$ (Definition~\ref{def:vs-structure}), $L$ is a homeomorphism, so $L(U)$ is open, and $L|_U : U \to L(U)$ is a single chart covering $U$. This applies to $\GL(n,\mathbb{R}) = \det^{-1}(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\})$ and $\GL(n,\mathbb{C}) = \det^{-1}(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\})$, which are open in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ and $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$ because $\det$ is continuous (a polynomial in the entries; Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups} for the complex case); the dimensions are $\dim\Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) = n^2$ (Definition~\ref{def:mat-euclid}) and $\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) = 2n^2$ (Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}).

Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent} makes sense verbatim for $U \subseteq V$, and we claim $T^{\geo}_pU = V$ for every $p \in U$. The inclusion $\subseteq$ holds because the velocity of a curve in $V$ is a vector of $V$. For $\supseteq$, every $v \in V$ is the velocity of the curve $t \mapsto p + tv$, which stays in $U$ for small $|t|$: fix a norm on $V$; as $U$ is open, a ball $B(p, r)$ lies in $U$, and for $|t| < r/(|v| + 1)$ we have $|(p + tv) - p| = |t|\,|v| < r$. The curve $\gamma(t) = p + tv$ is smooth, $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma'(0) = v$. So $T^{\geo}_pU = V$; at $p = I$ this gives $T^{\geo}_I\GL(n,\mathbb{R}) = \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ and $T^{\geo}_I\GL(n,\mathbb{C}) = \Mat(n,\mathbb{C})$.

\emph{$\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$.} Smoothness and dimension are Corollary~\ref{prop:SL-loc-euc} with Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}: $\SL(n,\mathbb{R}) = \det^{-1}(1)$ with $1$ a regular value of $\det$ on $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) = \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:regular-value}), a smooth manifold of dimension $n^2 - 1$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} with $F = \det$ and $c = 1$, $T^{\geo}_g\SL = \ker \det'(g)$, where $\det'(g)A = \nabla\det(g) \cdot A$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian} with $m = 1$). By Proposition~\ref{prop:jacobi}, $\nabla\det(g)\cdot A = \det(g)\,\tr(g^{-1}A) = \tr(g^{-1}A)$ for $g \in \SL(n,\mathbb{R})$, since $\det g = 1$. So
\[
T^{\geo}_g\SL = \{A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \mid \tr(g^{-1}A) = 0\} .
\]
\emph{Left translate.} Since $g$ is invertible, every $A$ is uniquely $A = gB$ with $B = g^{-1}A$, and then $\tr(g^{-1}A) = \tr B$; so $A \in T^{\geo}_g\SL$ iff $B \in \mathfrak{sl}(n)$, i.e.\ $T^{\geo}_g\SL = g\cdot\mathfrak{sl}(n)$. \emph{Right translate.} Every $A$ is uniquely $A = Bg$ with $B = Ag^{-1}$, and by $\tr(XY) = \tr(YX)$ with $X = g^{-1}$, $Y = Bg$,
\[
\tr(g^{-1}A) = \tr(g^{-1}Bg) = \tr(Bg\,g^{-1}) = \tr B ;
\]
so $T^{\geo}_g\SL = \mathfrak{sl}(n)\cdot g$. At $g = I$ either formula gives $T^{\geo}_I\SL = \mathfrak{sl}(n)$. The trace condition removes one dimension, consistently with $n^2 - 1$: $\tr : \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}$ is linear and surjective ($\tr(cE_{11}) = c$), so by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) $\dim\mathfrak{sl}(n) = n^2 - 1$.

\emph{$\Ogp(n)$ and $\SO(n)$.} Example~\ref{ex:On-smooth} gives that $\Ogp(n)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, and Corollary~\ref{cor:On-consequences} that $\SO(n)$ is an open subset of $\Ogp(n)$, a smooth manifold of the same dimension. Example~\ref{ex:tangent-On} gives $T^{\geo}_g\Ogp(n) = g\cdot\Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$ and $T^{\geo}_I\Ogp(n) = \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$. Since $\SO(n)$ is open in $\Ogp(n)$ its geometric tangent spaces are those of $\Ogp(n)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-local}): for $g \in \SO(n)$, $T^{\geo}_g\SO(n) = T^{\geo}_g\Ogp(n)$, and in particular $T^{\geo}_I\SO(n) = \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$. For the right translate, $\Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$ is preserved by conjugation by orthogonal $g$, exactly as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:Un-kernel}: if $X^{\mathsf T} = -X$ and $g^{-1} = g^{\mathsf T}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:orth-equiv}), then
\[
(gXg^{-1})^{\mathsf T} = (gXg^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = gX^{\mathsf T}g^{\mathsf T} = -gXg^{-1} .
\]
Hence $gX = (gXg^{-1})\,g \in \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})\cdot g$, so $g\cdot\Skew(n,\mathbb{R}) \subseteq \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})\cdot g$. Applying the same to the orthogonal matrix $g^{-1}$, $g^{-1}Xg$ is skew, so $Xg = g\,(g^{-1}Xg) \in g\cdot\Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$, which is the reverse inclusion. So $T^{\geo}_gG = g\cdot T^{\geo}_IG = T^{\geo}_IG\cdot g$ for $G = \Ogp(n)$, and for $G = \SO(n)$ by the equalities just noted.

\emph{$\Ugp(n)$.} Example~\ref{ex:Un-smooth} gives that $\Ugp(n)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $n^2$, and Example~\ref{ex:tangent-Un} gives $T^{\geo}_g\Ugp(n) = \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g = g\cdot\mathfrak{u}(n)$ and $T^{\geo}_I\Ugp(n) = \mathfrak{u}(n)$, which are the two translate formulas.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Adjoint Action]\deflabel{def:adjoint}
Let $G$ be one of $\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\Ogp(n)$, $\SO(n)$, $\Ugp(n)$, and $\mathfrak{g} = T^{\geo}_I G$. For $g \in G$, \textbf{conjugation} by $g$ is $\mathrm{Ad}_g(X) = gXg^{-1}$. The \textbf{adjoint action} of $G$ on $\mathfrak{g}$ is $g \mapsto \mathrm{Ad}_g|_{\mathfrak{g}}$; that each $\mathrm{Ad}_g$ maps $\mathfrak{g}$ onto itself is part of the next proposition.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Adjoint Action]\thmlabel{prop:adjoint}
Let $G$ be one of $\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\Ogp(n)$, $\SO(n)$, $\Ugp(n)$, and $\mathfrak{g} = T^{\geo}_I G$. For $g \in G$ the conjugation
\[
\mathrm{Ad}_g : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}, \qquad \mathrm{Ad}_g(X) = gXg^{-1},
\]
is a linear isomorphism, with $\mathrm{Ad}_{gh} = \mathrm{Ad}_g \circ \mathrm{Ad}_h$. Left and right multiplication $L_g(X) = gX$ and $R_g(X) = Xg$ satisfy $L_g = R_g \circ \mathrm{Ad}_g$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
There are four things to check: $\mathrm{Ad}_g$ maps $\mathfrak{g}$ into itself, it is linear, it is bijective on $\mathfrak{g}$ (with the composition law), and $L_g = R_g \circ \mathrm{Ad}_g$.

\emph{$\mathrm{Ad}_g$ maps $\mathfrak{g}$ into itself.} That $\mathrm{Ad}_g$ maps $\mathfrak{g}$ into itself is checked case by case, with $\mathfrak{g}$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}. For $\mathfrak{sl}(n)$: if $\tr X = 0$ then, by $\tr(YZ) = \tr(ZY)$ with $Y = gX$ and $Z = g^{-1}$, $\tr(gXg^{-1}) = \tr(Xg^{-1}g) = \tr X = 0$. For $g$ orthogonal (in $\Ogp(n)$ or $\SO(n)$, so $g^{-1} = g^{\mathsf T}$) and $X$ skew:
\[
(gXg^{-1})^{\mathsf T} = (gXg^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = gX^{\mathsf T}g^{\mathsf T} = -gXg^{-1} .
\]
For $g$ unitary ($g^{-1} = g^*$) and $X$ skew-Hermitian:
\[
(gXg^{-1})^* = (gXg^*)^* = gX^*g^* = -gXg^{-1} .
\]

\emph{Linear.} For $X, Y \in \mathfrak{g}$ and real $a, b$, by distributivity of matrix multiplication,
\[
\mathrm{Ad}_g(aX + bY) = g(aX + bY)g^{-1} = a\,gXg^{-1} + b\,gYg^{-1} = a\,\mathrm{Ad}_g X + b\,\mathrm{Ad}_g Y .
\]

\emph{Composition and inverse.} By associativity, and $(gh)^{-1} = h^{-1}g^{-1}$,
\[
\mathrm{Ad}_{gh}X = (gh)X(gh)^{-1} = g\big(hXh^{-1}\big)g^{-1} = \mathrm{Ad}_g(\mathrm{Ad}_h X) .
\]
Since $G$ is a group, $g^{-1} \in G$, so $\mathrm{Ad}_{g^{-1}} : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}$ is defined, and by the composition law $\mathrm{Ad}_{g^{-1}} \circ \mathrm{Ad}_g = \mathrm{Ad}_{g^{-1}g} = \mathrm{Ad}_I = \mathrm{id}$ and $\mathrm{Ad}_g \circ \mathrm{Ad}_{g^{-1}} = \mathrm{Ad}_{gg^{-1}} = \mathrm{id}$. So $\mathrm{Ad}_{g^{-1}}$ is an inverse, and $\mathrm{Ad}_g$ is a linear bijection of $\mathfrak{g}$ onto itself, i.e.\ a linear isomorphism.

\emph{Left and right multiplication.} Finally, for $X \in \mathfrak{g}$,
\[
R_g(\mathrm{Ad}_g X) = (gXg^{-1})\,g = gX\,(g^{-1}g) = gX = L_g X .
\]
This holds for every $X \in \mathfrak{g}$, so $L_g = R_g \circ \mathrm{Ad}_g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Left and Right Translates]\label{rem:left-right-translates}
The notes computed $T^{\geo}_g\Ogp(n) = g\cdot\Skew(n)$ by writing $A = gB$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:On-kernel}); Assignment~2 computed $T^{\geo}_g\Ugp(n) = \mathfrak{u}(n)\cdot g$ by writing $h = Xg$. Neither choice is privileged, and by the proposition the two agree, $g \cdot \mathfrak{g} = \mathrm{Ad}_g(\mathfrak{g}) \cdot g = \mathfrak{g} \cdot g$. This is the first structural fact about Lie groups to appear in the course: the geometric tangent space at the identity, carried to every other point by left or right multiplication, determines all the geometric tangent spaces. The spaces $\mathfrak{sl}(n)$, $\mathfrak{so}(n)$, $\mathfrak{u}(n)$ in the table will reappear as \emph{Lie algebras}.
\end{rembox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.8em, column sep=2.6em]
T^{\geo}_IG \arrow[rr, "\mathrm{Ad}_g \,:\, X \,\mapsto\, gXg^{-1}"] \arrow[dr, "L_g \,:\, X \,\mapsto\, gX"'] & & T^{\geo}_IG \arrow[dl, "R_g \,:\, X \,\mapsto\, Xg"] \\
& T^{\geo}_gG &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Left and right multiplication by $g$ both carry $T^{\geo}_IG$ isomorphically onto $T^{\geo}_gG$, and they differ by the adjoint action: $L_g = R_g \circ \mathrm{Ad}_g$, since $(gXg^{-1})g = gX$. The two descriptions of $T^{\geo}_gG$ agree precisely because $\mathrm{Ad}_g$ maps $T^{\geo}_IG$ onto itself.


\begin{defbox}[The Hat Map]\deflabel{def:hat-map}
The \textbf{hat map} $\mathbb{R}^3 \to \Skew(3,\mathbb{R})$ sends $v = (v_1, v_2, v_3)$ to
\[
\hat v = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -v_3 & v_2 \\ v_3 & 0 & -v_1 \\ -v_2 & v_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
a linear isomorphism, characterized by $\hat v\, x = v \times x$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{exbox}[$\SO(3)$ and Infinitesimal Rotations]\exlabel{ex:so3-infinitesimal}
$T^{\geo}_I\SO(3) = \Skew(3,\mathbb{R})$ is $3$-dimensional, and it is identified with $\mathbb{R}^3$ by the hat map of Definition~\ref{def:hat-map}
\[
v = (v_1,v_2,v_3) \longmapsto \hat v = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -v_3 & v_2 \\ v_3 & 0 & -v_1 \\ -v_2 & v_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad \hat v\, x = v \times x .
\]
Every tangent vector at the identity is the velocity of a family of rotations. For the axis $e_3$,
\[
R(t) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos t & -\sin t & 0 \\ \sin t & \cos t & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad R(0) = I, \qquad R'(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \hat e_3 .
\]
For a unit vector $n$, choose $Q \in \SO(3)$ with $Qe_3 = n$ (possible by Example~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}); the rotation about $n$ by angle $t$ is $QR(t)Q^{\mathsf T}$, with velocity $Q\hat e_3 Q^{\mathsf T} = \widehat{Qe_3} = \hat n$ at $t = 0$, using the identity $\widehat{Qv} = Q\hat vQ^{\mathsf T}$ for $Q \in \SO(3)$, which holds because rotations preserve the cross product. Scaling the speed, every $\hat v$ is attained: \emph{a tangent vector to $\SO(3)$ at the identity is an angular velocity}, with direction the axis and length the rate of rotation.
\end{exbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent-6}
This connects the $\SO(3)$ material of \ref{sec:actions} and \ref{sec:homogeneous} with the geometric tangent space. The three dimensions of $\SO(3)$ are the two needed to specify an axis, a point of $S^2$, and one for the angle about it --- matching $S^2 \cong \SO(3)/\SO(2)$ of Example~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}, with the isotropy $\SO(2)$ being exactly the rotations about the fixed axis.
\end{rembox}

The classical groups through the course: defined in Section~\ref{sec:topgroups}, with the examples of Section~\ref{sec:ex-classical}; topological manifolds as level sets in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-manifolds}; $\SO(2)$ and $\SO(3)$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so2-orbits} and~\ref{ex:so3-orbits}, and $\SO(3)$ on $S^2$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so3-isotropy} and~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}; $\Ogp(n)$ acting on the Grassmannians in Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}; smooth manifolds in Examples~\ref{ex:On-smooth} and~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}; their tangent spaces at the identity in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}, with the infinitesimal rotations of Example~\ref{ex:so3-infinitesimal}; the double cover $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \SO(3)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:double-cover}; the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and the cross product in Example~\ref{ex:cross-product-lie}; and Lie groups in Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}.


\begin{rembox}[Dimension Checks through Homogeneous Spaces]\label{rem:dimension-checks-through-homogeneous-spaces}
In every homogeneous space met so far, $\dim G/H = \dim G - \dim H$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $S^2 = \SO(3)/\SO(2)$: \ $3 - 1 = 2$;
    \item $\Gr_k(\mathbb{R}^n) = \Ogp(n)/\big(\Ogp(k)\times\Ogp(n-k)\big)$: \ $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} - \tfrac{k(k-1)}{2} - \tfrac{(n-k)(n-k-1)}{2} = k(n-k)$;
    \item $S^{2n+1} = \Ugp(n+1)/\Ugp(n)$: \ $(n+1)^2 - n^2 = 2n+1$;
    \item $\mathbb{CP}^n = \Ugp(n+1)/\big(\Ugp(1)\times\Ugp(n)\big)$: \ $(n+1)^2 - 1 - n^2 = 2n$, the real dimension found from charts in Theorem~\ref{thm:cpn-atlas}.
\end{itemize}
The first two identifications are proved in \ref{sec:homogeneous}--\ref{sec:GH-topology}; the last two are their complex analogues --- $\Ugp(n+1)$ acts transitively on unit vectors of $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ and on complex lines --- and are not proved here. The formula itself is heuristic until quotient manifolds are available, when it becomes a theorem; for now it is a consistency check linking four separate computations.
\end{rembox}

\subsection{The Dimension of the Geometric Tangent Space}\label{sub:geo-dimension}

\begin{thmbox}[Dimension of the Geometric Tangent Space]\thmlabel{thm:geo-tangent-dimension}
Let $M = F^{-1}(c) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}, a manifold of dimension $n$. Then for every $p \in M$,
\[
\dim T^{\geo}_pM = n = \dim M .
\]
The geometric tangent space has the same dimension at every point, and it is the dimension of the manifold.
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(The last sentence of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}, recorded as a theorem in its own right.)} By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}, $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$. Since $c$ is a regular value, the $k \times (n+k)$ matrix $F'(p)$ has rank $k$, so by rank--nullity $\dim \ker F'(p) = (n + k) - k = n$.
\end{proof}

The count is the geometric meaning of ``$k$ independent equations in $n + k$ unknowns'': each equation removes one tangent direction, and $n$ remain at every point. Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension} gives the same number for the abstract tangent space, as it must, since the two spaces are isomorphic (Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}).

\subsection{From Tangent Vectors to Derivations}\label{sub:derivations-motivation}

\textit{Motivation only; nothing in this subsection is used later, but it is where the abstract definition comes from.}

Keep $M = F^{-1}(c)$ and, by Lemmas \ref{lem:tangent-local} and \ref{lem:tangent-graph}, assume $M$ is the graph of a smooth $G : A \to \mathbb{R}^k$ over an open $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, with chart $\varphi : M \to A$ the projection $(x, G(x)) \mapsto x$ and $p = (x_0, G(x_0))$. Let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth, so that $f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1} : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}).

Given $v \in T^{\geo}_pM$, Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-graph} provides a unique $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $v = (u, G'(x_0)u)$. Lift the straight line $t \mapsto x_0 + tu$ from the chart to the manifold:
\[
\gamma(t) = \big(x_0 + tu,\; G(x_0 + tu)\big), \qquad \gamma(0) = p, \quad \gamma'(0) = v .
\]

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3.0em, column sep=3.6em]
M \arrow[r, "f"] \arrow[d, shift right=0.6ex, "\varphi"'] & \mathbb{R} \\
A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \arrow[u, shift right=0.6ex, "\varphi^{-1}"'] \arrow[ur, "f_\varphi"'] &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The chart triangle for the graph case, as drawn on the board. Downstairs is the open set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$; upstairs is the manifold. The chart $\varphi(x, G(x)) = x$ and its inverse $\varphi^{-1}(x) = (x, G(x))$ pass between them, and the triangle commutes: $f = f_\varphi \circ \varphi$. Smoothness of $f$ \emph{means} smoothness of $f_\varphi$, so every computation with $f$ can be pushed downstairs, done in ordinary calculus, and read back. That is the manoeuvre in the next definition: the curve is built downstairs as a straight line, lifted upstairs by $\varphi^{-1}$, and the derivative taken downstairs again. ``Upstairs and downstairs are very useful terminologies.''

\begin{defbox}[The Directional Derivative Attached to a Tangent Vector]\deflabel{def:Dv}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ be the graph of a smooth $G : A \to \mathbb{R}^k$ on an open $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, with chart $\varphi(x, G(x)) = x$, and $p = (x_0, G(x_0))$. Let $v \in T^{\geo}_pM$, let $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be the vector with $v = (u, G'(x_0)u)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-graph}), and let $\gamma(t) = (x_0 + tu, G(x_0 + tu))$ be the lifted line, a curve in $M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma'(0) = v$. For $f$ a smooth real-valued function on a neighbourhood of $p$ in $M$, set
\[
D_v(f) \;=\; \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f(\gamma(t)) \;=\; \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f_\varphi(x_0 + tu) \;=\; u \cdot \nabla f_\varphi(x_0),
\]
the second equality because $\varphi(\gamma(t)) = x_0 + tu$ and $f = f_\varphi \circ \varphi$, the third by the chain rule. So $D_v$ takes a smooth function defined near $p$ and returns a real number, and it depends only on the values of $f$ near $p$ --- which is what the germs of the next subsection make precise.
\leeref{Proposition 3.2 (in $\mathbb{R}^n$)}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Basic Properties of $D_v$]\thmlabel{prop:Dv-properties}
In the setting of Definition~\ref{def:Dv}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $D_v(f)$ depends only on the germ of $f$ at $p$;
    \item if $\sigma$ is \emph{any} smooth curve in $M$ with $\sigma(0) = p$ and $\sigma'(0) = v$, then $D_v(f) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} f(\sigma(t))$; so $D_v$ depends on $v$ alone, not on the curve used to define it;
    \item $D_v$ is linear and obeys the product rule $D_v(fg) = f(p)\,D_v(g) + g(p)\,D_v(f)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, $f$ is smooth on an open neighbourhood of $p$ in $M$, $f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$, so that $f = f_\varphi \circ \varphi$ on that neighbourhood, and by the third expression in Definition~\ref{def:Dv}, $D_v(f) = u \cdot \nabla f_\varphi(x_0)$.

\emph{(1)} $\gamma(t)$ lies in any given neighbourhood of $p$ for $|t|$ small, so only the values of $f$ near $p$ enter --- ``we don't need the whole manifold.'' In detail: suppose $f$ and $g$ are smooth near $p$ and agree on an open $W \ni p$ of $M$, say $W = M \cap O$ with $O$ open in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$. The curve $\gamma$ is continuous with values in $M$, so $\gamma^{-1}(W) = \gamma^{-1}(O)$ is open in its interval of definition and contains $0$; hence it contains some $(-\delta,\delta)$. For $|t| < \delta$, $\gamma(t) \in W$ and $f(\gamma(t)) = g(\gamma(t))$. Two functions of $t$ that agree on $(-\delta,\delta)$ have the same difference quotients at $0$ for $0 < |t| < \delta$, hence the same derivative at $0$:
\[
D_v(f) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f(\gamma(t)) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} g(\gamma(t)) = D_v(g) .
\]

\emph{(2)} The chart $\varphi$ is the restriction to $M$ of the linear projection $\pi(x,y) = x$, whose matrix is the $n \times (n+k)$ block row
\[
\pi = \left(\begin{array}{c|c} I_n & 0 \end{array}\right), \qquad \pi\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = I_n x + 0\,y = x \qquad (x \in \mathbb{R}^n,\ y \in \mathbb{R}^k),
\] so $\varphi \circ \sigma = \pi \circ \sigma$ is a smooth curve; it takes values in $A$, because $\sigma(t) \in M$ has the form $(x, G(x))$ with $x \in A$; and $(\varphi\circ\sigma)(0) = \varphi(p) = x_0$. Its velocity at $0$ is, since the derivative of the linear map $\pi$ is $\pi$ itself,
\[
(\varphi \circ \sigma)'(0) = \pi\big(\sigma'(0)\big) = \pi(v) = \pi\big(u, G'(x_0)u\big) = u ,
\]
the first component of $v$. For $|t|$ small, $\sigma(t)$ lies in the domain of $f$ (as in (1)) and $f(\sigma(t)) = f_\varphi\big((\varphi\circ\sigma)(t)\big)$, because $f = f_\varphi \circ \varphi$. So the chain rule for the curve $\varphi \circ \sigma$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}, case $m = 1$) gives
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f(\sigma(t)) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f_\varphi\big((\varphi\circ\sigma)(t)\big) = \nabla f_\varphi(x_0) \cdot (\varphi\circ\sigma)'(0) = \nabla f_\varphi(x_0) \cdot u = D_v(f) .
\]
The right side involves only $u$, which is determined by $v$; so the derivative along $\sigma$ is the same for every such $\sigma$, and $D_v$ depends on $v$ alone.

\emph{(3)} Linearity and the product rule are inherited from those of the gradient, $\nabla(f_\varphi g_\varphi) = f_\varphi \nabla g_\varphi + g_\varphi \nabla f_\varphi$, evaluated at $x_0$, where $f_\varphi(x_0) = f(p)$. In detail, let $f, g$ be smooth near $p$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$; on the common domain, composing with $\varphi^{-1}$ respects sums, scalar multiples and products:
\[
(af + bg)_\varphi = a f_\varphi + b g_\varphi, \qquad (fg)_\varphi = f_\varphi\, g_\varphi .
\]
\emph{Linearity.} Since the gradient is linear,
\[
D_v(af + bg) = u \cdot \nabla\big(af_\varphi + bg_\varphi\big)(x_0) = u \cdot \big(a\nabla f_\varphi(x_0) + b\nabla g_\varphi(x_0)\big) = a\,D_v(f) + b\,D_v(g) .
\]
\emph{Product rule.} The gradient of a product obeys $\nabla(f_\varphi g_\varphi) = f_\varphi \nabla g_\varphi + g_\varphi \nabla f_\varphi$ (the one-variable product rule in each partial derivative), and $f_\varphi(x_0) = f(\varphi^{-1}(x_0)) = f(p)$, $g_\varphi(x_0) = g(p)$, because $\varphi^{-1}(x_0) = (x_0, G(x_0)) = p$. So
\[
D_v(fg) = u \cdot \nabla(f_\varphi g_\varphi)(x_0) = f_\varphi(x_0)\, u \cdot \nabla g_\varphi(x_0) + g_\varphi(x_0)\, u\cdot\nabla f_\varphi(x_0) = f(p)\,D_v(g) + g(p)\,D_v(f) .
\]
This is the product rule of the statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[$D_v$ Determines $v$]\thmlabel{prop:Dv-determines-v}
The map $v \mapsto D_v$ is injective on $T^{\geo}_pM$: if $D_v = D_{v'}$ then $v = v'$.
\leeref{Proposition 3.2(b)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Write $v = (u, G'(x_0)u)$ and $v' = (u', G'(x_0)u')$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-graph}). Since $v$ is determined by $u$ and $v'$ by $u'$, it suffices to show $u = u'$, and for that to recover each component $u^i$ from $D_v$.

For $i = 1, \ldots, n$ let $x^i : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be the $i$-th coordinate of the chart, $x^i(x, G(x)) = x^i$, a smooth function on $M$. Then $(x^i)_\varphi = x^i \circ \varphi^{-1}$ sends $x \in A$ to the $i$-th coordinate of $\varphi^{-1}(x) = (x, G(x))$, which is $x^i$; so $(x^i)_\varphi = r^i$ is the $i$-th coordinate function on $A$, and $\nabla (x^i)_\varphi = e_i$, since $\partial r^i/\partial r^j = \delta^i_j$. By the third expression in Definition~\ref{def:Dv},
\[
D_v(x^i) = u \cdot \nabla (x^i)_\varphi(x_0) = u \cdot e_i = u^i .
\]
If $D_v = D_{v'}$, applying both to $x^i$ gives $u^i = D_v(x^i) = D_{v'}(x^i) = (u')^i$ for every $i$, so $u = u'$ and hence $v = (u, G'(x_0)u) = (u', G'(x_0)u') = v'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:abstract-tangent}
Uribe's version of this argument: the numbers $D_v(f) = u \cdot \nabla f_\varphi(x_0)$ range over the dot products of $u$ with an arbitrary vector, because the gradient of a function at a point can be prescribed freely; so knowing all of them determines $u$. Taking $f$ to be the coordinate functions is the cheapest way to prescribe it.

The conclusion is that a tangent vector loses nothing by being replaced by the operator it defines --- and the operator, unlike the vector, makes sense with no ambient space in sight. \emph{Tangent vectors will be defined as operators:} you feed them a function and they return a number.
\end{rembox}
