% SECTION: TRANSVERSALITY
% ============================================================================

\section{Transversality}\label{sec:transversality}\label{sub:transversality}

\roadmark{Stage: geometric}{When is the preimage of a regular level set again a regular level set? A condition that does not mention the defining map.}

\textit{Assignment 2, Problem 5. The problem ends with a parenthetical that is the point of the whole exercise: the transversality condition ``does not mention $G$ explicitly --- keep this in mind, for the future.''}

Throughout this section $F : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^k$ and $G : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^\ell$ are smooth, $0$ is a regular value of $G$, and
\[
S = G^{-1}(0) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k ,
\]
a smooth manifold of dimension $k - \ell$ with $T^{\geo}_qS = \ker G'(q)$ for $q \in S$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}). Its codimension, in the sense of the next definition, is $\operatorname{codim} S = k - \dim S = \ell$, the number of equations cutting it out.

\begin{defbox}[Codimension]\deflabel{def:codimension}
If $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ is a manifold of dimension $s$ --- for instance a regular level set --- its \textbf{codimension} in $\mathbb{R}^k$ is $\operatorname{codim} S = k - s$.
\leeref{Ch.~5, \emph{Embedded Submanifolds}}
\end{defbox} (Everything below works verbatim with $F$ and $G$ defined only on open subsets.)

\begin{defbox}[Transversality]\deflabel{def:transverse}
$F$ is \textbf{transverse} to $S$, written $F \pitchfork S$, if
\[
\operatorname{im} F'(p) \;+\; T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S \;=\; \mathbb{R}^k \qquad \text{for every } p \in F^{-1}(S).
\]
The condition is imposed only at points of the preimage, and holds vacuously if $F^{-1}(S) = \emptyset$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent-7}
In words: at each point where $F$ meets $S$, the directions $F$ can move in, together with the directions along $S$, fill up the whole ambient space. The condition involves $F$ and $S$ only --- not the function $G$ used to cut $S$ out.
\end{rembox}

\begin{thmbox}[Preimages of Transverse Level Sets]\thmlabel{thm:transverse-preimage}
If $F \pitchfork S$, then $M = F^{-1}(S)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $N - \ell$ (or empty), and for $p \in M$
\[
T^{\geo}_pM = F'(p)^{-1}\big(T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S\big) = \{\, v \in \mathbb{R}^N \mid F'(p)v \in T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S \,\}.
\]
In particular $\operatorname{codim} M = \operatorname{codim} S = \ell$.
\leeref{Theorem 6.30(a)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=3.6em]
M \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "F|_M"'] & \mathbb{R}^N \arrow[d, "F"'] \arrow[dr, "G \circ F"] & \\
S \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb{R}^k \arrow[r, "G"'] & \mathbb{R}^\ell
\end{tikzcd}
\\[1.2em]
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=3.6em]
T^{\geo}_pM \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "F'(p)|"'] & \mathbb{R}^N \arrow[d, "F'(p)"'] \arrow[dr, "(G \circ F)'(p)"] & \\
T^{\geo}_qS \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb{R}^k \arrow[r, "G'(q)"'] & \mathbb{R}^\ell
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Top, the spaces; bottom, their linearizations at $p$ and $q = F(p)$. In each, the square says the top-left corner is everything upstairs that lands in the bottom-left corner --- $M = F^{-1}(S)$ and $T^{\geo}_pM = F'(p)^{-1}(T^{\geo}_qS)$ --- and the triangle says the same set is cut out by the composite, $M = (G\circ F)^{-1}(0)$ and $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker (G\circ F)'(p)$. The theorem asserts that the preimage in the lower diagram is the geometric tangent space of the preimage in the upper one; Example~\ref{ex:transverse-failures}(b) shows this can fail without transversality.


\begin{proof}
If $M = \emptyset$ there is nothing to prove, so assume otherwise; then $S \neq \emptyset$ (a point $p \in M$ has $F(p) \in S$), and surjectivity of $G'(q) : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^\ell$ at some $q \in S$ gives $k \ge \ell$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)). The plan: write $M$ as a level set of $G \circ F$, show $0$ is a regular value, and read off the dimension and the geometric tangent space from the regular value theorem and Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}.

\emph{$M$ is a level set.} For $p \in \mathbb{R}^N$, by the definitions of preimage and of $S$,
\[
p \in F^{-1}(S) \iff F(p) \in G^{-1}(0) \iff G(F(p)) = 0 ,
\]
so $M = (G \circ F)^{-1}(0)$, with $G \circ F : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^\ell$ smooth as a composite of smooth maps.

\emph{$0$ is a regular value of $G \circ F$.} Let $p \in M$ and $q = F(p) \in S$. By the chain rule $(G \circ F)'(p) = G'(q)\,F'(p)$. We show this is surjective. Given $w \in \mathbb{R}^\ell$, choose $u \in \mathbb{R}^k$ with $G'(q)u = w$, possible as $G'(q)$ is surjective ($0$ is a regular value of $G$ and $q \in G^{-1}(0)$). Transversality at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse}) says $\operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS = \mathbb{R}^k$, so we can write $u = F'(p)v + t$ with $v \in \mathbb{R}^N$ and $t \in T^{\geo}_qS = \ker G'(q)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} for $S$). Then, by linearity of $G'(q)$ and $G'(q)t = 0$,
\[
w = G'(q)u = G'(q)F'(p)v + G'(q)t = G'(q)F'(p)v ,
\]
so $w$ is in the image and $(G\circ F)'(p)$ is surjective. As $p \in M$ was arbitrary, $0$ is a regular value (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}), and surjectivity at a point of $M$ forces $N \ge \ell$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)).

\emph{Conclusion.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} and Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}, applied to $G \circ F$ on $\mathbb{R}^N = \mathbb{R}^{(N-\ell)+\ell}$, $M$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $N - \ell$, so (Definition~\ref{def:codimension}) $\operatorname{codim} M = N - (N - \ell) = \ell = \operatorname{codim} S$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} applied to $M = (G\circ F)^{-1}(0)$, then the chain rule, then the definition of the kernel, then Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} for $S$,
\[
T^{\geo}_pM = \ker (G\circ F)'(p) = \ker\big(G'(q)F'(p)\big) = \{v \mid G'(q)\big(F'(p)v\big) = 0\} = \{v \mid F'(p)v \in \ker G'(q)\} = F'(p)^{-1}(T^{\geo}_qS). \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Surjectivity Step as an Image Computation]\label{rem:transverse-image-computation}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the route of the official solution of Assignment~2, Problem~5.)} For a linear map $B$ and a subspace $W$ of its domain, $B(W + \ker B) = B(W)$: an element of the left side is $B(w + t) = Bw + Bt = Bw$ with $w \in W$ and $t \in \ker B$, and $W \subseteq W + \ker B$ gives the other inclusion. Take $B = G'(q)$ and $W = \operatorname{im} F'(p)$. Then $\ker G'(q) = T^{\geo}_qS$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}), transversality says $\operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS = \mathbb{R}^k$, and
\[
\operatorname{im}\,(G \circ F)'(p) = G'(q)\big(\operatorname{im} F'(p)\big) = G'(q)\big(\operatorname{im} F'(p) + \ker G'(q)\big) = G'(q)\big(\mathbb{R}^k\big) = \mathbb{R}^\ell ,
\]
by the chain rule, the identity, transversality, and surjectivity of $G'(q)$ ($0$ is a regular value of $G$ and $q \in G^{-1}(0)$). This is the lifting step of the proof in one line; it is used again in the second proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}.
\end{rembox}

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} Lee's Theorem~6.30 states this for a smooth map transverse to an \emph{embedded submanifold} $S \subseteq M$, after the theory of submanifolds (Chapter~5). The course's version, for level sets in Euclidean space, needs only the regular value theorem. It is the case where $S$ is cut out by a single global defining map $G$, and the proof --- pull $G$ back along $F$ --- is the one Lee uses locally.

\begin{propbox}[Transversality Is the Regular Value Condition]\thmlabel{prop:transverse-iff}
For $p \in F^{-1}(S)$ with $q = F(p)$,
\[
\operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS = \mathbb{R}^k \iff (G \circ F)'(p) \text{ is surjective.}
\]
Consequently $F \pitchfork S$ if and only if $0$ is a regular value of $G \circ F$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, $T^{\geo}_qS = \ker G'(q)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}) and $(G \circ F)'(p) = G'(q)F'(p)$ (chain rule).

($\Rightarrow$) is the middle step of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}, written out here at the single point $p$. Suppose $\operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS = \mathbb{R}^k$ and let $w \in \mathbb{R}^\ell$. Since $q \in S$ and $0$ is a regular value of $G$, $G'(q)$ is surjective, so $w = G'(q)u$ for some $u \in \mathbb{R}^k$. By the hypothesis, $u = F'(p)v + t$ with $v \in \mathbb{R}^N$ and $t \in \ker G'(q)$, and then
\[
w = G'(q)u = G'(q)F'(p)v + G'(q)t = G'(q)F'(p)v = (G\circ F)'(p)\,v ,
\]
so $(G \circ F)'(p)$ is surjective.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $G'(q)F'(p)$ is surjective and let $u \in \mathbb{R}^k$. Then $G'(q)u = G'(q)F'(p)v$ for some $v \in \mathbb{R}^N$, so by linearity $G'(q)\big(u - F'(p)v\big) = 0$, i.e.\ $u - F'(p)v \in \ker G'(q) = T^{\geo}_qS$, and
\[
u = F'(p)v + \big(u - F'(p)v\big) \in \operatorname{im} F'(p) + T^{\geo}_qS.
\]

\emph{Consequently.} $F \pitchfork S$ means the left condition holds at every $p \in F^{-1}(S)$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse}); by the equivalence just proved, this says $(G\circ F)'(p)$ is surjective at every $p \in F^{-1}(S)$. Since $F^{-1}(S) = (G \circ F)^{-1}(0)$ (first step of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}), that is exactly the statement that $0$ is a regular value of $G \circ F$ (Definitions~\ref{def:regular-value} and~\ref{def:regular-point}).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[An Intrinsic Statement with a Chosen Proof]\label{rem:intrinsic-statement-chosen-proof}
Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-iff} is the precise content of the parenthetical. Transversality is not merely a sufficient condition: it \emph{is} the regular value condition for $G \circ F$, rewritten so that $G$ disappears. The hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} and both of its conclusions --- that $M$ is a manifold, and the formula for $T^{\geo}_pM$ --- involve only $F$ and $S$; only the proof picks a defining function $G$. This is the same pattern as for charts: a statement that does not depend on a choice, proved by making one. Two things remain for later. The smooth structure on $M$ is built through $G$, and its independence of $G$ is a statement about submanifolds. And $S$ need only be cut out by some $G$ \emph{near each point}, which will turn out to hold for every embedded submanifold, so the theorem localizes.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[The Regular Value Theorem as a Special Case]\thmlabel{cor:rvt-transverse}
Let $c \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and $S = \{c\}$. Then $F \pitchfork \{c\}$ if and only if $c$ is a regular value of $F$, and in that case Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} returns Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} together with $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
To apply the theorem we present $\{c\}$ as a regular level set. $\{c\} = G^{-1}(0)$ for $G(y) = y - c$, $G : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k$, since $y - c = 0 \iff y = c$. Its Jacobian is the identity, $G'(y) = I$ for every $y$, which is surjective, so $0$ is a regular value of $G$ with $\ell = k$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}, $T^{\geo}_c\{c\} = \ker G'(c) = \ker I = 0$.

\emph{Transversality is the regular value condition.} With $T^{\geo}_{F(p)}S = 0$, the condition of Definition~\ref{def:transverse} at $p \in F^{-1}(c)$ reads
\[
\operatorname{im} F'(p) + 0 = \operatorname{im} F'(p) = \mathbb{R}^k ,
\]
i.e.\ $F'(p)$ is surjective. Transversality then reads $\operatorname{im} F'(p) = \mathbb{R}^k$ at every $p \in F^{-1}(c)$ --- the definition of a regular value (Definitions~\ref{def:regular-value} and~\ref{def:regular-point}).

\emph{The conclusions.} With $\ell = k$, Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} gives that $M = F^{-1}(c)$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $\dim M = N - k$ --- the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} with $N = n + k$ --- and
\[
T^{\geo}_pM = F'(p)^{-1}\big(T^{\geo}_c\{c\}\big) = F'(p)^{-1}(0) = \ker F'(p) .
\]
This is the description of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} for the regular level set $F^{-1}(c)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Transverse Intersection]\deflabel{def:transverse-intersection}
Regular level sets $S_1, S_2 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ \textbf{intersect transversally} if
\[
T^{\geo}_qS_1 + T^{\geo}_qS_2 = \mathbb{R}^k \qquad\text{for every } q \in S_1 \cap S_2 ,
\]
a condition that holds vacuously when $S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset$.
\leeref{Theorem 6.30(b)}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Transverse Intersections]\thmlabel{prop:transverse-intersection}
Let $G_i : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{\ell_i}$, $i = 1,2$, be smooth with $0$ a regular value, and $S_i = G_i^{-1}(0)$. For $q \in S_1 \cap S_2$,
\[
T^{\geo}_qS_1 + T^{\geo}_qS_2 = \mathbb{R}^k \iff (G_1, G_2)'(q) : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{\ell_1 + \ell_2} \text{ is surjective.}
\]
If $S_1$ and $S_2$ intersect transversally (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-intersection}), then $S_1 \cap S_2$ is a smooth manifold with
\[
\operatorname{codim}(S_1 \cap S_2) = \operatorname{codim} S_1 + \operatorname{codim} S_2, \qquad T^{\geo}_q(S_1 \cap S_2) = T^{\geo}_qS_1 \cap T^{\geo}_qS_2 .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 6.30(b)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Write $T_i = T^{\geo}_qS_i = \ker G_i'(q)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}). Since $q \in S_i$ and $0$ is a regular value of $G_i$, $G_i'(q)$ is surjective, so by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) $T_i$ has dimension $k - \ell_i$. We show that both sides of the equivalence are the same condition on $\dim(T_1 \cap T_2)$.

\emph{The right side.} The rows of the Jacobian of $(G_1, G_2)$ are the gradients of the components (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}): first those of $G_1$, then those of $G_2$. So the Jacobian is the stacked matrix $(G_1,G_2)'(q) = \begin{pmatrix} G_1'(q) \\ G_2'(q)\end{pmatrix}$, and $(G_1,G_2)'(q)v = \big(G_1'(q)v,\ G_2'(q)v\big)$. This is $0$ iff $G_1'(q)v = 0$ and $G_2'(q)v = 0$, so the kernel is $T_1 \cap T_2$. By rank--nullity,
\[
\dim \operatorname{im}\,(G_1,G_2)'(q) = k - \dim(T_1 \cap T_2) ,
\]
and the image is all of $\mathbb{R}^{\ell_1+\ell_2}$ iff its dimension is $\ell_1 + \ell_2$. So $(G_1,G_2)'(q)$ is surjective iff $\dim(T_1 \cap T_2) = k - \ell_1 - \ell_2$.

\emph{The left side.} On the other hand, by the dimension formula for a sum of two subspaces,
\[
\dim(T_1 + T_2) = \dim T_1 + \dim T_2 - \dim(T_1 \cap T_2) = (k - \ell_1) + (k - \ell_2) - \dim(T_1 \cap T_2),
\]
and the subspace $T_1 + T_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^k$ is all of $\mathbb{R}^k$ iff its dimension is $k$, which happens iff $\dim(T_1 \cap T_2) = k - \ell_1 - \ell_2$. The two conditions coincide.

\emph{The transverse intersection.} A point $q$ lies in $S_1 \cap S_2$ iff $G_1(q) = 0$ and $G_2(q) = 0$, iff $(G_1,G_2)(q) = 0$; so $S_1 \cap S_2 = (G_1,G_2)^{-1}(0)$. When the conditions hold throughout $S_1 \cap S_2$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-intersection}), the equivalence shows that $(G_1,G_2)'(q)$ is surjective at every point of this level set, i.e.\ the point $0$ is a regular value of $(G_1, G_2)$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}). Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value} with Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} then makes $S_1 \cap S_2$ a smooth manifold of dimension $k - (\ell_1 + \ell_2)$, so by Definition~\ref{def:codimension}
\[
\operatorname{codim}(S_1 \cap S_2) = k - \big(k - \ell_1 - \ell_2\big) = \ell_1 + \ell_2 = \operatorname{codim} S_1 + \operatorname{codim} S_2 ,
\]
using $\operatorname{codim} S_i = k - (k - \ell_i) = \ell_i$. And Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} gives the geometric tangent space $T^{\geo}_q(S_1 \cap S_2) = \ker(G_1,G_2)'(q) = T_1 \cap T_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[The Sphere and the Plane Re-read]\exlabel{ex:sphere-plane-transverse}
The figure in \S\ref{sub:regular-values} was a transversality picture. Let $S_1 = S^2$ and $S_2 = \{z = c\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, so $T^{\geo}_qS_1 = q^\perp$ and $T^{\geo}_qS_2 = e_3^\perp$, the horizontal plane. Two planes through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$ sum to $\mathbb{R}^3$ iff they are distinct, so the intersection is transverse at $q$ iff $q^\perp \neq e_3^\perp$, i.e.\ iff $q \neq \pm e_3$ --- iff the two normals $q$ and $e_3$ are independent, which is what the figure's caption said in the language of gradients. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} In the form of Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-intersection}, cut out $S_1$ by $G_1(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1$ and $S_2$ by $G_2(x,y,z) = z - c$; at $q = (x,y,z)$ the stacked $2 \times 3$ Jacobian is
\[
(G_1, G_2)'(q) = \begin{pmatrix} G_1'(q) \\ G_2'(q) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2x & 2y & 2z \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},
\]
whose $2 \times 2$ minors are $2x$, $2y$ (columns $1,3$ and $2,3$) and $0$ (columns $1,2$); so it has rank $2$ iff $(x,y) \neq (0,0)$, which on $S^2$ means $q \neq \pm e_3$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $|c| < 1$: every point of $S_1 \cap S_2$ has $x^2 + y^2 = 1 - c^2 > 0$, so $q \neq \pm e_3$ and the intersection is transverse. Codimensions add, $1 + 1 = 2$, and $S_1 \cap S_2$ is a curve: the circle of radius $\sqrt{1-c^2}$.
    \item $c = \pm 1$: $S_1 \cap S_2 = \{\pm e_3\}$, where $T^{\geo}_qS_1 = T^{\geo}_qS_2$. Not transverse, and the intersection is a point rather than the predicted curve.
    \item $|c| > 1$: the intersection is empty, and transversality holds vacuously.
\end{itemize}
\end{exbox}

The sphere through the course: a topological manifold with hemisphere charts in Section~\ref{sec:ex-spheres}; the homogeneous space $\SO(3)/\SO(2)$ in Example~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}; the Riemann sphere $\mathbb{CP}^1$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:cp1-sphere}; its geometric tangent spaces in Example~\ref{ex:tangent-sphere} and its transverse intersection with a plane in Example~\ref{ex:sphere-plane-transverse}; the double cover $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ and the Hopf fibration $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$ in Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf}; and $S^3 = \mathrm{SU}(2)$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-su2}.


\begin{exbox}[Two Ways Transversality Can Fail]\exlabel{ex:transverse-failures}
Let $S$ be the $x$-axis in $\mathbb{R}^2$, cut out by $G(x,y) = y$, so $T^{\geo}_qS$ is the $x$-axis at every $q \in S$, and $\ell = 1$. For $F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ the theorem predicts $\dim F^{-1}(S) = 1 - 1 = 0$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] $F(t) = (t, 0)$. Then $F^{-1}(S) = \mathbb{R}$, of dimension $1$: the \emph{dimension} is wrong. Here $\operatorname{im} F'(t)$ is the $x$-axis, so $\operatorname{im} F'(t) + T S$ is the $x$-axis, not $\mathbb{R}^2$.
    \item[(b)] $F(t) = (t, t^2)$. Then $F^{-1}(S) = \{0\}$, which has the predicted dimension $0$; but $F'(0) = (1,0)$ lies in $T^{\geo}_0S$, so $F'(0)^{-1}(T^{\geo}_0S) = \mathbb{R}$, while the geometric tangent space of a point is $0$: the \emph{tangent formula} is wrong. Correspondingly $(G \circ F)(t) = t^2$ has $(G\circ F)'(0) = 0$, as Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-iff} predicts. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} As a product of Jacobians, with the $1 \times 2$ Jacobian $G'(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ of $G(x,y) = y$ and the $2 \times 1$ Jacobian $F'(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2t \end{pmatrix}$,
\[
(G \circ F)'(0) = G'(F(0))\,F'(0) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 0 .
\]
    \item[(c)] $F(t) = (t, t^2 - \varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Now $F^{-1}(S) = \{\pm\sqrt\varepsilon\}$, and at these points $F'(t) = (1, 2t)$ has nonzero second component, so $\operatorname{im} F'(t) + TS = \mathbb{R}^2$: transverse, two points, and every conclusion of the theorem holds.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:tangent-8}
Transversality protects the dimension and the tangent formula \emph{independently}: (a) loses the first, (b) keeps the first and loses the second. And (c) shows what happens to the tangency of (b) under an arbitrarily small perturbation: it disappears, replaced by two transverse crossings (for $\varepsilon > 0$) or by no intersection at all (for $\varepsilon < 0$). The same happens to the tangent plane of Example~\ref{ex:sphere-plane-transverse} when it is moved slightly up or down.
\end{rembox}

\begin{rembox}[Looking Ahead: Transversality Is Generic]\label{rem:looking-ahead-transversality-generic}
Two points of the remark above will be taken up once abstract manifolds and submanifolds are in place. First, the definition makes sense verbatim for a smooth map $F : X \to Y$ between abstract manifolds and a submanifold $S \subseteq Y$, with \emph{abstract} tangent spaces and the differential of \S\ref{sub:pushforward} in place of $T^{\geo}$ and the Jacobian:
\[
dF_p(T_pX) + T_{F(p)}S = T_{F(p)}Y \qquad \text{for all } p \in F^{-1}(S),
\]
and Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage} becomes the statement that \emph{the preimage of a submanifold under a transverse map is a submanifold of the same codimension}. Second, as Example~\ref{ex:transverse-failures}(c) suggests, transversality is the \emph{typical} situation: any smooth map can be made transverse to a given submanifold by an arbitrarily small perturbation, and tangencies are non-generic accidents. This is the transversality theorem of Thom, and it is the entry point to intersection theory (Guillemin--Pollack, Ch.~2). Neither is part of the course yet.
\end{rembox}

\begin{rembox}[What Is Still Missing]\label{rem:what-still-missing}
Everything above presupposes an ambient $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$: Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent} of the geometric tangent space $T^{\geo}_pM$ uses its vector space structure to differentiate $\gamma$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} uses the Jacobian of the defining map $F$. For an abstract smooth manifold neither is available --- ``if you have a sphere you can think of the tangent plane, but that is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$. If you do not have $\mathbb{R}^3$, then what do you do? You do not have room to put your vectors.'' The next sections build the \emph{abstract} tangent space $T_pM$ from the charts alone.
\end{rembox}

\section{Germs}\label{sub:germs}\label{sec:abstract-tangent}

\roadmark{Stage: abstract}{Germs of smooth functions at a point --- the objects that derivations act on, available on every manifold, including those built by quotients. The motivation from geometric tangent vectors closes \ref{sec:tangent}.}

Point (1) of Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-properties}, at the end of \ref{sec:tangent}, is made official here: the objects a derivation eats are not functions but germs.

\begin{defbox}[Agreement Near a Point]\deflabel{def:germ-relation}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $p \in M$. Consider pairs $(f, U)$ with $U \subseteq M$ open, $p \in U$, and $f : U \to \mathbb{R}$ smooth. Two such pairs \textbf{agree near $p$}, written $(f,U) \sim (g,V)$, if
\[
\text{there is an open } W \text{ with } p \in W \subseteq U \cap V \text{ and } f|_W = g|_W .
\]
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Agreement Near a Point Is an Equivalence Relation]\thmlabel{prop:germ-equivalence}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.
    \item Finitely many pairs in one equivalence class agree on a common open neighbourhood of $p$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
(1) Three properties of $\sim$ must be checked against Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation}.

\emph{Reflexive:} take $W = U$. It is open, contains $p$, lies in $U \cap U = U$, and $f|_U = f|_U$; so $(f,U) \sim (f,U)$.

\emph{Symmetric:} the condition is symmetric in the two pairs. Explicitly, if $W$ is open with $p \in W \subseteq U \cap V$ and $f|_W = g|_W$, then the same $W$ satisfies $p \in W \subseteq V \cap U$ and $g|_W = f|_W$; so $(f,U) \sim (g,V)$ implies $(g,V) \sim (f,U)$.

\emph{Transitive:} let $(f,U) \sim (g,V)$ and $(g,V) \sim (h,Z)$. So $f = g$ on an open $W_1 \ni p$ with $W_1 \subseteq U \cap V$, and $g = h$ on an open $W_2 \ni p$ with $W_2 \subseteq V \cap Z$. Then $f = h$ on $W_1 \cap W_2$: for $x \in W_1 \cap W_2$,
\[
f(x) = g(x) = h(x) .
\]
The set $W_1 \cap W_2$ is open (an intersection of two open sets), contains $p$, and lies in both domains, $W_1 \cap W_2 \subseteq U \cap Z$. So $(f,U) \sim (h,Z)$.

(2) If $(f_1,U_1), \ldots, (f_k,U_k)$ are equivalent, then for each $i$ there is an open $W_i \ni p$ with $W_i \subseteq U_1 \cap U_i$, on which $f_1 = f_i$ (since $(f_1,U_1) \sim (f_i,U_i)$). On $W = W_2 \cap \cdots \cap W_k$ (take $W = U_1$ if $k = 1$), which is open and contains $p$, all the $f_i$ equal $f_1$. Indeed $W \subseteq U_1 \cap U_2 \cap \cdots \cap U_k$, so every $f_i$ is defined on $W$, and for $x \in W$ and each $i$, $x \in W_i$ gives $f_i(x) = f_1(x)$. Both parts use only that a \emph{finite} intersection of open sets is open.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Germs of Smooth Functions]\deflabel{def:germ}
An equivalence class $[f]$ of the relation $\sim$ of Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation} is a \textbf{(}$C^\infty$\textbf{) germ at $p$}, and each pair $(f,U)$ in it is a \textbf{representative} of the germ. The set of all germs at $p$ is denoted $C_p^\infty(M)$.
\leeref{no counterpart; the course's germ-based route (Lee uses $C^\infty(M)$; see Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-global})}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.05]
\draw[violet!70!black, thick] (0,0) ellipse (1.55 and 0.95);
\draw[teal!60!black, thick] (2.0,0) ellipse (1.55 and 0.95);
\node[violet!70!black,font=\footnotesize] at (-1.12,0) {$U$};
\node[teal!60!black,font=\footnotesize] at (3.12,0) {$V$};
\draw[orange!85!black, thick] (1.0,0.06) circle (0.42);
\draw[gray!55,thin] (1.0,-0.36) -- (1.0,-1.12);
\node[orange!85!black,font=\footnotesize,anchor=north] at (1.0,-1.14) {$W$};
\fill (1.0,0.06) circle (1.7pt);
\node[font=\footnotesize,anchor=south west] at (1.06,0.10) {$p$};
\node[font=\footnotesize,anchor=west] at (3.95,0.34) {$f : U \to \mathbb{R}$, \quad $g : V \to \mathbb{R}$};
\node[font=\footnotesize,anchor=west] at (3.95,-0.04) {$f|_W = g|_W$};
\node[font=\footnotesize,anchor=west] at (3.95,-0.42) {$\Longrightarrow\ [f] = [g]$ in $C_p^\infty(M)$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\begin{exbox}[No Neighbourhood Serves a Whole Germ]\exlabel{ex:germ-no-common-nbhd}
Part (2) of Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-equivalence} fails for infinitely many representatives. Work at $p = 0 \in \mathbb{R}$. Let $h(s) = e^{-1/s}$ for $s > 0$ and $h(s) = 0$ for $s \le 0$, the smooth flat function (see Example~\ref{ex:taylor-germs} below), and put
\[
f_n(x) = h\big(x^2 - 1/n^2\big), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
\]
Each $f_n$ is smooth on all of $\mathbb{R}$ and vanishes exactly on $[-1/n, 1/n]$, so $(f_n, \mathbb{R}) \sim (0, \mathbb{R})$: every $f_n$ represents the zero germ. Yet the set on which all of them agree with $0$ is $\bigcap_n [-1/n, 1/n] = \{0\}$, which contains no open neighbourhood of $0$. The same happens, even more simply, with the representatives $\big(0, (-1/n, 1/n)\big)$: no open set around $0$ lies in all of their domains.
\end{exbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:abstract-tangent-2}
Nothing in the theory needs a common neighbourhood for a whole class. Every construction on germs --- sums, products and evaluation (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}), derivations, pullbacks --- handles finitely many representatives at a time, and part (2) supplies the common neighbourhood for those. The obstruction in the example is exactly that an \emph{infinite} intersection of open sets need not be open. This is also the precise sense in which a germ is not a function on any particular neighbourhood of $p$: its representatives can be shrunk at will, but there is no smallest domain to shrink them to.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[$C_p^\infty(M)$ Is an $\mathbb{R}$-Algebra]\thmlabel{prop:germ-algebra}
The operations
\[
[f] + [g] = [f|_W + g|_W], \qquad [f]\,[g] = [f|_W \cdot g|_W], \qquad \lambda[f] = [\lambda f],
\]
where $W$ is any open set with $p \in W \subseteq U \cap V$, are well defined and make $C_p^\infty(M)$ a commutative ring with unit $[1]$ and an $\mathbb{R}$-vector space --- that is, a commutative $\mathbb{R}$-algebra. Moreover the evaluation map
\[
[f] \longmapsto [f](p) := f(p)
\]
is a well-defined $\mathbb{R}$-algebra homomorphism $C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$.
\leeref{no counterpart; the course's germ-based route}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~8 sketched the operations --- ``taking representatives \ldots\ and shrinking to a common domain'' --- and skipped the checks as ``tedious''; they are filled in here.)} Let $(f,U)$ and $(g,V)$ be representatives of $[f]$ and $[g]$. Four things must be checked: the operations produce germs, they do not depend on the choices, they satisfy the algebra axioms, and evaluation is a well-defined homomorphism.

\emph{Existence of $W$ and smoothness.} $U \cap V$ is open and contains $p$, so $W = U \cap V$ will do; $f|_W + g|_W$ and $f|_W\, g|_W$ are smooth on $W$, so they define germs. Likewise $\lambda f$ is smooth on $U$.

\emph{Independence of representatives.} Suppose $(f,U) \sim (f', U')$ and $(g,V) \sim (g',V')$, say $f = f'$ on $W_1 \ni p$ and $g = g'$ on $W_2 \ni p$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation}). On the open set $W_1 \cap W_2 \ni p$ the four functions satisfy $f + g = f' + g'$ and $fg = f'g'$ pointwise: for $x \in W_1 \cap W_2$,
\[
f(x) + g(x) = f'(x) + g'(x), \qquad f(x)\,g(x) = f'(x)\,g'(x) ,
\]
so the resulting germs agree. To be precise about the auxiliary sets: if the sums are formed on $W \subseteq U \cap V$ and $W' \subseteq U' \cap V'$, then $f|_W + g|_W$ and $f'|_{W'} + g'|_{W'}$ agree on $W \cap W' \cap W_1 \cap W_2$, which is open, contains $p$, and lies in both domains; the same for products. For scalars, $f = f'$ on $W_1$ gives $\lambda f = \lambda f'$ on $W_1$, so $[\lambda f] = [\lambda f']$. Independence of the auxiliary $W$ is the same argument with $f = f'$, $g = g'$ (so $W_1 = U$, $W_2 = V$): two choices $W, W'$ give functions that agree on $W \cap W'$.

\emph{Algebra axioms.} Each is an identity between germs that holds for representatives on a common domain, hence holds after passing to classes. Explicitly: given finitely many germs $[f], [g], [h]$, choose representatives and restrict them to the common open set $W$, the intersection of their domains, which contains $p$; restricting does not change a germ, $(f,U) \sim (f|_W, W)$. By the previous step every operation may be computed on $W$, where it is the pointwise operation on functions. For example, distributivity reads
\[
\big([f] + [g]\big)[h] = [f + g]\,[h] = \big[(f+g)h\big] = [fh + gh] = [fh] + [gh] = [f][h] + [g][h],
\]
the middle equality because $(f + g)h = fh + gh$ pointwise on $W$, by distributivity in $\mathbb{R}$. In the same way, each of the remaining axioms reduces to the corresponding identity of real numbers at each point of $W$: associativity and commutativity of $+$ and of $\cdot$; the zero $[0]$, with $[f] + [0] = [f + 0] = [f]$; the negative $-[f] = [-f]$; the unit $[1]$, with $[1][f] = [1 \cdot f] = [f]$; the vector space axioms $\lambda([f] + [g]) = \lambda[f] + \lambda[g]$, $(\lambda + \mu)[f] = \lambda[f] + \mu[f]$, $(\lambda\mu)[f] = \lambda(\mu[f])$, $1[f] = [f]$; and the compatibility $\lambda([f][g]) = (\lambda[f])[g] = [f](\lambda[g])$.

\emph{Evaluation.} If $(f,U) \sim (g,V)$ then $f = g$ near $p$, in particular $f(p) = g(p)$, since $p$ lies in the set $W$ on which they agree; so $[f](p)$ is well defined. And evaluation of functions is compatible with sums and products: with representatives on a common $W \ni p$,
\[
\big([f] + [g]\big)(p) = (f + g)(p) = f(p) + g(p), \qquad \big([f][g]\big)(p) = (fg)(p) = f(p)\,g(p),
\]
\[
(\lambda[f])(p) = \lambda f(p), \qquad [1](p) = 1 ,
\]
so evaluation is an $\mathbb{R}$-algebra homomorphism $C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Evaluation of a Germ]\deflabel{def:germ-evaluation}
The \textbf{value} of a germ $[f] \in C_p^\infty(M)$ at $p$ is $[f](p) := f(p)$, independent of the representative by Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}. The map $C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$, $[f] \mapsto [f](p)$, is \textbf{evaluation} at $p$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}[How to Think About a Germ]\label{rem:how-think-about-germ}
Uribe: ``when I think of a germ, I think of a representative --- a smooth function defined in a neighbourhood --- but I know that it is a germ, which means I can shrink its domain arbitrarily, as long as I shrink it to a neighbourhood of $p$.'' In practice one works with representatives and checks at the end that the answer is unchanged by shrinking. The formal content of the definition is exactly that shrinking is free.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[Germs Versus Taylor Series]\exlabel{ex:taylor-germs}
Take $M = \mathbb{R}^n$ and $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$. All partial derivatives of a function at $x_0$ depend only on its germ, so the Taylor series construction descends to a map into the ring of formal power series,
\[
\mathcal{T} : C_{x_0}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}[[x^1, \ldots, x^n]], \qquad
\mathcal{T}[f] = \sum_{\alpha} \frac{1}{\alpha!}\, \frac{\partial^{|\alpha|} f}{\partial x^\alpha}(x_0)\, (x - x_0)^\alpha ,
\]
an $\mathbb{R}$-algebra homomorphism. It is \emph{surjective} but \emph{not injective}.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}[Justification]
Four claims: $\mathcal{T}$ is well defined on germs, it is an $\mathbb{R}$-algebra homomorphism, it is surjective, and it is not injective. Write $\alpha! = \alpha_1! \cdots \alpha_n!$ and $\partial^\alpha$ for the partial derivative of multi-index $\alpha$.

\emph{Well defined.} If $f$ and $g$ represent the same germ, they agree on an open $W \ni x_0$. A partial derivative at a point of an open set is a limit of difference quotients that, for small increments, only involve values on that open set; so the first partial derivatives of $f$ and $g$ agree on $W$, and, applying the same to them, by induction on the order all partial derivatives agree on $W$, in particular at $x_0$. Hence the coefficients $\frac{1}{\alpha!}\partial^\alpha f(x_0)$ of $\mathcal{T}[f]$ depend only on $[f]$.

\emph{Homomorphism.} Each $\partial^\alpha$ is linear, so $\mathcal{T}[af + bg] = a\,\mathcal{T}[f] + b\,\mathcal{T}[g]$; and $\mathcal{T}[1] = 1$, since all derivatives of positive order of a constant vanish. For products, the multi-index Leibniz rule (the product rule $\partial_i(fg) = (\partial_i f)g + f\,\partial_i g$ applied repeatedly, by induction on $|\alpha|$) gives
\[
\partial^\alpha(fg) = \sum_{\beta \le \alpha} \frac{\alpha!}{\beta!\,(\alpha - \beta)!}\, \partial^\beta f\; \partial^{\alpha-\beta} g .
\]
So the coefficient of $(x - x_0)^\alpha$ in $\mathcal{T}[fg]$ is
\[
\frac{1}{\alpha!}\,\partial^\alpha(fg)(x_0) = \sum_{\beta + \gamma = \alpha} \frac{\partial^\beta f(x_0)}{\beta!}\cdot\frac{\partial^\gamma g(x_0)}{\gamma!} ,
\]
which is the coefficient of $(x - x_0)^\alpha$ in the product of formal power series $\mathcal{T}[f]\,\mathcal{T}[g]$, since $(x - x_0)^\beta (x - x_0)^\gamma = (x - x_0)^{\beta+\gamma}$. Hence $\mathcal{T}\big([f][g]\big) = \mathcal{T}[fg] = \mathcal{T}[f]\,\mathcal{T}[g]$.

\emph{Surjective.} Surjectivity is \textbf{Borel's theorem}: every formal power series is the Taylor series at $x_0$ of some smooth function. It is cited, not proved --- Uribe: ``that's not so easy to show, but it's true.''

\emph{Not injective.} Failure of injectivity is elementary. Uribe: ``You can have totally flat functions that are not zero''; the example is filled in. The function
\[
f(x) = \begin{cases} e^{-1/|x-x_0|^2}, & x \neq x_0,\\ 0, & x = x_0,\end{cases}
\]
is smooth with all partial derivatives vanishing at $x_0$ (a standard computation, written out in the next two paragraphs), so $\mathcal{T}[f] = 0$, every coefficient being a partial derivative at $x_0$. On the other hand $[f] \neq 0$: $f(x) > 0$ for every $x \neq x_0$, and every open $W \ni x_0$ contains points $x \neq x_0$, so $f$ is not $0$ on any neighbourhood of $x_0$, i.e.\ $(f, \mathbb{R}^n) \not\sim (0, \mathbb{R}^n)$.

\emph{The one-variable function.} Let $h(s) = e^{-1/s}$ for $s > 0$ and $h(s) = 0$ for $s \le 0$. We show by induction on $j$: $h$ is $j$ times differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$, with $h^{(j)}(s) = 0$ for $s \le 0$ and $h^{(j)}(s) = P_j(1/s)\,e^{-1/s}$ for $s > 0$, where $P_j$ is a polynomial. For $j = 0$ take $P_0 = 1$. Assume the claim for $j$. For $s < 0$, $h^{(j)}$ vanishes on the open set $(-\infty, 0)$, so $h^{(j+1)}(s) = 0$. For $s > 0$, by the chain and product rules,
\[
\frac{d}{ds}\Big(P_j(1/s)\,e^{-1/s}\Big) = -\frac{1}{s^2}P_j'(1/s)\,e^{-1/s} + \frac{1}{s^2}P_j(1/s)\,e^{-1/s} = P_{j+1}(1/s)\,e^{-1/s}, \qquad P_{j+1}(y) = y^2\big(P_j(y) - P_j'(y)\big).
\]
At $s = 0$: the difference quotient $\big(h^{(j)}(s) - h^{(j)}(0)\big)/s$ is $0$ for $s < 0$, and for $s > 0$ it is
\[
\frac{P_j(1/s)\,e^{-1/s}}{s} = Q(1/s)\,e^{-1/s}, \qquad Q(y) = y\,P_j(y),
\]
which tends to $0$ as $s \to 0^+$, because $Q(y)e^{-y} \to 0$ as $y = 1/s \to \infty$ (the exponential grows faster than any polynomial). So $h^{(j+1)}(0) = 0$, completing the induction. Hence $h$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}$ and $h^{(j)}(0) = 0$ for every $j$.

\emph{Smoothness and flatness of $f$.} Put $q(x) = |x - x_0|^2 = \sum_i (x^i - x_0^i)^2$, a polynomial with $q(x_0) = 0$ and $q(x) > 0$ for $x \neq x_0$. Then $f = h \circ q$: for $x \neq x_0$, $h(q(x)) = e^{-1/|x-x_0|^2}$, and $h(q(x_0)) = h(0) = 0$. So $f$ is smooth, as a composite of smooth maps. By induction on $|\alpha|$, every partial derivative $\partial^\alpha f$ is a finite sum of terms $(h^{(j)} \circ q)\cdot P$ with $P$ a polynomial in $x$: this holds for $\alpha = 0$ ($f = (h \circ q)\cdot 1$), and by the chain and product rules
\[
\partial_i\big((h^{(j)} \circ q)\, P\big) = (h^{(j+1)} \circ q)\,(\partial_i q)\,P + (h^{(j)} \circ q)\,\partial_i P, \qquad \partial_i q = 2(x^i - x_0^i),
\]
again of that form. At $x_0$ every term contains a factor $h^{(j)}(q(x_0)) = h^{(j)}(0) = 0$, so $\partial^\alpha f(x_0) = 0$ for every $\alpha$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Flat Germ]\deflabel{def:flat-germ}
A germ $[f] \in C_{x_0}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is \textbf{flat} if all partial derivatives of $f$, of all orders, vanish at $x_0$; equivalently, $\mathcal{T}[f] = 0$. So the kernel of $\mathcal{T}$ consists exactly of the flat germs.
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:abstract-tangent-3}
The moral is that a germ carries strictly more information than its Taylor series --- ``one of the beauties of being in the $C^\infty$ category.'' This is the same phenomenon as the rigidity of $C^\omega$ noted after Definition~\ref{def:regularity-classes}: a real-analytic germ \emph{is} its Taylor series, which is why there are no analytic bump functions, whereas a $C^\infty$ germ has room to spare.
\end{rembox}

% SECTION: DERIVATIONS AND THE ABSTRACT TANGENT SPACE
% ============================================================================

\section{Derivations and the Abstract Tangent Space}\label{sec:derivations}\label{sub:derivations}

\roadmark{Stage: abstract}{The abstract tangent space $T_pM$ as the derivations at $p$, and the differential $F_{*p}$ that pushes them forward. The two notions of tangent space agree wherever both exist (Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}).}

\begin{rembox}[Two Faces of a Tangent Vector]\label{rem:two-faces-tangent-vector}
Lecture 9 opened with a framing that the rest of the course keeps returning to. A tangent vector has two faces --- ``like Janus.'' It is a \emph{velocity}, the $\gamma'(0)$ of a curve --- an element of the geometric tangent space $T^{\geo}_pM$, which is how \S\ref{sub:derivations-motivation} met it; and it is a \emph{derivation}, an operator that eats germs and returns numbers --- an element of the abstract tangent space $T_pM$, the formal definition below. Formally they are different objects, and the relation between them has to be proved (Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}). The same split will reappear for vector fields: as velocities attached to every point they \emph{generate dynamics}, and as operators they lead to the \emph{Lie derivative}.
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[Derivation at a Point]\deflabel{def:derivation}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $p \in M$. A \textbf{derivation at $p$} is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear map
\[
D : C_p^\infty(M) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]
satisfying the \textbf{Leibniz rule}
\[
D\big([f][g]\big) \;=\; f(p)\, D[g] \;+\; g(p)\, D[f] \qquad \text{for all } [f], [g] \in C_p^\infty(M),
\]
where $f(p) = [f](p)$ is the evaluation of Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Tangent Vectors}, on $C^\infty(M)$ rather than germs}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[The Abstract Tangent Space]\deflabel{def:abstract-tangent}
The \textbf{(abstract) tangent space} to $M$ at $p$ is
\[
T_pM \;=\; \{\, \text{all derivations at } p \,\},
\]
a real vector space under the pointwise operations $(D + D')[f] = D[f] + D'[f]$ and $(\lambda D)[f] = \lambda\, D[f]$. An element $D \in T_pM$ is a \textbf{tangent vector} at $p$. It is not an arrow in any ambient space but a function on germs, $D : C^\infty_p(M) \to \mathbb{R}$, so $D[f]$ is a real number for each germ $[f]$ at $p$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Tangent Vectors}, via $C^\infty(M)$ (see Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-global})}
\end{defbox}

\begin{proof}[Verification that $T_pM$ is a vector space]
What has to be shown. The set of \emph{all} maps $C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$ is a real vector space under the pointwise operations $(D + D')[f] = D[f] + D'[f]$ and $(\lambda D)[f] = \lambda\, D[f]$: each vector space axiom is an identity between values at a germ $[f]$, and it holds there because it holds in $\mathbb{R}$. $T_pM$ is a subset of this space, so it is a vector space under the same operations as soon as it contains the zero map and is closed under sums and scalar multiples, i.e.\ as soon as $D + D'$ and $\lambda D$ are again derivations whenever $D$ and $D'$ are (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}). $D + D'$ and $\lambda D$ are linear, being pointwise combinations of linear maps, and each satisfies the Leibniz rule because the rule is linear in $D$. In detail, fix germs $[f], [g] \in C_p^\infty(M)$ and numbers $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

\emph{Zero.} The zero map is linear, and it satisfies the Leibniz rule since $0 = f(p) \cdot 0 + g(p) \cdot 0$.

\emph{The sum is linear.} By the definition of $D + D'$, then the linearity of $D$ and of $D'$, then the definition of $D + D'$ again:
\[
(D+D')\big(a[f] + b[g]\big) = D\big(a[f] + b[g]\big) + D'\big(a[f] + b[g]\big) = a\,D[f] + b\,D[g] + a\,D'[f] + b\,D'[g] = a\,(D+D')[f] + b\,(D+D')[g] .
\]

\emph{The sum satisfies the Leibniz rule.} By the definition of $D + D'$, the Leibniz rules of $D$ and of $D'$ separately, regrouping the four terms, and the definition of $D + D'$ again:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(D+D')([f][g]) &= D([f][g]) + D'([f][g]) = f(p)D[g] + g(p)D[f] + f(p)D'[g] + g(p)D'[f] \\
&= f(p)\big(D[g] + D'[g]\big) + g(p)\big(D[f] + D'[f]\big) = f(p)(D+D')[g] + g(p)(D+D')[f].
\end{aligned}
\]

\emph{The scalar multiple.} By the definition of $\lambda D$ and the linearity, resp.\ the Leibniz rule, of $D$:
\[
(\lambda D)\big(a[f] + b[g]\big) = \lambda\big(a\,D[f] + b\,D[g]\big) = a\,(\lambda D)[f] + b\,(\lambda D)[g],
\]
\[
(\lambda D)([f][g]) = \lambda\big(f(p)D[g] + g(p)D[f]\big) = f(p)\,(\lambda D)[g] + g(p)\,(\lambda D)[f].
\]
So $T_pM$ is a linear subspace of the space of all maps $C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$, and the vector space axioms hold in it pointwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[The Ideal of Germs Vanishing at a Point]\deflabel{def:Ip}
The \textbf{ideal of germs vanishing at $p$} is
\[
I_p = \{\, [f] \in C_p^\infty(M) \mid f(p) = 0 \,\},
\]
the kernel of evaluation at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-evaluation}).
\leeref{Problem 11-4, where $I_p \subseteq C^\infty(M)$ consists of global functions}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[The Square of $I_p$]\deflabel{def:Ip-square}
The \textbf{square} $I_p^2$ of $I_p$ (Definition~\ref{def:Ip}) is the set of all finite sums $\sum_k [u_k][w_k]$ of products of two elements of $I_p$, the empty sum $0$ included.
\leeref{Problem 11-4, where $I_p \subseteq C^\infty(M)$ consists of global functions}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[$I_p$ and $I_p^2$]\thmlabel{lem:Ip-subspaces}
$I_p$ is an ideal of $C_p^\infty(M)$ and $I_p^2 \subseteq I_p$; both are linear subspaces.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
Three things are claimed: $I_p$ is a linear subspace and an ideal; $I_p^2$ is a linear subspace; and $I_p^2 \subseteq I_p$. Throughout, evaluation $[f] \mapsto f(p)$ is an algebra homomorphism $C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}, Definition~\ref{def:germ-evaluation}), so the value at $p$ of a sum, scalar multiple or product of germs is the sum, scalar multiple or product of the values.

\emph{$I_p$.} $I_p$ is the kernel of the algebra homomorphism of evaluation (Definition~\ref{def:Ip}), hence a linear subspace and an ideal. Explicitly: if $[f], [g] \in I_p$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, then $(a[f] + b[g])(p) = a\,f(p) + b\,g(p) = a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 0 = 0$, so $a[f] + b[g] \in I_p$; and $[g][f] \in I_p$ whenever $[f] \in I_p$ and $[g] \in C_p^\infty(M)$ is arbitrary, since $([g][f])(p) = g(p)f(p) = g(p) \cdot 0 = 0$.

\emph{$I_p^2$ is a subspace.} It contains $0$, the empty sum (Definition~\ref{def:Ip-square}). It is closed under sums by construction: the sum of two finite sums of products $[u][w]$ with $[u], [w] \in I_p$ is again such a finite sum. It is closed under scalars since $c\,[u][w] = [cu][w]$ (the algebra axioms of Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}) with $[cu] \in I_p$, because $(cu)(p) = c \cdot 0 = 0$; so
\[
c \sum_k [u_k][w_k] = \sum_k [cu_k][w_k] \in I_p^2 .
\]

\emph{$I_p^2 \subseteq I_p$.} Each product $[u][w]$ with $[u], [w] \in I_p$ lies in $I_p$, since $u(p)w(p) = 0 \cdot 0 = 0$; and $I_p$ is closed under finite sums, being a subspace. So every element $\sum_k [u_k][w_k]$ of $I_p^2$ lies in $I_p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[First Properties of Derivations]\thmlabel{lem:derivation-properties}
Let $D$ be a derivation at $p$, and $I_p$, $I_p^2$ as in Definitions~\ref{def:Ip} and~\ref{def:Ip-square}.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $D$ annihilates constants: if $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\underline{c}$ denotes the germ of the constant function $c$, then $D[\underline{c}] = 0$. Consequently $D[f] = D\big[f - \underline{f(p)}\big]$, so $D$ is determined by its values on $I_p$.
    \item $D$ annihilates products of vanishing germs: if $[f], [g] \in I_p$, then $D([f][g]) = 0$. Consequently $D$ vanishes on all of $I_p^2$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Lemmas 3.1 and 3.4}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
(1) The constant function $1$ satisfies $1 \cdot 1 = 1$, so its germ satisfies $[\underline 1] = [\underline 1][\underline 1]$ (products of germs are taken on representatives, Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}), and its value at $p$ is $1$. By the Leibniz rule (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}) with $[f] = [g] = [\underline 1]$,
\[
D[\underline 1] = D\big([\underline 1][\underline 1]\big) = 1 \cdot D[\underline 1] + 1 \cdot D[\underline 1] = 2\, D[\underline 1],
\]
whence, subtracting $D[\underline 1]$ from both sides, $D[\underline 1] = 0$. For general $c$, the constant germ is the scalar multiple $[\underline c] = c\,[\underline 1]$, and linearity gives $D[\underline c] = c\, D[\underline 1] = c \cdot 0 = 0$.

For the consequence, let $[f]$ be any germ. As germs, $[f] = \big[f - \underline{f(p)}\big] + \big[\underline{f(p)}\big]$, and $\big[f - \underline{f(p)}\big] \in I_p$, since its value at $p$ is $f(p) - f(p) = 0$. By linearity and the first part,
\[
D[f] = D\big[f - \underline{f(p)}\big] + D\big[\underline{f(p)}\big] = D\big[f - \underline{f(p)}\big] + 0 .
\]
So if two derivations agree on $I_p$, they agree on every germ: $D$ is determined by its values on $I_p$.

(2) Immediate from the Leibniz rule: if $[f], [g] \in I_p$ then $f(p) = g(p) = 0$, so $D([f][g]) = f(p)D[g] + g(p)D[f] = 0 \cdot D[g] + 0 \cdot D[f] = 0$. A general element of $I_p^2$ is a finite sum $\sum_k [u_k][w_k]$ of such products (Definition~\ref{def:Ip-square}), and $D$ is linear, so
\[
D\Big(\sum_k [u_k][w_k]\Big) = \sum_k D\big([u_k][w_k]\big) = \sum_k 0 = 0 .
\]
\end{proof}

Both parts were set as an exercise in Lecture 9, where Uribe noted that (2) is ``a very simple consequence of the product rule'' and is part of a problem on Assignment~3, which introduces the ideal $I_p$ under that name. In commutative algebra the same ideal is written $\mathfrak{m}_p$, the notation used in the remark at the end of \ref{sub:coordinate-derivations}.

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:abstract-tangent-4}
Uribe listed exactly these two as what must be shown before the basis theorem, and deferred them to the following lecture. They are the entire reason the Taylor--Hadamard expansion collapses: the constant term dies by (1), the quadratic remainder dies by (2), and only the linear term survives.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[Germ Derivations and Global Derivations]\thmlabel{prop:germ-global}
Lee defines $T_pM$ as the space of derivations of $C^\infty(M)$ at $p$: linear maps $v : C^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$ with $v(fg) = f(p)\,vg + g(p)\,vf$. For $D \in T_pM$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}, the formula $v_D(f) = D[f]$ defines such a derivation, and $D \mapsto v_D$ is a linear isomorphism between the two spaces.
\leeref{Ch.~3, with Propositions 2.25 and 3.8}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof, granting smooth bump functions]
Three things are to be shown: each $v_D$ is a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ at $p$; $D \mapsto v_D$ is linear; and it is bijective.

\emph{$v_D$ is a derivation, and $D \mapsto v_D$ is linear.} Taking germs, $f \mapsto [f]$ (the class of the pair $(f, M)$), is an algebra homomorphism $C^\infty(M) \to C_p^\infty(M)$ compatible with evaluation at $p$: by the definition of the germ operations (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}), with $W = M$, $[af + bg] = a[f] + b[g]$ and $[fg] = [f][g]$, and $[f](p) = f(p)$. Hence, for $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, by the linearity and the Leibniz rule of $D$ (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}),
\[
v_D(af + bg) = D\big(a[f] + b[g]\big) = a\,v_D(f) + b\,v_D(g), \qquad v_D(fg) = D\big([f][g]\big) = f(p)\,v_D(g) + g(p)\,v_D(f),
\]
so $v_D$ is a derivation in Lee's sense. And for $D, E \in T_pM$, by the pointwise operations of Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}, $v_{aD + bE}(f) = (aD + bE)[f] = a\,D[f] + b\,E[f] = a\,v_D(f) + b\,v_E(f)$ for every $f$, so $v_{aD + bE} = a\,v_D + b\,v_E$.

Both remaining steps use a \emph{bump function}: for an open $U \ni p$, a smooth $\psi : M \to [0,1]$ supported in $U$ with $\psi \equiv 1$ near $p$ (Lee, Proposition 2.25; these notes do not construct one).

\emph{Injective.} Every germ $[f]$, with $f$ defined on $U$, has the global representative $\psi f$, extended by zero. (It is smooth: on $U$ it is the product of smooth functions, on the open set $M \setminus \operatorname{supp}\psi$ it is $0$, and these two open sets cover $M$. It equals $f$ on the open set near $p$ where $\psi \equiv 1$, so $[\psi f] = [f]$.) So if $v_D = 0$ then $D[f] = D[\psi f] = v_D(\psi f) = 0$ for every germ, i.e.\ $D = 0$; a linear map with zero kernel is injective.

\emph{Surjective.} Given Lee's $v$, set $D[f] = v(\tilde f)$ for any global $\tilde f$ representing $[f]$; one exists by the previous paragraph. This is well defined because $v$ is local --- if $\tilde f = \tilde g$ near $p$ then $v\tilde f = v\tilde g$ (Lee, Proposition 3.8, whose proof uses a bump function) --- and two global representatives of the same germ agree near $p$. It is a derivation on germs: if $\tilde f$ and $\tilde g$ represent $[f]$ and $[g]$, then $a\tilde f + b\tilde g$ and $\tilde f \tilde g$ represent $a[f] + b[g]$ and $[f][g]$, so
\[
D\big(a[f] + b[g]\big) = v(a\tilde f + b\tilde g) = a\,v(\tilde f) + b\,v(\tilde g) = a\,D[f] + b\,D[g],
\]
\[
D\big([f][g]\big) = v(\tilde f\tilde g) = \tilde f(p)\, v(\tilde g) + \tilde g(p)\, v(\tilde f) = f(p)\, D[g] + g(p)\, D[f],
\]
using $\tilde f(p) = f(p)$ and $\tilde g(p) = g(p)$. Finally $v_D = v$: a global $f$ is itself a global representative of its germ, so $v_D(f) = D[f] = v(f)$.
\end{proof}

Both steps borrowed from Lee are now in these notes: bump functions are Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence} (existence stated, proof deferred in lecture), the global representative of a germ is Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}, and locality of derivations is Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-local} (Lecture~16).

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} This is where the course's algebraic route and Lee's part company. Lee works with global functions and pays for locality with bump functions: Proposition~3.8 shows a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ only sees a function near $p$, and Proposition~3.9 identifies $T_pU$ with $T_pM$. Germs build locality into the definition, so the course needs no bump functions at all --- Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local} is pure algebra. The proposition above is the bridge. Since the two spaces are isomorphic, every result about $T_pM$ in these notes transfers to Lee's, and conversely.


\subsection{Pushing Derivations Forward}\label{sub:pushforward}

\textit{Lecture 9. Derivations can be pushed forward along smooth maps. In lecture this appeared in the middle of the proof of the basis theorem, as a ``new derivation'' $\tilde D$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ built from one on $M$, and was defined properly only afterwards --- ``the order of my presentation is not ideal.'' Here it comes first, so the proof can cite it.}

Throughout, $F : M \to N$ is a smooth map of smooth manifolds and $p \in M$. The construction has two steps: functions are pulled back, and derivations, being linear functionals on functions, are pushed forward by duality.

\begin{defbox}[Pullback of Germs]\deflabel{def:germ-pullback}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map between smooth manifolds, and $p \in M$, so that $F(p)$ is a point of $N$. Let $[g] \in C^\infty_{F(p)}(N)$ be a germ \emph{at the point $F(p)$ of $N$}, with a representative $(g, V)$: $V \subseteq N$ is open with $F(p) \in V$, and $g : V \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth. Then $F^{-1}(V)$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$ in $M$, and $g \circ F : F^{-1}(V) \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), so $(g \circ F, F^{-1}(V))$ represents a germ at $p$ on $M$. The \textbf{pullback} of germs along $F$ at $p$ is the map
\[
F_p^* : C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \longrightarrow C^\infty_p(M), \qquad F_p^*[g] = [\,g \circ F\,],
\]
which takes a germ on $N$ at $F(p)$ to a germ on $M$ at $p$. It does not depend on the representative $(g, V)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-properties}).
\leeref{no counterpart; the course's germ-based route}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Properties of the Pullback]\thmlabel{prop:pullback-properties}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$. The map $F_p^* : C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \to C^\infty_p(M)$ is well defined, it is a homomorphism of $\mathbb{R}$-algebras, and it is compatible with evaluation: for every germ $[g] \in C^\infty_{F(p)}(N)$,
\[
\big(F_p^*[g]\big)(p) = g\big(F(p)\big).
\]
In particular $F_p^*$ maps the germs on $N$ vanishing at $F(p)$ to germs on $M$ vanishing at $p$: $F_p^*\big(I_{F(p)}\big) \subseteq I_p$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Well defined.} For a representative $(g, V)$, the set $F^{-1}(V)$ is open and contains $p$ because $F$ is continuous, and $g \circ F$ is smooth there by Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}. If $(g, V)$ and $(g', V')$ represent the same germ at $F(p)$, then $g = g'$ on some open $W$ with $F(p) \in W \subseteq V \cap V'$; so $g \circ F = g' \circ F$ on the open set $F^{-1}(W) \ni p$, and the two pulled-back germs at $p$ are equal.

\emph{Algebra homomorphism.} Composition with $F$ respects the pointwise operations: $(g + h)\circ F = g \circ F + h \circ F$, $(gh) \circ F = (g\circ F)(h \circ F)$, $(\lambda g)\circ F = \lambda (g \circ F)$, and $1 \circ F = 1$, since each side takes the same value at every point $q$ (for instance $((g+h) \circ F)(q) = g(F(q)) + h(F(q))$). To pass to germs, let $(g, V)$ and $(h, V')$ represent $[g]$ and $[h]$, and let $W$ be open with $F(p) \in W \subseteq V \cap V'$, so that $[g] + [h] = [g|_W + h|_W]$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}). The set $F^{-1}(W)$ is open, contains $p$, and lies in the domains of $g \circ F$ and $h \circ F$, so by the definition of the sum of germs at $p$,
\[
F_p^*\big([g] + [h]\big) = \big[(g|_W + h|_W) \circ F\big] = \big[(g \circ F)|_{F^{-1}(W)} + (h \circ F)|_{F^{-1}(W)}\big] = [g \circ F] + [h \circ F] = F_p^*[g] + F_p^*[h] .
\]
The same chain with every $+$ replaced by a product gives $F_p^*([g][h]) = F_p^*[g]\, F_p^*[h]$. For scalars, $F_p^*(\lambda[g]) = [(\lambda g) \circ F] = [\lambda (g \circ F)] = \lambda\, F_p^*[g]$, and for the unit, $F_p^*[1] = [1 \circ F] = [1]$.

\emph{Evaluation.} $(g \circ F)(p) = g(F(p))$ by definition of composition; this is the displayed formula, since the value of the germ $F_p^*[g] = [g \circ F]$ at $p$ is $(g \circ F)(p)$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-evaluation}).

\emph{In particular.} If $[g] \in I_{F(p)}$, i.e.\ $g(F(p)) = 0$ (Definition~\ref{def:Ip}), then by the evaluation formula $(F_p^*[g])(p) = g(F(p)) = 0$, so $F_p^*[g] \in I_p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Pushforward --- the Differential]\deflabel{def:pushforward}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$, and let $D \in T_pM$ be a tangent vector at $p$ --- that is, a derivation at $p$, a linear map $D : C^\infty_p(M) \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the Leibniz rule. The \textbf{pushforward} of $D$ along $F$ is the map
\[
F_{*p}D : C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}, \qquad \big(F_{*p}D\big)[g] \;:=\; D\big(F_p^*[g]\big) = D[\,g \circ F\,],
\]
defined on germs $[g]$ at $F(p)$ on $N$: pull the germ back to $p$, then apply $D$. In one line, $F_{*p}D = D \circ F_p^*$. It is a derivation at $F(p)$, i.e.\ an element of $T_{F(p)}N$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}). Letting $D$ vary gives the \textbf{pushforward}, or \textbf{differential}, of $F$ at $p$,
\[
F_{*p} : T_pM \longrightarrow T_{F(p)}N, \qquad D \longmapsto F_{*p}D,
\]
a map from tangent vectors at $p$ in $M$ to tangent vectors at $F(p)$ in $N$, also written $dF_p$. (Uribe: ``the awkward notation $F_{*p}$.'') So $F_{*p}$ acts on derivations; its value $F_{*p}D$ is again a derivation, which acts on germs at $F(p)$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{The Differential of a Smooth Map}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=4em]
C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \arrow[r, "F_p^*"] \arrow[dr, "F_{*p}D"'] & C^\infty_p(M) \arrow[d, "D"] \\
& \mathbb{R}
\end{tikzcd}
\\[1.4em]
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.1em, column sep=3.6em]
M \arrow[r, "F"] & N & \text{points: forward} \\
C^\infty_p(M) & C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \arrow[l, "F_p^*"'] & \text{germs: backward} \\
T_pM \arrow[r, "F_{*p}"] & T_{F(p)}N & \text{derivations: forward}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Above, the definition as a diagram: $F_{*p}D = D \circ F_p^*$, a derivation at $F(p)$ obtained by first pulling the germ back to $p$ and then applying $D$. Below, the directions. Points move forward along $F$; functions move backward, since a function on $N$ composed with $F$ is a function on $M$; and derivations, being dual to functions, reverse the arrow once more and move forward again.

\begin{propbox}[The Differential Is a Linear Map of Abstract Tangent Spaces]\thmlabel{prop:pushforward-derivation}
For every $D \in T_pM$, $F_{*p}D$ is a derivation at $F(p)$; and $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ is linear.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{The Differential of a Smooth Map}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Two claims: for fixed $D$, the map $F_{*p}D : C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \to \mathbb{R}$ is a derivation at $F(p)$ (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}), i.e.\ linear and satisfying the Leibniz rule with the values at $F(p)$; and $D \mapsto F_{*p}D$ is linear.

\emph{$F_{*p}D$ is linear.} $F_{*p}D = D \circ F_p^*$ is linear, as a composite of linear maps: $F_p^*$ is linear by Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-properties}, and $D$ is linear. Explicitly, for germs $[g], [h]$ at $F(p)$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, by Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}, the linearity of $F_p^*$, the linearity of $D$, and Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} again,
\[
\big(F_{*p}D\big)\big(a[g] + b[h]\big) = D\big(F_p^*(a[g] + b[h])\big) = D\big(a\,F_p^*[g] + b\,F_p^*[h]\big) = a\,D\big(F_p^*[g]\big) + b\,D\big(F_p^*[h]\big) = a\,\big(F_{*p}D\big)[g] + b\,\big(F_{*p}D\big)[h] .
\]

\emph{Leibniz rule.} Let $[g],[h] \in C^\infty_{F(p)}(N)$. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\big(F_{*p}D\big)\big([g][h]\big)
&= D\big(F_p^*([g][h])\big) = D\big(F_p^*[g]\cdot F_p^*[h]\big) \\
&= \big(F_p^*[g]\big)(p)\, D\big(F_p^*[h]\big) + \big(F_p^*[h]\big)(p)\, D\big(F_p^*[g]\big) \\
&= g(F(p))\,\big(F_{*p}D\big)[h] + h(F(p))\,\big(F_{*p}D\big)[g],
\end{aligned}
\]
using, in turn, Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}, that $F_p^*$ is multiplicative, the Leibniz rule for $D$ at $p$ applied to the two germs $F_p^*[g], F_p^*[h] \in C^\infty_p(M)$, and compatibility with evaluation, $(F_p^*[g])(p) = g(F(p))$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-properties}), together with Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} once more. So $F_{*p}D$ is a derivation at $F(p)$.

\emph{Linearity in $D$.} Linearity in $D$ holds because $(D + \lambda D')\circ F_p^* = D \circ F_p^* + \lambda\, D' \circ F_p^*$: for every germ $[g]$ at $F(p)$, by Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} and the pointwise operations on derivations (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}),
\[
\big(F_{*p}(D + \lambda D')\big)[g] = (D + \lambda D')\big(F_p^*[g]\big) = D\big(F_p^*[g]\big) + \lambda\, D'\big(F_p^*[g]\big) = \big(F_{*p}D + \lambda\, F_{*p}D'\big)[g] .
\]
The two derivations agree on every germ, so $F_{*p}(D + \lambda D') = F_{*p}D + \lambda\, F_{*p}D'$.
\end{proof}

Every object of this section, with what it is and where it lives. The rows go in order of the diagram above: germs travel backwards, from $N$ to $M$, and derivations forwards, from $M$ to $N$.

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.6cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{7.8cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.9cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Object} & \textbf{What it is} & \textbf{Lives in} \\ \midrule
$F$ & a smooth map & $M \to N$ \\
$p$, \ $F(p)$ & a point of $M$, and its image, a point of $N$ & $M$, \ $N$ \\
$[f]$ & a germ at $p$: a class of smooth functions defined near $p$ in $M$ & $C^\infty_p(M)$ \\
$[g]$ & a germ at $F(p)$: a class of smooth functions defined near $F(p)$ in $N$ & $C^\infty_{F(p)}(N)$ \\
$F_p^*$ & pullback, an algebra homomorphism, $[g] \mapsto [g \circ F]$ & $C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \to C^\infty_p(M)$ \\
$D$ & a tangent vector at $p$: a derivation, a linear map $C^\infty_p(M) \to \mathbb{R}$ & $T_pM$ \\
$F_{*p}$ & pushforward, a linear map, $D \mapsto D \circ F_p^*$ & $T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ \\
$F_{*p}D$ & a tangent vector at $F(p)$: a derivation, a linear map $C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \to \mathbb{R}$ & $T_{F(p)}N$ \\
$(F_{*p}D)[g]$ & a real number, equal to $D[g \circ F]$ & $\mathbb{R}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The board justified the derivation property with ``since $F_p^*$ is a ring morphism.'' That is one of the two facts used, and not quite enough on its own: the Leibniz rule \emph{at $F(p)$} needs the coefficients $g(F(p))$ and $h(F(p))$, and these appear only because pullback is compatible with evaluation, $(g \circ F)(p) = g(F(p))$ --- the third equality above. It is automatic here, but it is a separate property from multiplicativity, and it is the one that moves the base point from $p$ to $F(p)$.

\begin{thmbox}[The Chain Rule]\thmlabel{prop:pushforward-functorial}
If $F : M \to N$ and $G : N \to P$ are smooth and $p \in M$, then
\[
(G \circ F)_{*p} = G_{*F(p)} \circ F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{G(F(p))}P, \qquad (\mathrm{id}_M)_{*p} = \mathrm{id}_{T_pM} .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 3.6(b)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~10: ``the proof of the chain rule is one line'' --- pullbacks compose in the opposite order, because composition is associative. The dualization that follows was set as an exercise, ``use this to conclude the proof''; it is filled in.)} $G \circ F$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), so $(G \circ F)_{*p}$ is defined. Two linear maps $T_pM \to T_{G(F(p))}P$ are equal if they agree at every $D$, and two derivations at $G(F(p))$ are equal if they agree at every germ; so fix $D \in T_pM$ and a germ $[g]$ at $G(F(p))$.

\emph{Pullback reverses composition:} $(G\circ F)_p^* = F_p^* \circ G_{F(p)}^*$, since $g \circ (G \circ F) = (g \circ G) \circ F$. Indeed, by Definition~\ref{def:germ-pullback} applied three times (to $G \circ F$ at $p$, to $F$ at $p$, and to $G$ at $F(p)$),
\[
(G\circ F)_p^*[g] = \big[g \circ (G \circ F)\big] = \big[(g \circ G) \circ F\big] = F_p^*[g \circ G] = F_p^*\big(G_{F(p)}^*[g]\big).
\]

\emph{Dualization.} Hence
\[
\big((G\circ F)_{*p}D\big)[g] = D\big((G\circ F)_p^*[g]\big) = D\big(F_p^*\, G_{F(p)}^*[g]\big) = \big(F_{*p}D\big)\big(G_{F(p)}^*[g]\big) = \big(G_{*F(p)}\,F_{*p}D\big)[g].
\]
The first equality is Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} for $G \circ F$ at $p$; the second is the reversal just shown; the third is Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} for $F$ at $p$, applied to the germ $G_{F(p)}^*[g]$ at $F(p)$; the fourth is Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} for $G$ at $F(p)$, applied to the derivation $F_{*p}D \in T_{F(p)}N$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}).

\emph{Identity.} The identity pulls back every germ to itself, $(\mathrm{id}_M)_p^*[f] = [f \circ \mathrm{id}_M] = [f]$, so it pushes every derivation to itself: $\big((\mathrm{id}_M)_{*p}D\big)[f] = D\big((\mathrm{id}_M)_p^*[f]\big) = D[f]$ for every germ $[f]$ at $p$, i.e.\ $(\mathrm{id}_M)_{*p}D = D$.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3.2em, column sep=3.4em]
M \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[rr, bend left=28, "G \circ F"] & N \arrow[r, "G"] & P \\
T_pM \arrow[r, "F_{*p}"'] \arrow[rr, bend right=28, "(G \circ F)_{*p}"'] & T_{F(p)}N \arrow[r, "G_{*F(p)}"'] & T_{G(F(p))}P
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The upper row is the composite of maps; the lower row says its differential is the composite of the differentials. In coordinates (Corollary~\ref{cor:chain-rule-coords}) it becomes the multiplication of Jacobian matrices --- the chain rule of calculus, now as a statement about manifolds.

\textbf{Lecture 10.} Uribe stated this as the Chain Rule and proved the pullback identity $(G \circ F)_p^* = F_p^* \circ G_{F(p)}^*$ on the board --- ``see, you know that this is the right point of view when proofs become one line'' --- leaving the dualization as an exercise; the displayed computation above is that exercise. Pullbacks compose in the \emph{opposite} order, so pushforwards, being their duals, compose in the \emph{same} order as the maps. (The theorem appeared here, ahead of the lecture, because the two results below depend on it.)

\begin{corbox}[Diffeomorphisms Induce Isomorphisms]\thmlabel{lem:germs-diffeo}
If $\Phi : M \to N$ is a diffeomorphism, then $\Phi_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{\Phi(p)}N$ is a linear isomorphism, with inverse $(\Phi^{-1})_{*\Phi(p)}$.
\leeref{Proposition 3.6(d)}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Since $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism, $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$ are both smooth (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}), so their pushforwards are defined, and they are linear by Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}. Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial} to $\Phi^{-1} \circ \Phi = \mathrm{id}_M$ at $p$ and to $\Phi \circ \Phi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_N$ at $\Phi(p)$, using $\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(p)) = p$:
\[
(\Phi^{-1})_{*\Phi(p)} \circ \Phi_{*p} = (\Phi^{-1} \circ \Phi)_{*p} = (\mathrm{id}_M)_{*p} = \mathrm{id}_{T_pM}, \qquad
\Phi_{*p} \circ (\Phi^{-1})_{*\Phi(p)} = (\Phi \circ \Phi^{-1})_{*\Phi(p)} = (\mathrm{id}_N)_{*\Phi(p)} = \mathrm{id}_{T_{\Phi(p)}N} .
\]
So $\Phi_{*p}$ has the two-sided inverse $(\Phi^{-1})_{*\Phi(p)}$; a linear bijection is a linear isomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Open Subsets Have the Same Abstract Tangent Spaces]\thmlabel{lem:germs-local}
Let $U \subseteq M$ be open with $p \in U$, and $\iota : U \hookrightarrow M$ the inclusion. Then $\iota_p^* : C^\infty_p(M) \to C^\infty_p(U)$ is restriction of germs, an isomorphism of $\mathbb{R}$-algebras, and consequently $\iota_{*p} : T_pU \to T_pM$ is a linear isomorphism. We use it to identify $T_pU = T_pM$.
\leeref{Proposition 3.9}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
The inclusion $\iota$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}(1): in a chart of $M$ restricted to an open subset of $U$, a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), its coordinate representation is the identity), and by Definition~\ref{def:germ-pullback} it pulls back the germ of $(f, V)$ to $\iota_p^*[f] = [f \circ \iota] = [f|_{U \cap V}]$: restriction of germs.

\emph{Algebra homomorphism.} Restriction is well defined and an algebra homomorphism by Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-properties}, and it is compatible with evaluation: $(\iota_p^*[f])(p) = f(p)$.

\emph{Surjective.} It is surjective because a germ at $p$ on $U$ has a representative $(g, V')$ defined on an open subset $V'$ of $U$, which is open in $M$ ($U$ being open in $M$) and so already represents a germ on $M$; and $\iota_p^*[g] = [g|_{V' \cap U}] = [g|_{V'}]$, the given germ, since $V' \subseteq U$.

\emph{Injective.} It is injective because if $f|_U$ and $g|_U$ agree near $p$ then $f$ and $g$ agree near $p$: they agree on an open $W \ni p$ of $U$, and $W$ is also open in $M$, so $[f] = [g]$ in $C^\infty_p(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation}). A bijective algebra homomorphism is an algebra isomorphism; write $\rho = (\iota_p^*)^{-1}$ for its inverse, again an algebra homomorphism compatible with evaluation.

\emph{The derivations.} A derivation on one algebra corresponds to exactly one on the other by composing with this isomorphism. By Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}, $\iota_{*p}D = D \circ \iota_p^*$ for $D \in T_pU$. In the other direction, for $E \in T_pM$ the composite $E \circ \rho$ is a derivation at $p$ on $U$: it is linear, as a composite of linear maps, and for germs $[f], [g]$ on $U$, since $\rho$ is multiplicative and compatible with evaluation,
\[
(E \circ \rho)\big([f][g]\big) = E\big(\rho[f]\, \rho[g]\big) = f(p)\, E(\rho[g]) + g(p)\, E(\rho[f]) .
\]
The two assignments are mutually inverse: $\iota_{*p}(E \circ \rho) = E \circ \rho \circ \iota_p^* = E$ and $(\iota_{*p}D) \circ \rho = D \circ \iota_p^* \circ \rho = D$. So $\iota_{*p}$ is a bijection; it is linear by Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Charts Are Diffeomorphisms]\thmlabel{prop:chart-diffeo}
If $(U, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart of $M$, then $\varphi : U \to \varphi(U)$ is a diffeomorphism. Consequently, for every $p \in U$,
\[
T_pM \;=\; T_pU \xrightarrow[\ \cong\ ]{\ \varphi_{*p}\ } T_{\varphi(p)}\,\varphi(U)
\]
is a linear isomorphism of abstract tangent spaces.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{$\varphi$ is a diffeomorphism.} $\varphi : U \to \varphi(U)$ is a bijection, and a homeomorphism, so $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are continuous. In the charts $(U,\varphi)$ on $U$ and $(\varphi(U), \mathrm{id})$ on $\varphi(U)$, both $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ have coordinate representation the identity:
\[
\mathrm{id} \circ \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\varphi(U)}, \qquad \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ \mathrm{id}^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\varphi(U)},
\]
which is smooth; so both are smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}), and $\varphi$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}).

\emph{The isomorphism.} The isomorphism is then Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local} followed by Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo}: the first identifies $T_pM$ with $T_pU$ by the linear isomorphism $\iota_{*p}$; the second, applied to the diffeomorphism $\Phi = \varphi : U \to \varphi(U)$, says that $\varphi_{*p} : T_pU \to T_{\varphi(p)}\varphi(U)$ is a linear isomorphism with inverse $(\varphi^{-1})_{*\varphi(p)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Chart Pushforward]\label{rem:chart-pushforward}
This is the $\tilde D$ of the lecture: for $D \in T_pM$, $\tilde D = \varphi_{*p}D$ acts by $\tilde D[g] = D[g \circ \varphi]$, identifying tangent vectors on $M$ with derivations at a point of an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Everything about the abstract tangent space $T_pM$ can therefore be settled in $\mathbb{R}^n$, which is how the basis theorem is proved.
\end{rembox}

\begin{lembox}[The Pushforward Along a Constant Map]\thmlabel{lem:constant-pushforward}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Let $\kappa : X \to Y$ be a constant map of smooth manifolds, with value $q_0$. Then $\kappa$ is smooth, and $\kappa_{*x} = 0 : T_xX \to T_{q_0}Y$ for every $x \in X$.
    \item Let $\iota : S \to M$ and $F : M \to N$ be smooth maps such that $F \circ \iota$ is constant. Then for every $p \in S$
    \[
    F_{*\iota(p)} \circ \iota_{*p} = 0, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \iota_{*p}\big(T_pS\big) \subseteq \ker F_{*\iota(p)} .
    \]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)}

\emph{(1) $\kappa$ is smooth.} We check Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}. $\kappa$ is continuous: the preimage of any set is $X$ or $\emptyset$. Let $x \in X$, and choose smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $X$ at $x$ and $(V, \psi)$ of $Y$ at $q_0$ (the smooth charts cover $X$ and $Y$, Definition~\ref{def:atlas}). Then $\kappa(U) = \{q_0\} \subseteq V$, and the coordinate representation $\psi \circ \kappa \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is the constant map $\varphi(U) \to \mathbb{R}^{\dim Y}$ with value $\psi(q_0)$, which is smooth.

\emph{(1) $\kappa_{*x} = 0$.} Let $D \in T_xX$ and let $[g]$ be a germ at $q_0$, with $g$ defined on an open set $O \ni q_0$. Then $\kappa^{-1}(O) = X$, and $g \circ \kappa$ is the constant function $g(q_0)$ on $X$, whose germ at $x$ is the constant germ $\underline{g(q_0)}$. By the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}) and because derivations kill constants (Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(1)),
\[
(\kappa_{*x} D)[g] = D[g \circ \kappa] = D\big[\underline{g(q_0)}\big] = 0 .
\]
So $\kappa_{*x}D$ is the zero derivation, for every $D$: $\kappa_{*x} = 0$.

\emph{(2)} $F \circ \iota$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}) and constant, so by (1), $(F \circ \iota)_{*p} = 0$. By the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}),
\[
F_{*\iota(p)} \circ \iota_{*p} = (F \circ \iota)_{*p} = 0 .
\]
So for every $v \in T_pS$, $F_{*\iota(p)}\big(\iota_{*p}v\big) = 0$, i.e.\ $\iota_{*p}v \in \ker F_{*\iota(p)}$.
\end{proof}
