% SECTION: COORDINATE DERIVATIONS AND THE BASIS THEOREM
% ============================================================================

\section{Coordinate Derivations and the Basis Theorem}\label{sec:basis-theorem}\label{sub:coordinate-derivations}

\roadmark{Stage: abstract}{Charts give derivations $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$, and they form a basis of $T_pM$: $\dim T_pM = \dim M$. The proof needs Taylor's theorem with a smooth remainder.}

\begin{defbox}[Coordinate Functions of a Chart]\deflabel{def:coordinate-functions}
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The \textbf{standard coordinate functions} on $\mathbb{R}^n$ are the projections
    \[
    r^i : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad r^i(a^1, \ldots, a^n) = a^i, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n.
    \]
    \item For a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$, the \textbf{coordinate functions of the chart}, or \textbf{local coordinates} on $U$, are
    \[
    x^i := r^i \circ \varphi : U \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^n), \quad\text{i.e. } \varphi(q) = \big(x^1(q), \ldots, x^n(q)\big).
    \]
    \item For a function $f$ defined on $U$, its \textbf{coordinate representation} in the chart is $f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to \mathbb{R}$, as in Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}; thus $f = f_\varphi \circ \varphi$ on $U$. In particular $(x^i)_\varphi = r^i \circ \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = r^i$ on $\varphi(U)$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Coordinate Charts}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:abstract-tangent-5}
\textbf{A notational discipline.} Uribe stopped to insist on this. The $x^i$ live \emph{upstairs}, as functions on the manifold, and the $r^i$ \emph{downstairs}, as functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$; conflating them is the main source of confusion in what follows. The identity $(x^i)_\varphi = r^i$ is the bridge between the two rows: it says that the coordinate functions, written in their own chart, are the standard coordinates. It also shows that each $x^i$ is a smooth function on $U$, by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}, since $r^i$ is smooth.
\end{rembox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3.0em, column sep=3.4em]
& U \arrow[dl, "f"'] \arrow[d, "\varphi"] \arrow[dr, "x^i"] & \\
\mathbb{R} & \varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \arrow[l, "f_\varphi"] \arrow[r, "r^i"'] & \mathbb{R}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The board diagram for this section. Both triangles commute: the left one says $f = f_\varphi \circ \varphi$, which is what smoothness of $f$ means; the right one is the \emph{definition} $x^i = r^i \circ \varphi$ of the $i$-th coordinate function on $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}). Everything upstairs is expressed downstairs by composing with $\varphi$, and the derivation about to be defined does its differentiating entirely on the bottom row, where partial derivatives already make sense.

\begin{defbox}[Coordinate Derivations]\deflabel{def:coordinate-derivation}
Let $(U,\varphi)$ be a smooth chart with $p \in U$, with coordinate functions $x^1, \ldots, x^n$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}), and let $i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$. Define $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p : C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$ by
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p [f] \;:=\; \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi(p)\big),
\]
the ordinary $i$-th partial derivative at $\varphi(p)$ of the coordinate representation $f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$. For a function $f$ smooth near $p$ we also write
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p) \;:=\; \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p [f] \;=\; \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi(p)\big),
\]
the \textbf{partial derivative} of $f$ with respect to the coordinate $x^i$. It is defined by going downstairs: there is no other way to differentiate a function on a manifold with respect to a coordinate.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Computations in Coordinates}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Partial Derivatives of a Smooth Function Are Smooth]\thmlabel{lem:partials-smooth}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^n))$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and $f : U \to \mathbb{R}$ smooth, $f \in C^\infty(U)$ --- for instance the restriction to $U$ of a smooth function on $M$. For each $j$, the function $\partial f/\partial x^j : U \to \mathbb{R}$, $q \mapsto \partial f/\partial x^j(q)$, satisfies
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j} \circ \varphi^{-1} = \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^j} \qquad \text{on } \varphi(U),
\]
and it is smooth: $\partial f/\partial x^j \in C^\infty(U)$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} The open set $U$ is a smooth manifold whose smooth charts are the smooth charts of $M$ with domain in $U$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}); in particular $(U, \varphi)$ is a smooth chart of $U$. Two things are claimed: the identity of functions on $\varphi(U)$, and the smoothness of $\partial f/\partial x^j$.

\emph{The identity.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:some-any-function}, applied to the smooth function $f$ on the manifold $U$ and its smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$, the coordinate representation $f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$. So $f$ is smooth near every $q \in U$, and $\partial f/\partial x^j(q)$ is defined (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}). For $r \in \varphi(U)$, Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} at the point $q = \varphi^{-1}(r)$ gives
\[
\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j} \circ \varphi^{-1}\Big)(r) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big) = \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^j}\big(\varphi(\varphi^{-1}(r))\big) = \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^j}(r) .
\]

\emph{Smoothness.} $f_\varphi$ is smooth on the open set $\varphi(U)$, so its partial derivative $\partial f_\varphi/\partial r^j$ is smooth too: every partial derivative of it, of any order, is a partial derivative of $f_\varphi$, hence exists and is continuous. By the identity, $\partial f_\varphi/\partial r^j$ is the coordinate representation of $\partial f/\partial x^j$ in the chart $(U, \varphi)$, which contains every point of $U$; so $\partial f/\partial x^j$ is smooth on $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Coordinate Derivations Are Derivations]\thmlabel{prop:coord-is-derivation}
$\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p$ is well defined on germs and is a derivation at $p$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~8: ``it's linear, and the product rule will be inherited from the product rule of the ordinary partial derivatives'' --- the \emph{Linear} and \emph{Leibniz} steps below. Well-definedness is filled in.)}

Three things are to be shown: the value $\partial f_\varphi/\partial r^i(\varphi(p))$ does not depend on the representative of $[f]$; the resulting map is linear; and it satisfies the Leibniz rule of Definition~\ref{def:derivation}. For a representative $(f, U_1)$, $f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is defined on the open set $\varphi(U \cap U_1) \ni \varphi(p)$ and smooth there (Proposition~\ref{prop:some-any-function}, applied on the open set $U \cap U_1$ with the restricted chart, a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)), so its partial derivatives at $\varphi(p)$ exist.

\emph{Well defined.} If $(f,U_1) \sim (g,U_2)$, then $f = g$ on an open $W \ni p$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation}), so $f_\varphi = g_\varphi$ on the open set $\varphi(W \cap U) \ni \varphi(p)$ (open because $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism onto the open set $\varphi(U)$); partial derivatives at a point depend only on the function near that point, being limits of difference quotients that only use values in arbitrarily small neighbourhoods, so the two values agree. (Shrinking the chart domain also changes nothing, for the same reason.)

\emph{Linear.} $(\lambda f + g)_\varphi = \lambda f_\varphi + g_\varphi$ near $\varphi(p)$, since both sides take the value $\lambda f(\varphi^{-1}(r)) + g(\varphi^{-1}(r))$ at $r$; and partial differentiation is linear. So, by Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} at both ends,
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\big(\lambda[f] + [g]\big) = \frac{\partial (\lambda f + g)_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(\varphi(p)) = \lambda\,\frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(\varphi(p)) + \frac{\partial g_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(\varphi(p)) = \lambda\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p[f] + \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p[g] .
\]

\emph{Leibniz.} $(fg)_\varphi = f_\varphi\, g_\varphi$ near $\varphi(p)$, since $(fg)(\varphi^{-1}(r)) = f(\varphi^{-1}(r))\, g(\varphi^{-1}(r))$, so by the ordinary product rule at $\varphi(p)$,
\[
\frac{\partial (fg)_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(\varphi(p)) = f_\varphi(\varphi(p))\,\frac{\partial g_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(\varphi(p)) + g_\varphi(\varphi(p))\,\frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(\varphi(p)),
\]
and $f_\varphi(\varphi(p)) = f(\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(p))) = f(p)$, $g_\varphi(\varphi(p)) = g(p)$. By Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} the left side is $\partial/\partial x^i|_p([f][g])$ and the two partial derivatives on the right are $\partial/\partial x^i|_p[g]$ and $\partial/\partial x^i|_p[f]$, so
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\big([f][g]\big) = f(p)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p[g] + g(p)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p[f],
\]
which is the Leibniz rule.
\end{proof}

The proof of the Basis Theorem below needs a form of Taylor expansion whose remainder is not an estimate but an exact, \emph{smooth} term --- ``a theorem from calculus'' that is not usually taught there. It is built in two steps: first order, then the first-order statement applied again.

\begin{lembox}[Hadamard's Lemma]\thmlabel{lem:hadamard}
Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $a = (a^1,\ldots,a^n) \in W$, $f : W \to \mathbb{R}$ smooth, and $B \subseteq W$ an open ball centred at $a$. Then there are smooth functions $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ on $B$ with
\[
f(r) = f(a) + \sum_{i=1}^n (r^i - a^i)\, f_i(r) \quad (r \in B), \qquad f_i(a) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a) .
\]
Explicitly, $f_i(r) = \displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}\big(a + t(r-a)\big)\, dt$.
\leeref{cf.\ Theorem C.15, used in the proof of Proposition 3.2}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~9: ``the proof is delightfully simple.'')} Fix $r \in B$. The segment $t \mapsto a + t(r - a)$, $t \in [0,1]$, runs from $a$ to $r$ and stays in $B$, a ball being convex. Put $h(t) = f\big(a + t(r-a)\big)$. It is defined on the set of $t$ with $a + t(r-a) \in W$, which is open (the preimage of the open $W$ under a continuous map) and contains $[0,1]$, hence also open intervals around $0$ and $1$, hence an open interval containing $[0,1]$; there $h$ is smooth, as the composite of $f$ with an affine map. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $f(r) - f(a) = h(1) - h(0) = \int_0^1 h'(t)\, dt$, and by the chain rule, since $\frac{d}{dt}\big(a^i + t(r^i - a^i)\big) = r^i - a^i$,
\[
h'(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}\big(a + t(r-a)\big)\,(r^i - a^i) .
\]
Hence
\[
f(r) - f(a) = \int_0^1 \frac{d}{dt} f\big(a + t(r-a)\big)\, dt = \int_0^1 \sum_{i=1}^n (r^i - a^i)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}\big(a + t(r-a)\big)\, dt = \sum_{i=1}^n (r^i - a^i)\, f_i(r),
\]
the factors $r^i - a^i$ coming out of the integral because they do not depend on $t$ (linearity of the integral), and $f_i$ being the integral of the statement. Adding $f(a)$ to both sides gives the identity.

\emph{Smoothness.} Each $f_i$ is smooth on $B$: the integrand $(t, r) \mapsto \partial f/\partial r^i\big(a + t(r-a)\big)$ is the composite of the smooth map $(t,r) \mapsto a + t(r-a)$ with the smooth function $\partial f/\partial r^i$, so it is smooth in $(t, r)$ on an open set containing $[0,1] \times B$, and all its partial derivatives in $r$ are continuous there; so differentiation under the integral sign over the compact interval $[0,1]$ is legitimate to every order.

\emph{Value at $a$.} At $r = a$ the integrand is constant: $a + t(a - a) = a$ for every $t$, so the integrand is the number $\partial f/\partial r^i(a)$, and
\[
f_i(a) = \int_0^1 \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a)\, dt = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a) .
\]
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note.} In Lecture~9 the path in the integral was first written with the wrong endpoints; a student corrected it to the convex combination $t(r - a) + a$, which runs from $a$ at $t = 0$ to $r$ at $t = 1$, as above.

Uribe called the proof ``delightfully simple.'' A student corrected the path on the board: it must be the segment $a + t(r - a)$, equal to $a$ at $t = 0$ and to $r$ at $t = 1$. Convexity of $B$ is what the proof uses --- ``everything is local,'' but the neighbourhood must contain the segment from $a$ to each of its points, which is why a ball (or any set star-shaped about $a$) is taken.

\begin{lembox}[Taylor--Hadamard]\thmlabel{lem:taylor-hadamard}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:hadamard}, there are smooth functions $f_{ij}$ on $B$, $1 \le i, j \le n$, with
\[
f(r) \;=\; f(a) \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^n (r^i - a^i)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a) \;+\; \sum_{i,j=1}^n (r^i - a^i)(r^j - a^j)\, f_{ij}(r) \qquad (r \in B),
\]
and $f_{ij}(a) = \tfrac12\, \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^i\,\partial r^j}(a)$. This is an identity, not an approximation. In matrix form, with $r - a$ written as a column, the quadratic term is
\[
\sum_{i,j=1}^n (r^i - a^i)(r^j - a^j)\, f_{ij}(r) = (r - a)^{\mathsf T} \begin{pmatrix} f_{11}(r) & \cdots & f_{1n}(r) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ f_{n1}(r) & \cdots & f_{nn}(r) \end{pmatrix} (r - a),
\]
and at $r = a$ the $n \times n$ matrix of the $f_{ij}$ is half the Hessian of $f$:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} f_{11}(a) & \cdots & f_{1n}(a) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ f_{n1}(a) & \cdots & f_{nn}(a) \end{pmatrix} = \frac12 \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^1\,\partial r^1}(a) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^1\,\partial r^n}(a) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^n\,\partial r^1}(a) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^n\,\partial r^n}(a) \end{pmatrix} .
\]
\leeref{cf.\ Theorem C.15}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~9, exactly: first order, then ``apply the claim to each $f_i$'' and substitute back. Uribe wrote the quadratic term with a factor $\tfrac12$ --- ``doesn't matter'' --- which the notes absorb into $f_{ij}$; the value of $f_{ij}(a)$ at the end is a completion, the lecture needing only that the $f_{ij}$ are smooth.)}

\emph{Two applications of Hadamard.} Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:hadamard} to $f$, obtaining smooth $f_1, \ldots, f_n$ on $B$ with
\[
f(r) = f(a) + \sum_{i=1}^n (r^i - a^i)\, f_i(r) \quad (r \in B), \qquad f_i(a) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a) .
\]
Then apply it again to each $f_i$, now with the open set $B$ in place of $W$ and the same ball $B$ (which is centred at $a$), obtaining smooth $f_{ij}$ on $B$ with $f_{ij}(a) = \partial f_i/\partial r^j(a)$ and
\[
f_i(r) = f_i(a) + \sum_{j=1}^n (r^j - a^j)\, f_{ij}(r) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a) + \sum_{j=1}^n (r^j - a^j)\, f_{ij}(r),
\]
the second equality by the value $f_i(a)$ from the first application.

\emph{Substitution.} Substituting this into $f(r) = f(a) + \sum_i (r^i - a^i) f_i(r)$ and multiplying out gives the identity:
\[
f(r) = f(a) + \sum_{i=1}^n (r^i - a^i)\Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a) + \sum_{j=1}^n (r^j - a^j)\, f_{ij}(r)\Big) = f(a) + \sum_{i=1}^n (r^i - a^i)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a) + \sum_{i,j=1}^n (r^i - a^i)(r^j - a^j)\, f_{ij}(r) .
\]

\emph{The value at $a$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:hadamard} applied to $f_i$, $f_{ij}(a) = \partial f_i/\partial r^j(a)$. Differentiate the integral formula $f_i(r) = \int_0^1 \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}\big(a + t(r-a)\big)\, dt$ under the integral sign (legitimate, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:hadamard}). By the chain rule, since $\partial\big(a^k + t(r^k - a^k)\big)/\partial r^j = t\,\delta^k_j$, the $r^j$-derivative of the integrand is $\sum_k \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^k\,\partial r^i}\big(a + t(r-a)\big)\, t\,\delta^k_j = t\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^j\,\partial r^i}\big(a + t(r-a)\big)$. At $r = a$ the second derivative is the constant $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^j\,\partial r^i}(a)$, and $\int_0^1 t\, dt = \tfrac12$; the order of the two partial derivatives does not matter, $f$ being smooth (equality of mixed partials). So
\[
\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial r^j}(r) = \int_0^1 t\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^j\,\partial r^i}\big(a + t(r-a)\big)\, dt, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial r^j}(a) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^j\,\partial r^i}(a) \int_0^1 t\, dt = \frac12\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^i\,\partial r^j}(a). \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\textbf{On the factor $\tfrac12$.} The board states the lemma with $\tfrac12 \sum_{i,j}$ in front of the quadratic term; Uribe added it ``just for consistency,'' saying it ``doesn't matter.'' For the \emph{existence} statement that is right --- replacing $f_{ij}$ by $2f_{ij}$ converts one form into the other. But the two forms are not interchangeable as written: the iterated proof above produces the version \emph{without} the $\tfrac12$, and with $f_{ij}(a) = \tfrac12 \partial_{ij} f(a)$. The board's normalization is the one in which $f_{ij}(a) = \partial_{ij} f(a)$, matching the Hessian term $\tfrac12 \sum \partial_{ij}f(a)(r^i - a^i)(r^j - a^j)$ of the ordinary Taylor polynomial. A numerical check on a test function confirms the unscaled identity to machine precision and shows the scaled one, with the same $f_{ij}$, to be off. Nothing below depends on the normalization, since only the vanishing of the quadratic term under a derivation is used.

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:abstract-tangent-6}
\textbf{What matters.} ``The point is that these functions don't blow up at $a$'': the remainder is a product of two factors vanishing at $a$ with a \emph{smooth} function, not merely a quantity that is small compared with $|r - a|^2$. The same iteration continues to any order.
\end{rembox}

Taylor--Hadamard for $f(r) = e^r$ at $a = 0$, in one variable. Left: the remainder $f(r) - f(a) - f'(a)(r-a)$ is the gap between the graph and its tangent line. Right: the same gap divided by $(r - a)^2$. The quotient $f_{11}(r) = (e^r - 1 - r)/r^2$ has only a removable singularity at $a$: it is smooth there, with value $\tfrac12 = \tfrac12 f''(0)$, exactly as the lemma predicts, and as the iterated proof computes it --- $f_1(r) = (e^r - 1)/r$, then $f_{11}(r) = (f_1(r) - f_1(0))/r$. That the quotient extends smoothly across $a$ is the whole content of the lemma.

\begin{corbox}[Derivations on $\mathbb{R}^n$]\thmlabel{cor:derivations-Rn}
Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $a \in W$, and $D$ a derivation at $a$ on $W$. Then for every germ $[f]$ at $a$,
\[
D[f] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a)\, D[r^i], \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad D = \sum_{i=1}^n D[r^i]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_a .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 3.2 and Corollary 3.3}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Two formulas are claimed; the second is the first read as an equality of derivations.

\emph{Reduction to a ball.} Let $(f, V)$ represent $[f]$. Choose an open ball $B \subseteq V \cap W$ centred at $a$ (possible since $V \cap W$ is open and contains $a$). Then $(f|_B, B) \sim (f, V)$, so we may take the representative $f$ on $B$, which changes nothing since $D$ acts on germs.

\emph{The germ identity.} Lemma~\ref{lem:taylor-hadamard} gives smooth $f_{ij}$ on $B$ with $f(r) = f(a) + \sum_i (r^i - a^i)\,\partial f/\partial r^i(a) + \sum_{i,j} (r^i - a^i)(r^j - a^j) f_{ij}(r)$ for all $r \in B$. Functions equal on $B$ have equal germs, and the germ of a sum or product of functions on $B$ is the sum or product of their germs (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}); so, writing $\underline{c}$ for constants as in Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties},
\[
[f] = \big[\underline{f(a)}\big] + \sum_{i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a)\, \big[r^i - a^i\big] + \sum_{i,j} \big[r^i - a^i\big]\,\big[(r^j - a^j) f_{ij}\big] .
\]

\emph{Apply $D$.} Apply $D$ to this identity; $D$ is linear and the numbers $\partial f/\partial r^i(a)$ come out:
\[
D[f] = D\big[\underline{f(a)}\big] + \sum_{i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a)\, D\big[r^i - a^i\big] + \sum_{i,j} D\Big[(r^i - a^i)\cdot\big((r^j - a^j) f_{ij}\big)\Big].
\]
The constant term vanishes by Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(1). Each quadratic term is $D$ of a product of two germs in $I_a$ --- namely $r^i - a^i$ and $(r^j - a^j)f_{ij}$, both zero at $a$, the values at $a$ being $a^i - a^i = 0$ and $0 \cdot f_{ij}(a) = 0$ --- so it vanishes by Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(2). Finally $D[r^i - a^i] = D[r^i]$ by (1) again: $D[r^i - a^i] = D[r^i] - D[\underline{a^i}] = D[r^i] - 0$. What remains is
\[
D[f] = 0 + \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a)\, D[r^i] + 0 ,
\]
the first formula. So $D$ sees only the linear part of $f$: ``the ultimate formula in the Euclidean case.''

\emph{The second formula.} $\partial/\partial r^i|_a$ is the coordinate derivation (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}) of the identity chart $(W, \mathrm{id}_W)$, whose coordinate functions are the $r^i$ and in which $f_{\mathrm{id}} = f$; so $\partial/\partial r^i|_a[f] = \partial f/\partial r^i(a)$, and it is a derivation at $a$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:coord-is-derivation}). Derivations are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}), so for every germ $[f]$, by the first formula,
\[
\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n D[r^i]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_a\Big)[f] = \sum_{i=1}^n D[r^i]\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial r^i}(a) = D[f] .
\]
The two derivations agree on every germ, so they are equal.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Basis Theorem]\thmlabel{thm:tangent-basis}
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold, $p \in M$, and $(U, \varphi)$ any smooth chart with $p \in U$. Then
\[
\left\{ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^1}\Big|_p, \ \ldots, \ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^n}\Big|_p \right\}
\]
is a basis of $T_pM$; in particular $\dim T_pM = n$. Explicitly, every derivation $D$ at $p$ satisfies the \textbf{universal formula}
\[
D \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n D\big[x^i\big]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 3.15 and Corollary 3.3}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~9. In lecture the derivation $\tilde D$ was introduced inside this proof --- ``this is how you push forward derivations \ldots\ we'll come back to this construction immediately after'' --- and Uribe remarked that ``the order of my presentation is not ideal.'' The notes define the pushforward first, in \ref{sub:pushforward}, so that the proof can cite it.)} Let $D \in T_pM$ and put $a = \varphi(p) = (r_0^1, \ldots, r_0^n)$. What has to be shown: the $n$ derivations $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$, which lie in $T_pM$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:coord-is-derivation}, span $T_pM$ --- this is the universal formula, Steps 1--3 --- and are linearly independent, Step 4.

\emph{Step 1: push $D$ down.} Let $\tilde D = \varphi_{*p}D \in T_a\,\varphi(U)$, the chart pushforward of Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo} (with $D$ regarded as a derivation on germs on $U$, by the identification $T_pM = T_pU$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}). By Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} with $F = \varphi$, $\tilde D[g] = D\big(\varphi_p^*[g]\big) = D[g \circ \varphi]$ for germs $g$ at $a$.

\emph{Step 2: apply the Euclidean formula downstairs.} By Corollary~\ref{cor:derivations-Rn} on the open set $\varphi(U)$, applied to the derivation $\tilde D$ at $a$: for every germ $[g]$ at $a$,
\[
\tilde D[g] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial g}{\partial r^i}(a)\, \tilde D[r^i] .
\]

\emph{Step 3: read it back upstairs.} Let $[f]$ be a germ at $p$, with a representative $(f, V)$; replacing $V$ by $V \cap U$ does not change the germ, so assume $V \subseteq U$. Take $g = f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$, defined and smooth on the open set $\varphi(V) \ni a$. Three identities translate the terms of Step 2:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $f_\varphi \circ \varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = f$ on $V$, so by Step 1, $\tilde D[f_\varphi] = D[f_\varphi \circ \varphi] = D[f]$;
    \item by Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, $\partial f_\varphi/\partial r^i(a) = \partial/\partial x^i|_p[f]$;
    \item by Step 1 and Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions} ($x^i = r^i \circ \varphi$), $\tilde D[r^i] = D[r^i \circ \varphi] = D[x^i]$.
\end{itemize}
Substituting these into Step 2 with $g = f_\varphi$, and using that derivations are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}),
\[
D[f] = \tilde D[f_\varphi] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(a)\, \tilde D[r^i] = \sum_{i=1}^n D[x^i]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p[f] = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n D[x^i]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big)[f] \qquad\text{for every germ } [f],
\]
so $D = \sum_i D[x^i]\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p$, two derivations being equal when they agree on every germ. As $D$ was arbitrary, the coordinate derivations span.

\emph{Step 4: independence.} First, for all $i, j$: since $(x^j)_\varphi = r^j$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}(3)) and the projection $r^j$ has $i$-th partial derivative $1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise, Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} gives
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p[x^j] = \frac{\partial (x^j)_\varphi}{\partial r^i}(a) = \frac{\partial r^j}{\partial r^i}(a) = \delta^j_i .
\]
Now suppose $\sum_i c_i\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p = 0$, and apply it to $[x^j]$. Evaluating pointwise,
\[
0 = \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big)[x^j] = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p[x^j] = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i\, \delta^j_i = c_j ,
\]
hence $c_j = 0$, for every $j$. So the $n$ coordinate derivations form a basis, and $\dim T_pM = n$. The coefficients of $D$ are the numbers $D[x^i]$ --- uniquely: if also $D = \sum_i b_i\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p$, the same evaluation at $[x^j]$ gives $D[x^j] = \sum_i b_i\, \delta^j_i = b_j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3.2em, column sep=4.4em]
C^\infty_{a}\big(\varphi(U)\big) \arrow[r, "\varphi^*"] \arrow[dr, "\tilde D \,=\, \varphi_{*p}D"'] & C^\infty_p(U) = C^\infty_p(M) \arrow[d, "D"] \\
& \mathbb{R}
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad
\begin{tabular}{c}
$\varphi^*[r^i] = [x^i]$ \\[3pt]
$\varphi^*[f_\varphi] = [f]$
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The proof in one diagram --- the defining triangle of the pushforward, for the chart. Downstairs the Euclidean formula computes $\tilde D$ on everything; the two pullback identities on the right carry the answer back upstairs, turning $\tilde D[r^i]$ into $D[x^i]$ and $\tilde D[f_\varphi]$ into $D[f]$.

\textbf{Reconciliation with the lecture.} This is the lecture's proof, in the lecture's order of ideas but with the pushforward defined before it is used rather than after. Two details of the board version. It opens with ``$\forall\, [f] \in I_p$'': restricting to germs vanishing at $p$ is harmless, since $D[f] = D[f - f(p)]$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-properties}(1), but the argument works verbatim for every germ. And the notes had filled in a proof of this theorem before Lecture 9, via two reduction lemmas; those were the pushforward by an inclusion and by the chart in disguise, and they now appear as Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local} and Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo}.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 8).} Page 16 of the handwritten notes states Taylor--Hadamard for ``$f : U \to \mathbb{R}^2$''; the target is $\mathbb{R}$.

\begin{thmbox}[Ambient and Abstract Agree]\thmlabel{thm:ambient-abstract}
Let $M = F^{-1}(c) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ be a regular level set and $p \in M$. Then
\[
T^{\geo}_pM \longrightarrow T_pM, \qquad v \longmapsto D_v,
\]
from the geometric tangent space (a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$) to the abstract tangent space (derivations at $p$) is an isomorphism of vector spaces.
\leeref{Propositions 3.2, 5.37 and 5.38}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof]
\textbf{Announced in lecture.} Stated in lecture in answer to a student's question --- ``are the ambient and the abstract tangent spaces the same, just defined differently?'' --- with the answer that they are, but that it has to be proved. Injectivity is Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-determines-v}; that $D_v$ really is a derivation is Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-properties}; surjectivity follows from the basis theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), both spaces having dimension $n$. In detail:

\emph{The map lands in $T_pM$.} Near $p$, $M$ is the graph of a smooth function, after permuting coordinates (Step 2 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}), and passing to this open piece changes neither the geometric tangent space (Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-local}) nor the germs at $p$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}); so $D_v$ is defined by Definition~\ref{def:Dv}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-properties}(1), $D_v(f)$ depends only on the germ $[f]$, so $D_v$ is a map $C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$; by (3) it is linear and obeys the Leibniz rule, so it is a derivation at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}), $D_v \in T_pM$; and by (2) it does not depend on the graph piece used, only on $v$.

\emph{Linear.} In the graph chart, $v = (u, G'(x_0)u)$, so $u$ consists of the graph-variable components of $v$ and depends linearly on $v$; and $D_v(f) = u \cdot \nabla f_\varphi(x_0)$ is linear in $u$. Hence $D_{\lambda v + w}(f) = \lambda\, D_v(f) + D_w(f)$ for every $f$, i.e.\ $D_{\lambda v + w} = \lambda D_v + D_w$ (pointwise operations, Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}).

\emph{Injective.} If $D_v = D_{v'}$ then $v = v'$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-determines-v}).

\emph{Bijective.} $\dim T^{\geo}_pM = n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}) and $\dim T_pM = n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}, $M$ being a smooth $n$-manifold). A linear map between spaces of the same finite dimension is injective if and only if it is surjective (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)), so $v \mapsto D_v$ is a linear bijection, i.e.\ an isomorphism of vector spaces.

Even once it is proved, the notes keep the notations apart: $T^{\geo}_pM$ is the geometric tangent space, $T_pM$ the abstract one.
\end{proof}
\begin{corbox}[Consequences]\thmlabel{cor:tangent-basis-consequences}
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold and $p \in M$. Then the abstract tangent space has $\dim T_pM = n$, and for a regular level set $M = F^{-1}(c)$ the map $v \mapsto D_v$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}, from $T^{\geo}_pM$ to $T_pM$, is an isomorphism.
\leeref{Proposition 3.10}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{First claim.} The first claim is Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}: in any chart at $p$ the $n$ coordinate derivations $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$, so $\dim T_pM = n$.

\emph{Second claim.} For the second, $v \mapsto D_v$ is linear and injective (Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-determines-v}; it lands in $T_pM$ and is linear as shown in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}) between spaces of dimension $n$ --- the geometric tangent space $T^{\geo}_pM$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}, the abstract tangent space $T_pM$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis} --- hence an isomorphism: by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)), an injective linear map between spaces of equal finite dimension is also surjective.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} Lee meets the two kinds of tangent vector in the opposite order. He defines $T_pM$ by derivations first, identifies geometric and abstract tangent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Proposition~3.2), and only later, for embedded submanifolds, shows $T_pS = \ker d\Phi_p$ (Proposition~5.38). The course starts geometrically, with $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$ inside the ambient space (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}), and reaches derivations afterwards. The consequence above is where the two orders meet.

\begin{rembox}[A Derivation Sees Only the First Derivatives]\label{rem:derivation-sees-only-first-derivatives}
The basis theorem showed that, of the whole Taylor expansion of a germ, a derivation sees only the \emph{linear} term --- ``of the entire Taylor series of the germ, all I care about are the first partials.'' \ref{sec:cotangent-germs} says this algebraically: $I_p$ is a maximal ideal, being the kernel of evaluation; $I_p^2$ consists exactly of the germs vanishing to \emph{second} order (Proposition~\ref{prop:second-order}); and $I_p/I_p^2$ is canonically the \emph{cotangent space} $T_p^*M$ of Definition~\ref{def:cotangent}, built with no dualizing at all (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}). This is the sense in which, as Uribe remarked when he first set out to define the abstract tangent space, ``it is more natural to define the dual'': the cotangent space comes first, and the abstract tangent space is its dual. We follow Lee and do not take that route.
\end{rembox}

\begin{thmbox}[Dimension of the Tangent Space]\thmlabel{thm:tangent-dimension}
Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold. Then for every $p \in M$,
\[
\dim T_pM = n = \dim M ,
\]
the same at every point, and independent of the chart used to compute it.
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(The last clause of the basis theorem, recorded as a theorem in its own right.)} Fix $p \in M$. Since $M$ is a smooth $n$-manifold, there is a chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$, with $\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Any chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ has $n$ coordinate functions $x^1, \ldots, x^n$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}), and by Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis} the $n$ derivations $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$; so $\dim T_pM = n$. A different chart gives a different basis, but every basis of a finite-dimensional vector space has the same number of elements, namely its dimension; so every chart yields the same count $n$. Since $p$ was arbitrary, $\dim T_pM = n$ at every point.
\end{proof}

This is less obvious than it looks: the space of germs $C^\infty_p(M)$ on which the derivations act is infinite-dimensional, and it is the Hadamard lemma behind the basis theorem that cuts the derivations down to exactly $n$ dimensions.

\begin{corbox}[Smooth Invariance of Dimension]\thmlabel{cor:smooth-invariance-dim}
If $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ are nonempty open sets and $F : U \to V$ is a diffeomorphism, then $m = n$. Consequently two smooth charts of a smooth manifold at the same point have targets of the same dimension.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Give $U$ and $V$ their standard smooth structures, with the identity charts $(U, \mathrm{id}_U)$ and $(V, \mathrm{id}_V)$; they are smooth manifolds of dimensions $m$ and $n$, and $F$ and $F^{-1}$ are smooth maps between them (Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}). Let $p \in U$, which exists since $U$ is nonempty.

\emph{$F_{*p}$ is an isomorphism.} By the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), $(F^{-1})_{*F(p)} \circ F_{*p}$ and $F_{*p} \circ (F^{-1})_{*F(p)}$ are the pushforwards of the identity maps, hence identities:
\[
(F^{-1})_{*F(p)} \circ F_{*p} = (F^{-1} \circ F)_{*p} = (\mathrm{id}_U)_{*p} = \mathrm{id}_{T_pU}, \qquad F_{*p} \circ (F^{-1})_{*F(p)} = (F \circ F^{-1})_{*F(p)} = (\mathrm{id}_V)_{*F(p)} = \mathrm{id}_{T_{F(p)}V},
\]
using $F^{-1}(F(p)) = p$ in the second. So $F_{*p} : T_pU \to T_{F(p)}V$ is a linear isomorphism (linear by Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}); this is Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo} for $\Phi = F$.

\emph{The dimensions.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}, applied to the open sets $U$ and $V$ with their identity charts, these spaces have dimensions $m$ and $n$. A linear isomorphism is injective and surjective, so by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) $m \le n$ and $m \ge n$; so $m = n$.

\emph{Charts.} For two charts $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ and $(U_2, \varphi_2)$ at $p$ with targets $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$, apply this to the transition map $\varphi_2 \circ \varphi_1^{-1} : \varphi_1(U_1 \cap U_2) \to \varphi_2(U_1 \cap U_2)$, a diffeomorphism between nonempty open sets: the two sets are open because $U_1 \cap U_2$ is open and the charts are homeomorphisms onto open sets, nonempty because they contain $\varphi_1(p)$ and $\varphi_2(p)$, and the transition map is a bijection which is smooth with smooth inverse $\varphi_1 \circ \varphi_2^{-1}$ because the two charts are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}).
\end{proof}

Compare Theorem~\ref{thm:inv-dim}: the same statement for \emph{homeomorphisms} is true but genuinely hard, needing algebraic topology. For diffeomorphisms the derivative linearizes the problem, and linear algebra finishes it --- one of the first payoffs of having tangent spaces.
