% SECTION: THE DIFFERENTIAL IN COORDINATES
% ============================================================================

\section{The Differential in Coordinates}\label{sec:differential-coords}\label{sub:differential-coords}

\roadmark{Stage: abstract}{In charts the differential $F_{*p}$ is the Jacobian of the coordinate representation, and the chain rule is matrix multiplication.}

\textit{Lecture 9. The differential $F_{*p}$ is defined without coordinates; choosing charts on both sides turns it into a matrix, and the matrix is the Jacobian of the coordinate representation. ``This should be very much reminiscent of the things we said about vector spaces --- another instance of the same thing.''}

Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $\dim M = m$, $\dim N = n$, and $p \in M$. Choose smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ with $p \in U$ and $(V, \psi)$ of $N$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$ --- possible because $F$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}) --- and write
\[
\varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m), \qquad \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n), \qquad \tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}, \qquad F^j = y^j \circ F : U \to \mathbb{R}.
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis} there are bases
\[
\mathcal{B}_M = \Big\{ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p \Big\}_{i=1}^m \ \text{ of } T_pM, \qquad \mathcal{B}_N = \Big\{ \frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_{F(p)} \Big\}_{j=1}^n \ \text{ of } T_{F(p)}N .
\]

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=3.6em]
U \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\varphi"'] & V \arrow[d, "\psi"] \\
\varphi(U) \arrow[r, "\tilde F"'] & \psi(V)
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=4.4em]
T_pM \arrow[r, "F_{*p}"] \arrow[d, "\cong"'] & T_{F(p)}N \arrow[d, "\cong"] \\
\mathbb{R}^m \arrow[r, "\tilde F'(\varphi(p))"'] & \mathbb{R}^n
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Left, the maps: upstairs $F$ between manifolds, downstairs its coordinate representation $\tilde F$ between open sets of Euclidean space. Right, their linearizations: upstairs the differential, intrinsic; downstairs the Jacobian matrix, and the vertical isomorphisms send $\partial/\partial x^i|_p \mapsto e_i$ and $\partial/\partial y^j|_{F(p)} \mapsto e_j$. Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} below says the right-hand square commutes. It is the square of \ref{sub:vs-differential} again, with abstract tangent spaces in place of abstract vector spaces and coordinate bases in place of linear coordinates.

\begin{propbox}[Partial Derivatives Upstairs and Downstairs]\thmlabel{prop:upstairs-downstairs}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, with smooth charts $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ of $M$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ of $N$ such that $F(U) \subseteq V$. Let $F^j = y^j \circ F : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be the components of $F$, functions on the manifold, and $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to \mathbb{R}^n$ the coordinate representation, with components $\tilde F^j = r^j \circ \tilde F$, functions on Euclidean space. Then $F^j \circ \varphi^{-1} = \tilde F^j$, and therefore, for every $p \in U$,
\[
\underbrace{\frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p)}_{\text{upstairs, on } M} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{\partial \tilde F^j}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi(p)\big)}_{\text{downstairs, in } \mathbb{R}^m} .
\]
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Two things are claimed: the identity of functions $F^j \circ \varphi^{-1} = \tilde F^j$ on $\varphi(U)$, and the equality of the two partial derivatives at every $p \in U$.

\emph{The identity of functions.} Both sides are defined on all of $\varphi(U)$: for $r \in \varphi(U)$ the point $\varphi^{-1}(r)$ lies in $U$, so $F(\varphi^{-1}(r)) \in F(U) \subseteq V$, where $y^j$ and $\psi$ are defined. By Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}(2), applied to the chart $(V, \psi)$ of $N$, its coordinate functions are $y^j = r^j \circ \psi$ on $V$. Hence, on $\varphi(U)$,
\[
F^j \circ \varphi^{-1} = y^j \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} = r^j \circ \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} = r^j \circ \tilde F = \tilde F^j ,
\]
where the first equality is the definition $F^j = y^j \circ F$, the second is $y^j = r^j \circ \psi$, the third is the definition $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$, and the fourth is the definition $\tilde F^j = r^j \circ \tilde F$. By Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}(3), the left side is the coordinate representation $(F^j)_\varphi$ of the function $F^j$ in the chart $(U, \varphi)$. So the coordinate representation of $F^j$ is $\tilde F^j$, on all of $\varphi(U)$. In particular $(F^j)_\varphi$ is smooth, since $\tilde F$ is (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}), so $F^j$ is smooth on $U$ and its partial derivatives are defined.

\emph{The partial derivatives.} By Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, the upstairs partial derivative of $F^j$ at $p$ is the ordinary partial derivative of its coordinate representation at $\varphi(p)$; and the two functions $F^j \circ \varphi^{-1}$ and $\tilde F^j$, being equal on the open set $\varphi(U) \ni \varphi(p)$, have the same partial derivatives there. So
\[
\frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p) = \frac{\partial (F^j)_\varphi}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \frac{\partial (F^j \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \frac{\partial \tilde F^j}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi(p)\big) .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Why This Identity Carries So Much]\label{rem:why-this-identity-carries-so-much}
Uribe stated it in Lecture~10 and recalled it at the decisive moment of Lecture~11 --- it is marked with ``!!!'' on page~30 of the handwritten notes. When a student asked whether the matrix in the proof of the normal form should be written with $\tilde F$, the answer was: ``it's the same thing \ldots\ that's how we define partials.'' Partial derivatives on a manifold are \emph{defined} by going downstairs, so the matrix of partials of the components $F^j$ upstairs is literally the ordinary Jacobian of $\tilde F$ downstairs. This is what turns every local computation on a manifold into calculus in $\mathbb{R}^m$, and it is used in:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the matrix of the differential (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}), which is a one-line proof because of it;
    \item regular values in one chart (Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart}): the rank of $F_{*p}$ is the rank of $\tilde F'(\varphi(p))$;
    \item the proof of the local normal form (Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form}), where the matrix $\big[\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)\big]$ is built from the components $F^j$ but is the Jacobian of $\tilde F$;
    \item Assignment~3, Problem~4, whose ``matching coefficients'' step computes $F_{*p}(\partial/\partial u_k|_p)[x^j]$ as an ordinary partial derivative of $F_\varphi$.
\end{enumerate}
Both sides depend on the charts: changing $\varphi$ or $\psi$ changes the matrix (Corollary~\ref{cor:change-coords}), while $F_{*p}$ itself does not.
\end{rembox}

\begin{thmbox}[The Matrix of the Differential]\thmlabel{lem:differential-matrix}
$F_{*p}$ is linear, and
\[
F_{*p}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big) = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_{F(p)} .
\]
So the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the bases $\mathcal{B}_M$, $\mathcal{B}_N$ has the upstairs partials $\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)$ as entries, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs} it is the $n \times m$ Jacobian of the coordinate representation,
\[
\Big[\, \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p) \,\Big]_{j, i} = \tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big),
\]
with $j$ the row index and $i$ the column index. Written out,
\[
\Big[\, \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p) \,\Big]_{j, i} = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial \tilde F^1}{\partial r^1}\big(\varphi(p)\big) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^1}{\partial r^m}\big(\varphi(p)\big) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial \tilde F^n}{\partial r^1}\big(\varphi(p)\big) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^n}{\partial r^m}\big(\varphi(p)\big)
\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose $i$-th column lists the coefficients of $F_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$ in the basis $\mathcal{B}_N$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Computations in Coordinates}}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture 10 --- ``once you think about it a little bit, it's a one-line proof.'')} Three things are claimed: $F_{*p}$ is linear; the displayed formula for $F_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$; and the description of the matrix of $F_{*p}$.

\emph{Linearity.} This is Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}: $F_{*p}$ maps $T_pM$ into $T_{F(p)}N$ and is linear.

\emph{The formula.} Fix $i$ and put $E = F_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$, a derivation at $F(p)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}). The universal formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}, applied at the point $F(p)$ of $N$ with the chart $(V, \psi)$, whose coordinate functions are $y^1, \ldots, y^n$, says that the $j$-th coefficient of any derivation at $F(p)$ is its value on the germ $[y^j]$:
\[
E = \sum_{j=1}^n E\big[y^j\big]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_{F(p)} .
\]
So it suffices to compute $E[y^j]$. By the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}), $E[y^j] = \partial/\partial x^i|_p\,[y^j \circ F]$; the function $y^j \circ F$ is the component $F^j$, defined on $U$ because $F(U) \subseteq V$; and $\partial/\partial x^i|_p[F^j]$ is what Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} writes $\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)$. In one chain:
\[
F_{*p}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big)\big[y^j\big] = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\big[y^j \circ F\big] = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\big[F^j\big] = \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p).
\]
Substituting these coefficients into the universal formula gives $F_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = \sum_j \partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)\, \partial/\partial y^j|_{F(p)}$. That is the formula.

\emph{The matrix.} By Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3), with the basis $e_i = \partial/\partial x^i|_p$ of $T_pM$ (the basis $\mathcal{B}_M$) and the basis $f_j = \partial/\partial y^j|_{F(p)}$ of $T_{F(p)}N$ (the basis $\mathcal{B}_N$), the $i$-th column of the matrix of $F_{*p}$ consists of the coefficients of $F_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$ in the basis $\mathcal{B}_N$, and its entry in row $j$ is the coefficient of $f_j$. By the formula, that coefficient is $\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)$; so $j$ is the row index and $i$ the column index. For the identification with $\tilde F'(\varphi(p))$ --- the ``claim'' of the lecture --- this is Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs}: the partials are \emph{defined} through the chart, and $F^j \circ \varphi^{-1} = \tilde F^j$, so $\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p) = \partial \tilde F^j/\partial r^i(\varphi(p))$, which is the $(j,i)$ entry of $\tilde F'(\varphi(p))$, row $j$ of the Jacobian being the gradient of the $j$-th component $\tilde F^j$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}). So the two $n \times m$ matrices agree entry by entry. ``It's all the same.''
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:abstract-tangent-7}
\textbf{Which index is the row.} Uribe's mnemonic, ``from the mid-nineteenth century'': \emph{gradients go across}. Row $j$ of the matrix is the gradient of the single function $F^j$, so moving along a row changes $i$; the column $i$ is the image of the $i$-th basis vector, as it must be for the matrix of a linear map.
\end{rembox}

\textbf{Transcription notes.} Page 26 of the handwritten notes calls $\mathcal{B}_N$ a basis ``of $T_{F(p)}M$''. Page 27 (Lecture 10) repeats the lemma with the basis written $\{\partial/\partial y^j|_p,\ 1 \le j \le m\}$ ``of $T_{F(p)}M$'' --- three slips at once: the base point is $F(p)$, the index runs to $n = \dim N$, and the space is $T_{F(p)}N$. In the same proof the universal formula is written with $\partial/\partial y^j|_p$ for $\partial/\partial y^j|_{F(p)}$. A student asked whether the index on $F^j$ belongs upstairs or downstairs; upstairs, as for coordinates, with $j$ the row index. Uribe also announced that the partials will from now on be written in calculus notation, $\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)$ rather than $\partial/\partial x^i|_p[F^j]$.

\begin{corbox}[The Chain Rule in Coordinates]\thmlabel{cor:chain-rule-coords}
Let $F : M \to N$ and $G : N \to O$ be smooth, with charts $(U,\varphi)$ at $p$, $(V,\psi)$ at $F(p)$ and $(W,\chi)$ at $G(F(p))$ such that $F(U) \subseteq V$ and $G(V) \subseteq W$, and write $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$, $\tilde G = \chi \circ G \circ \psi^{-1}$ and $\widetilde{G \circ F} = \chi \circ (G \circ F) \circ \varphi^{-1}$ for the coordinate representations. Then $\widetilde{G \circ F} = \tilde G \circ \tilde F$ on $\varphi(U)$, and
\[
\big(\widetilde{G \circ F}\big)'\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \tilde G'\big(\psi(F(p))\big)\; \tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big):
\]
the matrix of $(G \circ F)_{*p}$ is the product of the matrices of $G_{*F(p)}$ and $F_{*p}$. Written out, with $\ell = \dim O$, the partials of $\widetilde{G \circ F}$ and $\tilde F$ taken at $\varphi(p)$ and those of $\tilde G$ at $\psi(F(p))$, this is the product of an $\ell \times n$ and an $n \times m$ matrix:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial (\widetilde{G \circ F})^1}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial (\widetilde{G \circ F})^1}{\partial r^m} \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial (\widetilde{G \circ F})^\ell}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial (\widetilde{G \circ F})^\ell}{\partial r^m}
\end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial \tilde G^1}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde G^1}{\partial r^n} \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial \tilde G^\ell}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde G^\ell}{\partial r^n}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial \tilde F^1}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^1}{\partial r^m} \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial \tilde F^n}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^n}{\partial r^m}
\end{pmatrix},
\]
that is, entry by entry, $\dfrac{\partial (\widetilde{G \circ F})^k}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n \dfrac{\partial \tilde G^k}{\partial r^j}\big(\psi(F(p))\big)\, \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^j}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi(p)\big)$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Computations in Coordinates}}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Two things are claimed: the equality $\widetilde{G \circ F} = \tilde G \circ \tilde F$ on $\varphi(U)$, and the matrix identity.

\emph{The coordinate representations.} First, the charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(W, \chi)$ are admissible for $G \circ F$: $(G \circ F)(U) = G(F(U)) \subseteq G(V) \subseteq W$. Let $r \in \varphi(U)$ and $q = \varphi^{-1}(r) \in U$. Then $F(q) \in F(U) \subseteq V$, so $\psi^{-1}(\psi(F(q))) = F(q)$: the identity $\psi^{-1} \circ \psi$ of $V$ may be inserted between $G$ and $F$. Hence $\chi \circ G \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} = (\chi \circ G \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ (\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1})$ on $\varphi(U)$, that is,
\[
\widetilde{G \circ F}(r) = \chi\big(G(F(q))\big) = \chi\Big(G\big(\psi^{-1}(\psi(F(q)))\big)\Big) = \big(\chi \circ G \circ \psi^{-1}\big)\big((\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1})(r)\big) = \tilde G\big(\tilde F(r)\big),
\]
where $\tilde F(r) = \psi(F(q))$ lies in $\psi(V)$, the domain of $\tilde G$.

\emph{The matrices.} Apply Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} three times, each time in the coordinate bases of the two charts named:
\begin{itemize}
    \item to $F$ at $p$, with $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$: the matrix of $F_{*p}$ is $\tilde F'(\varphi(p))$;
    \item to $G$ at $F(p)$, with $(V, \psi)$ and $(W, \chi)$: the matrix of $G_{*F(p)}$ is $\tilde G'(\psi(F(p)))$;
    \item to $G \circ F$ at $p$ (smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), with $(U, \varphi)$ and $(W, \chi)$, admissible by the inclusion above: the matrix of $(G \circ F)_{*p}$ is $(\widetilde{G \circ F})'(\varphi(p))$.
\end{itemize}
By the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), $(G \circ F)_{*p} = G_{*F(p)} \circ F_{*p}$. By Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3) the matrix of a composite is the product of the matrices, $[AB] = [A][B]$, provided the same basis is used on the middle space for both factors --- here the coordinate basis of $\psi$ at $F(p)$, which is the case. So
\[
\big(\widetilde{G \circ F}\big)'\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \big[(G \circ F)_{*p}\big] = \big[G_{*F(p)} \circ F_{*p}\big] = \big[G_{*F(p)}\big]\,\big[F_{*p}\big] = \tilde G'\big(\psi(F(p))\big)\; \tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big):
\]
the three matrices are the three Jacobians, and the matrix of $(G \circ F)_{*p}$ is the product of the matrices of $G_{*F(p)}$ and $F_{*p}$.

\emph{A second route.} The formula is also the Euclidean chain rule applied to $\widetilde{G \circ F} = \tilde G \circ \tilde F$ at $\varphi(p)$, where $\tilde F(\varphi(p)) = \psi(F(p))$: the Jacobian of a composite of smooth maps between open subsets of Euclidean spaces is the product of the Jacobians, the outer one taken at the image point. The two routes agree, as they must.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=3.6em]
U \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\varphi"'] & V \arrow[r, "G"] \arrow[d, "\psi"] & W \arrow[d, "\chi"] \\
\varphi(U) \arrow[r, "\tilde F"'] & \psi(V) \arrow[r, "\tilde G"'] & \chi(W)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Upstairs the composite of maps between manifolds; downstairs the composite of their coordinate representations. Each square commutes, so the outer rectangle does, and differentiating the bottom row at $\varphi(p)$ multiplies the Jacobians.

\begin{corbox}[Change of Coordinates]\thmlabel{cor:change-coords}
Let $(U, \varphi)$ and $(\tilde U, \tilde\varphi)$ be two smooth charts at $p$, with coordinates $x^i$ and $\tilde x^j$, and $n = \dim M$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The coordinate derivations transform by
    \[
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \tilde x^j}\Big|_p = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial \tilde x^j}(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p ,
    \]
    and the change-of-basis matrix is the Jacobian of the transition function $\varphi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}$ at $\tilde\varphi(p)$. Written out (row $i$, column $j$; the $j$-th column holds the old components of the $j$-th new basis vector):
    \[
    \begin{pmatrix}
    \dfrac{\partial x^1}{\partial \tilde x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial x^1}{\partial \tilde x^n}(p) \\[2mm]
    \vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
    \dfrac{\partial x^n}{\partial \tilde x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial x^n}{\partial \tilde x^n}(p)
    \end{pmatrix}
    = \big(\varphi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}\big)'\big(\tilde\varphi(p)\big) .
    \]
    \item The components of a tangent vector transform by
    \[
    v\big[\tilde x^j\big] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, v\big[x^i\big] \qquad (v \in T_pM,\ j = 1, \ldots, n).
    \]
    In matrix form, the column of new components is the matrix $A$ of (3) times the column of old components:
    \[
    \begin{pmatrix} v[\tilde x^1] \\ \vdots \\ v[\tilde x^n] \end{pmatrix}
    = \begin{pmatrix}
    \dfrac{\partial \tilde x^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde x^1}{\partial x^n}(p) \\[2mm]
    \vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
    \dfrac{\partial \tilde x^n}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde x^n}{\partial x^n}(p)
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix} v[x^1] \\ \vdots \\ v[x^n] \end{pmatrix} .
    \]
    \item The $n \times n$ matrices $A = \big[\partial \tilde x^j/\partial x^i(p)\big]$ (row $j$, column $i$) and $B = \big[\partial x^i/\partial \tilde x^j(p)\big]$ (row $i$, column $j$) are inverse to each other:
    \[
    \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial \tilde x^l}(p) = \delta^j_l, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial \tilde x^j}(p)\, \frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial x^k}(p) = \delta^i_k .
    \]
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Computations in Coordinates}}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Items (2) and (3) not from lecture; filled in.)} Item (1) is an equality of tangent vectors at $p$ for each $j$, together with the identification of the coefficient matrix; (2) and (3) then follow from the Basis Theorem.

\emph{(1) Setting up.} Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} needs a source chart whose domain is mapped into the domain of the target chart. Restrict both charts to the open set $U \cap \tilde U \ni p$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), applied to the open subset $U \cap \tilde U$ of $U$ and of $\tilde U$, the restrictions are again smooth charts. This changes neither the coordinate derivations at $p$ nor the partial derivatives at $p$, since these are ordinary partial derivatives at $\varphi(p)$, resp.\ $\tilde\varphi(p)$, which depend only on the functions near that point (the remark on shrinking the chart domain in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:coord-is-derivation}). So we may assume $U = \tilde U$.

\emph{(1) Applying the theorem.} Take $F = \mathrm{id}_M$, which is smooth, with the chart $(\tilde U, \tilde\varphi)$, coordinates $\tilde x^j$, on the source and the chart $(U, \varphi)$, coordinates $x^i$, on the target; then $\mathrm{id}_M(\tilde U) = U$. The components of $F$ in the target chart are $F^i = x^i \circ \mathrm{id}_M = x^i$, and the coordinate representation is $\varphi \circ \mathrm{id}_M \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1} = \varphi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}$, the transition function. Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, with $\tilde x^j$ in the role of the source coordinates and $x^i$ in the role of the target coordinates, gives
\[
(\mathrm{id}_M)_{*p}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial \tilde x^j}\Big|_p\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial \tilde x^j}(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p .
\]
By Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}, $(\mathrm{id}_M)_{*p} = \mathrm{id}_{T_pM}$, so the left side is $\partial/\partial \tilde x^j|_p$. That is the formula.

\emph{(1) The matrix.} The formula says that the $j$-th new basis vector $\partial/\partial \tilde x^j|_p$ has the coordinates $\partial x^i/\partial \tilde x^j(p)$ in the old basis $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$, so the change-of-basis matrix $P$ of Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(4) (defined by $e'_j = \sum_i P_{ij}\, e_i$) has entries $P_{ij} = \partial x^i/\partial \tilde x^j(p)$. This is the matrix of $(\mathrm{id}_M)_{*p}$ in the two coordinate bases, and by the second part of Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} it is the Jacobian of the coordinate representation $\varphi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}$ at $\tilde\varphi(p)$.

\emph{(2)} Fix $v \in T_pM$. The universal formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}, in the chart $(U, \varphi)$, gives $v = \sum_i v[x^i]\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p$. Apply both sides to the germ $[\tilde x^j]$ at $p$ ($\tilde x^j$ is smooth on $\tilde U \ni p$). Derivations are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}), and $\partial/\partial x^i|_p[\tilde x^j]$ is what Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} writes $\partial \tilde x^j/\partial x^i(p)$; so
\[
v\big[\tilde x^j\big] = \sum_{i=1}^n v\big[x^i\big]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\big[\tilde x^j\big] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, v\big[x^i\big] .
\]

\emph{(3)} First, a coordinate function differentiated with respect to the coordinates of its own chart gives the Kronecker delta: by Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} in the chart $(\tilde U, \tilde\varphi)$, and $(\tilde x^j)_{\tilde\varphi} = r^j$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}(3)),
\[
\frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial \tilde x^l}(p) = \frac{\partial (\tilde x^j)_{\tilde\varphi}}{\partial r^l}\big(\tilde\varphi(p)\big) = \frac{\partial r^j}{\partial r^l}\big(\tilde\varphi(p)\big) = \delta^j_l ,
\]
and in the same way $\partial x^i/\partial x^k(p) = \delta^i_k$ in the chart $(U, \varphi)$. Now evaluate the germ $[\tilde x^j]$ on the vector $\partial/\partial \tilde x^l|_p$ in two ways: directly it gives $\delta^j_l$; and by (2), applied to $v = \partial/\partial \tilde x^l|_p$, whose components are $v[x^i] = \partial x^i/\partial \tilde x^l(p)$,
\[
\delta^j_l = \frac{\partial}{\partial \tilde x^l}\Big|_p\big[\tilde x^j\big] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial \tilde x^l}\Big|_p\big[x^i\big] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial \tilde x^l}(p) = (AB)_{jl} .
\]
The second identity is the same computation with the two charts exchanged (rename $(U, \varphi, x^i) \leftrightarrow (\tilde U, \tilde\varphi, \tilde x^j)$). Written out: (2) for the exchanged charts reads $v[x^i] = \sum_j \partial x^i/\partial \tilde x^j(p)\, v[\tilde x^j]$, and with $v = \partial/\partial x^k|_p$,
\[
\delta^i_k = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}\Big|_p\big[x^i\big] = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial \tilde x^j}(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^k}\Big|_p\big[\tilde x^j\big] = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial \tilde x^j}(p)\, \frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial x^k}(p) = (BA)_{ik} .
\]
So $AB = I = BA$. (Either identity alone suffices: an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with $BA = I$ is injective, hence invertible by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1), and then $B = BAA^{-1} = A^{-1}$.) By (1), $B$ is the Jacobian of $\varphi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}$ at $\tilde\varphi(p)$, and, by (1) with the charts exchanged, $A$ is the Jacobian of $\tilde\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ at $\varphi(p)$: (3) says that the Jacobians of the two mutually inverse transition functions are inverse matrices, as the Euclidean chain rule predicts.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Polar Coordinates]\exlabel{ex:polar-derivations}
On $M = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{(x, 0) \mid x \le 0\}$ take the standard chart $(x, y)$ and the polar chart $(r, \theta)$, $0 < r$, $-\pi < \theta < \pi$, with $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:change-coords},
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial r} = \cos\theta\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x} + \sin\theta\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y}, \qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} = -r\sin\theta\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x} + r\cos\theta\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y},
\]
the coefficients being $\partial x/\partial r$, $\partial y/\partial r$ and $\partial x/\partial\theta$, $\partial y/\partial\theta$. In matrix form, the change-of-basis matrix of Corollary~\ref{cor:change-coords}(1) --- the Jacobian of the transition $(r, \theta) \mapsto (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ --- has these coefficients as its columns:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial r} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial r} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix} .
\]
\leeref{cf.\ Example C.37}
\end{exbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.15]
\draw[gray!40,->] (-0.4,0) -- (3.4,0) node[anchor=north west,font=\footnotesize]{$x$};
\draw[gray!40,->] (0,-0.4) -- (0,3.0) node[anchor=south east,font=\footnotesize]{$y$};
\draw[gray!40,dashed] (0,0) -- (35:3.3);
\draw[gray!40,dashed] (5:2.2) arc (5:85:2.2);
\draw[gray!55] (0.55,0) arc (0:35:0.55); \node[gray!60!black,font=\scriptsize] at (17:0.8) {$\theta$};
\fill (35:2.2) circle (1.6pt);
\node[font=\footnotesize,anchor=north west] at ($(35:2.2)+(0.05,-0.08)$) {$p$};
\draw[gray!65,->,thick] (35:2.2) -- ++(0.7,0) node[anchor=west,font=\scriptsize]{$\partial_x$};
\draw[gray!65,->,thick] (35:2.2) -- ++(0,0.7) node[anchor=south,font=\scriptsize]{$\partial_y$};
\draw[violet!75!black,->,very thick] (35:2.2) -- ++(35:0.7) node[anchor=south west,font=\footnotesize]{$\partial_r$};
\draw[orange!85!black,->,very thick] (35:2.2) -- ++(125:1.54) node[anchor=south east,font=\footnotesize]{$\partial_\theta$};
\node[font=\footnotesize,align=left,anchor=west] at (3.6,1.6) {same abstract $T_pM$, two bases:\\[2pt] $\partial_r$ has length $1$,\\ $\partial_\theta$ has length $r$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

At a point $p$ at radius $r$, the four coordinate derivations --- elements of the abstract tangent space $T_pM$ --- drawn as the vectors of $T^{\geo}_pM = \mathbb{R}^2$ they correspond to under the identification $\partial_x \leftrightarrow e_1$, $\partial_y \leftrightarrow e_2$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree} below (all at the common scale $0.7$). The polar ones are the radial and tangential directions, but $\partial_\theta$ is not a unit vector: it has length $r$, because it records the velocity of the curve $\theta \mapsto (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ along which the other coordinate is held fixed. A coordinate vector depends on the whole chart, not only on its own coordinate function --- the same abstract tangent space, and a different matrix for every map out of it.

\begin{propbox}[Agreement with the Vector-Space Differential]\thmlabel{prop:differential-agree}
Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open, $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth, and $a \in W$, and identify the abstract tangent spaces $T_aW \cong \mathbb{R}^m$ and $T_{F(a)}\mathbb{R}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^n$ by $\partial/\partial r^i \mapsto e_i$ --- that is, with the geometric tangent spaces $T^{\geo}_aW = \mathbb{R}^m$ and $T^{\geo}_{F(a)}\mathbb{R}^n = \mathbb{R}^n$. Then $F_{*a}$ corresponds to the Jacobian $F'(a)$, i.e.\ to the differential $dF_a$ of \ref{sub:vs-differential}. Under the same identification, $v = \sum_i v^i e_i$ corresponds to the derivation
\[
[g] \longmapsto \sum_i v^i\, \frac{\partial g}{\partial r^i}(a) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} g(a + tv),
\]
the directional derivative $D_v$ of \S\ref{sub:derivations-motivation}.
\leeref{Proposition 3.13 and Corollary 3.3}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
On $W$ use the identity chart $(W, \mathrm{id}_W)$, whose coordinate functions are the standard coordinates $r^1, \ldots, r^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}), and on $\mathbb{R}^n$ the identity chart, with coordinates $r^1, \ldots, r^n$. In an identity chart the coordinate representation of a function $g$ is $g$ itself, so by Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} the coordinate derivation $\partial/\partial r^i|_a$ sends $[g]$ to the ordinary partial derivative $\partial g/\partial r^i(a)$.

\emph{The differential.} Apply Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} with the identity charts; this is allowed, since $F(W) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. The coordinate representation is $\tilde F = \mathrm{id} \circ F \circ \mathrm{id}^{-1} = F$, so the theorem gives
\[
F_{*a}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_a\Big) = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial r^i}(a)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^j}\Big|_{F(a)} ,
\]
and the matrix of $F_{*a}$ in these bases is $F'(a)$. Under the identifications $\partial/\partial r^i|_a \mapsto e_i$ and $\partial/\partial r^j|_{F(a)} \mapsto e_j$, this says that the linear map $\mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ corresponding to $F_{*a}$ sends $e_i$ to $\sum_j \partial F^j/\partial r^i(a)\, e_j$, the $i$-th column of $F'(a)$, which is $F'(a)\,e_i$. Two linear maps that agree on a basis are equal (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(2)), so $F_{*a}$ corresponds to $F'(a)$. This is also the differential $dF_a$ of \ref{sub:vs-differential}: in Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential} with the identity coordinates $L = \mathrm{id}$ and $K = \mathrm{id}$, $dF_a = K^{-1} \circ F'(a) \circ L = F'(a)$.

\emph{The directional derivative.} Under the identification, $v = \sum_i v^i e_i$ corresponds to $D = \sum_i v^i\, \partial/\partial r^i|_a$. For a germ $[g]$ at $a$, since derivations are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}) and by the identity-chart partials above,
\[
D[g] = \sum_{i=1}^m v^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_a[g] = \sum_{i=1}^m v^i\, \frac{\partial g}{\partial r^i}(a) .
\]
For the second expression, apply the chain rule to $t \mapsto g(a + tv)$: the curve $c(t) = a + tv$ lies in the open domain of a representative $g$ for $|t|$ small, with $c(0) = a$ and $c'(0) = v$, so by the chain rule for a curve (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian})
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} g(a + tv) = \nabla g(a) \cdot c'(0) = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial g}{\partial r^i}(a)\, v^i ,
\]
the same number. So $D$ is the directional derivative $D_v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[The Tangent Space to a Vector Space]\thmlabel{cor:tangent-vs}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space with its standard smooth structure, and $a \in V$. The map
\[
V \to T_aV, \qquad v \mapsto D_v|_a, \qquad D_v|_a[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f(a + tv),
\]
is a linear isomorphism, defined without any choice of basis. For every linear map $L : V \to W$, $L_{*a}(D_v|_a) = D_{Lv}|_{La}$.
\leeref{Proposition 3.13}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Let $m = \dim V$. To show: $D_v|_a$ is a well-defined derivation at $a$; the transformation rule for linear $L$; that $v \mapsto D_v|_a$ is a linear isomorphism; and that no basis is involved.

\emph{Well defined on germs.} Let $b, w$ be vectors of a finite-dimensional vector space and $g$ smooth on an open neighbourhood of $b$. For $|t|$ small, $b + tw$ lies in that neighbourhood, and $t \mapsto g(b + tw)$ is smooth, as the composite of $g$ with the smooth curve $t \mapsto b + tw$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). Its derivative at $0$ depends only on the values of $g$ near $b$, hence only on the germ $[g]$. So $D_w|_b[g] = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_0\, g(b + tw)$ is a well-defined map on germs at $b$.

\emph{A computation on germs.} Let $L : V \to W$ be linear, $b, w \in V$, and $[g]$ a germ at $Lb$ on $W$. Since $L(b + tw) = Lb + t\,Lw$ by linearity,
\[
D_w|_b[g \circ L] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} g\big(L(b + tw)\big) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} g\big(Lb + t\,Lw\big) = D_{Lw}|_{Lb}[g] . \tag{A}
\]

\emph{$D_v|_a$ is a derivation.} Choose a linear coordinate system $L_0 : V \to \mathbb{R}^m$. It is a chart of $V$ with domain $V$ and image $\mathbb{R}^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:vs-structure}), hence a diffeomorphism $V \to \mathbb{R}^m$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), with linear inverse $L_0^{-1}$. Apply (A) to the linear map $L_0^{-1} : \mathbb{R}^m \to V$, at the point $b = L_0a$, with the vector $w = L_0v$: for every germ $[g]$ at $a$ on $V$,
\[
D_{L_0v}|_{L_0a}\big[g \circ L_0^{-1}\big] = D_v|_a[g] .
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree} (its second statement, on $\mathbb{R}^m$), $D_{L_0v}|_{L_0a} = \sum_i (L_0v)^i\, \partial/\partial r^i|_{L_0a}$, a linear combination of coordinate derivations (Proposition~\ref{prop:coord-is-derivation}), hence a derivation at $L_0a$. So by the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}) the left side is $\big((L_0^{-1})_{*L_0a} D_{L_0v}|_{L_0a}\big)[g]$, and
\[
D_v|_a = (L_0^{-1})_{*L_0a}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^m (L_0v)^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_{L_0a}\Big) . \tag{B}
\]
A pushforward of a derivation is a derivation (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}), here at $L_0^{-1}(L_0a) = a$. So $D_v|_a \in T_aV$.

\emph{Isomorphism.} By (B), $v \mapsto D_v|_a$ is the composite of three maps:
\[
V \xrightarrow{\ L_0\ } \mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow T_{L_0a}\mathbb{R}^m \xrightarrow{\ (L_0^{-1})_{*L_0a}\ } T_aV, \qquad v \mapsto w = L_0v \mapsto \sum_i w^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^i}\Big|_{L_0a} \mapsto D_v|_a .
\]
The first is a linear isomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:linear-coords}); the second is a linear isomorphism because the $\partial/\partial r^i|_{L_0a}$ form a basis of $T_{L_0a}\mathbb{R}^m$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}, identity chart); the third is a linear isomorphism because $L_0^{-1}$ is a diffeomorphism (Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo}). A composite of linear isomorphisms is one, so $v \mapsto D_v|_a$ is a linear isomorphism.

\emph{The rule for linear $L$.} A linear $L : V \to W$ is smooth: in linear coordinates $L_0$ on $V$ and $K$ on $W$ its coordinate representation $K \circ L \circ L_0^{-1}$ is linear, hence smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:vs-manifold}). Both $L_{*a}(D_v|_a)$ and $D_{Lv}|_{La}$ are derivations at $La$ (by the previous steps, applied in $V$ and in $W$), and for every germ $[g]$ at $La$, by the definition of the pushforward and then (A),
\[
L_{*a}(D_v|_a)[g] = D_v|_a[g \circ L] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0\, g(La + t\,Lv) = D_{Lv}|_{La}[g] .
\]
So $L_{*a}(D_v|_a) = D_{Lv}|_{La}$. In particular, for $L = L_0$, the isomorphism $(L_0)_{*a}$ carries $D_v|_a$ to $D_{L_0 v}|_{L_0 a}$, which is $\sum_i (L_0v)^i\,\partial/\partial r^i$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}: this is (B) read backwards, $(L_0)_{*a}$ being the inverse of $(L_0^{-1})_{*L_0a}$ (Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo}).

\emph{No basis.} The defining formula $D_v|_a[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_0 f(a + tv)$ mentions no basis; the linear coordinates $L_0$ entered only in the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:abstract-tangent-8}
This is what licenses the shared notation $dF_p$: on open subsets of Euclidean spaces the abstract differential \emph{is} the Jacobian, and between vector spaces it is the map of Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves}. It also closes a loop opened in \S\ref{sub:derivations-motivation}, where a tangent vector $v$ was traded for the operator $D_v$; in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that trade is exactly the identification $e_i \leftrightarrow \partial/\partial r^i$.
\end{rembox}

\begin{rembox}[Any Vector Space Will Do]\label{rem:translations-identify}
\textit{Lecture~17.} Nothing above needs $\mathbb{R}^N$: the ambient space can be any finite-dimensional vector space $V$, because the velocity
\[
\gamma'(0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{h}\big(\gamma(h) - \gamma(0)\big)
\]
makes sense in any vector space with a topology in which to take the limit (``you could take it in a Banach space \ldots\ if you're doing functional analysis'').
\end{rembox}

Moreover, all the tangent spaces of $V$ are identified with one another, and with $V$, by \emph{translations}.

\begin{defbox}[Translation]\deflabel{def:translation}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space and $p \in V$ (``I want to call it $p$ because I want to think of it as a point''). The \textbf{translation} by $p$ is
\[
\tau_p : V \to V, \qquad \tau_p(v) = v + p ,
\]
the unique translation mapping $0$ to $p$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Translations Identify the Tangent Spaces of a Vector Space]\thmlabel{prop:translations-identify}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space and $p \in V$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\tau_p$ is a diffeomorphism of $V$, with inverse $\tau_{-p}$.
    \item $(\tau_p)_{*0} : T_0V \to T_pV$ is a linear isomorphism, and $(\tau_p)_{*0}\big(D_v|_0\big) = D_v|_p$ for every $v \in V$.
\end{enumerate}
So the composite $V \cong T_0V \to T_pV$ is $v \mapsto D_v|_p$, the identification of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17: ``its pushforward is the identification''; filled in.)}

\emph{(1)} Fix a linear coordinate system $L : V \to \mathbb{R}^m$, a chart of $V$ with domain $V$ (Definition~\ref{def:vs-structure}), and put $\tilde p = L(p)$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$, by the definition of $\tau_p$ and the linearity of $L$,
\[
\big(L \circ \tau_p \circ L^{-1}\big)(x) = L\big(L^{-1}x + p\big) = x + \tilde p .
\]
So in linear coordinates $\tau_p$ is $x \mapsto x + \tilde p$, which is smooth; and $\tau_p = L^{-1} \circ (x \mapsto x + \tilde p) \circ L$ is continuous. By Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, $\tau_p$ is smooth. The same computation with $-p$ in place of $p$ shows that $\tau_{-p}$ is smooth, and $\tau_{-p}(\tau_p(v)) = v + p - p = v$, $\tau_p(\tau_{-p}(v)) = v - p + p = v$. So $\tau_p$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse $\tau_{-p}$, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}).

\emph{(2)} Since $\tau_p(0) = p$, the pushforward goes $(\tau_p)_{*0} : T_0V \to T_pV$. The pushforward along a diffeomorphism is a linear isomorphism (Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo}, applied to $\tau_p$ by (1)). For $v \in V$ and $g$ smooth near $p$, by the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}), the definition of $D_v|_0$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}) together with $(g \circ \tau_p)(0 + tv) = g(tv + p)$, and the definition of $D_v|_p$,
\[
(\tau_p)_{*0}\big(D_v|_0\big)[g] = D_v|_0[g \circ \tau_p] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} g(p + tv) = D_v|_p[g] .
\]
Both sides are derivations at $p$ that take the same value on every germ, so $(\tau_p)_{*0}(D_v|_0) = D_v|_p$.

\emph{The composite.} The identification $V \cong T_0V$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} is $v \mapsto D_v|_0$; following it by $(\tau_p)_{*0}$ gives, by (2), $v \mapsto D_v|_0 \mapsto D_v|_p$, the identification of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} at $p$.
\end{proof}

``This is a canonical way to identify all of these tangent vectors. \ldots\ That's what we did already'': a geometric tangent vector to the circle at $p$ was drawn as a vector in $\mathbb{R}^2$, which silently translates it back to the origin.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 17).} Page~45 of the handwritten notes writes the identification as ``$T_pM \cong T_0V \cong V$''; it is $T_pV \cong T_0V \cong V$.

Uribe added: ``this is actually kind of like a left-invariant vector field. It is a left-invariant vector field.'' For fixed $v$, the field $p \mapsto D_v|_p$ is the left-invariant field, with value $D_v|_0$ at the identity, of the Lie group $(V, +)$ (Example~\ref{ex:vs-lie-algebra}).

\begin{defbox}[Rank of a Smooth Map]\deflabel{def:manifold-rank}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map. The \textbf{rank} of $F$ at $p$ is the rank of the linear map $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ of abstract tangent spaces; by Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} it is the rank of the Jacobian of any coordinate representation.
\leeref{Ch.~4 and Ch.~5, p.~105}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Regular Point of a Smooth Map]\deflabel{def:manifold-regular-point}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map. A point $p$ is a \textbf{regular point} of $F$ if $F_{*p}$ is surjective.
\leeref{Ch.~4 and Ch.~5, p.~105}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Regular Value of a Smooth Map]\deflabel{def:manifold-regular}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map. A value $c \in N$ is a \textbf{regular value} if every $p \in F^{-1}(c)$ is a regular point (Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point}).
\leeref{Ch.~4 and Ch.~5, p.~105}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}[The Map Is Intrinsic --- the Matrix Is Not]\label{rem:map-intrinsic-matrix-not}
Uribe's closing point. The linear map $F_{*p}$ is defined with no choices, but its matrix depends on both charts: by Corollary~\ref{cor:change-coords}, changing them multiplies the matrix on each side by the Jacobian of a transition function. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} Explicitly, if $(U', \varphi')$ and $(V', \psi')$ are other charts at $p$ and $F(p)$ with $F(U') \subseteq V'$, and $\hat F = \psi' \circ F \circ \varphi'^{-1}$ is the coordinate representation in them, then near $\varphi'(p)$, $\hat F = (\psi' \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ \tilde F \circ (\varphi \circ \varphi'^{-1})$, and the Euclidean chain rule gives the product of an $n \times n$, an $n \times m$ and an $m \times m$ matrix,
\[
\hat F'\big(\varphi'(p)\big) = \big(\psi' \circ \psi^{-1}\big)'\big(\psi(F(p))\big)\; \tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big)\; \big(\varphi \circ \varphi'^{-1}\big)'\big(\varphi'(p)\big),
\]
the outer two factors being invertible. So only properties of $F_{*p}$ that survive such changes --- its rank, kernel and image, injectivity and surjectivity --- are properties of $F$, which is why the definition above is phrased through $F_{*p}$ rather than through a matrix. By Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree} it agrees with Definitions~\ref{def:regular-point} and~\ref{def:regular-value} in the Euclidean case. A regular point is exactly a point at which $F$ is a \emph{submersion}, in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:submersion}; maps with bijective, surjective and injective differentials are the subject of \ref{sec:special-maps}.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[Regular Values Inside One Chart]\thmlabel{prop:regular-one-chart}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map between smooth manifolds of dimensions $m$ and $n$, and $c \in N$. Suppose there are smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ and $(V, \psi)$ of $N$ with
\[
F^{-1}(c) \subseteq U, \qquad c \in V, \qquad F(U) \subseteq V .
\]
Let $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be the coordinate representation of $F$, a smooth map on the open set $\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$, and put $\tilde c = \psi(c) \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\varphi$ restricts to a homeomorphism from the level set $F^{-1}(c) \subseteq M$ onto the Euclidean level set $\tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c) \subseteq \varphi(U)$;
    \item $c$ is a regular value of $F$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular} if and only if $\tilde c$ is a regular value of $\tilde F$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:regular-value};
    \item in that case $F^{-1}(c)$ is a topological manifold of dimension $m - n$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{(1)} Let $x \in \varphi(U)$ and $q = \varphi^{-1}(x) \in U$. Then $F(q) \in F(U) \subseteq V$ and $c \in V$, and $\psi$ is injective on $V$; with the definitions $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ and $\tilde c = \psi(c)$,
\[
\tilde F(x) = \tilde c \iff \psi\big(F(q)\big) = \psi(c) \iff F(q) = c .
\]
So $x \in \tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c)$ exactly when $\varphi^{-1}(x) \in F^{-1}(c)$; as $\varphi : U \to \varphi(U)$ is a bijection, this says $\varphi\big(F^{-1}(c) \cap U\big) = \tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c)$. And $F^{-1}(c) \cap U = F^{-1}(c)$ by the hypothesis $F^{-1}(c) \subseteq U$. A homeomorphism restricts to a homeomorphism from any subset onto its image, both with the subspace topology (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(3)); applied to the chart $\varphi : U \to \varphi(U)$ and the subset $F^{-1}(c)$, it gives the homeomorphism $F^{-1}(c) \to \tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c)$.

\emph{(2)} The map $\tilde F$ is smooth on the open set $\varphi(U)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}), so its Jacobian is defined. Let $p \in F^{-1}(c)$. By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the coordinate bases of the two charts is the Jacobian $\tilde F'(\varphi(p))$. A linear map $A : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ is surjective exactly when its image, a subspace of dimension $\operatorname{rank} A$, is all of the $n$-dimensional target, i.e.\ when $\operatorname{rank} A = n$; and $\operatorname{rank} A$ is the rank of its matrix (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)). So
\[
F_{*p} \text{ surjective} \iff \operatorname{rank} \tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big) = n \iff \tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big) : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n \text{ surjective}:
\]
$p$ is a regular point of $F$ (Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point}) if and only if $\varphi(p)$ is a regular point of $\tilde F$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-point}, applied to $\tilde F$ on $\varphi(U)$). By (1), $p$ runs over $F^{-1}(c)$ exactly as $\varphi(p)$ runs over $\tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c)$. Hence every point of $F^{-1}(c)$ is a regular point of $F$ --- that is, $c$ is a regular value of $F$ (Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular}) --- if and only if every point of $\tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c)$ is a regular point of $\tilde F$ --- that is, $\tilde c$ is a regular value of $\tilde F$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}).

\emph{(3)} If $F^{-1}(c)$ is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, at a point $p$ of it $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ is surjective, so $m \ge n$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)). By (2), $\tilde c$ is a regular value of the smooth map $\tilde F$ on the open set $\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$, so Corollary~\ref{cor:rvt-open}, applied with $k = n$ and $m - n$ in place of its $n$ (so that $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ becomes $\mathbb{R}^m$), shows that the Euclidean level set $\tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c)$ is a topological manifold of dimension $m - n$. By (1), $F^{-1}(c)$ is homeomorphic to it, and being a topological manifold of a given dimension is preserved by homeomorphisms: second countability, the Hausdorff property and local Euclideanness (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}) are all defined through open sets, which a homeomorphism matches up.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=4.4em]
F^{-1}(c) \subseteq U \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\varphi"', "\cong"] & \{c\} \subseteq V \arrow[d, "\psi"] \\
\tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c) \subseteq \varphi(U) \arrow[r, "\tilde F"'] & \{\tilde c\} \subseteq \psi(V)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The proposition in one square. The level set upstairs is carried by the chart onto a level set downstairs, in Euclidean space, and the question ``is $c$ regular?'' is carried with it: surjectivity of $F_{*p}$ upstairs is the rank of $\tilde F'$ downstairs.

\begin{rembox}[The Strategy]\label{rem:strategy}
To show that $c$ is a regular value of a map between manifolds, and to see its level set:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{Locate the level set.} Show that $F^{-1}(c)$ lies inside a single chart domain $U$, and that $F(U)$ lies in a chart domain $V$ around $c$.
    \item \emph{Go downstairs.} Write the coordinate representation $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$, an ordinary map between open subsets of Euclidean spaces.
    \item \emph{Compute as in \ref{sec:rvt}.} Check that the Jacobian of $\tilde F$ has full rank $n$ at every point of the Euclidean level set $\tilde F^{-1}(\tilde c)$.
    \item \emph{Come back up.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart}, $c$ is a regular value of $F$, and $F^{-1}(c)$ is homeomorphic, through the chart, to a Euclidean regular level set: a manifold of dimension $\dim M - \dim N$.
\end{enumerate}
Assignment~3, Problem~4 is exactly this. For the moment map $F : \mathbb{CP}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ and $c$ in the interior of the simplex, every point of $F^{-1}(c)$ has all homogeneous coordinates nonzero, so $F^{-1}(c) \subseteq U_0$ (step 1). The target chart is the identity of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\varphi_0(U_0) = \mathbb{C}^n \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n}$, so $\tilde F$ is an explicit rational map $\mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ (step 2). Its Jacobian has rank $n$ on the level set (step 3; computed in Example~\ref{ex:moment-map}). So the fibre is an $n$-dimensional manifold (step 4) --- in this case a regular level set of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ itself, exactly the situation of \ref{sec:rvt}. When a level set does not fit in one chart, the same argument applies around each of its points separately, as the next corollary shows.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[The Moment Map on $\mathbb{CP}^n$]\exlabel{ex:moment-map}
Let $F : \mathbb{CP}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be the moment map,
\[
F\big([z_0 : \cdots : z_n]\big) = \Big( \frac{|z_1|^2}{|\vec z|^2}, \ldots, \frac{|z_n|^2}{|\vec z|^2} \Big), \qquad |\vec z|^2 = \sum_{i=0}^n |z_i|^2 ,
\]
and let $\mathring\Delta = \{\, t \in \mathbb{R}^n : t_j > 0 \text{ for all } j, \ \sum_j t_j < 1 \,\}$ be the open simplex. Every $c \in \mathring\Delta$ is a regular value of $F$.
\end{exbox}

\textit{Assignment~3, Problem~4.} Parts (a) and (b) show that $F$ is well defined and smooth, with image the closed simplex $\Delta = \{t : t_j \ge 0, \ \sum_j t_j \le 1\}$, whose interior is $\mathring\Delta$; part (c) is the statement above.

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~3, Problem~4(c); the route of the official solution. It supplies the computation that step~3 of the remark \emph{The Strategy} only asserts.)} We follow the four steps of the remark, with the chart $(U_0, \varphi_0)$ of Definition~\ref{def:cpn-charts} and the identity chart of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

\emph{Step 1: locate the level sets.} For $[\vec z] \in \mathbb{CP}^n$ with $F([\vec z]) = t$,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n t_j = \frac{|\vec z|^2 - |z_0|^2}{|\vec z|^2} = 1 - \frac{|z_0|^2}{|\vec z|^2} .
\]
So $t_j > 0$ for all $j \ge 1$ if and only if $z_j \neq 0$ for all $j \ge 1$, and $\sum_j t_j < 1$ if and only if $z_0 \neq 0$. Hence $F^{-1}(\mathring\Delta)$ is the set of points with all homogeneous coordinates nonzero. It lies in $U_0$, and $\varphi_0$ maps it onto the open set $O = \{ w \in \mathbb{C}^n : w_j \neq 0 \text{ for all } j \}$.

\emph{Step 2: go downstairs.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:cpn-chart}, $\varphi_0^{-1}(w) = [1 : w_1 : \cdots : w_n]$, so
\[
\tilde F(w) = F\big(\varphi_0^{-1}(w)\big) = \Big( \frac{|w_1|^2}{1 + |w|^2}, \ldots, \frac{|w_n|^2}{1 + |w|^2} \Big), \qquad |w|^2 = \sum_{l=1}^n |w_l|^2 .
\]
On $O$ it factors as $\tilde F = \Phi \circ \psi$, with $\mathbb{R}^n_{>0} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_j > 0 \text{ for all } j\}$ and
\[
\psi : O \to \mathbb{R}^n_{>0}, \quad \psi(w) = \big(|w_1|, \ldots, |w_n|\big), \qquad
\Phi : \mathbb{R}^n_{>0} \to \mathring\Delta, \quad \Phi(x) = \Big( \frac{x_1^2}{1 + |x|^2}, \ldots, \frac{x_n^2}{1 + |x|^2} \Big),
\]
since $\Phi(\psi(w))_j = |w_j|^2 / (1 + \sum_l |w_l|^2) = \tilde F(w)_j$.

\emph{Step 3a: $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism.} $\Phi$ takes values in $\mathring\Delta$: $\Phi(x)_j > 0$, and $\sum_j \Phi(x)_j = |x|^2/(1 + |x|^2) < 1$. Let
\[
H : \mathring\Delta \to \mathbb{R}^n_{>0}, \qquad H(t) = \Big( \sqrt{\frac{t_1}{1 - \sum_l t_l}}, \ldots, \sqrt{\frac{t_n}{1 - \sum_l t_l}} \Big) .
\]
Both maps are smooth: their components are rational functions with nonvanishing denominators, composed in $H$ with the square root on $(0, \infty)$. They are inverse to each other. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^n_{>0}$ and $t = \Phi(x)$: $1 - \sum_l t_l = 1/(1 + |x|^2)$, so $t_j/(1 - \sum_l t_l) = x_j^2$ and $H(t)_j = x_j$, as $x_j > 0$. For $t \in \mathring\Delta$ and $x = H(t)$: $|x|^2 = \sum_l t_l/(1 - \sum_l t_l)$, so $1 + |x|^2 = 1/(1 - \sum_l t_l)$ and $\Phi(x)_j = x_j^2\,(1 - \sum_l t_l) = t_j$. By the chain rule applied to $H \circ \Phi = \mathrm{id}$, $H'(\Phi(x))\,\Phi'(x) = I_n$, so the $n \times n$ matrix $\Phi'(x)$ is invertible.

\emph{Step 3b: $\psi'$ has rank $n$.} In the real coordinates $w_j = u_j + i v_j$, ordered $(u_1, v_1, \ldots, u_n, v_n)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:complex-groups}, $\psi_j = \sqrt{u_j^2 + v_j^2}$ is smooth on $O$, with $\partial\psi_j/\partial u_j = u_j/|w_j|$, $\partial\psi_j/\partial v_j = v_j/|w_j|$, and all other partials $0$:
\[
\psi'(w) = \begin{pmatrix}
\frac{u_1}{|w_1|} & \frac{v_1}{|w_1|} & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \frac{u_2}{|w_2|} & \frac{v_2}{|w_2|} & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\
\vdots & & & & \ddots & & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \frac{u_n}{|w_n|} & \frac{v_n}{|w_n|}
\end{pmatrix} \qquad (n \times 2n).
\]
Row $j$ is nonzero, its two entries forming the unit vector $(u_j, v_j)/|w_j|$, and different rows have nonzero entries in disjoint columns. So the rows are linearly independent and $\operatorname{rank}\psi'(w) = n$.

\emph{Step 3c: $\tilde F'$ has rank $n$ on $O$.} By the chain rule, $\tilde F'(w) = \Phi'(\psi(w))\,\psi'(w)$. Multiplying by the invertible matrix $\Phi'(\psi(w))$ does not change the rank, so $\operatorname{rank}\tilde F'(w) = n$. In words: if $F = \Phi \circ \psi$ with $\Phi$ a diffeomorphism, then $F$ is a submersion exactly where $\psi$ is.

\emph{Step 4: come back up.} Let $c \in \mathring\Delta$ and $p \in F^{-1}(c)$. By Step~1, $p \in U_0$ and $w = \varphi_0(p) \in O$. By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the coordinate bases of $\varphi_0$ and of the identity chart is $\tilde F'(w)$, of rank $n$ by Step~3c. So $F_{*p}$ is onto the $n$-dimensional space $T_c\mathbb{R}^n$, and $c$ is a regular value. By Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart}, $F^{-1}(c)$ is a manifold of dimension $2n - n = n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof (as submitted, Assignment~3)]
Step~3 by a direct computation of $\tilde F'$, without the factorization. Write $S = 1 + \sum_{l=1}^n (u_l^2 + v_l^2)$ and $|w_j|^2 = u_j^2 + v_j^2$, so that $\tilde F^j = |w_j|^2/S$ with $S \ge 1$. Since $\partial |w_j|^2/\partial u_k = 2u_k\delta_{jk}$ and $\partial S/\partial u_k = 2u_k$, the quotient rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial \tilde F^j}{\partial u_k} = \frac{2u_k}{S^2}\big(\delta_{jk}\,S - |w_j|^2\big), \qquad \frac{\partial \tilde F^j}{\partial v_k} = \frac{2v_k}{S^2}\big(\delta_{jk}\,S - |w_j|^2\big).
\]
With $\eta_k \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $(\eta_k)_j = \delta_{jk}S - |w_j|^2$, the $u_k$-column of $\tilde F'(w)$ is $\tfrac{2u_k}{S^2}\eta_k$ and the $v_k$-column is $\tfrac{2v_k}{S^2}\eta_k$. At a point of $O$, $w_k \neq 0$, so $u_k$ or $v_k$ is nonzero, and one of these two columns is a nonzero multiple of $\eta_k$. Choosing one such column for each $k$ gives $n$ columns, which are linearly independent once $\eta_1, \ldots, \eta_n$ are.

\emph{The $\eta_k$ are linearly independent.} Suppose $\sum_k a_k\eta_k = 0$ and put $\sigma = \sum_k a_k$. The $j$-th component reads $a_j S = |w_j|^2 \sigma$. Summing over $j$ gives $\sigma S = \sigma \sum_j |w_j|^2 = \sigma (S - 1)$, so $\sigma = 0$; then $a_j S = 0$ and $a_j = 0$, as $S \ge 1$. So $\tilde F'(w)$ has rank $n$, and Step~4 of the first proof concludes.
\end{proof}

Complex projective space through the course: the open quotient $S^{2n+1}/S^1$, Hausdorff, second countable and compact, in Section~\ref{sec:ex-cpn}; the circle group $\Ugp(1)$ acting there in Example~\ref{ex:1-circle}; an orbit space in Example~\ref{ex:cpn-orbit}; a smooth and complex manifold through its standard atlas in Section~\ref{sec:projective-smooth}; a homogeneous space of $\Ugp(n+1)$ in the remark \emph{Dimension Checks through Homogeneous Spaces} in \ref{sec:tangent}; the domain of the moment map in the remark \emph{The Strategy} in \ref{sec:differential-coords}; and the base of the Hopf fibration in Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf}.


\begin{corbox}[Regular Level Sets Are Topological Manifolds]\thmlabel{cor:manifold-level-sets}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map between smooth manifolds of dimensions $m$ and $n$, and $c \in N$ a regular value of $F$. Then $F^{-1}(c)$, with the subspace topology, is a topological manifold of dimension $m - n$ (or empty).
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:manifold}, three properties of $F^{-1}(c)$, with the subspace topology, must be shown: Hausdorff, second countable, and locally Euclidean of dimension $m - n$.

\emph{Hausdorff and second countable.} Both are inherited from $M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:subspace-inherit}).

\emph{Locally Euclidean.} Let $p \in F^{-1}(c)$. Choose smooth charts $(V, \psi)$ around $c$ and $(U_0, \varphi_0)$ around $p$, and put $U = U_0 \cap F^{-1}(V)$, an open neighbourhood of $p$ because $F$ is continuous and $F(p) = c \in V$; restricting $\varphi_0$ gives a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}(1)). Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart} to the restriction $F|_U : U \to N$, a smooth map on the open submanifold $U$ (of dimension $m$), with the charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$. Its hypotheses hold:
\begin{itemize}
    \item its level set $(F|_U)^{-1}(c) = F^{-1}(c) \cap U$ lies in $U$;
    \item $c \in V$;
    \item it maps $U$ into $V$, because $U \subseteq F^{-1}(V)$.
\end{itemize}
And $c$ is still a regular value of $F|_U$. Indeed, $F|_U = F \circ \iota$ with $\iota : U \hookrightarrow M$ the inclusion, so for $q \in F^{-1}(c) \cap U$ the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) gives $(F|_U)_{*q} = F_{*q} \circ \iota_{*q}$; since $\iota_{*q}$ is the isomorphism by which $T_qU = T_qM$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}), $(F|_U)_{*q} = F_{*q}$ under this identification, and it is surjective because $q \in F^{-1}(c)$ is a regular point of $F$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart}(3), $F^{-1}(c) \cap U$ is a topological manifold of dimension $m - n$.

It remains to place this inside $F^{-1}(c)$. The set $F^{-1}(c) \cap U$ is open in $F^{-1}(c)$, being the intersection of $F^{-1}(c)$ with the open set $U$ of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:subspace}), and its topology as a subspace of $U$ and as a subspace of $F^{-1}(c)$ are both the subspace topology from $M$. A chart of the manifold $F^{-1}(c) \cap U$ at $p$ has a domain open in $F^{-1}(c) \cap U$, hence open in $F^{-1}(c)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}). So $p$ has a neighbourhood in $F^{-1}(c)$ homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{m-n}$.
\end{proof}

This is the topological half of the regular value theorem for manifolds, and it is \ref{sec:rvt} applied chart by chart. The smooth half --- that $F^{-1}(c)$ is a smooth \emph{submanifold} of $M$, with tangent space $\ker F_{*p}$ --- came in Lecture~12, as Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}, proved with the local normal form for submersions (Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form}): near each point of the level set, $F$ is a projection, so the level set is a coordinate slice. It is Lee's Corollary~5.14 and Proposition~5.38. The corollary above is now a consequence of it, a submanifold being in particular a topological manifold, but its proof --- \ref{sec:rvt} applied chart by chart --- is more elementary.

\begin{propbox}[Maps with Zero Differential Are Constant]\thmlabel{prop:zero-differential}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, with $M$ connected. If $F_{*p} = 0$ for every $p \in M$, then $F$ is constant.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~4, Problem~1: the submitted solution, condensed.)} Two steps: first, every point has an open neighbourhood on which $F$ is constant; second, a map with this property on a connected space is constant. (If $M$ is empty there is nothing to prove.)

\emph{$F$ is locally constant.} Fix $p_0 \in M$.

\emph{Charts.} Take a chart $(V, \psi)$ at $F(p_0)$ and a chart $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ at $p_0$. The set $U_2 = U_1 \cap F^{-1}(V)$ is open, since $F$ is continuous, contains $p_0$, and satisfies $F(U_2) \subseteq V$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}(1)). Its image $\varphi_1(U_2)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^m$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-modify}(1)) and contains $\varphi_1(p_0)$, so it contains an open ball $B$ centred at $\varphi_1(p_0)$. Put $U_0 = \varphi_1^{-1}(B)$ and $\varphi = \varphi_1|_{U_0}$: a smooth chart at $p_0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)) whose image is the ball $B$ and whose domain satisfies $F(U_0) \subseteq V$ --- shrink by continuity of $F$, then to a ball.

\emph{Zero Jacobian.} The coordinate representation $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : B \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}). For $p \in U_0$, the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the coordinate bases is the Jacobian $\tilde F'(\varphi(p))$ (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}). By hypothesis $F_{*p} = 0$, which sends every basis vector to $0$, so every entry of its matrix is $0$. As $p$ runs over $U_0$, $\varphi(p)$ runs over $B$; so $\tilde F' \equiv 0$ on $B$, that is, $\partial \tilde F^j/\partial r^i = 0$ on $B$ for all $i$ and $j$.

\emph{Mean value theorem.} Let $p \in U_0$, and put $a = \varphi(p_0)$ and $b = \varphi(p)$. The ball $B$ is convex, so the segment $\sigma(s) = a + s\,(b - a)$, $s \in [0, 1]$, stays in $B$ (and, $B$ being open, $\sigma$ stays in $B$ for $s$ in an open interval containing $[0,1]$). For each $j$, the function $h_j(s) = \tilde F^j(\sigma(s))$ is differentiable there, and by the chain rule for a curve (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian})
\[
h_j'(s) = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial \tilde F^j}{\partial r^i}\big(\sigma(s)\big)\,(b^i - a^i) = 0 .
\]
The mean value theorem gives some $\xi \in (0,1)$ with $h_j(1) - h_j(0) = h_j'(\xi)\,(1 - 0) = 0$, so $\tilde F^j(b) = \tilde F^j(a)$ for every $j$. Hence
\[
\psi\big(F(p)\big) = \tilde F\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \tilde F\big(\varphi(p_0)\big) = \psi\big(F(p_0)\big),
\]
and since $F(p), F(p_0) \in V$ and $\psi$ is injective on $V$, $F(p) = F(p_0)$. So $F$ is constant on the open neighbourhood $U_0$ of $p_0$.

\emph{$F$ is constant.} Let $c = F(p_0)$ and $A = F^{-1}(c)$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $A$ is closed. $N$ is Hausdorff (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}), so each $q \ne c$ has a neighbourhood not containing $c$ (Definition~\ref{def:hausdorff-t2}); thus $N \setminus \{c\}$ is open and $\{c\}$ is closed, and $A = F^{-1}(\{c\})$ is closed since $F$ is continuous.
    \item $A$ is open. If $q \in A$, the first step at $q$ gives an open $U_q \ni q$ with $F \equiv F(q) = c$ on $U_q$, so $U_q \subseteq A$.
    \item $A$ is nonempty: $p_0 \in A$.
\end{itemize}
Then $A$ and $M \setminus A$ are disjoint open sets with union $M$. As $M$ is connected, one of them is empty, and $A \ne \emptyset$; so $M \setminus A = \emptyset$, that is, $F^{-1}(c) = M$.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis that $M$ is connected cannot be dropped: on a disconnected $M$, a map that takes different constant values on different components has zero differential everywhere. Locally, the proposition is the familiar fact from calculus that a function with zero derivative on an interval is constant.

\section{Tangent Vectors as Velocities of Curves}\label{sec:velocities}\label{sub:velocities}

\roadmark{Stage: abstract}{The other face of a tangent vector: every derivation is the velocity of a curve, on every manifold. Tangent spaces of products split.}

\textit{Assignment 3, Problem 2.} Tangent vectors were introduced with two faces: velocities of curves, and derivations (the remark at the start of \ref{sub:derivations}). For regular level sets the two were identified by Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}, through the ambient space. This section identifies them on \emph{every} smooth manifold, with no ambient space at all.

\begin{defbox}[Smooth Curve]\deflabel{def:smooth-curve}
Let $J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an open interval containing $0$, with its standard smooth structure and coordinate $t$. A \textbf{smooth curve} in $M$ is a smooth map $\gamma : J \to M$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Velocity of a Curve]\deflabel{def:velocity}
Let $\gamma : J \to M$ be a smooth curve (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-curve}). If $\gamma(0) = p$, the \textbf{velocity} of $\gamma$ at $0$ is the abstract tangent vector
\[
D_\gamma = \gamma_{*0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0\Big) \in T_pM, \qquad\text{explicitly}\qquad D_\gamma[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f\big(\gamma(t)\big).
\]
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}}
\end{defbox}

The explicit formula is the definition of the pushforward: $\gamma_{*0}(d/dt|_0)[f] = d/dt|_0\,[f \circ \gamma]$, the ordinary derivative at $0$ of the function $f \circ \gamma$, which is defined near $0$. Lee writes $\gamma'(0)$ for $D_\gamma$. These notes keep $\gamma'(0)$ for the ordinary derivative of a curve in $\mathbb{R}^N$, which is a \emph{geometric} tangent vector, and write $D_\gamma$ for the abstract one, as Assignment~3 does.

\begin{propbox}[Velocity in Coordinates]\thmlabel{prop:velocity-coords}
$D_\gamma$ is a derivation at $p$. In a chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ with coordinate functions $x^1, \ldots, x^n$,
\[
D_\gamma = \sum_{j=1}^n \big(x^j \circ \gamma\big)'(0)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p .
\]
In particular $D_\gamma$ depends only on the velocity $(\varphi \circ \gamma)'(0) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of the coordinate curve $\varphi \circ \gamma$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Three things are claimed: $D_\gamma$ is a derivation at $p$; its coefficients in the basis $\partial/\partial x^j|_p$ are the $(x^j \circ \gamma)'(0)$; and so it depends only on $(\varphi \circ \gamma)'(0)$.

\emph{$D_\gamma$ is a derivation.} The interval $J$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ with the identity chart $t$, and $d/dt|_0$ is the coordinate derivation of this chart at $0$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}: the coordinate representation of $f$ in the identity chart is $f$ itself, so $d/dt|_0[f] = f'(0)$); it is a derivation at $0$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:coord-is-derivation}. $D_\gamma = \gamma_{*0}(d/dt|_0)$ is a pushforward of a derivation along the smooth map $\gamma$, hence a derivation at $\gamma(0) = p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}) --- which is why Assignment~3 could waive the check.

\emph{The coefficients.} By the universal formula (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), applied to $D_\gamma \in T_pM$ in the chart $(U, \varphi)$,
\[
D_\gamma = \sum_{j=1}^n D_\gamma\big[x^j\big]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p ,
\]
so the $j$-th coefficient of $D_\gamma$ is $D_\gamma[x^j]$. The function $x^j \circ \gamma$ is defined on the open set $\gamma^{-1}(U) \ni 0$ ($\gamma$ is continuous), and by the explicit formula of Definition~\ref{def:velocity}, which is the definition of the pushforward,
\[
D_\gamma\big[x^j\big] = \gamma_{*0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0\Big)\big[x^j\big] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \big(x^j \circ \gamma\big)(t) = \big(x^j \circ \gamma\big)'(0) .
\]
Substituting into the universal formula gives the displayed formula.

\emph{Dependence on the coordinate curve.} By Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}(2), $x^j = r^j \circ \varphi$, so $x^j \circ \gamma = r^j \circ (\varphi \circ \gamma)$ is the $j$-th component of the coordinate curve $\varphi \circ \gamma$, and $(x^j \circ \gamma)'(0)$ is the $j$-th component of $(\varphi \circ \gamma)'(0) \in \mathbb{R}^n$. So all the coefficients of $D_\gamma$ are read off from $(\varphi \circ \gamma)'(0)$, and two curves through $p$ with the same velocity of their coordinate curves have the same $D_\gamma$.
\end{proof}

The same formula comes out of the chain rule directly, as in the assignment's solution. With $c = \varphi \circ \gamma$ and $c^j = r^j \circ c = x^j \circ \gamma$, near $0$ one has $f \circ \gamma = f_\varphi \circ c$, so
\[
D_\gamma[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0 f_\varphi\big(c(t)\big) = \sum_{j} \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^j}\big(\varphi(p)\big)\,(c^j)'(0) = \sum_j (c^j)'(0)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p[f].
\]
Each input $r^j$ of $f_\varphi$ moves at speed $(c^j)'(0)$ along the curve, and contributes $\partial f_\varphi/\partial r^j \cdot (c^j)'(0)$ to the rate of change.

\begin{defbox}[Velocity at Time $t$]\deflabel{def:velocity-at-t}
Let $\gamma : J \to M$ be a smooth curve and $t_0 \in J$. The \textbf{velocity} of $\gamma$ at time $t_0$ is
\[
\dot\gamma(t_0) = \frac{d\gamma}{dt}(t_0) := \gamma_{*t_0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t_0}\Big) \in T_{\gamma(t_0)}M, \qquad\text{explicitly}\qquad \dot\gamma(t_0)[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=t_0} f\big(\gamma(t)\big)
\]
for a germ $f$ at $\gamma(t_0)$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}}
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Added; the notes had the velocity only at time $0$, Definition~\ref{def:velocity}, and used it at other times informally.)} There is no difference quotient on $M$, so the velocity is a tangent vector: the pushforward of the coordinate tangent vector $\frac{d}{dt}|_{t_0}$ of the $1$-manifold $J$; and the right-hand side of the explicit formula is the ordinary derivative of the real function $f \circ \gamma$, so the definition makes sense on any manifold. It is the velocity at $0$ of the shifted curve $\sigma(s) = \gamma(t_0 + s)$, since $\frac{d}{ds}|_0 f(\gamma(t_0 + s)) = \frac{d}{dt}|_{t_0} f(\gamma(t))$: so $\dot\gamma(t_0) = D_\sigma$, and $\dot\gamma(0) = D_\gamma$ when $0 \in J$. (Lee writes $\gamma'(t_0)$; these notes keep $\gamma'$ for the ordinary derivative of a curve in $\mathbb{R}^N$, as for $D_\gamma$.)

\begin{corbox}[Velocity at Time $t$ in Coordinates]\thmlabel{cor:velocity-at-t-coords}
Let $\gamma : J \to M$ be smooth, $t_0 \in J$, and $(U, \varphi)$ a chart at $\gamma(t_0)$ with coordinate functions $x^1, \ldots, x^n$. Then
\[
\dot\gamma(t_0) = \sum_{j=1}^n \big(x^j \circ \gamma\big)'(t_0)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_{\gamma(t_0)} .
\]
Writing $x^j(t) = x^j(\gamma(t))$, this is $\dot\gamma = \sum_j \dot x^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Let $\sigma(s) = \gamma(t_0 + s)$, a smooth curve with $\sigma(0) = \gamma(t_0)$, so $\dot\gamma(t_0) = D_\sigma$ (Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t} and the paragraph after it). By Velocity in Coordinates (Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords}), $D_\sigma = \sum_j (x^j \circ \sigma)'(0)\, \partial/\partial x^j|_{\gamma(t_0)}$, and by the chain rule in one variable $(x^j \circ \sigma)'(0) = \frac{d}{ds}|_0\, x^j(\gamma(t_0 + s)) = (x^j \circ \gamma)'(t_0)$.
\end{proof}

The coefficients are ordinary derivatives, computed \emph{downstairs} on the coordinate curve $\varphi \circ \gamma$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$; the basis vectors live \emph{upstairs} in $T_{\gamma(t_0)}M$, and were themselves defined by going downstairs, $\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\big|_p[f] = \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^j}(\varphi(p))$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}).

\begin{propbox}[Velocity at Time $t$ in a Level Set]\thmlabel{prop:velocity-at-t-level-set}
Let $M = F^{-1}(c) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ be a regular level set and $\gamma : J \to M$ a smooth curve, $t_0 \in J$. Then the ordinary derivative $\gamma'(t_0)$ lies in $T^{\geo}_{\gamma(t_0)}M$, and $\dot\gamma(t_0) = D_{\gamma'(t_0)}$: under the isomorphism $v \mapsto D_v$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}, the abstract velocity is the ordinary derivative.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} $\gamma$ is smooth into $M$, hence smooth as a curve in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$. Let $\sigma(s) = \gamma(t_0 + s)$ for small $|s|$: a smooth curve in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ with values in $M$, $\sigma(0) = \gamma(t_0)$ and $\sigma'(0) = \gamma'(t_0)$. So $\gamma'(t_0) \in T^{\geo}_{\gamma(t_0)}M$ by Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent}. For a germ $f$ at $\gamma(t_0)$, Proposition~\ref{prop:Dv-properties}(2), applied to the curve $\sigma$, gives $D_{\gamma'(t_0)}[f] = \frac{d}{ds}\big|_{0} f(\sigma(s)) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t_0} f(\gamma(t)) = \dot\gamma(t_0)[f]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Every Tangent Vector Is a Velocity]\thmlabel{thm:every-vector-velocity}
For every $D \in T_pM$ there is a smooth curve $\gamma : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $D_\gamma = D$.
\leeref{Proposition 3.23}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment 3, Problem 2.)} Fix a chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ with coordinate functions $x^i$, and put $a^i = D[x^i]$ and $a = (a^1, \ldots, a^n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$. These are the coefficients of $D$ in the universal formula; the freedom lies in the curve.

\emph{The curve downstairs.} Let $c(t) = \varphi(p) + t\,a$. Since $\varphi(U)$ is open, some ball $B(\varphi(p), r)$ lies in it. If $a \ne 0$ take $\varepsilon = r/|a|$, so that $|c(t) - \varphi(p)| = |t|\,|a| < r$ for $|t| < \varepsilon$. If $a = 0$, which happens exactly when $D = 0$, take $\varepsilon = 1$. In either case $c : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to \varphi(U)$ is smooth, being affine, with $c(0) = \varphi(p)$ and $c'(0) = a$.

\emph{The curve upstairs.} Let $\gamma = \varphi^{-1} \circ c$. It is smooth, since its coordinate representation in the chart $(U,\varphi)$ is $\varphi \circ \gamma = c$, and $\gamma(0) = p$. Its coordinate curve is $\varphi \circ \gamma = c$, so $(x^j \circ \gamma)'(0) = (c^j)'(0) = a^j$.

\emph{Conclusion.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords} and the universal formula,
\[
D_\gamma = \sum_j a^j\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p = \sum_j D[x^j]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p = D. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

Assignment~3's solution first treats the basis vectors $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$, using curves with $c'(0) = e_i$, and then the general case. The general argument contains the basis case, with $a = e_i$ and $c(t) = \varphi(p) + t\,e_i$, so it is presented here alone.

\begin{corbox}[Velocity of a Composite --- Computing Differentials by Curves]\thmlabel{cor:velocity-composite}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $\gamma$ a smooth curve in $M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$. Then $D_{F \circ \gamma} = F_{*p}(D_\gamma)$. Consequently, for every $D \in T_pM$,
\[
F_{*p}(D) = D_{F \circ \gamma} \qquad \text{for any smooth curve } \gamma \text{ with } \gamma(0) = p \text{ and } D_\gamma = D,
\]
and such a curve exists by Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}.
\leeref{Proposition 3.24 and Corollary 3.25}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The identity $D_{F \circ \gamma} = F_{*p}(D_\gamma)$.} The composite $F \circ \gamma : J \to N$ is a smooth curve (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}) with $(F \circ \gamma)(0) = F(p)$, so its velocity $D_{F \circ \gamma} \in T_{F(p)}N$ is defined. The Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), applied to the maps $\gamma : J \to M$ and $F : M \to N$ at the point $0 \in J$, reads $(F \circ \gamma)_{*0} = F_{*\gamma(0)} \circ \gamma_{*0} = F_{*p} \circ \gamma_{*0}$. Hence, using Definition~\ref{def:velocity} at the first and last steps,
\[
D_{F \circ \gamma} = (F \circ \gamma)_{*0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0\Big) = F_{*p}\Big(\gamma_{*0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_0\Big)\Big) = F_{*p}(D_\gamma) .
\]

\emph{Consequence.} Let $D \in T_pM$ and let $\gamma$ be any smooth curve with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $D_\gamma = D$; such a curve exists by Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}. Then, by the identity just proved, $F_{*p}(D) = F_{*p}(D_\gamma) = D_{F \circ \gamma}$.
\end{proof}

This is Lee's main computational tool: to find $F_{*p}(D)$, choose any curve with velocity $D$ and differentiate $F$ along it. It is the manifold version of Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves}, and it is how Lee computes the differential of the determinant (Problem~7-4). \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} With $m = \dim M$, $n = \dim N$, charts $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$, and $F^j = y^j \circ F$, the coefficients of $D_\gamma$ and $D_{F \circ \gamma}$ are $(x^i \circ \gamma)'(0)$ and $(y^j \circ F \circ \gamma)'(0)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords}), and by Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} the identity $D_{F \circ \gamma} = F_{*p}(D_\gamma)$ reads
\[
\begin{pmatrix} (y^1 \circ F \circ \gamma)'(0) \\ \vdots \\ (y^n \circ F \circ \gamma)'(0) \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} (x^1 \circ \gamma)'(0) \\ \vdots \\ (x^m \circ \gamma)'(0) \end{pmatrix} :
\]
the Jacobian carries the velocity of the coordinate curve $\varphi \circ \gamma$ to that of $\psi \circ F \circ \gamma$.

\node[orange!85!black,font=\footnotesize,anchor=south east] at (1.550,2.710) {$\gamma$};
\node[violet!70!black,font=\footnotesize,anchor=east] at (1.15,4.3) {$U \subseteq M$};
\draw[gray!70,fill=gray!6] (0.85,-0.25) rectangle (4.45,1.45);

The proof in one picture. Downstairs, in the chart, the curve is the straight line through $\varphi(p)$ in the direction of the coefficient vector $a = (D[x^1], \ldots, D[x^n])$. The chart carries it upstairs to a curve $\gamma$ in $M$, bent by whatever distortion $\varphi^{-1}$ introduces. The bending is invisible to the velocity, which depends only on $(\varphi \circ \gamma)'(0) = a$ --- so the velocity is $D$.

\end{tikzcd}
