\subsection{Pulling Back Covectors}\label{sub:pullback-covectors}

\textit{Lecture 15. A smooth map pushes tangent vectors forward; dually, it pulls covectors back. ``Functions pull back by composition, and you can pull back actually any one-form by using the dual map of the forward star.''}

\begin{defbox}[Pullback of Covectors]\deflabel{def:pullback-covector}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$. The \textbf{pullback of covectors} at $p$ is the dual map (Definition~\ref{def:dual-map}) of the pushforward $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$:
\[
F_p^* : T^*_{F(p)}N \longrightarrow T_p^*M, \qquad (F_p^*\alpha)(v) = \alpha\big(F_{*p}v\big) .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Pullbacks of Covector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

Directions: points and vectors move \emph{forward} along $F$, from $M$ to $N$; functions and covectors move \emph{backward}, from $N$ to $M$, because they are things that eat --- to evaluate one on $M$, push the input to $N$ and evaluate there. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} With $m = \dim M$, $n = \dim N$ and charts $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$, $F^j = y^j \circ F$ and $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ as in Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, $(F_p^*\,dy^j|_{F(p)})(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = dy^j|_{F(p)}\big(F_{*p}\,\partial/\partial x^i|_p\big) = \partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)$, so $F_p^*\,dy^j|_{F(p)} = \sum_i \partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)\, dx^i|_p$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}). In the dual bases the $m \times n$ matrix of $F_p^*$ is therefore the transpose of the $n \times m$ matrix of $F_{*p}$:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) \\[2mm]
\vdots & & \vdots \\[1mm]
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix}
= \Big(\tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big)\Big)^{\mathsf T},
\]
its $j$-th column holding the components of $F_p^*\,dy^j|_{F(p)}$.

\begin{rembox}[One Symbol for Two Pullbacks]\label{rem:two-pullbacks}
The symbol $F_p^*$ now has two meanings. On germs it is the pullback $C^\infty_{F(p)}(N) \to C^\infty_p(M)$, $[g] \mapsto [g \circ F]$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-pullback}); on covectors it is the dual map $T^*_{F(p)}N \to T_p^*M$ of Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector}. Context decides which is meant, and the two are compatible: by the next proposition, pulling back the differential of $g$ is the same as differentiating the pulled-back germ, $F_p^*(dg_{F(p)}) = d\big(F_p^*[g]\big)_p$.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[Pullback Commutes with $d$]\thmlabel{prop:pullback-d}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $p \in M$, and $f$ smooth near $F(p)$. Then
\[
F_p^*\big(df_{F(p)}\big) = d(f \circ F)_p \quad \text{in } T_p^*M .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 11.25}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~15 --- ``every equal sign is a definition \ldots\ maybe this is best to be reflected upon at your coffee shop of choice.'')} For $v \in T_pM$:
\[
F_p^*\big(df_{F(p)}\big)(v) = df_{F(p)}\big(F_{*p}v\big) = \big(F_{*p}v\big)[f] = v[f \circ F] = d(f \circ F)_p(v) .
\]
The first equality is the definition of the dual map; the second, of the differential of a function, applied to the vector $F_{*p}v \in T_{F(p)}N$; the third, of the pushforward; the fourth, of the differential of $f \circ F$. Two covectors that agree on every $v$ are equal.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Two Differentials Meet]\label{rem:pullback-d-chain-rule}
In $\mathbb{R}^n$, with the dot-product identification $v \mapsto \xi_v$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}, under which $dh_p = \xi_{\nabla h(p)}$ (its part (3), with the gradient of Definition~\ref{def:gradient}), the proposition is the chain rule in the form $\nabla(f \circ F) = J_F^{\mathsf T}\, \nabla f$, with the gradients written as columns. (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian} writes the gradients $\nabla F_a(p)$ as the rows of the Jacobian; in that row convention the same identity reads $\nabla(f \circ F) = \nabla f \; J_F$, the transpose of this one.) Explicitly, for $F$ smooth on an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $J_F(p)$ its Jacobian, $F_{*p}(D_w|_p) = D_{J_F(p)w}|_{F(p)}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}), so for every $w \in \mathbb{R}^m$
\[
\xi_{\nabla(f \circ F)(p)}\big(D_w|_p\big) = d(f \circ F)_p\big(D_w|_p\big) = df_{F(p)}\big(D_{J_F(p)w}|_{F(p)}\big) = \nabla f(F(p)) \cdot J_F(p)w = \big(J_F(p)^{\mathsf T}\, \nabla f(F(p))\big) \cdot w = \xi_{J_F(p)^{\mathsf T} \nabla f(F(p))}\big(D_w|_p\big) ,
\]
the first and third equalities being part (3) of Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification} (for $f \circ F$ at $p$, and for $f$ at $F(p)$), the second the proposition above together with the definition of $F_p^*$; as $v \mapsto \xi_v$ is injective, $\nabla(f \circ F)(p) = J_F(p)^{\mathsf T}\, \nabla f(F(p))$. Uribe added that the pushforward $F_*$ ``we should have called the differential of $F$ ages ago'': for a function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$, $df_p$ is $f_{*p}$ followed by the identification $T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R} \cong \mathbb{R}$.
\end{rembox}

\textit{Not from lecture: the pullback of covectors in the germ picture of this section.} The pullback of germs (Definition~\ref{def:germ-pullback}) already moved functions backward along $F$, and the pushforward of derivations was built from it, $F_{*p}D = D \circ F_p^*$ (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}). Through the isomorphism $\Phi$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}, the pullback of covectors is that same pullback of germs.

\begin{propbox}[Pullback of Covectors from the Pullback of Germs]\thmlabel{prop:pullback-germ-picture}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $p \in M$, and $q = F(p)$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The pullback of germs $F_p^* : C^\infty_q(N) \to C^\infty_p(M)$ maps $I_q$ into $I_p$ and $I_q^2$ into $I_p^2$, so it induces a linear map
    \[
    \bar F_p^* : I_q/I_q^2 \longrightarrow I_p/I_p^2, \qquad [[g]] \longmapsto [[g \circ F]] .
    \]
    \item Under the isomorphisms $\Phi_q : I_q/I_q^2 \to T_q^*N$ and $\Phi_p : I_p/I_p^2 \to T_p^*M$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}, $\bar F_p^*$ is the pullback of covectors (Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector}):
    \[
    \Phi_p \circ \bar F_p^* = F_p^* \circ \Phi_q .
    \]
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4.2em, row sep=2.8em]
I_q/I_q^2 \arrow[r, "\bar F_p^*"] \arrow[d, "\Phi_q"', "\cong"] & I_p/I_p^2 \arrow[d, "\Phi_p", "\cong"'] \\
T_q^*N \arrow[r, "F_p^*"'] & T_p^*M
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{(1)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-properties}, $F_p^*$ is a homomorphism of $\mathbb{R}$-algebras with $F_p^*(I_q) \subseteq I_p$. An element of $I_q^2$ is a finite sum $\sum_k [u_k][w_k]$ with $[u_k], [w_k] \in I_q$ (Definition~\ref{def:Ip-square}), and since $F_p^*$ preserves sums and products,
\[
F_p^*\Big(\sum_k [u_k][w_k]\Big) = \sum_k F_p^*[u_k]\; F_p^*[w_k],
\]
a finite sum of products of two elements of $I_p$, that is, an element of $I_p^2$. So the composite of $F_p^*|_{I_q} : I_q \to I_p$ with the projection $I_p \to I_p/I_p^2$ is linear and vanishes on $I_q^2$. By the universal property of quotient spaces (Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-vs}(2)) it descends to a linear map $\bar F_p^*$ on $I_q/I_q^2$, with $\bar F_p^*[[g]] = [[F_p^*[g]]] = [[g \circ F]]$.

\emph{(2)} Let $[[g]] \in I_q/I_q^2$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}(2) at $p$, Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}(2) at $q$,
\[
\Phi_p\big(\bar F_p^*[[g]]\big) = \Phi_p\big([[g \circ F]]\big) = d(g \circ F)_p = F_p^*\big(dg_q\big) = F_p^*\big(\Phi_q[[g]]\big) .
\]
The two linear maps $\Phi_p \circ \bar F_p^*$ and $F_p^* \circ \Phi_q$ agree at every element, so they are equal.
\end{proof}

So in the germ picture no dual map is needed: a covector at $q$ is a class of germs vanishing at $q$, and it pulls back by composing with $F$, exactly as germs do. One operation, $[g] \mapsto [g \circ F]$, moves everything: tangent vectors act on germs, so they are pushed \emph{forward} by precomposing with it; covectors are classes of germs, so they are pulled \emph{back} by it. ``Functions pull back by composition'' (Lecture~15) covers covectors too.

\chapter{Submersions, Submanifolds and Fibrations}

% ============================================================================
\section{Local Diffeomorphisms}\label{sec:special-maps}

\roadmark{Stage: maps}{Properties of the linear maps $F_{*p}$ control the local behaviour of $F$ itself.}

\textit{References: Lee Ch.\ 4. Lecture 10.} Three special types of smooth maps $F : M \to N$ are singled out by the linear algebra of their differentials: \emph{local diffeomorphisms}, whose differentials are bijective; \emph{submersions}, whose differentials are surjective; and \emph{immersions}, whose differentials are injective. The theme of the section is that in each case a property of the linear maps $F_{*p}$ --- computable from a Jacobian --- controls the behaviour of $F$ itself near $p$. Immersions, listed with the others in Lecture~10, were treated only in Lecture~13, after the tangent bundle, and have their own section, \ref{sec:immersions}; everything up to the tangent bundle is the theory of submersions. ``That's why we're discussing them in this context.''

\label{sub:local-diffeo}

\begin{defbox}[Local Diffeomorphism]\deflabel{def:local-diffeo}
A smooth map $F : M \to N$ is a \textbf{local diffeomorphism} if for every $p \in M$ there are neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of $F(p)$ with $F(U) = V$ such that $F|_U^V : U \to V$ --- the restriction of $F$ to $U$, regarded as a map onto $V$ --- has a smooth inverse. Such an inverse $G : V \to U$ is a \textbf{local inverse} of $F$ at $p$.
\leeref{Ch.~2 and Ch.~4}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:special-maps}
Neighbourhoods are open (\ref{sec:review}). A local diffeomorphism need not be injective: the local inverses are local, and different ones need not fit together. The examples show both finite-to-one and infinite-to-one behaviour.
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[The Circle Covered by a Line]\exlabel{ex:line-circle}
$F : \mathbb{R} \to S^1$, $F(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$, is a local diffeomorphism, and so is its restriction to $(0, 4\pi)$. Neither is injective.
\leeref{cf.\ Ch.~4, \emph{Smooth Covering Maps}}
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~10 as an example, without proof --- the covering-map distinction was ``postponed''; filled in.)} Three things are claimed: $F$ is a local diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:local-diffeo}), so is its restriction to $(0, 4\pi)$, and neither map is injective. Two elementary facts about $F$ are used throughout: $F(t) = F(t')$ if and only if $t - t' \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, since cosine and sine together determine an angle up to a multiple of $2\pi$; and every point of $S^1$ is $F(s)$ for exactly one $s$ in any half-open interval of length $2\pi$.

\emph{$F$ is smooth into $S^1$.} Its components $\cos t$ and $\sin t$ are smooth, so $F$ is smooth as a map $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$; and $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$, so its values lie in the regular level set $S^1$, with the smooth structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:level-set-maps}(2), with $P = \mathbb{R}$ and $G = F$, $F$ is therefore smooth into $S^1$.

\emph{The neighbourhoods.} Fix $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$; Definition~\ref{def:local-diffeo} asks for neighbourhoods $U \ni t_0$ and $V \ni F(t_0)$ with $F(U) = V$ and $F|_U^V$ smoothly invertible. Let $U = (t_0 - \pi, t_0 + \pi)$ and $V = S^1 \setminus \{F(t_0 + \pi)\}$, which is open in $S^1$ because points of the Hausdorff space $S^1$ are closed. Then $F$ maps $U$ bijectively onto $V$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{injective:} if $t, t' \in U$ and $F(t) = F(t')$, then $t - t' \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ and $|t - t'| < 2\pi$, so $t = t'$;
    \item \emph{into $V$:} for $t \in U$, $t - (t_0 + \pi) \in (-2\pi, 0)$ is not a multiple of $2\pi$, so $F(t) \neq F(t_0 + \pi)$;
    \item \emph{onto $V$:} a point of $V$ is $F(s)$ for some $s \in [t_0 - \pi, t_0 + \pi)$, and $s \neq t_0 - \pi$ because $F(t_0 - \pi) = F(t_0 + \pi) \notin V$; so $s \in U$.
\end{itemize}
In particular $F(t_0) \in V$, and $F(U) = V$.

\emph{The local inverse.} The inverse of $F|_U^V$ is the angle chart $\theta : V \to U$ taking values in $U$, which belongs to the smooth structure of $S^1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:circle-atlases-same} and the remark on ranges in its proof); here $\theta(q)$ is the unique $s \in U$ with $F(s) = q$. Explicitly, this is the remark's ``rotate and add a constant'': let $R$ be the rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by the angle $\alpha = \pi - t_0$, so that $R(F(s)) = F(s + \alpha)$ for all $s$, and let $\varphi_a : U_a = S^1 \setminus \{(1,0)\} \to (0, 2\pi)$ be the angle chart of Example~\ref{ex:circle-angle}. Then $R$ maps $V$ onto $S^1 \setminus \{F(t_0 + \pi + \alpha)\} = S^1 \setminus \{F(2\pi)\} = U_a$, and for $q = F(s)$ with $s \in U$ we have $R(q) = F(s + \alpha)$ with $s + \alpha \in (0, 2\pi)$, so
\[
\varphi_a\big(R(q)\big) - \alpha = (s + \alpha) - \alpha = s = \theta(q) ;
\]
that is, $\theta = \varphi_a \circ R|_V + (t_0 - \pi)$. So $F|_U^V = \theta^{-1}$, and since the chart $\theta : V \to U$ is a diffeomorphism by Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}, so is its inverse $F|_U^V$; its smooth inverse $\theta$ is a local inverse of $F$ at $t_0$.

\emph{The restriction to $(0, 4\pi)$.} It is smooth, as the restriction of the smooth map $F$ to an open subset. For $t_0 \in (0,4\pi)$, replace $U$ by $U' = U \cap (0, 4\pi)$, an open interval containing $t_0$, and $V$ by its image $V' = F(U')$, which is open in $V$ --- hence in $S^1$, $V$ being open --- because $F|_U^V$ is a homeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(3)). Then $F$ maps $U'$ bijectively onto $V'$, with inverse $\theta|_{V'}$, smooth as the restriction of $\theta$ to an open subset.

\emph{Not injective.} Finally $F(t + 2\pi) = F(t)$ for every $t$, since cosine and sine have period $2\pi$; so $F$ is not injective. Nor is its restriction: $\pi$ and $3\pi$ both lie in $(0, 4\pi)$, and $F(\pi) = F(3\pi) = (-1, 0)$.
\end{proof}

The helix is the interval $(0, 4\pi)$, lifted so that $F$ becomes the vertical projection onto the circle. On the orange interval $U$ the projection is a diffeomorphism onto the arc $V$; but the point $q \in V$ has a second preimage $t_1 + 2\pi$, on the other turn and outside $U$. Local invertibility does not see it.

The circle through the course: the circle group $\Ugp(1)$ in Example~\ref{ex:1-circle}; the homogeneous space $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ in Example~\ref{ex:circle-RZ}; three atlases --- four charts, stereographic and angle --- in Examples~\ref{ex:circle-four}, \ref{ex:circle-stereo} and~\ref{ex:circle-angle}, with the remark \emph{Three Atlases and One Structure} in \ref{sec:smooth-structures}; $\mathbb{RP}^1$ homeomorphic to it in Proposition~\ref{prop:rpn-topologies}; its external, graph and internal descriptions, and the one smooth structure of its three atlases, in Section~\ref{sec:ex-circle}; and covered by a line, a local diffeomorphism that is not injective, in Example~\ref{ex:line-circle}.


The projection $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$, a two-to-one local diffeomorphism, is collected in Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf}.


\begin{rembox}[Covering Maps]\label{rem:covering-maps}
Uribe noted that $\mathbb{R} \to S^1$ and $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ are \emph{covering maps}, while $(0, 4\pi) \to S^1$ is a local diffeomorphism that is not: over the point $F(0) = (1,0)$ it has a single preimage, $2\pi$, where every other point of the circle has two. Covering maps were not defined in lecture and the distinction was postponed (``we're running a little bit behind schedule''); it is Lee Ch.\ 4.
\end{rembox}

The converse direction of the main theorem rests on one theorem from analysis --- ``that's really what's paying the bills here.''

\begin{thmbox}[Inverse Function Theorem]\thmlabel{thm:inverse-function}
Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $\Phi : W \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth, and $a \in W$ with $\Phi'(a)$ invertible. Then there are open sets $U_0 \ni a$ in $W$ and $V_0 \ni \Phi(a)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\Phi(U_0) = V_0$ and $\Phi|_{U_0} : U_0 \to V_0$ is bijective with smooth inverse.
\leeref{Theorem C.34}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (to be filled)]
Taken from analysis, not proved in this course (Lee, Theorem~C.34; MATH~452 proves the two-variable case). To be filled.
\end{proof}

Lee, Theorem C.34; taken from analysis, not proved in the course. It should not be confused with the \emph{implicit} function theorem of \S\ref{sub:ift} --- the board's ``IFT'' now means the inverse one. Each theorem can be derived from the other.

\begin{thmbox}[Local Diffeomorphisms Are Detected by the Differential]\thmlabel{thm:local-diffeo-criterion}
A smooth map $F : M \to N$ is a local diffeomorphism if and only if $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ is bijective for every $p \in M$.
\leeref{Theorem 4.5 and Proposition 4.8}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~10. The forward direction was supplied by a student at Uribe's prompting --- use the local inverse and the chain rule; for the converse the inverse function theorem ``is really what's paying the bills here.'' The identification of $(F|_U^V)_{*p}$ with $F_{*p}$ is a completion.)} ($\Rightarrow$) Fix $p \in M$, and let $U$, $V$ and the local inverse $G : V \to U$ at $p$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:local-diffeo}, so that $G \circ F|_U^V = \mathrm{id}_U$ and $F|_U^V \circ G = \mathrm{id}_V$. By the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), applied to these two composites at $p$ and at $F(p)$ respectively, together with $(\mathrm{id})_* = \mathrm{id}$,
\[
G_{*F(p)} \circ (F|_U^V)_{*p} = (\mathrm{id}_U)_{*p} = \mathrm{id}, \qquad (F|_U^V)_{*p} \circ G_{*F(p)} = (\mathrm{id}_V)_{*F(p)} = \mathrm{id},
\]
so $(F|_U^V)_{*p} : T_pU \to T_{F(p)}V$ is bijective with inverse $G_{*F(p)}$. Under the identifications $T_pU = T_pM$ and $T_{F(p)}V = T_{F(p)}N$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}, $(F|_U^V)_{*p}$ is $F_{*p}$, again by the Chain Rule applied to $F \circ \iota_U = \iota_V \circ F|_U^V$, where $\iota_U : U \hookrightarrow M$ and $\iota_V : V \hookrightarrow N$ are the inclusions. Explicitly, the Chain Rule gives $F_{*p} \circ (\iota_U)_{*p} = (\iota_V)_{*F(p)} \circ (F|_U^V)_{*p}$, and $(\iota_U)_{*p}$ is invertible (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}), so
\[
F_{*p} = (\iota_V)_{*F(p)} \circ (F|_U^V)_{*p} \circ \big((\iota_U)_{*p}\big)^{-1},
\]
a composite of three bijections (the outer two by Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}). So $F_{*p}$ is bijective, for every $p \in M$.

($\Leftarrow$) Fix $p$; we must produce neighbourhoods $U' \ni p$, $V' \ni F(p)$ with $F(U') = V'$ and a smooth inverse of $F|_{U'}^{V'}$. Choose smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}: take any chart $(V, \psi)$ at $F(p)$ and any chart $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ at $p$, and restrict $\varphi_1$ to the open set $U = U_1 \cap F^{-1}(V)$, open because $F$ is continuous. Let $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to \psi(V)$, smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}.

A bijective linear map forces $\dim M = \dim N$: $F_{*p}$ is a bijection $T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ between spaces of dimensions $m = \dim M$ and $n = \dim N$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), and rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) gives $m = \dim\ker F_{*p} + \operatorname{rank} F_{*p} = 0 + n$. By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} the matrix of $F_{*p}$ is the square matrix $\tilde F'(\varphi(p))$, written out in the standard coordinates $r^1, \ldots, r^n$ of $\varphi(U)$ as
\[
\tilde F'\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^1}{\partial r^1}\big(\varphi(p)\big) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^1}{\partial r^n}\big(\varphi(p)\big) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^n}{\partial r^1}\big(\varphi(p)\big) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde F^n}{\partial r^n}\big(\varphi(p)\big) \end{pmatrix} ;
\] so the latter is invertible, since its rank is the rank of $F_{*p}$, namely $n$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)).

By the Inverse Function Theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function}), applied to $\Phi = \tilde F$ on $W = \varphi(U)$ at $a = \varphi(p)$, there are open sets $\tilde A \ni \varphi(p)$ in $\varphi(U)$ and $\tilde B \ni \tilde F(\varphi(p))$ such that $\tilde F(\tilde A) = \tilde B$ and $\tilde F|_{\tilde A} : \tilde A \to \tilde B$ is bijective with smooth inverse; note $\tilde B = \tilde F(\tilde A) \subseteq \psi(V)$. Put $U' = \varphi^{-1}(\tilde A)$ and $V' = \psi^{-1}(\tilde B)$, neighbourhoods of $p$ and $F(p)$: they are open because $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are homeomorphisms onto open sets --- ``shrinking $\varphi(U)$ is the same as shrinking $U$.'' On $U$ we have $F = \psi^{-1} \circ \tilde F \circ \varphi$, by the definition of $\tilde F$ and $F(U) \subseteq V$; so
\[
F(U') = \psi^{-1}\big(\tilde F(\varphi(U'))\big) = \psi^{-1}\big(\tilde F(\tilde A)\big) = \psi^{-1}(\tilde B) = V' ,
\]
and the map $G = \varphi^{-1} \circ (\tilde F|_{\tilde A})^{-1} \circ \psi|_{V'} : V' \to U'$ is the inverse of $F|_{U'}^{V'}$. Indeed, for $y \in V'$ and $x \in U'$ (so that $\psi(y) \in \tilde B$ and $\varphi(x) \in \tilde A$),
\[
F\big(G(y)\big) = \psi^{-1}\Big(\tilde F\big((\tilde F|_{\tilde A})^{-1}(\psi(y))\big)\Big) = \psi^{-1}\big(\psi(y)\big) = y, \qquad G\big(F(x)\big) = \varphi^{-1}\Big((\tilde F|_{\tilde A})^{-1}\big(\tilde F(\varphi(x))\big)\Big) = \varphi^{-1}\big(\varphi(x)\big) = x .
\]
So
\[
\big(F|_{U'}^{V'}\big)^{-1} = \varphi^{-1} \circ \big(\tilde F|_{\tilde A}\big)^{-1} \circ \psi|_{V'},
\]
a composite of diffeomorphisms (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), hence smooth: $\psi|_{V'} : V' \to \tilde B$ and $\varphi^{-1} : \tilde A \to U'$ are restrictions of the chart diffeomorphisms $\psi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ to open sets, $(\tilde F|_{\tilde A})^{-1}$ is smooth in the Euclidean sense and hence as a map of manifolds (Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}), and a composite of smooth maps is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). So $G$ is a local inverse at $p$, and as $p$ was arbitrary, $F$ is a local diffeomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3.2em, column sep=5em]
U' \arrow[r, shift left=0.8ex, "F|_{U'}^{V'}"] \arrow[d, "\varphi"', "\cong"] & V' \arrow[l, shift left=0.8ex, "G"] \arrow[d, "\psi", "\cong"'] \\
\tilde A \arrow[r, shift left=0.8ex, "\tilde F"] & \tilde B \arrow[l, shift left=0.8ex, "\tilde F^{-1}"]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The converse in one picture. Downstairs the Inverse Function Theorem supplies $\tilde F^{-1}$; the charts carry it upstairs as the local inverse $G = \varphi^{-1} \circ \tilde F^{-1} \circ \psi$. The only input from the hypothesis is that the bottom arrow has an invertible Jacobian at $\varphi(p)$ --- which is where Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} enters.

A student asked why $\tilde F'(\varphi(p))$ is invertible; Uribe's answer was the lemma just cited: the Jacobian \emph{is} the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in coordinate bases, and $F_{*p}$ is bijective by hypothesis. The practical content of the theorem is that ``being a local diffeomorphism is detectable'' by computing one Jacobian at each point, rather than by exhibiting local inverses.

\begin{corbox}[Diffeomorphisms Are the Bijective Local Diffeomorphisms]\thmlabel{cor:bijective-local-diffeo}
A smooth map $F : M \to N$ is a diffeomorphism if and only if it is a bijective local diffeomorphism. Consequently, a smooth bijection with $F_{*p}$ bijective at every $p \in M$ is a diffeomorphism.
\leeref{Proposition 4.6}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{($\Rightarrow$)} A diffeomorphism is a local diffeomorphism with $U = M$ and $V = N$: these are neighbourhoods of every $p$ and $F(p)$, $F(M) = N$ because $F$ is surjective, and $F|_M^N = F$ has the smooth inverse $F^{-1}$ (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}). It is bijective by definition.

\emph{($\Leftarrow$)} Conversely, let $F$ be a bijective local diffeomorphism; $F$ is smooth and bijective, so by Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism} it remains to show that $F^{-1} : N \to M$ is smooth. Given $q \in N$, let $p = F^{-1}(q)$ and let $G : V \to U$ be a local inverse at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:local-diffeo}), so $V$ is an open neighbourhood of $q = F(p)$. For $y \in V$, $G(y) \in U$ and $F(G(y)) = (F|_U^V \circ G)(y) = y$; also $F(F^{-1}(y)) = y$; so $G(y) = F^{-1}(y)$ because $F$ is injective. Thus $F^{-1}$ agrees on the open neighbourhood $V$ of $q$ with the smooth map $G$.

As $q$ was arbitrary, the sets $V$ obtained in this way form an open cover of $N$, on each of which $F^{-1}$ equals a smooth, in particular continuous, map. So $F^{-1}$ is continuous and smooth, since both properties are local: for continuity, the preimage under $F^{-1}$ of an open $O \subseteq M$ is the union over the cover of the sets $G^{-1}(O \cap U)$, each open in an open $V$; for smoothness, Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} is checked with charts at each point, and on a chart domain inside $V$ the coordinate representations of $F^{-1}$ and of $G$ coincide, so they are smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}. Hence $F$ is a diffeomorphism.

\emph{The last sentence.} A smooth bijection with $F_{*p}$ bijective at every $p$ is a local diffeomorphism by Theorem~\ref{thm:local-diffeo-criterion}; being bijective, it is a diffeomorphism by the equivalence just proved.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}\label{rem:special-maps-2}
Not stated in lecture. Injectivity is the entire difference between the two notions, as the helix of Example~\ref{ex:line-circle} shows: there every local inverse exists, but they cannot be assembled into a global one, because the second preimage of $q$ lies outside the domain of the local inverse. The same argument shows that a bijective local homeomorphism is a homeomorphism.
\end{rembox}

% SECTION: SUBMERSIONS
% ============================================================================

\section{Submersions}\label{sec:submersions}\label{sub:submersions}

\roadmark{Stage: maps}{Maps with surjective differentials: locally projections, by the normal form --- the tool that makes the regular value theorem work on any manifold (\ref{sec:submanifolds}).}

\begin{defbox}[Submersion]\deflabel{def:submersion}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$. $F$ is a \textbf{submersion at $p$} if $F_{*p}$ is onto, and a \textbf{submersion} if it is a submersion at every point.
\leeref{Ch.~4, \emph{Maps of Constant Rank}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Immersion]\deflabel{def:immersion}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$. $F$ is an \textbf{immersion at $p$} if $F_{*p}$ is injective, and an \textbf{immersion} if it is one at every point.
\leeref{Ch.~4, \emph{Maps of Constant Rank}}
\end{defbox}

The submersion half is the lecture's definition. Immersions were listed as the third special type and treated in Lecture~13 (\ref{sub:immersions}); the definition is recorded here in Lee's form so that the three types can be compared. In the language of Definition~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point}, $F$ is a submersion at $p$ exactly when $p$ is a regular point.

\begin{propbox}[Dimension Constraints]\thmlabel{prop:dimension-constraints}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $m = \dim M$, $n = \dim N$, and $p \in M$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $F$ is a submersion at $p$ then $n \le m$; if $F$ is an immersion at $p$ then $m \le n$.
    \item $F$ is a local diffeomorphism if and only if it is both a submersion and an immersion; in that case $m = n$.
    \item If $m = n$ and $F$ is a submersion, or an immersion, at every point, then $F$ is a local diffeomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 4.8}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ is a linear map (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}) between spaces of dimensions $m$ and $n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), so rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) applies to it:
\[
m = \dim T_pM = \dim\ker F_{*p} + \operatorname{rank} F_{*p} .
\]

\emph{(1)} By rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)), a surjective linear map $T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ forces $n \le m$, and an injective one forces $m \le n$. In detail: if $F$ is a submersion at $p$, then $F_{*p}$ is onto (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}), so $\operatorname{rank} F_{*p} = n$ and $m = \dim\ker F_{*p} + n \ge n$. If $F$ is an immersion at $p$, then $F_{*p}$ is injective (Definition~\ref{def:immersion}), so $\ker F_{*p} = 0$ and $m = \operatorname{rank} F_{*p} \le n$, the image being a subspace of the $n$-dimensional $T_{F(p)}N$.

\emph{(2)} By Theorem~\ref{thm:local-diffeo-criterion}, $F$ is a local diffeomorphism if and only if $F_{*p}$ is bijective for every $p \in M$. A linear map is bijective if and only if it is injective and surjective, so this is Theorem~\ref{thm:local-diffeo-criterion}: ``$F_{*p}$ surjective for every $p$'' says that $F$ is a submersion, and ``$F_{*p}$ injective for every $p$'' that it is an immersion (Definitions~\ref{def:submersion} and~\ref{def:immersion}). Then (1) gives $m = n$: at any $p \in M$ (the claim tacitly assumes $M \neq \emptyset$), the submersion half gives $n \le m$ and the immersion half gives $m \le n$.

\emph{(3)} Between spaces of the same finite dimension, a linear map is injective iff surjective iff bijective (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)). So if $m = n$ and $F$ is a submersion at every point, each $F_{*p}$ is a surjection between spaces of the same dimension $m = n$, hence bijective; and if $F$ is an immersion at every point, each $F_{*p}$ is an injection between such spaces, hence again bijective. In either case apply Theorem~\ref{thm:local-diffeo-criterion}: $F$ is a local diffeomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Projections Are Submersions]\exlabel{ex:projection-submersion}
The projection $\pi : \mathbb{R}^k \times \mathbb{R}^l \to \mathbb{R}^k$, $(x, y) \mapsto x$, is a submersion.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
$\pi$ is linear, hence smooth; we show that $\pi_{*a}$ is onto $T_{\pi(a)}\mathbb{R}^k$ for every $a \in \mathbb{R}^k \times \mathbb{R}^l = \mathbb{R}^{k+l}$ (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}, applied with $W = \mathbb{R}^{k+l}$ and $F = \pi$, under the identifications $T_a\mathbb{R}^{k+l} \cong \mathbb{R}^{k+l}$ and $T_{\pi(a)}\mathbb{R}^k \cong \mathbb{R}^k$ the differential $\pi_{*a}$ is the Jacobian $\pi'(a)$. The components of $\pi$ are $\pi^i(r) = r^i$ for $i = 1, \ldots, k$, so $\partial \pi^i/\partial r^j(a) = \delta^i_j$ for $j = 1, \ldots, k+l$ (which is $0$ for every $j > k$), and row $i$ of the Jacobian is the $i$-th standard row vector (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}):
\[
\pi'(a) = \big(I_k \mid 0\big),
\]
a $k \times (k+l)$ matrix of rank $k$, since its first $k$ columns are the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^k$. So $\pi'(a) : \mathbb{R}^{k+l} \to \mathbb{R}^k$ is onto, and $\pi_{*a}$, which corresponds to it under linear isomorphisms, is onto as well. As $a$ was arbitrary, $\pi$ is a submersion.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page 28 of the handwritten notes writes the projection as $\mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^l \to \mathbb{R}^k$; for a projection onto a factor the factor must be the target, $\mathbb{R}^k \times \mathbb{R}^l \to \mathbb{R}^k$. Projections of \emph{product manifolds} $M_1 \times M_2 \to M_1$ are submersions for the same reason, but that needs the tangent space of a product --- ``they will be direct sums of tangent spaces'' --- which Uribe postponed to the next lecture.

Lecture~11 supplied it (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}):

\begin{exbox}[Projections of Product Manifolds Are Submersions]\exlabel{ex:product-projection-submersion}
The projection $\pi_1 : M_1 \times M_2 \to M_1$ is a submersion, and so is $\pi_2$.
\leeref{Proposition 3.14}
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
Fix $p = (p_1, p_2) \in M_1 \times M_2$, and let $\iota_1 = \iota^{p_2}$ and $\iota_2 = \iota^{p_1}$ be the slice inclusions through $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}), as in Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}. We must show that $\pi_{1*} : T_p(M_1 \times M_2) \to T_{p_1}M_1$ is onto. Two identities are needed. First, $\pi_1 \circ \iota_1 = \mathrm{id}_{M_1}$, since $\pi_1(\iota_1(q)) = \pi_1(q, p_2) = q$; so the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), which also gives $(\mathrm{id})_* = \mathrm{id}$, yields $\pi_{1*}\iota_{1*} = \mathrm{id}$. Second, $\pi_1 \circ \iota_2$ is constant, $\pi_1(\iota_2(q)) = \pi_1(p_1, q) = p_1$; so its pushforward is zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}), and the Chain Rule yields $\pi_{1*}\iota_{2*} = (\pi_1 \circ \iota_2)_{*} = 0$. With the linearity of $\pi_{1*}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}), for $v \in T_{p_1}M_1$ and $w \in T_{p_2}M_2$,
\[
\pi_{1*}\big(\Theta(v, w)\big) = \pi_{1*}\big(\iota_{1*}v + \iota_{2*}w\big) = \pi_{1*}\iota_{1*}v + \pi_{1*}\iota_{2*}w = v + 0 = v ,
\]
by the definition of $\Theta$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product} and the two identities; so $\pi_{1*}$ is onto $T_{p_1}M_1$: given $v$, the vector $\Theta(v, 0) = \iota_{1*}v$ is a preimage. As $p$ was arbitrary, $\pi_1$ is a submersion.

For $\pi_2$ the same two arguments, with the indices $1$ and $2$ exchanged, give $\pi_{2*}\iota_{2*} = \mathrm{id}$ from $\pi_2 \circ \iota_2 = \mathrm{id}_{M_2}$, and $\pi_{2*}\iota_{1*} = 0$ from the constant map $\pi_2 \circ \iota_1$, with value $p_2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}); hence
\[
\pi_{2*}\big(\Theta(v, w)\big) = \pi_{2*}\iota_{1*}v + \pi_{2*}\iota_{2*}w = 0 + w = w ,
\]
so $\Theta(0, w) = \iota_{2*}w$ is a preimage of any $w \in T_{p_2}M_2$, and $\pi_{2*}$ is onto.
\end{proof}

The projection $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$, a submersion, is collected in Section~\ref{sec:ex-hopf}.

\begin{defbox}[Regular Points and Critical Points]\deflabel{def:regular-critical}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $p \in M$ is a \textbf{regular point} of $F$ if $F$ is a submersion at $p$, i.e.\ $F_{*p}$ is onto --- which forces $n \le m$. Otherwise $p$ is a \textbf{critical point}, also called a \textbf{singular point}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Regular Values and Critical Values]\deflabel{def:regular-critical-value}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$.
\begin{enumerate}[start=2]
    \item $q \in N$ is a \textbf{regular value} of $F$ if $F$ is a submersion at every $p \in F^{-1}(q)$, and a \textbf{critical value} otherwise.
    \item In particular every $q \notin F(M)$ is a regular value: its preimage is empty, and ``everything is true for the empty set.''
\end{enumerate}
These are the notions of Definitions~\ref{def:manifold-regular-point} and~\ref{def:manifold-regular}, now with critical points and the empty-preimage convention made explicit; for maps between open subsets of Euclidean spaces they are those of Definitions~\ref{def:regular-point} and~\ref{def:regular-value}.
\end{defbox}

Uribe called (3) ``kind of a trivial way to be [regular], but important'': it matters in Sard's theorem, about the set of regular values, which is still to come. \textbf{Transcription note.} Page 29 of the handwritten notes has ``if $q \in \operatorname{Im} F$, then $q$ is regular''; the audio has ``if $q$ is not in the image of $F$'', as in (3). The same page writes the preimage in (2) as $F^{-1}(p)$ for $F^{-1}(q)$.

\begin{propbox}[Critical Points of Real-Valued Functions]\thmlabel{prop:critical-functions}
Let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth. Then $df_p$ is either onto or zero, so
\[
p \text{ is a critical point of } f \iff df_p = 0 \iff \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p) = 0 \text{ for all } i,
\]
in any chart at $p$.
\leeref{Exercise 11.24}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
Here $N = \mathbb{R}$, so $n = 1$, and by Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical} $p$ is a critical point of $f$ exactly when $f_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R}$ is not onto.

\emph{The dichotomy.} The image of the linear map $df_p$ is a subspace of the one-dimensional $T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R} \cong \mathbb{R}$ (Definition~\ref{def:identification-TR}), so it is $0$ or everything --- ``dimensions of images cannot be fractional.'' In detail: $df_p = \iota_{f(p)} \circ f_{*p}$ (Definition~\ref{def:differential-function}), where $\iota_{f(p)} : T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a linear isomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:tangent-space-R}(3)). The image of $df_p$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$, of dimension $0$ or $1$; so either $df_p = 0$ or $df_p$ is onto $\mathbb{R}$.

\emph{The first equivalence.} Since $\iota_{f(p)}$ is a bijection, $f_{*p}$ is onto $T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R}$ if and only if $df_p = \iota_{f(p)} \circ f_{*p}$ is onto $\mathbb{R}$. Hence
\[
p \text{ critical} \iff f_{*p} \text{ not onto} \iff df_p \text{ not onto} \iff df_p = 0 ,
\]
the last step by the dichotomy.

\emph{The second equivalence} is Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}: in any chart at $p$, $df_p = \sum_i \partial f/\partial x^i(p)\, dx^i|_p$, and the $dx^i|_p$ form a basis of $T_p^*M$, so this combination is $0$ if and only if every coefficient $\partial f/\partial x^i(p)$ is $0$.
\end{proof}

This is the definition of critical point Uribe sent to the class by email, and it agrees with Definition~\ref{def:regular-point} for $m = 1$: there $p$ is regular iff $\nabla F(p) \ne 0$.

\begin{defbox}[Critical Set]\deflabel{def:critical-set}
Let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth. The \textbf{critical set} of $f$ is
\[
\operatorname{Crit}(f) = \{\, p \in M : df_p = 0 \,\},
\]
the set of critical points of $f$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical}, by Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-functions}.
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Not from lecture: the notation of Assignment~5, Problem~3, used later, in \ref{sec:hessian}.)}

\begin{propbox}[Local Extrema Are Critical Points]\thmlabel{prop:extremum-critical}
Let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth and $p \in M$. If $f$ has a local extremum at $p$ --- $f(q) \le f(p)$ for all $q$ in some neighbourhood of $p$, or $f(q) \ge f(p)$ for all such $q$ --- then $df_p = 0$, that is, $p \in \operatorname{Crit}(f)$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. The argument is the one of Assignment~5, Problem~4(b), where it is applied to the restriction of a function to a regular level set; it works on any manifold.)} By Definition~\ref{def:critical-set} we must show $df_p = 0$, that is, $df_p(v) = 0$ for every $v \in T_pM$. Fix $v \in T_pM$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity} there is a smooth curve $\gamma : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $D_\gamma = v$. Let $W$ be a neighbourhood of $p$ --- an open subset of $M$ containing $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:neighborhood}) --- on which $f \le f(p)$ (or $f \ge f(p)$). As $\gamma$ is continuous, $\gamma^{-1}(W)$ is open in $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ and contains $0$, so it contains an interval $(-\delta, \delta)$; for $|t| < \delta$, $(f \circ \gamma)(t) \le f(p) = (f \circ \gamma)(0)$ (or $\ge$). So the function $f \circ \gamma$ of one variable, smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}, has a local maximum (or minimum) at the interior point $0$, and its derivative there is $0$ (the one-variable fact: at an interior local extremum of a differentiable function the derivative vanishes). By Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} and Definition~\ref{def:velocity},
\[
df_p(v) = D_\gamma[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} f\big(\gamma(t)\big) = (f \circ \gamma)'(0) = 0 .
\]
As $v$ was arbitrary, $df_p = 0$; by Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-functions}, $p$ is a critical point of $f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Submersions to $\mathbb{R}^k$ and Independent Differentials]\thmlabel{prop:submersion-independent-differentials}
Let $G = (G^1, \ldots, G^k) : M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ be smooth, where $G^j = r^j \circ G$ for the standard coordinates $r^1, \ldots, r^k$ of $\mathbb{R}^k$, and let $p \in M$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every $v \in T_pM$,
    \[
    G_{*p}v = \sum_{j=1}^k dG^j|_p(v)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^j}\Big|_{G(p)} .
    \]
    \item $G$ is a submersion at $p$ if and only if the covectors $dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p$ are linearly independent in $T_p^*M$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture. Assignment~5, Problem~4(b), at a point of a regular level set $G^{-1}(0)$: (1) and the direction ($\Rightarrow$) of (2) are the submitted solution's argument, written out; ($\Leftarrow$) is filled in. The Jacobian argument is the second proof below.)} Each $G^j = r^j \circ G$ is smooth, as a composite of smooth maps (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), so $dG^j|_p \in T_p^*M$ is defined.

\emph{(1) The components of $G_{*p}$.} For $v \in T_pM$, the vector $G_{*p}v \in T_{G(p)}\mathbb{R}^k$ is, by the universal formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis} in the identity chart of $\mathbb{R}^k$, $G_{*p}v = \sum_j (G_{*p}v)[r^j]\, \partial/\partial r^j|_{G(p)}$, and its coefficients are, by the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}) and Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation},
\[
\big(G_{*p}v\big)[r^j] = v\big[r^j \circ G\big] = v\big[G^j\big] = dG^j|_p(v) .
\]
Substituting these coefficients gives the formula of (1).

\emph{(2), ($\Rightarrow$): linear independence, without coordinates.} Let $G$ be a submersion at $p$, so that $G_{*p}$ is onto $T_{G(p)}\mathbb{R}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}). Suppose $\sum_{j=1}^k c_j\, dG^j|_p = 0$ for some $c = (c_1, \ldots, c_k) \in \mathbb{R}^k$; we show $c = 0$. Since $G_{*p}$ is onto, the vector $\sum_j c_j\, \partial/\partial r^j|_{G(p)}$ of $T_{G(p)}\mathbb{R}^k$ is $G_{*p}v$ for some $v \in T_pM$. Comparing with (1), and using that the coefficients of a vector in the basis $\partial/\partial r^j|_{G(p)}$ are unique (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), $dG^j|_p(v) = c_j$ for every $j$. Evaluating the assumed relation at this $v$, with the pointwise operations of $T_p^*M$,
\[
0 = \Big(\sum_{j=1}^k c_j\, dG^j|_p\Big)(v) = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j\, dG^j|_p(v) = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j^{\,2} = |c|^2 ,
\]
so $c = 0$. In the assignment's words: the relation says $c \cdot G_{*p}(v) = 0$ for every $v$, and since $G_{*p}$ is onto we may take $G_{*p}(v) = c$.

\emph{(2), ($\Leftarrow$).} Let $dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p$ be linearly independent; we show that $G_{*p}$ is onto. Let $\Lambda : T_pM \to \mathbb{R}^k$, $\Lambda(v) = \big(dG^1|_p(v), \ldots, dG^k|_p(v)\big)$, a linear map since each $dG^j|_p$ is linear. By (1), $G_{*p} = \beta \circ \Lambda$, where $\beta : \mathbb{R}^k \to T_{G(p)}\mathbb{R}^k$, $\beta(c) = \sum_j c_j\, \partial/\partial r^j|_{G(p)}$, is a linear isomorphism, the $\partial/\partial r^j|_{G(p)}$ being a basis (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}); so $G_{*p}$ is onto if and only if $\Lambda$ is. Suppose $\Lambda$ were not onto. Its image $E$ is then a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^k$ of some dimension $d < k$; choose a basis $a_1, \ldots, a_d$ of $E$ and let $B$ be the $d \times k$ matrix with rows $a_1^{\mathsf T}, \ldots, a_d^{\mathsf T}$. By rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) for $B : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^d$, $\dim\ker B \ge k - d \ge 1$, so there is $c \neq 0$ with $Bc = 0$, that is, $a_i \cdot c = 0$ for every $i$, and hence $w \cdot c = 0$ for every $w \in E$, by linearity of the dot product. Then for every $v \in T_pM$,
\[
\Big(\sum_{j=1}^k c_j\, dG^j|_p\Big)(v) = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j\, dG^j|_p(v) = c \cdot \Lambda(v) = 0 ,
\]
as $\Lambda(v) \in E$; so $\sum_j c_j\, dG^j|_p = 0$ with $c \neq 0$, contradicting the independence. Hence $\Lambda$, and with it $G_{*p}$, is onto: $G$ is a submersion at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof of (2), by the Jacobian]
\textit{(The second independence argument of the submitted solution, Assignment~5, Problem~4(b), run in both directions.)} Fix any chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ of $M$ at $p$, and let $J$ be the $k \times m$ matrix with entries $J_{ji} = \partial G^j/\partial x^i(p)$. Written out,
\[
J = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial G^k}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^k}{\partial x^m}(p) \end{pmatrix} .
\] By Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}, $dG^j|_p = \sum_{i=1}^m J_{ji}\, dx^i|_p$: row $j$ of $J$ holds the components of $dG^j|_p$. Hence, for $c \in \mathbb{R}^k$, collecting the coefficient of each $dx^i|_p$,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^k c_j\, dG^j|_p = \sum_{i=1}^m \Big(\sum_{j=1}^k c_j J_{ji}\Big) dx^i|_p ,
\]
and since the $dx^i|_p$ form a basis of $T_p^*M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}), this is $0$ if and only if $\sum_j c_j J_{ji} = 0$ for every $i$, that is, $J^{\mathsf T} c = 0$. So the $dG^j|_p$ are linearly independent if and only if $\ker J^{\mathsf T} = 0$. Next, $J$ is the matrix of $G_{*p}$ in the bases $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ and $\partial/\partial r^j|_{G(p)}$: by (1) with $v = \partial/\partial x^i|_p$ and Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, which gives $dG^j|_p(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = \partial G^j/\partial x^i(p)$, we have $G_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = \sum_j J_{ji}\, \partial/\partial r^j|_{G(p)}$, so the $i$-th column of $J$ holds the coordinates of the image of the $i$-th basis vector (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)). Therefore
\[
G \text{ submersion at } p \iff \operatorname{rank} G_{*p} = k \iff \operatorname{rank} J = k \iff \operatorname{rank} J^{\mathsf T} = k \iff \ker J^{\mathsf T} = 0 \iff dG^1|_p, \ldots, dG^k|_p \text{ independent}.
\]
The first equivalence holds because $G_{*p}$ is onto the $k$-dimensional $T_{G(p)}\mathbb{R}^k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}) exactly when its image has dimension $k$, a subspace of the same finite dimension being the whole space; the second and third because the rank of a linear map is the rank of its matrix, which equals the rank of the transpose (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)); the fourth by rank--nullity for $J^{\mathsf T} : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^m$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)), $\dim\ker J^{\mathsf T} = k - \operatorname{rank} J^{\mathsf T}$; and the last by the first part of this proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Diffeomorphisms onto Open Sets Are Charts]\thmlabel{lem:diffeo-chart}
Let $U \subseteq M$ be open and $\hat\varphi : U \to \mathbb{R}^m$ smooth, with $\hat\varphi(U)$ open and $\hat\varphi : U \to \hat\varphi(U)$ a diffeomorphism. Then $(U, \hat\varphi)$ is a smooth chart of $M$.
\leeref{cf.\ Ch.~2, \emph{Diffeomorphisms}}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{It is a chart.} $\hat\varphi : U \to \hat\varphi(U)$ is a diffeomorphism, so it is a bijection that is continuous with continuous inverse (smooth maps are continuous, Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}): it is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$, so it is a chart (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-chart}).

\emph{It is compatible with every smooth chart.} Let $(W, \chi)$ be any smooth chart of $M$; if $U \cap W = \emptyset$ there is nothing to check (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}). Otherwise the transition maps are
\[
\hat\varphi \circ \chi^{-1} : \chi(U \cap W) \to \hat\varphi(U \cap W), \qquad \chi \circ \hat\varphi^{-1} : \hat\varphi(U \cap W) \to \chi(U \cap W) .
\]
The first is the coordinate representation of the smooth map $\hat\varphi$, restricted to the open set $U \cap W$, in the charts $(U \cap W, \chi|_{U \cap W})$ of $M$ and $(\hat\varphi(U), \mathrm{id})$ of the open set $\hat\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$; the second is the coordinate representation of the smooth map $\hat\varphi^{-1}$ in the charts $(\hat\varphi(U \cap W), \mathrm{id})$ and $(U \cap W, \chi|_{U \cap W})$. Both are smooth, because these maps are (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}, which allows any pair of smooth charts). They are inverse to each other, so the transition function is a diffeomorphism, and $(U, \hat\varphi)$ is compatible with $(W, \chi)$.

\emph{Conclusion.} So $(U, \hat\varphi)$ is compatible with every chart of the maximal atlas $\mathcal{A}$ of $M$, and therefore belongs to it (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}): the set $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ of charts compatible with every chart of $\mathcal{A}$ is the unique maximal atlas containing $\mathcal{A}$, which is $\mathcal{A}$ itself.
\end{proof}
\begin{thmbox}[Local Normal Form for Submersions]\thmlabel{thm:submersion-normal-form}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a submersion at $p$, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$. Then there are charts $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi)$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$ in which the coordinate representation $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to \psi(V)$ is the projection onto the first $n$ coordinates:
\[
\tilde F\big(r^1, \ldots, r^m\big) = \big(r^1, \ldots, r^n\big).
\]
Equivalently, with coordinate functions $x^i = r^i \circ \varphi$ on $U$ and $y^j = r^j \circ \psi$ on $V$: $\;y^j \circ F = x^j$ on $U$ for $j = 1, \ldots, n$. In particular $n \le m$.
\leeref{Theorem 4.12, the rank theorem}
\end{thmbox}

Stated in Lecture 10 and proved in Lecture 11, below. The inequality $n \le m$ needs no theorem --- a surjective linear map cannot raise dimension --- but the normal form does: it says that every submersion, in suitable coordinates, \emph{is} a projection.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=3em, column sep=11em]
U \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\varphi"'] & V \arrow[d, "\psi"] \\
\varphi(U) \arrow[r, "{(r^1, \ldots, r^m) \,\mapsto\, (r^1, \ldots, r^n)}"'] & \psi(V)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}

What the normal form says, for $m = 2$ and $n = 1$. Left: near $p$ the fibres $F^{-1}(c)$ of a submersion are curves, one through each point, which $F$ collapses to the points of an interval. Right: in the charts of the theorem the fibres are straightened into vertical lines, and $\tilde F$ forgets the second coordinate. Every submersion looks, locally and up to a change of coordinates, like the projection of Example~\ref{ex:projection-submersion}.

% ============================================================
% Lecture 11 (Fri Sep 25, 2026)
% ============================================================

\textit{Lecture 11. ``Back to submersions.'' Uribe now made the vocabulary official, with the letters matched to the dimensions: $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$. (In \ref{sec:rvt}, following the earlier lecture, $F : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^m$ had $m$ as the dimension of the target.)}


Uribe singled out Lemma~\ref{lem:diffeo-chart} as ``an intellectual step that should not be overlooked'': in the proof below, a map is shown to be a local diffeomorphism, and this lemma is what makes it a coordinate system.

\begin{proof}[Proof (Lecture 11)]
The steps are the lecture's, in the lecture's order. Sentences marked \textit{(Completion.)} fill in details the lecture passed over.

\emph{1. Start with any coordinates.} ``I start with any coordinates'': smooth charts $(U_0, \varphi_0 = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U_0) \subseteq V$. \textit{(Completion.)} Such charts exist by Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}, applied to $F$ at $p$: take any charts and replace $U_0$ by the open set $U_0 \cap F^{-1}(V)$, open because $F$ is continuous, and $\varphi_0$ by its restriction, again a smooth chart (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)).

\emph{2. The components and their matrix.} As before, define the components of $F$, $F^j = y^j \circ F : U_0 \to \mathbb{R}$. The submersion condition says that the matrix
\[
J = \Big[\frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\Big]
\]
has rank $n$. It ``has $m$ columns, which are the $x$'s, and $n$ rows, that are the gradients'' of the $F^j$. Written out,
\[
J = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p) \end{pmatrix} \qquad (n \text{ rows}, \ m \text{ columns}).
\] \textit{(Completion.)} By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, $J$ is the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the coordinate bases, and $F_{*p}$ is onto, so $J$ has rank $n$: the rank of $F_{*p}$ is $\dim T_{F(p)}N = n$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), and the rank of a linear map is the rank of its matrix (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)).

\emph{3. ``It's the same matrix.''} A student asked whether the matrix should be written with $\tilde F$. Uribe: ``It's the same thing\ldots\ That's how we define partials. We define them by going downstairs and taking the ordinary partial derivative downstairs. So it's the same matrix.'' That is Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs}: writing $G = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi_0^{-1}$ for the coordinate representation in these first charts (the lecture's $\tilde F$ at this stage),
\[
\frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p) = \frac{\partial G^j}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi_0(p)\big), \qquad J = G'\big(\varphi_0(p)\big).
\]
\textit{(Completion.)} The same proposition gives the identity of functions $F^j \circ \varphi_0^{-1} = G^j$ on $\varphi_0(U_0)$, used in step 7.

\emph{4. Reindex --- ``the only thing we need to do.''} $J$ has $n$ linearly independent columns; ``I just put them at the beginning.'' \textit{(Completion.)} The rank of a matrix is the dimension of its column space, so among the $m$ columns of $J$, which has rank $n$, some $n$ are linearly independent. Rearranging the $x^i$, we can write $J$ in block form
\[
J = \big(\, A \ \big|\ B \,\big), \qquad A \text{ an } n \times n \text{ non-singular matrix}, \quad B \text{ of size } n \times (m - n),
\]
where $B$ is ``the stuff that remains here that I'm not going to care about.'' \textit{(Completion.)} $A$ consists of the $n$ independent columns, so it is a square matrix with independent columns, hence non-singular. Rearranging the coordinates replaces $\varphi_0$ by $P \circ \varphi_0$ for a permutation $P$ of $\mathbb{R}^m$. This is again a smooth chart, by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(2) with $h = P$: a linear isomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^m$, hence a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^m$ onto itself (it and its inverse $P^{-1}$ are linear, hence smooth), defined on all of $\mathbb{R}^m \supseteq \varphi_0(U_0)$. It permutes the columns of $J$ in the same way. From now on $\varphi_0 = (x^1, \ldots, x^m)$, $G$ and $J$ denote the rearranged chart, its coordinate representation, and its matrix.

\emph{5. The coordinates we want.} ``The thing to do, you see, is to take the first $n$ components of $F$ as the first $n$ coordinate functions, and then we keep the remaining ones'':
\[
\hat\varphi = \big(F^1, \ldots, F^n, x^{n+1}, \ldots, x^m\big) : U_0 \to \mathbb{R}^m .
\]
\textit{(Completion.)} This makes sense because $n \le m$ --- the theorem's ``in particular'', true since $F_{*p}$ is onto (Proposition~\ref{prop:dimension-constraints}) --- so there are $m - n \ge 0$ remaining coordinates. $\hat\varphi$ is smooth because its components are. It has $m$ components, so it maps into $\mathbb{R}^m$ (see the transcription note below).

\emph{6. The claim.} $\hat\varphi$ is a local diffeomorphism in a neighbourhood of $p$.

\emph{7. The Jacobian of $\hat\varphi$ in the old coordinates.} ``Gradient across'': the first $n$ rows are the gradients of $F^1, \ldots, F^n$, which give the matrix $J = (A \mid B)$; the last $m - n$ rows are the gradients of $x^{n+1}, \ldots, x^m$. These give the $(m-n) \times (m-n)$ identity, and zero in the first $n$ columns, ``because I would be taking partials of these $x$'s with respect to $x$'s that come before.'' So
\[
\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & I_{m-n} \end{pmatrix},
\]
and ``by the block nature, the fact that we have a big zero there, this is non-degenerate'' at $p$: its determinant is $\det A \ne 0$. \textit{(Completion.)} ``The Jacobian of $\hat\varphi$ in the $x$-coordinates'' is the Jacobian at $\varphi_0(p)$ of the ordinary map $H = \hat\varphi \circ \varphi_0^{-1} : \varphi_0(U_0) \to \mathbb{R}^m$. Its rows are the partials of the components of $\hat\varphi$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs}, applied with the identity chart on $\mathbb{R}^m$, and $\partial x^k/\partial x^i = \delta^k_i$ gives the identity and zero blocks. Concretely, for $r \in \varphi_0(U_0)$ put $q = \varphi_0^{-1}(r)$; then $F^j(q) = G^j(r)$ by step 3, and $x^k(q) = r^k$ because $x^k = r^k \circ \varphi_0$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}), so
\[
H(r) = \hat\varphi(q) = \big(F^1(q), \ldots, F^n(q), x^{n+1}(q), \ldots, x^m(q)\big) = \big(G^1(r), \ldots, G^n(r), r^{n+1}, \ldots, r^m\big).
\]
The first $n$ rows of $H'(\varphi_0(p))$ are therefore the rows of $G'(\varphi_0(p)) = J = (A \mid B)$, and row $n + l$ is the gradient of $r^{n+l}$, the standard row vector with $1$ in place $n + l$. Written out, with all partials at $\varphi_0(p)$,
\[
H'\big(\varphi_0(p)\big) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial r^n} & \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial r^{n+1}} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial r^m} \\ \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial G^n}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^n}{\partial r^n} & \dfrac{\partial G^n}{\partial r^{n+1}} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^n}{\partial r^m} \\ \hline 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \end{array}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & I_{m-n} \end{pmatrix} .
\] The matrix is block upper triangular, so its determinant is the product $\det A \cdot \det I_{m-n} = \det A$ of the determinants of the diagonal blocks.

\emph{8. The inverse function theorem, ``possibly after shrinking $U$.''} By the inverse function theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function}), possibly after shrinking, $\hat\varphi$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\hat\varphi(U)$. \textit{(Completion.)} The theorem gives an open $W \ni \varphi_0(p)$, contained in $\varphi_0(U_0)$, with $H|_W$ a diffeomorphism onto the open set $H(W) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$. (This is Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function} with $\Phi = H$ on the open set $\varphi_0(U_0)$ and $a = \varphi_0(p)$, where $H'(a)$ is invertible by step 7; the open sets that theorem calls $U_0$ and $V_0$ are here $W$ and $H(W)$, not to be confused with the chart domain $U_0$.) Put $U = \varphi_0^{-1}(W)$, an open neighbourhood of $p$. Then $\hat\varphi|_U = H|_W \circ \varphi_0|_U$ is a composite of diffeomorphisms (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}, Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), mapping $U$ onto the open set $\hat\varphi(U) = H(W)$. In detail: $H \circ \varphi_0 = \hat\varphi \circ \varphi_0^{-1} \circ \varphi_0 = \hat\varphi$ on $U_0$; $\varphi_0|_U : U \to W$ is the restriction of the diffeomorphism $\varphi_0 : U_0 \to \varphi_0(U_0)$ to the open set $U$, onto $\varphi_0(U) = W$; $H|_W$ is a diffeomorphism of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^m$, hence of manifolds (Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}); and the composite has the smooth inverse $(\varphi_0|_U)^{-1} \circ (H|_W)^{-1}$.

\emph{9. The intellectual step: $\hat\varphi$ is a chart.} ``There's an intellectual step here that should not be overlooked. If I have a local diffeomorphism like this from an open set in $M$ into its image, which is open in $\mathbb{R}^m$, that is a chart'': it is a homeomorphism, and being smooth with smooth inverse makes it compatible with every other smooth chart, so it lies in the maximal atlas. This is Lemma~\ref{lem:diffeo-chart}. So $(U, \hat\varphi)$ is a smooth chart at $p$, and $F(U) \subseteq F(U_0) \subseteq V$.

\emph{10. Do not change the $y$-coordinates.} The chart $(V, \psi)$ on $N$ stays as it was. Only the chart on $M$ is new.

\emph{11. Going up and coming down.} Let $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \hat\varphi^{-1} : \hat\varphi(U) \to \psi(V)$ be the coordinate representation of $F$ in the new chart. ``I take a point down here, $r^1$ up to $r^m$, and I go upstairs'': going up means finding the point $q = \hat\varphi^{-1}(r)$ of $U$ whose values of the first $n$ functions $F^1, \ldots, F^n$ are the first $n$ coordinates of $r$. By the definition of $\hat\varphi$,
\[
F^i\big(\hat\varphi^{-1}(r^1, \ldots, r^m)\big) = r^i \qquad (i = 1, \ldots, n).
\]
\textit{(Completion.)} For $r \in \hat\varphi(U)$ the point $q = \hat\varphi^{-1}(r) \in U$ satisfies $\hat\varphi(q) = r$, that is, $\big(F^1(q), \ldots, F^n(q), x^{n+1}(q), \ldots, x^m(q)\big) = (r^1, \ldots, r^m)$; comparing the first $n$ entries gives the display. Coming back down by $\psi$, the $i$-th coordinate of $\tilde F(r)$ is $y^i(F(q)) = F^i(q) = r^i$. \textit{(Completion.)} In one chain, using the definition of $\tilde F$, then $y^i = r^i \circ \psi$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}), then $F^i = y^i \circ F$, then the display:
\[
r^i\big(\tilde F(r)\big) = r^i\big(\psi(F(q))\big) = y^i\big(F(q)\big) = F^i(q) = r^i \qquad (i = 1, \ldots, n).
\]
So $\tilde F(r^1, \ldots, r^m) = (r^1, \ldots, r^n)$: ``this coordinate system labels every point in $U$; the first $n$ labels are the values of the $F$'s at that point.''

\textit{(Completion.)} The charts of the theorem are $(U, \hat\varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$, with $F(U) \subseteq V$ by step 9. For the equivalent form, the coordinate functions of the new chart are $r^j \circ \hat\varphi$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}), and for $j \le n$ this is the $j$-th component of $\hat\varphi$, namely $F^j = y^j \circ F$. So, calling the new coordinate functions $x^j$ as in the statement, $y^j \circ F = F^j = x^j$ on $U$ for $j = 1, \ldots, n$. Finally $n \le m$ was shown in step 5.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.8em, column sep=3.8em]
& U \arrow[dl, "\varphi_0"'] \arrow[dr, "\hat\varphi"] \arrow[rr, "F"] & & V \arrow[d, "\psi"] \\
W \subseteq \varphi_0(U_0) \arrow[rr, "H = \hat\varphi \circ \varphi_0^{-1}"', "\cong"] & & \hat\varphi(U) \arrow[r, "\tilde F"'] & \psi(V)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The change of chart in one diagram. The first chart $\varphi_0$ and the new chart $\hat\varphi$ differ by $H$, a diffeomorphism near $\varphi_0(p)$ by step~8. In the new chart, $F$ becomes $\tilde F$, the projection (step~11). The lecture used the letters $\phi$ and $\tilde F$ both for the first charts and for the new ones. The notes write $\varphi_0$ and $G$ for the first, and $\hat\varphi$ and $\tilde F$ for the new, to keep the two stages apart.

\textbf{Transcription note.} In the lecture, $\hat\varphi$ was twice called ``a map from $U$ into $\mathbb{R}^n$'', and page 30 of the handwritten notes writes $\phi : U \to \mathbb{R}$; it has $m$ components, so $\hat\varphi : U \to \mathbb{R}^m$. The matrix of partials was spoken as ``$\partial x^j/\partial x^i$'', for $\partial F^j/\partial x^i$.

\begin{corbox}[Being a Submersion Is an Open Condition]\thmlabel{cor:submersion-open-condition}
If $F : M \to N$ is a submersion at $p$, then $F$ is a submersion at every point of some neighbourhood of $p$.
\leeref{Proposition 4.1}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Let $(U, \hat\varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ be the charts of the theorem: $p \in U$, $F(U) \subseteq V$, and $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \hat\varphi^{-1}$ is the projection $\tilde F(r^1, \ldots, r^m) = (r^1, \ldots, r^n)$ on $\hat\varphi(U)$. The open set $U$ is a neighbourhood of $p$; we show that $F$ is a submersion at every $q \in U$.

In the charts of the theorem, $\tilde F$ is the projection, whose Jacobian $(I_n \mid 0)$ has rank $n$ at every point of $\hat\varphi(U)$: its components are $\tilde F^j(r) = r^j$ ($j \le n$), so $\partial \tilde F^j/\partial r^i = \delta^j_i$ for $i = 1, \ldots, m$ at every point, and the first $n$ columns of the resulting matrix are the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Written out, for every $r \in \hat\varphi(U)$,
\[
\tilde F'(r) = \left(\begin{array}{cccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{array}\right) = (I_n \mid 0) \qquad (n \text{ rows}, \ m \text{ columns}).
\] Now fix $q \in U$. The same two charts are charts at $q$ and at $F(q)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$, so by Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} the matrix of $F_{*q}$ in the coordinate bases is $\tilde F'(\hat\varphi(q)) = (I_n \mid 0)$. Hence $\operatorname{rank} F_{*q} = n$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)), and the image of $F_{*q}$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of the $n$-dimensional space $T_{F(q)}N$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), so it is all of it. By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, $F_{*q}$ is onto for every $q \in U$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[The Critical Set Is Closed]\thmlabel{cor:critical-set-closed}
Let $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth. Then $\operatorname{Crit}(f)$ (Definition~\ref{def:critical-set}) is a closed subset of $M$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} We show that the complement $M \setminus \operatorname{Crit}(f)$ is open, by finding around each of its points an open set contained in it. Let $p \in M \setminus \operatorname{Crit}(f)$, so $df_p \neq 0$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-functions}, $p$ is not a critical point of $f$, that is (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical}), $f$ is a submersion at $p$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-open-condition}, applied to $F = f : M \to \mathbb{R}$, there is a neighbourhood $U_p$ of $p$ --- an open set containing $p$ --- such that $f$ is a submersion at every $q \in U_p$. Each such $q$ is a regular point of $f$, so $df_q \neq 0$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-functions} again, that is, $q \notin \operatorname{Crit}(f)$. Thus $U_p \subseteq M \setminus \operatorname{Crit}(f)$, and $M \setminus \operatorname{Crit}(f) = \bigcup_p U_p$ is open, as a union of open sets. Hence $\operatorname{Crit}(f)$ is closed.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Submersions Are Open Maps]\thmlabel{cor:submersion-open-map}
If $F : M \to N$ is a submersion, then $F(W)$ is open in $N$ for every open $W \subseteq M$.
\leeref{Proposition 4.28}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
$F$ is smooth, hence continuous, so by Definition~\ref{def:open-map} it remains to show that $F(W)$ is open for every open $W \subseteq M$. It suffices to find, for each point $q$ of $F(W)$, an open set containing $q$ and contained in $F(W)$, since then $F(W)$ is the union of these open sets.

Let $q = F(p)$ with $p \in W$, and take the charts of the theorem at $p$, shrinking $U$ to $U \cap W$: the restriction of $\hat\varphi$ to the open set $U \cap W \ni p$ is again a smooth chart (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), with $U' = U \cap W$), still $F(U \cap W) \subseteq V$, and the coordinate representation is still the projection, now on $\hat\varphi(U \cap W)$. We write $U$ for $U \cap W$. Then $F(U) = \psi^{-1}\big(\mathrm{pr}(\hat\varphi(U))\big)$, where $\mathrm{pr} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is the projection onto the first $n$ coordinates. Indeed, on $U$ we have $F = \psi^{-1} \circ \tilde F \circ \hat\varphi$ (the definition of $\tilde F$, with $F(U) \subseteq V$), and $\tilde F = \mathrm{pr}$ on $\hat\varphi(U)$, so
\[
F(U) = \psi^{-1}\big(\tilde F(\hat\varphi(U))\big) = \psi^{-1}\big(\mathrm{pr}(\hat\varphi(U))\big) .
\]
Projections are open (Lemma~\ref{lem:proj-open}, for $\mathbb{R}^m = \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^{m-n}$), and $\hat\varphi(U)$ is open, being the image of a chart, so $\mathrm{pr}(\hat\varphi(U))$ is an open subset of $\psi(V)$; it lies in $\psi(V)$ because it equals $\tilde F(\hat\varphi(U))$. Since $\psi : V \to \psi(V)$ is a homeomorphism, $\psi^{-1}$ maps open subsets of $\psi(V)$ to open subsets of $V$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(2)), and $V$ is open in $N$; so $F(U)$ is open in $N$. It contains $q$ and lies in $F(W)$: $q = F(p)$ with $p \in U$, and $U \subseteq W$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Submersions from Compact Manifolds]\thmlabel{thm:compact-submersion}
Let $M$ be compact and nonempty, $N$ connected, and $F : M \to N$ a submersion. Then $F$ is surjective, and $N$ is compact.
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~4, Problem~2, where $N = \mathbb{R}^k$; the same argument gives the general statement.)} $F(M)$ is open in $N$ because a submersion is an open map (Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-open-map}), and compact, hence closed in the Hausdorff space $N$, because $M$ is compact. It is nonempty, and $N$ is connected, so $F(M) = N$. Then $N = F(M)$ is compact.

In detail, the three properties of the subset $F(M) \subseteq N$ are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{open:} Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-open-map} with $W = M$;
    \item \emph{closed:} $F$ is continuous (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}), so $F(M)$ is compact as the continuous image of the compact space $M$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(2)); $N$ is Hausdorff, being a manifold; and a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space is closed (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(4));
    \item \emph{nonempty:} $M \neq \emptyset$.
\end{itemize}
In a connected space the only subsets that are both open and closed are $\emptyset$ and the whole space; $F(M)$ is such a subset and is not empty, so $F(M) = N$, i.e.\ $F$ is surjective. And $N = F(M)$ is compact, by the second item.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[No Submersions from Compact Manifolds to Euclidean Space]\thmlabel{cor:no-submersion-Rk}
If $M$ is compact and nonempty and $k \ge 1$, there is no submersion $M \to \mathbb{R}^k$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~4, Problem~2.)} $\mathbb{R}^k$ is connected but not compact, since it is unbounded; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:compact-submersion}.

In detail, suppose $F : M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ were a submersion. The hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:compact-submersion} hold: $M$ is compact and nonempty, and $N = \mathbb{R}^k$ is connected (Proposition~\ref{fact:conn}(4)). So the theorem gives that $\mathbb{R}^k$ is compact. But for $k \ge 1$, $\mathbb{R}^k$ is not bounded --- it contains the points $(t, 0, \ldots, 0)$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ --- so it is not compact by Heine--Borel (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(1)). This contradiction shows that no such $F$ exists.
\end{proof}

The submitted solution also noted the edge cases: for $k = 0$ the constant map $M \to \mathbb{R}^0$ is a submersion, since every differential maps onto the zero space; and for $M = \emptyset$ the empty map is vacuously one. In particular, a compact manifold carries no nonconstant submersion to $\mathbb{R}$ --- the maximum of any smooth function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is a critical point. \textit{(Filled in.)} Directly: if $M$ is compact and nonempty, $f(M)$ is a compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(2)), hence closed and bounded (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(1)), nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$, so it contains its supremum $f(p)$, $p \in M$. Then $f(q) \le f(p)$ for every $q$ in the neighbourhood $M$ of $p$, so $df_p = 0$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:extremum-critical}, and $f$ is not a submersion at $p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-functions}). (Constant functions are not submersions either, their differentials being zero; so for $M$ compact and nonempty there is no submersion $M \to \mathbb{R}$ at all, as Corollary~\ref{cor:no-submersion-Rk} says.)

\section{Regular Submanifolds}\label{sec:submanifolds-fibrations}\label{sec:submanifolds}

\roadmark{Stage: submanifolds}{Subsets of a manifold that are locally coordinate slices --- the equations thread, completed.}

\textit{References: Lee Ch.~5. Lecture 12.} The subsets of a manifold that look locally like $\mathbb{R}^{m-k} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$. The regular value theorem for manifolds, proved from the submersion normal form of \ref{sec:submersions}, produces them as level sets --- the end of the equations thread that began in \ref{sec:rvt}.

\subsection{Open Submanifolds}\label{sub:open-submanifolds}

\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Which subsets of a smooth manifold $M$ inherit a smooth structure from $M$? An arbitrary subset with the subspace topology need not even be a manifold --- $\mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is not locally Euclidean (the remark \emph{What Subspaces Do Not Inherit} in \ref{sec:new-spaces}) --- and when it is a lower-dimensional one, the charts of $M$ do not restrict to charts of it: for a chart $(U, \varphi)$, the set $\varphi(U \cap S)$ is in general not open in $\mathbb{R}^m$ (for the circle in $\mathbb{R}^2$ it is a piece of a curve). Open subsets are the easy case: the charts of $M$ simply restrict (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}). Regular submanifolds, in the rest of this section, are the general answer, and the two meet in codimension $0$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-codim0}).

\begin{defbox}[Open Submanifold of a Smooth Manifold]\deflabel{def:open-submanifold-smooth}
An \textbf{open submanifold} of a smooth manifold $M$ is an open subset $S \subseteq M$ with the subspace topology and the smooth structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}, whose charts are the smooth charts of $M$ with domain in $S$. It is the smooth counterpart of Definition~\ref{def:open-submanifold}; its inclusion into $M$ is smooth, and maps into $S$ are smooth exactly when they are smooth into $M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}).
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Open Subsets of a Product]\thmlabel{prop:open-product}
Let $M_1$, $M_2$ be smooth manifolds and $U \subseteq M_1$ open. Then $U \times M_2$ is open in $M_1 \times M_2$, and the open submanifold $U \times M_2$ of $M_1 \times M_2$ (Definition~\ref{def:open-submanifold-smooth}) is the same smooth manifold as the product manifold $U \times M_2$ of the open submanifold $U$ with $M_2$ (Definition~\ref{def:product-manifold}). In particular the projection $\mathrm{pr}_1 : U \times M_2 \to U$ is the restriction to $U \times M_2$ of the projection $\mathrm{pr}_1 : M_1 \times M_2 \to M_1$ (Definition~\ref{def:projections}).
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{Open.} $U \times M_2 = \mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}(U)$, open because $\mathrm{pr}_1$ is continuous (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}).

\emph{Same topology.} The product topology of $U \times M_2$ has the basis of sets $A' \times B$ with $A'$ open in $U$ and $B$ open in $M_2$ (Definition~\ref{def:product-topology}); since $U$ is open, the sets $A'$ open in $U$ are the sets $A \cap U$ with $A$ open in $M_1$. The subspace topology of $U \times M_2$ in $M_1 \times M_2$ has the basis of sets $(A \times B) \cap (U \times M_2) = (A \cap U) \times B$. The two bases are the same, so the topologies agree.

\emph{Same smooth structure.} A product chart of $U \times M_2$ is $(U_1 \times U_2, \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)$ with $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ a smooth chart of the open submanifold $U$ and $(U_2, \varphi_2)$ one of $M_2$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(2), $(U_1, \varphi_1)$ is a smooth chart of $M_1$ with $U_1 \subseteq U$, so $(U_1 \times U_2, \varphi_1 \times \varphi_2)$ is a product chart of $M_1 \times M_2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-manifold}) with domain in $U \times M_2$ --- a smooth chart of the open submanifold $U \times M_2$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(2) again. So the product charts of $U \times M_2$, an atlas generating its product structure, all lie in the smooth structure of the open submanifold; by the uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas} the two smooth structures are equal.

\emph{The projection.} Both maps send $(b, y)$ to $b$.
\end{proof}
