\subsection{Regular Submanifolds}\label{sub:submanifolds}

\textit{Lecture 12 (Mon Sep 28). ``I know we're in the middle of discussing submersions and fibrations, but we need the notion of submanifold. So let's pause to discuss that. It's not difficult.'' The local model is a lower-dimensional Euclidean space inside a higher-dimensional one: $\mathbb{R}^{m-k} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ as the points whose last $k$ coordinates vanish, $x \mapsto (x, \vec 0)$.}

\begin{defbox}[Regular Submanifold]\deflabel{def:submanifold}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$, $S \subseteq M$ a subset with the subspace topology, and $0 \le k \le m$. For a chart $\varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ write $x_a = (x^1, \ldots, x^{m-k})$ for its first $m - k$ components and $x_b = (x^{m-k+1}, \ldots, x^m)$ for its last $k$. Then $S$ is a \textbf{regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $k$} if every $p \in S$ lies in the domain of a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ with
\[
U \cap S = \{\, q \in U : x_b(q) = \vec 0 \,\}.
\]
Regular submanifolds are also called \textbf{embedded} submanifolds, as opposed to the immersed submanifolds of Definition~\ref{def:immersed-submanifold}. In these notes, ``submanifold'' without qualification means a regular submanifold.
\leeref{Theorem 5.8}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Adapted Chart]\deflabel{def:adapted-chart}
Let $M$, $S$ and $k$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}. Such charts --- smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ with $U \cap S = \{\, q \in U : x_b(q) = \vec 0 \,\}$ --- are \textbf{adapted} to $S$; ``a random chart of $M$ is not adapted.'' In an adapted chart, $U \cap S$ is cut out by the $k$ equations $x^{m-k+1} = \cdots = x^m = 0$, exactly as in the local model.
\leeref{Theorem 5.8}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Two Observations on Adapted Charts]\thmlabel{prop:adapted-flex}
Let $(U, \varphi)$ be a smooth chart of $M$, and suppose that $U \cap S$ is cut out in it by setting some $k$ of the coordinates equal to constants:
\[
U \cap S = \{\, q \in U : x^{i_1}(q) = c_1, \ \ldots, \ x^{i_k}(q) = c_k \,\}.
\]
Then there is an adapted chart with the same domain $U$. That is:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the value $\vec 0$ in the definition may be replaced by any constant vector $\vec c$;
    \item the last $k$ coordinates may be replaced by any $k$ of them.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~12: ``obvious observations''; filled in.)} Let $P : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be the permutation of coordinates that moves positions $i_1, \ldots, i_k$ to the last $k$ places, and $T(r) = r - (\vec 0, \vec c)$. Explicitly, if $j_1 < \cdots < j_{m-k}$ are the remaining indices,
\[
P(r) = \big(r^{j_1}, \ldots, r^{j_{m-k}}, r^{i_1}, \ldots, r^{i_k}\big), \qquad T(s) = \big(s^1, \ldots, s^{m-k}, s^{m-k+1} - c_1, \ldots, s^m - c_k\big).
\]
Then $A = T \circ P$ is an affine diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^m$, with inverse $A^{-1}(s) = P^{-1}\big(s + (\vec 0, \vec c)\big)$, so $(U, A \circ \varphi)$ is a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(2), applied with $h = A$: a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^m$ onto itself (the components of $A$ and of $A^{-1}$ are affine, hence smooth), defined on all of $\mathbb{R}^m \supseteq \varphi(U)$. (In that lemma the transition maps with a smooth chart $(V, \chi)$ are $(A \circ \varphi) \circ \chi^{-1} = A \circ (\varphi \circ \chi^{-1})$ and $\chi \circ (A \circ \varphi)^{-1} = (\chi \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ A^{-1}$, composites of smooth maps.) Its last $k$ coordinates are $x^{i_1} - c_1, \ldots, x^{i_k} - c_k$, which vanish exactly on $U \cap S$: for $q \in U$,
\[
(A \circ \varphi)(q) = \big(x^{j_1}(q), \ldots, x^{j_{m-k}}(q),\ x^{i_1}(q) - c_1, \ldots, x^{i_k}(q) - c_k\big),
\]
and its last $k$ entries are all $0$ if and only if $x^{i_l}(q) = c_l$ for $l = 1, \ldots, k$, that is (by hypothesis), if and only if $q \in U \cap S$. So $(U, A \circ \varphi)$ is adapted (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}). Observation (1) is the case $(i_1, \ldots, i_k) = (m-k+1, \ldots, m)$, where $P$ is the identity; observation (2) is the case $\vec c = \vec 0$, where $T$ is the identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Induced Smooth Structure]\thmlabel{prop:submanifold-structure}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold of codimension $k$. For each adapted chart $(U, \varphi = (x_a, x_b))$ put
\[
\varphi_S = x_a|_{U \cap S} : U \cap S \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{m-k}.
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $U \cap S$ is open in $S$, and $\varphi_S$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{m-k}$;
    \item the charts $(U \cap S, \varphi_S)$, over all adapted charts, form a smooth atlas $\mathcal{A}_S$ on $S$.
\end{enumerate}
So $S$ is a topological manifold of dimension $m - k$, and with the smooth structure generated by $\mathcal{A}_S$ it is a smooth manifold --- ``a manifold in its own right.''
\leeref{Theorem 5.8}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~12 claimed (1) --- ``easy to check'' --- and gave the reason for (2); completed here.)} $S$ is Hausdorff and second countable as a subspace of $M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:subspace-inherit}) --- ``back to week one of the class.'' Let $j : \mathbb{R}^{m-k} \to \mathbb{R}^m$, $j(r) = (r, \vec 0)$, and $\mathrm{pr} : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}^{m-k}$, $\mathrm{pr}(r, s) = r$. Both are linear, hence smooth, and $\mathrm{pr} \circ j = \mathrm{id}$; also $x_a = \mathrm{pr} \circ \varphi$ on $U$, so $\varphi_S = \mathrm{pr} \circ \varphi|_{U \cap S}$.

(1) $U \cap S$ is open in $S$ by the definition of the subspace topology, $U$ being open in $M$. Since $U \cap S = \{x_b = \vec 0\}$, the chart $\varphi$ maps $U \cap S$ bijectively onto $\varphi(U) \cap j(\mathbb{R}^{m-k}) = j(W)$, where $W = j^{-1}(\varphi(U))$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^{m-k}$ because $j$ is continuous. Indeed, for $q \in U$: $q \in S$ iff the last $k$ entries of $\varphi(q)$ vanish iff $\varphi(q) \in j(\mathbb{R}^{m-k})$; so $\varphi(U \cap S) = \varphi(U) \cap j(\mathbb{R}^{m-k})$, and a point $j(r)$ lies in $\varphi(U)$ exactly when $r \in W$. So $\varphi_S = \mathrm{pr} \circ \varphi|_{U \cap S}$ is a continuous bijection $U \cap S \to W$, with continuous inverse $r \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(j(r))$. In detail: $\varphi_S$ is continuous as a composite of continuous maps; $r \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(j(r))$ is continuous $W \to U$, with values in $U \cap S$ because $j(r) \in \varphi(U \cap S)$, hence continuous into the subspace $U \cap S$; and the two maps are inverse to each other,
\[
\varphi_S\big(\varphi^{-1}(j(r))\big) = \mathrm{pr}\big(j(r)\big) = r, \qquad \varphi^{-1}\big(j(\varphi_S(q))\big) = \varphi^{-1}\big(j(\mathrm{pr}(\varphi(q)))\big) = \varphi^{-1}\big(\varphi(q)\big) = q ,
\]
the last because $\varphi(q) = (x_a(q), \vec 0) = j(\mathrm{pr}(\varphi(q)))$ for $q \in U \cap S$. So $\varphi_S$ is a homeomorphism of the open set $U \cap S$ of $S$ onto the open set $W$ of $\mathbb{R}^{m-k}$; as every point of $S$ lies in an adapted chart, $S$ is locally Euclidean of dimension $m - k$, and with the first paragraph it is a topological manifold of dimension $m - k$.

(2) Every point of $S$ lies in an adapted chart, so the domains cover $S$. For adapted charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$, since $\varphi_S^{-1} = \varphi^{-1} \circ j$,
\[
\psi_S \circ \varphi_S^{-1} = \mathrm{pr} \circ (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ j \qquad \text{on } \varphi_S(U \cap V \cap S) = j^{-1}\big(\varphi(U \cap V)\big) .
\]
Here $\psi_S = \mathrm{pr} \circ \psi$ on $V \cap S$ gives the formula, and the domain is computed as in (1) with the open set $U \cap V$ in place of $U$ (the restriction of $\varphi$ to $U \cap V$ is again adapted). This is the transition map of $M$, which is smooth, composed with the linear maps $j$ and $\mathrm{pr}$: the transition maps of $S$ are ``restrictions to $\mathbb{R}^{m-k}$ of $C^\infty$ maps between open sets of $\mathbb{R}^m$.'' Exchanging the roles of the two charts, $\varphi_S \circ \psi_S^{-1} = \mathrm{pr} \circ (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}) \circ j$ is smooth as well, and the two transition maps are inverse to each other; so they are diffeomorphisms, and any two charts of $\mathcal{A}_S$ are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}). Thus $\mathcal{A}_S$ is a smooth atlas, and it generates a smooth structure (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Open Submanifolds Are the Regular Submanifolds of Codimension 0]\thmlabel{prop:open-codim0}
Let $M$ be a smooth $m$-manifold and $S \subseteq M$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $S$ is open, it is a regular submanifold of codimension $0$, and its induced smooth structure (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}) is that of the open submanifold $S$ (Definition~\ref{def:open-submanifold-smooth}).
    \item Conversely, a regular submanifold of codimension $0$ is open in $M$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} For $k = 0$ the chart has no last coordinates: $x_a = \varphi$ and $x_b$ is empty, so the condition $x_b(q) = \vec 0$ in Definition~\ref{def:submanifold} holds for every $q$. A chart $(U, \varphi)$ is therefore adapted to $S$ with $k = 0$ exactly when $U \cap S = U$, that is, when $U \subseteq S$.

\emph{(1)} Let $S$ be open and $p \in S$. For a smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$, its restriction $(U \cap S, \varphi|_{U \cap S})$ is a smooth chart of $M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(2)) with domain inside $S$, hence adapted with $k = 0$. So $S$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $0$. The induced chart of an adapted chart $(U, \varphi)$ with $U \subseteq S$ is $\varphi_S = x_a|_{U \cap S} = \varphi$, the chart itself; so the atlas $\mathcal{A}_S$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure} consists of the smooth charts of $M$ with domain in $S$, which generate the open-submanifold structure (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(2)). The two smooth structures are therefore equal (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}).

\emph{(2)} Let $S$ be a regular submanifold of codimension $0$. Each $p \in S$ lies in the domain $U_p$ of an adapted chart, and $U_p \subseteq S$ by the observation above. So $S = \bigcup_{p \in S} U_p$ is a union of open sets of $M$, hence open.
\end{proof}

An adapted chart ($m = 2$, $k = 1$). The chart $\varphi$ straightens $U \cap S$ onto the part of the $x_a$-axis inside $\varphi(U)$ --- exactly the set $\varphi(U) \cap \{x_b = 0\}$, running from rim to rim --- and the induced chart $\varphi_S$ keeps only the coordinate $x_a$, landing on an open interval of $\mathbb{R}^{m-k}$.

\textbf{Extending charts.} A student asked whether every chart of $S$ extends to an adapted chart of $M$. Uribe: ``The answer is yes'' --- since everything reduces to the local Euclidean picture, the $m - k$ functions of a chart of $S$ extend to a neighbourhood in $M$. This is stated, not proved, here; likewise his remark that smooth functions on $S$ extend to smooth functions near $S$.

\begin{lembox}[Smooth Maps and Regular Submanifolds]\thmlabel{lem:maps-into-submanifold}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold, with its induced structure, and $\iota : S \to M$ the inclusion.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\iota$ is smooth; in an adapted chart and its induced chart, its coordinate representation is $j(r) = (r, \vec 0)$.
    \item If $G : X \to M$ is smooth and $G(X) \subseteq S$, then $G$ is smooth as a map into $S$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Corollary 5.30}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{((1) is Uribe's ``immediate from the definitions''; filled in, and (2) is not from lecture.)} Recall from the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure} that for an adapted chart $(U, \varphi)$, $\varphi_S = \mathrm{pr} \circ \varphi$ on $U \cap S$ and $\varphi_S^{-1} = \varphi^{-1} \circ j$, with $j(r) = (r, \vec 0)$ and $\mathrm{pr}(r, s) = r$.

(1) $\iota$ is continuous for the subspace topology: the preimage of an open $O \subseteq M$ is $O \cap S$, open in $S$. For an adapted chart, $\varphi \circ \iota \circ \varphi_S^{-1} = \varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ j = j$ on $\varphi_S(U \cap S)$, which is smooth, so $\iota$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}). In detail: every $p \in S$ lies in an adapted chart $(U, \varphi)$, whose induced chart $(U \cap S, \varphi_S)$ is a chart of $S$ at $p$ with $\iota(U \cap S) \subseteq U$; the coordinate representation in these charts is the linear map $j$; so $\iota$ is smooth by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, and this computation shows that its coordinate representation is $j$ in every adapted chart and its induced chart.

(2) $G$ is continuous into $S$, since $G^{-1}(O \cap S) = G^{-1}(O)$ for $O$ open in $M$ (because $G(X) \subseteq S$), and the sets $O \cap S$ are the open sets of $S$. Given $x \in X$, take an adapted chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $G(x)$ and a chart $\chi$ of $X$ at $x$ with domain inside $G^{-1}(U)$ --- the restriction of any smooth chart at $x$ to its intersection with the open set $G^{-1}(U)$, again a smooth chart (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)). Its domain is then mapped by $G$ into $U \cap S$, the domain of the induced chart $\varphi_S$. Then $\varphi_S \circ G \circ \chi^{-1} = \mathrm{pr} \circ (\varphi \circ G \circ \chi^{-1})$, a linear map composed with a coordinate representation of the smooth map $G$, hence smooth: $\varphi \circ G \circ \chi^{-1}$ is smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}, and $\varphi_S = \mathrm{pr} \circ \varphi$ on $U \cap S$. So $G : X \to S$ is smooth by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Tangent Spaces of a Regular Submanifold]\thmlabel{prop:submanifold-tangent}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold of codimension $k$ and $p \in S$. Then $\iota_{*p} : T_pS \to T_pM$ is injective. In an adapted chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ at $p$, writing $\partial/\partial x^i|^S_p$ for the coordinate derivations of the induced chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^{m-k})$ of $S$,
\[
\iota_{*p}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|^S_p\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p \quad (i \le m - k), \qquad \iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \Span\Big\{\frac{\partial}{\partial x^1}\Big|_p, \ldots, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{m-k}}\Big|_p\Big\}.
\]
Equivalently, by curves: for a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $S$ with $\gamma(0) = p$, $\iota_{*p} D_\gamma = D_{\iota \circ \gamma}$ --- a curve in $S$ is a curve in $M$, with the same velocity.
\leeref{Propositions 5.35 and 5.37}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~12: ``immediate from the definitions''; filled in.)} Fix an adapted chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and its induced chart $(U \cap S, \varphi_S)$ of $S$, whose coordinate functions are $x^1, \ldots, x^{m-k}$ restricted to $U \cap S$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis} the $\partial/\partial x^i|^S_p$, $i \le m - k$, form a basis of $T_pS$, and the $\partial/\partial x^l|_p$, $l \le m$, a basis of $T_pM$.

\emph{The formula.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1) the coordinate representation of $\iota$ is $j$, whose Jacobian is the $m \times (m-k)$ matrix $\binom{I_{m-k}}{0}$: the components of $j(r) = (r, \vec 0)$ are $j^l(r) = r^l$ for $l \le m - k$ and $j^l(r) = 0$ for $l > m - k$, so $\partial j^l/\partial r^i = \delta^l_i$ for $l \le m - k$ and $0$ for $l > m - k$. Written out, at every point,
\[
j'(r) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 1 \\ \hline 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{array}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} I_{m-k} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \qquad (m \text{ rows}, \ m - k \text{ columns}).
\] By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} this is the matrix of $\iota_{*p}$ in the coordinate bases; its $i$-th column gives the formula. Explicitly, the formula of that theorem, with the upstairs partials replaced by the entries of the Jacobian of $j$, reads
\[
\iota_{*p}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|^S_p\Big) = \sum_{l=1}^m \frac{\partial j^l}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi_S(p)\big)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^l}\Big|_p = \sum_{l=1}^{m-k} \delta^l_i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^l}\Big|_p = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p \qquad (i \le m - k).
\]

\emph{The image.} $\iota_{*p}$ is linear, so it maps $T_pS$, the span of the basis $\partial/\partial x^i|^S_p$ ($i \le m - k$), onto the span of their images, which by the formula is $\Span\{\partial/\partial x^1|_p, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^{m-k}|_p\}$.

\emph{Injectivity.} The columns of $\binom{I_{m-k}}{0}$ are independent, so $\iota_{*p}$ is injective. In terms of vectors: if $\iota_{*p}\big(\sum_i a_i\, \partial/\partial x^i|^S_p\big) = \sum_i a_i\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p = 0$, then every $a_i = 0$, because the $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ are part of a basis of $T_pM$.

\emph{Curves.} The statement for curves is Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}, applied to the smooth map $F = \iota$ and a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $S$ with $\gamma(0) = p$: it gives $\iota_{*p} D_\gamma = D_{\iota \circ \gamma}$, where $\iota \circ \gamma$ is $\gamma$ regarded as a curve in $M$, smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}.
\end{proof}

So $T_pS$ is identified with the $(m-k)$-dimensional subspace $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) \subseteq T_pM$, the ``intrinsic tangent space'' inside the ambient one --- ``for some reason this class, and maybe all abstract classes, keep identifying things with each other.'' The second description is the one from Assignment~3, Problem~2: think of a curve in $S$ composed with the inclusion as a curve in $M$, and take its velocity there.

\begin{propbox}[Adapted Charts Give Local Defining Maps]\thmlabel{prop:adapted-defining-map}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold of codimension $k$ and $(U, \varphi = (x_a, x_b))$ a chart adapted to $S$, with $x_b = (x^{m-k+1}, \ldots, x^m) : U \to \mathbb{R}^k$, a map from the open submanifold $U$ to $\mathbb{R}^k$ with its standard coordinates $r^1, \ldots, r^k$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $x_b$ is smooth, and for every $q \in U$
    \[
    (x_b)_{*q}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_q\Big) = \begin{cases} 0, & i \le m - k, \\[2pt] \dfrac{\partial}{\partial r^{\,i-(m-k)}}\Big|_{x_b(q)}, & i > m - k. \end{cases}
    \]
    \item $x_b$ is a submersion at every point of $U$.
    \item $U \cap S = x_b^{-1}(\vec 0)$, and $\vec 0$ is a regular value of $x_b$.
    \item For every $q \in U \cap S$, $\iota_{*q}(T_qS) = \ker (x_b)_{*q}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, a regular submanifold is locally a regular level set: every point of $S$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ in $M$ on which $U \cap S$ is the preimage of the regular value $\vec 0$ of a smooth map $U \to \mathbb{R}^k$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. The computation is Step~2 of the submitted solution of Assignment~5, Problem~2, and the last sentence is the remark of Assignment~5, Problem~4, that a regular submanifold is locally a regular level set.)} Throughout, the tangent space of the open set $U$ at $q$ is identified with $T_qM$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}), and $\mathbb{R}^k$ carries the identity chart, whose coordinate functions are $r^1, \ldots, r^k$.

\emph{(1)} The coordinate representation of $x_b$ in the charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(\mathbb{R}^k, \mathrm{id})$ is
\[
\mathrm{id} \circ x_b \circ \varphi^{-1}\big(r^1, \ldots, r^m\big) = \big(r^{m-k+1}, \ldots, r^m\big) \qquad \text{on } \varphi(U),
\]
because the $l$-th entry of $\varphi(q')$ is $x^l(q')$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}). This is a linear map, hence smooth, so $x_b$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}). Its components are $x_b^{\,j} = r^j \circ x_b = x^{m-k+j}$, $j = 1, \ldots, k$, and the Jacobian of the coordinate representation at every point is the $k \times m$ matrix $(0 \mid I_k)$: $\partial r^{m-k+j}/\partial r^i = \delta^{m-k+j}_i$. Written out,
\[
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \end{array}\right) = (0 \mid I_k) \qquad (k \text{ rows}; \ m - k \text{ zero columns, then } k).
\] By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, whose upstairs partials $\partial x_b^{\,j}/\partial x^i(q) = \partial x^{m-k+j}/\partial x^i(q)$ are the entries of this Jacobian, for $q \in U$
\[
(x_b)_{*q}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_q\Big) = \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{\partial x^{m-k+j}}{\partial x^i}(q)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^j}\Big|_{x_b(q)} = \sum_{j=1}^k \delta^{m-k+j}_i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^j}\Big|_{x_b(q)} =
\begin{cases} 0, & i \le m - k, \\[2pt] \dfrac{\partial}{\partial r^{\,i-(m-k)}}\Big|_{x_b(q)}, & i > m - k. \end{cases}
\]

\emph{(2)} Let $q \in U$. The image of $(x_b)_{*q}$ is a subspace containing, by the second case of (1), every vector $\partial/\partial r^j|_{x_b(q)}$ of the coordinate basis of $T_{x_b(q)}\mathbb{R}^k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), hence their span, which is everything. So $(x_b)_{*q}$ is onto, and $x_b$ is a submersion at $q$ (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}).

\emph{(3)} By Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}, $U \cap S = \{\, q \in U : x_b(q) = \vec 0 \,\} = x_b^{-1}(\vec 0)$. Every point of $x_b^{-1}(\vec 0)$ is a point of $U$, at which $x_b$ is a submersion by (2); so $\vec 0$ is a regular value of $x_b$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}).

\emph{(4)} Let $q \in U \cap S$; then $(U, \varphi)$ is an adapted chart at $q$. By the first case of (1), $(x_b)_{*q}$ kills $\partial/\partial x^1|_q, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^{m-k}|_q$, hence, being linear, their span; by Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent} that span is $\iota_{*q}(T_qS)$, so $\iota_{*q}(T_qS) \subseteq \ker (x_b)_{*q}$. The span has dimension $m - k$, its spanning vectors being part of a basis of $T_qM$. On the other side, by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) with $\dim T_qM = m$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}) and $\operatorname{rank}(x_b)_{*q} = k$ by (2),
\[
\dim \ker (x_b)_{*q} = \dim T_qM - \operatorname{rank}(x_b)_{*q} = m - k .
\]
A subspace of the same finite dimension is the whole space, so $\iota_{*q}(T_qS) = \ker (x_b)_{*q}$.

\emph{The last sentence.} Every $p \in S$ lies in the domain $U$ of an adapted chart (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}), an open neighbourhood of $p$ in $M$, and by (1) and (3) $U \cap S = x_b^{-1}(\vec 0)$ with $x_b : U \to \mathbb{R}^k$ smooth and $\vec 0$ a regular value.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Conormal Space]\deflabel{def:conormal}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold and $p \in S$. The \textbf{conormal space} of $S$ at $p$ is
\[
N_pS = \{\, \xi \in T_p^*M : \xi(v) = 0 \text{ for all } v \in \iota_{*p}(T_pS) \,\},
\]
the covectors at $p$ that vanish on the tangent space of $S$ --- the annihilator of $T_pS$ in $T_p^*M$.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[A Basis of the Conormal Space]\thmlabel{prop:conormal-basis}
Let $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ be an adapted chart at $p$, and write a covector $\xi \in T_p^*M$ as $\xi = \sum_i \xi_i\, dx^i|_p$, with components $\xi_i = \xi(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}).
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\xi \in N_pS$ if and only if $\xi_i = 0$ for every $i \le m - k$.
    \item $N_pS$ has basis $dx^{m-k+1}|_p, \ldots, dx^m|_p$. In particular $\dim N_pS = k$, the codimension of $S$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Fix an adapted chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ at $p$. Write $\xi = \sum_j \xi_j\, dx^j|_p$ in the dual basis (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}), so that $\xi(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = \xi_i$. (By Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} the $dx^j|_p$ are the basis dual to the $\partial/\partial x^j|_p$, and the coefficients are the components $\xi_i = \xi(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}.)

\emph{(1)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}, $\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$ is the span of $\partial/\partial x^1|_p, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^{m-k}|_p$, and a linear functional vanishes on a span if and only if it vanishes on each spanning vector; so, by Definition~\ref{def:conormal},
\[
\xi \in N_pS \iff \xi\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big) = 0 \ \ (i \le m - k) \iff \xi_i = 0 \ \ (i \le m - k) .
\]

\emph{(2)} By (1), and since a covector is the sum of its components times the dual basis,
\[
\xi \in N_pS \iff \xi = \sum_{j = m-k+1}^m \xi_j\, dx^j\big|_p .
\]
So $N_pS$ is spanned by the $dx^j|_p$ with $j > m - k$, which are linearly independent as part of a basis. (Each of them does lie in $N_pS$, by (1): for $j > m - k$ and $i \le m - k$, the $i$-th component of $dx^j|_p$ is $dx^j|_p(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = \delta^j_i = 0$.) So they form a basis of $N_pS$, and $\dim N_pS = m - (m - k) = k$, the codimension of $S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof that $\dim N_pS = k$ (without a chart)]
\textit{(Not from lecture; the chart-free count of the official solution of Assignment~5, Problem~4.)} Let $\iota_p^* : T_p^*M \to T_p^*S$ be the pullback of covectors by the inclusion (Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector}), $\iota_p^*\xi = \xi \circ \iota_{*p}$. By Definition~\ref{def:conormal}, $\xi \in N_pS$ if and only if $\xi(\iota_{*p}v) = 0$ for all $v \in T_pS$, that is, $\iota_p^*\xi = 0$; so $N_pS = \ker\iota_p^*$. The map $\iota_{*p}$ is injective (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), so its dual map $\iota_p^*$ is surjective (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-map}(3)). Concretely, a functional on the subspace $\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$ extends to $T_pM$: extend a basis of the subspace to a basis of $T_pM$ and send the new vectors to $0$. The dimensions are $\dim T_p^*M = m$ and $\dim T_p^*S = \dim T_pS = m - k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}, Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}, and $\dim S = m - k$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}). Rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) gives
\[
\dim N_pS = \dim\ker\iota_p^* = \dim T_p^*M - \operatorname{rank}\iota_p^* = m - (m - k) = k .
\]
This is the linear-algebra fact that the annihilator of a $d$-dimensional subspace of an $m$-dimensional space has dimension $m - d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[No Normal Vectors Without a Metric]\label{rem:no-normal-vectors-without-metric}
``We don't have normal vectors, because we don't have a metric \ldots\ There is no notion of orthogonality, but there is an intrinsic'' definition: the conormal space. ``If we had a metric, [an] inner product on $T_pM$, we could identify $T^*_pM$ with $T_pM$, and this would be the normal space.'' Uribe added that he regards the cotangent side as ``actually more natural'' than the tangent side --- ``that's where Hamiltonian mechanics takes place.''
\end{rembox}

How to draw a conormal covector. Without a metric, a covector $\xi$ on $T_pM$ is drawn by its level lines $\{\xi = \text{const}\}$. For $\xi \in N_pS$ the level line $\xi = 0$ contains $T_pS$, so all of its level lines run \emph{parallel} to $T_pS$ (left). Only once an inner product is chosen does $\xi$ become a vector, perpendicular to its level lines, and $N_pS$ becomes the normal line $(T_pS)^\perp$ (right). The board, and page~33 of the handwritten notes, draw $N_pS$ as a line perpendicular to $T_pS$: that is the right-hand, metric picture.

\subsection{Regular Submanifolds of Euclidean Space}\label{sub:submanifolds-euclidean}

\textit{Not from lecture: the link back to the geometric stage.} Inside a Euclidean space, Section~\ref{sec:euclidean} described a manifold $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ near a point in three ways --- externally, by equations (Definition~\ref{def:ext-int}); internally, by a parametrization (Definition~\ref{def:internal-description}); and as a graph --- and Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int} showed that they agree. Definition~\ref{def:submanifold} adds a fourth, the \emph{slice} description: a chart of the ambient space in which $X$ is a coordinate plane. The fourth agrees with the other three, so in $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ the submanifolds of codimension $k$ are exactly the manifolds of Section~\ref{sec:euclidean}, and Definition~\ref{def:submanifold} is their description made intrinsic to the ambient manifold.

\begin{propbox}[Regular Submanifolds of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$: The Fourth Description]\thmlabel{prop:submanifold-euclidean}
Let $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ and $p \in X$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item near $p$, $X$ is described externally (Definition~\ref{def:ext-int}) --- equivalently, internally or as a graph (Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int});
    \item \emph{(slice)} there is a smooth chart $(U, \varphi = (x_a, x_b))$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ with $p \in U$, $x_a$ its first $n$ and $x_b$ its last $k$ components, such that $U \cap X = \{\, q \in U : x_b(q) = \vec 0 \,\}$, that is, a chart adapted to $X$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}).
\end{enumerate}
In particular $X$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ of codimension $k$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}) if and only if every point of $X$ has the descriptions of Section~\ref{sec:euclidean}.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} By Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int} the external, internal and graph descriptions near $p$ are equivalent, so for (1)$\iff$(2) it suffices to prove graph $\Rightarrow$ slice and slice $\Rightarrow$ external; together with external $\Rightarrow$ graph (Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int}) these close the cycle.

\emph{Graph $\Rightarrow$ slice.} Permuting coordinates is a linear isomorphism, so we may assume $X \cap (V \times V') = \{(x, h(x)) : x \in V\}$ as in (G) of Theorem~\ref{thm:ext-int}. (If a permutation $P$ is needed, the construction below gives a chart $\Phi$ adapted to $P(X)$, with domain $U$, and $\Phi \circ P$, on the open set $P^{-1}(U)$, is a chart adapted to $X$. It is a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}: (2), applied to the identity chart of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ with the linear isomorphism $h = P$, and (1), restricting to $P^{-1}(U)$, make $P$ a smooth chart on $P^{-1}(U)$, and (2) again, with the diffeomorphism $h = \Phi$ of $U = P(P^{-1}(U))$ onto an open set, gives $\Phi \circ P$. Its last $k$ components vanish at $q \in P^{-1}(U)$ iff $P(q) \in P(X)$, i.e.\ iff $q \in X$.) Let $U = V \times V'$, an open set containing $p$, and $\Phi(x, y) = (x,\, y - h(x))$ on $U$. Then:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\Phi$ is smooth, its components $x$ and $y - h(x)$ being smooth;
    \item $\Phi$ is injective: $\Phi(x, y) = \Phi(x', y')$ gives $x = x'$ and then $y - h(x) = y' - h(x)$, so $y = y'$;
    \item its image $\{(x, z) : x \in V,\ z + h(x) \in V'\}$ is open: it is the preimage of the open set $V \times V'$ under the continuous map $\Psi(x, z) = (x, z + h(x))$ on the open set $V \times \mathbb{R}^k$;
    \item its inverse is $\Psi$ restricted to the image, $(x, z) \mapsto (x, z + h(x))$, which is smooth.
\end{itemize}
\textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} In matrix form, with $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^k$, the Jacobians of $\Phi$ and of its inverse $\Psi$ are block lower triangular with identity diagonal blocks,
\[
\Phi'(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} I_n & 0 \\ -Dh(x) & I_k \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Psi'(x, z) = \begin{pmatrix} I_n & 0 \\ Dh(x) & I_k \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Phi'(x, y)\, \Psi'\big(\Phi(x, y)\big) = I_{n+k},
\]
where $Dh(x)$ is the $k \times n$ Jacobian of $h$; in particular $\det \Phi' = 1$ everywhere.
So $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism of $U$ onto an open set (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}), hence a smooth chart of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$: it is a homeomorphism onto an open set, and its transition maps with the identity chart are $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$, so it is compatible with the atlas $\{(\mathbb{R}^{n+k}, \mathrm{id})\}$ and lies in the maximal atlas it generates (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}). Its last $k$ components $y - h(x)$ vanish exactly on $X \cap U$: for $(x, y) \in U$, $y - h(x) = 0$ iff $y = h(x)$ iff $(x, y) \in X \cap (V \times V')$. So $\Phi$ is a chart adapted to $X$ at $p$.

\emph{Slice $\Rightarrow$ external.} Let $F = x_b : U \to \mathbb{R}^k$, the last $k$ components of $\varphi$; it is smooth, its components being components of the smooth map $\varphi$. A chart is a diffeomorphism onto its image (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}; it is a diffeomorphism of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}), so the Jacobian $\varphi'(q)$ is invertible at every $q \in U$: the ordinary chain rule applied to $\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi = \mathrm{id}_U$ gives $(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q))\, \varphi'(q) = I$. Its last $k$ rows, which form $F'(q)$, are linearly independent, since the rows of an invertible matrix are; and row $l$ of $\varphi'(q)$ is the gradient of the $l$-th component of $\varphi$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}), so these rows are exactly the rows of $F'(q)$. In block form, with $\varphi = (\varphi^1, \ldots, \varphi^{n+k})$,
\[
\varphi'(q) = \left(\begin{array}{c} \nabla \varphi^1(q) \\ \vdots \\ \nabla \varphi^n(q) \\ \hline \nabla \varphi^{n+1}(q) \\ \vdots \\ \nabla \varphi^{n+k}(q) \end{array}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} x_a'(q) \\ F'(q) \end{pmatrix} \qquad (F = x_b).
\] Hence $F'(q)$ has rank $k$ everywhere, $\vec 0$ is a regular value of $F$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}: every point of $F^{-1}(\vec 0)$, indeed every point of $U$, is a regular point), and
\[
X \cap U = \{\, q \in U : x_b(q) = \vec 0 \,\} = F^{-1}(\vec 0) ,
\]
by (2): the external description with $W = U$ (Definition~\ref{def:ext-int}).

The final statement follows, since Definition~\ref{def:submanifold} asks for (2) at every point of $X$: $X$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $k$ iff every $p \in X$ has an adapted chart, i.e.\ satisfies (2), iff every $p \in X$ satisfies (1), by the equivalence just proved.
\end{proof}

Straightening a graph. The map $\Phi(x, y) = (x, y - h(x))$ keeps $x$ and measures the height above the graph; it carries the graph $X$ to the slice $z = 0$, and the parallel graphs $y = h(x) + c$ to the slices $z = c$. This is the passage from the graph charts of Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}, which flatten $X$ \emph{alone}, to an adapted chart, which straightens a whole neighbourhood of $X$ in the ambient space.

For the unit sphere $S^2 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ near the north pole, the graph is $z = \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}$, and $(x, y, z) \mapsto (x, y, z - \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2})$ is an adapted chart; so is $(x, y, z) \mapsto (x, y, x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1)$ near any point with $z \neq 0$, whose last coordinate is the defining function of the external description.

\begin{lembox}[An Adapted Chart of a Submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$]\thmlabel{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m$, that is, of codimension $n - m$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}), and let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^n))$ be a smooth chart of $\mathbb{R}^n$ adapted to $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}), so that
\[
U \cap M = \{\, q \in U : x^{m+1}(q) = \cdots = x^n(q) = 0 \,\}.
\]
Put
\[
G = (G^1, \ldots, G^{n-m}) = (x^{m+1}, \ldots, x^n) : U \to \mathbb{R}^{n-m}, \qquad J(q) = G'(q) \quad (q \in U),
\]
the $(n-m) \times n$ Jacobian of $G$ in the standard coordinates, whose $s$-th row is the gradient $\nabla G^s(q)$ (Definitions~\ref{def:jacobian} and~\ref{def:gradient}):
\[
J(q) = \begin{pmatrix} \nabla G^1(q) \\ \vdots \\ \nabla G^{n-m}(q) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial r^1}(q) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial r^n}(q) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial G^{n-m}}{\partial r^1}(q) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^{n-m}}{\partial r^n}(q) \end{pmatrix} .
\] Tangent spaces are the geometric ones (Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent}, whose formula makes sense verbatim for any subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$), and $v \cdot w = \sum_l v^l w^l$ is the dot product.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every $q \in U$, $\varphi'(q)$ is invertible, with inverse $(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q))$, and $J(q)$ has rank $n - m$.
    \item For every $q \in U \cap M$,
    \[
    T^{\geo}_qM = T^{\geo}_q(U \cap M) = \ker J(q), \qquad \dim T^{\geo}_qM = m.
    \]
    \item For $q \in U$ and $j = 1, \ldots, n$ let $X_j(q) = \dfrac{\partial \varphi^{-1}}{\partial r^j}\big(\varphi(q)\big) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the $j$-th column of $(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q))$, with components $X_j^l(q)$:
\[
(\varphi^{-1})'\big(\varphi(q)\big) = \big(\, X_1(q) \ \big|\ X_2(q) \ \big|\ \cdots \ \big|\ X_n(q) \,\big) = \begin{pmatrix} X_1^1(q) & \cdots & X_n^1(q) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ X_1^n(q) & \cdots & X_n^n(q) \end{pmatrix} .
\] Each $X_j^l$ is smooth on $U$; $X_1(q), \ldots, X_n(q)$ form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$, with $\varphi'(q)\, X_j(q) = e_j$ (in particular $X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)$ are linearly independent for every $q \in U$); and for $q \in U \cap M$, $X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)$ form a basis of $T^{\geo}_qM$.
    \item For $q \in U \cap M$, the gradients $\nabla G^1(q), \ldots, \nabla G^{n-m}(q)$ form a basis of the orthogonal complement
    \[
    (T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp = \{\, v \in \mathbb{R}^n : v \cdot w = 0 \text{ for all } w \in T^{\geo}_qM \,\} ;
    \]
    equivalently, $(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp = \{\, J(q)^{\mathsf T} c : c \in \mathbb{R}^{n-m} \,\}$, and $c \mapsto J(q)^{\mathsf T} c$ is injective.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. These are the facts about an adapted chart used for the normal bundle of Assignment~5, Problem~5.)} Every point of $M$ lies in such a chart (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}).

\emph{(1)} The chart $\varphi : U \to \varphi(U)$ is a diffeomorphism of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Propositions~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo} and~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}), and the chain rule applied to $\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\varphi(U)}$ at $\varphi(q)$ gives
\[
\varphi'(q)\, (\varphi^{-1})'\big(\varphi(q)\big) = I_n ,
\]
so the square matrix $\varphi'(q)$ is invertible, with inverse $(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q))$. The rows of an invertible matrix are linearly independent, and row $l$ of $\varphi'(q)$ is $\nabla x^l(q)$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}); the rows of $J(q)$ are the last $n - m$ of these, $\nabla x^{m+1}(q), \ldots, \nabla x^n(q)$, so they are independent and $J(q)$ has rank $n - m$ (Definition~\ref{def:rank}). This is the computation in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean} (slice $\Rightarrow$ external, with $m$ and $n - m$ in place of $n$ and $k$).

\emph{(2)} By (1), $\vec 0$ is a regular value of $G$ on the open set $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}), and $U \cap M = G^{-1}(\vec 0)$ by the displayed description of $U \cap M$. The first equality is Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-local}, since $U \cap M$ is open in $M$ (its proof uses only that $U \cap M$ is open in the subset $M$ of the Euclidean space). The second, and the dimension, are Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} for the regular level set $U \cap M = G^{-1}(\vec 0)$, with $W = U$, $F = G$, $c = \vec 0$ and $m$, $n - m$ in place of $n$, $k$: the kernel of the surjective $J(q) : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ has dimension $n - (n - m) = m$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)).

\emph{(3)} $X_j(q)$ is the velocity of the $j$-th coordinate line $t \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(\varphi(q) + t e_j)$ at $t = 0$, by the chain rule: the coordinate field $\partial/\partial x^j$ regarded as a vector field on $U$ in the sense of multivariable calculus. Each $X_j^l$ is smooth on $U$, as the composite of the smooth $\varphi$ with the partial derivative $\partial(\varphi^{-1})^l/\partial r^j$ of the smooth map $\varphi^{-1}$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{$X_1(q), \ldots, X_n(q)$ form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $\varphi'(q)\, X_j(q) = e_j$.} By (1), $(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q))$ is the inverse of $\varphi'(q)$; so it is invertible, its columns $X_1(q), \ldots, X_n(q)$ form a basis, and $\varphi'(q)\, X_j(q)$, the $j$-th column of $\varphi'(q)\,(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q)) = I_n$, is $e_j$. Any $m$ of the $n$ basis vectors, in particular $X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)$, are linearly independent, for every $q \in U$.
    \item \emph{For $q \in U \cap M$, $X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)$ form a basis of $T^{\geo}_qM$.} The rows of $J(q)$ are the last $n - m$ rows of $\varphi'(q)$ (proof of (1)), so $J(q)\, X_j(q)$ consists of the last $n - m$ entries of $\varphi'(q)\, X_j(q) = e_j$. For $j \le m$ these entries are all $0$, so $X_j(q) \in \ker J(q) = T^{\geo}_qM$ by (2). The $m$ vectors $X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)$ are linearly independent, as part of the basis just found, and lie in the $m$-dimensional space $T^{\geo}_qM$ (2); $m$ independent vectors in an $m$-dimensional space form a basis. So
    \[
    T^{\geo}_qM = \Span\{X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)\}.
    \]
\end{itemize}

\emph{(4)} Fix $q \in U \cap M$. \emph{The gradients are normal:} for $w \in T^{\geo}_qM = \ker J(q)$ (2), the $s$-th entry of $J(q)\, w$ is $\nabla G^s(q) \cdot w$ (the $s$-th row of $J(q)$ is $\nabla G^s(q)$, Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}), and $J(q)\, w = 0$; so $\nabla G^s(q) \cdot w = 0$, and $\nabla G^s(q) \in (T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$. \emph{They are independent:} $J(q)$ has rank $n - m$ by (1), so its $n - m$ rows are linearly independent (Definition~\ref{def:rank}). \emph{The orthogonal complement has dimension $n - m$:} choose a basis $w_1, \ldots, w_m$ of $T^{\geo}_qM$ ($\dim = m$ by (2)), and let $B$ be the $m \times n$ matrix with rows $w_1^{\mathsf T}, \ldots, w_m^{\mathsf T}$. A vector $v$ is orthogonal to every element $\sum_i a_i w_i$ of $T^{\geo}_qM$ if and only if it is orthogonal to each $w_i$, because $v \cdot \sum_i a_i w_i = \sum_i a_i\, (v \cdot w_i)$ by linearity of the dot product (``if'' by this formula, ``only if'' by taking $a = e_i$); that is, iff $Bv = 0$. So $(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp = \ker B$. The rows of $B$ are independent, so $B$ has rank $m$, and rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) gives $\dim \ker B = n - m$. So the $n - m$ independent vectors $\nabla G^s(q)$ lie in the $(n-m)$-dimensional space $(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$, and form a basis of it. \emph{Matrix form:} for $c = (c^1, \ldots, c^{n-m}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$, $J(q)^{\mathsf T} c = \sum_s c^s\, \nabla G^s(q)$, since the columns of $J(q)^{\mathsf T}$ are the rows of $J(q)$,
\[
J(q)^{\mathsf T} = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial r^1}(q) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^{n-m}}{\partial r^1}(q) \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial G^1}{\partial r^n}(q) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial G^{n-m}}{\partial r^n}(q) \end{pmatrix} \qquad (\text{column } s \text{ holds the entries of } \nabla G^s(q));
\] so the set of all $J(q)^{\mathsf T} c$ is the span of the gradients, which is $(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$, and $c \mapsto J(q)^{\mathsf T} c$ is injective because the gradients are independent.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Tangent Spaces Match]\label{rem:tangent-spaces-match}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The two tangent spaces of the geometric and the abstract stage correspond as well. Externally, $T^{\geo}_pX = \ker F'(p)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}). In the slice chart of Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean}, with $F = x_b$, this kernel is the set of vectors on which the differentials of the last $k$ coordinates vanish, the span of the first $n$ coordinate directions; and that span is $\iota_{*p}(T_pX)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}). Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree} below makes the identification precise, together with the agreement of the two smooth structures.
\end{rembox}

% SECTION: THE REGULAR VALUE THEOREM FOR MANIFOLDS

\section{The Regular Value Theorem for Manifolds}\label{sec:rvt-manifolds}\label{sub:rvt-manifolds}

\roadmark{Stage: submanifolds}{Regular level sets of smooth maps between manifolds are regular submanifolds --- the regular submanifolds of \ref{sec:submanifolds} as solution sets of equations.}

\textit{Lecture 12. ``And now we go back to submersions'' --- to ``[the] wonderful version of the regular value theorem.''}

The local half of the theorem below holds at a single point where a map is a submersion. It is isolated as a lemma because it is used twice: for level sets here, and for preimages of transverse submanifolds in \ref{sec:transversality-submanifolds}.

\begin{lembox}[Level Sets Near a Regular Point]\thmlabel{lem:rvt-local}
Let $V \subseteq M$ be open, $\dim M = m$, $G : V \to N$ smooth with $\dim N = n$, $p \in V$ a point at which $G$ is a submersion (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}), and $c = G(p)$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item There are a smooth chart $(W, \theta = (z^1, \ldots, z^m))$ of $M$ at $p$ with $W \subseteq V$ and a smooth chart $(Y, \chi)$ of $N$ at $c$ with $G(W) \subseteq Y$, such that $\chi\big(G(p')\big) = \big(z^1(p'), \ldots, z^n(p')\big)$ for $p' \in W$; consequently, with $\vec c = \chi(c) = (c_1, \ldots, c_n)$,
    \[
    W \cap G^{-1}(c) = \{\, p' \in W : z^1(p') = c_1, \ \ldots, \ z^n(p') = c_n \,\} .
    \]
    In particular $n \le m$.
    \item $\hat\theta = \big(z^{n+1}, \ldots, z^m,\ z^1 - c_1, \ldots, z^n - c_n\big)$ is a smooth chart of $M$ with domain $W$, whose last $n$ components vanish exactly on $W \cap G^{-1}(c)$. Hence, if $S \subseteq M$ is a subset with $S \cap W = G^{-1}(c) \cap W$, then $(W, \hat\theta)$ is a chart adapted to $S$ of codimension $n$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}).
    \item Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold of codimension $n$ with inclusion $\iota$ and $p \in S$, and suppose $S \cap W' = G^{-1}(c) \cap W'$ for some open $W' \subseteq V$ containing $p$. Then $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \ker G_{*p}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~12's argument for the regular value theorem below, and Steps~6--7 and part~(2) of the submitted solution of Assignment~5, Problem~2; isolated here, with the details filled in.)} Throughout, the tangent spaces of the open sets $V$ and $W'$ at their points are identified with those of $M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}).

\emph{(1)} $V$ is an open submanifold of $M$, of dimension $m$. The normal form (Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form}) requires $G$ to be a submersion only at the one point $p$. (That $G$ is then a submersion on a whole neighbourhood of $p$, Corollary~\ref{cor:submersion-open-condition}, is a consequence of the normal form, not a hypothesis of it; no shrinking of $V$ is needed.) Applied to $G : V \to N$ at $p$, it gives smooth charts $(W, \theta = (z^1, \ldots, z^m))$ of $V$ at $p$ and $(Y, \chi)$ of $N$ at $G(p) = c$, with $G(W) \subseteq Y$, $n \le m$, and
\[
\chi \circ G \circ \theta^{-1}\big(r^1, \ldots, r^m\big) = \big(r^1, \ldots, r^n\big) \quad \text{on } \theta(W) ;
\]
applying this identity at $\theta(p')$, and using $z^i = r^i \circ \theta$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-functions}), gives $\chi\big(G(p')\big) = \big(z^1(p'), \ldots, z^n(p')\big)$ for $p' \in W$. Since $W \subseteq V$ is open in $V$, hence in $M$, $(W, \theta)$ is also a smooth chart of $M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(2)). For $p' \in W$,
\[
p' \in G^{-1}(c) \iff G(p') = c \iff \chi\big(G(p')\big) = \chi(c) \iff \big(z^1(p'), \ldots, z^n(p')\big) = (c_1, \ldots, c_n) .
\]
The first equivalence is the definition of the preimage; the second holds because $G(p')$ and $c = G(p)$ both lie in $Y$ (as $G(W) \subseteq Y$ and $p, p' \in W$), on which $\chi$ is injective; the third is the identity just derived from the normal form.

\emph{(2)} By (1), $W \cap G^{-1}(c)$ is cut out in the smooth chart $(W, \theta)$ of $M$ by setting $n$ of its coordinates, $z^1, \ldots, z^n$, equal to the constants $c_1, \ldots, c_n$; and so is $W \cap S$ for any subset $S$ with $S \cap W = G^{-1}(c) \cap W$. Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-flex}, with $k = n$, the coordinates $z^1, \ldots, z^n$ and the constant vector $\vec c$, therefore gives the chart $(W, A \circ \theta)$ of $M$ adapted to $S$, where, in the notation of its proof, $A(r) = \big(r^{n+1}, \ldots, r^m,\ r^1 - c_1, \ldots, r^n - c_n\big)$; explicitly $A \circ \theta = \hat\theta$. Its last $n$ components $z^1 - c_1, \ldots, z^n - c_n$ vanish at $p' \in W$ if and only if $z^i(p') = c_i$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$, that is, by (1), if and only if $p' \in G^{-1}(c)$; this is the case $S = G^{-1}(c)$.

\emph{(3): $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) \subseteq \ker G_{*p}$.} The set $S \cap W'$ is open in $S$ (subspace topology) and contains $p$, so its tangent space at $p$ is $T_pS$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}). On it the composite $G \circ \iota$ is defined --- $\iota$ maps it into $W' \subseteq V$, and its restriction is smooth into the open set $V$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1) and Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}(3) --- and constant with value $c$, since $S \cap W' \subseteq G^{-1}(c)$. The pushforward along a constant map is zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}), so by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial})
\[
G_{*p} \circ \iota_{*p} = (G \circ \iota)_{*p} = 0 ,
\]
that is, $G_{*p}(\iota_{*p}v) = 0$ for every $v \in T_pS$.

\emph{(3): dimensions.} $\iota_{*p}$ is injective (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), so, by Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension} and Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure},
\[
\dim \iota_{*p}\big(T_pS\big) = \dim T_pS = \dim S = m - n .
\]
On the other side, $G_{*p}$ is onto the $n$-dimensional space $T_cN$, so by rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1))
\[
\dim \ker G_{*p} = \dim T_pM - \operatorname{rank} G_{*p} = m - n .
\]
A subspace of the same finite dimension is the whole space, so $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \ker G_{*p}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Regular Value Theorem for Manifolds]\thmlabel{thm:rvt-manifolds}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$, and let $q \in N$ be a regular value of $F$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}). Then $S = F^{-1}(q)$ is a regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $n$ (possibly empty), so $\dim S = m - n$, and for every $p \in S$
\[
\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \ker F_{*p} .
\]
\leeref{Corollary 5.14 and Proposition 5.38}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\emph{$S$ is a submanifold (Lecture~12).} We check the definition at each $p \in S$: we need an adapted chart at $p$. (If $S = \emptyset$ there is nothing to check.) By assumption $F$ is a submersion at $p$, so the normal form (Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form}) gives charts $(U, \hat\varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $q = F(p)$, with $F(U) \subseteq V$ and $\tilde F(r^1, \ldots, r^m) = (r^1, \ldots, r^n)$. What are the equations of $S \cap U$ in these coordinates? For $q' \in U$,
\begin{align*}
q' \in S &\iff F(q') = q \iff \psi\big(F(q')\big) = \psi(q) \\
&\iff \tilde F\big(\hat\varphi(q')\big) = \psi(q) \iff \big(x^1(q'), \ldots, x^n(q')\big) = \big(y^1(q), \ldots, y^n(q)\big).
\end{align*}
``These are not of the type $x_b = 0$, but of the type $x_a$ equals a constant'': the first $n$ coordinates equal a constant vector. By the observations after the definition (Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-flex}) --- any constant, and any $n$ of the coordinates --- $S$ has an adapted chart at $p$, of codimension $n$. \textit{(Completion.)} This is Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local}, applied with $V = M$, $G = F$ and $c = q$, so that $G^{-1}(c) = S$; its proof gives the details. Part~(1) of the lemma is the computation above, with the normal-form charts $(U, \hat\varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ and the constant vector $\vec c = \psi(q) = (y^1(q), \ldots, y^n(q))$: the first equivalence is $S = F^{-1}(q)$; the second holds because $F(q')$ and $q$ both lie in $V$, on which $\psi$ is injective; the third because $\psi \circ F = \tilde F \circ \hat\varphi$ on $U$; the last because $\tilde F(\hat\varphi(q'))$ consists of the first $n$ entries of $\hat\varphi(q')$. Part~(2), with $S \cap U = F^{-1}(q) \cap U$, is Proposition~\ref{prop:adapted-flex} with $k = n$, the coordinates $x^1, \ldots, x^n$ and $\vec c = \psi(q)$: it gives the adapted chart $\big(x^{n+1}, \ldots, x^m,\ x^1 - y^1(q), \ldots, x^n - y^n(q)\big)$ at $p$, of codimension $n$, and $n \le m$ by the normal form. As $p \in S$ was arbitrary, $S$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $n$, and $\dim S = m - n$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}.

\emph{The tangent space.} \textit{(Completion. In lecture: ``I won't bother checking the kernel thing, because everything really reduces to the Euclidean [case].'')} By Lemma~\ref{lem:rvt-local}(3), applied with $V = W' = M$, $G = F$, $c = q$ and the regular submanifold $S$ of codimension $n$ itself (so that $S \cap M = F^{-1}(q) \cap M$), $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \ker F_{*p}$. In that lemma's proof: the composite $F \circ \iota : S \to N$ is constant, with value $q$, so $F_{*p} \circ \iota_{*p} = (F \circ \iota)_{*p} = 0$ by the Chain Rule and Lemma~\ref{lem:constant-pushforward}, and $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) \subseteq \ker F_{*p}$; the left side has dimension $m - n$, since $\iota_{*p}$ is injective (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), and the right side has dimension $m - n$ by rank--nullity, since $F_{*p}$ is onto (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)); and a subspace of the same finite dimension is everything. This is the argument of Lecture~8 for $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}), one level up.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=6em, row sep=3em]
S \cap U \subseteq U \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\hat\varphi"'] & V \ni q \arrow[d, "\psi"] \\
\big\{ r : (r^1, \ldots, r^n) = \psi(q) \big\} \subseteq \hat\varphi(U) \arrow[r, "\tilde F"'] & \psi(V) \ni \psi(q)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The proof in one square, as on the board. In the normal-form charts $\tilde F$ is the projection onto the first $n$ coordinates, so the level set $S \cap U = F^{-1}(q) \cap U$ is carried by $\hat\varphi$ onto a fibre of a projection: the slice where the first $n$ coordinates equal $\psi(q)$.

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page~33 of the handwritten notes states the theorem for ``$q \in M$ a regular value''; the regular value lies in the target, $q \in N$.

\begin{corbox}[Fibres of Submersions Are Regular Submanifolds]\thmlabel{cor:submersion-fibres}
If $F : M \to N$ is a submersion, then every fibre $F^{-1}(q)$, $q \in N$, is a regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $n$ --- ``they could be empty, some of them.''
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
Every $q \in N$ is a regular value: every point of $F^{-1}(q)$ is a regular point, and if $F^{-1}(q)$ is empty the condition holds vacuously. Indeed, $F$ is a submersion at every point of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:submersion}), in particular at every $p \in F^{-1}(q)$, which is what Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}(2) asks of a regular value; and if $q \notin F(M)$, it is a regular value by Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}(3). Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}: $F^{-1}(q)$ is a regular submanifold of $M$ of codimension $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[The Regular Value Theorems --- Old and New]\label{rem:regular-value-theorems-old-new}
The notes now contain the regular value theorem in five forms. They are one idea met at increasing generality, not competing statements.
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.5cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.9cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.0cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.0cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Where} & \textbf{Setting} & \textbf{Conclusion} & \textbf{Role now} \\ \midrule
Thm.~\ref{thm:regular-value}, Cor.~\ref{cor:rvt-open} & $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^k$, $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ open & topological manifold & the first version (Lecture~3); Chapter~2 needs it \\
Prop.~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth} & the same & smooth manifold, by graph charts & the Euclidean case (Lecture~6) \\
Prop.~\ref{prop:regular-one-chart} & $F : M \to N$, level set inside one chart & regular for $F$ iff for $\tilde F$ & a computational tool \\
Cor.~\ref{cor:manifold-level-sets} & $F : M \to N$ & topological manifold & subsumed; a more elementary proof \\
Thm.~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds} & $F : M \to N$ & submanifold, with $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \ker F_{*p}$ & the general theorem (Lecture~12) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The general theorem contains the others: taking $M$ an open subset of Euclidean space recovers the first two. Its proof goes through the normal form, which rests on the inverse function theorem and not on \ref{sec:rvt}, so nothing is circular. The next proposition shows that the old and new versions give the same smooth structure and the same tangent spaces.
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[The Old and New Versions Agree]\thmlabel{prop:rvt-agree}
Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ be open, $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^k$ smooth, $c$ a regular value, and $S = F^{-1}(c)$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The smooth structure on $S$ given by the graph charts (Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}) is the induced structure of $S$ as a regular submanifold of $W$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}).
    \item In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}, under the identification $T_pW = \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}, the subspace $\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$ is $T^{\geo}_pS = \ker F'(p)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} First, $c$ is a regular value in both senses, since the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the standard coordinates is $F'(p)$ (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}). In detail: with the identity charts on $W$ and on $\mathbb{R}^k$, the coordinate representation of $F$ is $F$ itself, so Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} says the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the coordinate bases is $F'(p)$. A linear map is onto $T_{F(p)}\mathbb{R}^k$ iff its rank is $k$, and its rank is that of its matrix (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)); so $F_{*p}$ is onto (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}) iff $F'(p)$ has rank $k$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}). Hence Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds} applies to $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^k$, and $S$ is a regular submanifold of $W$ of codimension $k$.

(1) Let $p \in S$. As in the construction of the graph charts, after reordering the coordinates write the points of $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ as $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^k$ with $\partial F/\partial y\,(p)$ invertible, so that the graph chart near $p$ is $(x, y) \mapsto x$ on $S$. (Here $x = x_I$, $y = x_J$ in the notation of the construction before Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}, and the graph chart is $\varphi_J = \pi_I|_{U_J}$. The reordering is a permutation $P$ of coordinates; the chart produced below is then $\Phi \circ P$, with the same last $k$ components, a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}: (2), applied to the identity chart with the linear isomorphism $h = P$, and (1), restricting to an open set, make $P$ a smooth chart on $P^{-1}(U)$, and (2) again, with the diffeomorphism $h = \Phi|_U$, gives $\Phi \circ P$. We suppress $P$.) Let $\Phi(x, y) = (x, F(x, y) - c)$. Its Jacobian at $p$ is $\begin{pmatrix} I_n & 0 \\ \partial F/\partial x & \partial F/\partial y \end{pmatrix}$, which is invertible: it is block lower triangular, so its determinant is $\det I_n \cdot \det\big(\partial F/\partial y\,(p)\big) \ne 0$. Written out, with $x = (x^1, \ldots, x^n)$, $y = (y^1, \ldots, y^k)$, $F = (F^1, \ldots, F^k)$ and all partials at $p$,
\[
\Phi'(p) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \hline \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^n} & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial y^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial y^k} \\ \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial F^k}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^k}{\partial x^n} & \dfrac{\partial F^k}{\partial y^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^k}{\partial y^k} \end{array}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} I_n & 0 \\ \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix} .
\] So by the inverse function theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function}, with $\Phi$ on $W$ and $a = p$) $\Phi$ restricts to a diffeomorphism of an open $U \ni p$ onto an open set, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:diffeo-chart} (with $M = W$, the diffeomorphism being one of manifolds by Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}) it is a smooth chart of $W$. Its last $k$ components are $F - c$, which vanish exactly on $S \cap U$, so $\Phi$ is adapted, and its induced chart is $\Phi_S = x|_{S \cap U}$: the graph chart. More precisely, $\Phi_S$ and the graph chart $\varphi_J$ are both restrictions of the projection $(x, y) \mapsto x$, so they agree on $S \cap U \cap U_J$, an open neighbourhood of $p$ in $S$. The same construction works at every point $p'$ of the graph chart's domain $U_J$, with the same splitting $(x, y)$: there $S$ is the graph $y = h_J(x)$, and differentiating $F(x, h_J(x)) = c$ gives $\partial F/\partial x = -\,\partial F/\partial y \cdot h_J'$, so $F'(p') = \partial F/\partial y\,(p') \cdot \big({-h_J'} \mid I_k\big)$; as $F'(p')$ has rank $k$, the $k \times k$ matrix $\partial F/\partial y\,(p')$ has rank $k$, i.e.\ is invertible. So near each of its points, every graph chart is an induced chart. Induced charts are pairwise compatible, and smoothness of a transition map is local, so every graph chart is compatible with every induced chart, and the two atlases determine the same maximal atlas (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}). In detail: let $(U_J, \varphi_J)$ be a graph chart and $(V \cap S, \psi_S)$ an induced chart. Near each point $\varphi_J(p')$ of the domain of $\psi_S \circ \varphi_J^{-1}$, by what was just shown, $\varphi_J$ agrees with an induced chart $\Phi_S$ on an open neighbourhood $O$ of $p'$ in $S$; on $\varphi_J(O \cap V)$ the map $\psi_S \circ \varphi_J^{-1}$ equals $\psi_S \circ \Phi_S^{-1}$, a transition map between induced charts, smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}(2). The same holds for $\varphi_J \circ \psi_S^{-1}$ near each point. So the two charts are compatible, the union of the two atlases is an atlas, and both generate the maximal atlas containing it.

(2) Let $v \in T^{\geo}_pS$, and let $\gamma$ be the lifted line of Definition~\ref{def:Dv}, a curve in $S$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $\gamma'(0) = v$, so that $D_v = D_\gamma$. (It is smooth into $\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ with values in $S$, hence smooth into $S$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:level-set-maps}(2); by (1) the structure there is the induced one, so $T_pS$ and $\iota_{*p}$ are unambiguous. And $D_v = D_\gamma$ because both send $f$ to $\frac{d}{dt}|_{t=0} f(\gamma(t))$, by Definitions~\ref{def:Dv} and~\ref{def:velocity}.) By Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}, $\iota_{*p}D_v = D_{\iota \circ \gamma}$, the derivation $g \mapsto (g \circ \gamma)'(0) = \nabla g(p) \cdot v$ at $p$ --- the directional derivative in the direction $v$, which is $v$ under Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}. In detail, for a germ $[g]$ at $p$ on $W$, by Definition~\ref{def:velocity} and the chain rule (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}),
\[
(\iota_{*p}D_v)[g] = D_{\iota \circ \gamma}[g] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} g\big(\gamma(t)\big) = \nabla g(p) \cdot \gamma'(0) = \nabla g(p) \cdot v = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} g(p + tv) = D_v|_p[g] ,
\]
where $D_v|_p \in T_pW$ is the derivation of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}, the vector $v$ under the identification $T_pW = \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$; the fifth equality is the chain rule for the line $t \mapsto p + tv$. Since $v \mapsto D_v$ is onto $T_pS$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:ambient-abstract}), $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = T^{\geo}_pS$: every element of $T_pS$ is $D_v$ for some $v \in T^{\geo}_pS$, and its image is the vector $v$. And $T^{\geo}_pS = \ker F'(p)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}. This matches $\ker F_{*p}$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}, $F_{*p}$ being $F'(p)$: by Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}, $F_{*p}$ corresponds to $F'(p)$ under the identification $\partial/\partial r^i|_p \mapsto e_i$, which is the identification of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}, since $D_{e_i}|_p[g] = \frac{d}{dt}|_{t=0}\, g(p + te_i) = \partial g/\partial r^i(p)$; so $\ker F_{*p}$ corresponds to $\ker F'(p)$.
\end{proof}
