\section{Examples of Fibrations}\label{sec:fibration-examples}

\roadmark{Stage: bundles}{The trivial fibrations, the Möbius band with its two trivializations and their half-twist, and where the other fibrations of the course appear; the normal bundle of a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$ follows in the next section.}

\textit{The examples of \ref{sec:fibrations}, collected: the product fibrations, which every fibration imitates locally, and the Möbius band (Lecture~12), the first fibration that is not a product. The non-examples --- a submersion that is not a fibration, and one whose fibres are all diffeomorphic but which is still not a fibration --- stay with Ehresmann's theorem in \ref{sub:ehresmann}, whose hypotheses they explain. The normal bundle of a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Assignment~5), a fibration with fibre $\mathbb{R}^{n-m}$, has the next section to itself (\ref{sec:normal-bundle}), with its endpoint map and focal points.}

\begin{rembox}[Where Explicit Trivializations Come From]\label{rem:canonical-trivializations}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} In Definition~\ref{def:fibration} the local trivializations $\phi_\alpha$ are part of the data: a fibration has some, and nothing in the definition says how to find them --- the charts of the base $B$ carry no information about the total space or the fibre. So a fibration is a map that is, over each $U_\alpha$, a product fibration (Example~\ref{ex:product-fibration}), but there is no general formula for $\phi_\alpha$. Explicit trivializations come from extra structure:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{The tangent and cotangent bundles} (\ref{sec:tangent-bundle}, \ref{sub:cotangent-bundle}) reverse the order: $TM$ and $T^*M$ start out as sets (Definitions~\ref{def:tangent-bundle-set} and~\ref{def:cotangent-bundle}), with no topology, and the trivializations are written down first. A chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ of $M$ gives every fibre a basis, $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ of $T_pM$ and $dx^i|_p$ of $T_p^*M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}, Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}), and writing a tangent vector $v \in T_pM$ or a covector $\xi \in T_p^*M$ in that basis,
\[
v = \sum_{i=1}^m v^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p, \quad v^i = v[x^i], \qquad\qquad \xi = \sum_{i=1}^m \xi_i\, dx^i\big|_p, \quad \xi_i = \xi\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big)
\]
(Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}, Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}), is the trivialization: $(p, v) \mapsto (p, v^1, \ldots, v^m)$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-charts}) and $(p, \xi) \mapsto (p, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m)$ (Definition~\ref{def:ctb-trivialization}). The topology is then \emph{defined} from them: it is the unique topology for which every $TU$ is open and every chart $\tilde\varphi = (\varphi \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \Phi : TU \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ is a homeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-topology}; for $T^*M$, Proposition~\ref{prop:ctb-topology}), and the smooth structure is the one generated by these charts (Propositions~\ref{prop:tb-atlas} and~\ref{prop:cotangent-transition}). So the trivializations make the total space a manifold, and are local trivializations in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:fibration} by construction (Corollaries~\ref{cor:tb-fibration} and~\ref{cor:ctb-fibration}). For a general fibration the order is the other way: the total space is a manifold to begin with, and trivializations have to be found.
    \item \emph{A quotient description} of the total space lies in between, as for the Möbius band (Proposition~\ref{prop:mobius-fibration}): the topology is the quotient topology, given in advance, but the smooth structure is defined by the same charts that give the trivializations.
    \item \emph{Local sections} (Definition~\ref{def:local-section}) give them for the Hopf fibration (Proposition~\ref{prop:hopf-section-trivialization}), whose total space $S^{2n+1}$ is a manifold in advance.
\end{itemize}
Ehresmann's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:ehresmann}) produces trivializations for proper submersions, but not by a formula.
\end{rembox}

\subsection{Product Fibrations}\label{sub:product-fibrations}

\begin{exbox}[Product Fibrations]\exlabel{ex:product-fibration}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} For smooth manifolds $B$ and $F$, the projection $\mathrm{pr}_1 : B \times F \to B$, $\mathrm{pr}_1(b, y) = b$, is a trivial fibration with fibre $F$, with one open set $U = B$ and one local trivialization $\phi = \mathrm{id}_{B \times F}$. Every trivial fibration is this one up to the diffeomorphism $\phi$: if $\phi : M \to B \times F$ is a global trivialization of $\pi$, then $\pi = \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
Check Definition~\ref{def:fibration} with $M = B \times F$ and $\pi = \mathrm{pr}_1$. The map $\mathrm{pr}_1$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}). The single set $U = B$ covers $B$, and $\mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}(B) = B \times F$. The identity $\mathrm{id}_{B \times F}$ is a diffeomorphism $\mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}(B) \to B \times F$, and $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \mathrm{id}_{B \times F} = \mathrm{pr}_1 = \pi|_{\pi^{-1}(B)}$. So $\mathrm{pr}_1$ is a fibration with fibre $F$, trivial by Definition~\ref{def:trivial-fibration}. The last sentence is the condition $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi = \pi$ of that definition.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Möbius Band}\label{sub:mobius}

\begin{exbox}[The Möbius Band]\exlabel{ex:mobius}
The Möbius band fibres over its core circle, with an interval as fibre: ``no matter where you cut it, it just looks like a [strip]. But globally, it's not a product.'' Concretely, let $E = \big(\mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1)\big)/{\sim}$ with $(s, t) \sim (s + n, (-1)^n t)$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, and $\pi[s, t] = [s] \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} \cong S^1$.
\leeref{Example 10.3}
\end{exbox}

\textit{Status.} In lecture this was a picture, not a proof: the claim that $\pi$ is a fibration with fibre $(-1, 1)$ is proved, with explicit local trivializations, in Proposition~\ref{prop:mobius-fibration} below; the claim that $E$ is not globally the product $S^1 \times (-1, 1)$ is stated, not proved, here. Over any arc of the circle shorter than the whole, the twist can be undone, which is the local product structure; the obstruction is global, and it is visible in the picture: the band has a single boundary curve, while the product $S^1 \times (-1, 1)$ closed up would have two. Lee's Möbius bundle takes the fibre $\mathbb{R}$ in place of $(-1, 1)$.

Left: the strip $[0, 1] \times (-1, 1)$, ruled by its fibres, with the core circle in orange; glue the two ends with a half-twist, matching the arrows. Right: the band itself. Each grey segment is a fibre, lying over one point of the orange core circle, and the boundary is a single curve.

\begin{propbox}[The Möbius Band Is a Fibration]\thmlabel{prop:mobius-fibration}
Let $E = \big(\mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1)\big)/{\sim}$ and $\pi[s, t] = [s]$ be as in Example~\ref{ex:mobius}, let $q : \mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1) \to E$ be the quotient map, and identify $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with $S^1$ by $h[s] = (\cos 2\pi s, \sin 2\pi s)$. For $a \in \{0, \tfrac12\}$ put $I_a = (a, a + 1)$, $U_a = \{[s] : s \in I_a\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ and $W_a = q\big(I_a \times (-1, 1)\big) \subseteq E$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $E$ is a topological $2$-manifold, and the two maps $\psi_a = \big(q|_{I_a \times (-1,1)}\big)^{-1} : W_a \to I_a \times (-1, 1)$ form a smooth atlas, with transition
    \[
    \psi_{1/2} \circ \psi_0^{-1}(s, t) = \begin{cases} (s, t), & \tfrac12 < s < 1, \\ (s + 1, -t), & 0 < s < \tfrac12. \end{cases}
    \]
    \item With this smooth structure $\pi$ is smooth, $\pi^{-1}(U_a) = W_a$, and
    \[
    \phi_a : \pi^{-1}(U_a) \to U_a \times (-1, 1), \qquad \phi_a[s, t] = \big([s], t\big) \quad (s \in I_a),
    \]
    are local trivializations. So $\pi$ is a fibration with fibre $(-1, 1)$.
    \item On $U_0 \cap U_{1/2}$ the two trivializations differ by a sign on one arc:
    \[
    \phi_{1/2} \circ \phi_0^{-1}\big([s], t\big) = \begin{cases} \big([s], t\big), & \tfrac12 < s < 1, \\ \big([s], -t\big), & 0 < s < \tfrac12. \end{cases}
    \]
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Write $g_n(s, t) = \big(s + n, (-1)^n t\big)$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, so that $(s, t) \sim (s', t')$ exactly when $(s', t') = g_n(s, t)$ for some $n$. Each $g_n$ is a homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1)$, with inverse $g_{-n}$, since $g_n \circ g_m = g_{n+m}$ and $g_0 = \mathrm{id}$.

\emph{$q$ is open.} The relation $\sim$ is the orbit relation (Definition~\ref{def:orbit-relation}) of the action $n \cdot (s, t) = g_n(s, t)$ of the additive group $\mathbb{Z}$ on $\mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1)$, which is an action (Definition~\ref{def:action}) because $g_0 = \mathrm{id}$ and $g_n \circ g_m = g_{n+m}$. With the discrete topology $\mathbb{Z}$ is a topological group (Example~\ref{ex:discrete-groups}), and the action is continuous (Definition~\ref{def:continuous-action}): $\mathbb{Z} \times \big(\mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1)\big)$ is the union of the open sets $\{n\} \times \big(\mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1)\big)$, on each of which the action map is the continuous $g_n$. So by Lemma~\ref{lem:orbit-open} the orbit relation is open: for $O$ open in $\mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1)$, the saturation $q^{-1}(q(O))$ is open --- explicitly, it is $\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} g_n(O)$, a union of open sets, as in that lemma --- so $q(O)$ is open in the quotient topology (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-topology}, Proposition~\ref{prop:saturation}).

\emph{$q$ restricted to $I_a \times (-1, 1)$.} It is injective: if $q(s, t) = q(s', t')$ with $s, s' \in I_a$, then $(s', t') = g_n(s, t)$, so $s' - s = n$ is an integer with $|s' - s| < 1$, hence $n = 0$ and $(s', t') = (s, t)$. It is continuous, as a restriction of $q$, and open, since an open subset of $I_a \times (-1, 1)$ is open in $\mathbb{R} \times (-1, 1)$ and $q$ is open. So it is a homeomorphism onto the open set $W_a$, and $\psi_a$ is a homeomorphism of $W_a$ onto the open subset $I_a \times (-1, 1)$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

\emph{(1) $E$ is a topological $2$-manifold.} The sets $W_0, W_{1/2}$ cover $E$: every $s \in \mathbb{R}$ has $s - n \in (0, 1)$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ unless $s$ is an integer, and then $s - n = 1 \in I_{1/2}$ for $n = s - 1$; and $q(s, t) = q\big(g_{-n}(s, t)\big)$. \emph{Hausdorff:} let $x \ne y$ in $E$. If both lie in one $W_a$, separate them there, $W_a$ being homeomorphic to a subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and open in $E$. Otherwise one lies in $W_0 \setminus W_{1/2} = q\big(\{\tfrac12\} \times (-1, 1)\big)$ and the other in $W_{1/2} \setminus W_0 = q\big(\{1\} \times (-1, 1)\big)$; then $q\big((\tfrac14, \tfrac34) \times (-1, 1)\big)$ and $q\big((\tfrac34, \tfrac54) \times (-1, 1)\big)$ are open neighbourhoods of them, disjoint because two of their points with first coordinates $s \in (\tfrac14, \tfrac34)$, $s' \in (\tfrac34, \tfrac54)$ have $0 < s' - s < 1$, not an integer. \emph{Second countable:} each $W_a$ has a countable basis of sets open in $W_a$, hence in $E$, and the union of the two bases is a countable basis of $E$. With the charts $\psi_a$, $E$ is a topological $2$-manifold (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}).

\emph{(1) The transition.} $W_0 \cap W_{1/2} = q\big(((0, \tfrac12) \cup (\tfrac12, 1)) \times (-1, 1)\big)$. Let $(s, t) \in \psi_0(W_0 \cap W_{1/2})$. If $\tfrac12 < s < 1$, then $s \in I_{1/2}$ and $\psi_{1/2}(q(s, t)) = (s, t)$. If $0 < s < \tfrac12$, then $q(s, t) = q\big(g_1(s, t)\big) = q(s + 1, -t)$ with $s + 1 \in I_{1/2}$, so $\psi_{1/2}(q(s, t)) = (s + 1, -t)$. Both branches are smooth, and so is the inverse, $(s, t) \mapsto (s, t)$ or $(s - 1, -t)$. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} Their Jacobians are constant on each branch,
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \big(\tfrac12 < s < 1\big), \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \big(0 < s < \tfrac12\big),
\]
the second being the half-twist $t \mapsto -t$. So the two charts are compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}) and form a smooth atlas (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}).

\emph{The base.} $h$ is well defined and bijective because $(\cos 2\pi s, \sin 2\pi s)$ depends exactly on $s$ modulo $1$; $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ carries the topology and smooth structure of $S^1$ transported along $h$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}). For $s \in I_0 = (0, 1)$ the angle $2\pi s$ lies in $(0, 2\pi)$, and for $s \in I_{1/2}$ in $(\pi, 3\pi)$; so the maps $\chi_a : U_a \to I_a$, $\chi_a[s] = s$ ($s \in I_a$), are $\chi_0 = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\,\varphi_a \circ h$ and $\chi_{1/2} = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\,\varphi_b \circ h$, with $\varphi_a, \varphi_b$ the angle charts of Example~\ref{ex:circle-angle}. Rescaling by the diffeomorphism $\theta \mapsto \theta/2\pi$ of $\mathbb{R}$ keeps a smooth chart smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(2), applied to the smooth charts $\varphi_a \circ h$ and $\varphi_b \circ h$ of $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, with the transported structure, and to this rescaling as the diffeomorphism), so $\chi_0, \chi_{1/2}$ are smooth charts of $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with domains $U_0, U_{1/2}$.

\emph{(2) $\pi$ is smooth and $\pi^{-1}(U_a) = W_a$.} $\pi$ is well defined, since $\pi[g_n(s, t)] = [s + n] = [s]$. If $[s] \in U_a$ then $s - n \in I_a$ for some $n$ and $q(s, t) = q(g_{-n}(s, t)) \in W_a$; conversely $\pi(W_a) \subseteq U_a$. So $\pi^{-1}(U_a) = W_a$, and in the charts $\psi_a$ and $\chi_a$,
\[
\chi_a \circ \pi \circ \psi_a^{-1}(s, t) = \chi_a[s] = s \qquad \big((s, t) \in I_a \times (-1, 1)\big),
\]
a smooth map. The $W_a$ cover $E$, so $\pi$ is smooth (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}).

\emph{(2) The trivializations.} $\phi_a = (\chi_a^{-1} \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \psi_a$, since $\psi_a[s, t] = (s, t)$ and $\chi_a^{-1}(s) = [s]$ for $s \in I_a$. Here $\psi_a : W_a \to I_a \times (-1, 1)$ is a diffeomorphism, a chart of the open submanifold $W_a$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), and $\chi_a^{-1} \times \mathrm{id} : I_a \times (-1, 1) \to U_a \times (-1, 1)$ is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $\chi_a \times \mathrm{id}$, both having the identity as coordinate representation in the product chart $(U_a \times (-1, 1), \chi_a \times \mathrm{id})$. So $\phi_a$ is a diffeomorphism, and $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \phi_a[s, t] = [s] = \pi[s, t]$. With the open cover $\{U_0, U_{1/2}\}$ of $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, Definition~\ref{def:fibration} holds with fibre $(-1, 1)$.

\emph{(3)} Let $[s] \in U_0 \cap U_{1/2}$ with $s \in I_0$. Then $\phi_0^{-1}([s], t) = q(s, t)$, and by the transition in (1), $q(s, t) = q(s, t)$ with $s \in I_{1/2}$ if $\tfrac12 < s < 1$, and $q(s, t) = q(s + 1, -t)$ with $s + 1 \in I_{1/2}$ if $0 < s < \tfrac12$. Applying $\phi_{1/2}$ gives $([s], t)$ in the first case and $([s + 1], -t) = ([s], -t)$ in the second.
\end{proof}

The sign in (3) is the half-twist: going once around the circle, the two trivializations agree on one arc and differ by $t \mapsto -t$ on the other. Over either arc alone the band is a product; the sign is what a global product would have to remove.

\subsection{Further Examples}\label{sub:fibration-examples-more}

\textit{(Not from lecture: a guide to the fibrations that appear later.)}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{The Hopf fibration} $S^{2n+1} \to \mathbb{CP}^n$, with fibre $S^1$ and the explicit trivializations $\phi_j(z) = ([z], z_j/|z_j|)$ (Example~\ref{ex:hopf-fibration}); it has local sections but no global one (Corollary~\ref{cor:hopf-local-sections}).
    \item \emph{The normal bundle} $\mathcal{N} \to M$ of a submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, with fibre $\mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}, in the next section, \ref{sec:normal-bundle}).
    \item \emph{The tangent and cotangent bundles} $TM \to M$ and $T^*M \to M$, with fibre $\mathbb{R}^m$, whose trivializations come from charts of $M$ (Corollaries~\ref{cor:tb-fibration} and~\ref{cor:ctb-fibration}).
    \item \emph{Two-to-one local diffeomorphisms}: $S^n \to \mathbb{RP}^n$ (Example~\ref{ex:sn-rpn}) and $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \SO(3)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:double-cover}). These are fibrations with a two-point fibre (two-sheeted coverings); the notes prove the local-diffeomorphism and two-to-one statements, not the fibration property.
\end{itemize}

% SECTION: THE NORMAL BUNDLE OF A SUBMANIFOLD OF EUCLIDEAN SPACE
% ============================================================================

\section{The Normal Bundle of a Submanifold of Euclidean Space}\label{sec:normal-bundle}\label{sub:normal-bundle}

\roadmark{Stage: bundles}{The vectors perpendicular to a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$, collected into an $n$-dimensional manifold that fibres over it; its endpoint map and focal points; and, through the dot product, normal vectors as conormal covectors.}

\textit{Assignment~5, Problem~5.} A submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has, at each of its points, the vectors perpendicular to it; collecting all pairs (point, perpendicular vector) gives the \emph{normal bundle}. Part~(a) of the problem shows that it is a manifold of dimension $n$, whatever the dimension of $M$; part~(b) introduces the endpoint map and finds the focal points of a parabola. The normal bundle is the Euclidean shadow of the conormal bundle (the remark \emph{The Conormal Bundle} in \ref{sec:transversality-submanifolds}; Definition~\ref{def:conormal-bundle}, later, in \ref{sub:ctb-zero-section}): Uribe's ``if we had a metric \ldots\ this would be the normal space'' (the remark \emph{No Normal Vectors Without a Metric} in \ref{sec:submanifolds}) is realized here by the dot product of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-conormal} makes the identification explicit. That the projection to $M$ is a fibration (Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}) --- which is why the normal bundle stands next to the examples of fibrations (\ref{sec:fibration-examples}) --- and what focal points mean geometrically (the remark \emph{Focal Points Are Centres of Curvature} below), are added.

\emph{Three meanings of ``normal''.} \textit{(Not from lecture.)} For a regular submanifold $S$ of a manifold $M$ and $p \in S$, three spaces in these notes carry the name:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the \emph{conormal space} $N_pS \subseteq T_p^*M$, the covectors that vanish on $\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$ (Definition~\ref{def:conormal}, \ref{sec:submanifolds}, Lecture~12) --- intrinsic, defined without any metric;
    \item the \emph{normal space} $T_pM/\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$, a quotient (Definition~\ref{def:normal-space}, \ref{sec:transversality-submanifolds}) --- also intrinsic; $N_pS$ consists of the covectors that vanish on $\iota_{*p}(T_pS)$, which are the same as the linear forms on this quotient;
    \item for a submanifold of Euclidean space --- in this section, following the assignment, the submanifold is called $M$ and the ambient space is $\mathbb{R}^n$ --- the \emph{Euclidean normal space} $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ of vectors perpendicular to $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:normal-bundle}), studied here; it needs the dot product.
\end{enumerate}
With the dot product the three agree: $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$ is a complement of $T^{\geo}_pM$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, so it maps isomorphically onto the quotient $\mathbb{R}^n/T^{\geo}_pM$, which is the normal space $T_p\mathbb{R}^n/\iota_{*p}(T_pM)$ under $w \mapsto D_w|_p$; and $v \mapsto \xi_v$ maps it isomorphically onto the conormal space $N_pM$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-conormal}).

\subsection{The Normal Bundle}\label{sub:normal-bundle-def}

\emph{Setting.} Throughout this section $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a regular submanifold of dimension $m < n$, that is, of codimension $n - m$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}), and $v \cdot w = \sum_l v^l w^l$ is the dot product of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Tangent spaces are the geometric ones: for $p \in M$, $T^{\geo}_pM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is the set of velocities $\gamma'(0)$ of smooth curves $\gamma$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\gamma(0) = p$ that stay in $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:geometric-tangent}, whose formula makes sense verbatim for any subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). This is the assignment's ``$T_pM$ identified with the ambient tangent space''; its identification with $\iota_{*p}(T_pM)$ is the remark \emph{The Tangent Spaces Match} in \ref{sec:submanifolds}. It is computed in an adapted chart: $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^n))$ is a smooth chart of $\mathbb{R}^n$ adapted to $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}), so that
\[
U \cap M = \{\, q \in U : x^{m+1}(q) = \cdots = x^n(q) = 0 \,\},
\]
and
\[
G = (G^1, \ldots, G^{n-m}) = (x^{m+1}, \ldots, x^n) : U \to \mathbb{R}^{n-m}, \qquad J(q) = G'(q) \quad (q \in U),
\]
the $(n-m) \times n$ Jacobian of $G$ in the standard coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^n$, whose $s$-th row is the gradient $\nabla G^s(q)$ (Definitions~\ref{def:jacobian} and~\ref{def:gradient}). Every point of $M$ lies in such a chart (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}). The facts about such a chart that are used throughout are collected in Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart} (\ref{sub:submanifolds-euclidean}):
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\varphi'(q)$ is invertible and $J(q)$ has rank $n - m$, for every $q \in U$;
    \item $T^{\geo}_qM = \ker J(q)$, of dimension $m$, for every $q \in U \cap M$;
    \item the vectors $X_j(q) = \dfrac{\partial \varphi^{-1}}{\partial r^j}\big(\varphi(q)\big)$, $j = 1, \ldots, m$, form a basis of $T^{\geo}_qM$, for every $q \in U \cap M$;
    \item the gradients $\nabla G^1(q), \ldots, \nabla G^{n-m}(q)$ form a basis of the orthogonal complement $(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$, for every $q \in U \cap M$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{defbox}[Normal Bundle]\deflabel{def:normal-bundle}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m < n$. For $p \in M$ write
\[
(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp = \{\, v \in \mathbb{R}^n : v \cdot w = 0 \text{ for all } w \in T^{\geo}_pM \,\}
\]
for the orthogonal complement of the geometric tangent space with respect to the dot product. The \textbf{normal bundle} of $M$ is
\[
\mathcal{N} = \{\, (p, v) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n : p \in M \text{ and } v \in (T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp \,\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n},
\]
with the \textbf{projection} $\pi : \mathcal{N} \to M$, $\pi(p, v) = p$. Its fibre over $p$ is $\pi^{-1}(p) = \{p\} \times (T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$, a copy of the normal space at $p$.
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Tubular Neighborhoods}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Normal Bundle Is a Submanifold]\thmlabel{prop:normal-bundle-submanifold}
$\mathcal{N}$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{2n} = \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n$ of codimension $n$, hence a smooth manifold of dimension $n$ with the induced structure (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}).
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Tubular Neighborhoods}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~5, Problem~5(a); the student's route, following the hint. Two steps are completed: that the first $m$ coordinate vectors span the tangent space is proved, in Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(3) (cited in Step~1(ii)), and the Jacobian, which the hint computes in the coordinates $(x, v)$, is converted to the standard coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, so that the external description of \ref{sec:euclidean} applies.)} By the last statement of Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean}, applied to $X = \mathcal{N} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2n} = \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ with $k = n$, it suffices to describe $\mathcal{N}$ externally near each of its points (Definition~\ref{def:ext-int}): for each $(p_0, v_0) \in \mathcal{N}$ we need an open $W \ni (p_0, v_0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ and a smooth $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^n$ having $\vec 0$ as a regular value with $\mathcal{N} \cap W = F^{-1}(\vec 0)$. Fix $(p_0, v_0) \in \mathcal{N}$. Then $p_0 \in M$, so there is an adapted chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^n))$ at $p_0$ as in the Setting; put $W = U \times \mathbb{R}^n$, open in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ as a product of open sets, and containing $(p_0, v_0)$.

\emph{Step 1: the vector fields $X_j$.} For $q \in U$ and $j = 1, \ldots, n$ put
\[
X_j(q) = \frac{\partial \varphi^{-1}}{\partial r^j}\big(\varphi(q)\big) \in \mathbb{R}^n ,
\]
the $j$-th column of the Jacobian $(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q))$, with components $X_j^l(q)$, $l = 1, \ldots, n$. This is the hint's coordinate field $\partial/\partial x^j$ ``regarded as a vector field on $U$ in the sense of Calc~III'': the velocity of the $j$-th coordinate line $t \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(\varphi(q) + t e_j)$ at $t = 0$, by the chain rule. Each $X_j^l$ is smooth on $U$, as the composite of the smooth $\varphi$ with the partial derivative $\partial(\varphi^{-1})^l/\partial r^j$ of the smooth map $\varphi^{-1}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] \emph{$X_1(q), \ldots, X_n(q)$ form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$, for every $q \in U$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(1), $\varphi'(q)$ is invertible, and the chain rule applied to $\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}_{\varphi(U)}$ at $\varphi(q)$ gives $\varphi'(q)\,(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q)) = I_n$; so $(\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q))$ is the inverse of $\varphi'(q)$, hence invertible, and its columns $X_1(q), \ldots, X_n(q)$ form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$. In particular $X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)$ are linearly independent at every $q \in U$, not only on $M$; this is what Step~4 uses.
    \item[(ii)] \emph{For $q \in U \cap M$, $X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)$ form a basis of $T^{\geo}_qM$.} This is Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(3), for the chart $(U, \varphi)$ and the point $q$:
    \[
    T^{\geo}_qM = \Span\{X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)\}.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
The submitted solution quotes this span from the computation of Problem~2 for the inclusion of a regular submanifold in an adapted chart: $\iota_{*q}(T_qM) = \Span\{\partial/\partial x^1|_q, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^m|_q\}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), read in $\mathbb{R}^n$ through the remark \emph{The Tangent Spaces Match} in \ref{sec:submanifolds}.

\emph{Step 2: the map $F$.} Define $F : W = U \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ by
\[
F(q, v) = \big( x^{m+1}(q), \ldots, x^n(q),\ y^1(q, v), \ldots, y^m(q, v) \big), \qquad y^j(q, v) = X_j(q) \cdot v = \sum_{l=1}^n X_j^l(q)\, v^l .
\]
It is smooth: its first $n - m$ components are components of the smooth chart $\varphi$, and each $y^j$ is a sum of products of the smooth functions $X_j^l(q)$ and the coordinates $v^l$.

\emph{Step 3: $F^{-1}(\vec 0) = \mathcal{N} \cap W$.} For $(q, v) \in W$,
\begin{align*}
F(q, v) = \vec 0 &\iff x^{m+s}(q) = 0 \ (1 \le s \le n - m) \ \text{ and } \ X_j(q) \cdot v = 0 \ (1 \le j \le m) \\
&\iff q \in U \cap M \ \text{ and } \ X_j(q) \cdot v = 0 \ (1 \le j \le m) \\
&\iff q \in U \cap M \ \text{ and } \ v \in (T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp \\
&\iff (q, v) \in \mathcal{N} \cap W .
\end{align*}
The first equivalence is the definition of $F$. The second is the adapted-chart description $U \cap M = \{x^{m+1} = \cdots = x^n = 0\}$, with $q \in U$. For the third, $q \in U \cap M$, so $T^{\geo}_qM = \Span\{X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)\}$ by Step~1(ii); a vector $v$ is orthogonal to every element $\sum_j c_j X_j(q)$ of this span if and only if it is orthogonal to each $X_j(q)$, because $v \cdot \sum_j c_j X_j(q) = \sum_j c_j\, \big(v \cdot X_j(q)\big)$ by linearity of the dot product (``if'' by this formula, ``only if'' by taking $c = e_j$). The fourth is Definition~\ref{def:normal-bundle}, together with $q \in U$ and $W = U \times \mathbb{R}^n$.

\emph{Step 4: the Jacobian in the coordinates $(x, v)$ (the submitted computation).} On $W$ use the coordinates $(x, v) = (x^1(q), \ldots, x^n(q), v^1, \ldots, v^n)$, i.e.\ the map $\varphi \times \mathrm{id} : W \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^n$, $(q, v) \mapsto (\varphi(q), v)$, a bijection with inverse $\varphi^{-1} \times \mathrm{id}$; in them the $x$'s and the $v$'s are independent variables. The coordinate representation of $F$ is $\tilde F = F \circ (\varphi^{-1} \times \mathrm{id}) : \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$,
\[
\tilde F(r, v) = \Big( r^{m+1}, \ldots, r^n,\ \tilde X_1(r) \cdot v, \ldots, \tilde X_m(r) \cdot v \Big), \qquad \tilde X_j(r) = \frac{\partial \varphi^{-1}}{\partial r^j}(r),
\]
using $x^{m+s}(\varphi^{-1}(r)) = r^{m+s}$ and $X_j(\varphi^{-1}(r)) = \tilde X_j(r)$. Its partial derivatives at $(r, v)$, for $1 \le i, l \le n$, are as follows.
\begin{itemize}
    \item The component $r^{m+s}$ ($1 \le s \le n - m$) depends only on $r$, and is the $(m+s)$-th coordinate:
    \[
    \frac{\partial r^{m+s}}{\partial r^i} = \delta^{m+s}_i, \qquad \frac{\partial r^{m+s}}{\partial v^l} = 0 .
    \]
    \item The component $\tilde y^j(r, v) = \tilde X_j(r) \cdot v = \sum_l \tilde X_j^l(r)\, v^l$: differentiating each term by the product rule, with $v$ independent of $r$ and $\tilde X_j$ independent of $v$,
    \[
    \frac{\partial \tilde y^j}{\partial r^i} = \sum_{l=1}^n v^l\, \frac{\partial^2 (\varphi^{-1})^l}{\partial r^i\, \partial r^j}(r), \qquad \frac{\partial \tilde y^j}{\partial v^l} = \tilde X_j^l(r) .
    \]
\end{itemize}
Grouping the columns as $(r^1, \ldots, r^m)$, $(r^{m+1}, \ldots, r^n)$, $(v^1, \ldots, v^n)$, the $n \times 2n$ Jacobian at $(\varphi(q), v)$ is therefore
\[
\tilde F'\big(\varphi(q), v\big) = \begin{pmatrix} 0_{(n-m) \times m} & I_{n-m} & 0_{(n-m) \times n} \\ \ast & \ast & X(q) \end{pmatrix},
\]
where the entries $\ast$ are the second-derivative sums above, and $X(q)$ is the $m \times n$ matrix whose $j$-th row is $X_j(q)^{\mathsf T} = \big(X_j^1(q), \ldots, X_j^n(q)\big)$ (recall $\tilde X_j(\varphi(q)) = X_j(q)$). Written out, with the partials of the $\tilde y^j$ taken at $(\varphi(q), v)$,
\[
\tilde F'\big(\varphi(q), v\big) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc|ccc} 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \hline \dfrac{\partial \tilde y^1}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde y^1}{\partial r^m} & \dfrac{\partial \tilde y^1}{\partial r^{m+1}} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde y^1}{\partial r^n} & X_1^1(q) & \cdots & X_1^n(q) \\ \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial \tilde y^m}{\partial r^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde y^m}{\partial r^m} & \dfrac{\partial \tilde y^m}{\partial r^{m+1}} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial \tilde y^m}{\partial r^n} & X_m^1(q) & \cdots & X_m^n(q) \end{array}\right) ,
\]
with $n - m$ rows above the line and $m$ below, and $m$, $n - m$, $n$ columns in the three groups.

\emph{It has rank $n$.} Write the $s$-th of the first $n - m$ rows as $(0, e_s, 0)$, with $e_s \in \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$, and the $j$-th of the last $m$ rows as $(\ast, \ast, X_j(q)^{\mathsf T})$, and suppose a linear combination of the rows vanishes:
\[
\sum_{s=1}^{n-m} c_s\, (0, e_s, 0) + \sum_{j=1}^m b_j\, \big(\ast, \ast, X_j(q)^{\mathsf T}\big) = 0, \qquad c_s, b_j \in \mathbb{R}.
\]
In the last $n$ columns the first $n - m$ rows have zeros, so these columns give $\sum_j b_j X_j(q)^{\mathsf T} = 0$; since $X_1(q), \ldots, X_m(q)$ are linearly independent (Step~1(i)), $b_1 = \cdots = b_m = 0$. With all $b_j = 0$, columns $m+1, \ldots, n$ give $\sum_s c_s e_s = 0$, so $c_1 = \cdots = c_{n-m} = 0$. So the $n$ rows are linearly independent, and $\tilde F'(\varphi(q), v)$ has rank $n$ (Definition~\ref{def:rank}).

\emph{Step 5: back to the standard coordinates.} On $W$, $F = \tilde F \circ (\varphi \times \mathrm{id})$, and $\varphi \times \mathrm{id}$ is smooth with the block-diagonal Jacobian
\[
(\varphi \times \mathrm{id})'(q, v) = \begin{pmatrix} \varphi'(q) & 0 \\ 0 & I_n \end{pmatrix},
\]
which is invertible, with inverse $\operatorname{diag}\big((\varphi^{-1})'(\varphi(q)), I_n\big)$, by Step~1(i) (Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(1) and the chain rule). By the chain rule,
\[
F'(q, v) = \tilde F'\big(\varphi(q), v\big)\, (\varphi \times \mathrm{id})'(q, v) .
\]
Multiplying on the right by an invertible matrix does not change the image: $\operatorname{im}(AB) = A(\operatorname{im} B) = A(\mathbb{R}^{2n}) = \operatorname{im} A$ when $B$ is onto. So $F'(q, v)$ has the same image as $\tilde F'(\varphi(q), v)$, which is all of $\mathbb{R}^n$ by Step~4. Thus every point of $W$ is a regular point of $F$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-point}), and in particular $\vec 0$ is a regular value of $F$ on $W$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}, applied on the open set $W$ as in Corollary~\ref{cor:rvt-open}).

\emph{Step 6: conclusion.} By Steps~2, 3 and~5, $W$ is an open neighbourhood of $(p_0, v_0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, $F : W \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is smooth with $\vec 0$ as a regular value, and $\mathcal{N} \cap W = F^{-1}(\vec 0)$: $\mathcal{N}$ is described externally near $(p_0, v_0)$ (Definition~\ref{def:ext-int}, with $n + k = 2n$ and $k = n$). As $(p_0, v_0) \in \mathcal{N}$ was arbitrary, Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean} gives that $\mathcal{N}$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ of codimension $n$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure} it is a smooth manifold of dimension $2n - n = n$.

\emph{The submitted ending.} The solution as submitted concludes without leaving the coordinates $(x, v)$. By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, $\tilde F'(\varphi(q), v)$ is the matrix of $F_{*(q,v)}$, so by Step~4 $F$ is a submersion on the open submanifold $W$ of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, and the regular value theorem for manifolds (Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}) makes $F^{-1}(\vec 0) = \mathcal{N} \cap W$ a regular submanifold of $W$ of codimension $n$. An adapted chart $(W', \theta)$ of $W$ at $(p_0, v_0)$ is a smooth chart of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(2)), and since $W' \subseteq W$,
\[
W' \cap \mathcal{N} = W' \cap \mathcal{N} \cap W = W' \cap F^{-1}(\vec 0) ,
\]
so it is adapted to $\mathcal{N}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}), with $n$ vanishing coordinates. The two endings are the same argument: Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean} packages the passage from a regular level set to an adapted chart.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Normal Bundle Is a Fibration]\thmlabel{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^n))$ be a chart of $\mathbb{R}^n$ adapted to $M$, with $G = (x^{m+1}, \ldots, x^n)$ and $J(q) = G'(q)$ as in the Setting, and let $\mathcal{N}$ carry the smooth structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-submanifold}.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $q \in U \cap M$ the gradients $\nabla G^1(q), \ldots, \nabla G^{n-m}(q)$, the rows of $J(q)$, form a basis of $(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$; and for every $q \in U$ the $(n-m) \times (n-m)$ matrix $J(q) J(q)^{\mathsf T}$ is invertible.
    \item The map
    \[
    \Phi_U : \pi^{-1}(U \cap M) \longrightarrow (U \cap M) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}, \qquad \Phi_U(q, v) = \Big(q,\ \big(J(q) J(q)^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} J(q)\, v\Big),
    \]
    is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $(q, c) \mapsto \big(q, J(q)^{\mathsf T} c\big)$, and $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \Phi_U = \pi|_{\pi^{-1}(U \cap M)}$. On each fibre $\pi^{-1}(q) = \{q\} \times (T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$ it is a linear isomorphism $(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp \to \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$.
    \item $\pi : \mathcal{N} \to M$ is a fibration with fibre $\mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ (Definition~\ref{def:fibration}), the maps $\Phi_U$ of (2), over all adapted charts, being local trivializations.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment; filled in.)} Throughout, $M$ carries its induced structure as a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$, $U \cap M$ is open in $M$ (subspace topology, $U$ being open in $\mathbb{R}^n$) and is an open submanifold of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:open-submanifold-smooth}), and $(U \cap M) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ is a product manifold (Definition~\ref{def:product-manifold}).

\emph{$\pi$ is smooth, and $\pi^{-1}(U \cap M)$.} Let $\iota_{\mathcal{N}} : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ be the inclusion, smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1), and $\mathrm{pr} : \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $\mathrm{pr}(p, v) = p$, which is linear, hence smooth. Then $\pi = \mathrm{pr} \circ \iota_{\mathcal{N}}$ as maps into $\mathbb{R}^n$, smooth as a composite (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}); its values lie in $M$ by Definition~\ref{def:normal-bundle}, so $\pi$ is smooth as a map into $M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)). Next,
\[
\mathcal{N}_U := \pi^{-1}(U \cap M) = \{\, (q, v) \in \mathcal{N} : q \in U \,\} = \mathcal{N} \cap (U \times \mathbb{R}^n),
\]
the first equality because $\pi(q, v) = q$ and $q \in M$ for every $(q, v) \in \mathcal{N}$. It is open in $\mathcal{N}$, being the intersection of $\mathcal{N}$ with an open set of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, and is an open submanifold of $\mathcal{N}$.

\emph{(1) The gradients span the normal space.} Fix $q \in U \cap M$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(4), for the chart $(U, \varphi)$ and the point $q$, the $n - m$ gradients $\nabla G^1(q), \ldots, \nabla G^{n-m}(q)$ --- the rows of $J(q)$ (Definition~\ref{def:jacobian}) --- form a basis of $(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$; in particular $\dim (T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp = n - m$. In matrix form, since $J(q)^{\mathsf T} c = \sum_s c^s\, \nabla G^s(q)$ for $c = (c^1, \ldots, c^{n-m}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ (the columns of $J(q)^{\mathsf T}$ are the rows of $J(q)$):
\[
(T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp = \{\, J(q)^{\mathsf T} c : c \in \mathbb{R}^{n-m} \,\}, \qquad c \mapsto J(q)^{\mathsf T} c \ \text{ injective}. \tag{$\flat$}
\]
\emph{The Gram matrix.} Now let $q \in U$ be arbitrary; $J(q)$ still has rank $n - m$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(1)), so $c \mapsto J(q)^{\mathsf T} c$ is injective (its columns are the independent rows of $J(q)$). If $J(q) J(q)^{\mathsf T} c = 0$, then
\[
0 = c \cdot \big(J(q) J(q)^{\mathsf T} c\big) = c^{\mathsf T} J(q) J(q)^{\mathsf T} c = \big(J(q)^{\mathsf T} c\big) \cdot \big(J(q)^{\mathsf T} c\big) = \big|J(q)^{\mathsf T} c\big|^2 ,
\]
so $J(q)^{\mathsf T} c = 0$, and $c = 0$ by injectivity. A square matrix with zero kernel is invertible (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)). ($J J^{\mathsf T}$ is the Gram matrix of the gradients: its $(s, s')$ entry is $\nabla G^s(q) \cdot \nabla G^{s'}(q)$.) Written out,
\[
J(q) J(q)^{\mathsf T} = \begin{pmatrix} \nabla G^1(q) \cdot \nabla G^1(q) & \cdots & \nabla G^1(q) \cdot \nabla G^{n-m}(q) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \nabla G^{n-m}(q) \cdot \nabla G^1(q) & \cdots & \nabla G^{n-m}(q) \cdot \nabla G^{n-m}(q) \end{pmatrix} .
\]

\emph{(2) The map and its inverse.} For $q \in U$ put $A(q) = \big(J(q) J(q)^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} J(q)$, an $(n-m) \times n$ matrix. Its entries are smooth functions on $U$: the entries of $J(q)$ are partial derivatives $\partial x^{m+s}/\partial r^l(q)$ of components of the smooth chart $\varphi$; those of $J J^{\mathsf T}$ are sums of products of these; and by the cofactor formula $(J J^{\mathsf T})^{-1} = \adj(J J^{\mathsf T}) / \det(J J^{\mathsf T})$, each entry of the inverse is a polynomial in the entries of $J J^{\mathsf T}$ divided by $\det(J J^{\mathsf T})$, which is smooth and, by (1), nowhere zero on $U$. Define
\[
\Phi_U(q, v) = \big(q, A(q)\, v\big) \quad \big((q, v) \in \mathcal{N}_U\big), \qquad \Theta_U(q, c) = \big(q, J(q)^{\mathsf T} c\big) \quad \big((q, c) \in (U \cap M) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}\big).
\]
\emph{Targets.} For $(q, v) \in \mathcal{N}_U$, $q \in U \cap M$, so $\Phi_U(q, v) \in (U \cap M) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$. For $q \in U \cap M$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$, $J(q)^{\mathsf T} c \in (T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$ by $(\flat)$, so $(q, J(q)^{\mathsf T} c) \in \mathcal{N}$, and it lies in $\mathcal{N}_U$ since $q \in U$.

\emph{Mutually inverse.} For $(q, c) \in (U \cap M) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$,
\[
\Phi_U\big(\Theta_U(q, c)\big) = \Big(q,\ \big(J J^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} J\, J^{\mathsf T} c\Big) = \Big(q,\ \big(J J^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} \big(J J^{\mathsf T}\big) c\Big) = (q, c),
\]
with $J = J(q)$. For $(q, v) \in \mathcal{N}_U$, $v \in (T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$, so by $(\flat)$ $v = J^{\mathsf T} c$ for some $c \in \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$, and
\[
\Theta_U\big(\Phi_U(q, v)\big) = \Big(q,\ J^{\mathsf T} \big(J J^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} J\, v\Big) = \Big(q,\ J^{\mathsf T} \big(J J^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} \big(J J^{\mathsf T}\big) c\Big) = \big(q, J^{\mathsf T} c\big) = (q, v).
\]
So $\Phi_U$ is a bijection with inverse $\Theta_U$.

\emph{Commuting triangle and linearity on fibres.} $\mathrm{pr}_1\big(\Phi_U(q, v)\big) = q = \pi(q, v)$ for every $(q, v) \in \mathcal{N}_U$. On the fibre $\pi^{-1}(q) = \{q\} \times (T^{\geo}_qM)^\perp$, $\Phi_U$ is $v \mapsto A(q)\, v$ in the second component, a linear map; it is a bijection onto $\mathbb{R}^{n-m}$, because $\Phi_U$ and $\Theta_U$ are mutually inverse and both keep the first component $q$, so that $c \mapsto J(q)^{\mathsf T} c$ is its inverse.

\emph{$\Phi_U$ is smooth.} Let $\varphi_M = (x^1, \ldots, x^m)|_{U \cap M}$ be the induced chart of $M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}); its domain is all of $U \cap M$, so it is also a chart of the open submanifold $U \cap M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-smooth}(2)), with image $V_M = \varphi_M(U \cap M)$ open in $\mathbb{R}^m$. With the identity chart of $\mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ it gives the product chart $\big((U \cap M) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}, \varphi_M \times \mathrm{id}\big)$, whose domain is the whole product (Proposition~\ref{prop:product-manifold}); so $\varphi_M \times \mathrm{id} : (U \cap M) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m} \to V_M \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ is a diffeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}). Now
\[
(\varphi_M \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \Phi_U(q, v) = \big(x^1(q), \ldots, x^m(q),\ A(q)\, v\big) = \hat\Phi(q, v), \qquad \hat\Phi : U \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m},
\]
where $\hat\Phi$ is defined by the same formula on all of $U \times \mathbb{R}^n$ and is smooth, its components being components of $\varphi$ and sums of products of the smooth entries of $A(q)$ with the coordinates $v^l$. The inclusion $\iota_U : \mathcal{N}_U \to U \times \mathbb{R}^n$ is smooth: the inclusion $\mathcal{N}_U \to \mathcal{N}$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}(1)), and so is $\iota_{\mathcal{N}}$; their composite $\mathcal{N}_U \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ takes values in the open set $U \times \mathbb{R}^n$, hence is smooth into it (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}(3)). So $\hat\Phi \circ \iota_U$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}); it takes values in the open set $V_M \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, hence is smooth into it (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}(3)); and
\[
\Phi_U = (\varphi_M \times \mathrm{id})^{-1} \circ \big(\hat\Phi \circ \iota_U\big)
\]
is a composite of smooth maps, hence smooth.

\emph{$\Theta_U$ is smooth.} First, $\varphi_M^{-1}(r) = \varphi^{-1}(r, \vec 0)$ for $r \in V_M$: such an $r$ is $\varphi_M(q) = \big(x^1(q), \ldots, x^m(q)\big)$ for a $q \in U \cap M$, and $x^{m+1}(q) = \cdots = x^n(q) = 0$ by the description of $U \cap M$ in the Setting, so $\varphi(q) = (r, \vec 0)$ and $\varphi_M^{-1}(r) = q = \varphi^{-1}(r, \vec 0)$. So for $(r, c) \in V_M \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$,
\[
\Theta_U \circ (\varphi_M \times \mathrm{id})^{-1}(r, c) = \Big(\varphi^{-1}(r, \vec 0),\ J\big(\varphi^{-1}(r, \vec 0)\big)^{\mathsf T} c\Big) =: \hat\Theta(r, c) \in \mathbb{R}^{2n},
\]
and $\hat\Theta : V_M \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m} \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is smooth: $r \mapsto (r, \vec 0)$ is linear with values in $\varphi(U)$ for $r \in V_M$, $\varphi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$, and the entries of $J$ are smooth on $U$. Hence $\Theta_U = \hat\Theta \circ (\varphi_M \times \mathrm{id})$ is smooth as a map into $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). Its values lie in $\mathcal{N}$ (\emph{Targets} above), so it is smooth into $\mathcal{N}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)), and they lie in the open subset $\mathcal{N}_U$, so it is smooth into $\mathcal{N}_U$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:open-inclusion-smooth}(3)).

So $\Phi_U$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse $\Theta_U$, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}).

\emph{(3) The fibration.} The sets $U \cap M$, over all charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ adapted to $M$, are open in $M$ and cover $M$, since every point of $M$ lies in an adapted chart (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}). The projection $\pi$ is smooth (first paragraph), and over each $U \cap M$ the map $\Phi_U$ of (2) is a diffeomorphism $\pi^{-1}(U \cap M) \to (U \cap M) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ with $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \Phi_U = \pi|_{\pi^{-1}(U \cap M)}$. This is Definition~\ref{def:fibration} with total space $\mathcal{N}$, base $M$, fibre $\mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ and the cover $\{U \cap M\}$.
\end{proof}

The trivialization is the recipe of the remark \emph{Where Explicit Trivializations Come From} in \ref{sec:fibration-examples}: a basis of each fibre that depends smoothly on the base point --- here the gradients $\nabla G^s(q)$ --- and, for a vector $v$ of the fibre, its components $c = (J J^{\mathsf T})^{-1} J v$ in that basis, $v = \sum_s c^s\, \nabla G^s(q)$. The gradients are the vectors that the dot product attaches to the covectors $dG^s|_q = dx^{m+s}|_q$: by Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}, applied to the smooth function $h = G^s$ on the open set $U$, $\xi_{\nabla G^s(q)} = dG^s|_q$, that is, for $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
\[
dG^s|_q\big(D_w|_q\big) = D_w|_q[G^s] = \nabla G^s(q) \cdot w
\]
(the middle expression by Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}, the last by Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}). Those covectors form a basis of the conormal space $N_qM$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}; for a general defining map, Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-defining-functions}). So (1) is the basis of the conormal space, read through the metric; Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-conormal} below says this for every point and for the whole bundle.

\subsection{The Endpoint Map and Focal Points}\label{sub:endpoint-focal}

\begin{defbox}[Endpoint Map]\deflabel{def:endpoint-map}
The \textbf{endpoint map} of $M$ is
\[
E : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n, \qquad E(p, v) = p + v ,
\]
the endpoint of the normal vector $v$ drawn from $p$. It is smooth: $E = L \circ \iota_{\mathcal{N}}$, where $\iota_{\mathcal{N}} : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is the inclusion, smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1), and $L(p, v) = p + v$ is linear, hence smooth; a composite of smooth maps is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}).
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Tubular Neighborhoods}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Focal Point]\deflabel{def:focal-point}
A point $q \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a \textbf{focal point} of $M$ if $q = E(p, v)$ for some critical point $(p, v) \in \mathcal{N}$ of the endpoint map $E$ (Definition~\ref{def:endpoint-map}), that is, for some $(p, v)$ at which $E_{*(p,v)} : T_{(p,v)}\mathcal{N} \to T_q\mathbb{R}^n$ (written $dE_{(p,v)}$ in the assignment) is not of maximal rank. Since $\dim \mathcal{N} = n = \dim \mathbb{R}^n$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-submanifold}), maximal rank means rank $n$, so $(p, v)$ is critical exactly when $E_{*(p,v)}$ is not onto --- a critical point in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical} --- equivalently (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) not bijective.
\end{defbox}

\begin{exbox}[Focal Points of the Parabola]\exlabel{ex:parabola-focal}
Let $M = \{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : y = x^2\}$. The set of focal points of $M$ is the image of the smooth curve
\[
\mathbf{r} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2, \qquad \mathbf{r}(a) = \Big(-4a^3,\ 3a^2 + \tfrac12\Big),
\]
where $\mathbf{r}(a) = E(p, v)$ for the unique critical point $(p, v)$ of $E$ with $p = (a, a^2)$: the focal point on the normal line to the parabola at $(a, a^2)$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}[Working out the example]
\textit{(Assignment~5, Problem~5(b), as submitted; the smoothness of the parametrization and the passage from $E_*$ to a Jacobian are made explicit.)} In this example $(x, y)$ are the standard coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^2$, so $n = 2$ and $m = 1$.

\emph{$M$ is a submanifold.} $M = g^{-1}(0)$ for $g(x, y) = y - x^2$, $g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$, whose Jacobian $g'(x, y) = (-2x, 1)$ is nonzero, i.e.\ has rank $1$, at every point. So $0$ is a regular value (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}), and $M = g^{-1}(0)$ is an external description of $M$ near each of its points with $W = \mathbb{R}^2$ (Definition~\ref{def:ext-int}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean}, $M$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$ of codimension $1$, i.e.\ of dimension $1$; and by Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-submanifold}, $\mathcal{N}$ is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^4$ of dimension $2$.

\emph{Tangent and normal spaces.} Every $p \in M$ is $p = (a, a^2)$ for a unique $a \in \mathbb{R}$, namely its first coordinate. By Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel} with $W = \mathbb{R}^2$, $F = g$, $c = 0$,
\[
T^{\geo}_pM = \ker g'(p) = \{\, (u, w) : -2a\, u + w = 0 \,\} = \{\, (u, 2a\, u) : u \in \mathbb{R} \,\} = \Span\{(1, 2a)\}.
\]
(The submission finds the same line as the velocity of the curve $t \mapsto (a + t, (a + t)^2)$ in $M$ at $t = 0$, which is $(1, 2a)$, together with $\dim M = 1$.) The vector $(-2a, 1)$ is nonzero and
\[
(-2a, 1) \cdot (1, 2a) = -2a + 2a = 0 ,
\]
so it lies in $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$; and $\dim (T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp = n - m = 2 - 1 = 1$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}(1) (equivalently Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(4)) for the adapted chart $\varphi$ below, in which $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$ has a basis of $n - m = 1$ vector, the gradient $\nabla G^1(p) = \nabla g(p)$. Hence
\[
(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp = \Span\{(-2a, 1)\}, \qquad \mathcal{N} = \Big\{\, \big((a, a^2),\ \lambda(-2a, 1)\big) : a, \lambda \in \mathbb{R} \,\Big\}.
\]
Note that $(-2a, 1) = \nabla g(p)$, as Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}(1) predicts: $\varphi(x, y) = (x, y - x^2)$ is a chart of $\mathbb{R}^2$ adapted to $M$ with $U = \mathbb{R}^2$ and $G = g$. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} Its Jacobian is $\varphi'(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2x & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $1$; the second row is $\nabla g(x, y) = (-2x, 1)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto itself, smooth with the smooth inverse $(x, z) \mapsto (x, z + x^2)$, so $(\mathbb{R}^2, \varphi) = (\mathbb{R}^2, \varphi \circ \mathrm{id})$ is a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(2), applied to the identity chart of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the diffeomorphism $\varphi$; and its second coordinate $y - x^2 = g(x, y)$ vanishes exactly on $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}, with $k = 1$). It is the chart $\Phi$ of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-euclidean}, graph $\Rightarrow$ slice, for $h(x) = x^2$.

\emph{A global parametrization of $\mathcal{N}$.} Define
\[
\Psi : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathcal{N}, \qquad \Psi(a, \lambda) = \big((a, a^2),\ \lambda(-2a, 1)\big) = \big(a,\ a^2,\ -2\lambda a,\ \lambda\big).
\]
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{Smooth.} As a map into $\mathbb{R}^4$ its components are polynomials, so it is smooth; its values lie in $\mathcal{N}$ by the description of $\mathcal{N}$ just found, so it is smooth into $\mathcal{N}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)).
    \item \emph{Bijective.} It is onto $\mathcal{N}$ by that description. It is injective: if $\Psi(a, \lambda) = \Psi(a', \lambda')$, the first coordinates give $a = a'$ and the fourth give $\lambda = \lambda'$.
    \item \emph{Its differential is bijective.} The Jacobian of $\Psi$ as a map into $\mathbb{R}^4$,
    \[
    D\Psi(a, \lambda) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2a & 0 \\ -2\lambda & -2a \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},
    \]
    has rank $2$, since its first and fourth rows form $I_2$; so $D\Psi(a, \lambda) u = 0$ forces $u = 0$. With $\iota_{\mathcal{N}} : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{R}^4$ the inclusion, $\iota_{\mathcal{N}} \circ \Psi$ is $\Psi$ regarded as a map into $\mathbb{R}^4$, and its differential corresponds to $D\Psi(a, \lambda)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}). By the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), $(\iota_{\mathcal{N}})_{*} \circ \Psi_{*(a,\lambda)} = (\iota_{\mathcal{N}} \circ \Psi)_{*(a,\lambda)}$, which is injective; so $\Psi_{*(a,\lambda)}$ is injective (if $\Psi_{*}u = 0$ then $(\iota_{\mathcal{N}} \circ \Psi)_{*}u = 0$, so $u = 0$). It is a linear map between spaces of the same dimension $2$, $T_{(a,\lambda)}\mathbb{R}^2$ and $T_{\Psi(a,\lambda)}\mathcal{N}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), hence bijective (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)).
\end{itemize}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:bijective-local-diffeo} (a smooth bijection with bijective differential everywhere; this is where the inverse function theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function}, enters), $\Psi : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathcal{N}$ is a diffeomorphism, and $\Psi^{-1}$ is a global chart of $\mathcal{N}$: its transition maps with any smooth chart $\chi$ of $\mathcal{N}$ are $\chi \circ \Psi$ and $\Psi^{-1} \circ \chi^{-1}$, smooth as composites of smooth maps. (In the language of Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}, $\Psi(a, \lambda) = \Theta_U\big((a, a^2), \lambda\big)$ with $G = g$: the normal bundle of the parabola is trivial.)

\emph{The endpoint map in coordinates.} Put
\[
\hat E = E \circ \Psi : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2, \qquad \hat E(a, \lambda) = (a, a^2) + \lambda(-2a, 1) = \big(a - 2\lambda a,\ a^2 + \lambda\big).
\]
By the Chain Rule, $\hat E_{*(a,\lambda)} = E_{*\Psi(a,\lambda)} \circ \Psi_{*(a,\lambda)}$. Since $\Psi_{*(a,\lambda)}$ is a bijection onto $T_{\Psi(a,\lambda)}\mathcal{N}$, the two maps $\hat E_{*(a,\lambda)}$ and $E_{*\Psi(a,\lambda)}$ have the same image; so $E_{*\Psi(a,\lambda)}$ is onto iff $\hat E_{*(a,\lambda)}$ is onto, iff (Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}) the $2 \times 2$ Jacobian $D\hat E(a, \lambda)$ has rank $2$, iff $\det D\hat E(a, \lambda) \neq 0$.

\emph{Critical points of $E$.} Differentiating the components $a - 2\lambda a$ and $a^2 + \lambda$ with respect to $a$ and $\lambda$,
\[
D\hat E(a, \lambda) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - 2\lambda & -2a \\ 2a & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det D\hat E(a, \lambda) = (1 - 2\lambda)\cdot 1 - (-2a)(2a) = 1 - 2\lambda + 4a^2 .
\]
So $\Psi(a, \lambda)$ is a critical point of $E$ (Definition~\ref{def:focal-point}) if and only if $1 - 2\lambda + 4a^2 = 0$, that is,
\[
\lambda = \frac{4a^2 + 1}{2} .
\]
For each $a$ there is exactly one such $\lambda$, and every point of $\mathcal{N}$ is $\Psi(a, \lambda)$ for exactly one $(a, \lambda)$; so the critical points of $E$ are exactly the points $\Psi\big(a, \tfrac{4a^2+1}{2}\big)$, one over each $p = (a, a^2) \in M$.

\emph{The focal points.} A point of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a focal point iff it is $E(\Psi(a, \lambda)) = \hat E(a, \lambda)$ with $\lambda = \frac{4a^2+1}{2}$, for some $a \in \mathbb{R}$. Substituting,
\[
a - 2\lambda a = a - a(4a^2 + 1) = -4a^3, \qquad a^2 + \lambda = a^2 + 2a^2 + \tfrac12 = 3a^2 + \tfrac12 .
\]
So the set of focal points is the image of $\mathbf{r}(a) = \big(-4a^3, 3a^2 + \frac12\big)$, a smooth curve, its components being polynomials in $a$; and $\mathbf{r}(a) = E(p, v)$ for the critical point over $p = (a, a^2)$.

\emph{Shape.} $\mathbf{r}(-a) = \big(4a^3, 3a^2 + \frac12\big)$ is the reflection of $\mathbf{r}(a)$ in the $y$-axis, so the curve is symmetric about the axis of the parabola. Its velocity $\mathbf{r}'(a) = (-12a^2, 6a)$ vanishes only at $a = 0$, where the curve has a cusp at $\mathbf{r}(0) = (0, \frac12)$ (the remark \emph{Focal Points Are Centres of Curvature} gives its equation, $(y - \frac12)^3 = \frac{27}{16}x^2$).
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.3]
\draw[->, gray!70!black] (-2.4,0) -- (2.4,0) node[right, font=\scriptsize, text=black] {$x$};
\draw[->, gray!70!black] (0,-0.3) -- (0,2.9) node[above, font=\scriptsize, text=black] {$y$};
\draw[blue, thick, domain=-1.6:1.6, samples=100, variable=\t] plot ({\t}, {(\t)*(\t)});
\draw[red, thick, domain=-0.82:0.82, samples=200, variable=\t] plot ({-4*(\t)*(\t)*(\t)}, {3*(\t)*(\t) + 0.5});
\fill (0,0.5) circle (1.5pt);
\node[font=\scriptsize, anchor=west] at (0.1,0.58) {$(0, \tfrac12)$};
\draw[blue, thick] (-2.2,-0.7) -- (-1.8,-0.7) node[right, font=\scriptsize, text=black] {parabola $y = x^2$};
\draw[red, thick] (0.3,-0.7) -- (0.7,-0.7) node[right, font=\scriptsize, text=black] {focal points $\mathbf{r}(a)$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

The parabola $y = x^2$ (blue, drawn for $|x| \le 1.6$) and its set of focal points, the curve $\mathbf{r}$ (red, drawn for $|a| \le 0.82$). The red curve is symmetric about the $y$-axis and has a cusp at $(0, \frac12)$ (the dot), the focal point over the vertex; as $|a|$ grows the focal points move out and up, $\mathbf{r}(a)$ lying on the normal line at $(a, a^2)$, on the concave side. The cusp is not the optical focus $(0, \frac14)$ of the parabola: ``focal'' here refers to the endpoint map, and the remark \emph{Focal Points Are Centres of Curvature} explains what these points are.

\begin{rembox}[Focal Points Are Centres of Curvature]\label{rem:focal-curvature}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} At the critical point over $p = (a, a^2)$ the normal vector is $v = \lambda(-2a, 1)$ with $\lambda = \frac{1 + 4a^2}{2}$, of length
\[
|v| = \lambda\, \big|(-2a, 1)\big| = \frac{1 + 4a^2}{2}\, \sqrt{1 + 4a^2} = \frac{(1 + 4a^2)^{3/2}}{2} .
\]
This is the radius of curvature of the graph $y = f(x)$ at $x = a$, $R = (1 + f'(a)^2)^{3/2} / |f''(a)|$, for $f(x) = x^2$: $f'(a) = 2a$ and $f''(a) = 2$ give $R = (1 + 4a^2)^{3/2}/2$. And $v$ points to the concave (upper) side, since $\lambda > 0$ and $(-2a, 1)$ has positive second component. So the focal point $p + v$ on the normal line at $p$ is the \emph{centre of curvature}, the centre of the osculating circle at $p$, and the curve $\mathbf{r}$ of focal points is the \emph{evolute} of the parabola. As a check, the classical formula for the centre of curvature of a graph, $\big(a - f'(1 + f'^2)/f'',\ f + (1 + f'^2)/f''\big)$, gives
\[
\Big(a - \frac{2a(1 + 4a^2)}{2},\ a^2 + \frac{1 + 4a^2}{2}\Big) = \Big(-4a^3,\ 3a^2 + \tfrac12\Big) = \mathbf{r}(a).
\]
\emph{The evolute as a curve.} From $x = -4a^3$ and $y - \frac12 = 3a^2$: $(y - \frac12)^3 = 27a^6$ and $x^2 = 16a^6$, so
\[
\Big(y - \tfrac12\Big)^3 = \tfrac{27}{16}\, x^2 ,
\]
a semicubical parabola with its cusp at $(0, \frac12)$. Conversely every point of this curve is on $\mathbf{r}$: given $(x, y)$ with $(y - \frac12)^3 = \frac{27}{16}x^2$, let $a$ be the real cube root of $-x/4$; then $-4a^3 = x$, and $y - \frac12 = \big(\frac{27}{16}x^2\big)^{1/3} = 3\,(x/4)^{2/3} = 3a^2$. The cusp is the centre of curvature at the vertex, where the radius of curvature is $R = \frac12$: the osculating circle there is $x^2 + (y - \frac12)^2 = \frac14$.

\emph{In general} (stated, not proved here): for a submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, $(p, v) \in \mathcal{N}$ is a critical point of $E$ if and only if $1$ is an eigenvalue of the shape operator (second fundamental form) of $M$ at $p$ in the normal direction $v$, and the dimension of $\ker E_{*(p,v)}$ is the multiplicity of that eigenvalue (Milnor, \emph{Morse Theory}, \S6). For a curve in the plane the shape operator in the direction of a normal $v$ is multiplication by $\kappa\, (v \cdot \mathbf{n})$, with $\kappa$ the curvature and $\mathbf{n}$ the unit normal toward the concave side; so the focal point on each normal line is at distance $|v| = 1/\kappa$ on the concave side, the centre of curvature, as found above. For the parabola, $\kappa = 2/(1 + 4a^2)^{3/2}$.
\end{rembox}

\subsection{Normal and Conormal}\label{sub:normal-conormal}

\begin{propbox}[Normal and Conormal Spaces]\thmlabel{prop:normal-conormal}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m < n$, $p \in M$, and $v \mapsto \xi_v$, $\xi_v(D_w|_p) = v \cdot w$, the isomorphism $\mathbb{R}^n \to T_p^*\mathbb{R}^n$ given by the dot product (Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}).
\begin{enumerate}
    \item It restricts to an isomorphism
    \[
    (T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } N_pM, \qquad v \mapsto \xi_v ,
    \]
    of the Euclidean normal space onto the conormal space of $M$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Definition~\ref{def:conormal}), both of dimension $n - m$.
    \item In a chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ at $p$ adapted to $M$, with $G = (x^{m+1}, \ldots, x^n)$ as in the Setting of \ref{sub:normal-bundle-def}, it sends the gradient $\nabla G^s(p)$ to the differential $dG^s|_p = dx^{m+s}|_p$, for $s = 1, \ldots, n - m$: the basis of $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}(1) to the basis of $N_pM$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}.
    \item Fibre by fibre, $(p, v) \mapsto (p, \xi_v)$ maps the normal bundle $\mathcal{N}$ bijectively onto the set $\{\, (p, \xi) : p \in M,\ \xi \in N_pM \,\}$, linearly on each fibre.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from the assignment; filled in.)} Fix $p \in M$ and a chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ at $p$ adapted to $M$, with $G$ and $J$ as in the Setting (every point of $M$ lies in one, Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}).

\emph{The tangent space of $M$ inside $T_p\mathbb{R}^n$.} By Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} every tangent vector of $\mathbb{R}^n$ at $p$ is $D_w|_p$ for a unique $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Under $w \mapsto D_w|_p$ the subspace $\iota_{*p}(T_pM)$ is $T^{\geo}_pM$ (the remark \emph{The Tangent Spaces Match} in \ref{sec:submanifolds}). In detail: by Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(1), $J(q) = G'(q)$ has rank $n - m$ for every $q \in U$, so $\vec 0$ is a regular value of $G : U \to \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-value}), and $U \cap M = G^{-1}(\vec 0)$ by the description of $U \cap M$ in the Setting. Proposition~\ref{prop:rvt-agree}(2), with $W = U$, $F = G$, $c = \vec 0$ and $S = U \cap M$, says that the image of $T_p(U \cap M)$ in $T_pU$ is $\ker J(p)$ under $w \mapsto D_w|_p$; and $\ker J(p) = T^{\geo}_pM$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:euclidean-adapted-chart}(2). Since $U \cap M$ is open in $M$ and $U$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$, these tangent spaces are those of $M$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}). So
\[
\iota_{*p}(T_pM) = \big\{\, D_w|_p : w \in T^{\geo}_pM \,\big\} .
\]

\emph{(1)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}, $v \mapsto \xi_v$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathbb{R}^n \to T_p^*\mathbb{R}^n$. For $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$, by Definition~\ref{def:conormal} and the description of $\iota_{*p}(T_pM)$ just obtained,
\[
\xi_v \in N_pM \iff \xi_v\big(D_w|_p\big) = 0 \ \text{ for all } w \in T^{\geo}_pM \iff v \cdot w = 0 \ \text{ for all } w \in T^{\geo}_pM \iff v \in (T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp .
\]
So the isomorphism maps $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$ into $N_pM$, injectively, as the restriction of an injective map; and onto $N_pM$: every $\xi \in N_pM$ is $\xi_v$ for some $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $v \mapsto \xi_v$ being onto, and this $v$ lies in $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$ by the equivalence. A restriction of a linear map is linear, so $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp \to N_pM$ is a linear isomorphism. Both spaces have dimension $n - m$: $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}(1), which gives it a basis of $n - m$ gradients, and $N_pM$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis}, $n - m$ being the codimension of $M$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

\emph{(2)} $G^s = x^{m+s}$ is a smooth function on the open set $U$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:dot-product-identification}, applied to $h = G^s$, gives $\xi_{\nabla G^s(p)} = dG^s|_p$, with $T_p^*U = T_p^*\mathbb{R}^n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}); explicitly, for $w \in \mathbb{R}^n$,
\[
\xi_{\nabla G^s(p)}\big(D_w|_p\big) = \nabla G^s(p) \cdot w = D_w|_p[G^s] = dG^s|_p\big(D_w|_p\big),
\]
as in the paragraph after Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-bundle-fibration}(1) the $\nabla G^s(p)$ form a basis of $(T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:conormal-basis} (the adapted chart $(U, \varphi)$ has codimension $n - m$, so its last $n - m$ coordinates are $x^{m+1}, \ldots, x^n$) the $dx^{m+s}|_p = dG^s|_p$ form a basis of $N_pM$.

\emph{(3)} By Definition~\ref{def:normal-bundle}, $(p, v) \in \mathcal{N}$ means $p \in M$ and $v \in (T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$; then $\xi_v \in N_pM$ by (1), so the map takes values in the set $\{(p, \xi) : p \in M,\ \xi \in N_pM\}$. It is injective: if $(p, \xi_v) = (p', \xi_{v'})$, then $p = p'$, and $\xi_v = \xi_{v'}$ in $T_p^*\mathbb{R}^n$ gives $v = v'$ by (1). It is onto: given $p \in M$ and $\xi \in N_pM$, (1) gives $v \in (T^{\geo}_pM)^\perp$ with $\xi_v = \xi$, and $(p, v) \in \mathcal{N}$ is mapped to $(p, \xi)$. It keeps the base point $p$, and on the fibre over $p$ it is the linear map $v \mapsto \xi_v$ of (1).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Normal Bundle and Conormal Bundle]\label{rem:normal-conormal}
\textit{(Not from the assignment.)} The set $\{(p, \xi) : p \in M,\ \xi \in N_pM\}$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-conormal}(3) is the conormal bundle $N^*M$ of $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, announced in the remark \emph{The Conormal Bundle} in \ref{sec:transversality-submanifolds} and defined later, in \ref{sub:ctb-zero-section} (Definition~\ref{def:conormal-bundle}), once the cotangent bundle $T^*\mathbb{R}^n$ is available. So $\mathcal{N}$ is the conormal bundle read through the metric of $\mathbb{R}^n$. This is Uribe's remark that with an inner product the conormal space ``would be the normal space'' (the remark \emph{No Normal Vectors Without a Metric} in \ref{sec:submanifolds}), and it is why both bundles have dimension $n$: $m$ dimensions of base point, plus $n - m$ of normal vector or conormal covector.
\end{rembox}

\chapter{Immersions, Embeddings and Examples}

\section{Immersions}\label{sec:immersions}

\roadmark{Stage: maps}{The maps with injective differentials: locally inclusions, globally more subtle.}

\textit{References: Lee Ch.~4. Lecture 13.} The third special type of map, dual to the submersions of \ref{sec:submersions}: the differential is injective instead of surjective, and the local model is an inclusion instead of a projection.

\subsection{Immersions}\label{sub:immersions}

\textit{Lecture 13. ``Next class of special maps'': Lecture~10 listed immersions among the special types of map, and the definition has been on record since (Definition~\ref{def:immersion}); Lecture~13 is where they were first treated seriously, after the tangent bundle (\ref{sec:tangent-bundle}).}

\begin{defbox}[Immersions]\deflabel{def:immersion-lecture}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$. $F$ is an \textbf{immersion at $p$} if $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ is injective --- which forces $m \le n$, since an injective linear map cannot lower dimension --- and an \textbf{immersion} if it is an immersion at every point. ``Go from a lower-dimensional manifold to a bigger one.''
\leeref{Ch.~4, \emph{Immersions}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{thmbox}[Local Normal Form for Immersions]\thmlabel{thm:immersion-normal-form}
Let $F : M \to N$ be an immersion at $p$, with $\dim M = m \le n = \dim N$. Then there are charts $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$ in which the coordinate representation $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is the standard inclusion:
\[
\tilde F(r^1, \ldots, r^m) = (r^1, \ldots, r^m, \underbrace{0, \ldots, 0}_{n - m}) .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 4.12, the rank theorem}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (Lecture~14)]
The steps are the lecture's, in the lecture's order; sentences marked \textit{(Completion.)} fill in details. The first half runs as for submersions (Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form}); the new step is that here the chart on $N$ changes too.

\emph{1. Start with any coordinates.} Take charts $(U_0, \varphi_0 = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and $(V_0, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U_0) \subseteq V_0$, shrinking $U_0$ if necessary, and write $F^j = y^j \circ F$. \textit{(Completion.)} Such charts exist by Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}. Shrinking means: replace $U_0$ by $U_0 \cap F^{-1}(V_0)$, which is open because $F$ is continuous and contains $p$; the restriction of the smooth chart $\varphi_0$ to it is again a smooth chart (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1); its transition maps are restrictions of the old ones). The components $F^j : U_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ are smooth, since $F^j \circ \varphi_0^{-1}$ is the $j$-th component of the smooth coordinate representation $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi_0^{-1}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs}).

\emph{2. The Jacobian is taller than wide.} $J = \big[\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)\big]$ is the matrix of $F_{*p}$ (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}): $n$ rows and $m$ columns, ``fewer columns than rows.'' Written out,
\[
J = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p) \end{pmatrix} .
\] $F_{*p}$ is injective, so $J$ has rank $m$: it has $m$ linearly independent row vectors. \textit{(Completion.)} By Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}, $F_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = \sum_j \partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)\, \partial/\partial y^j|_{F(p)}$, so the $i$-th column of $J$ holds the coordinates of $F_{*p}(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$, and $J$ is the matrix of $F_{*p}$ in the coordinate bases (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)). Since $F_{*p}$ is injective, $\ker F_{*p} = 0$, and rank--nullity (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(1)) gives $\operatorname{rank} F_{*p} = \dim T_pM = m$. So $J$ has rank $m$, and so does its transpose (Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(3)), whose columns are the rows of $J$: among the $n$ rows of $J$ there are $m$ linearly independent ones.

\emph{3. Relabel the $y$'s.} Reordering the coordinates of $\psi$ --- again a smooth chart, by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(2) with a permutation of coordinates, a linear isomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^n$, as the diffeomorphism --- we may assume the top $m \times m$ block $A$ of $J$ is invertible:
\[
J = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial F^m}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^m}{\partial x^m}(p) \\ \hline \dfrac{\partial F^{m+1}}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^{m+1}}{\partial x^m}(p) \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p) \end{array}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} A \\ \ast \end{pmatrix}, \qquad A \ (m \times m) \text{ invertible}.
\] \textit{(Completion.)} Let rows $j_1, \ldots, j_m$ of $J$ be linearly independent, and let $P : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a permutation of coordinates moving positions $j_1, \ldots, j_m$ to positions $1, \ldots, m$. Replacing $\psi$ by $P \circ \psi$ lists the same coordinate functions $y^j$ in a new order; so it lists the components $F^j = y^j \circ F$, and hence the rows of $J$, in the same new order. Afterwards rows $1, \ldots, m$ of $J$ are linearly independent, so the top block $A$, which consists of them, is an $m \times m$ matrix of rank $m$, that is, invertible. We keep the names $\psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n)$, $F^j$ and $J$ for the reordered chart, components and matrix.

\emph{4. The first $m$ components of $F$ are coordinates on $M$.} $A$ is the Jacobian at $p$, in the $x$-coordinates, of the map $U_0 \to \mathbb{R}^m$ that sends $q$ to the first $m$ components $\big(F^1(q), \ldots, F^m(q)\big)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs}). \textit{(Completion.)} Read in the $x$-coordinates, this map is $\Phi = (F^1, \ldots, F^m) \circ \varphi_0^{-1} : \varphi_0(U_0) \to \mathbb{R}^m$, with components $F^j \circ \varphi_0^{-1}$. By Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, $\partial F^j/\partial x^i(p) = \partial (F^j \circ \varphi_0^{-1})/\partial r^i\big(\varphi_0(p)\big)$, so
\[
\Phi'\big(\varphi_0(p)\big) = \Big[\frac{\partial (F^j \circ \varphi_0^{-1})}{\partial r^i}\big(\varphi_0(p)\big)\Big]_{1 \le j, i \le m} = \Big[\frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\Big]_{1 \le j, i \le m} = A .
\]
It is invertible, so by the inverse function theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function}) --- ``I always say implicit, but in this case I want the inverse function theorem'' --- this map is a local diffeomorphism near $p$, and, possibly after shrinking $U_0$ to some $U \ni p$, it is a chart:
\[
\tilde\varphi = \big(F^1, \ldots, F^m\big)\big|_U : U \longrightarrow \tilde\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m .
\]
\textit{(Completion.)} As in step~8 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form}: the inverse function theorem gives an open $W \ni \varphi_0(p)$ on which $\tilde\varphi \circ \varphi_0^{-1}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open set; put $U = \varphi_0^{-1}(W)$; then $\tilde\varphi$ maps $U$ diffeomorphically onto an open set, and is a chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:diffeo-chart}. In detail: $\tilde\varphi \circ \varphi_0^{-1} = \Phi$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function}, applied to $\Phi$ at $a = \varphi_0(p)$, gives open sets $W \ni \varphi_0(p)$ in $\varphi_0(U_0)$ and $W' \ni \Phi(\varphi_0(p))$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with $\Phi(W) = W'$ and $\Phi|_W : W \to W'$ bijective with smooth inverse. The set $U = \varphi_0^{-1}(W)$ is open in $M$ and contains $p$, and on it
\[
\tilde\varphi = \Phi|_W \circ \varphi_0|_U ,
\]
a composite of the diffeomorphism $\varphi_0|_U : U \to W$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}) and the diffeomorphism $\Phi|_W : W \to W'$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeo-agree}). So $\tilde\varphi$ is a diffeomorphism of $U$ onto the open set $\tilde\varphi(U) = W'$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), and $(U, \tilde\varphi)$ is a smooth chart at $p$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:diffeo-chart}. Also $F(U) \subseteq F(U_0) \subseteq V_0$.

\emph{5. In the new chart, $F$ is a graph.} Let $\hat F = \psi \circ F \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1} : \tilde\varphi(U) \to \psi(V_0)$, defined because $F(U) \subseteq V_0$. By the definition of $\tilde\varphi$, the first $m$ components of $\hat F(r)$ are $F^i(\tilde\varphi^{-1}(r)) = r^i$. \textit{(Completion.)} Fix $r \in \tilde\varphi(U)$ and put $u = \tilde\varphi^{-1}(r) \in U$, so that $\big(F^1(u), \ldots, F^m(u)\big) = \tilde\varphi(u) = r$. The $j$-th component of $\hat F(r) = \psi(F(u))$ is $y^j(F(u)) = F^j(u)$: for $j = i \le m$ it is $r^i$, and for $j = m + k$ it is $F^{m+k}(\tilde\varphi^{-1}(r))$. So
\[
\hat F(r) = \big(r, \ G^1(r), \ldots, G^{n-m}(r)\big), \qquad G^k = F^{m+k} \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1} ,
\]
with $G = (G^1, \ldots, G^{n-m})$ smooth on $\tilde\varphi(U)$: $G^k = r^{m+k} \circ \hat F$ is a component of $\hat F$, the coordinate representation of the smooth map $F$ in smooth charts (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}). ``I don't get zeros yet. I get something'': $\hat F$ is the graph of $G$ over $\tilde\varphi(U)$.

\emph{6. Straighten the graph.} ``You can always straighten out a graph to make it zero.'' Define new coordinates on $N$ by keeping the first $m$ and shifting the rest: ``I always mess up my indices \ldots\ so I'm going to cheat''
\[
\tilde y^i = y^i \quad (1 \le i \le m), \qquad \tilde y^i = y^i - G^{i-m}\big(y^1, \ldots, y^m\big) \quad (m+1 \le i \le n),
\]
and $\tilde\psi = (\tilde y^1, \ldots, \tilde y^n)$. \textit{(Completion.)} This is $\tilde\psi = \Sigma \circ \psi$, where $\Sigma(y_a, y_b) = \big(y_a, \, y_b - G(y_a)\big)$ for $y_a = (y^1, \ldots, y^m)$ and $y_b = (y^{m+1}, \ldots, y^n)$: the components of $\Sigma \circ \psi$ are exactly the $\tilde y^i$ above. $\Sigma$ is defined on $\tilde\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$, and is a diffeomorphism of that open set onto itself, with inverse $(y_a, z) \mapsto (y_a, z + G(y_a))$. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} In matrix form its Jacobian is block lower triangular,
\[
\Sigma'(y_a, y_b) = \begin{pmatrix} I_m & 0 \\ -DG(y_a) & I_{n-m} \end{pmatrix},
\]
with $DG(y_a)$ the $(n-m) \times m$ Jacobian of $G$, so $\det \Sigma' = 1$. In detail: $\tilde\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$, a product of open sets; $\Sigma$ and the proposed inverse both leave the first block $y_a$ unchanged, so both map this set into itself; the two composites are the identity, since $\big(y_a, (y_b - G(y_a)) + G(y_a)\big) = (y_a, y_b)$ and $\big(y_a, (z + G(y_a)) - G(y_a)\big) = (y_a, z)$; and both are smooth, their components being $y_a$ and $y_b \mp G(y_a)$ with $G$ smooth (step~5). So on the open set $V = \psi^{-1}\big(\tilde\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}\big) \cap V_0$ the map $\tilde\psi$ is a smooth chart. In detail: $V$ is open, the preimage of an open set under the continuous $\psi$, and $V \subseteq V_0$, so $(V, \psi|_V)$ is a smooth chart (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)), whose image $\psi(V) = \psi(V_0) \cap \big(\tilde\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}\big)$ lies in the domain of $\Sigma$. On $V$, $\tilde\psi = \Sigma \circ \psi|_V$, so $(V, \tilde\psi)$ is a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(2), applied to $(V, \psi|_V)$ and the diffeomorphism $\Sigma$ of $\tilde\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ onto itself. (Equivalently: $\psi|_V$ is a diffeomorphism of $V$ onto the open set $\psi(V)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}, for the restricted chart), and $\Sigma$ restricts to a diffeomorphism of $\psi(V)$ onto $\Sigma(\psi(V))$, which is open because $\Sigma$ is a homeomorphism of the open set $\tilde\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^{n-m}$ onto itself (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(3)); so $\tilde\psi$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, hence a chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:diffeo-chart}.) And $F(U) \subseteq V$, because the first $m$ coordinates of $\psi(F(u))$ are $\tilde\varphi(u) \in \tilde\varphi(U)$: by step~5, $\psi(F(u)) = \hat F(\tilde\varphi(u)) = \big(\tilde\varphi(u), G(\tilde\varphi(u))\big)$, and $F(u) \in V_0$. In particular $F(p) \in V$.

\emph{7. These do the job.} ``We're not changing the first $m$ --- we already have the inclusion here --- but we're fixing the other ones.'' \textit{(Completion.)} For $r \in \tilde\varphi(U)$,
\[
\tilde\psi \circ F \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}(r) = \Sigma\big(\hat F(r)\big) = \Sigma\big(r, G(r)\big) = \big(r, \, G(r) - G(r)\big) = (r, \vec 0) .
\]
The first equality is $\tilde\psi = \Sigma \circ \psi$ on $V \supseteq F(U)$ (step~6) together with $\hat F = \psi \circ F \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}$ (step~5); the second is the graph form of $\hat F$ (step~5); the third is the definition of $\Sigma$. So in the charts $(U, \tilde\varphi)$ and $(V, \tilde\psi)$, $F$ is the standard inclusion: these are the charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ of the statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5.4em, row sep=3em]
