\textbf{Transcription note.} Page~38 of the handwritten notes begins the proof with ``start with any coordinates with $\varphi(U) \subset V$''; the condition is $F(U) \subseteq V$. In the lecture the shifted coordinates were first spoken as $G^{i-m}(y^1, \ldots, y^n)$; the arguments are the first $m$ coordinates, $y^1, \ldots, y^m$, as on page~38.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=8em, row sep=3em]
U \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\varphi"'] & V \arrow[d, "\psi"] \\
\varphi(U) \arrow[r, "{\tilde F :\ r \,\mapsto\, (r, \vec 0)}"'] & \psi(V)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The immersion normal form, as on the board: the mirror image of the submersion normal form (Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form}). There $\tilde F$ forgot the last $m - n$ coordinates; here it appends $n - m$ zeros. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} In Jacobians, at every point, the $n \times m$ matrix here and the $n \times m$ matrix of Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form} there (with the letters of each theorem):
\[
\tilde F'(r) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 1 \\ \hline 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{array}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} I_m \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{(immersion)}, \qquad \tilde F'(r) = \big(I_n \mid 0\big) \quad \text{(submersion)}.
\]

\textit{Status.} Stated in Lecture~13 --- ``a little bit technical \ldots\ better do it fresh at the beginning of the class'' --- and proved at the start of Lecture~14, above. It is the counterpart of Theorem~\ref{thm:submersion-normal-form}: there $F$ was locally a projection, here it is locally an inclusion.

What the image of an immersion looks like --- locally a submanifold, globally not necessarily --- is taken up next, in \ref{sub:immersion-images}.

\subsection{Images of Immersions}\label{sub:immersion-images}

\textit{Lecture 13, continuing \ref{sub:immersions}. What the image of an immersion looks like. These results use submanifolds (\ref{sub:submanifolds}).}

\begin{corbox}[The Local Image of an Immersion]\thmlabel{cor:immersion-local-image}
In the charts of Theorem~\ref{thm:immersion-normal-form}, $F|_U$ is injective and $F(U)$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $n - m$.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~13 gave the idea --- the image of $\tilde F$ is an open set times zeros, ``and so since what happens below happens upstairs too'', $F(U)$ is a submanifold --- adding ``I'm feeling a little bit uneasy, because I want to say after restriction, possibly after restricting $U$.'' Completed here: shrinking $V$ instead of $U$ settles it.)} Let $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ be the charts of Theorem~\ref{thm:immersion-normal-form}: $F(U) \subseteq V$ and $\psi\big(F(\varphi^{-1}(r))\big) = \tilde F(r) = (r, \vec 0)$ for $r \in \varphi(U)$. Putting $r = \varphi(u)$, this reads
\[
\psi\big(F(u)\big) = \big(\varphi(u), \vec 0\big) \qquad (u \in U).
\]

\emph{$F|_U$ is injective.} $\tilde F$ is injective, so $F|_U$ is: if $F(u_1) = F(u_2)$ with $u_1, u_2 \in U$, then
\[
\big(\varphi(u_1), \vec 0\big) = \psi\big(F(u_1)\big) = \psi\big(F(u_2)\big) = \big(\varphi(u_2), \vec 0\big),
\]
so $\varphi(u_1) = \varphi(u_2)$, and $u_1 = u_2$ because $\varphi$ is injective.

\emph{The set $V'$.} Let
\[
V' = \big\{\, q \in V : \big(y^1(q), \ldots, y^m(q)\big) \in \varphi(U) \,\big\},
\]
open in $N$ because $\varphi(U)$ is open: with $\mathrm{pr} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ the projection onto the first $m$ coordinates, $V' = (\mathrm{pr} \circ \psi)^{-1}\big(\varphi(U)\big)$, the preimage of an open set under the continuous map $\mathrm{pr} \circ \psi : V \to \mathbb{R}^m$, so $V'$ is open in $V$, hence in $N$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}). And $V'$ contains $F(U)$ because $\psi(F(u)) = (\varphi(u), \vec 0)$: the first $m$ coordinates of $\psi(F(u))$ are $\varphi(u) \in \varphi(U)$.

\emph{The equations of $F(U)$.} We claim $F(U) = \{ q \in V' : y^{m+1}(q) = \cdots = y^n(q) = 0 \}$. The inclusion $\subseteq$ is clear: if $q = F(u)$, then $q \in V'$ as just shown, and $y^{m+1}(q), \ldots, y^n(q)$ are the last $n - m$ coordinates of $\psi(q) = (\varphi(u), \vec 0)$, all zero. Conversely, if $q \in V'$ has $\psi(q) = (r, \vec 0)$ with $r \in \varphi(U)$, then $\psi(q) = \tilde F(r) = \psi\big(F(\varphi^{-1}(r))\big)$, so $q = F(\varphi^{-1}(r))$ because $\psi$ is injective.

\emph{An adapted chart.} The restriction $(V', \psi|_{V'})$ is a smooth chart of $N$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), $V'$ being an open subset of $V$). Apply Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart} with ambient manifold $N$ of dimension $n$, $S = F(U)$ and $k = n - m$, so that $x_b = (y^{m+1}, \ldots, y^n)$ are the last $k$ coordinates. Since $F(U) \subseteq V'$, the claim says $V' \cap F(U) = F(U) = \{ q \in V' : x_b(q) = \vec 0 \}$. So $(V', \psi|_{V'})$ is an adapted chart at every point of $F(U)$, and $F(U)$ is a submanifold of codimension $n - m$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}). No restriction of $U$ was needed: the worry was that $\psi(V) \cap (\mathbb{R}^m \times \{\vec 0\})$ might contain points not of the form $\tilde F(r)$ with $r \in \varphi(U)$, and passing to $V'$ removes exactly those.
\end{proof}

``But the really interesting thing about these immersions is that globally it doesn't have to be the case'': the whole image of an immersion need not be a submanifold. There are two ways for this to fail.

\begin{exbox}[An Immersion That Crosses Itself]\exlabel{ex:nodal-cubic}
$\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$, $\gamma(t) = (t^2 - 1, \ t^3 - t)$, is an immersion, but it is not injective, and its image is not a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$: near the origin the image looks like an X.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~13 drew a curve crossing itself and gave the argument below; the specific curve is filled in.)} Three things are claimed: $\gamma$ is an immersion, it is not injective, and its image is not a submanifold.

\emph{Immersion.} $\gamma'(t) = (2t, 3t^2 - 1)$, as a $2 \times 1$ Jacobian
\[
\gamma'(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 2t \\ 3t^2 - 1 \end{pmatrix} ,
\]
never vanishes --- the first component vanishes only at $t = 0$, where the second is $-1$ --- so $\gamma$ is an immersion. In detail: in the identity charts of $\mathbb{R}$ (coordinate $r$) and of $\mathbb{R}^2$ (coordinates $r^1, r^2$), Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} gives
\[
\gamma_{*t}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big|_t\Big) = 2t\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^1}\Big|_{\gamma(t)} + (3t^2 - 1)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^2}\Big|_{\gamma(t)} ,
\]
the velocity $\dot\gamma(t)$ (Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t}), which is nonzero, because the coordinate derivations are linearly independent (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}) and the two coefficients do not both vanish. $T_t\mathbb{R}$ is spanned by $\partial/\partial r|_t$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), so a linear map on it that is nonzero on this vector has kernel $0$. Hence $\gamma_{*t}$ is injective for every $t$ (Definition~\ref{def:immersion-lecture}).

\emph{Not injective.} $\gamma(1) = (1 - 1, \ 1 - 1) = (0, 0)$ and $\gamma(-1) = (1 - 1, \ -1 + 1) = (0, 0)$, so $\gamma(1) = \gamma(-1) = (0, 0)$, and $\gamma$ is not injective.

\emph{Not a submanifold: the lecture's argument.} Near the origin the image consists of two arcs crossing transversally, one through $\gamma(-1)$ and one through $\gamma(1)$, with tangent directions $\gamma'(\mp 1) = (\mp 2, 2)$. ``What is the proof? If you remove the point of intersection from an X, you get four connected components. If you remove a point from an interval, you get two.'' This is the lecture's level of rigour: made precise, it compares small connected neighbourhoods of the crossing point in the image with those of a point of a $1$-manifold.

\emph{Not a submanifold: a complete argument.} \textit{(Completion, by tangent spaces instead of connected components.)} Let $C = \gamma(\mathbb{R})$, and suppose that $C$ were a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$ of some codimension $k$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}), with its induced structure (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}). By the display above at $t = \pm 1$,
\[
\gamma_{*1}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big|_1\Big) = 2\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^1}\Big|_0 + 2\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^2}\Big|_0, \qquad \gamma_{*(-1)}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big|_{-1}\Big) = -2\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^1}\Big|_0 + 2\, \frac{\partial}{\partial r^2}\Big|_0 ,
\]
two linearly independent vectors of $T_0\mathbb{R}^2$: the determinant of their coefficients is $2 \cdot 2 - (-2) \cdot 2 = 8 \neq 0$:
\[
\det \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = 8 ,
\]
the columns holding the coefficients of $\gamma_{*1}(\partial/\partial r|_1)$ and $\gamma_{*(-1)}(\partial/\partial r|_{-1})$. Both lie in $\iota_{*0}(T_0C)$. Indeed $\gamma$ is smooth into $\mathbb{R}^2$ with values in $C$, so $\gamma = \iota \circ c$ with $c : \mathbb{R} \to C$ smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)), and by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) $\gamma_{*t} = \iota_{*0} \circ c_{*t}$ for $t = \pm 1$, where $\gamma(\pm 1) = 0$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}, $\iota_{*0}(T_0C)$ is spanned by the first $2 - k$ coordinate derivations of an adapted chart, so it has dimension $2 - k$. Containing two independent vectors, it has dimension $2$, so $k = 0$. But for $k = 0$ the condition of Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart} on an adapted chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $(0, 0)$ has no equations, and reads $U \cap C = U$: the open set $U \ni (0, 0)$ would lie in $C$. That is false. $U$ contains a point $(0, s)$ with $s \neq 0$, and $(0, s) \notin C$, since $\gamma(t) = (0, s)$ forces $t^2 - 1 = 0$ and then $s = t^3 - t = t(t^2 - 1) = 0$. So $C$ is not a regular submanifold.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[An Injective Immersion That Is Not a Homeomorphism onto Its Image]\exlabel{ex:hook}
Let $\gamma : (a, b) \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be an injective immersion that passes through a point $P = \gamma(t_0)$ and whose other end returns to $P$: $\gamma(t) \to P$ as $t \to b$. Then $\gamma$ is not a homeomorphism onto its image, and near $P$ the image looks like a T.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~13: ``it's like you're making a hook with a piece of wire \ldots\ but the wire is open, it doesn't have an end''; the discontinuity argument is filled in.)} Since $\gamma$ is injective, it is a bijection of $(a, b)$ onto its image $\gamma\big((a,b)\big)$, which carries the subspace topology of $\mathbb{R}^2$ (Definition~\ref{def:subspace}); we show that the inverse $\gamma^{-1} : \gamma\big((a,b)\big) \to (a, b)$ is not continuous at $P$, so that $\gamma$ is not a homeomorphism onto its image.

Choose $t_k \to b$, with $t_k \in (a, b)$. Then $\gamma(t_k) \to P = \gamma(t_0)$ in the image: by hypothesis $\gamma(t_k) \to P$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and every open set of the image containing $P$ has the form $O \cap \gamma\big((a,b)\big)$ with $O$ open in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $P \in O$, so it contains $\gamma(t_k)$ for all large $k$. But $t_k \to b \ne t_0$, so $\gamma^{-1}(\gamma(t_k)) = t_k$ does not converge to $\gamma^{-1}(P) = t_0$: choose $\varepsilon > 0$ with $t_0 + \varepsilon < b$; since $t_k \to b$, eventually $t_k > t_0 + \varepsilon$, so $t_k \notin (t_0 - \varepsilon, t_0 + \varepsilon)$. If $\gamma^{-1}$ were continuous at $P$, the preimage under $\gamma^{-1}$ of the open interval $(t_0 - \varepsilon, t_0 + \varepsilon) \ni t_0$ would contain an open set of the image containing $P$, hence $\gamma(t_k)$ for all large $k$, and then $t_k = \gamma^{-1}(\gamma(t_k)) \in (t_0 - \varepsilon, t_0 + \varepsilon)$ for those $k$ --- a contradiction. So $\gamma^{-1} : \gamma\big((a,b)\big) \to (a, b)$ is not continuous at $P$.

The image near $P$ consists of the strand through $P$ together with the end arriving at it: ``this point now doesn't look like an X, but it looks like a T''; removing it leaves three pieces, not two.
\end{proof}

The hook. The domain is an open interval, so neither end is attained: the left end of the image is missing (hollow), and the right end only approaches $P$. But $P$ is in the image, reached at $t_0$ by the strand passing through it --- so points of the image near $P$ come from parameters near $t_0$ \emph{and} from parameters near $b$, which is exactly the failure of continuity of $\gamma^{-1}$. Lee's figure-eight (Example~4.19) is an explicit instance with both ends returning, $\beta(t) = (\sin 2t, \sin t)$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, where the image near the origin is an X although $\beta$ is injective.

\begin{rembox}[Embeddings --- Next Time]\label{rem:embeddings-next-time}
To make the image of an immersion a submanifold, ``you have to add a topological condition'': an \emph{embedding} is an immersion that is a homeomorphism onto its image, and its image is a submanifold. Both were done in Lecture~14, together with the proof of the normal form above: see \ref{sec:embeddings}.
\end{rembox}

\section{Embeddings}\label{sec:embeddings}

\roadmark{Stage: maps}{Immersions that are homeomorphisms onto their images --- their images are submanifolds.}

\textit{References: Lee Ch.~4 and Ch.~5. Lecture 14.} The normal form makes every immersion locally an inclusion, but an immersion's image can still fail to be a submanifold (\ref{sub:immersion-images}). Embeddings are the immersions for which it cannot: the normal form is local in the domain, and the topological condition makes it local in the image too.

\subsection{Embeddings and Their Images}\label{sub:embeddings}

\begin{defbox}[Embedding]\deflabel{def:embedding}
A smooth map $F : M \to N$ is an \textbf{embedding} if it is an immersion and, as a map onto its image, $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism, $F(M)$ carrying the subspace topology of $N$. Injectivity is part of being a homeomorphism; Uribe wrote ``(injective) immersion'' and called the word redundant.
\leeref{Ch.~4, \emph{Embeddings}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4.2em, row sep=2.8em]
M \arrow[r, "\cong", "F"'] \arrow[dr, "F"'] & F(M) \arrow[d, hook] \\
& N
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

An embedding factors through its image as a homeomorphism followed by the inclusion --- ``you're taking the manifold $M$ and you're putting it inside $N$.'' The figure-eight of Lee's Example~4.19 (\ref{sub:immersion-images}) is an injective immersion for which the top arrow is not a homeomorphism.

The standard non-example is the \emph{irrational line on the torus}: for $\alpha$ irrational, $F : \mathbb{R} \to T^2 = \mathbb{R}^2/\mathbb{Z}^2$, $F(t) = [t, \alpha t]$. It is an injective immersion whose image is dense in $T^2$, and it is not an embedding (Proposition~\ref{prop:irrational-line} below, from Assignment~4, Problem~5; Lee, Example~4.20). In lecture its image was also said not to be a regular submanifold of $T^2$.

\textit{In lecture.} Given as ``a very important category: non-examples.'' ``You're wrapping a line, but the slope of the line is irrational, so it never closes \ldots\ like one of those spirographs.'' The normal form still applies: around any $p$ there are neighbourhoods $U$ and $V$ for which $F(U)$ is ``a very nice submanifold.'' But ``it's local in the domain'', while being a submanifold is a statement about the whole image. Points outside $U$ ``contribute segments like this, and they're going to be dense. No matter how you shrink this $V$, you won't be able to isolate only the yellow guy.''

\begin{thmbox}[The Image of an Embedding Is a Regular Submanifold]\thmlabel{thm:embedding-image}
If $F : M \to N$ is an embedding, with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$, then $F(M)$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $n - m$.
\leeref{Proposition 5.2}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~14. The final equality is completed with Corollary~\ref{cor:immersion-local-image}; see the remark after the proof.)} Let $q = F(p) \in F(M)$. We need a chart of $N$ at $q$ in which $F(M)$ is cut out by the vanishing of the last $n - m$ coordinates: an adapted chart at $q$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}, with $k = n - m$). Since $q$ is arbitrary, this shows that $F(M)$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $n - m$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}).

\emph{Start with the normal form.} $F$ is an immersion (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}). Take the charts $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $q$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:immersion-normal-form}. By Corollary~\ref{cor:immersion-local-image}, after replacing $V$ by the smaller open set
\[
V' = \big\{\, x \in V : \big(y^1(x), \ldots, y^m(x)\big) \in \varphi(U) \,\big\},
\]
which contains $F(U)$, we have
\[
F(U) = \{\, x \in V' : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0 \,\}. \tag{$*$}
\]
This describes $F(U)$, not $F(M) \cap V'$: ``other pieces of the image'' may still pass through $V'$, as in the irrational line.

\emph{The key step: the topological hypothesis.} ``Here's where we use the very strong condition that $F$ is a topological homeomorphism to its image.'' $U$ is open in $M$ and $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism, so $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$ (homeomorphisms are open maps, Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(2)). Since $F(M)$ carries the subspace topology, this means (Definition~\ref{def:subspace}) that there is an open $W \subseteq N$ with
\[
F(U) = W \cap F(M) .
\]

\emph{Shrink $V'$ to $V' \cap W$, and keep the same coordinates.} Since $F(U) \subseteq V' \cap W$ --- $F(U) \subseteq V'$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:immersion-local-image}, and $F(U) = W \cap F(M) \subseteq W$ ---
\[
F(M) \cap (V' \cap W) = F(U) = \{\, x \in V' \cap W : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0 \,\},
\]
the first equality because $F(M) \cap W = F(U) \subseteq V'$, the second by $(*)$ intersected with $W$. In full, using in turn the regrouping of intersections, $F(M) \cap W = F(U)$, $F(U) \subseteq V'$, $F(U) \subseteq W$, and $(*)$:
\[
F(M) \cap (V' \cap W) = \big(F(M) \cap W\big) \cap V' = F(U) \cap V' = F(U) = F(U) \cap W = \{\, x \in V' : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0 \,\} \cap W .
\]
The set $V' \cap W$ is open and contains $q \in F(U)$, and $(V' \cap W, \psi|_{V' \cap W})$ is a smooth chart (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), $V' \cap W$ being an open subset of $V$). So $(V' \cap W, \psi)$ is an adapted chart at $q$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}), and $F(M)$ is a submanifold of codimension $n - m$.
\end{proof}

Because $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$, it is $W \cap F(M)$ for an open $W$ (shaded), and $W$ cuts the other parts away; $F(M)$ continues beyond $F(U)$ only by leaving $W$. For the irrational line no such $W$ exists, which is exactly the failure of openness.

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page~39 of the handwritten notes writes the target as $F(M) \cap V = \{0 = y^{n-m+1} = \cdots = y^m\}$; the vanishing coordinates are the last $n - m$ of them, $y^{m+1}, \ldots, y^n$, as the lecture said.

\begin{rembox}[Where Is Injectivity Used?]\label{rem:where-injectivity-used}
In lecture the last equality caused trouble, and a discussion. Uribe first located the use of injectivity there; a student pointed out that $(*)$ concerns only $F(U)$, and that the proof seems to need only that $F$ be an immersion which is open onto its image. Another student added covering-type examples: maps that are not injective but whose images are manifolds, such as $\mathbb{R} \to S^1$, $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$, or the two-to-one map $S^2 \to \mathbb{RP}^2$. Uribe agreed --- ``I don't think we're using injectivity'' --- and promised ``a definite conclusion by email.''

\emph{The conclusion, from Uribe's follow-up email.} The students were right: ``a proof that we did today does show that for an immersion that is open as a map onto its image (so for all $U$ open in $M$, $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$), $F(M)$ is a submanifold. The map $F$ does not have to be injective.'' The proof uses exactly two things: the normal form (the immersion hypothesis), and that $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$ for the $U$ of the normal form; with the completion via Corollary~\ref{cor:immersion-local-image} nothing else enters. Injectivity belongs to the \emph{idea} of an embedding --- ``the idea of an embedding is that it is an isomorphism between $M$ and its image'' (Corollary~\ref{cor:embedding-diffeo}) --- not to this proof. He added that ``being an immersion and an open map onto its image'' is ``an unusual class of maps.\@''
\end{rembox}

\begin{propbox}[Immersions That Are Open onto Their Images]\thmlabel{prop:immersion-open-image}
Let $F : M \to N$ be an immersion such that $F : M \to F(M)$ is an open map, $F(M)$ carrying the subspace topology. Then $F(M)$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $n - m$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(The conclusion of the class discussion, confirmed in Uribe's follow-up email.)} The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, word for word: openness of $F$ onto its image is all it used to produce $W$. Written out, with the one changed justification marked:

Let $q = F(p) \in F(M)$; we need an adapted chart at $q$. \emph{Normal form.} $F$ is an immersion, so Theorem~\ref{thm:immersion-normal-form} gives charts $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $q$, and Corollary~\ref{cor:immersion-local-image} gives an open $V' \subseteq V$ containing $F(U)$ with
\[
F(U) = \{\, x \in V' : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0 \,\}. \tag{$*$}
\]
Neither result uses injectivity of $F$: the injectivity used in the corollary is that of the chart $\psi$. \emph{Openness} (the changed step). $U$ is open in $M$ and, by hypothesis, $F : M \to F(M)$ is an open map, so $F(U)$ is open in $F(M)$; since $F(M)$ carries the subspace topology, $F(U) = W \cap F(M)$ for some open $W \subseteq N$ (Definition~\ref{def:subspace}). In Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image} this step used that $F$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, but only through its consequence that $F$ is open onto its image. \emph{Shrinking.} Since $F(U) \subseteq V'$ and $F(U) = W \cap F(M) \subseteq W$,
\[
F(M) \cap (V' \cap W) = \big(F(M) \cap W\big) \cap V' = F(U) \cap V' = F(U) = F(U) \cap W = \{\, x \in V' \cap W : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0 \,\},
\]
the last equality by $(*)$ intersected with $W$. So the smooth chart $(V' \cap W, \psi|_{V' \cap W})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), $V' \cap W$ being an open subset of $V$), whose domain contains $q$, is adapted at $q$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}, with $k = n - m$), and $F(M)$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $n - m$.

For example, $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ is an immersion of $\mathbb{R}$, open onto $S^1$ and far from injective --- every point of $S^1$ has infinitely many preimages --- and its image $S^1$ is a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$. (It is an immersion into $\mathbb{R}^2$ because its velocity $(-\sin t, \cos t)$ never vanishes, as in Example~\ref{ex:nodal-cubic}. It is open onto $S^1$ because it is a local diffeomorphism onto $S^1$ (Example~\ref{ex:line-circle}): each $t$ has an open neighbourhood $U_t$ mapped homeomorphically onto an open subset of $S^1$, so for $O \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ open the image of $O \cap U_t$ is open in that subset, hence in $S^1$, and the image of $O$ is the union of these open sets.) The figure-eight is not open onto its image, consistent with its image not being a submanifold. (For $\beta(t) = (\sin 2t, \sin t)$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, the set $\beta\big((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\big)$ is not open in the image: every open set of $\mathbb{R}^2$ around $\beta(0) = (0, 0)$ contains $\beta(t)$ for $t$ near $\pm\pi$, because $\beta(t) \to (\sin(\pm 2\pi), \sin(\pm\pi)) = (0, 0)$ as $t \to \pm\pi$, and these points are not in $\beta\big((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\big)$ since $\beta$ is injective.)
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[An Embedding Is a Diffeomorphism onto Its Image]\thmlabel{cor:embedding-diffeo}
If $F : M \to N$ is an embedding, then $F : M \to F(M)$ is a diffeomorphism, $F(M)$ carrying its induced smooth structure as a regular submanifold.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~14 --- ``an embedding restricts to a diffeomorphism between $M$ and the image''; filled in.)} Write $\bar F : M \to F(M)$ for $F$ regarded as a map onto its image and $\iota : F(M) \hookrightarrow N$ for the inclusion, so that $F = \iota \circ \bar F$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, $F(M)$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ of codimension $n - m$, so with its induced structure it is a smooth manifold of dimension $n - (n - m) = m$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}).

\emph{Smooth.} $F$ is smooth into $N$ with values in $F(M)$, so $\bar F : M \to F(M)$ is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2).

\emph{Immersion.} Its differential followed by the injective $\iota_*$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}) is the injective $F_*$: by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), $F_{*p} = \iota_{*F(p)} \circ \bar F_{*p}$ for $p \in M$. If $\bar F_{*p} v = 0$, then $F_{*p} v = \iota_{*F(p)}(0) = 0$, so $v = 0$ because $F$ is an immersion. So $\bar F_{*p}$ is injective for every $p$.

\emph{Local diffeomorphism.} Both manifolds have dimension $m$ and $\bar F$ is an immersion at every point, so it is a local diffeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:dimension-constraints}(3)).

\emph{Diffeomorphism.} $\bar F$ is bijective: injective because $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}), and onto $F(M)$ by the definition of $F(M)$. Being a bijective local diffeomorphism, it is a diffeomorphism, its inverse being smooth near every point (Corollary~\ref{cor:bijective-local-diffeo}).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proper Maps}\label{sub:proper-maps}

\textit{Lecture 14. When is an injective immersion an embedding? The homeomorphism condition is point-set topology, and a convenient sufficient condition is properness --- the same hypothesis as in Ehresmann's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:ehresmann}).}

\begin{defbox}[Proper Map]\deflabel{def:proper-map}
A continuous map $F : X \to Y$ is \textbf{proper} if $F^{-1}(K)$ is compact for every compact $K \subseteq Y$.
\leeref{App.~A, \emph{Proper Maps}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Proper Maps into Manifolds Are Closed]\thmlabel{prop:proper-closed}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a continuous proper map, $N$ a topological manifold. Then $F$ is closed: $F(C)$ is closed in $N$ for every closed $C \subseteq M$.
\leeref{Theorem A.57}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~14 --- ``it's a very funny proof. You go back and forth literally.'' Uribe did not finish Claim~2 in lecture and sent the complete proof in his follow-up email; the completion of Claim~2 below is the notes' own.)} Let $C \subseteq M$ be closed. We show $\overline{F(C)} \subseteq F(C)$, so that $F(C)$ is closed. Recall that $N$, a topological manifold, is Hausdorff, and that a point lies in the closure of a set $A$ exactly when every open set containing the point meets $A$.

\emph{Claim 1: $F(C) \cap K$ is closed for every compact $K \subseteq N$.} $F^{-1}(K)$ is compact, because $F$ is proper (Definition~\ref{def:proper-map}). So $C \cap F^{-1}(K)$, a closed subset of it, is compact: it is closed in the subspace $F^{-1}(K)$, its complement there being $(M \setminus C) \cap F^{-1}(K)$, and a closed subset of a compact space is compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(5)). Its image $F\big(C \cap F^{-1}(K)\big)$ is compact, as the continuous image of a compact space (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(2)), hence closed in the Hausdorff space $N$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(4)). And $F\big(C \cap F^{-1}(K)\big) = F(C) \cap K$: a point of the left side is $F(c)$ with $c \in C$ and $F(c) \in K$, hence lies in $F(C) \cap K$; and conversely, a point $y \in F(C) \cap K$ is $y = F(c)$ with $c \in C$, and $F(c) = y \in K$ gives $c \in F^{-1}(K)$.

\emph{Claim 2.} Let $q \in \overline{F(C)}$, and let $V$ be a neighbourhood of $q$ with compact closure (Proposition~\ref{prop:locally-compact}). Then $q \in \overline{F(C) \cap \overline V}$. \textit{(Completion.)} If $O$ is any open set containing $q$, then $O \cap V$ is an open set containing $q$, so it meets $F(C)$; hence $O$ meets $F(C) \cap V \subseteq F(C) \cap \overline V$.

\emph{Conclusion.} By Claim~1 with $K = \overline V$, the set $F(C) \cap \overline V$ is closed, so it equals its closure, and $q \in F(C) \cap \overline V \subseteq F(C)$. As $q \in \overline{F(C)}$ was arbitrary, $\overline{F(C)} \subseteq F(C)$; the reverse inclusion always holds. Thus $\overline{F(C)} = F(C)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Injective Proper Immersions Are Embeddings]\thmlabel{thm:proper-embedding}
An injective proper immersion $F : M \to N$ is an embedding.
\leeref{Proposition 4.22}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~14 reduced this to Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-closed}; the last step is filled in.)} $F$ is an immersion by hypothesis, so by Definition~\ref{def:embedding} it remains to see that $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism, $F(M)$ carrying the subspace topology.

It is a continuous bijection: continuous into $F(M)$ because it is continuous into $N$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:univ-subspace}(2)), injective by hypothesis, and onto $F(M)$ by the definition of $F(M)$. Let $G : F(M) \to M$ be its inverse. A map is continuous when the preimage of every closed set is closed (take complements in the definition of continuity), and for $C \subseteq M$ the preimage $G^{-1}(C)$ is $F(C)$. If $C \subseteq M$ is closed, then $F(C)$ is closed in $N$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-closed} ($F$ is continuous and proper, and $N$ is a manifold), hence $F(C) = F(C) \cap F(M)$ is closed in $F(M)$: its complement in $F(M)$ is $(N \setminus F(C)) \cap F(M)$, open in the subspace topology (Definition~\ref{def:subspace}). So the inverse $F(M) \to M$ is continuous, and $F : M \to F(M)$ is a homeomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Injective Immersions of Compact Manifolds]\thmlabel{cor:compact-embedding}
If $M$ is compact, every injective immersion $F : M \to N$ is an embedding.
\leeref{Proposition 4.22}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Uribe's follow-up email: ``Note that $F$ is proper if $M$ is compact, a fact that can be very useful!''; the proof is filled in.)} $F$ is proper (Definition~\ref{def:proper-map}): if $K \subseteq N$ is compact, it is closed, as a compact subset of the Hausdorff space $N$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(4)); so $F^{-1}(K)$ is closed in $M$, $F$ being continuous; and a closed subset of the compact $M$ is compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(5)). So $F$ is an injective proper immersion. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}: $F$ is an embedding.
\end{proof}

\textit{An aside from the end of the lecture.} Uribe mentioned that he is developing his own notes for the course, ``based on notes that somebody took a few years ago'', edited ``the night before'', and asked whether they would help, perhaps shared through Overleaf.

\subsection{Closedness and Density}\label{sub:closedness-density}

\textit{Why does density of the irrational line rule out an embedding? Because the image of an embedding is always closed \emph{locally}, and a dense set that is locally closed is open. Prompted by Assignment~4, Problem~5.}

\begin{defbox}[Locally Closed Subset]\deflabel{def:locally-closed}
A subset $S$ of a topological space $N$ is \textbf{locally closed} if every point of $S$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ in $N$ such that $S \cap V$ is closed in $V$. Equivalently, $S$ is closed in some open subset of $N$ containing it, namely the union $U$ of these $V$'s.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Images of Embeddings Are Locally Closed]\thmlabel{prop:embedding-locally-closed}
Every regular submanifold of $N$ --- in particular the image of an embedding (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}) --- is locally closed in $N$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Let $S$ be a regular submanifold of $N$, of codimension $k$, and put $n = \dim N$ and $m = n - k$. (By Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, the image of an embedding is such an $S$, so the ``in particular'' follows.)

\emph{Locally closed.} At each point of the submanifold $S$ there is an adapted chart $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ (Definitions~\ref{def:submanifold} and~\ref{def:adapted-chart}), in which $S \cap V = \{x \in V : y^{m+1}(x) = \cdots = y^n(x) = 0\}$, a closed subset of $V$ as the zero set of continuous functions: it is the preimage of the closed set $\{\vec 0\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{k}$ under the continuous map $(y^{m+1}, \ldots, y^n) : V \to \mathbb{R}^k$. This is the condition of Definition~\ref{def:locally-closed}, with this $V$.

\emph{The equivalence in the definition.} If $U$ is the union of these $V$ --- one for each point of $S$ --- then $U$ is open and contains $S$. A point of $U \setminus S$ lies in some $V \setminus S$, which is open: it is open in $V$, as the complement of the closed set $S \cap V$, hence open in $N$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}); and $V \setminus S \subseteq U \setminus S$. So $U \setminus S$ is open, and $S = U \setminus (U \setminus S)$ is closed in $U$. Conversely, if $S$ is closed in an open $U \supseteq S$, then every point of $S$ has the open neighbourhood $V = U$, with $S \cap V = S$ closed in $V$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Dense Regular Submanifolds Are Open]\thmlabel{cor:dense-submanifold}
A dense regular submanifold $S$ of $N$ is an open subset of $N$, and has codimension $0$. In particular, the image of an embedding $F : M \to N$ with $\dim M < \dim N$ is never dense.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{$S$ is open.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:embedding-locally-closed}, $S$ is closed in an open $U \supseteq S$. $S$ is dense in $N$, hence in $U$: a point $u \in U$ lies in the closure of $S$ in $U$ when every open set of $U$ containing $u$ meets $S$, and such a set is open in $N$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}), so it meets $S$ by density. A closed dense subset of $U$ is all of $U$, since it equals its closure in $U$, which is $U$; so $S = U$ is open.

\emph{Codimension $0$.} If $S = \emptyset$, density forces $N = \overline{S} = \emptyset$, and there is nothing to prove; so let $x \in S$. If $S$ had codimension $k \ge 1$, take an adapted chart $(V, \psi)$ at $x$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}): then $\psi(S \cap V)$ would be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n-k} \times \{0\}$, open in $\mathbb{R}^n$ because $S \cap V$ is open in $V$ --- impossible, since no nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ lies in a hyperplane. In detail: $S \cap V$ is open in $V$ because $S$ is open in $N$; $\psi$ is a homeomorphism of $V$ onto the open set $\psi(V)$, so $\psi(S \cap V)$ is open in $\psi(V)$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(3)), hence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}). It contains $\psi(x) = (a, \vec 0)$, hence an open ball of some radius $\varepsilon > 0$ around it, which contains the point obtained from $(a, \vec 0)$ by changing its last coordinate from $0$ to $\varepsilon/2$; since $k \ge 1$, that coordinate is one of the last $k$, so this point is not in $\mathbb{R}^{n-k} \times \{0\}$, a contradiction. So $k = 0$.

\emph{In particular.} Let $F : M \to N$ be an embedding with $m = \dim M < \dim N = n$, and $M \neq \emptyset$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, $F(M)$ is a nonempty regular submanifold with adapted charts of codimension $n - m \ge 1$ at each of its points. If $F(M)$ were dense, it would be open by the first part, and the argument just given, applied to one of these adapted charts, would give a contradiction. So $F(M)$ is not dense.
\end{proof}

This is the precise form of Uribe's ``no matter how you shrink $V$, you won't be able to isolate only the yellow guy'': at every point of the irrational line, local closedness fails.

\begin{propbox}[Closed Embeddings Are the Proper Ones]\thmlabel{prop:proper-iff-closed}
An embedding $F : M \to N$ is proper if and only if its image $F(M)$ is closed in $N$. In particular, an injective proper immersion is exactly an embedding with closed image.
\leeref{Proposition 5.5}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{Proper $\Rightarrow$ closed image.} If $F$ is proper, it is closed (Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-closed}, $N$ being a manifold), so $F(M)$, the image of the closed set $M$, is closed.

\emph{Closed image $\Rightarrow$ proper.} Conversely, let $F(M)$ be closed and $K \subseteq N$ compact. Then $K \cap F(M)$ is a closed subset of $K$ (in the subspace topology of $K$, as the intersection of $K$ with a closed subset of $N$), hence compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(5)). Since $F$ takes all its values in $F(M)$, $F^{-1}(K) = F^{-1}\big(K \cap F(M)\big)$. And $F^{-1}\big(K \cap F(M)\big)$ is its image under the inverse of the homeomorphism $F : M \to F(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}), a continuous map, hence compact (Proposition~\ref{fact:compact}(2)). So $F$ is proper (Definition~\ref{def:proper-map}).

\emph{The last sentence.} The last sentence combines this with Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}. An injective proper immersion is an embedding by that theorem, and its image is closed by the first part. Conversely, an embedding with closed image is proper by the second part, and it is an injective immersion by Definition~\ref{def:embedding}.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Sections Are Closed Embeddings]\thmlabel{prop:sections-embeddings}
Let $\pi : E \to M$ and $s : M \to E$ be smooth with $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_M$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $s$ is an embedding (Definition~\ref{def:embedding});
    \item its image $s(M) = \{ y \in E : s(\pi(y)) = y \}$ is closed in $E$.
\end{enumerate}
So $s(M)$ is a closed regular submanifold of $E$ of dimension $\dim M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}), and $s$ is proper (Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-iff-closed}). In particular the image of every section of a fibration (Definition~\ref{def:section}) is one.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~5, Problem~1, which assumed $\pi$ to be a surjective submersion; the proof uses only $\pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_M$. Part (2) is not from the assignment.)} Throughout, $p, p'$ denote points of $M$ and $y$ points of $E$.

\emph{(1) $s$ is an immersion.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:section-splitting}(1), $s_{*p}$ is injective for every $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:immersion}).

\emph{(1) $s : M \to s(M)$ is a homeomorphism.} It is injective: if $s(p) = s(p')$, then $p = \pi(s(p)) = \pi(s(p')) = p'$. It is onto $s(M)$ by definition, so it is a bijection. Its inverse is the restriction $\pi|_{s(M)}$: on one hand $\pi|_{s(M)} \circ s = \pi \circ s = \mathrm{id}_M$; on the other, for $y = s(p) \in s(M)$,
\[
s\big(\pi|_{s(M)}(y)\big) = s\big(\pi(s(p))\big) = s(p) = y .
\]
Both maps are continuous: $s : M \to E$ is continuous with values in $s(M)$, which carries the subspace topology, so $s : M \to s(M)$ is continuous; and $\pi|_{s(M)}$ is the restriction of the continuous map $\pi$ to a subspace. So $s$ is an immersion and a homeomorphism onto its image, an embedding.

\emph{(2) The image.} If $y = s(p)$, then $s(\pi(y)) = s(p) = y$; conversely, if $s(\pi(y)) = y$, then $y \in s(M)$. So $s(M) = \{ y : s(\pi(y)) = y \}$. Its complement is open: let $s(\pi(y)) \ne y$. $E$ is Hausdorff (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}), so there are disjoint open sets $O \ni s(\pi(y))$ and $O' \ni y$. The set $(s \circ \pi)^{-1}(O) \cap O'$ is open, as $s \circ \pi$ is continuous, and contains $y$; for $y'$ in it, $s(\pi(y')) \in O$ and $y' \in O'$, so $s(\pi(y')) \ne y'$. So every point outside $s(M)$ has a neighbourhood outside $s(M)$, and $s(M)$ is closed.

The last two sentences: $s(M)$ is a regular submanifold of codimension $\dim E - \dim M$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, closed by (2), so $s$ is proper by Proposition~\ref{prop:proper-iff-closed}. For a fibration, a section is such an $s$ (Definition~\ref{def:section}).
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Sections of the Tangent and Cotangent Bundles]\label{rem:sections-embeddings-bundles}
The main examples come later: the zero sections of $TM$ and $T^*M$ (Definitions~\ref{def:tb-zero-section} and~\ref{def:ctb-zero-section}, later, in \ref{sec:tangent-bundle} and \ref{sec:cotangent-bundle}), and the section $p \mapsto (p, df_p)$ of $T^*M$ given by a smooth function $f$, smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:d-operator} (later, in \ref{sec:d-operator}). Each is such an $s$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:sections-embeddings} its image --- the zero section, resp.\ the image $\{(p, df_p)\}$ of the one-form $df$ --- is a closed regular submanifold of dimension $\dim M$.
\end{rembox}


\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.27\textwidth} p{0.33\textwidth} p{0.3\textwidth}}
\hline
Map & Image & Example separating it from the row above \\
\hline
injective proper immersion & closed regular submanifold & --- \\
embedding & locally closed regular submanifold & an open interval embedded in $\mathbb{R}^2$ \\
injective immersion & possibly not locally closed, even dense & the irrational line \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Closedness of the image alone is not enough: the image of the figure-eight (Lee's Example~4.19) is compact, hence closed, but the figure-eight is not an embedding. Local closedness is necessary for an embedding, not sufficient.

\begin{lembox}[Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem]\thmlabel{lem:dirichlet}
For every $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and every integer $N \ge 1$ there are integers $n, m$ with $1 \le n \le N$ and $|n\alpha - m| < 1/N$.
\leeref{Lemma 4.21}
\end{lembox}

\textit{Status.} Used in Assignment~4, Problem~5, citing Lee; not proved here. (Lee's proof is a pigeonhole argument on the fractional parts of $0, \alpha, \ldots, N\alpha$.)

\begin{propbox}[The Irrational Line on the Torus]\thmlabel{prop:irrational-line}
Let $\alpha$ be irrational and $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to T^2 = S^1 \times S^1$, $\gamma(t) = (e^{2\pi i t}, e^{2\pi i \alpha t})$ --- the curve $F(t) = [t, \alpha t]$ introduced before Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, under the identification $[x, y] \mapsto (e^{2\pi i x}, e^{2\pi i y})$. Then $\gamma$ is an injective immersion, its image is dense in $T^2$, and $\gamma$ is not an embedding.
\leeref{Example 4.20}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Assignment~4, Problem~5: the submitted solution, condensed; the second proof of the last claim is new.)} Distances below are taken in $\mathbb{C}^2$, whose subspace topology $T^2$ carries; write $\gamma_{\mathbb{C}} = \iota \circ \gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}^2$ for $\gamma$ followed by the inclusion $\iota : T^2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}^2$. Two elementary facts are used: $e^{2\pi i s} = 1$ if and only if $s \in \mathbb{Z}$; and $|e^{is} - e^{it}| \le |s - t|$ for real $s, t$ (a chord of the unit circle is no longer than the arc it subtends).

\emph{Immersion.} $\gamma$ is smooth into $\mathbb{C}^2$ with values in the submanifold $T^2$, hence smooth into $T^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2)). Its velocity in $\mathbb{C}^2$, $\big(2\pi i e^{2\pi i t}, 2\pi i\alpha e^{2\pi i \alpha t}\big)$, has first entry of modulus $2\pi \ne 0$, so by the chain rule $\gamma_{*t}$ is nonzero, hence injective. In detail: by Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix} in the identity charts, $(\gamma_{\mathbb{C}})_{*t}(\partial/\partial r|_t)$ is the velocity above, which is nonzero; by the Chain Rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) $(\gamma_{\mathbb{C}})_{*t} = \iota_{*\gamma(t)} \circ \gamma_{*t}$, so $\gamma_{*t}(\partial/\partial r|_t) \neq 0$, for otherwise its image under $\iota_{*\gamma(t)}$ would be $0$. As $T_t\mathbb{R}$ is spanned by $\partial/\partial r|_t$, the linear map $\gamma_{*t}$ has kernel $0$.

\emph{Injective.} If $\gamma(t_1) = \gamma(t_2)$, then $e^{2\pi i (t_1 - t_2)} = 1$ and $e^{2\pi i \alpha(t_1 - t_2)} = 1$, so $t_1 - t_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $\alpha(t_1 - t_2) \in \mathbb{Z}$; if $t_1 \ne t_2$ this makes $\alpha = \alpha(t_1 - t_2)/(t_1 - t_2)$ a quotient of integers with nonzero denominator, that is, rational. So $t_1 = t_2$.

\emph{Dense.} Using $|e^{is} - e^{it}| \le |s - t|$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet} there are $n_N \ge 1$ and $m_N$ with $|n_N\alpha - m_N| < 1/N$, so $w_N = e^{2\pi i \alpha n_N} = e^{i\theta_N}$ with $\theta_N = 2\pi(n_N\alpha - m_N)$, $0 < |\theta_N| < 2\pi/N$ (nonzero by injectivity). Here $e^{2\pi i \alpha n_N} = e^{2\pi i (\alpha n_N - m_N)}$ because $e^{-2\pi i m_N} = 1$; and $\theta_N = 0$ would give $\gamma(n_N) = (1, 1) = \gamma(0)$ with $n_N \neq 0$, contradicting injectivity. The powers $w_N^k = e^{2\pi i \alpha (k n_N)}$ are $2\pi/N$-dense in $S^1$, since consecutive ones differ in angle by $|\theta_N|$. In detail: let $\delta = |\theta_N|$, and note $e^{ik\delta} = w_N^{\pm k} = e^{2\pi i \alpha (\pm k n_N)}$, with the sign of $\theta_N$. Given $e^{i\phi} \in S^1$ with $\phi \in [0, 2\pi)$, let $k \ge 0$ be the integer with $k\delta \le \phi < (k+1)\delta$; then $0 \le \phi - k\delta < \delta$, so $|e^{i\phi} - e^{ik\delta}| \le |\phi - k\delta| < \delta < 2\pi/N$, and $e^{ik\delta}$ is a power of $w_N$. So $D = \{e^{2\pi i\alpha k} : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ is dense in $S^1$: every point of $S^1$ lies within $2\pi/N$ of $D$, for every $N$. Given $(e^{2\pi i a}, e^{2\pi i b}) \in T^2$, the points $\gamma(a + k) = (e^{2\pi i a}, e^{2\pi i \alpha a} e^{2\pi i \alpha k})$ have the right first coordinate, and their second coordinates come arbitrarily close to $e^{2\pi i b}$ because $D$ is dense. In detail: given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|e^{2\pi i \alpha k} - e^{2\pi i (b - \alpha a)}| < \varepsilon$; multiplying by $e^{2\pi i \alpha a}$, of modulus $1$,
\[
\big|\gamma(a + k) - (e^{2\pi i a}, e^{2\pi i b})\big| = \big|e^{2\pi i \alpha a} e^{2\pi i \alpha k} - e^{2\pi i \alpha a} e^{2\pi i (b - \alpha a)}\big| = \big|e^{2\pi i \alpha k} - e^{2\pi i (b - \alpha a)}\big| < \varepsilon .
\]
So every open set of $T^2$ meets $\gamma(\mathbb{R})$: the image is dense.

\emph{Not an embedding: the submitted proof.} $\gamma(n_N) \to \gamma(0)$, since
\[
|\gamma(n_N) - \gamma(0)| = \big|(e^{2\pi i n_N}, e^{2\pi i \alpha n_N}) - (1, 1)\big| = \big|e^{2\pi i \alpha n_N} - e^{2\pi i m_N}\big| \le 2\pi|n_N\alpha - m_N| < 2\pi/N ,
\]
using $e^{2\pi i n_N} = 1 = e^{2\pi i m_N}$. So $\gamma(n_N) \to \gamma(0)$ in the image $\gamma(\mathbb{R})$ with its subspace topology. If $\gamma^{-1} : \gamma(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}$ were continuous, as it is for an embedding (Definition~\ref{def:embedding}), then $n_N = \gamma^{-1}(\gamma(n_N)) \to \gamma^{-1}(\gamma(0)) = 0$, which is false because $n_N \ge 1$ for every $N$.

\emph{Not an embedding: via density.} The image is dense and $\dim \mathbb{R} = 1 < 2 = \dim T^2$, so by Corollary~\ref{cor:dense-submanifold} it is not the image of an embedding.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Regular and Immersed Submanifolds}\label{sub:immersed-submanifolds}

\textit{Not from lecture: the notion announced with Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}.} A regular submanifold carries the subspace topology, and its smooth structure is forced on it by the ambient manifold. The images of the injective immersions of \ref{sec:immersions} --- the figure-eight, the irrational line on the torus --- do not fit that definition, but each is a perfectly good manifold in the topology it inherits from its \emph{domain}. Allowing that topology gives the second kind of submanifold.

\begin{defbox}[Immersed Submanifold]\deflabel{def:immersed-submanifold}
Let $N$ be a smooth manifold. An \textbf{immersed submanifold} of $N$ is a subset $S \subseteq N$ together with a topology on $S$, in which it is a topological manifold, and a smooth structure on $S$, such that the inclusion $\iota : S \hookrightarrow N$ is a smooth immersion (Definition~\ref{def:immersion-lecture}). The topology need not be the subspace topology.
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Images of Injective Immersions]\thmlabel{prop:immersion-image}
Let $F : M \to N$ be an injective immersion and $S = F(M)$. There is exactly one topology and smooth structure on $S$ for which $F : M \to S$ is a diffeomorphism, and with them $S$ is an immersed submanifold of $N$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} \emph{The topology.} Declare $U \subseteq S$ open if $F^{-1}(U)$ is open in $M$. This is a topology on $S$, because $F^{-1}(\emptyset) = \emptyset$, $F^{-1}(S) = M$, and preimages commute with unions and intersections. Let $h = F^{-1} : S \to M$ be the inverse of the bijection $F : M \to S$ ($F$ is injective). For $U \subseteq S$, $h(U) = F^{-1}(U)$, so $U$ is open in $S$ exactly when $h(U)$ is open in $M$: $h$ is a bijection that matches open sets with open sets, a homeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(2)).

\emph{The smooth structure.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}, applied to the homeomorphism $h : S \to M$, $S$ is a topological manifold and carries exactly one smooth structure for which $h$, and hence $F = h^{-1}$, is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:transported}); a map is a diffeomorphism exactly when its inverse is (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}).

\emph{Uniqueness.} The topology is forced as well, since a diffeomorphism is a homeomorphism: if some topology on $S$ makes $F : M \to S$ a homeomorphism, then a set $U \subseteq S$ is open in it exactly when $F^{-1}(U)$ is open in $M$ (Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(2)), which is the topology declared above. And for that topology the smooth structure is unique by Proposition~\ref{prop:transport-structure}(3).

\emph{Immersed submanifold.} The inclusion is $\iota = F \circ h$, with $F : M \to N$: indeed $F(h(q)) = q$ for $q \in S$. It is a composite of smooth maps (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}); by the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) $\iota_{*q} = F_{*h(q)} \circ h_{*q}$, which is injective because $h_{*q}$ is an isomorphism (Corollary~\ref{lem:germs-diffeo}) and $F_{*h(q)}$ is injective: if $\iota_{*q}v = 0$, then $h_{*q}v \in \ker F_{*h(q)} = 0$, so $v = 0$. So $\iota$ is an immersion, and $S$, with this topology and smooth structure, is an immersed submanifold of $N$ (Definition~\ref{def:immersed-submanifold}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Every Regular Submanifold Is an Immersed Submanifold]\thmlabel{prop:regular-is-immersed}
A regular submanifold $S \subseteq N$, with the subspace topology and its induced smooth structure (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}), is an immersed submanifold of $N$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Check Definition~\ref{def:immersed-submanifold}. With the subspace topology and the induced smooth structure, $S$ is a topological manifold and a smooth manifold (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}). The inclusion $\iota : S \hookrightarrow N$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}) and $\iota_{*p}$ is injective at every $p \in S$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), so $\iota$ is a smooth immersion (Definition~\ref{def:immersion-lecture}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[When an Immersed Submanifold Is Regular]\thmlabel{prop:immersed-regular}
Let $F : M \to N$ be an injective immersion, and give $S = F(M)$ the structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $F$ is an embedding (Definition~\ref{def:embedding});
    \item the topology of $S$ is the subspace topology;
    \item $S$ is a regular submanifold of $N$ whose induced smooth structure is the structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Write $\mathcal{T}_S$ for the topology of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image} and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ for the subspace topology on $S$. We show (1)~$\Leftrightarrow$~(2), (1)~$\Rightarrow$~(3) and (3)~$\Rightarrow$~(2), which together give all the equivalences.

\emph{(1)~$\Leftrightarrow$~(2).} The topology of $S$ is the one for which $F : M \to S$ is a homeomorphism; it equals the subspace topology exactly when $F$ is a homeomorphism onto its image with the subspace topology, which, for an immersion, is the definition of an embedding. In detail: $F$ is an immersion by hypothesis, so by Definition~\ref{def:embedding}, (1) says that $F : M \to (S, \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}})$ is a homeomorphism. If $\mathcal{T}_S = \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}}$, this holds, because $F : M \to (S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a homeomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}). Conversely, if $F : M \to (S, \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}})$ is a homeomorphism, then for $U \subseteq S$, by Proposition~\ref{fact:cont}(2) applied to both homeomorphisms,
\[
U \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}} \iff F^{-1}(U) \text{ is open in } M \iff U \in \mathcal{T}_S ,
\]
so $\mathcal{T}_S = \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}}$.

\emph{(1)~$\Rightarrow$~(3).} $S$ is a regular submanifold by Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}, and $F : M \to S$ is a diffeomorphism for its induced structure by Corollary~\ref{cor:embedding-diffeo}. By the uniqueness in Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image} --- exactly one topology and smooth structure on $S$ make $F : M \to S$ a diffeomorphism --- the two structures coincide.

\emph{(3)~$\Rightarrow$~(2).} The induced structure of a regular submanifold has the subspace topology (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-structure}, and Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}, where $S$ carries the subspace topology). By (3) the induced structure is the structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}, so its topology $\mathcal{T}_S$ is $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sub}}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Immersed but Not Regular]\exlabel{ex:immersed-not-regular}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{The figure-eight.} $\beta(t) = (\sin 2t, \sin t)$, $t \in (-\pi, \pi)$ (Lee, Example~4.19), is an injective immersion, so its image is an immersed submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:immersion-image}). It is not a regular submanifold: in the subspace topology every small neighbourhood of the origin in the image is an X --- the strand through $\beta(0)$ and the two ends returning as $t \to \pm\pi$ --- and removing the origin leaves four components, which cannot happen in a $1$-manifold (as in Example~\ref{ex:nodal-cubic}).
    \item \emph{The irrational line.} The curve $\gamma$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:irrational-line} is an injective immersion, so its image is an immersed submanifold of $T^2$, a copy of $\mathbb{R}$ in its own topology. It is not a regular submanifold. The image is dense, so if it were regular it would be open in $T^2$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:dense-submanifold}). But a nonempty open subset of $T^2$ containing $(e^{2\pi i a}, w)$ meets the circle $\{e^{2\pi i a}\} \times S^1$ in an open arc, which is uncountable, while the image meets that circle only in the countable set $\{\gamma(a + k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exbox}

In the immersed topology, a short interval of the irrational line is an open subset of the image; in the subspace topology, every neighbourhood of a point of the image also contains points from arbitrarily far along the line, because the line comes back densely. That is the whole difference between the two kinds of submanifold.
