Then $\{dx^1|_p, \ldots, dx^m|_p\}$ is the dual basis of $\{\partial/\partial x^1|_p, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^m|_p\}$, so $\dim T_p^*M = m$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-basis}), and for every smooth $f$ defined near $p$,
\[
df_p = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}(p)\, dx^i\big|_p .
\]
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components} (Components of a Covector).} In a chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ near $p$, every covector $\alpha \in T_p^*M$ is
\[
\alpha = \sum_{j=1}^m a_j\, dx^j\big|_p, \qquad a_j = \alpha\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big) .
\]
The numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_m$ are the \textbf{components} of $\alpha$ in the chart.
\end{quote}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.95]
\begin{scope}
\clip (-1.7,-1.9) rectangle (2.7,2.3);
\foreach \c in {-4,...,6} \draw[violet!55, thick] ({(\c+2)/2},-2) -- ({(\c-2.4)/2},2.4);
\end{scope}
\draw[gray!60] (-1.7,-1.9) rectangle (2.7,2.3);
\foreach \c in {0,1,2,3} \node[violet!75!black, font=\scriptsize] at ({(\c-2.45)/2+0.13},2.48) {$\c$};
\fill (0,0) circle (1.6pt) node[below left, font=\scriptsize] {$p$};
\draw[->, very thick, teal!65!black] (0,0) -- (1,1) node[above right, font=\scriptsize] {$v$};
\draw[->, very thick, orange!85!black] (0,0) -- (0.6,-1.2) node[below right, font=\scriptsize] {$w$};
\node[font=\scriptsize, align=left, anchor=west] at (2.9,0.9) {$\alpha = 2\,dx + dy$:\\ the lines $\alpha = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots$};
\node[font=\scriptsize, align=left, anchor=west, teal!65!black] at (2.9,0.0) {$\alpha(v) = 3$: $v$ crosses three lines};
\node[font=\scriptsize, align=left, anchor=west, orange!85!black] at (2.9,-0.6) {$\alpha(w) = 0$: $w$ runs along them};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

A covector drawn as a stack of parallel lines. In $\mathbb{R}^2$ (or in one tangent space, after choosing a basis) the covector $\alpha = 2\,dx + dy$ is pictured by its level lines $\{\alpha = 0\}, \{\alpha = 1\}, \ldots$; its value on an arrow is the number of lines the arrow crosses, with sign. $v = \partial_x + \partial_y$ crosses three, so $\alpha(v) = 3$; $w = 0.6\,\partial_x - 1.2\,\partial_y$ runs along the lines, so $\alpha(w) = 0$. For $\alpha = df_p$ the lines are the level sets of the linear approximation of $f$ at $p$: closely spaced lines mean a steep $f$. An arrow and a stack of lines are different kinds of objects; only an inner product turns one into the other.

\textbf{Step 4: the cotangent space from germs alone.} The differential of $f$ depends only on $f$ to first order: $T_p^*M \cong I_p/I_p^2$, the germs vanishing at $p$ modulo those vanishing to second order, by $[[f - f(p)]] \mapsto df_p$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}). So covectors can be built from functions without mentioning tangent vectors at all --- the cotangent space is ``very extremely natural from the point of view of functions'' (the remark \emph{The Most Natural Description} in \ref{sec:cotangent-germs}).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:Ip-quotient} (The Space $I_p/I_p^2$).} $I_p/I_p^2$ is the quotient vector space (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-vs}) of $I_p$ by its subspace $I_p^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:Ip-subspaces}). The class of $[f] \in I_p$ is written $[[f]] = [f] + I_p^2$, and $[[f]] = [[f']]$ iff $[f'] - [f] \in I_p^2$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal} (The Cotangent Space from Germs).} \begin{enumerate}
    \item The pairing induces isomorphisms
    \[
    T_pM \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } \big(I_p/I_p^2\big)^*, \qquad\qquad \Phi : I_p/I_p^2 \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } (T_pM)^* = T_p^*M .
    \]
    \item $\Phi([[f]]) = df_p$: the isomorphism sends the class of a germ to its differential.
    \item In any chart, $\Phi$ carries the basis $[[x^i - x^i(p)]]$ of $I_p/I_p^2$ to the basis $dx^i|_p$ of $T_p^*M$, which is dual to the basis $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ of $T_pM$.
\end{enumerate}
The isomorphisms are defined without any chart.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Step 5: covectors pull back.} For $F : M \to N$, the dual map of $F_{*p}$ is the \emph{pullback of covectors} $F_p^* : T^*_{F(p)}N \to T_p^*M$, $(F_p^*\alpha)(v) = \alpha(F_{*p}v)$ (Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector}). It commutes with differentials: $F_p^*(df_{F(p)}) = d(f \circ F)_p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d}), which is the chain rule in covector form. The same symbol $F_p^*$ already denoted the pullback of germs (Step~5 of \ref{sec:recap-tangent}); the two are compatible, as the remark \emph{One Symbol for Two Pullbacks} in \ref{sec:cotangent-germs} explains. In charts $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ near $p$ and $(y^1, \ldots, y^n)$ near $F(p)$, the matrix of $F_p^*$ in the dual bases $dy^j|_{F(p)}$ and $dx^i|_p$ is the transpose of the Jacobian of Step~5 of \ref{sec:recap-tangent} (Proposition~\ref{prop:dual-map}(2)):
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(p) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix},
\]
an $m \times n$ matrix whose $j$-th column lists the components of $F_p^*(dy^j|_{F(p)}) = d(F^j)_p$.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector} (Pullback of Covectors).} Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $p \in M$. The \textbf{pullback of covectors} at $p$ is the dual map (Definition~\ref{def:dual-map}) of the pushforward $F_{*p} : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$:
\[
F_p^* : T^*_{F(p)}N \longrightarrow T_p^*M, \qquad (F_p^*\alpha)(v) = \alpha\big(F_{*p}v\big) .
\]
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d} (Pullback Commutes with $d$).} Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $p \in M$, and $f$ smooth near $F(p)$. Then
\[
F_p^*\big(df_{F(p)}\big) = d(f \circ F)_p \quad \text{in } T_p^*M .
\]
\end{quote}

\textbf{Step 6: the word ``differential''.} The course uses it for four objects. They are one idea at four levels of generality.

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.25\textwidth} p{0.13\textwidth} p{0.27\textwidth} p{0.25\textwidth}}
\hline
Name & Symbol & Takes \ldots\ to \ldots & Defined in \\
\hline
differential of a map between vector spaces & $dF_p$ & a vector in $X$ to a vector in $Y$ (the Jacobian) & Definition~\ref{def:vs-differential} \\
differential (pushforward) of a smooth map & $F_{*p}$ & $T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ & Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} \\
differential of a function at $p$ & $df_p$ & $T_pM \to \mathbb{R}$, a covector & Definition~\ref{def:differential-function} \\
the operator $d$ & $d$ & a function $f$ to the one-form $df$ & Proposition~\ref{prop:d-operator} \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

How they fit: on open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ the second is the first (Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}); Lee writes $dF_p$ for what these notes call $F_{*p}$, and Uribe said in Lecture~15 that $F_{*p}$ ``we should have called the differential of $F$ ages ago''. The third is the second for maps into $\mathbb{R}$. The fourth collects the third over all points: $df$ is the field $p \mapsto df_p$, a one-form (\ref{sec:d-operator}).

\textbf{Step 7: forward and backward.} Given $F : M \to N$:

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.27\textwidth} p{0.14\textwidth} p{0.48\textwidth}}
\hline
Object & Moves & Rule \\
\hline
point $p \in M$ & forward & $p \mapsto F(p)$ \\
tangent vector $v \in T_pM$ & forward & $F_{*p}v \in T_{F(p)}N$ (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}) \\
function $f$ on $N$ & backward & $F^*f = f \circ F$ on $M$ \\
germ $[g]$ at $F(p)$ & backward & $F_p^*[g] = [g \circ F]$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-pullback}) \\
covector $\alpha \in T^*_{F(p)}N$ & backward & $(F_p^*\alpha)(v) = \alpha(F_{*p}v)$ (Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector}) \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Things that \emph{are} somewhere move forward with the points; things that \emph{eat} move backward, because to evaluate one on $M$ you push its input forward and evaluate on $N$.

\textbf{What this chapter builds.} So far every object lives at a single point. This chapter lets the point vary. The tangent spaces are assembled into one manifold, the tangent bundle $TM$ (\ref{sec:tangent-bundle}), and the cotangent spaces into the cotangent bundle $T^*M$ (\ref{sec:cotangent-bundle}). A smooth choice of a covector at every point is a one-form; $d$ turns functions into one-forms, and $F^*$ pulls one-forms back (\ref{sec:d-operator}). The next chapter turns to the sections of $TM$: a smooth choice of a tangent vector at every point is a vector field, and a vector field differentiates functions everywhere at once (\ref{sec:fields}).

\begin{exbox}[Covectors in the Plane]\exlabel{ex:recap-covectors-plane}
Continue Example~\ref{ex:recap-vectors-plane}: $p = (1, 2)$, $f = x^2 y$, $v = 3\,\partial_x - \partial_y$, and $F(x, y) = (x^2, x + y)$ with $F(p) = (1, 3)$ and $F_{*p}v = 6\,\partial_u + 2\,\partial_w$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{The differential of $f$.} $df_p = \partial_x f(p)\, dx + \partial_y f(p)\, dy = 4\, dx + dy$, and $df_p(v) = 4 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot (-1) = 11 = v[f]$, as Step~3 promises.
    \item \emph{A covector at $F(p)$.} Let $g(u, w) = u w^2$ on the target. Then $dg_{F(p)} = w^2\, du + 2uw\, dw = 9\, du + 6\, dw$ at $(1, 3)$.
    \item \emph{Its pullback, by definition.} $(F_p^* dg_{F(p)})(v) = dg_{F(p)}(F_{*p}v) = 9 \cdot 6 + 6 \cdot 2 = 66$.
    \item \emph{Its pullback, by the chain rule.} $g \circ F = x^2 (x + y)^2$, with $\partial_x (g \circ F)(p) = 2x(x+y)^2 + 2x^2(x+y) = 18 + 6 = 24$ and $\partial_y (g \circ F)(p) = 2x^2(x+y) = 6$. So $d(g \circ F)_p = 24\, dx + 6\, dy$, and $d(g \circ F)_p(v) = 72 - 6 = 66$: the two agree, as Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d} says.
    \item \emph{The transpose.} The components of $F_p^*$ come from the \emph{transpose} of the Jacobian: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 9 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 24 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$. Vectors are pushed forward by the Jacobian, covectors pulled back by its transpose.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exbox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; the conversion diagram of the midterm check sheet, added on request.)} The differential of a smooth $F : M \to N$ at $p$, in four equivalent forms. Charts $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^n))$ at $F(p)$, $F^i = y^i \circ F$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3.4em, row sep=3.4em, font=\footnotesize]
F_{*p}D = D \circ F^* \ \text{(germs)} \arrow[r, leftrightarrow, "(1)"] \arrow[d, leftrightarrow, "(2)"'] & (F \circ \gamma)'(0) \ \text{(curves)} \\
\Big[\dfrac{\partial F^i}{\partial x^j}(p)\Big] \ \text{(Jacobian)} \arrow[r, leftrightarrow, "(3)"'] & \dfrac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} F(p + tv) \ \text{(vector spaces)}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{rembox}[Conversion Diagram for the Differential]\label{rem:conversion-differential}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{Germs and curves.} $(F_{*p}D)[g] = D[g \circ F]$ (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}); for $D = D_\gamma$, $F_{*p}D_\gamma = D_{F \circ \gamma}$, i.e.\ $F_{*}(\gamma'(0)) = (F \circ \gamma)'(0)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-composite}).
    \item \emph{Germs and the Jacobian.} $F_{*p}\big(\partial/\partial x^j|_p\big) = \sum_i \frac{\partial F^i}{\partial x^j}(p)\, \partial/\partial y^i|_{F(p)}$: column $j$ of the Jacobian of $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}); on components, $(F_{*p}v)^i = \sum_j \frac{\partial F^i}{\partial x^j}(p)\, v^j$.
    \item \emph{The Jacobian and the vector-space formula.} Between open subsets of vector spaces, $F_{*p}v = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} F(p + tv)$ once $F$ is known to be smooth, and any curve with velocity $v$ may replace the line (Theorem~\ref{thm:vs-differential-curves}, Proposition~\ref{prop:differential-agree}).
\end{enumerate}
\emph{For a function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$}, five faces of $df_p \in T_p^*M$:
\[
df_p(v) = v[f] = f_{*p}(v) = (f \circ \gamma)'(0) = \sum_j \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(p)\, v^j ,
\]
with $f_{*p}(v)$ read through $T_{f(p)}\mathbb{R} \cong \mathbb{R}$ and $\gamma$ any curve with velocity $v$; $df_p = \sum_j \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(p)\, dx^j|_p$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}); in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $df_p(v) = \nabla f(p) \cdot v$; and, on germs, $df_p$ corresponds to the class of $f - f(p)$ in $I_p/I_p^2$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}).

\emph{Covectors.} Components $\xi_j = \xi(\partial/\partial x^j|_p)$, $\xi = \sum_j \xi_j\, dx^j|_p$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}); under a change of chart $\xi_i = \sum_j \frac{\partial \tilde x^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, \tilde\xi_j$, the transpose of the rule for vectors. The pullback $F_p^*\xi = \xi \circ F_{*p}$ has the transposed Jacobian as its matrix (Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector}), and $F_p^*\big(dg_{F(p)}\big) = d(g \circ F)_p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d}).
\end{rembox}


% ============================================================================
% SECTION: THE TANGENT BUNDLE
% ============================================================================

\section{The Tangent Bundle}\label{sec:tangent-bundle}

\roadmark{Stage: bundles}{All the tangent spaces of $M$, assembled into a single manifold that fibres over $M$.}

\textit{Lecture 12. ``Again, these constructions, especially the cotangent [bundle], are basic parts of the basic theory.'' The tangent bundle was introduced as a set, with its projection and zero section; its topology, smooth structure and charts come next lecture.}

\begin{defbox}[The Tangent Bundle as a Set]\deflabel{def:tangent-bundle-set}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Its \textbf{tangent bundle} is the set
\[
TM = \bigcup_{p \in M} \{p\} \times T_pM = \{\, (p, v) : p \in M,\ v \in T_pM \,\},
\]
all the tangent spaces ``put together in one big set.''
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{The Tangent Bundle}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[The Projection of $TM$]\deflabel{def:tb-projection}
The \textbf{projection} of the tangent bundle is
\[
\pi : TM \longrightarrow M, \qquad \pi(p, v) = p .
\]
Its fibre over $p$, $\pi^{-1}(p) = \{p\} \times T_pM$, is identified with $T_pM$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{The Tangent Bundle}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[The Zero Section of $TM$]\deflabel{def:tb-zero-section}
The \textbf{zero section} of the tangent bundle is
\[
\zeta : M \longrightarrow TM, \qquad \zeta(p) = (p, 0) .
\]
It is one-to-one because every tangent space has a distinguished element, its zero.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{The Tangent Bundle}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}[The Picture Changes]\label{rem:picture-changes}
``There are several psychological inflection steps that one needs to make. The most important one is that we're going to think of $TM$ as fibering over $M$.'' A tangent space is usually drawn touching $M$, lying along it. In the bundle picture it stands \emph{vertically}, as the fibre over its point, and $M$ itself sits horizontally inside $TM$ as the zero section --- the tangent spaces become ``transversal'' to it.
\end{rembox}

The tangent bundle as a fibration. Each fibre $\pi^{-1}(p) = T_pM$ is a vertical line over $p$ (in general a copy of $\mathbb{R}^m$); the point $(p, v)$ lies on it, and the zero section $\zeta$ lifts each $p$ straight up to $(p, 0)$, placing a copy of $M$ horizontally inside $TM$.


\textit{Status.} Proposition~\ref{prop:tangent-bundle-claim}, below, was stated in Lecture~12 --- ``the claim, which takes a lot of detail to prove'' --- and made precise in Lecture~13 (\ref{sub:tb-charts}), which wrote down the charts. Their idea was given: a chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ of $M$ gives the basis $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ of every $T_pM$, $p \in U$, hence an identification of each of these tangent spaces with $\mathbb{R}^m$; ``putting all that together gives us a map'' $\pi^{-1}(U) \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2m}$, the chart of $TM$. The dimension $2m$ is $m$ coordinates for the point and $m$ for the vector.

\subsection{Trivializations and Charts}\label{sub:tb-charts}

\textit{Lecture 13. ``Back to the tangent bundle.'' $TM$ has been defined as a set; its charts come from charts of $M$ and the coordinate bases.}

\begin{defbox}[Local Trivializations of $TM$]\deflabel{def:tb-charts}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ be a smooth chart of $M$, and $TU = \pi^{-1}(U) = \{(p, v) \in TM : p \in U\}$, the tangent vectors at points of $U$. The \textbf{local trivialization} over $U$ is
\[
\Phi : TU \longrightarrow U \times \mathbb{R}^m, \qquad \Phi(p, v) = (p, v^1, \ldots, v^m), \qquad \text{where } v = \sum_{i=1}^m v^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p ,
\]
the components of $v$ in the coordinate basis (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). It is a bijection, and $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \Phi = \pi$ --- ``that's why I call it a trivialization.''
\leeref{Proposition 3.18}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Charts of $TM$]\deflabel{def:tb-chart}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and $\Phi$ the local trivialization over $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-charts}). The \textbf{chart} of $TM$ over $U$ is $\tilde\varphi = (\varphi \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \Phi : TU \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2m}$, which acts in two steps:
\[
(p, v) \;\overset{\Phi}{\longmapsto}\; (p,\, v^1, \ldots, v^m) \;\overset{\varphi \times \mathrm{id}}{\longmapsto}\; \big(x^1(p), \ldots, x^m(p),\, v^1, \ldots, v^m\big),
\]
where $v^1, \ldots, v^m$ are the components of $v$ in the coordinate basis at $p$,
\[
v = \sum_{i=1}^m v^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p, \qquad v^i = v[x^i]
\]
(the universal formula, Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). So the first $m$ coordinates of $\tilde\varphi(p, v)$ locate the point $p$, and the last $m$ list the components of the vector $v$. $\tilde\varphi$ is a bijection, with inverse
\[
(r, a^1, \ldots, a^m) \longmapsto \Big(\varphi^{-1}(r),\ \sum_{i=1}^m a^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_{\varphi^{-1}(r)}\Big), \qquad r \in \varphi(U),\ (a^1, \ldots, a^m) \in \mathbb{R}^m .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 3.18}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4.6em, row sep=3em]
TU \arrow[r, "\Phi"] \arrow[dr, "\pi"'] \arrow[rr, bend left=28, "\tilde\varphi"] & U \times \mathbb{R}^m \arrow[r, "\varphi \times \mathrm{id}"] \arrow[d, "\mathrm{pr}_1"] & \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2m} \\
& U &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The trivialization and the chart, as on the board. The triangle commutes, $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \Phi = \pi$ --- the fibration diagram of Definition~\ref{def:fibration} --- and the chart $\tilde\varphi$ is $\Phi$ followed by $\varphi$ on the first factor.

\begin{lembox}[Building a Manifold from Charts]\thmlabel{lem:chart-lemma}
Let $X$ be a set and $n \ge 0$ an integer. Suppose given subsets $U_\alpha \subseteq X$, indexed by $\alpha$ in some set $A$, and injective maps $\varphi_\alpha : U_\alpha \to \mathbb{R}^n$, such that:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item each $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$;
    \item each $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$, $\alpha, \beta \in A$, is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$;
    \item each map $\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1} : \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta) \to \varphi_\beta(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$, $\alpha, \beta \in A$, is smooth;
    \item countably many of the sets $U_\alpha$ cover $X$;
    \item for distinct points $p, q \in X$, either some $U_\alpha$ contains both, or there are disjoint sets $U_\alpha \ni p$ and $U_\beta \ni q$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $X$ has a unique topology for which every $U_\alpha$ is open and every $\varphi_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism of $U_\alpha$ onto $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$. With it, $X$ is a topological manifold of dimension $n$, and the charts $(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)$ form a smooth atlas on $X$, so they determine a smooth structure (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}).
\leeref{Lemma 1.35}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture: Lee's smooth manifold chart lemma. Lecture~13 called the construction of the topology of $TM$ ``all point-set topology \ldots\ see Lee''. The argument is written once here, in general, and applied to $TM$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-topology} and to $T^*M$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:ctb-topology}.)} Three things have to be shown: a topology with the two stated properties exists; it is the only one; and with it $X$ is second countable, Hausdorff and locally Euclidean of dimension $n$ (Definition~\ref{def:manifold}), with the $(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)$ a smooth atlas.

\emph{The transition maps are homeomorphisms.} Let $\alpha, \beta \in A$. Since $\varphi_\alpha$ and $\varphi_\beta$ are injective, $\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}$ is a bijection of $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$ onto $\varphi_\beta(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$, both open by (2), with inverse $\varphi_\alpha \circ \varphi_\beta^{-1}$. Both maps are smooth by (3) (the second with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ exchanged), hence continuous; so each transition map is a homeomorphism between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

\emph{The topology.} Declare $W \subseteq X$ open if $\varphi_\alpha(W \cap U_\alpha)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$ for every $\alpha \in A$, and call the collection of these sets $\tau$. It is a topology; the three axioms are checked chart by chart.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\emptyset \in \tau$, since $\varphi_\alpha(\emptyset) = \emptyset$; and $X \in \tau$, since $\varphi_\alpha(X \cap U_\alpha) = \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$ is open by (1).
    \item For any family $W_\lambda \in \tau$, images under any map commute with unions, so $\varphi_\alpha\big((\bigcup_\lambda W_\lambda) \cap U_\alpha\big) = \bigcup_\lambda \varphi_\alpha(W_\lambda \cap U_\alpha)$, a union of open sets.
    \item For $W_1, W_2 \in \tau$, an injective map carries intersections to intersections, and $\varphi_\alpha$ is injective, so $\varphi_\alpha(W_1 \cap W_2 \cap U_\alpha) = \varphi_\alpha(W_1 \cap U_\alpha) \cap \varphi_\alpha(W_2 \cap U_\alpha)$, an intersection of two open sets.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Each $U_\alpha$ is open.} For every $\beta \in A$, $\varphi_\beta(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$ is open by (2). So $U_\alpha \in \tau$.

\emph{Each $\varphi_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism onto the open set $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$.} Give $U_\alpha$ the subspace topology. $\varphi_\alpha : U_\alpha \to \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$ is a bijection; it remains to show that it is open and continuous.

\emph{Open:} if $W \subseteq U_\alpha$ is open in $U_\alpha$, then $W$ is open in $X$, because $U_\alpha$ is open (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}); so, by the definition of $\tau$ applied with $\alpha$, $\varphi_\alpha(W) = \varphi_\alpha(W \cap U_\alpha)$ is open.

\emph{Continuous:} let $O \subseteq \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$ be open and $W = \varphi_\alpha^{-1}(O) \subseteq U_\alpha$. For any $\beta \in A$, the set $W \cap U_\beta$ consists of the points of $U_\alpha \cap U_\beta$ whose image under $\varphi_\alpha$ lies in $O$, so $\varphi_\alpha(W \cap U_\beta) = O \cap \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$, and therefore
\[
\varphi_\beta(W \cap U_\beta) = \big(\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}\big)\Big(O \cap \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)\Big).
\]
The set in parentheses is open (an intersection of two open sets) and lies in the domain of the transition map; a homeomorphism carries it to a set open in the target $\varphi_\beta(U_\alpha \cap U_\beta)$, which is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$, so the image is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}). This holds for every $\beta$, so $W \in \tau$; as $W \subseteq U_\alpha$, it is open in $U_\alpha$. A continuous open bijection is a homeomorphism.

\emph{Uniqueness.} Let $\tau'$ be any topology in which every $U_\alpha$ is open and every $\varphi_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism onto its image; we show $\tau' = \tau$. If $W \in \tau'$, then for each $\alpha$, $W \cap U_\alpha$ is open in $U_\alpha$ (subspace topology of $\tau'$), so its image $\varphi_\alpha(W \cap U_\alpha)$ under the homeomorphism $\varphi_\alpha$ is open in $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$, hence in $\mathbb{R}^n$; so $W \in \tau$. Conversely, let $W \in \tau$. For each $\alpha$, $\varphi_\alpha(W \cap U_\alpha)$ is open, so $W \cap U_\alpha = \varphi_\alpha^{-1}\big(\varphi_\alpha(W \cap U_\alpha)\big)$ is open in $U_\alpha$ for $\tau'$, by continuity of $\varphi_\alpha$; it is then open in $X$ for $\tau'$, since $U_\alpha \in \tau'$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}). The $U_\alpha$ cover $X$ by (4), so $W = \bigcup_\alpha (W \cap U_\alpha)$, a union of members of $\tau'$; hence $W \in \tau'$.

\emph{Locally Euclidean.} Let $p \in X$. By (4), $p$ lies in some $U_\alpha$, which is open, and $\varphi_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism of $U_\alpha$ onto the open subset $\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha)$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$. This is Definition~\ref{def:locally-euclidean}.

\emph{Hausdorff.} Let $p \ne q$ in $X$; we need disjoint open sets containing them (Definition~\ref{def:hausdorff-t2}). By (5) there are two cases. \emph{Both lie in one $U_\alpha$.} Their images under the injective map $\varphi_\alpha$ are distinct points of the Hausdorff space $\mathbb{R}^n$, so they have disjoint open neighbourhoods $O_1$, $O_2$. The sets $\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(O_1 \cap \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha))$ and $\varphi_\alpha^{-1}(O_2 \cap \varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha))$ are disjoint, contain $p$ and $q$ respectively, and are open in $U_\alpha$ by continuity of $\varphi_\alpha$, hence open in $X$ because $U_\alpha$ is (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}). \emph{Disjoint $U_\alpha \ni p$ and $U_\beta \ni q$.} These are the required open sets.

\emph{Second countable.} By (4) there are $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots \in A$ with $X = \bigcup_k U_{\alpha_k}$. Each $U_{\alpha_k}$ is homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, which has a countable basis (for instance the balls with rational centres and rational radii contained in it), so $U_{\alpha_k}$ has a countable basis $\mathcal{C}_k$, whose members are open in $U_{\alpha_k}$ and hence in $X$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:open-in-open}). The union $\mathcal{C} = \bigcup_k \mathcal{C}_k$ is a countable union of countable sets, so countable. It is a basis of $X$ (Definition~\ref{def:basis}): if $W$ is open in $X$ and $p \in W$, choose $k$ with $p \in U_{\alpha_k}$; then $W \cap U_{\alpha_k}$ is open in $U_{\alpha_k}$ and contains $p$, so some $C \in \mathcal{C}_k$ has $p \in C \subseteq W \cap U_{\alpha_k} \subseteq W$ (Definition~\ref{def:second-countable}).

\emph{The smooth atlas.} Each $(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)$ is a chart of the topological manifold $X$: a homeomorphism of an open set onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$. The domains cover $X$ by (4), and any two charts are $C^\infty$-compatible (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}), because each transition map $\varphi_\beta \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}$ is smooth with smooth inverse $\varphi_\alpha \circ \varphi_\beta^{-1}$ by (3), a diffeomorphism between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}). So the charts form a smooth atlas (Definition~\ref{def:atlas}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Transition Maps of $TM$]\thmlabel{prop:tb-atlas}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^i))$ and $(V, \psi = (y^j))$ be smooth charts of $M$. Then $\tilde\varphi(TU \cap TV) = \varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$, an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$, and the transition map is
\[
\tilde\psi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}(r, v) = \Big( \psi \circ \varphi^{-1}(r), \ \ \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{\partial y^1}{\partial x^j}\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big)\, v^j, \ \ldots, \ \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{\partial y^m}{\partial x^j}\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big)\, v^j \Big) .
\]
In matrix form, the last $m$ components are the column $v$ multiplied by the Jacobian $\big[\partial y^i/\partial x^j\big]$ of the change of coordinates (row $i$, column $j$), evaluated at $\varphi^{-1}(r)$:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial y^1}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial y^1}{\partial x^m} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial y^m}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial y^m}{\partial x^m}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} v^1 \\ \vdots \\ v^m \end{pmatrix} .
\]
It is a diffeomorphism of $\varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ onto $\psi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$. No topology on $TM$ is used: the statement concerns only the bijections $\tilde\varphi$, $\tilde\psi$ of Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}.
\leeref{Proposition 3.18}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~13: ``the only thing that I want to have a look at is \ldots\ the transition functions of the atlas, because this is how people handle tangent vectors.'' Completed here.)} Three things have to be shown: the domain and target of the transition map; its formula; and that it is a diffeomorphism, that is (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}), smooth with smooth inverse.

\emph{The domain of the transition map.} A point $(p, v)$ lies in $TU \cap TV$ exactly when $p \in U \cap V$; for such $p$ every list of components $(v^1, \ldots, v^m) \in \mathbb{R}^m$ occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). So the domain is $\tilde\varphi(TU \cap TV) = \varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$, open in $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ since $\varphi(U \cap V)$ is open (Proposition~\ref{prop:transition-homeo}); likewise the target is $\psi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$.

\emph{The formula.} Let $(r, v) = (r, v^1, \ldots, v^m)$ be a point of the domain and $p = \varphi^{-1}(r) \in U \cap V$. By the inverse formula of Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}, $\tilde\varphi^{-1}(r, v) = (p, u)$ with $u \in T_pM$ the tangent vector whose components in the basis $\partial/\partial x^j|_p$ are the $v^j$. Write $u$ in both bases (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}):
\[
u = \sum_j v^j \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p = \sum_i w^i \frac{\partial}{\partial y^i}\Big|_p .
\]
By Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart} for the chart $\psi$, $\tilde\psi(p, u) = \big(\psi(p), w^1, \ldots, w^m\big)$, and $\psi(p) = \psi \circ \varphi^{-1}(r)$; so the first component of the transition is $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$, smooth because the charts of $M$ are compatible. For the rest we need the $w$'s in terms of the $v$'s: ``a change of basis formula from 217, which I always forget.'' By the universal formula (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}) in the chart $\psi$, the $i$-th coefficient of a derivation $D$ in the basis $\partial/\partial y^i|_p$ is $D[y^i]$. Applied to $D = \partial/\partial x^j|_p$, whose value on $y^i$ is $\partial y^i/\partial x^j(p)$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}), it gives the change of basis formula
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p = \sum_i \frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}(p) \frac{\partial}{\partial y^i}\Big|_p .
\]
Substitute this into the first expression for $u$ and collect terms, using that derivations are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}):
\[
u = \sum_j v^j \sum_i \frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}(p) \frac{\partial}{\partial y^i}\Big|_p = \sum_i \Big( \sum_j \frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}(p)\, v^j \Big) \frac{\partial}{\partial y^i}\Big|_p .
\]
The coefficients of $u$ in the basis $\partial/\partial y^i|_p$ are unique, so comparing with $u = \sum_i w^i\, \partial/\partial y^i|_p$,
\[
w^i = \sum_j \frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}(p)\, v^j .
\]
(In lecture Uribe expanded $\partial/\partial y^j$ in the other basis and first solved for the $v$'s --- ``I did it backwards'' --- then took the other direction ``by the same argument''.) With $p = \varphi^{-1}(r)$ this is the displayed formula.

\emph{Smoothness.} The coefficients are smooth functions of $r$. Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs} to $F = \mathrm{id}_M$, with the chart $(U \cap V, \varphi|_{U \cap V})$ on the source and $(V, \psi)$ on the target (so $F(U \cap V) \subseteq V$): then $F^i = y^i$ and the coordinate representation is $\tau = \psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ on $\varphi(U \cap V)$, and it gives
\[
\frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big) = \frac{\partial \tau^i}{\partial r^j}(r) ,
\]
the entries of the Jacobian $\tau'(r)$ of the transition map of $M$. (Restricting the chart to $U \cap V$ does not change partial derivatives at points of $U \cap V$: the coordinate representation of a function only gets restricted to an open set around $\varphi(p)$.) So the transition map of $TM$ is
\[
(r, v) \longmapsto \big(\tau(r),\ \tau'(r)\, v\big), \qquad \tau = \psi \circ \varphi^{-1} .
\]
Its first $m$ components $\tau^i(r)$ are smooth because $\tau$ is; its last $m$ components $\sum_j \partial\tau^i/\partial r^j(r)\, v^j$ are sums of products of the smooth functions $\partial\tau^i/\partial r^j(r)$ with the coordinate functions $v^j$, hence smooth in $(r, v)$. A map into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ is smooth if all its components are, so $\tilde\psi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}$ is smooth.

\emph{The inverse.} The inverse of $\tilde\psi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}$ is $\tilde\varphi \circ \tilde\psi^{-1}$, and the computation above with the names exchanged --- $(U, \varphi, x^i)$ and $(V, \psi, y^i)$ swapped --- shows that it is $(s, w) \mapsto \big(\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}(s), (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1})'(s)\, w\big)$, smooth. So every transition map is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}).
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5.4em, row sep=3em]
& TU \cap TV \arrow[dl, "\tilde\varphi"'] \arrow[dr, "\tilde\psi"] & \\
\varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m \arrow[rr, "{(r, v) \,\mapsto\, (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}(r),\ (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})'(r)\, v)}"'] & & \psi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The transition map of the charts $\tilde\varphi$ and $\tilde\psi$ of $TM$, as drawn in lecture over a point $(p, v)$ of $TU \cap TV$.

The transition map of $TM$, in one line: the base point moves by the transition map of $M$, and the vector by its Jacobian. This is Uribe's identity at work once more --- the partials $\partial y^i/\partial x^j$, taken upstairs on $M$, are the Jacobian downstairs.

\begin{propbox}[The Topology and Smooth Structure of $TM$]\thmlabel{prop:tb-topology}
There is a unique topology on $TM$ for which every $TU$ is open and every chart $\tilde\varphi : TU \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ is a homeomorphism. With it, $TM$ is a topological manifold of dimension $2m$, and the charts $(TU, \tilde\varphi)$, as $(U, \varphi)$ ranges over the smooth charts of $M$, form a smooth atlas on it.
\leeref{Lemma 1.35 and Proposition 3.18}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~13 without proof --- ``it's all point-set topology, and of course everything is in Lee \ldots\ see Lee''; filled in.)} Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-lemma} with $X = TM$, $n = 2m$, and the sets $TU$ with the maps $\tilde\varphi$, indexed by the smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$. Each $\tilde\varphi$ is injective, being a bijection of $TU$ onto $\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}). We check the five conditions of the lemma.

\emph{(1) and (2).} By Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-atlas}, $\tilde\varphi(TU \cap TV) = \varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ for any two charts; this is (2), and with $V = U$ it is (1), $\tilde\varphi(TU) = \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$.

\emph{(3)} Each transition map $\tilde\psi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}$ is smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-atlas}.

\emph{(4)} Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a countable basis of $M$ (Definition~\ref{def:second-countable}). For each $B \in \mathcal{B}$ contained in some chart domain, choose one such chart $(U_B, \varphi_B)$, so $B \subseteq U_B$. These countably many charts cover $M$: each $p$ lies in some chart domain $U$, and then, by Definition~\ref{def:basis}, in some $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $p \in B \subseteq U$; this $B$ is contained in a chart domain, so $(U_B, \varphi_B)$ was chosen, and $p \in B \subseteq U_B$. A point $(p, v) \in TM$ lies in $TU_B$ for any $B$ with $p \in U_B$, so the countably many sets $TU_B$ cover $TM$.

\emph{(5)} Let $(p, v) \ne (q, w)$. \emph{Case $p = q$.} Both points lie in $TU$ for any chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$. \emph{Case $p \ne q$.} $M$ is Hausdorff, so there are disjoint open sets $U_0 \ni p$ and $V_0 \ni q$. Take charts $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi)$ at $q$ and shrink their domains to $U \cap U_0$ and $V \cap V_0$; the restrictions are still smooth charts (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1), applied to the open subsets $U \cap U_0 \subseteq U$ and $V \cap V_0 \subseteq V$; their transition maps are restrictions of those of $\varphi$ and $\psi$ to open subsets). Then $T(U \cap U_0) \ni (p, v)$ and $T(V \cap V_0) \ni (q, w)$ are disjoint: a common point $(x, u)$ would have $x \in U_0 \cap V_0 = \emptyset$.

So Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-lemma} applies: $TM$ has a unique topology in which every $TU$ is open and every $\tilde\varphi$ is a homeomorphism onto $\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$; with it, $TM$ is a topological manifold of dimension $2m$, and the charts $(TU, \tilde\varphi)$ form a smooth atlas.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-lemma} builds the topology and smooth structure of the cotangent bundle (\ref{sub:cotangent-bundle}) in the same way, with the dual bases in place of the coordinate bases (Proposition~\ref{prop:ctb-topology}).

\begin{corbox}[The Tangent Bundle Is a Fibration]\thmlabel{cor:tb-fibration}
With the smooth structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-topology}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $TM$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $2m$, and $\pi : TM \to M$ is smooth;
    \item the $\Phi$ are local trivializations, so $\pi$ is a fibration with fibre $\mathbb{R}^m$, and each $\Phi$ restricts on the fibre $T_pM$ to a linear isomorphism $T_pM \to \{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^m$;
    \item the image $\zeta(M)$ of the zero section is a submanifold of $TM$ of codimension $m$.
\end{enumerate}
With Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-topology}, this proves Proposition~\ref{prop:tangent-bundle-claim} below in full.
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{((1) and (2) are the lecture's observations --- ``in these coordinates, the projection is just projection onto the first $m$ components \ldots\ so we get a beautiful fibration''; the details and (3) are filled in.)}

\emph{(1)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-topology}, $TM$ is a topological manifold of dimension $2m$ and the charts $(TU, \tilde\varphi)$ form a smooth atlas on it; so $TM$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $2m$, with the smooth structure determined by this atlas (Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-atlas}). To see that $\pi$ is smooth, check Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}. \emph{Continuity:} on each open set $TU$, by Definitions~\ref{def:tb-projection} and~\ref{def:tb-chart}, $\pi = \varphi^{-1} \circ \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \tilde\varphi$ with $\mathrm{pr}_1(r, v) = r$, a composite of continuous maps; the open sets $TU$ cover $TM$, so $\pi$ is continuous. \emph{Coordinate representation:} for $(p, v) \in TM$ take a chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$; then $(TU, \tilde\varphi)$ is a chart at $(p, v)$ with $\pi(TU) \subseteq U$, and for $(r, v) \in \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$, with $\tilde\varphi^{-1}(r, v) = (\varphi^{-1}(r), u)$ for some $u$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}),
\[
\varphi \circ \pi \circ \tilde\varphi^{-1}(r, v) = \varphi\big(\pi(\varphi^{-1}(r), u)\big) = \varphi\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big) = r .
\]
So in the charts $\tilde\varphi$ and $\varphi$, $\pi$ is $(r, v) \mapsto r$, a linear projection, which is smooth.

\emph{(2)} By Definition~\ref{def:fibration} we need an open cover of $M$ and, over each member $U$, a diffeomorphism $\pi^{-1}(U) = TU \to U \times \mathbb{R}^m$ commuting with the projections. Take the chart domains $U$, which cover $M$, and the maps $\Phi$ of Definition~\ref{def:tb-charts}. Since $\tilde\varphi = (\varphi \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \Phi$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}) and $\varphi \times \mathrm{id} : U \times \mathbb{R}^m \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ is a bijection with inverse $\varphi^{-1} \times \mathrm{id}$,
\[
\Phi = (\varphi^{-1} \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \tilde\varphi .
\]
Both factors are diffeomorphisms (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}): $\tilde\varphi$ is a chart of the smooth manifold $TU$, and $\varphi^{-1} \times \mathrm{id}$ is the inverse of the product chart $\varphi \times \mathrm{id}$ of the product manifold $U \times \mathbb{R}^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:product-manifold}, with the chart $\mathrm{id}$ of $\mathbb{R}^m$). A composite of diffeomorphisms is a diffeomorphism, since the composite and its inverse are composites of smooth maps (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). And for $(p, v) \in TU$, $\mathrm{pr}_1(\Phi(p, v)) = \mathrm{pr}_1(p, v^1, \ldots, v^m) = p = \pi(p, v)$, so $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \Phi = \pi$ on $TU$. Hence $\pi$ is a fibration with fibre $\mathbb{R}^m$.

\emph{Linearity on fibres.} Fix $p \in U$. On $T_pM$ (that is, on the fibre $\{p\} \times T_pM$), $\Phi$ is $v \mapsto (p, v^1, \ldots, v^m)$ with $v^i = v[x^i]$ (universal formula, Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). Each $v \mapsto v[x^i]$ is linear, because tangent vectors are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}): $(av + bw)[x^i] = a\,v[x^i] + b\,w[x^i]$. It is bijective onto $\mathbb{R}^m$ because the $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ form a basis (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}): the components of $v$ exist and are unique, and every list $(a^1, \ldots, a^m)$ is the list of components of $\sum_i a^i\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p$. So taking components in a basis is a linear isomorphism $T_pM \to \{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^m$.

\emph{(3)} By Definition~\ref{def:submanifold} (with $2m$ coordinates and $k = m$), it suffices to find, around each point of $\zeta(M)$, a smooth chart of $TM$ in which $\zeta(M)$ is cut out by the vanishing of the last $m$ coordinates. A point of $\zeta(M)$ is $\zeta(p) = (p, 0)$; take a chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$, so $(p, 0) \in TU$. A point $\zeta(q) = (q, 0)$ lies in $TU$ exactly when $q \in U$, so $\zeta(M) \cap TU = \{(q, 0) : q \in U\}$. For $(q, v) \in TU$, the last $m$ coordinates of $\tilde\varphi(q, v)$ are $v^i = v[x^i]$, and by the universal formula $v = \sum_i v^i\, \partial/\partial x^i|_q$, so $v = 0$ exactly when $v^1 = \cdots = v^m = 0$. Hence
\[
\zeta(M) \cap TU = \{\, (q, v) \in TU : v^1 = \cdots = v^m = 0 \,\},
\]
so the charts $\tilde\varphi$ are adapted to $\zeta(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}), and $\zeta(M)$ is a submanifold of codimension $m$.
\end{proof}
\begin{propbox}[The Tangent Bundle Is a Manifold (Claim)]\thmlabel{prop:tangent-bundle-claim}
$TM$ has a natural topology and smooth structure making it a smooth manifold of dimension $2m$, for which $\pi : TM \to M$ is a fibration with fibre $\mathbb{R}^m$, and the image $\zeta(M)$ of the zero section is a submanifold of $TM$.
\leeref{Proposition 3.18}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof]
Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-topology} gives the topology, and Corollary~\ref{cor:tb-fibration} the smooth structure, the fibration with fibre $\mathbb{R}^m$, and the zero section as a submanifold.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Vector Bundles]\label{rem:vector-bundles}
$TM$ is in fact a \emph{vector bundle}: a fibration whose fibres are vector spaces, with trivializations that are linear isomorphisms on each fibre. Uribe postponed the general definition --- ``it takes another 10 minutes of axioms'' --- but these are the two features: ``the fibres are abstract vector spaces, and you can find trivializations which restrict to linear isomorphisms fibrewise.'' Vector bundles are ``fun objects'' in their own right; K-theory is built from them.
\end{rembox}

\begin{rembox}[Trivializations and Frames]\label{rem:same-principle-elsewhere}
Proposition~\ref{prop:trivialization-section} turns local trivializations into local sections. For the tangent bundle the dictionary is between trivializations and \emph{frames}: the trivialization $\Phi$ of a chart (Definition~\ref{def:tb-charts}) corresponds to the $m$ local sections $u \mapsto \partial/\partial x^i|_u$, since $\Phi^{-1}(u, e_i) = \partial/\partial x^i|_u$; for a vector bundle of rank $m$ one local section is not enough, and it takes $m$ sections that are linearly independent at every point (Lee, Example~10.18 and Proposition~10.19). For the Hopf fibration one section suffices because the fibre is a single orbit of the free $S^1$-action. That is the general pattern of \emph{principal bundles}, where a group acts freely and transitively on each fibre; it is stated here, not proved.
\end{rembox}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: THE COTANGENT BUNDLE
% ============================================================================

\section{The Cotangent Bundle}\label{sec:cotangent-bundle}\label{sub:cotangent-bundle}

\roadmark{Stage: bundles}{The cotangent spaces assembled into $T^*M$, with charts from the dual bases; covector components transform by the inverse transpose.}

\textit{Lecture 13 defined the cotangent bundle --- ``completely analogous'' to the tangent bundle, with the dual bases in place of the coordinate bases; Lecture 15 returned to it for the homework.}

\begin{defbox}[The Cotangent Bundle as a Set]\deflabel{def:cotangent-bundle}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Its \textbf{cotangent bundle} is the set
\[
T^*M = \bigcup_{p \in M} \{p\} \times T_p^*M = \{\, (p, \xi) : p \in M,\ \xi \in T_p^*M \,\},
\]
all the cotangent spaces (Definition~\ref{def:cotangent}) put together.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{The Cotangent Bundle}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[The Projection of $T^*M$]\deflabel{def:ctb-projection}
The \textbf{projection} of the cotangent bundle is
\[
\pi : T^*M \longrightarrow M, \qquad \pi(p, \xi) = p .
\]
Its fibre over $p$, $\pi^{-1}(p) = \{p\} \times T_p^*M$, is identified with $T_p^*M$.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{The Cotangent Bundle}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[The Zero Section of $T^*M$]\deflabel{def:ctb-zero-section}
The \textbf{zero section} of the cotangent bundle is
\[
\zeta : M \longrightarrow T^*M, \qquad \zeta(p) = (p, 0) .
\]
It is one-to-one, as for $TM$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-zero-section}): every cotangent space has a distinguished element, its zero.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{The Cotangent Bundle}}
\end{defbox}

The definitions and results of this section run parallel to those for the tangent bundle in \ref{sec:tangent-bundle}, item for item, with the dual bases $dx^i|_p$ in place of the coordinate bases $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$. Lecture~13 gave the charts and the transition maps; the rest is filled in, following Section~\ref{sec:tangent-bundle}.

\subsection{Trivializations and Charts}\label{sub:ctb-charts}

\begin{defbox}[Local Trivializations of $T^*M$]\deflabel{def:ctb-trivialization}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ be a smooth chart of $M$, and $T^*U = \pi^{-1}(U) = \{(p, \xi) \in T^*M : p \in U\}$, the covectors at points of $U$. The \textbf{local trivialization} of $T^*M$ over $U$ is
\[
\Psi : T^*U \longrightarrow U \times \mathbb{R}^m, \qquad \Psi(p, \xi) = (p, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m), \qquad \text{where } \xi = \sum_{i=1}^m \xi_i\, dx^i\big|_p ,
\]
the components of $\xi$ in the dual basis. Because the bases $dx^i|_p$ and $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ are dual to each other, the components are computed by evaluation, $\xi_i = \xi\big(\partial/\partial x^i|_p\big)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}). $\Psi$ is a bijection, and $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \Psi = \pi$.
\leeref{Proposition 11.9}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Charts of $T^*M$]\deflabel{def:ctb-chart}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and $\Psi$ the local trivialization over $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:ctb-trivialization}). The \textbf{chart} of $T^*M$ over $U$ --- the \textbf{standard coordinates} on $T^*U$ --- is $\hat\varphi = (\varphi \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \Psi : T^*U \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2m}$, which acts in two steps:
\[
(p, \xi) \;\overset{\Psi}{\longmapsto}\; (p,\, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m) \;\overset{\varphi \times \mathrm{id}}{\longmapsto}\; \big(x^1(p), \ldots, x^m(p),\, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m\big),
\]
where $\xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m$ are the components of $\xi$ in the dual basis at $p$,
\[
\xi = \sum_{i=1}^m \xi_i\, dx^i\big|_p, \qquad \xi_i = \xi\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big)
\]
(Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}). So the first $m$ coordinates of $\hat\varphi(p, \xi)$ locate the point $p$, and the last $m$ list the components of the covector $\xi$. $\hat\varphi$ is a bijection, with inverse
\[
(r, b_1, \ldots, b_m) \longmapsto \Big(\varphi^{-1}(r),\ \sum_{i=1}^m b_i\, dx^i\big|_{\varphi^{-1}(r)}\Big), \qquad r \in \varphi(U),\ (b_1, \ldots, b_m) \in \mathbb{R}^m .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 11.9}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[The Transition Maps of $T^*M$]\thmlabel{prop:cotangent-transition}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^i))$ and $(V, \psi = (y^j))$ be smooth charts of $M$. Then $\hat\varphi(T^*U \cap T^*V) = \varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$, an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$. For $p \in U \cap V$, if $\xi = \sum_i \xi_i\, dx^i|_p = \sum_j \eta_j\, dy^j|_p$, then
\[
dx^i|_p = \sum_j \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^j}(p)\, dy^j|_p, \qquad \eta_j = \sum_i \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^j}(p)\, \xi_i .
\]
In matrix form, with row index $j$ and column index $i$,
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \eta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \eta_m \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial x^1}{\partial y^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial x^m}{\partial y^1}(p) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial x^1}{\partial y^m}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial x^m}{\partial y^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \xi_1 \\ \vdots \\ \xi_m \end{pmatrix} ,
\]
the matrix being the transpose of $\big[\partial x^i/\partial y^j(p)\big]$ (row $i$, column $j$).
So the covector components transform by the transpose of the inverse of the matrix that transforms tangent components: with $\tau = \psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$, the transition map is
\[
\hat\psi \circ \hat\varphi^{-1}(r, \xi) = \Big( \tau(r),\ \big(\tau'(r)^{-1}\big)^{\mathsf T} \xi \Big) ,
\]
a diffeomorphism of $\varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ onto $\psi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$. No topology on $T^*M$ is used.
\leeref{Proposition 11.9}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~13: ``completely analogous'', with the change ``we use the dual basis'', and the formula for $dx^i$ given; the rest is filled in.)} Fix $p \in U \cap V$. Four things are to be shown, in order: the formula for $dx^i|_p$; the formula for $\eta_j$; that $\big[\partial x^i/\partial y^j(p)\big]$ is the inverse of $\big[\partial y^i/\partial x^j(p)\big]$, which gives the transition map; and that the transition maps are diffeomorphisms.

\emph{The formula for $dx^i|_p$.} It is Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} applied to the function $f = x^i$, smooth near $p$, in the chart $\psi = (y^1, \ldots, y^m)$ at $p$: the lemma gives $d(x^i)_p = \sum_j \partial x^i/\partial y^j(p)\, dy^j|_p$.

\emph{The formula for $\eta_j$.} Substituting it into $\sum_i \xi_i\, dx^i|_p$ and collecting terms (covectors are added and scaled pointwise, Definition~\ref{def:dual}),
\[
\xi = \sum_i \xi_i\, dx^i\big|_p = \sum_i \xi_i \sum_j \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^j}(p)\, dy^j\big|_p = \sum_j \Big( \sum_i \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^j}(p)\, \xi_i \Big)\, dy^j\big|_p .
\]
The $dy^j|_p$ form a basis of $T_p^*M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} for the chart $\psi$), so the coefficients of $\xi$ in it are unique; comparing coefficients of $dy^j|_p$ with $\xi = \sum_j \eta_j\, dy^j|_p$ gives $\eta_j = \sum_i \partial x^i/\partial y^j(p)\, \xi_i$.

\emph{The inverse matrix.} Write $A = \big[\partial y^i/\partial x^j(p)\big]$ (row $i$, column $j$) and $B = \big[\partial x^i/\partial y^j(p)\big]$. Written out,
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial y^1}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial y^1}{\partial x^m}(p) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial y^m}{\partial x^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial y^m}{\partial x^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial x^1}{\partial y^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial x^1}{\partial y^m}(p) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial x^m}{\partial y^1}(p) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial x^m}{\partial y^m}(p)
\end{pmatrix} .
\]
 That $B = A^{-1}$ is the chain rule: Corollary~\ref{cor:change-coords}(3), applied to the two charts $\varphi = (x^i)$ and $\psi = (y^j)$ at $p$, says that $A$ is invertible with inverse $B$. (With the covectors of this section it can also be read off the formula for $dx^i|_p$: evaluating it on $\partial/\partial x^k|_p$ and using $dx^i|_p(\partial/\partial x^k|_p) = \delta^i_k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}) and $dy^j|_p(\partial/\partial x^k|_p) = \partial y^j/\partial x^k(p)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}) gives $\delta^i_k = \sum_j \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^j}(p)\, \frac{\partial y^j}{\partial x^k}(p) = (BA)_{ik}$.) By Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-atlas} the tangent components transform by $A$, $w = Av$; and the formula for $\eta_j$ reads $\eta_j = \sum_i B_{ij}\, \xi_i = (B^{\mathsf T} \xi)_j$, so the covector components transform by $B^{\mathsf T} = (A^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$.

\emph{The transition map.} Explicitly, let $(r, \xi) \in \hat\varphi(T^*U \cap T^*V) = \varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ (an open set, by the same argument as for $TM$ in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-atlas}, with Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} giving the basis $dx^i|_p$) and $p = \varphi^{-1}(r)$. By the inverse formula of Definition~\ref{def:ctb-chart}, $\hat\varphi^{-1}(r, \xi) = \big(p, \sum_i \xi_i\, dx^i|_p\big)$, and by the same definition for $\psi$ and the formula for $\eta$, $\hat\psi$ sends this point to $(\psi(p), \eta) = (\tau(r), B^{\mathsf T}\xi)$. With $p = \varphi^{-1}(r)$, the matrix $A = \big[\partial y^i/\partial x^j(p)\big]$ is $\tau'(r)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs}, applied to $F = \mathrm{id}_M$ exactly as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-atlas}), so $B = \big[\partial x^i/\partial y^j(p)\big] = \tau'(r)^{-1}$ and $\eta = \big(\tau'(r)^{-1}\big)^{\mathsf T}\xi$, which is the displayed transition map.

\emph{Smoothness.} Its entries are smooth in $r$: those of $\tau'(r)$ are, since $\tau$ is smooth (the charts of $M$ are compatible); $\det \tau'(r) \ne 0$ because $\tau'(r)$ is invertible; and the inverse of an invertible matrix is given by Cramer's rule, each entry a polynomial in the entries (a cofactor) divided by the nonzero determinant, hence smooth in $r$. So the first $m$ components $\tau^i(r)$ and the last $m$ components $\sum_i \big(\tau'(r)^{-1}\big)_{ij}\, \xi_i$ of the transition map are smooth in $(r, \xi)$, and the transition maps are smooth, as in Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-atlas}. The inverse transition map $\hat\varphi \circ \hat\psi^{-1}$ is the same formula with the two charts exchanged (rename $(U, \varphi, x^i) \leftrightarrow (V, \psi, y^j)$), hence smooth too, so each transition map is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeo-euclidean}).
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Topology and Smooth Structure of $T^*M$]\thmlabel{prop:ctb-topology}
There is a unique topology on $T^*M$ for which every $T^*U$ is open and every chart $\hat\varphi : T^*U \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ is a homeomorphism. With it, $T^*M$ is a topological manifold of dimension $2m$, and the charts $(T^*U, \hat\varphi)$, as $(U, \varphi)$ ranges over the smooth charts of $M$, form a smooth atlas on it.
\leeref{Lemma 1.35 and Proposition 11.9}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture --- ``completely analogous''; filled in.)} Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-lemma} with $X = T^*M$, $n = 2m$, and the sets $T^*U$ with the maps $\hat\varphi$, indexed by the smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$. Each $\hat\varphi$ is injective, being a bijection of $T^*U$ onto $\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:ctb-chart}). The five conditions:

\emph{(1) and (2).} By Proposition~\ref{prop:cotangent-transition}, $\hat\varphi(T^*U \cap T^*V) = \varphi(U \cap V) \times \mathbb{R}^m$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$; with $V = U$ this is $\hat\varphi(T^*U) = \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$.

\emph{(3)} Each transition map $\hat\psi \circ \hat\varphi^{-1}$ is smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:cotangent-transition}.

\emph{(4)} As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-topology}, a countable basis of $M$ gives countably many charts $(U_B, \varphi_B)$ whose domains cover $M$. A covector $(p, \xi)$ lies in $T^*U_B$ whenever $p \in U_B$, so the countably many sets $T^*U_B$ cover $T^*M$.

\emph{(5)} Let $(p, \xi) \ne (q, \zeta)$. If $p = q$, both lie in $T^*U$ for any chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$. If $p \ne q$, take disjoint open sets $U_0 \ni p$, $V_0 \ni q$ ($M$ is Hausdorff) and charts $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$, $(V, \psi)$ at $q$, shrunk to $U \cap U_0$ and $V \cap V_0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)); then $T^*(U \cap U_0) \ni (p, \xi)$ and $T^*(V \cap V_0) \ni (q, \zeta)$ are disjoint, since a common point $(x, \eta)$ would have $x \in U_0 \cap V_0 = \emptyset$.

So Lemma~\ref{lem:chart-lemma} applies: $T^*M$ has a unique topology in which every $T^*U$ is open and every $\hat\varphi$ is a homeomorphism onto $\varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$; with it, $T^*M$ is a topological manifold of dimension $2m$, and the charts $(T^*U, \hat\varphi)$, whose domains cover $T^*M$, form a smooth atlas. The fibration and linearity statements follow as in Corollary~\ref{cor:tb-fibration}; they are written out in the next corollary.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[The Cotangent Bundle Is a Fibration]\thmlabel{cor:ctb-fibration}
With the smooth structure of Proposition~\ref{prop:ctb-topology}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $T^*M$ is a smooth manifold of dimension $2m$, and $\pi : T^*M \to M$ is smooth; for each smooth chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$, its coordinate representation in the charts $\hat\varphi$ of $T^*M$ (Definition~\ref{def:ctb-chart}) and $\varphi$ of $M$ is $\varphi \circ \pi \circ \hat\varphi^{-1}(r, \xi) = r$, $(r, \xi) \in \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m$;
    \item the $\Psi$ are local trivializations, so $\pi$ is a fibration with fibre $\mathbb{R}^m$, and each $\Psi$ restricts on the fibre $T_p^*M$ to a linear isomorphism $T_p^*M \to \{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^m$; so $T^*M$ is a vector bundle;
    \item the image $\zeta(M)$ of the zero section is a submanifold of $T^*M$ of codimension $m$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 11.9}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, as Corollary~\ref{cor:tb-fibration}.)}

\emph{(1)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:ctb-topology}, $T^*M$ is a topological manifold of dimension $2m$ with a smooth atlas, hence a smooth manifold of dimension $2m$. To see that $\pi$ is smooth, check Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}. \emph{Continuity:} on each open set $T^*U$, $\pi = \varphi^{-1} \circ \mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \hat\varphi$ (Definitions~\ref{def:ctb-projection} and~\ref{def:ctb-chart}), a composite of continuous maps, and the $T^*U$ cover $T^*M$. \emph{Coordinate representation:} for $(p, \xi) \in T^*M$ take a chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$; then $(T^*U, \hat\varphi)$ is a chart at $(p, \xi)$ with $\pi(T^*U) \subseteq U$, and, as $\hat\varphi^{-1}(r, \xi) = \big(\varphi^{-1}(r), \sum_i \xi_i\, dx^i|_{\varphi^{-1}(r)}\big)$,
\[
\varphi \circ \pi \circ \hat\varphi^{-1}(r, \xi) = \varphi\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big) = r .
\]
So in the charts $\hat\varphi$ and $\varphi$, $\pi$ is $(r, \xi) \mapsto r$, which is smooth.

\emph{(2)} By Definition~\ref{def:fibration}, take the open cover of $M$ by chart domains $U$ and the maps $\Psi$ of Definition~\ref{def:ctb-trivialization}. Since $\hat\varphi = (\varphi \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \Psi$ (Definition~\ref{def:ctb-chart}),
\[
\Psi = (\varphi^{-1} \times \mathrm{id}) \circ \hat\varphi ,
\]
a composite of diffeomorphisms (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}: $\hat\varphi$ is a chart of $T^*U$, and $\varphi^{-1} \times \mathrm{id}$ is the inverse of the product chart $\varphi \times \mathrm{id}$ of $U \times \mathbb{R}^m$), hence a diffeomorphism (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}, applied to the composite and to its inverse). For $(p, \xi) \in T^*U$, $\mathrm{pr}_1(\Psi(p, \xi)) = \mathrm{pr}_1(p, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m) = p = \pi(p, \xi)$, so $\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ \Psi = \pi$; the $T^*U$ cover $T^*M$ and the $U$ cover $M$. So $\pi$ is a fibration with fibre $\mathbb{R}^m$.

\emph{Linearity on fibres.} Fix $p \in U$. On $T_p^*M$, $\Psi$ is $\xi \mapsto (p, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m)$ with $\xi_i = \xi(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}), taking components in a basis. Each $\xi \mapsto \xi(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$ is linear, since covectors are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:dual}): $(a\xi + b\zeta)(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = a\,\xi(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) + b\,\zeta(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$. It is bijective onto $\mathbb{R}^m$ because the $dx^i|_p$ form a basis of $T_p^*M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}): the components of $\xi$ exist and are unique, and every list $(b_1, \ldots, b_m)$ is the list of components of $\sum_i b_i\, dx^i|_p$. So $\Psi$ restricts to a linear isomorphism $T_p^*M \to \{p\} \times \mathbb{R}^m$. The fibres are vector spaces and the trivializations are fibrewise linear isomorphisms --- the two features of a vector bundle (the remark \emph{Vector Bundles} in \ref{sec:tangent-bundle}); so $T^*M$ is a vector bundle.

\emph{(3)} A point of $\zeta(M)$ is $\zeta(p) = (p, 0)$; take a chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$, so $(p, 0) \in T^*U$, and $\zeta(M) \cap T^*U = \{(q, 0) : q \in U\}$. For $(q, \xi) \in T^*U$, the last $m$ coordinates of $\hat\varphi(q, \xi)$ are the components $\xi_i$, and $\xi = \sum_i \xi_i\, dx^i|_q$, so $\xi = 0$ exactly when $\xi_1 = \cdots = \xi_m = 0$. Hence, in the chart $\hat\varphi$,
\[
\zeta(M) \cap T^*U = \{\, (q, \xi) \in T^*U : \xi_1 = \cdots = \xi_m = 0 \,\},
\]
so the charts $\hat\varphi$ are adapted to $\zeta(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}), and $\zeta(M)$ is a submanifold of codimension $m$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}, with $2m$ coordinates and $k = m$).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Lecture 15 and the Standard Coordinates}\label{sub:ctb-lecture15}

\textit{Lecture~15 returned to the cotangent bundle --- ``we did define it, but it was all very quick'' --- because the homework uses it: ``the standard coordinates on $T^*M$, which are also trivializations'', with the components found by evaluating on the dual basis, as in Definitions~\ref{def:ctb-trivialization} and~\ref{def:ctb-chart}. He also recalled that the cotangent space has a description from germs, $T_p^*M \cong I_p/I_p^2$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}): ``the cotangent space is, in a way, very extremely natural from the point of view of functions.''}

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page~40 of the handwritten notes writes the standard coordinates as a map on $T^*M$; they are defined on $T^*U$, the part of the bundle over the chart domain, as Uribe corrected in lecture.

``We'll see that the cotangent bundle has a natural structure that the tangent bundle doesn't have.'' $TM$ and $T^*M$ are isomorphic as vector bundles, ``but not naturally isomorphic --- we have to make choices to construct an isomorphism'' (a metric, for instance, as in the remark on conormal spaces). This is stated, not proved, here.

\begin{rembox}[Review Session: The Standard Atlases]\label{rem:review-standard-atlases}
\textit{Review session, Friday Oct 16, in answer to ``can you go over the construction of the atlas for the tangent bundle and cotangent bundle?''} Any manifold has ``some sort of large infinity of coordinate charts''; the \emph{standard} ones are the most useful. Start with any chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
TU = \pi^{-1}(U) &\longrightarrow U \times \mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^m \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2m}, \\
(p, v) &\longmapsto (p, v^1, \ldots, v^m) \longmapsto \big(x^1(p), \ldots, x^m(p), v^1, \ldots, v^m\big),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first arrow is ``in the language of bundles, a trivialization'' (Definitions~\ref{def:tb-charts} and~\ref{def:tb-chart}). ``What makes this thing hard is that I don't have an explicit formula for the $v^i$'' --- they are defined as the coefficients of $v = \sum_i v^i\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p$ --- to which a student answered that there is one, $v^i = v[x^i]$: ``That's true. Thank you. That's very good'' (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}). For $T^*M$ the same, with covectors: $\alpha = \sum_i \alpha_i\, dx^i|_p$, and again ``a dual way of writing what the $\alpha_i$ are'': $\alpha_i = \alpha(\partial/\partial x^i|_p)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components}). There is a unique topology on $TM$ making these charts homeomorphisms (``we didn't prove this; we just accepted it'' in lecture; Proposition~\ref{prop:ctb-topology} for $T^*M$), and the transition functions are smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:cotangent-transition}).

\emph{Coordinates on $T^*M$.} By a ``slight abuse of notation'' the first $m$ components of the chart of $T^*U$ are written $x^1, \ldots, x^m$ again, and the last $m$ are ``traditionally called $p_1, \ldots, p_m$'', $p_i(\alpha) = \alpha_i$ --- the $\xi_i$ of these notes. A student asked about tangent vectors to $T^*M$ and germs on it: ``at this point you have to say, okay, I just have a manifold that has dimension $2m$ \ldots\ and now I apply the general theory'': $\sum_i a^i\, \partial/\partial x^i + \sum_j \beta_j\, \partial/\partial p_j$. ``You can keep taking tangent bundles forever.'' In November, with differential forms, the cotangent bundle will turn out to carry an intrinsically defined two-form, the \emph{symplectic form} --- ``and you who are interested in physics will see how this comes up in Hamiltonian mechanics.''
\end{rembox}

\section{One-Forms}\label{sub:one-forms}\label{sec:d-operator}

\roadmark{Stage: fields}{Smooth sections of $T^*M$, a covector at every point; functions give one-forms through $d$, but not every one-form is a $df$; one-forms pull back along smooth maps, and $d$ commutes with pulling back.}

\textit{Lecture 15. The sections of the cotangent bundle, and the operator $d$ that produces them from functions --- ``which will be the beginning of a chain of operators when we discuss the de Rham cohomology.''}

A one-form is a section of the cotangent bundle (Definition~\ref{def:section}): it picks a covector in every fibre $T_p^*M$. Every vector bundle has sections, the zero section at least --- unlike a general fibration: the Hopf fibration has none (the remark \emph{Sections Need Not Exist} in \ref{sec:ex-hopf}).

\subsection{One-Forms and Their Coordinates}\label{sub:one-forms-def}

\begin{defbox}[One-Form]\deflabel{def:one-form}
A \textbf{one-form} (or \emph{$1$-form}, or \emph{covector field}) on $M$ is a smooth map
\[
\theta : M \longrightarrow T^*M
\]
such that
\[
\theta_p \in T_p^*M \qquad \text{for every } p \in M .
\]
Equivalently, $\pi \circ \theta = \mathrm{id}_M$ for the projection $\pi : T^*M \to M$: a one-form is a section of the cotangent bundle (Definition~\ref{def:section}).
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Covector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

In words: a one-form chooses one covector at every point of $M$, and the choice varies smoothly. Its value at $p$ is written $\theta_p$, not $\theta(p)$; it is a linear function $\theta_p : T_pM \to \mathbb{R}$, $v \mapsto \theta_p(v)$.

Uribe on the notation: ``$\theta$ is really a function of two variables, a point and a vector, and you want to make room for the vector variable'' --- so the point goes into the subscript and the vector into the parentheses. A student asked where a $\theta_p$ comes from; the answer is that the definition describes \emph{every} one-form, and the examples come next.

\begin{defbox}[The Space of One-Forms]\deflabel{def:one-forms-space}
The set of all one-forms on $M$ is written $C^\infty(M, T^*M)$ (Uribe's notation; also $\Omega^1(M)$).
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Covector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[One-Forms in Coordinates]\thmlabel{prop:one-form-coords}
Let $\theta$ be a section of $T^*M \to M$ (not assumed smooth) and $(U, \varphi = (x^i))$ a chart.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item On $U$,
    \[
    \theta = \sum_{j=1}^m \theta_j\, dx^j, \qquad \theta_j(p) = \theta_p\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big).
    \]
    \item $\theta$ maps $U$ into $T^*U$, and its coordinate representation in the charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ and $(T^*U, \hat\varphi)$ of $T^*M$ (Definition~\ref{def:ctb-chart}) is
    \[
    \hat\varphi \circ \theta \circ \varphi^{-1}(r) = \big(r,\ \theta_1(\varphi^{-1}(r)), \ldots, \theta_m(\varphi^{-1}(r))\big), \qquad r \in \varphi(U) .
    \]
    \item $\theta$ is smooth on $U$ if and only if the coefficient functions $\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m$ are smooth on $U$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition 11.11}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~15 stated it --- ``smoothness of the form will translate into these functions being smooth''; the proof is filled in.)} Three things are claimed: the expansion of $\theta$ on $U$ with the stated coefficients, (1); the coordinate representation, (2); and the smoothness criterion, (3). Since $\theta$ is a section, $\pi \circ \theta = \mathrm{id}_M$, so $\theta(p) = (p, \theta_p)$ with $\theta_p \in T_p^*M$ for every $p$.

\emph{(1) The expansion.} The equation $\theta = \sum_j \theta_j\, dx^j$ on $U$ means $\theta_p = \sum_j \theta_j(p)\, dx^j|_p$ for every $p \in U$. At each $p \in U$ the $dx^j|_p$ form a basis of $T_p^*M$ dual to the $\partial/\partial x^j|_p$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}), and Corollary~\ref{cor:covector-components} with $\alpha = \theta_p$ gives
\[
\theta_p = \sum_{j=1}^m \theta_p\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p\Big)\, dx^j\big|_p = \sum_{j=1}^m \theta_j(p)\, dx^j\big|_p ,
\]
which is the expansion, with $\theta_j(p) = \theta_p(\partial/\partial x^j|_p)$.

\emph{(2) The coordinate representation.} Since $\pi(\theta(p)) = p$, $\theta$ maps $U$ into $T^*U = \pi^{-1}(U)$, so the charts $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$ and $(T^*U, \hat\varphi)$ of $T^*M$ (Definition~\ref{def:ctb-chart}) are admissible for $\theta|_U$. For $r \in \varphi(U)$ put $p = \varphi^{-1}(r)$; by Definition~\ref{def:ctb-chart}, whose last $m$ entries are the components $\theta_p(\partial/\partial x^j|_p) = \theta_j(p)$,
\[
\hat\varphi \circ \theta \circ \varphi^{-1}(r) = \hat\varphi(p, \theta_p) = \big(\varphi(p), \theta_1(p), \ldots, \theta_m(p)\big) = \big(r,\ \theta_1(\varphi^{-1}(r)), \ldots, \theta_m(\varphi^{-1}(r))\big) .
\]
A map into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ is smooth exactly when all its components are; the first $m$ components, $r \mapsto r$, are smooth. So this coordinate representation is smooth exactly when every $\theta_j \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$.

\emph{(3) If $\theta$ is smooth on $U$,} then its coordinate representation in these charts is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}), so every $\theta_j \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$; this is the coordinate representation $(\theta_j)_\varphi$ of $\theta_j$, so $\theta_j$ is smooth on $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}, with the chart $(U, \varphi)$ at every point).

\emph{If every $\theta_j$ is smooth on $U$,} then each $\theta_j \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:some-any-function}, applied on the manifold $U$ with its chart $(U, \varphi)$), so the coordinate representation above is smooth. Moreover $\theta|_U$ is continuous: it equals $\hat\varphi^{-1} \circ (\hat\varphi \circ \theta \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ \varphi$, a composite of continuous maps ($\hat\varphi$ is a homeomorphism by Proposition~\ref{prop:ctb-topology}). So $\theta$ is smooth on $U$ by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}, using these two charts at every point of $U$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Operator $d$}\label{sub:d-operator}

\begin{propbox}[The Differential of a Function Is a One-Form]\thmlabel{prop:d-operator}
For $f \in C^\infty(M)$, the section $df : p \mapsto df_p$ is a one-form, given in a chart by
\[
df = \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\, dx^j .
\]
The resulting operator $d : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M, T^*M)$, $f \mapsto df$, is $\mathbb{R}$-linear and satisfies $d(fg) = f\, dg + g\, df$.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{The Differential of a Function}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(The coordinate formula is Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}, which Lecture~15 recalled; the rest is filled in.)} Four things are claimed: $df$ is a section of $T^*M$, it has the stated coordinate formula, it is smooth, and $d$ is linear and satisfies the product rule.

\emph{A section, and the formula.} For each $p \in M$, $df_p \in T_p^*M$ (Definition~\ref{def:differential-function}), so $df(p) = (p, df_p)$ satisfies $\pi \circ df = \mathrm{id}_M$. In a chart $(U, \varphi = (x^j))$, Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords} at each $p \in U$ gives $df_p = \sum_j \partial f/\partial x^j(p)\, dx^j|_p$, which is the formula $df = \sum_j (\partial f/\partial x^j)\, dx^j$ on $U$; its coefficient functions are $\partial f/\partial x^j : U \to \mathbb{R}$, in agreement with Proposition~\ref{prop:one-form-coords}, since $df_p(\partial/\partial x^j|_p) = \partial f/\partial x^j(p)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation}).

\emph{Smoothness.} The coefficients $\partial f/\partial x^j$ are smooth on $U$: Lemma~\ref{lem:partials-smooth}, applied to the restriction of $f$ to the chart domain $U$ (smooth, as $f \in C^\infty(M)$), gives $\partial f/\partial x^j \in C^\infty(U)$, with $(\partial f/\partial x^j) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \partial f_\varphi/\partial r^j$ on $\varphi(U)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:one-form-coords}(3), $df$ is smooth on $U$. The chart domains cover $M$, and smoothness of a map is checked near each point (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}), so $df$ is smooth on $M$: a one-form, $df \in C^\infty(M, T^*M)$.

\emph{Linearity and the product rule.} One-forms are added, and multiplied by functions, pointwise: $(a\,\theta + b\,\sigma)_p = a\,\theta_p + b\,\sigma_p$ and $(f\theta)_p = f(p)\,\theta_p$. So the two identities are equalities of covectors at each $p$, and two covectors are equal when they agree at every $v \in T_pM$. Fix $p$ and $v \in T_pM$, and let $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$, $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} ($dk_p(v) = v[k]$), the $\mathbb{R}$-linearity of the derivation $v$ (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}), and the pointwise operations of $T_p^*M$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual}),
\[
d(af + bg)_p(v) = v[af + bg] = a\, v[f] + b\, v[g] = a\, df_p(v) + b\, dg_p(v) = \big(a\, df_p + b\, dg_p\big)(v) ;
\]
and, by the Leibniz rule of $v$ instead of its linearity,
\[
d(fg)_p(v) = v[fg] = f(p)\, v[g] + g(p)\, v[f] = f(p)\, dg_p(v) + g(p)\, df_p(v) = \big(f(p)\, dg_p + g(p)\, df_p\big)(v) .
\]
These are Corollary~\ref{cor:df-properties}(1) and (2) at the point $p$. As $p$ and $v$ were arbitrary, $d(af + bg) = a\, df + b\, dg$ and $d(fg) = f\, dg + g\, df$.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[Two One-Forms on the Plane]\exlabel{ex:two-one-forms}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ with coordinates $x, y$, any expression $a(x,y)\, dx + b(x,y)\, dy$ with smooth $a, b$ is a one-form. Uribe's two examples:
\[
\theta = \tfrac12\,(x\, dy - y\, dx), \qquad \sigma = \tfrac12\,(x\, dx + y\, dy) .
\]
$\sigma$ is the differential of a function: $\sigma = d\big(\tfrac14(x^2 + y^2)\big)$.
\end{exbox}

$\theta$ is not the differential of any function, as the next proposition shows.

\begin{propbox}[A Necessary Condition for Being a Differential]\thmlabel{prop:exactness-test}
If $\theta = \sum_j \theta_j\, dx^j = df$ on a chart domain $U$ for some $f \in C^\infty(U)$, then
\[
\frac{\partial \theta_j}{\partial x^k} = \frac{\partial \theta_k}{\partial x^j} \qquad \text{for all } j, k .
\]
In particular, $\theta = \tfrac12(x\,dy - y\,dx)$ is not $df$ for any $f$ on any open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~15.)} \emph{The condition.} Suppose $\theta = df$ on $U$. Then $\theta_p = df_p$ for every $p \in U$, and the coefficients of a covector in the basis $dx^j|_p$ are unique (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}); comparing $\theta_p = \sum_j \theta_j(p)\, dx^j|_p$ with $df_p = \sum_j \partial f/\partial x^j(p)\, dx^j|_p$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:d-operator}) gives $\theta_j = \partial f/\partial x^j$ for every $j$. By Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, $(\partial f/\partial x^j) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \partial f_\varphi/\partial r^j$ on $\varphi(U)$, where $f_\varphi = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:some-any-function}). Applying Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} once more, now to the function $\theta_j$,
\[
\frac{\partial \theta_j}{\partial x^k}(p) = \frac{\partial (\theta_j \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial r^k}\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial r^k}\Big(\frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^j}\Big)\big(\varphi(p)\big) = \frac{\partial^2 f_\varphi}{\partial r^k\, \partial r^j}\big(\varphi(p)\big) ,
\]
which is what $\partial\theta_j/\partial x^k = \partial^2 f/\partial x^k \partial x^j$ means. By equality of mixed partials (Clairaut's theorem) for the smooth function $f_\varphi$ on the open set $\varphi(U)$, this is $\partial^2 f_\varphi/\partial r^j\, \partial r^k(\varphi(p))$, i.e.\ $\partial^2 f/\partial x^j \partial x^k$, and the same computation with $j$ and $k$ exchanged identifies it with $\partial\theta_k/\partial x^j(p)$. So $\partial\theta_j/\partial x^k = \partial\theta_k/\partial x^j$ on $U$.

\textit{(Completion.)} \emph{The example.} Let $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a nonempty open set and suppose $\theta = \tfrac12(x\,dy - y\,dx) = df$ on $W$ for some $f \in C^\infty(W)$. $W$ is a chart domain, with the chart $\mathrm{id}_W$ and coordinates $x, y$; in it, coordinate partial derivatives are the ordinary ones (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation} with $\varphi = \mathrm{id}$). The coefficients of $\theta$ are read off from $\theta = -\tfrac{y}{2}\, dx + \tfrac{x}{2}\, dy$: $\theta_x = -\tfrac{y}{2}$ and $\theta_y = \tfrac{x}{2}$. The condition just proved, with $j = x$ and $k = y$, would require $\partial\theta_y/\partial x = \partial\theta_x/\partial y$ at every point of $W$. But at every point
\[
\frac{\partial\theta_y}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\Big(\frac{x}{2}\Big) = \tfrac12 \neq -\tfrac12 = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\Big(-\frac{y}{2}\Big) = \frac{\partial\theta_x}{\partial y} ,
\]
and $W$ has at least one point. So no such $f$ exists.
\end{proof}

``You know this from multivariable calculus in various different forms. Not every vector field is a gradient field'': the condition is the vanishing of the curl, ``a curl condition.''
