The two forms of Example~\ref{ex:two-one-forms}, drawn as arrows. A one-form is not an arrow --- it eats arrows --- so the picture uses the Euclidean dot product to turn $a\,dx + b\,dy$ into the vector $(a, b)$; this identification is available in $\mathbb{R}^2$, not on a general manifold, and it is how ``$df$'' becomes the ``gradient'' of calculus. Right: $\sigma = df$ for $f = \tfrac14(x^2+y^2)$, and its arrows cross the level circles of $f$ at right angles, as a gradient's must. Left: $\theta$'s arrows run \emph{along} the circles. If $\theta$ were $df$, then $f$ would increase steadily all the way around a circle and return to its starting value --- impossible.

\begin{rembox}[The Condition Is Not Sufficient]\label{rem:condition-not-sufficient}
The mixed-partials condition is necessary but not sufficient, and Uribe flagged this as ``the beginning of de Rham theory'': whether it suffices ``has to do with the topology of the domain.'' The standard example (Lee, Example~11.36; not from lecture) is
\[
\omega = \frac{x\, dy - y\, dx}{x^2 + y^2} \quad \text{on } \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\} .
\]
It satisfies the condition: both mixed partials equal $(y^2 - x^2)/(x^2 + y^2)^2$. But it is not $df$. Along the circle $c(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$, with velocity $c'(t) = -\sin t\, \partial_x + \cos t\, \partial_y$ (\ref{sec:velocities}), one finds $\omega(c'(t)) = 1$. If $\omega = df$, then $(f \circ c)'(t) = df(c'(t)) = 1$, so $f(c(2\pi)) - f(c(0)) = 2\pi$; but $c(2\pi) = c(0)$. The hole at the origin is what makes this possible: on all of $\mathbb{R}^2$ --- indeed on any star-shaped domain --- the condition is sufficient (Lee, Corollary~11.50).
\end{rembox}

\begin{exbox}[The Angle Form on the Punctured Plane]\exlabel{ex:angle-form}
\textit{(Not from lecture; added on request: the remark above, written out.)} The form is $\omega = (x\,dy - y\,dx)/(x^2+y^2)$. Names, used below: a one-form $\omega$ is \textbf{closed} if its coefficients satisfy the mixed-partials condition of Proposition~\ref{prop:exactness-test} in every chart, and \textbf{exact} if $\omega = df$ for some smooth function $f$. Proposition~\ref{prop:exactness-test} says exact $\Rightarrow$ closed. This example shows closed $\not\Rightarrow$ exact.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{The manifold.} $M = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}$, an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$, hence an open submanifold (Definition~\ref{def:open-submanifold-smooth}), with the single chart $\mathrm{id}_M$ and coordinates $x, y$. Its coordinate derivations $\partial_x, \partial_y$ are the ordinary partial derivatives.
    \item \emph{The one-form.} $\omega = a\, dx + b\, dy$ with coefficient functions
    \[
    a, b : M \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad a(x,y) = \frac{-y}{x^2 + y^2}, \qquad b(x,y) = \frac{x}{x^2 + y^2} .
    \]
    They are smooth on $M$ because $x^2 + y^2 > 0$ there; so $\omega$ is a one-form on $M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:one-form-coords}): at each $p \in M$ it is the covector $\omega_p = a(p)\, dx|_p + b(p)\, dy|_p \in T_p^*M$, a linear map $T_pM \to \mathbb{R}$. It is not defined at $0$.
    \item \emph{$\omega$ is closed.} By the quotient rule,
    \[
    \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} = \frac{(x^2 + y^2) - x \cdot 2x}{(x^2 + y^2)^2} = \frac{y^2 - x^2}{(x^2 + y^2)^2},
    \qquad
    \frac{\partial a}{\partial y} = -\frac{(x^2 + y^2) - y \cdot 2y}{(x^2 + y^2)^2} = \frac{y^2 - x^2}{(x^2 + y^2)^2} ,
    \]
    so $\partial a/\partial y = \partial b/\partial x$ on $M$: the necessary condition of Proposition~\ref{prop:exactness-test} holds. (Compare $\theta = \tfrac12(x\,dy - y\,dx)$ of Example~\ref{ex:two-one-forms}, where the two sides are $\tfrac12$ and $-\tfrac12$.)
    \item \emph{The test curve.} $c : \mathbb{R} \to M$, $c(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$, the unit circle run once around in time $2\pi$. It is smooth and lands in $M$ ($|c(t)| = 1$). Its velocity at time $t$ (Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t}) is the tangent vector (Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords}, components $(x \circ c)'(t)$, $(y \circ c)'(t)$)
    \[
    D_c(t) = -\sin t\; \partial_x|_{c(t)} + \cos t\; \partial_y|_{c(t)} \in T_{c(t)}M .
    \]
    \item \emph{$\omega$ along the curve.} Evaluating the covector $\omega_{c(t)}$ on this tangent vector, with $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ on the circle,
    \[
    \omega_{c(t)}\big(D_c(t)\big) = a(c(t))\,(-\sin t) + b(c(t))\,\cos t = (-\sin t)(-\sin t) + (\cos t)(\cos t) = 1 \qquad \text{for every } t .
    \]
    \item \emph{$\omega$ is not exact.} Suppose $\omega = df$ for some $f \in C^\infty(M)$. The function $f \circ c : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth, and by the definition of the velocity (Definition~\ref{def:velocity}) and Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation},
    \[
    (f \circ c)'(t) = D_c(t)[f] = df_{c(t)}\big(D_c(t)\big) = \omega_{c(t)}\big(D_c(t)\big) = 1 .
    \]
    By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $f(c(2\pi)) - f(c(0)) = \int_0^{2\pi} (f \circ c)'(t)\, dt = 2\pi$. But $c(2\pi) = (1, 0) = c(0)$, so the left side is $0$. Contradiction: no such $f$ exists on $M$.
    \item \emph{What $f$ would have to be: the angle.} Let $U = M \setminus \{(x, 0) : x < 0\}$, the plane slit along the negative $x$-axis, and $\vartheta : U \to (-\pi, \pi)$ the polar angle, so that $x = r\cos\vartheta$, $y = r\sin\vartheta$ with $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ (the polar coordinates of Example~\ref{ex:polar-derivations}; $(r, \vartheta)$ is a chart on $U$, so $\vartheta$ is smooth there). In that chart
    \[
    dx = \cos\vartheta\, dr - r\sin\vartheta\, d\vartheta, \qquad dy = \sin\vartheta\, dr + r\cos\vartheta\, d\vartheta ,
    \]
    \[
    x\,dy - y\,dx = r\cos\vartheta\,(\sin\vartheta\, dr + r\cos\vartheta\, d\vartheta) - r\sin\vartheta\,(\cos\vartheta\, dr - r\sin\vartheta\, d\vartheta) = r^2\, d\vartheta ,
    \]
    so $\omega = r^2\, d\vartheta / r^2 = d\vartheta$ on $U$: on the slit plane $\omega$ \emph{is} exact, with $f = \vartheta$. The obstruction is global: going once around the hole, $\vartheta$ increases by $2\pi$ (step 6), so it cannot be continued continuously across the slit, where it jumps from near $\pi$ (just above) to near $-\pi$ (just below). Any $f$ with $df = \omega$ on all of $M$ would be such a continuation (two functions with the same differential on a connected open set differ by a constant).
    \item \emph{Why the hole matters.} On $\mathbb{R}^2$ itself, or on any star-shaped open set (a disk, the slit plane $U$), a closed form is exact (Poincaré lemma; Lee, Corollary~11.50, not proved in these notes). $M$ is not star-shaped, and step 6 shows the lemma cannot extend to it: whether closed forms are exact depends on the topology of the domain, which is what de Rham cohomology measures.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exbox}

\subsection{Pullbacks of One-Forms}\label{sub:pullback-one-forms}

\begin{defbox}[Pullback of Functions]\deflabel{def:pullback-function}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth. The \textbf{pullback} of functions is $F^*f = f \circ F$.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Pullbacks of Covector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Pullback of One-Forms]\deflabel{def:pullback-one-form}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth. For a one-form $\theta$ on $N$, the \textbf{pullback} $F^*\theta$ is the section of $T^*M$ whose value at $p$ is the pullback of the covector $\theta_{F(p)}$ (Definition~\ref{def:pullback-covector}):
\[
(F^*\theta)_p = F_p^*\big(\theta_{F(p)}\big), \qquad (F^*\theta)_p(v) = \theta_{F(p)}\big(F_{*p}v\big) .
\]
It is smooth, hence a one-form, by Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-coords} below.
\leeref{Ch.~11, \emph{Pullbacks of Covector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{corbox}[Pullback Commutes with $d$]\thmlabel{cor:pullback-d-forms}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and $f \in C^\infty(N)$. Then $F^*(df) = d(F^*f)$ as one-forms on $M$.
\leeref{Proposition 11.25}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~15 stated it in this form, ``one says that the pullback map commutes with $d$''.)} Both sides are sections of $T^*M$, and two sections are equal when their values agree at every point; so fix $p \in M$ and compute the two values.

\emph{Left side.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:d-operator}, $df$ is a one-form on $N$ whose value at $F(p)$ is $df_{F(p)}$. By Definition~\ref{def:pullback-one-form} with $\theta = df$,
\[
\big(F^*(df)\big)_p = F_p^*\big((df)_{F(p)}\big) = F_p^*\big(df_{F(p)}\big) .
\]

\emph{Right side.} By Definition~\ref{def:pullback-function}, $F^*f = f \circ F$, which is smooth on $M$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}); so $d(F^*f)$ is a one-form on $M$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:d-operator}) with value $d(f \circ F)_p$ at $p$.

\emph{Comparison.} Proposition~\ref{prop:pullback-d}, applied to this $F$, the point $p$, and $f$ (smooth on $N$, so in particular near $F(p)$), gives $F_p^*\big(df_{F(p)}\big) = d(f \circ F)_p$ in $T_p^*M$. So the two sides agree at $p$, and $p$ was arbitrary.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Pullbacks in Coordinates]\thmlabel{prop:pullback-coords}
In charts $(x^i)$ on $M$ and $(y^j)$ on $N$, with $F^j = y^j \circ F$,
\[
F^*\Big(\sum_j \theta_j\, dy^j\Big) = \sum_i \Big( \sum_j (\theta_j \circ F)\, \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i} \Big)\, dx^i .
\]
In matrix form, with $m = \dim M$ and $n = \dim N$, the column of coefficients of $F^*\theta$ is the transpose of the Jacobian $\big[\partial F^j/\partial x^i\big]$ (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}) applied to the column of the $\theta_j \circ F$:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_j (\theta_j \circ F)\, \dfrac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^1} \\ \vdots \\ \sum_j (\theta_j \circ F)\, \dfrac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^m}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \theta_1 \circ F \\ \vdots \\ \theta_n \circ F \end{pmatrix} .
\]
In particular $F^*\theta$ is smooth whenever $\theta$ is.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Let $(U, \varphi = (x^i))$ and $(V, \psi = (y^j))$ be the charts, with $F(U) \subseteq V$ so that $F^j = y^j \circ F$ is defined on $U$ (otherwise replace $U$ by $U \cap F^{-1}(V)$, open since $F$ is continuous; the restriction of $\varphi$ to it is a smooth chart by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)). Write $\theta = \sum_j \theta_j\, dy^j$ on $V$, with $\theta_j(q) = \theta_q(\partial/\partial y^j|_q)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:one-form-coords}), and let $c_i = \sum_j (\theta_j \circ F)\, \partial F^j/\partial x^i$ be the coefficients on the right. Two things are claimed: the identity on $U$, and the smoothness of $F^*\theta$.

\emph{The identity.} Fix $p \in U$. Both sides have values in $T_p^*M$, linear functionals on $T_pM$, so by Proposition~\ref{fact:linalg}(2) it suffices that they agree on each basis vector $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$. The right side, evaluated pointwise and using $dx^l|_p(\partial/\partial x^i|_p) = \delta^l_i$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}), gives $\sum_l c_l(p)\, \delta^l_i = c_i(p)$. For the left side, use in turn Definition~\ref{def:pullback-one-form}; the expansion $\theta_{F(p)} = \sum_k \theta_k(F(p))\, dy^k|_{F(p)}$; the formula $F_{*p}\, \partial/\partial x^i|_p = \sum_j \partial F^j/\partial x^i(p)\, \partial/\partial y^j|_{F(p)}$ (Theorem~\ref{lem:differential-matrix}); linearity of the covectors $dy^k|_{F(p)}$; and $dy^k|_{F(p)}(\partial/\partial y^j|_{F(p)}) = \delta^k_j$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:df-coords}):
\[
\begin{aligned}
(F^*\theta)_p\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big) &= \theta_{F(p)}\Big(F_{*p}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big) = \sum_k \theta_k(F(p))\, dy^k\big|_{F(p)}\Big(F_{*p}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p\Big) \\
&= \sum_k \theta_k(F(p))\, \sum_j \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, dy^k\big|_{F(p)}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\Big|_{F(p)}\Big) = \sum_k \theta_k(F(p))\, \sum_j \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p)\, \delta^k_j \\
&= \sum_j \theta_j(F(p))\, \frac{\partial F^j}{\partial x^i}(p) = c_i(p) .
\end{aligned}
\]
The two covectors agree on every basis vector, so they are equal; as $p \in U$ was arbitrary, the identity holds on $U$.

\emph{Smoothness.} Let $\theta$ be smooth. By Proposition~\ref{prop:one-form-coords} the $\theta_j$ are smooth on $V$, so $\theta_j \circ F$ is smooth on $U$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}, with $F|_U : U \to V$). By Proposition~\ref{prop:upstairs-downstairs}, $F^j \circ \varphi^{-1} = \tilde F^j$, a component of the coordinate representation $\tilde F = \psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}$, which is smooth (Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}); so $F^j$ is smooth on $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}), and Lemma~\ref{lem:partials-smooth}, applied to $F^j \in C^\infty(U)$, gives $\partial F^j/\partial x^i \in C^\infty(U)$, with $(\partial F^j/\partial x^i) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \partial \tilde F^j/\partial r^i$ on $\varphi(U)$. Sums and products of smooth functions are smooth, so each $c_i$ is smooth on $U$, and $F^*\theta$ is smooth on $U$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:one-form-coords}(3). Every $p \in M$ lies in such a $U$: Lemma~\ref{lem:charts-around-map}, applied to $F$ at $p$, gives smooth charts $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$ and $(V, \psi)$ at $F(p)$ with $F(U) \subseteq V$. So $F^*\theta$ is smooth on $M$.
\end{proof}
