\draw[gray!60, dashed] (0,-0.78) -- (1.2,-0.78);
\fill (1.2,0) circle (1.4pt) node[above=1pt] {$u$};
\fill (0,-0.78) circle (1.4pt) node[left] {$h_p(u)$};
\fill[blue!70!black] (1.2,-0.78) circle (1.7pt);
\node[blue!70!black, anchor=west] at (1.3,-0.5) {$(s_f)_{*p}u = (u, h_p(u))$};
\draw[orange!85!black, thick, ->] (-0.9,0) arc (180:146:0.9);
\node[orange!85!black, anchor=south east, align=right] at (-1.05,0.1) {slope $= h_p$,\\ i.e.\ $\operatorname{Hess}_pf(u,\cdot)$};
\node[gray!70!black, anchor=north west, align=left] at (-2.3,-1.0) {a line through $(p,0)$ meeting\\ the fibre only in $0$: a graph};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

The splitting at a point of the zero section, and the image of $(s_f)_{*p}$ in it: a line through the origin that ``passes the vertical line test'', the graph of $h_p$. Its slope is the Hessian: $h_p(u) = \operatorname{Hess}_p f(u, \cdot\,)$. A line through the origin is such a graph exactly when it meets the vertical axis (the fibre direction) only in $0$.

\textit{Away from a critical point.} The horizontal summand ``has nothing to do with $f$. It's just because \ldots\ we have the zero section, and then we have the fibre, and they're just sitting there''; at $(p, df_p)$ with $df_p \neq 0$ the fibre is still there, but there is no zero section through the point. A student asked why one cannot use some other section through $(p, df_p)$: ``Yeah, you can put a section, but you have to make a choice \ldots\ because you make a choice, you don't have a well-defined'' Hessian. In coordinates (``which we haven't done much of''), with two charts $(x^i)$ and $(y^j)$, $\partial f/\partial x^i = \sum_j (\partial y^j/\partial x^i)\, \partial f/\partial y^j$, and differentiating again,
\[
\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^k \partial x^i} = \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 y^j}{\partial x^k \partial x^i}\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y^j} + \sum_{j,l} \frac{\partial y^j}{\partial x^i}\, \frac{\partial y^l}{\partial x^k}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^l \partial y^j} :
\]
the first sum ``will not go away in general'', so the matrix ``doesn't transform like a quadratic form unless these guys are zero'' (Proposition~\ref{prop:hessian-transformation}).

\begin{rembox}[Natural Is Not Canonical]\label{rem:natural-canonical}
``Natural is not the same thing as canonical. This was [drilled] into me when I was your age. \emph{Canonical} means that this is how we do it: we follow the canon, an established set of traditions. \emph{Natural} means that this is how nature does it. It's not a convention. It's just sitting there, in the mathematical world.'' The splitting $T_{(p,0)}(T^*M) = T_pM \oplus T_p^*M$ ``is natural. It's not canonical.''
\end{rembox}

\textit{Jets.} ``In the same sort of direction'': for every $k$ the quotient of germs by a power of $I_p$ makes sense, generalizing $T_p^*M \cong I_p/I_p^2$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}).

\begin{defbox}[Jets]\deflabel{def:jets}
Let $p \in M$ and $k \ge 0$. The space of \textbf{$k$-jets} at $p$ is
\[
J^k_p = C^\infty_p(M) \big/ I_p^{k+1},
\]
where $I_p^{k+1}$ is spanned by products of $k + 1$ germs vanishing at $p$. The class of a germ is its $k$-jet.
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Multi-Index Notation]\deflabel{def:multi-index}
A \textbf{multi-index} is an $m$-tuple $\alpha = (\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m)$ of integers $\alpha_i \ge 0$, with \textbf{order} $|\alpha| = \alpha_1 + \cdots + \alpha_m$ and $\alpha! = \alpha_1! \cdots \alpha_m!$. In a chart $(U, (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$, with $\partial_i = \partial/\partial x^i$ acting on $C^\infty(U)$,
\[
\partial^\alpha = \partial_1^{\alpha_1} \circ \cdots \circ \partial_m^{\alpha_m}, \qquad (x - c)^\alpha = (x^1 - c^1)^{\alpha_1} \cdots (x^m - c^m)^{\alpha_m} \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}^m),
\]
and $\partial^{(0, \ldots, 0)} = \mathrm{id}$. Write $\beta \le \alpha$ if $\beta_i \le \alpha_i$ for every $i$, and $e_j$ for the multi-index with $1$ in place $j$ and $0$ elsewhere.
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Derivatives of Monomials]\thmlabel{lem:monomial-derivatives}
Let $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ be a chart, $p \in U$, $c = \varphi(p)$, and $\alpha$, $\beta$ multi-indices. On $U$,
\[
\partial^\alpha (x - c)^\beta = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\beta!}{(\beta - \alpha)!}\, (x - c)^{\beta - \alpha} & \text{if } \alpha \le \beta, \\[4pt] 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}
\]
with $(\beta - \alpha)_i = \beta_i - \alpha_i$. In particular $\partial^\alpha (x - c)^\beta(p) = \beta!$ if $\alpha = \beta$ and $0$ if $\alpha \ne \beta$; so the coefficients of a polynomial $P = \sum_{|\beta| \le k} c_\beta\, (x - c)^\beta$ are $c_\beta = \partial^\beta P(p)/\beta!$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Partial derivatives on $U$ are computed from coordinate representations: $(\partial_i u) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \partial(u \circ \varphi^{-1})/\partial r^i$ (Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}), so, applying this $|\alpha|$ times, $(\partial^\alpha u) \circ \varphi^{-1} = \partial^{|\alpha|}(u \circ \varphi^{-1})/\partial r^\alpha$. In coordinates, $(x - c)^\beta \circ \varphi^{-1}(r) = \prod_i (r^i - c^i)^{\beta_i}$, a product of factors each depending on one variable, so
\[
\frac{\partial^{|\alpha|}}{\partial r^\alpha} \prod_{i=1}^m (r^i - c^i)^{\beta_i} = \prod_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial^{\alpha_i}}{\partial (r^i)^{\alpha_i}} (r^i - c^i)^{\beta_i}, \qquad \frac{\partial^{\alpha_i}}{\partial (r^i)^{\alpha_i}} (r^i - c^i)^{\beta_i} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\beta_i!}{(\beta_i - \alpha_i)!} (r^i - c^i)^{\beta_i - \alpha_i} & \alpha_i \le \beta_i, \\ 0 & \alpha_i > \beta_i . \end{cases}
\]
That is, $\partial^\alpha (x - c)^\beta = \frac{\beta!}{(\beta - \alpha)!} (x - c)^{\beta - \alpha}$ if $\alpha \le \beta$, and $0$ otherwise. At $x = c$, i.e.\ at the point $p$, the factor $(r^i - c^i)^{\beta_i - \alpha_i}$ is $1$ if $\alpha_i = \beta_i$ and $0$ if $\alpha_i < \beta_i$; so $\partial^\alpha (x - c)^\beta(p)$ vanishes unless $\alpha = \beta$, where it is $\beta!$. For the last statement, apply $\partial^\alpha$ to $P$ and evaluate at $p$: $\partial^\alpha P(p) = \sum_\beta c_\beta\, \partial^\alpha (x - c)^\beta(p) = c_\alpha\, \alpha!$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Jets Are Taylor Polynomials]\thmlabel{prop:jets-taylor}
In a chart $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ centred at $p$, two germs have the same $k$-jet if and only if their partial derivatives of all orders $\le k$ agree at $p$, that is, their Taylor polynomials of degree $k$ at $p$ agree. So $J^k_p$ is isomorphic to the space of polynomials of degree $\le k$ in $m$ variables.
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~20: ``this just isolates \ldots\ the partial sum of the Taylor series. You kill derivatives of order $k+1$ and higher.'' Filled in.)} It suffices to show that $[g] \in I_p^{k+1}$ if and only if all partials of $g$ of orders $0, \ldots, k$ vanish at $p$. \emph{Only if.} A product $g_1 \cdots g_{k+1}$ of germs vanishing at $p$: by the Leibniz rule, a partial derivative of order $\le k$ of the product is a sum of products in each of which some factor $g_i$ is not differentiated, and so vanishes at $p$; sums of such products behave the same. \emph{If.} Applying Hadamard's lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:hadamard}) repeatedly to the coefficient functions, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:taylor-hadamard}, gives, on a ball about $p$,
\[
g = \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} \frac{\partial^\alpha g(p)}{\alpha!}\, x^\alpha + \sum_{|\beta| = k+1} x^\beta\, g_\beta
\]
with $g_\beta$ smooth. If all $\partial^\alpha g(p)$ with $|\alpha| \le k$ vanish, then $[g] = \sum_\beta [x^\beta][g_\beta]$, and each $x^\beta$, $|\beta| = k+1$, is a product of $k + 1$ coordinate functions vanishing at $p$; so $[g] \in I_p^{k+1}$. Finally, a polynomial $P = \sum_{|\beta| \le k} c_\beta\, x^\beta$ is the Taylor polynomial of its own germ, since $\partial^\beta P(p)/\beta! = c_\beta$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:monomial-derivatives}, with $c = 0$ for the chart centred at $p$); so the map from $J^k_p$ to Taylor polynomials is onto.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.25, font=\scriptsize]
\draw[->, gray!60] (-2.2,0) -- (2.4,0) node[right, text=black] {$x$};
\draw[->, gray!60] (0,-0.3) -- (0,2.6);
% f(x) = 1 + 0.5 x + 0.4 x^2 + 0.25 x^3 around p = 0
\draw[violet!75!black, very thick] plot[smooth, domain=-2:1.7] (\x,{1+0.5*\x+0.4*\x*\x+0.15*\x*\x*\x});
\draw[gray!70!black, thick] (-2,1) -- (2.2,1) node[right] {$T_0$: $0$-jet (value)};
\draw[teal!60!black, thick] (-1.6,0.2) -- (2.2,2.1) node[right] {$T_1$: $1$-jet};
\draw[orange!85!black, thick, dashed] plot[smooth, domain=-2:1.75] (\x,{1+0.5*\x+0.4*\x*\x});
\node[orange!85!black, anchor=west] at (1.6,2.55) {$T_2$: $2$-jet};
\node[violet!75!black, anchor=east] at (-2.05,0.4) {$f$};
\fill (0,1) circle (1.6pt); \node[below right] at (0,1) {$p$};
\node[align=center] at (0.1,-0.75) {germs at $p$ modulo $I_p^{k+1}$ $=$ Taylor polynomials of degree $k$;\\ $k = 1$, value removed: $I_p/I_p^2 \cong T_p^*M$, the differential};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} The jets of a function $f$ of one variable at $p$, drawn as its Taylor polynomials (Proposition~\ref{prop:jets-taylor}): the $0$-jet $T_0$ is the value $f(p)$, the $1$-jet $T_1$ the tangent line, the $2$-jet $T_2$ the osculating parabola. Two germs have the same $k$-jet when their difference lies in $I_p^{k+1}$, that is, vanishes to order $k + 1$ at $p$. For $k = 1$, removing the value leaves $I_p/I_p^2 \cong T_p^*M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}): the $1$-jet of a germ vanishing at $p$ is its differential.

``This is called a space of jets \ldots\ they are useful in some circles. If you take $k = 2$, you can package the information contained in the function --- the value, the first derivative, the second derivative --- in some abstract object.'' But ``within them you cannot separate naturally the first and the second partials, unless you have a special situation'' --- a critical point being the special situation that gives the Hessian.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 20).} Page~53 of the handwritten notes writes the jet space as $C^\infty_p(M)/I_p^k$, which keeps derivatives through order $k - 1$; Uribe corrected it in lecture (``maybe I should put $k + 1$ here''), and the $k$-jet is $C^\infty_p(M)/I_p^{k+1}$. The splitting there is written at ``$(0, p)$''; in these notes the point of the zero section over $p$ is $(p, 0)$.

\chapter{Vector Fields and Lie Groups}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: VECTOR FIELDS
% ============================================================================

\section{Vector Fields}\label{sec:fields}\label{sub:sections}\label{sub:vector-fields}\label{sec:vf-operators}

\roadmark{Stage: fields}{Smooth sections of $TM$, a tangent vector at every point --- and vector fields acting on functions, as derivations of $C^\infty(M)$.}

\textit{Lecture 15: ``now we want to start a big chapter, new chapter, and now it is on vector fields.'' References: Lee Ch.~8.} The definition itself was given in Lectures~12 and~13, with the tangent bundle; Lecture~15 restated it ``analogously'' to one-forms.

\subsection{Vector Fields and Their Coordinates}\label{sub:vf-def}

\begin{defbox}[Vector Field]\deflabel{def:vector-field}
A \textbf{vector field} on $M$ is a smooth map
\[
\mathbf{X} : M \longrightarrow TM
\]
such that
\[
\mathbf{X}(p) \in T_pM \qquad \text{for every } p \in M .
\]
Equivalently, $\pi \circ \mathbf{X} = \mathrm{id}_M$ for the projection $\pi : TM \to M$: a vector field is a section of the tangent bundle (Definition~\ref{def:section}).
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Vector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

In words: a vector field chooses one tangent vector at every point of $M$, and the choice varies smoothly --- ``for every point, [it] selects a tangent vector at that point.''

\begin{center}

A vector field in two pictures, on the circle $M = S^1$ with $\mathbf{X} = c(\theta)\,\partial/\partial\theta$, $c(\theta) = 0.55 + 0.35\sin\theta$. Left: the usual picture, an arrow $\mathbf{X}(p)$ at each point $p$. Right: the tangent bundle $TS^1$, with $S^1$ cut open at $(1,0)$; each fibre $T_pM$ is a vertical line over $p$, and the height of a point on it measures the vector $c\,\partial/\partial\theta$ (above the dashed zero section: counterclockwise). The vector field is the curve $\mathbf{X}(M)$, which meets every fibre exactly once --- that is the condition $\mathbf{X}(p) \in T_pM$ --- and $\pi \circ \mathbf{X} = \mathrm{id}_M$ says that the point of the curve above $p$ projects back to $p$. The points $p_1, p_2, p_3$ carry the same colour in both pictures.

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page~36 of the handwritten notes writes ``Section of $TM \xrightarrow{F} M$''; the map is the projection $\pi$.

\textbf{Notation.} The value of a vector field $\mathbf{X}$ (Definition~\ref{def:vector-field}) at $p$ is written $\mathbf{X}_p \in T_pM$, again with $p$ as a subscript, to make room for the function a tangent vector acts on.

\begin{defbox}[The Space of Vector Fields]\deflabel{def:vector-fields-space}
The set of all vector fields on $M$ is denoted
\[
\mathfrak{X}(M) \qquad \text{(\LaTeX: \texttt{\textbackslash mathfrak\{X\}})}.
\]
For $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the sum and the scalar multiple are defined pointwise, in the vector space $T_pM$:
\[
(\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y})_p = \mathbf{X}_p + \mathbf{Y}_p, \qquad (c\mathbf{X})_p = c\, \mathbf{X}_p, \qquad p \in M .
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-vector-space} shows that these are again vector fields and that $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ is a real vector space. Multiplying by a function rather than a constant is the next definition.
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Vector Fields on Manifolds}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Product of a Function and a Vector Field]\deflabel{def:function-times-field}
For $f \in C^\infty(M)$ and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, the product $f\mathbf{X}$ is defined pointwise:
\[
(f\mathbf{X})_p = f(p)\, \mathbf{X}_p \qquad \text{for every } p \in M .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Vector Fields on Manifolds}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{propbox}[Vector Fields in Coordinates]\thmlabel{prop:vf-coords}
Let $\mathbf{X}$ be a section of $TM$ (not assumed smooth), $m = \dim M$, and $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ a chart \emph{of $M$}: $U \subseteq M$ open, with coordinate functions $x^j : U \to \mathbb{R}$. Then on $U$
\[
\mathbf{X} = \sum_{j=1}^m \mathbf{X}^j\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}, \qquad \mathbf{X}^j(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[x^j] = dx^j|_p(\mathbf{X}_p),
\]
where $\partial/\partial x^j$ is the coordinate vector field of the chart ($p \mapsto \partial/\partial x^j|_p \in T_pM$) and the coefficients $\mathbf{X}^j : U \to \mathbb{R}$ are functions on $U \subseteq M$. Moreover $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth on $U$ if and only if the coefficient functions $\mathbf{X}^1, \ldots, \mathbf{X}^m$ are smooth on $U$; smoothness of $\mathbf{X} : U \to TU$ is tested in the chart $\tilde\varphi$ of $TM$ induced by $\varphi$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}), whose $2m$ coordinates are $x^1, \ldots, x^m$ and the components $v^j = dx^j(v)$.
\leeref{Proposition 8.1}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~15, ``analogously'' to one-forms; filled in.)} Three things are claimed: the expansion of $\mathbf{X}$ at each point of $U$, the two formulas for its coefficients, and the smoothness criterion.

\emph{The expansion.} Fix $p \in U$. Since $\mathbf{X}$ is a section of $TM$, $\mathbf{X}_p \in T_pM$ is a derivation at $p$. The universal formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}, applied to $D = \mathbf{X}_p$, gives
\[
\mathbf{X}_p = \sum_{j=1}^m \mathbf{X}_p[x^j]\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p = \sum_{j=1}^m \mathbf{X}^j(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p , \qquad \mathbf{X}^j(p) := \mathbf{X}_p[x^j] .
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:df-derivation} with $f = x^j$ and $D = \mathbf{X}_p$, $\mathbf{X}_p[x^j] = dx^j|_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$, which is the second formula for $\mathbf{X}^j(p)$. As $p \in U$ was arbitrary, $\mathbf{X} = \sum_j \mathbf{X}^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$ on $U$, the equality holding at every point.

\emph{The coordinate representation.} For $p \in U$ the point $\mathbf{X}(p) = (p, \mathbf{X}_p)$ of $TM$ lies over $p \in U$, so $\mathbf{X}$ maps $U$ into $TU = \pi^{-1}(U)$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-charts}), the domain of the chart $\tilde\varphi$ of $TM$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}). That chart sends $(p, v)$ to $\big(x^1(p), \ldots, x^m(p), v[x^1], \ldots, v[x^m]\big)$. Let $r \in \varphi(U)$ and $p = \varphi^{-1}(r)$; then $(x^1(p), \ldots, x^m(p)) = \varphi(p) = r$, and for $v = \mathbf{X}_p$ the last $m$ entries are $\mathbf{X}_p[x^j] = \mathbf{X}^j(p)$. Hence
\[
\tilde\varphi \circ \mathbf{X} \circ \varphi^{-1}(r) = \big(r,\ \mathbf{X}^1(\varphi^{-1}(r)), \ldots, \mathbf{X}^m(\varphi^{-1}(r))\big), \qquad r \in \varphi(U) .
\]
A map into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ is smooth if and only if each of its $2m$ components is; the first $m$ components $r \mapsto r^i$ are smooth, so this coordinate representation is smooth exactly when every $\mathbf{X}^j \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$.

\emph{Smooth $\Rightarrow$ smooth coefficients.} Suppose $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth on $U$, i.e.\ $\mathbf{X}|_U : U \to TM$ is smooth, $U$ being an open submanifold (Definition~\ref{def:open-submanifold}). Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-map-charts}, applied to the chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $U$ and the chart $(TU, \tilde\varphi)$ of $TM$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-atlas}), with $\mathbf{X}(U) \subseteq TU$, says that the coordinate representation above is smooth. So every $\mathbf{X}^j \circ \varphi^{-1} = (\mathbf{X}^j)_\varphi$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$, and by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}, tested with the chart $(U, \varphi)$ at every point of $U$, each $\mathbf{X}^j$ is smooth on $U$.

\emph{Smooth coefficients $\Rightarrow$ smooth.} Suppose every $\mathbf{X}^j$ is smooth on $U$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:some-any-function}, applied in the chart $(U, \varphi)$, every $\mathbf{X}^j \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$, so the coordinate representation is smooth. $\mathbf{X}|_U$ is also continuous: on $U$,
\[
\mathbf{X} = \tilde\varphi^{-1} \circ \big(\tilde\varphi \circ \mathbf{X} \circ \varphi^{-1}\big) \circ \varphi ,
\]
a composite of continuous maps ($\varphi$ is a homeomorphism onto $\varphi(U)$, the middle map is smooth, and $\tilde\varphi^{-1}$ is continuous by Proposition~\ref{prop:tb-topology}). So Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map} holds at every $p \in U$ with the charts $(U, \varphi)$ and $(TU, \tilde\varphi)$: $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth on $U$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Space of Vector Fields Is a Real Vector Space]\thmlabel{prop:vf-vector-space}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, then $\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y}$ and $c\mathbf{X}$ (Definition~\ref{def:vector-fields-space}) are vector fields.
    \item The zero field $\mathbf{0}$, $\mathbf{0}_p = 0_p \in T_pM$, is a vector field.
    \item With these operations $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ is a real vector space, with zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ and additive inverse $-\mathbf{X} = (-1)\mathbf{X}$.
    \item More generally, if $f \in C^\infty(M)$ and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, then $f\mathbf{X}$ (Definition~\ref{def:function-times-field}) is a vector field.
\end{enumerate}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture: the notes stated the vector-space structure without proof; filled in.)} \emph{The operations give sections.} At each $p$, $\mathbf{X}_p + \mathbf{Y}_p$, $c\,\mathbf{X}_p$, $f(p)\,\mathbf{X}_p$ and $0_p$ lie in $T_pM$, a real vector space (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}); so each of $\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y}$, $c\mathbf{X}$, $f\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{0}$ assigns to every $p$ a tangent vector at $p$, a section of $TM$.

\emph{(1), (2), (4): smoothness.} Let $(U, (x^j))$ be a chart. By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, $\mathbf{X} = \sum_j \mathbf{X}^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$ and $\mathbf{Y} = \sum_j \mathbf{Y}^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$ on $U$ with smooth coefficients. At each $p \in U$, by linearity in $T_pM$,
\[
(\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y})_p = \sum_j \big(\mathbf{X}^j(p) + \mathbf{Y}^j(p)\big) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p, \qquad (f\mathbf{X})_p = \sum_j f(p)\, \mathbf{X}^j(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p, \qquad \mathbf{0}_p = \sum_j 0 \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p ,
\]
so the coefficients of $\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y}$, $f\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{0}$ are $\mathbf{X}^j + \mathbf{Y}^j$, $f\mathbf{X}^j$ and $0$, smooth on $U$ as sums and products of smooth functions. By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords} again these sections are smooth on $U$; the chart domains cover $M$, and smoothness is local, so they are smooth. The scalar multiple $c\mathbf{X}$ is the case $f \equiv c$ of (4).

\emph{(3): the axioms.} Each axiom is an equality of vector fields, that is, of their values at every $p \in M$, and there it is the corresponding axiom of the vector space $T_pM$. Explicitly, for $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $p \in M$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item commutativity: $(\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y})_p = \mathbf{X}_p + \mathbf{Y}_p = \mathbf{Y}_p + \mathbf{X}_p = (\mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{X})_p$;
    \item associativity: $\big((\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y}) + \mathbf{Z}\big)_p = (\mathbf{X}_p + \mathbf{Y}_p) + \mathbf{Z}_p = \mathbf{X}_p + (\mathbf{Y}_p + \mathbf{Z}_p) = \big(\mathbf{X} + (\mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{Z})\big)_p$;
    \item zero: $(\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{0})_p = \mathbf{X}_p + 0_p = \mathbf{X}_p$;
    \item inverses: $\big(\mathbf{X} + (-1)\mathbf{X}\big)_p = \mathbf{X}_p - \mathbf{X}_p = 0_p = \mathbf{0}_p$;
    \item unit: $(1\mathbf{X})_p = 1 \cdot \mathbf{X}_p = \mathbf{X}_p$;
    \item compatibility: $\big((ab)\mathbf{X}\big)_p = (ab)\,\mathbf{X}_p = a\,(b\,\mathbf{X}_p) = \big(a(b\mathbf{X})\big)_p$;
    \item distributivity: $\big(a(\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y})\big)_p = a\,\mathbf{X}_p + a\,\mathbf{Y}_p = (a\mathbf{X} + a\mathbf{Y})_p$ and $\big((a + b)\mathbf{X}\big)_p = a\,\mathbf{X}_p + b\,\mathbf{X}_p = (a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{X})_p$.
\end{itemize}
So $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ is a real vector space.
\end{proof}

By (4), $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ is moreover a module over the ring $C^\infty(M)$ --- the same pointwise check gives $(fg)\mathbf{X} = f(g\mathbf{X})$, $(f + g)\mathbf{X} = f\mathbf{X} + g\mathbf{X}$ and $f(\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y}) = f\mathbf{X} + f\mathbf{Y}$ --- which is what Uribe meant by ``an algebra over the smooth functions'' in Lecture~17. It is infinite-dimensional as a real vector space (for $\dim M \ge 1$), but over $C^\infty(U)$ the fields on a chart domain $U$ have the basis $\partial/\partial x^1, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^m$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}).

\begin{rembox}[Vector Fields and One-Forms Side by Side]\label{rem:fields-side-by-side}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.2\textwidth} p{0.26\textwidth} p{0.2\textwidth} p{0.22\textwidth}}
\hline
Field & A section of & In a chart & Picture \\
\hline
vector field $\mathbf{X}$ & $TM$ (Definition~\ref{def:vector-field}) & $\sum_j \mathbf{X}^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$ & wind on the surface \\
one-form $\theta$ & $T^*M$ (Definition~\ref{def:one-form}) & $\sum_j \theta_j\, dx^j$ & a rule pricing every step \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Every function gives a one-form, $f \mapsto df$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:d-operator}), but not every one-form is a $df$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:exactness-test}). A one-form and a vector field together give a function, $p \mapsto \theta_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$. And a vector field acting on a function gives a function, $p \mapsto \mathbf{X}_p[f]$ --- the starting point of the next subsection.
\end{rembox}

\subsection{Vector Fields as Derivations}\label{sub:vf-derivations}

\begin{rembox}[Two Faces of a Vector Field]\label{rem:two-faces-vector-field}
``Just as tangent vectors, fields have a double life.'' Tangent vectors were defined as derivations and then shown to be velocities of curves (\ref{sec:velocities}). Vector fields likewise have two faces: \emph{operators on functions}, studied first because it continues the definition by derivations; and \emph{dynamics on $M$} --- integral curves, the trajectories that follow the field, to come later.
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[Operator on $C^\infty(M)$]\deflabel{def:operator}
An \textbf{operator} on $C^\infty(M)$ is a map
\[
P : C^\infty(M) \longrightarrow C^\infty(M), \qquad f \longmapsto Pf ,
\]
taking smooth functions on $M$ to smooth functions on $M$.
\end{defbox}

\textit{(Not from lecture: Uribe uses the word without defining it --- ``it's an $\mathbb{R}$-linear operator''.)} $C^\infty(M)$ is a real vector space under pointwise addition and scalar multiplication, and an operator $P$ is \emph{$\mathbb{R}$-linear}, or a \emph{linear operator}, if it is a linear map of this space: $P(af + bg) = a\,Pf + b\,Pg$ for $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$. Operators can be added, $(P + Q)f = Pf + Qf$, and composed, $(P \circ Q)f = P(Qf)$, and sums and composites of linear operators are linear. Examples: $f \mapsto D_\mathbf{X}f$ for a vector field $\mathbf{X}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation} below), and multiplication by a fixed function, $f \mapsto gf$ (Definition~\ref{def:multiplication-operator} below). A derivation, a local operator and a differential operator, defined below, are operators with extra properties; the Lie bracket of \ref{sec:lie-bracket} is the commutator of two operators.

\begin{defbox}[Derivation of $C^\infty(M)$]\deflabel{def:global-derivation}
A \textbf{derivation} of $C^\infty(M)$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear operator $D : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:operator}) satisfying the product rule
\[
D(fg) = f\, Dg + g\, Df \qquad \text{for all } f, g \in C^\infty(M).
\]
Compare a derivation \emph{at a point} (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}), which takes values in $\mathbb{R}$ and acts on germs.
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Vector Fields as Derivations}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[A Vector Field Is a Derivation]\thmlabel{lem:vf-derivation}
For $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $f \in C^\infty(M)$, the function $D_\mathbf{X}f : p \mapsto \mathbf{X}_p[f]$ is smooth, and $D_\mathbf{X} : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M)$ is a derivation. In a chart, $D_\mathbf{X}f = \sum_j \mathbf{X}^j\, \partial f/\partial x^j$. (Lee writes $\mathbf{X}f$ for $D_\mathbf{X}f$.)
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~15: linearity and the product rule are ``an immediate consequence of the corresponding properties for tangent vectors'', applied at each point. Smoothness of $D_\mathbf{X}f$, which the lecture did not address, is filled in.)} Three things are claimed: the chart formula, smoothness of $D_\mathbf{X}f$, and that $D_\mathbf{X}$ is $\mathbb{R}$-linear and satisfies the product rule (Definition~\ref{def:global-derivation}). Throughout, $[f]$ denotes the germ at $p$ of $f \in C^\infty(M)$.

\emph{The chart formula.} Let $(U, \varphi = (x^j))$ be a chart and $p \in U$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, $\mathbf{X}_p = \sum_j \mathbf{X}^j(p)\, \partial/\partial x^j|_p$. Derivations at $p$ are added and scaled pointwise (Definition~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}), so evaluating at $[f]$ and using Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation},
\[
(D_\mathbf{X}f)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[f] = \sum_{j=1}^m \mathbf{X}^j(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_p[f] = \sum_{j=1}^m \mathbf{X}^j(p)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(p) .
\]

\emph{Smoothness.} Fix $p \in M$ and a chart $(U, \varphi)$ at $p$; by Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function} it suffices that $(D_\mathbf{X}f) \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth on $\varphi(U)$. By the chart formula, for $r \in \varphi(U)$,
\[
(D_\mathbf{X}f)\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big) = \sum_{j=1}^m \mathbf{X}^j\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big)\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}\big(\varphi^{-1}(r)\big) = \sum_{j=1}^m \big(\mathbf{X}^j \circ \varphi^{-1}\big)(r)\, \frac{\partial f_\varphi}{\partial r^j}(r),
\]
the second equality by Definition~\ref{def:coordinate-derivation}, $\partial f/\partial x^j(q) = \partial f_\varphi/\partial r^j(\varphi(q))$ with $q = \varphi^{-1}(r)$. Here $\mathbf{X}^j \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is smooth because $\mathbf{X}^j$ is smooth on $U$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, $\mathbf{X}$ being smooth) and by Proposition~\ref{prop:some-any-function}; and $\partial f_\varphi/\partial r^j$ is smooth because $f_\varphi$ is (Proposition~\ref{prop:some-any-function}). A sum of products of smooth functions is smooth, so $D_\mathbf{X}f \in C^\infty(M)$.

\emph{Linearity.} Let $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$, $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $p \in M$. The germ of $af + bg$ is $a[f] + b[g]$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}), and $\mathbf{X}_p$ is $\mathbb{R}$-linear (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}):
\[
\big(D_\mathbf{X}(af + bg)\big)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p\big(a[f] + b[g]\big) = a\,\mathbf{X}_p[f] + b\,\mathbf{X}_p[g] = \big(a\, D_\mathbf{X}f + b\, D_\mathbf{X}g\big)(p) .
\]

\emph{Product rule.} The germ of $fg$ is $[f][g]$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}), and $\mathbf{X}_p$ satisfies the Leibniz rule at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:derivation}):
\[
\big(D_\mathbf{X}(fg)\big)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p\big([f][g]\big) = f(p)\, \mathbf{X}_p[g] + g(p)\, \mathbf{X}_p[f] = \big(f\, D_\mathbf{X}g + g\, D_\mathbf{X}f\big)(p) .
\]
Both identities hold at every $p$, so they hold as identities of functions, and $D_\mathbf{X}$ is a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$.
\end{proof}

The goal of this section is the converse of the lemma: every derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ comes from a vector field (Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}, at the end). Tangent vectors act on germs, which only see a neighbourhood of a point, while a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ acts on functions on all of $M$. The bridge is locality (Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-local}), and its proof needs bump functions, so these come first.

\begin{defbox}[Local Operator]\deflabel{def:local-operator}
An operator $D : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:operator}) is \textbf{local} if for every open $U \subseteq M$ and all $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$,
\[
f|_U = g|_U \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (Df)|_U = (Dg)|_U .
\]
\end{defbox}

``Even though $D$ a priori is defined on functions on $M$, it's actually going to be given by local data'': knowing $f$ on $U$ determines $Df$ on $U$.

\begin{defbox}[Support]\deflabel{def:support}
The \textbf{support} of a function $\chi : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is the \emph{closure} of the set where it is nonzero,
\[
\operatorname{supp}\chi = \overline{\{ q \in M : \chi(q) \neq 0 \}} .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Partitions of Unity}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Compactly Supported Functions]\deflabel{def:compact-support}
$C^\infty_0(M)$ is the set of smooth functions $\chi : M \to \mathbb{R}$ whose support (Definition~\ref{def:support}) is compact.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Partitions of Unity}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{defbox}[Bump Function]\deflabel{def:bump-function}
Let $p \in M$. A \textbf{bump function at $p$} is a $\chi \in C^\infty_0(M)$ (Definition~\ref{def:compact-support}) with $\chi \equiv 1$ on a neighbourhood of $p$.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Partitions of Unity}}
\end{defbox}

``It's a technical term, and it's not a joke'': the graph is a plateau, equal to $1$ near $p$ and dying off to $0$ outside a compact set --- ``smooth, but not analytic'', since an analytic function equal to $1$ on an open set would equal $1$ on the whole connected domain.

A bump function at $p$, after the board sketch, with the front quarter cut away. $M$ is a plane, and the graph of $\chi$ is a surface over it: $\chi \equiv 1$ on a disc around $p$ (the blue plateau, at height $1$); from its edge the graph falls smoothly to $0$ (orange); and $\chi = 0$ outside the compact set $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, whose boundary is the dashed circle on $M$. The two cut faces show the profile of $\chi$ along two rays from $p$, and $p$ lies on $M$ at their inner corner, directly below the plateau, where $\chi(p) = 1$. The cross-section below shows the same profile along a whole line through $p$.

A bump function, drawn over a one-dimensional slice of $M$ (the graph is the plateau of Uribe's picture, in cross-section). It equals $1$ on a neighbourhood of $p$, is smooth everywhere, and vanishes outside its support, which is compact and lies inside the given open set $U$. This one is built from $h(t) = e^{-1/t}$ for $t > 0$, $h(t) = 0$ for $t \le 0$, as $\chi(x) = h(b - |x|)/\big(h(b - |x|) + h(|x| - a)\big)$, which is $1$ for $|x| \le a$ and $0$ for $|x| \ge b$.

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page~41 of the handwritten notes defines $\operatorname{supp}(\chi) = \{q \in M : \chi(q) \neq 0\}$; the support is the \emph{closure} of that set, as Uribe said (``and then you take the closure of that''). Without the closure, the support of a bump function would not be compact.

\begin{propbox}[Bump Functions Exist]\thmlabel{prop:bump-existence}
For every open $U \subseteq M$ and every $p \in U$ there is a bump function $\chi$ at $p$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq U$.
\leeref{Proposition 2.25}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~15, and again in Lecture~16 --- ``we're going to prove it next week, but not this week'' --- as ``technical things that you will not be using in homework.'' ``The existence is not so obvious, but it's true.'' Lecture~21 gave the recipe while proving the Whitney embedding theorem: the function ``is constructed in the Euclidean space first, and then you pull back with the chart.'' Filled in along that recipe, following Lee, Lemmas 2.20--2.22.)} We prove slightly more, needed in Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney}: \emph{if $(V, \varphi)$ is a chart at $p$ with $V \subseteq U$, and $0 < r < r'$ with $\overline{B}(\varphi(p), r') \subseteq \varphi(V)$, there is a bump function $\chi$ at $p$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq V$ and $\chi \equiv 1$ on the closed coordinate ball $\varphi^{-1}\big(\overline{B}(\varphi(p), r)\big)$.} Such a chart exists: restrict any chart at $p$ to its intersection with $U$, and choose a small ball.

\emph{1. A smooth function vanishing to infinite order.} Let $h(t) = e^{-1/t}$ for $t > 0$ and $h(t) = 0$ for $t \le 0$. By induction, for $t > 0$, $h^{(k)}(t) = P_k(1/t)\, e^{-1/t}$ with $P_k$ a polynomial, since $\frac{d}{dt}\big(P(1/t) e^{-1/t}\big) = \big(-P'(1/t)/t^2 + P(1/t)/t^2\big) e^{-1/t}$. As $s^j e^{-s} \to 0$ for $s = 1/t \to \infty$, every $h^{(k)}(t) \to 0$ as $t \to 0^+$, and the right difference quotient $\big(h^{(k)}(t) - 0\big)/t = (1/t)\, P_k(1/t)\, e^{-1/t} \to 0$ as well. So by induction every $h^{(k)}$ exists at $0$ and equals $0$, and $h$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}$, with $h > 0$ exactly on $(0, \infty)$.

\emph{2. A plateau on $\mathbb{R}^m$.} Put
\[
H(x) = \frac{h\big(r'^2 - |x|^2\big)}{h\big(r'^2 - |x|^2\big) + h\big(|x|^2 - r^2\big)}, \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}^m .
\]
The denominator never vanishes: if $|x| < r'$ the first term is positive, and if $|x| \ge r' > r$ the second is. So $H$ is smooth, $0 \le H \le 1$, $H(x) = 1$ when $|x| \le r$ (the second term vanishes), and $H(x) = 0$ when $|x| \ge r'$.

\emph{3. Pull back by the chart.} Define $\chi = H\big(\varphi - \varphi(p)\big)$ on $V$ and $\chi = 0$ on $M \setminus V$. The set $K = \varphi^{-1}\big(\overline{B}(\varphi(p), r')\big)$ is compact, as the image of a compact set under the continuous map $\varphi^{-1}$, hence closed in the Hausdorff space $M$, and $K \subseteq V$. $\chi$ is smooth on the open set $V$ and zero on the open set $M \setminus K$; these two open sets cover $M$, so $\chi$ is smooth. Its support lies in $K$, so it is compact and inside $V \subseteq U$; and $\chi \equiv 1$ on $\varphi^{-1}\big(\overline{B}(\varphi(p), r)\big)$, which contains the open neighbourhood $\varphi^{-1}\big(B(\varphi(p), r)\big)$ of $p$. So $\chi$ is a bump function at $p$ (Definition~\ref{def:bump-function}).
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} The two steps of the construction for $m = 1$. Left: $h(t) = e^{-1/t}$ for $t > 0$ and $h = 0$ for $t \le 0$ is smooth, with all derivatives $0$ at $t = 0$, so it switches on without a corner (Step~1). Right: the plateau $H(x) = h(r'^2 - x^2) / \big(h(r'^2 - x^2) + h(x^2 - r^2)\big)$ is $1$ on $|x| \le r$, $0$ for $|x| \ge r'$, and smooth in between (Step~2); pulling it back by a chart gives the bump function (Step~3).
%% <<< END ADDED


\textit{Terminology (Lecture~16).} A function $\chi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq U$ is said to be \emph{subordinate to $U$}, ``because this is a condition that is going to show up several times.''

\textit{Lecture~16: the corollary of the bump function lemma that the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields} uses.}

\begin{corbox}[Every Germ Has a Global Representative]\thmlabel{cor:germ-extension}
Let $p \in M$ and $\gamma \in C^\infty_p(M)$, represented by $f \in C^\infty(U)$ with $U \ni p$ open. If $\chi$ is a bump function at $p$ subordinate to $U$, then
\[
\tilde f = \begin{cases} \chi f & \text{on } U, \\ 0 & \text{on } M \setminus U \end{cases}
\]
is smooth on all of $M$ and represents $\gamma$. In particular every germ at $p$ has a representative defined on all of $M$.
\leeref{Lemma 2.26 (extension lemma)}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~16.)} Two things are claimed: $\tilde f \in C^\infty(M)$, and $[\tilde f] = [f] = \gamma$ in $C^\infty_p(M)$.

\emph{$\tilde f$ is smooth.} Smoothness of a function is tested at each point with a chart at that point (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-function}), and a smooth chart may be shrunk to any smaller open neighbourhood of the point (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)); so it suffices to cover $M$ by open sets on each of which $\tilde f$ is smooth. Take the two sets $U$ and $M \setminus \operatorname{supp}\chi$. The second is open because $\operatorname{supp}\chi$ is closed, being a closure (Definition~\ref{def:support}). They cover $M$: a point $q \notin U$ is not in $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, because $\operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq U$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item On $U$, $\tilde f = \chi f$ is a product of the smooth functions $\chi|_U$ and $f$, hence smooth.
    \item On $M \setminus \operatorname{supp}\chi$, $\tilde f \equiv 0$. Let $q \notin \operatorname{supp}\chi$. Then $\chi(q) = 0$, since every point where $\chi \ne 0$ lies in $\operatorname{supp}\chi$. If $q \in U$, $\tilde f(q) = \chi(q)\, f(q) = 0 \cdot f(q) = 0$; if $q \notin U$, $\tilde f(q) = 0$ by definition. A constant function is smooth.
\end{itemize}
So $\tilde f \in C^\infty(M)$.

\emph{$\tilde f$ represents $\gamma$.} Since $\chi$ is a bump function at $p$, there is an open $V \ni p$ with $\chi \equiv 1$ on $V$ (Definition~\ref{def:bump-function}). For $q \in V \cap U$,
\[
\tilde f(q) = \chi(q)\, f(q) = 1 \cdot f(q) = f(q) .
\]
$V \cap U$ is open, contains $p$, and lies in the intersection $M \cap U$ of the two domains, so $(\tilde f, M) \sim (f, U)$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation}), that is, $[\tilde f] = [f] = \gamma$.

\emph{In particular.} Every germ $\gamma$ at $p$ has some representative $f \in C^\infty(U)$ with $U \ni p$ open (Definition~\ref{def:germ}), and a bump function at $p$ subordinate to $U$ exists by Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence}; so the construction applies to every germ.
\end{proof}

The extension of a germ. Above: $f$ is defined only on $U$ (its ends are open), and $\chi$ (dashed) is a bump function at $p$ subordinate to $U$. Below: $\tilde f = \chi f$, extended by $0$. On $V$, where $\chi \equiv 1$, it agrees with $f$ (dotted), so it has the same germ at $p$; it dies off inside $U$ and is $0$ outside $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, so it is smooth on all of $M$.


\begin{lembox}[Derivations Are Local]\thmlabel{lem:derivation-local}
Every derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ is a local operator.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~16, in full: ``you'll see how incredibly powerful the product rule is.'')} Let $D$ be a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$, $U \subseteq M$ open, and $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$ with $f|_U = g|_U$; we must show $(Df)|_U = (Dg)|_U$.

\emph{Reduction to the kernel.} Put $h = f - g \in C^\infty(M)$; then $h|_U = 0$. By linearity of $D$, $Df - Dg = D(f - g) = Dh$. So it suffices to show: if $h|_U = 0$ then $(Dh)|_U = 0$ --- ``like showing that something is injective by showing that the kernel is zero.''

\emph{The kernel.} Let $h|_U = 0$ and fix $p \in U$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence} there is a bump function $\chi$ at $p$ subordinate to $U$: $\chi \in C^\infty(M)$, $\operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq U$, and $\chi \equiv 1$ near $p$, in particular $\chi(p) = 1$ (Definition~\ref{def:bump-function}). The product $\chi h$ is the zero function on $M$. Indeed, for $q \in U$, $h(q) = 0$; and for $q \notin U$, $q \notin \operatorname{supp}\chi$, so $\chi(q) = 0$ (every point where $\chi \ne 0$ lies in the support, Definition~\ref{def:support}). A linear map sends $0$ to $0$, so $D(\chi h) = D(0) = 0$; and by the product rule (Definition~\ref{def:global-derivation}),
\[
0 = D(\chi h) = \chi\, Dh + h\, D\chi ,
\]
an equality of functions on $M$. Evaluate it at $p$, using $\chi(p) = 1$ and $h(p) = 0$ (as $p \in U$):
\[
0 = \chi(p)\,(Dh)(p) + h(p)\,(D\chi)(p) = 1 \cdot (Dh)(p) + 0 \cdot (D\chi)(p) = (Dh)(p) .
\]
As $p \in U$ was arbitrary, $(Dh)|_U = 0$, and therefore $(Df)|_U = (Dg)|_U$.
\end{proof}

``Derivations are local, thanks to the product rule and the existence of bump functions.\@''


\textit{Lecture~15, after stating the lemma (proved above in Lecture~16): ``I want to make an observation.''} The observation was the ring of differential operators, generated by the operators $D_\mathbf{X}$ and the multiplications by functions, all of whose elements are local; it is collected, with what follows from it, in the next section, \ref{sec:diff-ops}.

\textit{Lecture~16 proved the converse of Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}. ``It's not an immediate thing at all \ldots\ tangent vectors are defined in terms of germs'', local objects near a point, ``whereas'' a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ ``a priori'' acts on functions on all of $M$. Locality (Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-local}) is half the bridge; the other half is that germs can be globalized (Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}).}

\begin{propbox}[Derivations Are Vector Fields]\thmlabel{prop:derivations-are-fields}
Conversely, every derivation $D$ of $C^\infty(M)$ is of the form $D = D_\mathbf{X}$ for a unique $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.
\leeref{Proposition 8.15}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~16, in the lecture's steps. Uribe ``skip[ped] a little bit the details'' of smoothness; they are completed below, as are two steps the lecture did not state: that each $\mathbf{X}_p$ is a derivation at $p$, and uniqueness.)} Let $D$ be a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$. We must produce $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, i.e.\ a smooth section of $TM$, with $D_\mathbf{X} = D$, and show that it is the only one.

\emph{1. Define $\mathbf{X}$ pointwise.} For $p \in M$ and a germ $\gamma \in C^\infty_p(M)$, set
\[
\mathbf{X}_p(\gamma) = (Df)(p), \qquad f \in C^\infty(M) \text{ a global representative of } \gamma,
\]
which exists by Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension} (with a bump function supplied by Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence}).

\emph{2. It is well defined.} Let $f, f' \in C^\infty(M)$ both represent $\gamma$. Then $(f, M) \sim (f', M)$, so there is an open $W \ni p$ with $f|_W = f'|_W$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation}). By Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-local}, applied with the open set $W$, $(Df)|_W = (Df')|_W$; since $p \in W$, $(Df)(p) = (Df')(p)$. So $\mathbf{X}_p(\gamma)$ does not depend on the choice of $f$. ``So you see, we need all these lemmas.''

\emph{3. Each $\mathbf{X}_p$ is a derivation at $p$.} \textit{(Completion.)} Let $\gamma, \delta \in C^\infty_p(M)$ with global representatives $f, g$, and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. Germ operations are computed on representatives (Proposition~\ref{prop:germ-algebra}), here on the common domain $M$, so $af + bg$ is a global representative of $a\gamma + b\delta$, and $fg$ one of $\gamma\delta$. By step 1 and the linearity of $D$,
\[
\mathbf{X}_p(a\gamma + b\delta) = \big(D(af + bg)\big)(p) = a\,(Df)(p) + b\,(Dg)(p) = a\,\mathbf{X}_p(\gamma) + b\,\mathbf{X}_p(\delta) .
\]
By step 1, the product rule of $D$, and $\gamma(p) = f(p)$, $\delta(p) = g(p)$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-evaluation}),
\[
\mathbf{X}_p(\gamma\delta) = \big(D(fg)\big)(p) = f(p)\,(Dg)(p) + g(p)\,(Df)(p) = \gamma(p)\,\mathbf{X}_p(\delta) + \delta(p)\,\mathbf{X}_p(\gamma) .
\]
So $\mathbf{X}_p$ is a derivation at $p$, i.e.\ $\mathbf{X}_p \in T_pM$ (Definitions~\ref{def:derivation} and~\ref{def:abstract-tangent}). Thus $\mathbf{X} : p \mapsto \mathbf{X}_p$ is a section of $TM$, so far not known to be smooth.

\emph{4. $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth.} In a chart $(U, (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ at $p$, $\mathbf{X}_q = \sum_j \mathbf{X}_q(x^j)\, \partial/\partial x^j|_q$ for $q \in U$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), and ``$\mathbf{X}_p(x^j)$ is $D(\tilde x^j)(p)$, where $\tilde x^j$ is a smooth extension of $x^j$.'' \textit{(Completion.)} Smoothness of a map is a condition at each point (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}), so it suffices to find an open $V \ni p$ on which $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth. Take one bump function $\chi$ at $p$ subordinate to $U$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence}), equal to $1$ on an open $V \ni p$. Then $V \subseteq U$, since $V \subseteq \{\chi \ne 0\} \subseteq \operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq U$. Let $\tilde x^j = \chi x^j$, extended by $0$ outside $U$: the single extension of Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}, smooth on $M$. For $q \in V$, $\tilde x^j$ and $x^j$ agree on the open set $V \ni q$ (because $\chi = 1$ there), so $\tilde x^j$ is a global representative of the germ of $x^j$ at $q$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation}), and by step 1
\[
\mathbf{X}_q(x^j) = D(\tilde x^j)(q) \qquad \text{for all } q \in V .
\]
The right side is the function $D(\tilde x^j) \in C^\infty(M)$ evaluated at $q$; its restriction to $V$ is smooth. Now $(V, (x^1|_V, \ldots, x^m|_V))$ is a smooth chart (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)), and in it the coefficients of $\mathbf{X}$ are $\mathbf{X}^j(q) = \mathbf{X}_q(x^j)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}), which we have just shown to be smooth on $V$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}, $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth on $V$. As $p$ was arbitrary, $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth, and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.

\emph{5. $D = D_\mathbf{X}$.} Let $f \in C^\infty(M)$ and $p \in M$. The function $f$ is a global representative of its own germ $[f]$ at $p$, so step 1 with $\gamma = [f]$ and the definition of $D_\mathbf{X}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}) give
\[
(D_\mathbf{X} f)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[f] = (Df)(p) .
\]
This holds for every $p$ and every $f$, so $D_\mathbf{X} f = Df$ for all $f$, i.e.\ $D_\mathbf{X} = D$.

\emph{6. Uniqueness.} \textit{(Completion.)} Suppose $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ with $D_\mathbf{X} = D_\mathbf{Y}$. Fix $p$ and a germ $\gamma$ at $p$, with global representative $f$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}), so $\gamma = [f]$. Then
\[
\mathbf{X}_p(\gamma) = \mathbf{X}_p[f] = (D_\mathbf{X} f)(p) = (D_\mathbf{Y} f)(p) = \mathbf{Y}_p[f] = \mathbf{Y}_p(\gamma) .
\]
So $\mathbf{X}_p$ and $\mathbf{Y}_p$ agree on every germ, $\mathbf{X}_p = \mathbf{Y}_p$, for every $p$; that is, $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{Y}$.
\end{proof}

So $\mathbf{X} \mapsto D_\mathbf{X}$ is a bijection from $\mathfrak{X}(M)$ onto the derivations of $C^\infty(M)$. \textit{Notation (Lecture~16).} From now on $D_\mathbf{X}$ is written $\mathbf{X}$: ``you say to yourself, I'm thinking of $\mathbf{X}$ as an operator \ldots\ if you say $\mathbf{X}(f)$, then it's an operator.''

\textbf{Transcription note.} Page~43 of the handwritten notes asks ``is $\mathbf{X}_p$ $C^\infty$?''; the question is whether the field $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth, $\mathbf{X}_p$ being a single tangent vector. The same line writes the coordinates as $(x^1, \ldots, x^n)$ and then sums to $m$; the dimension is $m$ throughout.

\begin{lembox}[A Smoothness Criterion for Vector Fields]\thmlabel{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}
Let $\mathbf{X}$ be a section of $TM$, not assumed smooth, and for $f \in C^\infty(M)$ let $\mathbf{X}f$ be the function $p \mapsto \mathbf{X}_p[f]$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth if and only if $\mathbf{X}f$ is smooth for every $f \in C^\infty(M)$.
\leeref{Proposition 8.14}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, for use in Lecture~17's theorem on Lie algebras. The argument is step~4 of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}.)} Two implications.

\emph{$\mathbf{X}$ smooth $\Rightarrow$ every $\mathbf{X}f$ smooth.} If $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth, then $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $\mathbf{X}f$ is the function $D_\mathbf{X}f$, which is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}.

\emph{Every $\mathbf{X}f$ smooth $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbf{X}$ smooth.} Smoothness of a map is a condition at each point (Definition~\ref{def:smooth-map}), so it suffices to show that every $p \in M$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ on which $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth. Let $p \in M$ and $(U, (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ a chart at $p$. Take a bump function $\chi$ at $p$ subordinate to $U$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence}), equal to $1$ on an open $V \ni p$; then $V \subseteq \{\chi \ne 0\} \subseteq \operatorname{supp}\chi \subseteq U$. Let $\tilde x^j = \chi x^j$ (extended by $0$ outside $U$) be the global function of Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}. For $q \in V$, $\tilde x^j$ and $x^j$ agree on the open set $V \ni q$, so they have the same germ at $q$ (Definition~\ref{def:germ-relation}), and the derivation $\mathbf{X}_q$, which acts on germs, gives them the same value. In the smooth chart $(V, (x^j|_V))$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-chart-modify}(1)) the coefficients of $\mathbf{X}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}) are therefore
\[
\mathbf{X}^j(q) = \mathbf{X}_q[x^j] = \mathbf{X}_q[\tilde x^j] = (\mathbf{X}\tilde x^j)(q), \qquad q \in V,
\]
and $\mathbf{X}\tilde x^j$ is smooth on $M$ by hypothesis, since $\tilde x^j \in C^\infty(M)$; so each $\mathbf{X}^j$ is smooth on $V$. So $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth on $V$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}; $p$ was arbitrary.
\end{proof}
