\textit{The operator viewpoint.} The definition is geometric --- ``arrows''. There is an equivalent characterization in terms of operators, using the pullback of functions, $F^*g = g \circ F$.

\begin{propbox}[Related Fields as Operators]\thmlabel{prop:F-related-operator}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are $F$-related if and only if
\[
\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F \qquad \text{for every } g \in C^\infty(N),
\]
that is, $\mathbf{X} \circ F^* = F^* \circ \mathbf{Y}$: the pullback $F^*$ intertwines $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ as derivations.
\leeref{Proposition 8.16}
\end{propbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=4em, row sep=2.6em]
C^\infty(N) \arrow[r, "\mathbf{Y}"] \arrow[d, "F^*"'] & C^\infty(N) \arrow[d, "F^*"] \\
C^\infty(M) \arrow[r, "\mathbf{X}"'] & C^\infty(M)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17, ``let's have a peek at the proof''; the step for the converse is filled in.)} The two forms of the condition are the same, since $(\mathbf{X} \circ F^*)(g) = \mathbf{X}(g \circ F)$ and $(F^* \circ \mathbf{Y})(g) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F$; and both sides are functions on $M$, so the condition says that they agree at every $p \in M$, for every $g$. Let $g \in C^\infty(N)$ and $p \in M$. The value at $p$ of a field applied to a function is the tangent vector at $p$ applied to its germ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}). With this, and the definition of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}) for $D = \mathbf{X}_p$ --- ``we pull back germs, so we push forward derivations'' ---
\[
\mathbf{X}(g \circ F)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[g \circ F] = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)[g],
\qquad
\big((\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F\big)(p) = (\mathbf{Y}g)\big(F(p)\big) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}[g] .
\]

\emph{Related implies intertwining.} If the fields are $F$-related, then $dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$ (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}), so the right-hand sides agree, for every $g$ and $p$; that is, $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F$.

\emph{Intertwining implies related.} Conversely, suppose $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F$ for every $g \in C^\infty(N)$, and fix $p \in M$. By the display, the two derivations $dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$ and $\mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$ at $F(p)$ agree on every global function $g$. Every germ $[h]$ at $F(p)$ has a global representative $g \in C^\infty(N)$, $[g] = [h]$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}), so
\[
dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)[h] = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)[g] = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}[g] = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}[h] .
\]
So the two derivations agree on every germ, and are equal as maps on $C^\infty_{F(p)}(N)$: $dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$. As $p$ was arbitrary, the fields are $F$-related. ``It's a trivial if and only if once you realize'' this.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Pushforward by a Diffeomorphism]\thmlabel{prop:vf-pushforward}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a diffeomorphism and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. Then $F_*\mathbf{X}$ is smooth, it is the unique vector field on $N$ that is $F$-related to $\mathbf{X}$, and for every $g \in C^\infty(N)$
\[
(F_*\mathbf{X})\, g = \big(\mathbf{X}(g \circ F)\big) \circ F^{-1} .
\]
\leeref{Proposition 8.19, Corollary 8.21}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} Four things are claimed: the formula, smoothness, $F$-relatedness, and uniqueness. Here $(F_*\mathbf{X})\,g$ denotes the function $q \mapsto (F_*\mathbf{X})_q[g]$ on $N$, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}.

\emph{The formula.} For $q \in N$ put $p = F^{-1}(q)$. By Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}, then Definition~\ref{def:pushforward} with $D = \mathbf{X}_p$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation},
\[
(F_*\mathbf{X})_q[g] = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)[g] = \mathbf{X}_p[g \circ F] = \mathbf{X}(g \circ F)(p) = \big(\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) \circ F^{-1}\big)(q) ,
\]
which is the formula.

\emph{Smoothness.} At each $q$, $(F_*\mathbf{X})_q = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$ lies in $T_{F(p)}N = T_qN$, so $F_*\mathbf{X}$ is a section of $TN$. In the formula, $g \circ F \in C^\infty(M)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}), so $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F)$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}); and $F^{-1}$ is smooth because $F$ is a diffeomorphism (Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}), so the composite $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) \circ F^{-1}$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). This holds for every $g \in C^\infty(N)$, so $F_*\mathbf{X}$ is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}.

\emph{$F$-related.} For $p \in M$, $F^{-1}(F(p)) = p$, so Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward} at $q = F(p)$ reads $(F_*\mathbf{X})_{F(p)} = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$. This is Definition~\ref{def:F-related} with $\mathbf{Y} = F_*\mathbf{X}$.

\emph{Uniqueness.} If $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$ is also $F$-related to $\mathbf{X}$, let $q \in N$. Since $F$ is onto, $q = F(p)$ with $p = F^{-1}(q)$, and by Definition~\ref{def:F-related} and then Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward},
\[
\mathbf{Y}_q = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)} = dF_p(\mathbf{X}_p) = (F_*\mathbf{X})_q .
\]
This holds for every $q$, so $\mathbf{Y} = F_*\mathbf{X}$.
\end{proof}

\textit{``Now the reason I wanted to do it this way''} --- through operators --- is the following proposition.

\begin{propbox}[Naturality of the Bracket]\thmlabel{prop:bracket-naturality}
Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth, $\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2 \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2 \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$. If $\mathbf{X}_i$ is $F$-related to $\mathbf{Y}_i$ for $i = 1, 2$, then $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ is $F$-related to $[\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2]$.
\leeref{Proposition 8.30}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Omitted in Lecture~17 as an exercise: ``it's just a matter of chasing the definitions \ldots\ being $F$-related means that $F^*$ commutes with the derivations. So you just play with the symbols; it all comes out.'' Filled in.)} The brackets $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2] \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $[\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2] \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$ are vector fields (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}). By Proposition~\ref{prop:F-related-operator}, it suffices to show
\[
[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2](g \circ F) = \big([\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2]\, g\big) \circ F \qquad \text{for every } g \in C^\infty(N).
\]
Let $g \in C^\infty(N)$. The same proposition, applied to the pairs $(\mathbf{X}_i, \mathbf{Y}_i)$, gives $\mathbf{X}_i(h \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}_i h) \circ F$ for every $h \in C^\infty(N)$ and $i = 1, 2$.

\emph{The composite $\mathbf{X}_1\mathbf{X}_2$.} Apply this first for $i = 2$ with $h = g$, and then for $i = 1$ with $h = \mathbf{Y}_2 g$, which lies in $C^\infty(N)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}:
\[
\mathbf{X}_1\mathbf{X}_2(g \circ F) = \mathbf{X}_1\big((\mathbf{Y}_2 g) \circ F\big) = (\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{Y}_2 g) \circ F .
\]

\emph{The composite $\mathbf{X}_2\mathbf{X}_1$.} Apply it first for $i = 1$ with $h = g$, and then for $i = 2$ with $h = \mathbf{Y}_1 g$:
\[
\mathbf{X}_2\mathbf{X}_1(g \circ F) = \mathbf{X}_2\big((\mathbf{Y}_1 g) \circ F\big) = (\mathbf{Y}_2\mathbf{Y}_1 g) \circ F .
\]

\emph{Subtracting.} By Definition~\ref{def:lie-bracket}, and since $u \circ F - v \circ F = (u - v) \circ F$ for functions $u, v$ on $N$,
\[
[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2](g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{Y}_2 g) \circ F - (\mathbf{Y}_2\mathbf{Y}_1 g) \circ F = \big(\mathbf{Y}_1\mathbf{Y}_2 g - \mathbf{Y}_2\mathbf{Y}_1 g\big) \circ F = \big([\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2]\, g\big) \circ F ,
\]
and Proposition~\ref{prop:F-related-operator} again, with $\mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ and $\mathbf{Y} = [\mathbf{Y}_1, \mathbf{Y}_2]$, gives the claim.
\end{proof}

On omitting this proof: ``In a class like this, you cannot prove everything. First of all, there is no time, and second, you would be bored to tears. \ldots\ But on the other hand, if we just say, oh, you can read the proof, then you don't get a feeling for the subject. So there is a line there somewhere, or a zone, where you have to prove enough, but not too much.'' Feedback on where that line should sit is ``always welcome.''

\begin{corbox}[Diffeomorphisms Preserve Brackets]\thmlabel{cor:diffeo-bracket}
If $F : M \to N$ is a diffeomorphism and $\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2 \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, then $F_*[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2] = [F_*\mathbf{X}_1, F_*\mathbf{X}_2]$.
\leeref{Corollary 8.31}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} By Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}, each $F_*\mathbf{X}_i$ is a vector field on $N$ and $\mathbf{X}_i$ is $F$-related to $F_*\mathbf{X}_i$, for $i = 1, 2$. So Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}, with $\mathbf{Y}_i = F_*\mathbf{X}_i$, shows that $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ is $F$-related to $[F_*\mathbf{X}_1, F_*\mathbf{X}_2]$. On the other hand $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2] \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}), so Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}, applied to this field, says that the only field on $N$ that is $F$-related to $[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ is $F_*[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$. Both $[F_*\mathbf{X}_1, F_*\mathbf{X}_2]$ and $F_*[\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2]$ are such fields, so they are equal.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture; the conversion diagram of the midterm check sheet, added on request.)} A vector field $\mathbf{X}$ on $M$, pointwise, globally and in components. Chart $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$; the numbers on the arrows refer to the remark below.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3.6em, row sep=3.2em, font=\footnotesize]
\text{section } p \mapsto \mathbf{X}_p \in T_pM \arrow[r, shift left, "(1)"] \arrow[d, shift left, "(3)"] & \text{operator } \mathbf{X} : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M) \arrow[l, shift left, "(2)"] \\
\mathbf{X} = \sum_j X^j \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x^j} \ \text{on } U \arrow[u, shift left, "(4)"] &
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{rembox}[Conversion Diagram for Vector Fields]\label{rem:conversion-vector-fields}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{Section to operator.} $(\mathbf{X}f)(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[f]$, a derivation of $C^\infty(M)$: $\mathbf{X}(fg) = f\,\mathbf{X}g + g\,\mathbf{X}f$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-derivation}); $\mathbf{X}f$ is smooth for every smooth $f$ exactly when $\mathbf{X}$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}).
    \item \emph{Operator to section.} Every derivation of $C^\infty(M)$ is a vector field: $\mathbf{X}_p[f] = (\mathbf{X}\tilde f)(p)$ for a global $\tilde f$ with the same germ at $p$, which exists by bump functions and does not depend on the choice (Corollary~\ref{cor:germ-extension}, Lemma~\ref{lem:derivation-local}, Proposition~\ref{prop:derivations-are-fields}).
    \item \emph{Section to components.} On $U$, $X^j = \mathbf{X}(x^j)$, that is, $X^j(p) = \mathbf{X}_p[x^j] = dx^j|_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$.
    \item \emph{Components to section.} $\mathbf{X}_p = \sum_j X^j(p)\, \partial/\partial x^j|_p$, smooth if and only if all $X^j$ are (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}); then $\mathbf{X}f = \sum_j X^j\, \partial f/\partial x^j$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{The same three faces for:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{the bracket.} Globally $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]f = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{Y}f) - \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{X}f)$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-bracket}). Pointwise $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p[f] = \mathbf{X}_p[\mathbf{Y}f] - \mathbf{Y}_p[\mathbf{X}f]$, which needs the global function $\mathbf{Y}f$, not only the vector $\mathbf{Y}_p$. In components $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]^j = \mathbf{X}(Y^j) - \mathbf{Y}(X^j) = \sum_i \big(X^i\, \partial Y^j/\partial x^i - Y^i\, \partial X^j/\partial x^i\big)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}).
    \item \emph{$F$-related fields.} Pointwise $F_{*p}\mathbf{X}_p = \mathbf{Y}_{F(p)}$ (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}). Globally $\mathbf{X}(g \circ F) = (\mathbf{Y}g) \circ F$ for all $g$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:F-related-operator}). In components $Y^i(F(p)) = \sum_j \frac{\partial F^i}{\partial x^j}(p)\, X^j(p)$. For a diffeomorphism, $\mathbf{Y} = F_*\mathbf{X}$ with $(F_*\mathbf{X})_q = F_{*}\mathbf{X}_{F^{-1}(q)}$ (Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}).
    \item \emph{one-forms.} Pointwise $\theta_p \in T_p^*M$; globally the function $p \mapsto \theta_p(\mathbf{X}_p)$ for each vector field $\mathbf{X}$; in components $\theta_j = \theta(\partial/\partial x^j)$ and $\theta = \sum_j \theta_j\, dx^j$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:one-form-coords}). For $\theta = df$, $df(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{X}f$.
    \item \emph{the tangent bundle.} The section $\mathbf{X}$ in the standard chart of $TM$ (\ref{sec:tangent-bundle}) is $p \mapsto (x^1, \ldots, x^m, X^1, \ldots, X^m)$, with transition $(r, v) \mapsto (\tau(r), \tau'(r)v)$, $\tau$ the transition function of the base.
\end{itemize}
\end{rembox}


\textit{Lecture 21 opened with the last problem of the midterm --- ``there's always a question that is hard, but it's okay \ldots\ I hope we're still friends.''}

\begin{defbox}[Vector Field Tangent to a Submanifold]\deflabel{def:field-tangent}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold, $\iota : S \hookrightarrow M$ the inclusion, and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. Then $\mathbf{X}$ is \textbf{tangent to $S$} if
\[
\mathbf{X}_p \in \iota_{*p}(T_pS) \qquad \text{for every } p \in S .
\]
Identifying $T_pS$ with the subspace $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) \subseteq T_pM$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}), this reads $\mathbf{X}_p \in T_pS$ for every $p \in S$. Nothing is required at points of $M \setminus S$.
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Vector Fields on Submanifolds}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Tangency in an Adapted Chart]\thmlabel{lem:tangent-adapted}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $k$, and $(U, (x, y)) = (U, (x^1, \ldots, x^k, y^1, \ldots, y^{m-k}))$ an adapted chart with $S \cap U = \{ y = 0 \}$ (Definition~\ref{def:adapted-chart}). Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ be written on $U$ as
\[
\mathbf{X} = \sum_{i=1}^k f^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} + \sum_{a=1}^{m-k} g^a\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}
\]
(Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}). Then $\mathbf{X}_p \in T_pS$ for every $p \in S \cap U$ if and only if $g^a(x, 0) = 0$ for every $a$ and every point $(x, 0)$ of $S \cap U$: along $S$, ``there is no $y$ component.''
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the step the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-tangent} uses, written out.)} Let $p \in S \cap U$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:submanifold-tangent}, applied to the adapted chart with the coordinates along $S$ listed first, $\iota_{*p}(T_pS) = \Span\{ \partial/\partial x^1|_p, \ldots, \partial/\partial x^k|_p \}$. The $m$ vectors $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$, $\partial/\partial y^a|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-basis}), and
\[
\mathbf{X}_p = \sum_i f^i(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\Big|_p + \sum_a g^a(p)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}\Big|_p .
\]
Since coefficients in a basis are unique, $\mathbf{X}_p$ lies in the span of the $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ exactly when every $g^a(p) = 0$. The points of $S \cap U$ are those with $y = 0$, so the condition for all $p \in S \cap U$ is $g^a(x, 0) = 0$ for all $a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Brackets of Fields Tangent to a Submanifold]\thmlabel{prop:bracket-tangent}
Let $S \subseteq M$ be a regular submanifold and $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ tangent to $S$ (Definition~\ref{def:field-tangent}). Then $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ is also tangent to $S$.
\leeref{Corollary 8.32}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~21, ``not in excruciating detail''; the bookkeeping is filled in.)} ``Use adapted coordinates'': near $p \in S$ take a slice chart $(x, y) = (x^1, \ldots, x^k, y^1, \ldots, y^{m-k})$ with $S = \{ y = 0 \}$ (Definition~\ref{def:submanifold}); on the exam, $M$ was two-dimensional, ``but they could be vector-valued \ldots\ the codimension or the dimension doesn't matter.'' Write
\[
\mathbf{X} = \sum_i f^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} + \sum_a g^a\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}, \qquad
\mathbf{Y} = \sum_i u^i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} + \sum_a v^a\, \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a} .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:tangent-adapted}, tangency says $g^a(x, 0) = 0$ and $v^a(x, 0) = 0$: ``there is no $y$ component.'' We show the $\partial/\partial y^b$ components of $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ have the same property. By Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, that component is
\[
\mathbf{X}(v^b) - \mathbf{Y}(g^b) = \sum_i f^i\, \frac{\partial v^b}{\partial x^i} + \sum_a g^a\, \frac{\partial v^b}{\partial y^a} - \sum_i u^i\, \frac{\partial g^b}{\partial x^i} - \sum_a v^a\, \frac{\partial g^b}{\partial y^a} .
\]
Evaluate at $y = 0$. The terms with $\partial/\partial x^i$ vanish for one reason: ``how do you evaluate the partial with respect to $x$ at $y = 0$? You fix $y$ to zero and differentiate with respect to $x$, but when I set $y$ to zero, I get zero'' --- $\frac{\partial v^b}{\partial x^i}(x, 0) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\big(v^b(x, 0)\big) = 0$, and likewise for $g^b$. The terms with $\partial/\partial y^a$ vanish ``for a different reason'': ``I don't know that these partials are zero, but these guys are'' --- the coefficients $g^a(x, 0)$ and $v^a(x, 0)$. So the $y$-components of $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ vanish on $S$, and $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]_p \in T_pS$ for $p \in S$.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} Lee proves this (Corollary~8.32) with related fields: on $S$, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ restrict to fields $\iota$-related to them, and the naturality of the bracket (Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}) applied to the inclusion $\iota : S \to M$ does the rest. The coordinate proof above is the one given in class.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 21).} Page~55 of the handwritten notes records the $\partial_y$ component of $[f\partial_x, v\partial_y]$ as $\partial v/\partial x|_{y = 0}$; it is $f\, \partial v/\partial x|_{y = 0}$, which vanishes for the same reason.

\section{Lie Groups and Left-Invariant Vector Fields}\label{sec:lie-groups}

\roadmark{Stage: symmetry}{Groups that are manifolds, and the vector fields that respect the group: the start of Lie theory.}

\textit{Lecture 16, last three minutes, to be continued. References: Lee Ch.~7 and Ch.~8. ``Lie algebras and Lie groups are related, and in one direction the relationship is very nice: any Lie group has a Lie algebra associated to it.''}

\begin{defbox}[Lie Group]\deflabel{def:lie-group}
A \textbf{Lie group} is a topological group $G$ (Definition~\ref{def:top-group}) together with a smooth structure, such that multiplication $G \times G \to G$, $(g, h) \mapsto gh$, and inversion $G \to G$, $g \mapsto g^{-1}$, are smooth maps.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Basic Definitions}}
\end{defbox}

For a topological group the two maps had to be continuous; ``now we ask that they be smooth maps, because we have a manifold structure, so we can make sense of that.''

\begin{propbox}[The Classical Groups Are Lie Groups]\thmlabel{prop:classical-lie-groups}
$\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$, $\SL(n,\mathbb{R})$, $\Ogp(n)$, $\SO(n)$, $\Ugp(n)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, with the smooth structures of Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary} and \ref{sec:double-cover}, are Lie groups.
\leeref{Examples 7.3, 7.27--7.30}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~16 --- ``all the matrix groups that we have seen \ldots\ are Lie groups''; filled in.)} By Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}, for each group $G$ of the list it has to be shown that multiplication $G \times G \to G$ and inversion $G \to G$ are smooth; they are then continuous, so $G$ is also a topological group (Definition~\ref{def:top-group}).

\emph{The setting.} Each group $G$ is an open subset or a submanifold of a space of matrices $\Mat$, which is $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) = \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ or $\Mat(n,\mathbb{C}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{2n^2}$ (real and imaginary parts of the entries) (Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}; for $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-su2}). The inclusion $\iota : G \hookrightarrow \Mat$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}). And a smooth map into $\Mat$ that lands in $G$ is smooth into $G$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(2) for a submanifold; for an open subset because its chart is the restriction of the linear chart of $\Mat$ (proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}), so the map has the same coordinate representations as a map into $G$ and as a map into $\Mat$.

\emph{Multiplication} is the composite of $\iota \times \iota : G \times G \to \Mat \times \Mat$, $(g, h) \mapsto (g, h)$, with matrix multiplication $\Mat \times \Mat \to \Mat$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\iota \times \iota$ is smooth since its components are: they are $\iota \circ \pi_1$ and $\iota \circ \pi_2$, smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps} and Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}, and a map into the Euclidean space $\Mat \times \Mat$ is smooth when its components are.
    \item Matrix multiplication is smooth: the entries $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj}$ are polynomials in the real coordinates (in the complex case, the real and imaginary parts of $\sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj}$ are polynomials in the real and imaginary parts of the entries).
\end{itemize}
So the composite $(g, h) \mapsto gh$ is smooth into $\Mat$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). It lands in $G$, because $G$ is a group under matrix multiplication; so it is smooth into $G$, by the last sentence of the setting.

\emph{Inversion} is the restriction of a smooth map on the open set of invertible matrices --- $g \mapsto \adj(g)/\det g$ by the cofactor formula, a rational map with nonvanishing denominator --- landing in $G$, hence smooth into $G$ in the same way. In detail: the set of invertible matrices in $\Mat$ is $\det^{-1}$ of the nonzero numbers, open since $\det$ is continuous. On it, the entries of $\adj(g)$ and $\det g$ are polynomials in the entries of $g$, and $\det g \ne 0$, so $g \mapsto \adj(g)/\det g = g^{-1}$ is smooth; in the complex case, dividing by $\det g$ is multiplying by $\overline{\det g}/|\det g|^2$, again rational in the real coordinates with nonvanishing denominator $|\det g|^2$. Every $G$ of the list consists of invertible matrices, so $g \mapsto g^{-1}$ on $G$ is this map composed with $\iota$, smooth into $\Mat$; it lands in $G$, because $G$ is closed under inverses; so it is smooth into $G$. (For $\Ogp(n)$ and $\Ugp(n)$ it is even linear: $g \mapsto g^{\mathsf T}$, $g \mapsto g^*$.)
\end{proof}

The classical groups through the course: defined in Section~\ref{sec:topgroups}, with the examples of Section~\ref{sec:ex-classical}; topological manifolds as level sets in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-manifolds}; $\SO(2)$ and $\SO(3)$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so2-orbits} and~\ref{ex:so3-orbits}, and $\SO(3)$ on $S^2$ in Examples~\ref{ex:so3-isotropy} and~\ref{ex:s2-homogeneous}; $\Ogp(n)$ acting on the Grassmannians in Corollary~\ref{cor:grassmannian}; smooth manifolds in Examples~\ref{ex:On-smooth} and~\ref{ex:Un-smooth}; their tangent spaces at the identity in Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}, with the infinitesimal rotations of Example~\ref{ex:so3-infinitesimal}; the double cover $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \SO(3)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:double-cover}; the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and the cross product in Example~\ref{ex:cross-product-lie}; and Lie groups in Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}.

The unit quaternions $S^3$ are a Lie group as well (Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-lie-group}), isomorphic to $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:s3-su2}).

\begin{defbox}[Left Translation]\deflabel{def:left-translation-lie}
For $g$ in a Lie group $G$, \textbf{left translation} by $g$ is $L_g : G \to G$, $L_g(h) = gh$.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Basic Definitions}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Left Translations Are Diffeomorphisms]\thmlabel{lem:Lg-diffeo}
$L_g$ is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $L_{g^{-1}}$.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Basic Definitions}}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in, as for topological groups in Lemma~\ref{lem:Lg}.)} By Definition~\ref{def:diffeomorphism}, it has to be shown that $L_g$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, and that the inverse is $L_{g^{-1}}$.

\emph{Smooth.} $L_g$ is smooth as the composite of $h \mapsto (g, h)$ with multiplication: $L_g(h) = gh = \mu\big(\iota^{g}(h)\big)$, where $\iota^{g} : G \to G \times G$, $h \mapsto (g, h)$, is the slice inclusion of Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions} (with $M_1 = M_2 = G$ and $p_1 = g$), smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-maps}, and $\mu : G \times G \to G$ is multiplication, smooth by Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}. So $L_g = \mu \circ \iota^{g}$ is smooth (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). The same holds for every element of $G$, in particular for $g^{-1}$: $L_{g^{-1}}$ is smooth.

\emph{Inverse.} For $h \in G$, by associativity of the group product,
\[
L_g\big(L_{g^{-1}}(h)\big) = g\,(g^{-1}h) = (gg^{-1})\,h = h, \qquad L_{g^{-1}}\big(L_g(h)\big) = g^{-1}(gh) = (g^{-1}g)\,h = h .
\]
So $L_g \circ L_{g^{-1}} = L_{g^{-1}} \circ L_g = \mathrm{id}$: $L_g$ is a bijection with inverse $L_{g^{-1}}$, and both are smooth, so $L_g$ is a diffeomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[Left-Invariant Vector Field]\deflabel{def:left-invariant}
A vector field $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ is \textbf{left-invariant} if for all $g, h \in G$
\[
(L_g)_{*h}\, \mathbf{X}_h = \mathbf{X}_{gh} .
\]
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Lie Algebras}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=6em, row sep=3em]
T_hG \arrow[r, "(L_g)_{*h}"] & T_{gh}G \\[-2.2em]
\mathbf{X}_h \arrow[r, mapsto] & \mathbf{X}_{gh}
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Left invariance in one line: ``using [left translations], you can push vectors of the field to get other vectors; and whenever you do that, you get the corresponding vector of the field.'' The value at one point determines the field everywhere: taking $h = e$, $\mathbf{X}_g = (L_g)_{*e}\, \mathbf{X}_e$. This is the left translation of tangent spaces from the discussion of moving the base point (Lemma~\ref{lem:group-morphism-translation}), applied to a whole field.

\begin{exbox}[Left-Invariant Fields on $\GL({n,\mathbb{R}})$]\exlabel{ex:left-invariant-GL}
On $G = \GL(n,\mathbb{R})$, open in $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, so that $T_gG = \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, the left-invariant vector fields are exactly
\[
\mathbf{X}^A_g = gA, \qquad A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) = T_IG .
\]
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in.)} \emph{The identification.} $G$ is open in the vector space $\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, so $T_gG = T_g\Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}), and $T_g\Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \cong \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ by $v \leftrightarrow D_v|_g$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}); this is the identification $T_gG = \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$ of the statement.

\emph{The differential of $L_g$.} $L_g$ is the restriction to $G$ of the linear map $\ell_g : \Mat(n,\mathbb{R}) \to \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, $h \mapsto gh$, so its differential at every point is that same linear map: $(L_g)_{*h}(v) = gv$. Indeed, $\iota \circ L_g = \ell_g \circ \iota$ for the inclusion $\iota : G \hookrightarrow \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$, so by the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) $\iota_{*gh} \circ (L_g)_{*h} = (\ell_g)_{*h} \circ \iota_{*h}$, and $\iota_{*}$ is the identification of Lemma~\ref{lem:germs-local}; and by Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} for the linear map $\ell_g$, $(\ell_g)_{*h}(D_v|_h) = D_{gv}|_{gh}$.

\emph{Left-invariant fields are of the form $\mathbf{X}^A$.} By the last step, left invariance (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}) reads
\[
g\,\mathbf{X}_h = \mathbf{X}_{gh} \qquad \text{for all } g, h \in G,
\]
with $\mathbf{X}_h \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$. Taking $h = I$ gives $\mathbf{X}_g = \mathbf{X}_{gI} = g\,\mathbf{X}_I$, so $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}^A$ with $A = \mathbf{X}_I$.

\emph{Every $\mathbf{X}^A$ is a left-invariant field.} Conversely, let $A \in \Mat(n,\mathbb{R})$. By associativity of matrix multiplication,
\[
(L_g)_{*h}\big(\mathbf{X}^A_h\big) = g\,(hA) = (gh)A = \mathbf{X}^A_{gh},
\]
so every $\mathbf{X}^A$ is left-invariant. It is smooth because its entries are linear in those of $g$: in the global chart of $G$ given by the matrix entries $x^{ij}$, the coefficients of $\mathbf{X}^A$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}) are $\mathbf{X}^A_g[x^{ij}] = D_{gA}|_g[x^{ij}] = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\, x^{ij}(g + t\,gA) = (gA)_{ij} = \sum_k g_{ik} A_{kj}$, linear in the entries of $g$, hence smooth.
\end{proof}

Compare Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}, where $T^{\geo}_g G = g \cdot T^{\geo}_I G$ for the classical groups: a left-invariant field moves the tangent space at the identity around the group by left multiplication. In the language of \ref{sub:lie-algebra-TeG}, later in this section, $\mathbf{X}^A$ is the left-invariant extension of $A \in T_IG$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}): by the differential of $L_g$ computed in the proof above, $(L_g)_{*I}(A) = gA = \mathbf{X}^A_g$.

\begin{defbox}[The Lie Algebra of a Lie Group]\deflabel{def:lie-algebra-of-group}
The \textbf{Lie algebra} of a Lie group $G$ is
\[
\mathfrak{g} = \{\, \mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(G) \mid \mathbf{X} \text{ is left-invariant} \,\},
\]
with the Lie bracket of vector fields.
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Lie Algebras}}
\end{defbox}

\textit{Status.} Defined in Lecture~16 --- ``this is going to be quickly identified with the tangent space at the identity. But originally we think of them as a certain very special type of vector field, because that's where the Lie bracket comes from.'' For $\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ the identification is $\mathbf{X}^A \mapsto A$ (Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}). The two facts announced then were proved in Lecture~17, in \S\ref{sub:lie-algebra-TeG} below: $\mathfrak{g}$ is closed under the bracket, and $\mathbf{X} \mapsto \mathbf{X}_e$ is an isomorphism onto $T_eG$ (its last step, smoothness, completed in Lecture~18).

\subsection{The Lie Algebra and the Tangent Space at the Identity}\label{sub:lie-algebra-TeG}

\textit{Lecture 17. ``Back to Lie groups.'' With the language of related fields, ``we can rephrase some of the definitions.''}

\begin{lembox}[Left-Invariance as Relatedness]\thmlabel{lem:left-invariant-related}
A vector field $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ is left-invariant (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}) if and only if, for every $g \in G$, $\mathbf{X}$ is \emph{$L_g$-related to itself} (Definition~\ref{def:F-related} with $F = L_g$ and $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}$).
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17, a rephrasing of the definition: ``we can rephrase some of the definitions''.)} Being $L_g$-related to itself means $d(L_g)_h(\mathbf{X}_h) = \mathbf{X}_{L_g(h)} = \mathbf{X}_{gh}$ for every $h \in G$, which is the condition of Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant} for this $g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Why Left?]\label{rem:left-invariant-related}
Lecture~17 abbreviates ``left-invariant'' to l.i. ``And you can ask why left. What's wrong with right? There's nothing wrong with right. You have to choose \ldots\ and this is the universal choice.'' Right-invariant fields, $R_g$-related to themselves for $R_g(h) = hg$, give an equivalent theory; the one place the choice shows is the sign of the bracket, at the end of this subsection.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[$\mathfrak{g}$ Is a Lie Subalgebra of $\mathfrak{X}(G)$]\thmlabel{cor:lie-subalgebra}
If $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$ then $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] \in \mathfrak{g}$. So $\mathfrak{g}$, a linear subspace of $\mathfrak{X}(G)$, is a Lie algebra under the bracket of vector fields.
\leeref{Proposition 8.33}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17: ``the big observation, which is actually a consequence of'' Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}.)} \emph{Closed under the bracket.} Let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$ and fix $g \in G$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-related}, $\mathbf{X}$ is $L_g$-related to $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$. So by Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality} with $F = L_g$, $\mathbf{X}_1 = \mathbf{Y}_1 = \mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{X}_2 = \mathbf{Y}_2 = \mathbf{Y}$, $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$ is $L_g$-related to $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}]$. This holds for every $g$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-related} again (in the converse direction) this for every $g$ is left-invariance: $[\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}] \in \mathfrak{g}$.

\textit{(Filled in.)} \emph{A linear subspace.} $\mathfrak{g}$ is a linear subspace because each $d(L_g)_h$ is linear (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}). Explicitly, let $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. For all $g, h \in G$, by the pointwise operations of Definition~\ref{def:vector-fields-space}, the linearity of $d(L_g)_h$, and left-invariance of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$,
\[
d(L_g)_h\big((a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y})_h\big) = d(L_g)_h\big(a\,\mathbf{X}_h + b\,\mathbf{Y}_h\big) = a\, d(L_g)_h(\mathbf{X}_h) + b\, d(L_g)_h(\mathbf{Y}_h) = a\,\mathbf{X}_{gh} + b\,\mathbf{Y}_{gh} = (a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y})_{gh} .
\]
So $a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$; and the zero field is in $\mathfrak{g}$, since a linear map sends $0$ to $0$.

\emph{A Lie algebra.} By the first step the bracket of vector fields restricts to a map $\mathfrak{g} \times \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}$. The bracket on $\mathfrak{g}$ is bilinear, skew and satisfies Jacobi because it does on $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:vf-lie-algebra}): these are identities for all elements of $\mathfrak{X}(G)$, so in particular for all elements of $\mathfrak{g}$. So $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra}).
\end{proof}

``It's a Lie subalgebra of the infinite-dimensional algebra of all vector fields on $G$.'' Vector fields can be added and scaled, so $\mathfrak{X}(G)$ is a vector space (``in fact, it's an algebra over the smooth functions, but I want to think of it as a vector space''). ``At this point, maybe it's not clear what [$\mathfrak{g}$] is. It could be, I don't know, still infinite-dimensional, or something, or empty.'' The theorem below settles it. Its proof rests on a construction, made in Lecture~17 and finished in Lecture~18, which comes first.

\begin{defbox}[Left-Invariant Extension]\deflabel{def:left-invariant-extension}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$, and $v \in T_eG$. The \textbf{left-invariant extension} of $v$ is the map $\mathbf{X}^v : G \to TG$, $g \mapsto \mathbf{X}^v_g$, with
\[
\mathbf{X}^v_g = d(L_g)_e(v) \in T_gG, \qquad g \in G :
\]
the vector $v$ carried from $e$ to $g$ by the differential of the left translation $L_g$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-translation-lie}). It is a \emph{rough} vector field (Lee's term), a tangent vector at every point, not yet known to be smooth.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 8.37}
\end{defbox}

``Just as with vector fields'' on a vector space (Proposition~\ref{prop:translations-identify}), there is a unique left translation carrying $e$ to $g$, and $\mathbf{X}^v_g$ is $v$ carried along it.

\begin{lembox}[The Left-Invariant Extension Is Left-Invariant]\thmlabel{lem:left-invariant-extension}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $v \in T_eG$, $\mathbf{X}^v_g \in T_gG$ for every $g \in G$, and $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$.
    \item For $v \in T_eG$, $\mathbf{X}^v$ satisfies the identity of Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}: $d(L_g)_h\big(\mathbf{X}^v_h\big) = \mathbf{X}^v_{gh}$ for all $g, h \in G$.
    \item Every $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{g}$ is the left-invariant extension of its value at $e$: $\mathbf{X}_g = d(L_g)_e(\mathbf{X}_e)$ for every $g \in G$, that is, $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}^{\mathbf{X}_e}$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{proof of Theorem 8.37}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17, steps of the proof that $\mathfrak{g}$ is $T_eG$; (2) was left to check --- ``not a bad thing to do'' --- and done in the review at the start of Lecture~19.)}

\emph{(1)} $L_g$ maps $e$ to $g$, so $d(L_g)_e : T_eG \to T_{L_g(e)}G = T_{ge}G = T_gG$, and $\mathbf{X}^v_g = d(L_g)_e(v)$ lies in $T_gG$. And $L_e = \mathrm{id}_G$ (as $eh = h$), so $\mathbf{X}^v_e = (\mathrm{id}_G)_{*e}(v) = v$ by Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}.

\emph{(2)} \textit{(Lecture~19.)} Fix $h, g \in G$. ``If I want to end up at $g$, I have to start at $h^{-1}g$'': $L_h$ maps $h^{-1}g$ to $g$. By Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension} and the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}),
\[
d(L_h)_{h^{-1}g}\big(\mathbf{X}^v_{h^{-1}g}\big) = d(L_h)_{h^{-1}g}\, d(L_{h^{-1}g})_e(v) = d\big(L_h \circ L_{h^{-1}g}\big)_e(v) = d(L_g)_e(v) = \mathbf{X}^v_g ,
\]
because $L_h \circ L_{h^{-1}g} = L_g$: ``you multiply on the left by $h^{-1}g$, and then you multiply on the left by $h$, so the $h$ and the $h^{-1}$ cancel.'' Writing $k = h^{-1}g$, this says $d(L_h)_k(\mathbf{X}^v_k) = \mathbf{X}^v_{hk}$ for all $h, k \in G$, the identity of Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}.

\emph{(3)} Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $g \in G$. Left-invariance (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}) with $h = e$ reads $d(L_g)_e(\mathbf{X}_e) = \mathbf{X}_{ge} = \mathbf{X}_g$, and by Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension} with $v = \mathbf{X}_e$ the left side is $\mathbf{X}^{\mathbf{X}_e}_g$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[The Left-Invariant Extension Is Smooth]\thmlabel{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$ and $v \in T_eG$. For $f \in C^\infty(G)$ let $\varphi : G \times G \to \mathbb{R}$, $\varphi(g, x) = f(gx)$. Then $\varphi$ is smooth, and
\[
\mathbf{X}^v f = \partial_v\varphi \in C^\infty(G),
\]
the partial derivative of $\varphi$ in the second variable in the direction $v$ (Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor}). Hence $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth: $\mathbf{X}^v \in \mathfrak{g}$, a left-invariant vector field with $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 8.37}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~18, completing the proof of Lecture~17.)} Lecture~17 stopped here: ``The incompleteness in the proof is that we want to show that this is $C^\infty$. It's an important technical point \ldots\ and we don't have the tools to do that at this point.'' Lecture~18 finished it --- ``in fact, we can just use this partial derivative construction'' (Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor}). So far $\mathbf{X}^v$ is a left-invariant \emph{rough} field (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(1) and (2)), Lee's term for a section not yet known to be smooth: ``the piece of the construction that has not been justified is that this thing is smooth.''

\emph{The claim.} It suffices to show that for every $f \in C^\infty(G)$ the function $\mathbf{X}^v f : g \mapsto \mathbf{X}^v_g[f]$ is smooth. ``This function is still well defined regardless of whether $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth or not \ldots\ because I have a vector at every point, and I can let that act on any function.'' The lecture's proof of the claim: in local coordinates $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$, $m = \dim G$, there is still a pointwise expansion $\mathbf{X}^v = \sum_j a^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$, and $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth exactly when the $a^j$ are (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}); ``but the $a^j$ are precisely the action of $\mathbf{X}^v$ on the coordinate $x^j$.'' This is Lemma~\ref{lem:vf-smooth-criterion}, whose proof also handles the point that $x^j$ is defined only on the chart, by extending it with a bump function.

\emph{The construction.} Let $f \in C^\infty(G)$ and $g \in G$. By the definition of $\mathbf{X}^v$ and of the pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:pushforward}),
\[
(\mathbf{X}^v f)(g) = d(L_g)_e(v)[f] = v[f \circ L_g] \in \mathbb{R},
\]
and ``we want to show that as a function of $g$, this is smooth.'' Construct ``a trick that occurred to me''
\[
\varphi : G \times G \xrightarrow{\ \text{multiplication}\ } G \xrightarrow{\ f\ } \mathbb{R}, \qquad \varphi(g, x) = f(gx) = (f \circ L_g)(x).
\]
It is smooth, as the composite of the multiplication, smooth by Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}, with $f$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:composition-smooth}). Fixing $g$ in the first variable, $f \circ L_g = \varphi(g, \cdot)$, so by Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor}, in the second variable with $w = v \in T_eG$,
\[
(\mathbf{X}^v f)(g) = v\big[\varphi(g, \cdot)\big] = \partial_v\varphi(g) .
\]
``We're letting $v$ act on the second variable, and so that means that it is smooth'': $\partial_v\varphi \in C^\infty(G)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:partial-derivative-factor}(3). By the claim, $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth. It is left-invariant (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(2)), so $\mathbf{X}^v \in \mathfrak{g}$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-of-group}), and $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(1)).
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Lie Algebra Is the Tangent Space at the Identity]\thmlabel{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}
Let $G$ be a Lie group with identity $e$. The evaluation map
\[
\mathrm{ev} : \mathfrak{g} \to T_eG, \qquad \mathbf{X} \mapsto \mathbf{X}_e ,
\]
is a linear isomorphism. In particular $\dim \mathfrak{g} = \dim G$.
\leeref{Theorem 8.37}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~17 --- ``it'll be an incomplete proof \ldots\ there is one detail that we're not prepared to prove'' --- completed in Lecture~18. The lecture's steps.)} $\mathrm{ev}$ is linear: for $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y} \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{ev}(a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y}) = (a\mathbf{X} + b\mathbf{Y})_e = a\,\mathbf{X}_e + b\,\mathbf{Y}_e$ by Definition~\ref{def:vector-fields-space}. It remains to show that $\mathrm{ev}$ is injective and surjective.

\textit{The basic idea.} For $g \in G$, $L_g$ maps $e$ to $g$, so $d(L_g)_e : T_eG \to T_gG$, and for $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{g}$, left-invariance (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant}) with $h = e$ reads
\[
d(L_g)_e(\mathbf{X}_e) = \mathbf{X}_g ;
\]
more generally $d(L_g)_h(\mathbf{X}_h) = \mathbf{X}_{gh}$ for all $h$. ``There's only one choice really'': $\mathbf{X}$ is the left-invariant extension of $\mathbf{X}_e$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(3)).

\emph{Injective.} By the basic idea, $\mathbf{X}$ is determined by its value at $e$. So $\mathbf{X}_e = 0$ forces $\mathbf{X}_g = d(L_g)_e(0) = 0$ for all $g$, since $d(L_g)_e$ is linear (Proposition~\ref{prop:pushforward-derivation}). So the kernel of the linear map $\mathrm{ev}$ is $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, and $\mathrm{ev}$ is injective.

\emph{Surjective.} Start with $v \in T_eG$; we want a left-invariant $\mathbf{X}$ with $\mathbf{X}_e = v$. The basic idea says there is no choice: we must take the left-invariant extension of $v$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}),
\[
\mathbf{X}^v_g = d(L_g)_e(v), \qquad g \in G .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(1) and (2), which are Lecture~17's steps, $\mathbf{X}^v$ is a rough vector field, a tangent vector at every point, with $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$ and satisfying the left-invariance identity. \emph{Smooth.} This is where Lecture~17 stopped; Lecture~18 finished it, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth} $\mathbf{X}^v$ is smooth, through $\mathbf{X}^v f = \partial_v\varphi$ for $\varphi(g, x) = f(gx)$. So $\mathbf{X}^v \in \mathfrak{g}$ and $\mathrm{ev}(\mathbf{X}^v) = v$. ``So this finishes completely the proof of that theorem.''

Finally, a linear isomorphism preserves dimension, so $\dim \mathfrak{g} = \dim T_eG = \dim G$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}).
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.95]
\draw[thick, gray!70!black, fill=gray!4] (0,0) ellipse (2.4 and 1.15);
\node[gray!70!black, font=\footnotesize] at (-2.25,0.95) {$G$};
\fill (-1.2,-0.2) circle (1.6pt) node[below left, font=\scriptsize] {$e$};
\fill (1.15,0.05) circle (1.6pt) node[below right, font=\scriptsize] {$g$};
\draw[->, very thick, orange!85!black] (-1.2,-0.2) -- ++(0.35,0.55) node[above, font=\scriptsize] {$v$};
\draw[->, very thick, orange!85!black] (1.15,0.05) -- ++(0.55,0.45) node[right, xshift=16pt, font=\scriptsize] {$\mathbf{X}^v_g = d(L_g)_e(v)$};
\draw[->, dashed, gray!65] (-0.95,-0.35) .. controls (-0.2,-0.85) and (0.5,-0.7) .. (1.0,-0.08);
\node[gray!70!black, font=\scriptsize] at (0.0,-0.95) {$L_g$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\textbf{Comparison with Lee.} Lee's proof (Theorem~8.37) differentiates $f(g\,\gamma(t))$ along a curve $\gamma$ adapted to $v$, which is Proposition~\ref{prop:partial-derivative-factor}(1) applied to the function $\varphi(g, x) = f(gx)$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}: $(\mathbf{X}^v f)(g) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} \varphi(g, \gamma(t))$. The course packages that step once and for all as the partial derivative $\partial_v\varphi$.

On the proof as a whole, Uribe passed on a remark a student made in office hours: ``this subject is not so much about solving problems \ldots\ it's about constructing an architecture inside one's brain.''

\begin{exbox}[The Additive Group of a Vector Space]\exlabel{ex:vs-lie-algebra}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space, a Lie group under addition with identity $0$, so that $L_p = \tau_p$ is translation by $p$. Its left-invariant vector fields are the constant fields $\mathbf{X}^v : p \mapsto D_v|_p$, $v \in V$, and all their brackets vanish: $\mathfrak{g} \cong V$ with the zero bracket.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, after the remark in Lecture~17 that the translations of a vector space give ``a left-invariant vector field''.)} \emph{$V$ is a Lie group.} In linear coordinates (Definition~\ref{def:vs-structure}), addition $(p, q) \mapsto p + q$ and inversion $p \mapsto -p$ are linear, hence smooth; so $V$ is a Lie group (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}), with $L_p(q) = p + q = \tau_p(q)$.

\emph{The left-invariant fields.} By Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}, every element of $T_0V$ is $D_v|_0$ for a unique $v \in V$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG} and Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(3), the left-invariant fields are exactly the left-invariant extensions $\mathbf{X}^w$, $w \in T_0V$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}), with $\mathbf{X}^w_p = d(L_p)_0(w)$. For $w = D_v|_0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:translations-identify}(2) gives
\[
\mathbf{X}^{w}_p = d(\tau_p)_0\big(D_v|_0\big) = D_v|_p ,
\]
so the field $\mathbf{X}^v$ of the example, the left-invariant extension of $D_v|_0$, is $p \mapsto D_v|_p$; by the theorem these are all the left-invariant fields. The map $v \mapsto \mathbf{X}^v$ is the composite of the isomorphism $v \mapsto D_v|_0$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} with $\mathrm{ev}^{-1}$, so it is a linear isomorphism $V \cong \mathfrak{g}$.

\emph{The brackets vanish.} Choose a basis of $V$ and the corresponding linear coordinates $x^1, \ldots, x^n$, a global chart, and write $v = \sum_i v^i e_i$. The coefficients of $\mathbf{X}^v$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}) are, using Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs} and the linearity of $x^i$,
\[
\mathbf{X}^v_p[x^i] = D_v|_p[x^i] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} x^i(p + tv) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} \big(x^i(p) + t\,v^i\big) = v^i .
\]
So in linear coordinates $\mathbf{X}^v = \sum_i v^i\, \partial_i$ has constant coefficients, and likewise $\mathbf{X}^w = \sum_i w^i\, \partial_i$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, the $j$-th coefficient of $[\mathbf{X}^v, \mathbf{X}^w]$ is $\sum_i \big(v^i\, \partial w^j/\partial x^i - w^i\, \partial v^j/\partial x^i\big) = 0$, since the partial derivatives of constants vanish. So $[\mathbf{X}^v, \mathbf{X}^w] = 0$ for all $v, w$: $\mathfrak{g} \cong V$ with the zero bracket.
\end{proof}

\begin{defbox}[The Lie Bracket on $T_eG$]\deflabel{def:bracket-TeG}
Let $G$ be a Lie group and, for $v \in T_eG$, let $\mathbf{X}^v \in \mathfrak{g}$ be its left-invariant extension (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension} and Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}), the left-invariant field with $\mathbf{X}^v_e = v$, unique by Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}. The \textbf{Lie bracket} on $T_eG$ is
\[
[v, w] = \big[\mathbf{X}^v, \mathbf{X}^w\big]_e , \qquad v, w \in T_eG .
\]
\end{defbox}

By construction $\mathrm{ev}$ is then an isomorphism of Lie algebras: $T_eG$ inherits the bracket that makes it one. The question is what this bracket is.

\begin{thmbox}[{The Lie Algebra of $\GL({d,\mathbb{R}})$}]\thmlabel{thm:gl-bracket}
Let $G = \GL(d, \mathbb{R})$, the $d \times d$ invertible matrices, an open subset of $\Mat(d, \mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{d^2}$, so that $T_IG = \Mat(d,\mathbb{R})$. The Lie bracket on $T_IG$ (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}) is the matrix commutator
\[
[A, B] = AB - BA .
\]
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19 --- ``we have run out of diagrams to chase. We actually have to compute something.'' The lecture's computation, with the index bookkeeping written out. Lecture~19 proved this together with Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket}, which reduces every linear group to this case.)}

\emph{Coordinates.} Write $A = (a^i_j)$, with $i$ the row index and $j$ the column index, and call a general group element $X = (x^i_j) \in \GL(d, \mathbb{R})$ rather than $g$, ``because I want to think of it as a variable.'' Written out,
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix} a^1_1 & \cdots & a^1_d \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a^d_1 & \cdots & a^d_d \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
X = \begin{pmatrix} x^1_1 & \cdots & x^1_d \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ x^d_1 & \cdots & x^d_d \end{pmatrix},
\]
the upper index numbering the rows and the lower index the columns. The entries $x^i_j$ are the standard coordinates of $\Mat(d,\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{d^2}$, ``indexed in a funny way'', and a tangent vector $V = (V^i_j) \in \Mat(d, \mathbb{R}) = T_X\GL(d,\mathbb{R})$ is $\sum_{i,j} V^i_j\, \partial/\partial x^i_j|_X$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}). The basic computation is
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i_j}\big(x^l_n\big) = \delta_{il}\, \delta_{jn} ,
\]
``one or zero depending on whether I'm differentiating the same coordinate as I'm taking the partial.''

\emph{The left-invariant field.} $\mathbf{X}^A_X = d(L_X)_I(A)$, and $L_X : \mathbb{R}^{d^2} \to \mathbb{R}^{d^2}$, $Y \mapsto XY$, is linear, ``so it's its own differential'' (Corollary~\ref{cor:tangent-vs}): $\mathbf{X}^A_X = XA$ (Example~\ref{ex:left-invariant-GL}). The $(i,j)$ entry of $XA$ is $\sum_k x^i_k a^k_j$, so
\[
\mathbf{X}^A = \sum_{i,j} \Big( \sum_k x^i_k\, a^k_j \Big) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i_j}, \qquad
\mathbf{X}^B = \sum_{l,n} \Big( \sum_m x^l_m\, b^m_n \Big) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^l_n},
\]
with independent indices for the second field, ``because these are independent.'' The $a^k_j$ and $b^m_n$ are constants; the $x$'s are functions. (A student asked why the sums can come out of the commutator: ``because the commutator is bilinear \ldots\ over constants, \ldots\ but you cannot pull the $x$'s out, because those are functions.'')

\emph{The bracket.} ``We know that we don't care about the second derivatives because they're going to go away'' (Lemma~\ref{lem:bracket-field}): by Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-coords}, the coefficient of $\partial/\partial x^l_n$ in $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]$ is $\mathbf{X}^A$ applied to the coefficient of $\mathbf{X}^B$, minus the same with $A$ and $B$ exchanged. Applying the basic computation,
\[
\mathbf{X}^A\Big( \sum_m x^l_m\, b^m_n \Big) = \sum_{i,j,k,m} x^i_k\, a^k_j\, b^m_n\, \delta_{il}\, \delta_{jm} = \sum_{k} x^l_k \Big( \sum_j a^k_j\, b^j_n \Big) = \sum_k x^l_k\, (AB)^k_n :
\]
setting $i = l$ and $m = j$ is all that happens, and then ``these two guys together \ldots\ it's an entry of a matrix'', the $(k, n)$ entry of $AB$. So
\[
[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B] = \sum_{l,n} \Big( \sum_k x^l_k\, (AB)^k_n \Big) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^l_n} - \big(\text{the same with } A \text{ and } B \text{ exchanged}\big) = \mathbf{X}^{AB} - \mathbf{X}^{BA},
\]
comparing with the formula for $\mathbf{X}^A$ with $AB$, resp.\ $BA$, in place of $A$.

\emph{Evaluate at the identity.} By Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG} and $\mathbf{X}^C_I = C$,
\[
[A, B] = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_I = \mathbf{X}^{AB}_I - \mathbf{X}^{BA}_I = AB - BA . \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

``You have to think about this on your own \ldots\ think about indices and so on. But this is essentially the reason.'' Coordinate-free, the computation says: a field $X \mapsto XC$ on an open subset of $\Mat(d,\mathbb{R})$ is linear in $X$, and the bracket of the linear fields $X \mapsto XA$ and $X \mapsto XB$ is the linear field $X \mapsto X(AB - BA)$.

\begin{rembox}[Left or Right: The Sign of the Bracket]\label{rem:bracket-on-TeG}
``This is the case because we use left-invariant fields. If we use right-invariant fields, we would have minus that.'' Why left, then? An aside: ``Did you ever think what the world would look like if, instead of writing $f(x)$ \ldots\ we would have written $(x)f$? \ldots\ Imagine composing functions with that rule. \ldots\ Everything works much better if you write $(x)f$'': in that notation, composites read in the order the maps are applied.
\end{rembox}

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 17).} Page~46 of the handwritten notes says the construction gives ``$\mathbf{X} : M \to TM$''; the manifold is the group, $\mathbf{X} : G \to TG$.

% SECTION: LIE GROUP MORPHISMS AND LINEAR GROUPS
% ============================================================================

\section{Lie Group Morphisms and Linear Groups}\label{sec:lie-morphisms}\label{sub:lie-group-morphisms}

\roadmark{Stage: symmetry}{Maps of Lie groups induce maps of Lie algebras that preserve brackets; for a linear group the bracket is the matrix commutator.}

\textit{Lecture 18. ``Next, we want to talk about Lie group morphisms and the Lie algebra, because we can do something now that we couldn't before.''}

\begin{rembox}[From Now On: $\mathfrak{g}$ Is $T_eG$]\label{rem:g-is-TeG}
``From now on, as you can imagine, we will identify'' the Lie algebra with the tangent space at the identity, $\mathfrak{g} \cong T_eG$ by $\mathrm{ev}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}), as vector spaces, ``keeping in mind that the Lie bracket comes from \ldots\ commuting left-invariant fields.'' That is Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-of-group} read through Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}: to compute the bracket of $A, B \in T_eG$,
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item extend $A$ and $B$ to the left-invariant fields $\mathbf{X}^A$, $\mathbf{X}^B$, their left-invariant extensions (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}; they lie in $\mathfrak{g}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth});
\item take the commutator $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]$ of vector fields;
\item evaluate it at the identity: $[A, B] = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_e$.
\end{enumerate}
``That's the definition.'' Elements of $T_eG$ are now written with capital letters: ``I really kind of think of them as matrices.''
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[Linear Group]\deflabel{def:linear-group}
A \textbf{linear group}, or \textbf{matrix group}, is a Lie group $G$ (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group}) that is a subgroup of $\GL(n,\mathbb{R})$ or $\GL(n,\mathbb{C})$ for some $n$, with matrix multiplication as its group product --- for instance each classical group of Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}.
\end{defbox}

\begin{rembox}[Nonlinear Groups]\label{rem:linear-groups}
Matrix groups ``are called linear groups, by the way'' (Definition~\ref{def:linear-group}). ``And not every Lie group is isomorphic to a matrix group \ldots\ the nonlinear groups arise naturally from making covers'' of matrix groups. \textit{(Filled in: the standard example is the universal cover of $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, a Lie group isomorphic to no group of matrices.)} The question of Lecture~17, restated: for a matrix group, ``can we identify the bracket directly on the tangent space at the identity?'' The answer is the matrix commutator (Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket}); to get there, the course uses the general idea below.
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[Lie Group Morphism]\deflabel{def:lie-group-morphism}
Let $H$ and $G$ be Lie groups. A \textbf{Lie group morphism} (homomorphism) $F : H \to G$ is a map that is both smooth and a group morphism: $F(gh) = F(g)F(h)$ for all $g, h \in H$.
\leeref{Ch.~7, \emph{Lie Group Homomorphisms}}
\end{defbox}

A Lie group is ``a manifold and a group, and the various maps are smooth'', so a morphism ``preserves both structures.'' In particular $F(e_H) = e_G$. \textit{(Filled in: $F(e_H) = F(e_He_H) = F(e_H)F(e_H)$; multiply on the left by $F(e_H)^{-1}$.)} So $F$ has a differential at the identity,
\[
dF_e : T_{e}H \longrightarrow T_{e}G, \qquad \text{that is,} \qquad dF_e : \mathfrak{h} \longrightarrow \mathfrak{g},
\]
a linear map between the Lie algebras, and ``the natural question is whether this map preserves commutators.''

\begin{defbox}[Lie Algebra Morphism]\deflabel{def:lie-algebra-morphism}
Let $\mathfrak{h}$ and $\mathfrak{g}$ be Lie algebras (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra}). A \textbf{Lie algebra morphism} is a linear map $\phi : \mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{g}$ that preserves brackets: $\phi([A, B]) = [\phi(A), \phi(B)]$ for all $A, B \in \mathfrak{h}$.
\leeref{Ch.~8, \emph{Induced Lie Algebra Homomorphisms}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{lembox}[Left-Invariant Fields Related by a Morphism]\thmlabel{lem:morphism-related}
Let $F : H \to G$ be a Lie group morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism}) and $A \in T_eH$, and put $\tilde A = dF_e(A) \in T_eG$. Let $\mathbf{X}^A \in \mathfrak{X}(H)$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ be the left-invariant extensions of $A$ and of $\tilde A$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}; smooth by Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}). Then $\mathbf{X}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ are $F$-related (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}):
\[
dF_h\big(\mathbf{X}^A_h\big) = \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_{F(h)} \in T_{F(h)}G \qquad \text{for every } h \in H .
\]
\leeref{proof of Theorem 8.44}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~18: the ``claim'' in the proof that Lie group morphisms preserve brackets. The final diagram chase, left to the class as the lecture ran out of time, is completed.)} Fix $h \in H$; the displayed equality is to be shown. \emph{$F(e) = e$.} As noted after Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism}, $F(e_H) = F(e_He_H) = F(e_H)F(e_H)$, and multiplying on the left by $F(e_H)^{-1}$ gives $F(e_H) = e_G$; so $dF_e$ maps $T_eH$ to $T_eG$, and $\tilde A \in T_eG$.

\emph{The square.} ``We have to use very much that $F$ is a group morphism.'' Consider the square
\[
F \circ L_h = L_{F(h)} \circ F : H \to G .
\]
It commutes: for $x \in H$, $F(L_h(x)) = F(hx) = F(h)F(x) = L_{F(h)}(F(x))$, where $L$ is ``always left multiplication in the corresponding group.'' Differentiate it at $e \in H$. Since $L_h(e) = h$ and $F(e) = e$, the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}) gives the commutative square of differentials
\[
dF_h \circ d(L_h)_e = d\big(L_{F(h)}\big)_e \circ dF_e : T_eH \to T_{F(h)}G .
\]

\emph{The chase.} \textit{(Completed.)} ``Chase where $A$ goes under this diagram'':
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{along the bottom, then up:} && A \mapsto d(L_h)_e(A) = \mathbf{X}^A_h \mapsto dF_h(\mathbf{X}^A_h), \\
&\text{up, then along the top:} && A \mapsto dF_e(A) = \tilde A \mapsto d(L_{F(h)})_e(\tilde A) = \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_{F(h)},
\end{aligned}
\]
both by Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension}, for $H$ at the point $h$ and for $G$ at the point $F(h)$. The square commutes, so $dF_h(\mathbf{X}^A_h) = \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_{F(h)}$; as $h$ was arbitrary, this is the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em, row sep=3em]
G \arrow[r, "L_{F(h)}"] & G \\
H \arrow[u, "F"] \arrow[r, "L_h"'] & H \arrow[u, "F"']
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em, row sep=3em]
T_eG \arrow[r, "d(L_{F(h)})_e"] & T_{F(h)}G \\
T_eH \arrow[u, "dF_e"] \arrow[r, "d(L_h)_e"'] & T_hH \arrow[u, "dF_h"']
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5em, row sep=3em]
\tilde A \arrow[r, mapsto] & \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_{F(h)} \\
A \arrow[u, mapsto] \arrow[r, mapsto] & \mathbf{X}^A_h \arrow[u, mapsto]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

Top left: the group square, which commutes because $F$ is a morphism. Top right: its differential at $e$, which commutes by the chain rule. Below: where $A$ goes. Both routes end at the same vector, which is the statement that $\mathbf{X}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ are $F$-related.

\begin{propbox}[Lie Group Morphisms Preserve Brackets]\thmlabel{prop:morphism-preserves-bracket}
Let $F : H \to G$ be a Lie group morphism. For all $A, B \in T_eH$,
\[
dF_e\big([A, B]\big) = \big[dF_e(A), dF_e(B)\big] \in T_eG ,
\]
that is, $dF_e : \mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-algebra-morphism}).
\leeref{Theorem 8.44}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~18 --- ``kind of a soft proof''.)} ``Since the bracket is defined in terms of vector fields, I have to pass to vector fields to do the proof.'' For $A \in T_eH$ let $\mathbf{X}^A \in \mathfrak{X}(H)$ be the left-invariant extension of $A$, the left-invariant field with $\mathbf{X}^A_e = A$; put $\tilde A = dF_e(A) \in T_eG$, and let $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A} \in \mathfrak{X}(G)$ be the left-invariant extension of $\tilde A$, with $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}_e = \tilde A$ (Definition~\ref{def:left-invariant-extension} and Proposition~\ref{prop:left-invariant-extension-smooth}, applied to $H$ and to $G$).

\emph{Claim.} $\mathbf{X}^A$ and $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ are $F$-related (Definition~\ref{def:F-related}).

\emph{The proposition follows from the claim.} Let also $B \in T_eH$ and $\tilde B = dF_e(B)$. By the claim, $\mathbf{X}^A$ is $F$-related to $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}$ and $\mathbf{X}^B$ to $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:bracket-naturality}, $[\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]$ is $F$-related to $[\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}, \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}]$. Evaluate at $e \in H$, using $F(e) = e$:
\[
dF_e\big([\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_e\big) = [\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}, \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}]_{F(e)} = [\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde A}, \mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}]_e .
\]
By Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG} the left side is $dF_e([A, B])$ and the right side is $[\tilde A, \tilde B] = [dF_e(A), dF_e(B)]$: ``that's exactly'' the proposition. ``So the fight is to prove the claim'': it is Lemma~\ref{lem:morphism-related}, applied to $F$ and $A$, whose proof is the diagram chase above.
\end{proof}

Next: the commutator, ``first for the general linear group, and then \ldots\ for any linear group'' (Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket}).

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 18).} Page~47 of the handwritten notes begins the proof with ``take $A \in T_hH$''; $A \in T_eH$. Page~48 writes the second field as $\mathbf{Y}^{\hat B}$ in one place; it is $\mathbf{Y}^{\tilde B}$, with $\tilde B = dF_e(B)$.

% Lecture 19 (Wed Oct 14, 2026): the bracket of a matrix group
% ============================================================================

\subsection{The Bracket of a Matrix Group}\label{sub:matrix-group-bracket}

\textit{Lecture 19 began with a review, ``just because last time was a little bit complex'': the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ of left-invariant fields, closed under commutators (Corollary~\ref{cor:lie-subalgebra}); the isomorphism $\mathrm{ev} : \mathfrak{g} \to T_eG$ with inverse $A \mapsto \mathbf{X}^A$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:lie-algebra-TeG}), including the check that $\mathbf{X}^A$ is left-invariant (Lemma~\ref{lem:left-invariant-extension}(2)); and the bracket on $T_eG$, ``I keep forgetting to do it, but it's important to write it'' (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}), defined so that $\mathrm{ev}$ is an isomorphism of Lie algebras.}

\begin{rembox}[The Lie Algebra in Practice]\label{rem:lie-algebra-practice}
``In practice, when you say, `What's the Lie algebra of the orthogonal group?', the answer is never `some left-invariant fields', right? The answer is always: well, it's the tangent space at the identity'' --- with the bracket of Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}, which for matrix groups is the matrix commutator (Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-group-bracket} below). The notation $\mathfrak{gl}(d, \mathbb{R}) = T_I\GL(d,\mathbb{R}) = \Mat(d,\mathbb{R})$ is standard.
\end{rembox}

\begin{thmbox}[The Bracket of a Linear Group]\thmlabel{thm:linear-group-bracket}
Let $G \subseteq \GL(d, \mathbb{R})$ be a linear group (Definition~\ref{def:linear-group}) that is a \emph{Lie subgroup}: the inclusion $i : G \hookrightarrow \GL(d, \mathbb{R})$ is smooth and $di_I$ is injective --- for instance, $G$ a regular submanifold of $\Mat(d, \mathbb{R})$, as are the classical groups (Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-lie-groups}). Identify $T_IG$ with its image $di_I(T_IG) \subseteq \mathfrak{gl}(d,\mathbb{R}) = \Mat(d,\mathbb{R})$. Then the Lie bracket on $T_IG$ is
\[
[A, B] = AB - BA ,
\]
with matrix multiplication.
\leeref{Proposition 8.41, Theorem 8.46}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19.)} ``By assumption, $G$ is included in some general linear group \ldots\ as a Lie subgroup, and the differential of the inclusion map at the identity is the inclusion'' $di_I : T_IG \hookrightarrow \mathfrak{gl}(d, \mathbb{R})$. The inclusion is a Lie group morphism (Definition~\ref{def:lie-group-morphism}): smooth by hypothesis, and a group morphism because the product on $G$ is matrix multiplication. So by Proposition~\ref{prop:morphism-preserves-bracket}, for $A, B \in T_IG$,
\[
di_I\big([A, B]_G\big) = \big[di_I(A), di_I(B)\big]_{\GL(d,\mathbb{R})} = di_I(A)\, di_I(B) - di_I(B)\, di_I(A),
\]
the last step by Theorem~\ref{thm:gl-bracket}. Under the identification of $T_IG$ with its image, which $di_I$ injective makes legitimate, this is $[A, B] = AB - BA$. ``If we know that the bracket for the general linear group is a commutator, then for every linear group, it's got to be the commutator too, \ldots\ just some algebra.'' \textit{(Filled in: a regular submanifold qualifies, since $i$ is smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}(1), with coordinate representation $r \mapsto (r, \vec 0)$ in an adapted chart, whose differential is injective.)}
\end{proof}

In particular $di_I(T_IG)$ is closed under the matrix commutator, as the image of a bracket. Lecture~19 checked this directly in one case: ``we have a theorem, but it's good to check.''

\begin{exbox}[The Commutator of Skew-Symmetric Matrices]\exlabel{ex:skew-bracket}
$T_I\Ogp(n) = \Skew(n, \mathbb{R}) = \{A : A^{\mathsf T} = -A\}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:classical-summary}). Written out, an element of $\Skew(n, \mathbb{R})$ has zero diagonal, and its entries below the diagonal are the negatives of those above:
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1n} \\
-a_{12} & 0 & \cdots & a_{2n} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
-a_{1n} & -a_{2n} & \cdots & 0
\end{pmatrix} .
\]
 If $A, B \in \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$, then $[A, B] = AB - BA \in \Skew(n,\mathbb{R})$.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19.)} $[A, B]^{\mathsf T} = (AB - BA)^{\mathsf T} = B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T} - A^{\mathsf T}B^{\mathsf T} = (-B)(-A) - (-A)(-B) = BA - AB = -[A, B]$. ``You can do the same for the unitary [group] --- that was the homework problem. Instead of transpose, you have star, complex transpose conjugate, and the same computation works.''
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 19).} Page~49 of the handwritten notes writes the evaluation map as $\mathfrak{g} \to T_eM$ and its inverse from $T_eM$; the group is $G$, so $T_eG$. The definition of the bracket there reads ``$[A, B] = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]$''; the field bracket is evaluated at the identity, $[A, B] = [\mathbf{X}^A, \mathbf{X}^B]_e$ (Definition~\ref{def:bracket-TeG}), as Uribe said in lecture (``now we go back by evaluating at $e$'').

\chapter{Sard's Theorem}

\textit{Lecture 19. ``I want to switch gears \ldots\ to a theorem that is very useful \ldots\ It's not about vector fields.'' Sard's theorem ``is a very important theorem that is proved using techniques that are never used again in the course. So I never prove this. It's a complicated proof, actually, and I never do it in class. It's of course in Lee, because everything is in Lee.'' The proofs below are filled in, following Lee, Chapter~6, and marked as such. The dynamical side of vector fields resumes after the midterm; meanwhile, ``topics that are kind of self-contained.''}

% SECTION: SETS OF MEASURE ZERO

\section{Sets of Measure Zero}\label{sec:measure-zero}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Sets that are negligible, in Euclidean space and then on manifolds: ``this is not really measure theory. It's just the notion of sets of measure zero.''}

\begin{defbox}[Measure Zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$]\deflabel{def:measure-zero-Rn}
A set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has \textbf{measure zero} if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a countable cover $\{C_a\}$ of $S$ such that each $C_a$ is an open \textbf{rectangle}, a product of open intervals $C_a = (\alpha_1, \beta_1) \times \cdots \times (\alpha_n, \beta_n)$, and
\[
\sum_a \operatorname{Vol}(C_a) < \varepsilon, \qquad \operatorname{Vol}(C_a) = \prod_{i=1}^n (\beta_i - \alpha_i) \ \ \text{(Euclidean volume)}.
\]
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Sets of Measure Zero}; Appendix C}
\end{defbox}

``They could be closed, but let's say open.'' In three dimensions the rectangles are solid boxes. ``You should think of them as being very small, very thin. And for example, they cannot contain an open set. But it's much more than that, actually.''

A curve $S$ in the plane, covered by rectangles. Refining the cover shrinks the total area: about $0.79$ with $8$ rectangles, about $0.34$ with $32$, and as small as desired with more --- so $S$ has measure zero.

\begin{lembox}[Basic Properties of Measure Zero]\thmlabel{lem:measure-zero-basic}
In $\mathbb{R}^n$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item a subset of a set of measure zero has measure zero;
\item a countable union of sets of measure zero has measure zero;
\item in Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-Rn}, the open rectangles may be replaced by closed rectangles, or by open or closed cubes;
\item a nonempty open set does not have measure zero (for $n \ge 1$).
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Proposition C.18, Exercise 6.1, Corollary C.25}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in. Item (4) is Uribe's ``they cannot contain an open set''.)}

\emph{(1)} A cover of the larger set covers the smaller one.

\emph{(2)} Let $S = \bigcup_{k \ge 1} S_k$ with each $S_k$ of measure zero, and $\varepsilon > 0$. Cover $S_k$ by countably many open rectangles of total volume $< \varepsilon/2^k$. All of these together, a countable family, cover $S$ with total volume $< \sum_k \varepsilon/2^k = \varepsilon$.

\emph{(3)} \emph{Closed rectangles.} A closed rectangle $\prod[\alpha_i, \beta_i]$ lies in the open rectangle $\prod(\alpha_i - \eta, \beta_i + \eta)$, whose volume tends to $\prod(\beta_i - \alpha_i)$ as $\eta \to 0$; so given a cover by closed rectangles of total volume $< \varepsilon/2$, enlarging the $a$-th rectangle ($a = 1, 2, \ldots$) so that its volume grows by less than $\varepsilon/2^{a+1}$ gives an open cover of total volume $< \varepsilon$. Conversely an open rectangle lies in its closure, of the same volume.
\emph{Cubes.} Cubes are rectangles, so a cover by cubes is a cover by rectangles. Conversely, let $R = \prod(\alpha_i, \beta_i)$ with sides $\ell_i = \beta_i - \alpha_i > 0$, and $0 < \delta \le \min_i \ell_i$. The closed cubes of side $\delta$ with corners in $\prod_i (\alpha_i + \delta\mathbb{Z})$ that meet $\overline R$ cover $R$; in the $i$-th direction at most $\lfloor \ell_i / \delta \rfloor + 2 \le \ell_i/\delta + 2 \le 3\ell_i/\delta$ of the intervals $[\alpha_i + t\delta, \alpha_i + (t+1)\delta]$ meet $[\alpha_i, \beta_i]$, so there are at most $\prod_i 3\ell_i/\delta$ such cubes, of total volume at most $3^n \operatorname{Vol}(R)$. Doing this for each rectangle of a cover of total volume $< \varepsilon/3^n$ gives a countable cover by closed cubes of total volume $< \varepsilon$; enlarging them as before gives open cubes.

\emph{(4)} A nonempty open set contains a closed cube $Q$ of some side $s > 0$, so by (1) it suffices to show that $Q$ is not covered by open rectangles of total volume $< s^n = \operatorname{Vol}(Q)$. Suppose $Q \subseteq \bigcup_a C_a$. $Q$ is compact, so finitely many $C_1, \ldots, C_r$ cover it. Cut $\mathbb{R}^n$ by the hyperplanes $x^i = $ (an endpoint of a side of $Q$ or of some $C_b$): this divides $Q$ into finitely many closed grid cells $P$, and each $\overline{C_b} \cap Q$ into cells too, with $\operatorname{Vol}(Q) = \sum_{P \subseteq Q} \operatorname{Vol}(P)$ and $\operatorname{Vol}(C_b) \ge \sum_{P \subseteq \overline{C_b}} \operatorname{Vol}(P)$, since the volume of a rectangle is the sum of the volumes of the cells it is divided into (expand the product of the side lengths). An interior point of a cell $P \subseteq Q$ lies in some $C_b$; no cutting hyperplane passes through the interior of $P$, so $P$ lies on one side of each face of $C_b$, hence $P \subseteq \overline{C_b}$. So every cell of $Q$ is counted in some $\operatorname{Vol}(C_b)$, and $\operatorname{Vol}(Q) \le \sum_{b=1}^r \operatorname{Vol}(C_b) \le \sum_a \operatorname{Vol}(C_a)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Smooth Maps Preserve Measure Zero]\thmlabel{lem:smooth-measure-zero}
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open, $F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth, and $S \subseteq U$ a set of measure zero. Then $F(S)$ has measure zero.
\leeref{Proposition 6.5}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19 gave the idea: ``I'm not going to prove this, but I want to tell you the idea of the proof.'' The details are filled in.)}

\emph{The idea.} ``Differentiable maps, $C^\infty$ maps, are locally Lipschitz'': for every compact $K \subseteq U$ there is a constant $C$ with
\[
|F(x) - F(y)| \le C\, |x - y| \qquad \text{for all } x, y \in K,
\]
and ``somehow $C$ has to do with --- not quite, but it's essentially --- the sup of the partial derivatives over $K$.'' This ``of course implies continuity, but it's a lot more strong'': ``it's going to map cubes to cubes of comparable volume.''

\emph{Reduction to a closed cube.} $U$ is the union of the countably many closed cubes with rational corners and rational side lengths that lie in $U$ (each $x \in U$ has an open ball in $U$ about it, and a small rational cube containing $x$ inside that ball). So $F(S) = \bigcup_Q F(S \cap Q)$ over countably many closed cubes $Q \subseteq U$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2) it suffices to show that $F(S \cap Q)$ has measure zero.

\emph{The Lipschitz estimate on $Q$, in the sup norm $\|x\|_\infty = \max_i |x^i|$.} The partial derivatives $\partial F^i/\partial x^j$ are continuous on the compact set $Q$, so $M = \max_{i,j} \sup_Q |\partial F^i/\partial x^j|$ is finite. $Q$ is convex, so for $x, y \in Q$ the segment between them lies in $Q$, and the mean value theorem applied to $t \mapsto F^i(x + t(y - x))$ gives a point $\xi$ on the segment with
\[
|F^i(y) - F^i(x)| = \Big| \sum_j \frac{\partial F^i}{\partial x^j}(\xi)\, (y^j - x^j) \Big| \le n M\, \|y - x\|_\infty ,
\]
so $\|F(y) - F(x)\|_\infty \le C \|y - x\|_\infty$ with $C = nM + 1 > 0$.

\emph{Cubes go to cubes.} A cube of side $t$ is a sup-norm ball. Let $\varepsilon > 0$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(3) cover $S \cap Q$ by countably many open cubes $Q_a$, of sides $t_a$, with $\sum_a t_a^n < \varepsilon$. For each $a$ with $Q_a \cap Q \ne \varnothing$ pick $c_a \in Q_a \cap Q$. For $x \in Q_a \cap Q$, $\|x - c_a\|_\infty < t_a$, so $\|F(x) - F(c_a)\|_\infty < C t_a$: $F(Q_a \cap Q)$ lies in the open cube of side $2Ct_a$ centred at $F(c_a)$. These cubes cover $F(S \cap Q)$, with total volume $\sum_a (2C t_a)^n < (2C)^n \varepsilon$, as small as desired.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Continuity Is Not Enough]\label{rem:cantor-function}
``You have to be careful. Just for fun, this is not true'': $F(S)$ may not have measure zero if $F$ is only continuous --- ``Cantor's function. It's a standard counterexample.'' \textit{(Filled in.)} The Cantor function $c : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ is continuous, nondecreasing, and maps the Cantor set, which has measure zero, onto all of $[0,1]$, which does not (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4)). The smoothness used above is exactly the Lipschitz estimate, which $c$ lacks. ``As you can see, we're really talking about analysis here.''
\end{rembox}
