\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The Cantor function $c$: constant on each removed middle third, it climbs only on the Cantor set. So $c$ maps a set of measure zero (orange; shown at the second stage of the construction) onto the whole interval $[0,1]$ (teal). Its slopes are unbounded near the Cantor set, which is the Lipschitz estimate of Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero} failing.

\textit{``Because of this lemma, we can define sets of measure zero on a manifold.''}

\begin{defbox}[Measure Zero in a Manifold]\deflabel{def:measure-zero-manifold}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$ and $S \subseteq M$ any subset (``I'm not assuming it's a submanifold. It's just a set''). $S$ has \textbf{measure zero} if $S$ can be covered by coordinate charts $\{(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)\}$, $S \subseteq \bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha$, such that for every $\alpha$ the set $\varphi_\alpha(S \cap U_\alpha) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ has measure zero (Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-Rn}).
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{Sets of Measure Zero}; Lemma 6.6}
\end{defbox}

A student asked whether any number of charts is allowed. ``Yeah, but you can always do with a countable [number], because of second countability'' --- the next lemma.

\begin{lembox}[Countable Subcovers]\thmlabel{lem:countable-subcover}
Let $X$ be a second-countable space (Definition~\ref{def:second-countable}), $A \subseteq X$, and $\{U_\alpha\}$ a family of open sets covering $A$. Then countably many of the $U_\alpha$ cover $A$.
\leeref{Proposition A.16}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in.)} Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a countable basis. For each $B \in \mathcal{B}$ that is contained in some $U_\alpha$, choose one such $U_{\alpha(B)}$; there are countably many choices. If $x \in A$, then $x \in U_\alpha$ for some $\alpha$, and since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U_\alpha$; so $B$ was given a set $U_{\alpha(B)} \supseteq B \ni x$. So the chosen sets cover $A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{propbox}[Measure Zero Is Seen in Every Chart]\thmlabel{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}
If $S \subseteq M$ has measure zero, then $\varphi(S \cap U)$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^m$ for \emph{every} chart $(U, \varphi)$ of $M$. Consequently subsets and countable unions of sets of measure zero in $M$ have measure zero in $M$.
\leeref{Lemma 6.6, Exercise 6.7}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~19 as an observation, ``by the lemma''; filled in.)} Let $\{(U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha)\}$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-manifold}, and $(U, \varphi)$ any chart. By Lemma~\ref{lem:countable-subcover} (manifolds are second countable), countably many $U_\alpha$ cover $S \cap U$, and
\[
\varphi(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha) = \big(\varphi \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}\big)\big(\varphi_\alpha(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha)\big),
\]
where the transition map $\varphi \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1} : \varphi_\alpha(U \cap U_\alpha) \to \varphi(U \cap U_\alpha)$ is a smooth map between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:compatible}), and $\varphi_\alpha(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha) \subseteq \varphi_\alpha(S \cap U_\alpha)$ has measure zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(1)). By Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero}, each $\varphi(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha)$ has measure zero, and $\varphi(S \cap U)$ is their countable union (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2)).

For the consequences: if $T \subseteq S$, the charts covering $S$ cover $T$, and $\varphi_\alpha(T \cap U_\alpha) \subseteq \varphi_\alpha(S \cap U_\alpha)$. If $S = \bigcup_k S_k$ with each $S_k$ of measure zero, cover $S$ by all charts of $M$: for each chart, $\varphi(S \cap U) = \bigcup_k \varphi(S_k \cap U)$ is a countable union of sets of measure zero, by the first part.
\end{proof}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.2em, row sep=3.2em]
 & S \cap U \cap U_\alpha \arrow[dl, "\varphi_\alpha"'] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"] & \\
\varphi_\alpha(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha) \arrow[rr, "\varphi \circ \varphi_\alpha^{-1}"'] & & \varphi(S \cap U \cap U_\alpha)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The same piece of $S$ seen in two charts. The transition map carries one picture to the other, and it is smooth, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero} measure zero in one picture means measure zero in the other.

\begin{lembox}[A Fubini Lemma for Compact Sets]\thmlabel{lem:fubini-measure-zero}
Let $n \ge 2$ and $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ compact, such that for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$ the slice $A_c = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1} : (c, x) \in A \}$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$. Then $A$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\leeref{Lemma 6.2}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, as a tool for Sard's theorem.)} Choose $a < b$ with $A \subseteq [a, b] \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$, and let $\delta > 0$.

\emph{Each slice, thickened.} Fix $c \in [a, b]$. $A_c$ is compact (its image $\{c\} \times A_c = A \cap (\{c\} \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1})$ is compact) and has measure zero, so it is covered by countably many open rectangles of total volume $< \delta$, hence by finitely many of them; let $U_c \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ be their union. There is an open interval $J_c \ni c$, which we may take inside $(a - 1, b + 1)$, with $A \cap (J_c \times \mathbb{R}^{n-1}) \subseteq J_c \times U_c$. Otherwise there are points $(c_k, x_k) \in A$ with $c_k \to c$ and $x_k \notin U_c$; by compactness a subsequence converges to some $(c, x) \in A$, with $x \notin U_c$ because the complement of $U_c$ is closed; but $x \in A_c \subseteq U_c$.

\emph{Finitely many strips.} The $J_c$ cover $[a, b]$; take a finite subcover, and from it a minimal one, $J_1, \ldots, J_r$ (for $c_1, \ldots, c_r$). No point lies in three of them: if $x$ lay in three, the one with the smallest left endpoint and the one with the largest right endpoint would both contain $x$, so their union, an interval, would contain the third, contradicting minimality. So $\sum_k \operatorname{length}(J_k) \le 2\,\operatorname{length}\big(\bigcup_k J_k\big) \le 2(b - a + 2)$.

\emph{The cover.} $A \subseteq \bigcup_k J_k \times U_{c_k}$, and $J_k \times U_{c_k}$ is a union of finitely many open rectangles, (interval) $\times$ (rectangle of $U_{c_k}$), of total volume $< \operatorname{length}(J_k)\,\delta$. In total, finitely many open rectangles of total volume $< 2(b - a + 2)\,\delta$, which is as small as desired.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture.)} The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:fubini-measure-zero} for a compact $A$ in the plane ($n = 2$). The slice of $A$ at $c$ (teal) has measure zero, so it is covered by finitely many small intervals, $U_c$. By compactness the same intervals still cover the slices at all $c'$ near $c$, in an interval $J_c$, so $A \cap (J_c \times \mathbb{R})$ lies in the thin boxes $J_c \times U_c$ (orange). Finitely many $J_c$ cover the first coordinate's range, overlapping at most twice, and the total area is at most $2 \times$ (length) $\times$ (the slices' cover size).

\begin{rembox}[Measure Zero and Lebesgue Measure]\label{rem:measure-zero-lebesgue}
\textit{(Not from lecture.)} Uribe: ``this is not really measure theory. It's just the notion of sets of measure zero.'' For readers who know Lebesgue measure the dictionary is short.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has measure zero in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-Rn} exactly when its Lebesgue outer measure is $m^*(S) = 0$ (outer measure is defined with countable covers by rectangles, open or closed, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(3)); such sets are Lebesgue measurable.
\item Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(1)--(2) are monotonicity and countable subadditivity of $m^*$; item (4) is $m^*(\text{closed rectangle}) = $ its volume.
\item Lemma~\ref{lem:fubini-measure-zero} is the cross-section theorem (a consequence of Tonelli's theorem) for a compact, hence measurable, set: $m(A) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} m(A_c)\, dc = 0$. The proof above avoids measurability and integration and uses only compactness.
\end{enumerate}
\end{rembox}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: SARD'S THEOREM

\section{Sard's Theorem}\label{sec:sard}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Almost every value of a smooth map is regular.}

\begin{rembox}[Recall: Regular and Singular Values]\label{rem:singular-values}
For $F : M \to N$ smooth, $q \in N$ is a regular value if $dF_p$ is onto for every $p \in F^{-1}(q)$ (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value}); in particular every $q \notin F(M)$ is a regular value. A value that is not regular is a \emph{singular value} --- Uribe's word in Lecture~19; ``critical value'' in Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical-value} and in Lee. Likewise $p \in M$ is a critical (singular) point if $dF_p$ is not onto (Definition~\ref{def:regular-critical}).
\end{rembox}

\begin{lembox}[Sard's Theorem Reduces to Euclidean Space]\thmlabel{lem:sard-reduction}
Let $m, n \ge 0$. Suppose that for every open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and every smooth $G : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$, the set of singular values of $G$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then for every smooth map $F : M \to N$ with $\dim M = m$ and $\dim N = n$, the set of singular values of $F$ has measure zero in $N$.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 6.10}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the first step of Lee's proof of Theorem~6.10.)} Let $C \subseteq M$ be the set of critical points of $F$, so that its set of singular values is $S = F(C)$. If $n = 0$, every $dF_p$ is onto the zero space $T_{F(p)}N$, so $S = \varnothing$. Let $n \ge 1$. Each $p \in M$ has a chart $(U_p, \varphi_p)$ with $F(U_p)$ inside the domain of a chart $(V_p, \psi_p)$ of $N$ (shrink a chart at $p$ into $F^{-1}(V_p)$, by continuity). By Lemma~\ref{lem:countable-subcover} countably many $U_i = U_{p_i}$ cover $M$, so $S = \bigcup_i F(C \cap U_i)$. In the charts, $\hat F_i = \psi_i \circ F \circ \varphi_i^{-1} : \varphi_i(U_i) \to \mathbb{R}^n$, and since charts are diffeomorphisms (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), $p$ is a critical point of $F$ exactly when $\varphi_i(p)$ is one of $\hat F_i$; so $\psi_i\big(F(C \cap U_i)\big)$ is the set of singular values of $\hat F_i$. By hypothesis, applied to $\hat F_i$ on the open set $\varphi_i(U_i) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$, that set has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$. So $F(C \cap U_i)$, covered by the single chart $(V_i, \psi_i)$, has measure zero in $N$, and so does the countable union $S$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lembox}[Where All Derivatives up to Order $k$ Vanish]\thmlabel{lem:sard-flat-points}
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open, $F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth with $n \ge 1$, and $k \ge 1$ an integer with $n(k + 1) > m$. Let $Z \subseteq U$ be a set at each point of which all partial derivatives of $F$ of orders $1, \ldots, k$ vanish. Then $F(Z)$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 6.10}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; the last step of Lee's proof of Theorem~6.10.)} $U$ is the union of countably many closed cubes $E \subseteq U$ (the reduction to a closed cube in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero}), so by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2) it suffices to show that $F(Z \cap E)$ has measure zero for a closed cube $E \subseteq U$, of side $R$. Let $A > 0$ bound the absolute values of all partial derivatives of order $k + 1$ of $F$ on $E$ (continuous functions on a compact set; taking $A > 0$ keeps the cubes below nondegenerate). If $x' \in Z \cap E$ and $x \in E$, Taylor's theorem along the segment from $x'$ to $x$, which lies in the convex set $E$, applied to each component $F^i$, has no terms of orders $1, \ldots, k$, so
\[
|F^i(x) - F^i(x')| \le \sum_{|\beta| = k + 1} \frac{A}{\beta!}\, |(x - x')^\beta| \le A'\, \|x - x'\|_\infty^{k + 1},
\]
with $A'$ depending only on $A$, $k$ and $m$. Divide $E$ into $K^m$ closed cubes $E_1, \ldots, E_{K^m}$ of side $R/K$. If $E_j$ contains a point $x'_j \in Z$, then $F(E_j)$ lies in the closed cube of side $2A'(R/K)^{k + 1}$ centred at $F(x'_j)$. So $F(Z \cap E)$ lies in at most $K^m$ cubes of total volume
\[
K^m \big(2A'\big)^n \Big(\frac{R}{K}\Big)^{n(k + 1)} = \big(2A'\big)^n R^{\,n(k + 1)}\, K^{\,m - n(k + 1)} ,
\]
which tends to $0$ as $K \to \infty$ because $n(k + 1) > m$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(3), $F(Z \cap E)$ has measure zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Sard's Theorem]\thmlabel{thm:sard}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a smooth map, and
\[
S = \{\, q \in N : q \text{ is not a regular value of } F \,\},
\]
the set of singular values. Then $S$ has measure zero in $N$ (Definition~\ref{def:measure-zero-manifold}).
\leeref{Theorem 6.10}
\end{thmbox}

``So almost all values are regular \ldots\ and this is going to have a lot of applications. Trust me, we're going to see them. They're very cute.''

The simplest picture: $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$ on $M = N = \mathbb{R}$. The critical points are $x = \pm 1$, where $f' = 0$, so the singular values are just $f(\pm 1) = \mp 2$, two points, a set of measure zero. Every other $c$ is a regular value: at each of its preimages the slope is nonzero.

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not given in lecture --- ``it's a big theorem. It's a long proof'' --- filled in, following Lee's proof of Theorem~6.10.)} By Lemma~\ref{lem:sard-reduction}, it suffices to prove, for every $m \ge 0$, the Euclidean statement

\textbf{$(\mathrm{S}_m)$:} for every open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$, every $n \ge 0$ and every smooth $F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$, the set $F(C)$ has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $C = \{ x \in U : \operatorname{rank} DF(x) < n \}$.

Here $C$ is the set of critical points of $F$, so $F(C)$ is its set of singular values. We prove $(\mathrm{S}_m)$ by induction on $m$.

\emph{$m = 0$.} $\mathbb{R}^0$ is a single point, so $F(C)$ has at most one point. If $n = 0$, then $C = \varnothing$, as no rank is $< 0$. If $n \ge 1$, a point lies in cubes of arbitrarily small volume, so it has measure zero. (Through Lemma~\ref{lem:sard-reduction} this covers manifolds of dimension $0$; directly, such an $M$ is countable, being second countable and discrete, so $F(M)$ is countable and has measure zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(2).)

\emph{$m \ge 1$.} Assume $(\mathrm{S}_{m-1})$, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open and $F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ smooth. If $n = 0$, then $C = \varnothing$; so let $n \ge 1$. Here $DF(x)$ is the $n \times m$ Jacobian
\[
DF(x) = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(x) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(x) \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^1}(x) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^n}{\partial x^m}(x)
\end{pmatrix} .
\]

\emph{A filtration of $C$.} For $k \ge 1$ let $C_k \subseteq C$ be the set of $x \in C$ at which all partial derivatives of $F$ of orders $1, \ldots, k$ vanish, so $C \supseteq C_1 \supseteq C_2 \supseteq \cdots$. These sets are closed in $U$: $C$ is where all $n \times n$ minors of $DF$ vanish, and $C_k$ is cut out of $C$ by finitely many more continuous functions. Fix an integer $k_0 \ge 1$ with $k_0 > m/n - 1$, that is, $n(k_0 + 1) > m$ (for instance $k_0 = \max(1, \lfloor m/n \rfloor)$; the condition $k_0 \ge 1$ matters when $m < n$). Then
\[
C = (C \setminus C_1) \cup \bigcup_{k=1}^{k_0 - 1} (C_k \setminus C_{k+1}) \cup C_{k_0},
\]
and it suffices to show that the image of each piece has measure zero.

\emph{Step 1: $F(C \setminus C_1)$ has measure zero.} If $n = 1$ then $C \setminus C_1 = \varnothing$: a nonzero first partial at $x$ makes the $1 \times m$ matrix $DF(x)$ have rank $1$. Let $n \ge 2$. Replacing $U$ by the open set $U \setminus C_1$, we may assume $C_1 = \varnothing$. Let $a \in C$. Some first partial of $F$ is nonzero at $a$; renumbering coordinates, $\partial F^1/\partial x^1(a) \neq 0$. Then $h(x) = (F^1(x), x^2, \ldots, x^m)$ has invertible derivative at $a$, so by the inverse function theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:inverse-function}) it is a diffeomorphism from an open $W_a \ni a$ onto an open set; choose a closed ball $K_a \ni a$ in $W_a$ with $a$ in its interior. \textit{(Computed; not from lecture.)} The derivative of $h$ is upper triangular,
\[
Dh(a) = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^1}(a) & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^2}(a) & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F^1}{\partial x^m}(a) \\
0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
so $\det Dh(a) = \partial F^1/\partial x^1(a) \neq 0$. In the coordinates $(u, v) = h(x)$, $u \in \mathbb{R}$, $v \in \mathbb{R}^{m-1}$, the map $G = F \circ h^{-1}$ has the form $G(u, v) = (u, G^2(u,v), \ldots, G^n(u, v))$, so
\[
DG(u, v) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ * & \big(\partial G^i/\partial v^j\big) \end{pmatrix},
\]
and $(u, v)$ is a critical point of $G$ exactly when the $(n-1) \times (m-1)$ block has rank $< n - 1$. For $c \in \mathbb{R}$ let $G_c(v) = (G^2(c, v), \ldots, G^n(c, v))$, defined on the open set $\{ v : (c, v) \in h(W_a) \} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m-1}$; then $(c, v)$ is a critical point of $G$ exactly when $v$ is a critical point of $G_c$. The set $F(C \cap K_a) = G(h(C \cap K_a))$ is compact ($C \cap K_a$ is closed in the compact $K_a$), and its slice at $u = c$ consists of points $(c, G_c(v))$ with $v$ a critical point of $G_c$: it lies in $\{c\} \times$ (the singular values of $G_c$), which has measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ by $(\mathrm{S}_{m-1})$, $G_c$ having an $(m-1)$-dimensional domain. By Lemma~\ref{lem:fubini-measure-zero}, $F(C \cap K_a)$ has measure zero. The interiors of the $K_a$ cover $C$, so countably many do (Lemma~\ref{lem:countable-subcover}), and $F(C \setminus C_1)$ is a countable union of sets of measure zero.

\emph{Step 2: $F(C_k \setminus C_{k+1})$ has measure zero, $k \ge 1$.} Replacing $U$ by $U \setminus C_{k+1}$, we may assume that at each $a \in C_k$ some partial derivative of order $k + 1$ of $F$ is nonzero. So there is a $k$-th order partial derivative $y = \partial^\alpha F^i$, $|\alpha| = k$, with $dy_a \neq 0$. Choose an open $V_a \ni a$ on which $dy \neq 0$. Then $0$ is a regular value of $y|_{V_a}$, and $Y = \{ x \in V_a : y(x) = 0 \}$ is a regular submanifold of $V_a$ of dimension $m - 1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:rvt-manifolds}). All $k$-th order partials of $F$ vanish on $C_k$, so $C_k \cap V_a \subseteq Y$. At $p \in C_k \cap V_a$, all first partials vanish ($k \ge 1$), so $dF_p = 0$, and $d(F|_Y)_p = dF_p \circ d\iota_p = 0$ is not onto $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n \ge 1$ (chain rule, $\iota : Y \to U$ the inclusion, smooth by Lemma~\ref{lem:maps-into-submanifold}). So $F(C_k \cap V_a)$ lies in the set of singular values of $F|_Y : Y \to \mathbb{R}^n$, which has measure zero by $(\mathrm{S}_{m-1})$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:sard-reduction}, applied to the $(m-1)$-dimensional manifold $Y$ and $N = \mathbb{R}^n$. Countably many $V_a$ cover $C_k$, so $F(C_k \setminus C_{k+1})$ has measure zero.

\emph{Step 3: $F(C_{k_0})$ has measure zero.} At each point of $C_{k_0}$ all partial derivatives of $F$ of orders $1, \ldots, k_0$ vanish, and $n(k_0 + 1) > m$. So Lemma~\ref{lem:sard-flat-points}, with $k = k_0$ and $Z = C_{k_0}$, shows that $F(C_{k_0})$ has measure zero.

Steps 1--3 cover all of $C$, which completes the induction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corbox}[Maps from Lower Dimension]\thmlabel{cor:sard-low-dim}
If $F : M \to N$ is smooth and $\dim M < \dim N$, then the regular values of $F$ are exactly the points of $N \setminus F(M)$, and $F(M)$ has measure zero in $N$.
\leeref{Corollary 6.11}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~19.)} ``By linear algebra, no point in the image can be a regular value, because \ldots\ the dimensions don't work out'': for $p \in M$, the image of $dF_p : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$ has dimension at most $\dim M < \dim N$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-dimension}), so $dF_p$ is never onto. So the regular values are exactly the points with empty preimage --- ``this is a vacuous thing'' --- and $F(M)$ is the set of singular values, of measure zero by Sard's theorem.
\end{proof}

``That's one observation, but there will be many other nice applications of this.'' For instance, a smooth curve $\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ never fills an open set of the plane: its image has measure zero, and so does every subset of it (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(1)), while an open set does not (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4)) --- in contrast with continuous space-filling curves.

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 19).} Page~50 of the handwritten notes states the image lemma for ``$F : U \to \mathbb{R}^n$, $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ open''. As written, with $m$ unrestricted, it is false for $m > n$: the projection $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$, $(x, y) \mapsto x$, maps the $x$-axis, of measure zero in $\mathbb{R}^2$, onto $\mathbb{R}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-measure-zero} takes $m = n$, as Lee does and as the application to transition maps needs. (For $m < n$ the conclusion holds for every $S$, by Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim}.)

\section{Parametric Transversality}\label{sec:parametric-transversality}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Transversality of a whole family passes, by Sard's theorem, to almost every member.}

\textit{Lecture 20. ``Next topic \ldots\ one of my favorite theorems in the whole course \ldots\ a really beautiful, useful theorem, called the transversality theorem of René Thom, or parametric transversality, that will have really beautiful consequences together with Sard's theorem.''}

\begin{defbox}[Smooth Family of Maps]\deflabel{def:smooth-family}
Let $S$, $M$, $N$ be smooth manifolds. A \textbf{smooth family} of maps $M \to N$, parametrized by $S$, is a collection $\{F_s\}_{s \in S}$ of maps $F_s : M \to N$ such that $F : S \times M \to N$, $F(s, p) = F_s(p)$, is smooth. $S$ is the \textbf{parameter space}.
\leeref{Ch.~6, \emph{The Transversality Homotopy Theorem}}
\end{defbox}

``Smoothness of the family is the same as smoothness of the big map'' --- jointly in $s$ and $p$. Each $F_s = F \circ \iota_s$, with $\iota_s : M \to S \times M$, $p \mapsto (s, p)$, the slice inclusion (Definition~\ref{def:slice-inclusions}), so each $F_s$ is smooth.

\begin{thmbox}[Parametric Transversality]\thmlabel{thm:parametric-transversality}
Let $F : S \times M \to N$ be smooth, $Z \subseteq N$ a regular submanifold, and suppose $F \pitchfork Z$ (Definition~\ref{def:transverse-submanifold}). Then $W = F^{-1}(Z)$ is a regular submanifold of $S \times M$, and with $\pi : W \to S$ the restriction of the projection $(s, p) \mapsto s$: for $s \in S$,
\[
s \text{ is a regular value of } \pi \iff F_s : M \to N \text{ is transverse to } Z .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 6.35 (proof)}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~20 --- ``a nice exercise'' --- proved the direction ``that matters for applications'', $(\Rightarrow)$; the converse is filled in.)}

\emph{Preliminaries.} $W$ is a regular submanifold of $S \times M$ and, for $(s, p) \in W$ with $q = F(s, p)$,
\[
T_{(s,p)}W = \big(dF_{(s,p)}\big)^{-1}\big(T_qZ\big) \tag{1}
\]
(Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-submanifold-preimage}; a student supplied this in class: ``it's the preimage of the tangent space of $Z$ by the differential''). $\pi$ is smooth, as the restriction of the smooth projection to a regular submanifold. Write tangent vectors to $S \times M$ as pairs $(\sigma, u) \in T_sS \oplus T_pM$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-product}); then $d\pi(\sigma, u) = \sigma$, and
\[
dF_{(s,p)}(0, u) = d(F_s)_p(u), \tag{2}
\]
because $F_s = F \circ \iota_s$ and $d(\iota_s)_p(u) = (0, u)$: ``it's a partial derivative \ldots\ when I compute this derivative, I freeze the first entry to $s$'' (Definition~\ref{def:partial-derivative-factor}).

\emph{$(\Rightarrow)$} Let $s$ be a regular value of $\pi$, and $p \in M$ with $q = F_s(p) = F(s,p) \in Z$. We must show $\operatorname{Im} d(F_s)_p + T_qZ = T_qN$; ``clearly we have one inclusion.'' Let $w \in T_qN$. Since $F \pitchfork Z$, there are $(\sigma, u) \in T_{(s,p)}(S \times M)$ and $v \in T_qZ$ with
\[
w = dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, u) + v . \tag{$*$}
\]
``Since $s$ is a regular value of $\pi$ \ldots\ I can hit $\sigma$'': there is a tangent vector to $W$ at $(s, p)$ projecting to $\sigma$, and since $d\pi$ only reads the first component, it has the form $(\sigma, \tau)$ for some $\tau \in T_pM$. Write $(\sigma, u) = (\sigma, \tau) + (0, u - \tau)$ and substitute into $(*)$:
\[
w = dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, \tau) + dF_{(s,p)}(0, u - \tau) + v = d(F_s)_p(u - \tau) + \big(dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, \tau) + v\big),
\]
by (2). By (1), $dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, \tau) \in T_qZ$, so the bracket is tangent to $Z$, and $w \in \operatorname{Im} d(F_s)_p + T_qZ$. ``So this implies that $F_s$ intersects $Z$ transversely.''

\emph{$(\Leftarrow)$} \textit{(Filled in.)} Suppose $F_s \pitchfork Z$, and let $(s, p) \in \pi^{-1}(s)$, so $q = F_s(p) \in Z$; we show $d\pi_{(s,p)}$ is onto $T_sS$. Let $\sigma \in T_sS$. By transversality of $F_s$, $dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, 0) = d(F_s)_p(u) + v$ for some $u \in T_pM$, $v \in T_qZ$. By (2), $dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, -u) = dF_{(s,p)}(\sigma, 0) - d(F_s)_p(u) = v \in T_qZ$, so $(\sigma, -u) \in T_{(s,p)}W$ by (1), and $d\pi(\sigma, -u) = \sigma$.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} An explicit instance of the cartoon. Take $S = M = \mathbb{R}$, $N = \mathbb{R}^2$, $Z = \{ y = x^2 \}$ and $F(s, x) = (x, s)$, so $F_s$ parametrizes the horizontal line at height $s$. Then $F$ is a diffeomorphism, so $F \pitchfork Z$, and $W = F^{-1}(Z) = \{ (s, x) : s = x^2 \}$. Parametrizing $W$ by $x \mapsto (x^2, x)$, the projection is $\pi(x^2, x) = x^2$, with derivative $2x$: the only critical point is $x = 0$, and the only critical value is $s = 0$. For $s > 0$, $F_s$ crosses $Z$ transversally at $x = \pm\sqrt{s}$; for $s < 0$, $F_s^{-1}(Z) = \varnothing$; at $s = 0$, $\operatorname{Im} d(F_0)_0 = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 0)\} = T_{(0,0)}Z$, so $F_0$ is tangent to $Z$, not transverse --- exactly as Theorem~\ref{thm:parametric-transversality} predicts.

\begin{corbox}[Almost Every Member Is Transverse]\thmlabel{cor:parametric-sard}
If $F : S \times M \to N$ is smooth and $F \pitchfork Z$, then $F_s \pitchfork Z$ for almost every $s \in S$: the set of $s$ with $F_s$ not transverse to $Z$ has measure zero in $S$.
\leeref{Theorem 6.35}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~20: ``pairing this with Sard's theorem''.)} By Sard's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:sard}) applied to $\pi : W \to S$, the singular values of $\pi$ form a set of measure zero; for every other $s$, $F_s \pitchfork Z$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:parametric-transversality}.
\end{proof}

``You go from transversality of the family to transversality of individual elements in the family. That's the beauty of this.''

\begin{exbox}[Translates Are Generically Transverse]\exlabel{ex:translates-transverse}
Let $Y, Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be regular submanifolds. For almost every $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translate $a + Y$ intersects $Z$ transversally.
\end{exbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~20, the ``first classical, very geometric application''; details filled in.)} The parameter space is $\mathbb{R}^d$ itself: $F : \mathbb{R}^d \times Y \to \mathbb{R}^d$, $F(a, p) = a + p$, ``I use the vector space structure to translate.'' Then $F_a(Y) = a + Y$. \emph{$F$ is a submersion}: fixing $p$ and varying $a$, $dF_{(a,p)}(\sigma, 0) = \sigma$ for every $\sigma \in T_a\mathbb{R}^d = \mathbb{R}^d$ --- ``if you just vary $a$, you get anything.'' So $F \pitchfork Z$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:transverse-special-cases}(3)), and $F^{-1}(Z) = \{ (a, p) : a + p \in Z \}$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:parametric-sard}, $F_a \pitchfork Z$ for almost every $a$. Finally $F_a : Y \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is the inclusion of $a + Y$ composed with the diffeomorphism $Y \to a + Y$, $p \mapsto a + p$ (``the translate \ldots\ just the inclusion''), and $a + Y$ is a regular submanifold, a translate of one, so $F_a \pitchfork Z$ says $(a + Y) \pitchfork Z$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:transverse-submanifolds-maps}).
\end{proof}

``Isn't that nice?'' If $\dim Y + \dim Z < d$, a transverse intersection must be empty, since $T_qY + T_qZ$ has dimension at most $\dim Y + \dim Z$. So two curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$ ($1 + 1 < 3$): ``translate one by a generic vector, it'll cease to intersect the other one.'' For two curves in the plane that are tangent, a generic translate either separates them or makes them cross transversally. This is the idea of \emph{general position}: a configuration is not in general position if moving one of the objects a little changes the geometry radically. ``General position things are transverse, which may mean that they don't intersect. But vacuous intersection is a statement. It's a powerful statement.''

``I will give you a homework problem, an application of this \ldots\ to show that if you have a manifold inside $\mathbb{R}^2$ [as transcribed], almost all linear functions restricted to the manifold are Morse. So you have a lot of Morse functions'' (Definition~\ref{def:morse-function}).

\section{The Whitney Embedding Theorem}\label{sec:whitney}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Every manifold sits inside some Euclidean space; Sard's theorem pushes the dimension down to $2m + 1$.}

\textit{Lecture 21. ``There isn't enough time in the semester to cover everything that's on the syllabus, and the only way to cover more is to skip some proofs \ldots\ I never quite get to degree theory, which is a really cool topic that is officially on the syllabus. So I will be assigning reading.'' Then: ``Today we're going to talk about the Whitney embedding and immersion theorems.''}

The proof, for $M$ compact, has two parts with ``totally different'' ideas: bump functions embed $M$ in some $\mathbb{R}^k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds}), and projections along well-chosen lines lower the dimension (Lemmas~\ref{lem:projection-injective} and~\ref{lem:projection-immersion}). The lemmas come first; Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact} assembles them. The general case, Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney}, is sketched in \ref{sub:whitney-noncompact}.

\begin{lembox}[Compact Manifolds Embed in Some $\mathbb{R}^k$]\thmlabel{lem:compact-embeds}
Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Then there is an embedding $F : M \to \mathbb{R}^k$ for some $k$.
\leeref{proof of Theorem 6.15}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~21, Part~I of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact}, in the lecture's steps with details filled in.)} ``We're going to use bump functions'' --- ``this idea of partition of unity \ldots\ is kind of behind it.''

\emph{The cover.} For every $x \in M$ choose a chart $(U_x, \varphi_x)$ at $x$ and an open coordinate ball $B_x \ni x$ with $\overline{B_x} \subseteq U_x$ and $\varphi_x(\overline{B_x})$ a closed ball in $\mathbb{R}^m$ --- possible because $\varphi_x(U_x)$ is open, so it contains a closed Euclidean ball about $\varphi_x(x)$, ``and then I pull it back.'' Let $\chi_x \in C^\infty_0(M)$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi_x \subseteq U_x$ and $\chi_x \equiv 1$ on $\overline{B_x}$ (the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence}). The \emph{open} balls $B_x$ cover $M$ --- in lecture Uribe first wrote the cover with the $U_x$, and corrected it: ``I want to put a $B$. It's very important.'' $M$ is compact, so finitely many cover; relabel them $B_1, \ldots, B_n$, with charts $(U_i, \varphi_i)$ and bump functions $\chi_i$.

\emph{The map.} Each $\chi_i\varphi_i : M \to \mathbb{R}^m$, defined as $\chi_i \varphi_i$ on $U_i$ and $0$ outside, is smooth: it is smooth on $U_i$ and zero on the open set $M \setminus \operatorname{supp}\chi_i$, and these cover $M$ ($\operatorname{supp}\chi_i$ is compact, hence closed). Define
\[
F = \big(\chi_1\varphi_1, \ldots, \chi_n\varphi_n, \chi_1, \ldots, \chi_n\big) : M \to \mathbb{R}^{nm + n},
\]
``a super big'' Euclidean space: $n$ blocks of $m$ components, then $n$ scalars. ``It's really very, very clever.''

\emph{$F$ is injective.} Suppose $F(p) = F(q)$. There is $i$ with $p \in B_i$, so $\chi_i(p) = 1$. The last $n$ components of $F$ are the $\chi$'s, so $\chi_i(q) = \chi_i(p) = 1$; in particular $\chi_i(q) \neq 0$, so $q \in U_i$, because $\chi_i$ vanishes outside $U_i$. ``I don't know that $q$ is in $B_i$, but I don't care.'' The $i$-th block gives $\chi_i(p)\varphi_i(p) = \chi_i(q)\varphi_i(q)$, that is, $\varphi_i(p) = \varphi_i(q)$; ``the charts are bijective, so $p = q$.'' ``Because we put the $\chi$'s here, we are able to conclude that $p$ and $q$ \ldots\ are in the same coordinate chart.''

\emph{$F$ is an immersion.} Write $F = (F_1, \ldots, F_n, \chi_1, \ldots, \chi_n)$ with $F_j = \chi_j\varphi_j : M \to \mathbb{R}^m$. Let $p \in M$, $v \in T_pM$, and $\gamma$ a curve with $\gamma(0) = p$ and $D_\gamma = v$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:every-vector-velocity}). ``Use curves'': $dF_p(v) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} F(\gamma(t)) = (v_1, \ldots, v_n, \ldots)$, with $v_j = d(F_j)_p(v) \in \mathbb{R}^m$, componentwise. Choose $i$ with $p \in B_i$. Then $\chi_i \equiv 1$ on the open set $B_i \ni p$, so $F_i = \varphi_i$ near $p$ and $v_i = d(\varphi_i)_p(v)$ --- equivalently $d(\chi_i)_p = 0$, since $\chi_i \equiv 1$ in a neighbourhood of $p$. As $\varphi_i$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), $v \neq 0$ gives $v_i \neq 0$, so $dF_p(v) \neq 0$: $dF_p$ is injective.

\emph{An embedding.} An injective immersion of a compact manifold is an embedding (Corollary~\ref{cor:compact-embedding}). ``End of Part~I.''
\end{proof}

Uribe's cartoon for injectivity: $\chi_i \equiv 1$ on $\overline{B}_i$ (``it could be one a little bit outside too''), and zero outside $U_i$. So $\chi_i(q) = 1$ forces $q \in U_i$, where the chart $\varphi_i$ separates points.


\textit{Part~II: lower the ambient dimension.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds}, a compact $M$ may be taken to be a regular submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ (the image of the embedding, Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}). Regard $\mathbb{R}^{N-1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ by $x \mapsto (x, 0)$. To every line $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ through $0$ that is transverse to $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, that is, not contained in it, so that $\mathbb{R}^N = \mathbb{R}^{N-1} \oplus \ell$, associate the projection along $\ell$, a linear map $\mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ with kernel $\ell$, and its restriction
\[
\pi_\ell : M \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N-1} .
\]
(``Do you guys know the difference between complementary and supplementary? I learned that in elementary school, and I'm still trying to figure out what the difference is.'') We want: \emph{if $N > 2m + 1$, there is an $\ell$ such that $\pi_\ell$ is an embedding.} Applying this repeatedly lowers $N$ to $2m + 1$, ``until we're out of parameters.''

\begin{lembox}[Projections That Stay Injective]\thmlabel{lem:projection-injective}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m$, with $N > 2m + 1$. Then the lines $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ through $0$ for which $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, or $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is not injective, form a set of measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$. In particular there are lines $\ell \not\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ with $\pi_\ell$ injective.
\leeref{Lemma 6.13}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~21, Part~II of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact}.)} ``The clever idea'': let $\Delta = \{ (p, p) : p \in M \}$, closed in $M \times M$ since $M$ is Hausdorff, and
\[
\sigma : (M \times M) \setminus \Delta \longrightarrow \mathbb{RP}^{N-1}, \qquad (p, q) \longmapsto \operatorname{span}(q - p),
\]
the line through $0$ parallel to the secant from $p$ to $q$, ``the vector $\vec{pq}$, as in Calc~3''; $q - p \neq 0$ because $p \neq q$. \textit{(Filled in.)} $\sigma$ is smooth: it is $(p, q) \mapsto q - p \in \mathbb{R}^N \setminus \{0\}$ followed by the quotient map to $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$, which in the chart $\varphi_i$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:rpn-atlas} is $w \mapsto (w_k/w_i)_{k \neq i}$, rational with nonvanishing denominator. Its domain is open in $M \times M$, of dimension $2m$, and $\dim \mathbb{RP}^{N-1} = N - 1$. If $2m < N - 1$, the image of $\sigma$ has measure zero (Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim}). So do the lines contained in $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$: they form a copy of $\mathbb{RP}^{N-2}$, of lower dimension --- ``the things that are not transverse to $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is a projective space of lower dimension'' --- whose image under the smooth inclusion has measure zero by the same corollary. A union of two sets of measure zero has measure zero (Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}), so its complement is dense (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4), in charts): ``pick $\ell$ not in the image and transverse to $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$.'' For such $\ell$, $\pi_\ell$ is injective: $\pi_\ell(p) = \pi_\ell(q)$ means $q - p \in \ker = \ell$, so for $p \neq q$, $\ell = \operatorname{span}(q - p) = \sigma(p, q)$, contrary to the choice. ``I'm going to lose injectivity precisely when I have a $p$ and a $q$ parallel to the line of projection.'' The condition $2m < N - 1$ is $N > 2m + 1$, ``precisely the bound.''
\end{proof}

Projection along a line $\ell$, in the plane ($N = 2$). Points of $M$ slide along lines parallel to $\ell$ onto $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$. Two points $p \neq q$ collide exactly when the secant $q - p$ is parallel to $\ell$; choosing $\ell$ outside the image of $\sigma$ avoids every such pair. ``That's a beautiful proof of the non-optimal Whitney embedding theorem.''

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} Why the bound is $2m + 1$. For a curve ($m = 1$) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ ($N = 3$), $(M \times M) \setminus \Delta$ has dimension $2m = 2 = N - 1$, so the secant directions $\sigma(p, q)$ can fill an open set of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ and Corollary~\ref{cor:sard-low-dim} does not apply. Indeed, projecting a curve in space onto a plane along $\ell$ typically produces crossings: here $q - p$ is parallel to $\ell$, and $\pi_\ell(p) = \pi_\ell(q)$. The shadow is still an immersed curve, matching the immersion into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney}, but not an embedded one.
%% <<< END ADDED

\begin{lembox}[Projections That Stay Immersions]\thmlabel{lem:projection-immersion}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ be a regular submanifold of dimension $m$, with $N > 2m + 1$. Then the lines $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ through $0$ for which $\ell \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, or $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is not an immersion, form a set of measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$.
\leeref{Lemma 6.13}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (to be filled)]
\textit{(A homework problem. Uribe's sketch from Lecture~21 is recorded as given; the proof is to be filled in after the assignment is submitted.)} ``The same idea \ldots\ instead of pairs $(p, q)$ to create a line, you take tangent vectors. You take $p$ and $q$ infinitesimally close together'': map nonzero tangent vectors to lines,
\[
TM \setminus \mathcal{Z} \longrightarrow \mathbb{RP}^{N-1}, \qquad (p, v) \longmapsto \mathbb{R}v ,
\]
with $T_pM \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$ (``in the homework you replace this by $v$ of length one''), and choose $\ell$ also outside its image. ``What remains to be proved is that if you have a line that is not in here, then you get an immersion, and that's going to be precisely because the differential of the projection is just the projection.'' To be filled.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[The Whitney Theorems for Compact Manifolds]\thmlabel{thm:whitney-compact}
Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Then there is an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ and an immersion $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$.
\leeref{Theorems 6.15 and 6.18, compact case}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~21, ``two steps \ldots\ totally different. The technology, the ideas are totally different.'' The steps are Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds} and Lemmas~\ref{lem:projection-injective}--\ref{lem:projection-immersion}; the immersion lemma is a homework problem, to be filled in after the assignment.)}

\emph{Step 1: some Euclidean space.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-embeds} there is an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^N$ for some $N$. Its image is a regular submanifold diffeomorphic to $M$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}); replace $M$ by it.

\emph{Step 2: one dimension less.} Suppose $N > 2m + 1$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:projection-injective} and~\ref{lem:projection-immersion}, the lines $\ell$ that lie in $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$, or for which $\pi_\ell$ is not injective, or not an immersion, form the union of two sets of measure zero in $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$, which has measure zero (Proposition~\ref{prop:measure-zero-every-chart}). A set of measure zero contains no nonempty open set (Lemma~\ref{lem:measure-zero-basic}(4), in a chart), so it is not all of $\mathbb{RP}^{N-1}$: choose $\ell$ outside it. Then $\pi_\ell : M \to \mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ is an injective immersion of a compact manifold, hence an embedding (Corollary~\ref{cor:compact-embedding}), and its image is a regular submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^{N-1}$ diffeomorphic to $M$.

\emph{Step 3: repeat.} Apply Step~2 while $N > 2m + 1$, lowering $N$ by one each time, ``until we're out of parameters'': this ends with an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$. The immersion into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ is part of the same homework, and is likewise to be filled.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Noncompact Case: A Sketch}\label{sub:whitney-noncompact}

\textit{Lecture 22. ``An indication of a sketch of proof, very sketchy \ldots\ I already said several times we can't prove everything,'' with ``chapter and verse'' of the rest in Lee to follow by email. The noncompact proof has the same two parts as the compact one --- first put $M$ in some Euclidean space, then project as much as you can --- and Uribe sketched only the first. ``The main tool is going to be a theorem that I hope to prove later'': the existence of exhaustion functions. ``Notation and terminology are key to doing math. It's a nice name, exhaustion function.''}

\begin{defbox}[Exhaustion Function]\deflabel{def:exhaustion-function}
An \textbf{exhaustion function} on $M$ is a smooth function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$, $f \ge 0$, such that for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$ the \textbf{sublevel set} $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big)$ is compact.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Exhaustion Functions}}
\end{defbox}

``The cartoon, which is used in Morse theory'': stand $M$ up with $f$ as the height. The level set at $c$ is the slice at height $c$, and the sublevel set is everything below it, compact for every $c$ --- ``and it's not obvious, but these things always exist.''

\begin{propbox}[Exhaustion Functions Exist]\thmlabel{prop:exhaustion-exists}
Every smooth manifold admits an exhaustion function.
\leeref{Proposition 2.28}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (Lecture~23)]
Announced in Lecture~22 and proved with partitions of unity --- ``right now we're sort of buying on credit. We have to pay the bill.'' Uribe's email of Oct 26: ``On Wednesday I will discuss the construction of exhaustion functions, which is Proposition 2.28.'' The proof is in \ref{sub:exhaustion-proof}, after partitions of unity (\ref{sec:partitions-of-unity}).
\end{proof}

\textit{Slicing $M$ into compact pieces.} ``The idea is going to be that we're going to use these level sets \ldots\ to slice the manifold into compact pieces. They will have a boundary, but I'm going to ignore that. And basically, we're going to be able to embed each piece and keep track of overlaps.'' Let $f$ be an exhaustion function. Its singular values have measure zero (Theorem~\ref{thm:sard}), so every interval contains regular values; for each $i = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ pick regular values $a_i, b_i$ with $i < a_i < b_i < i + 1$, and put
\[
E_i = f^{-1}\big([b_{i-1}, a_{i+1}]\big), \qquad D_i = f^{-1}\big([i, i+1]\big) \qquad (i \ge 1),
\]
with $E_0 = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, a_1]\big)$ and $D_0 = f^{-1}\big((-\infty, 1]\big)$ (``you have to do something a little bit different at the beginning''). Each $E_i$ is compact (a closed subset of a sublevel set), and a manifold with boundary, because $b_{i-1}$ and $a_{i+1}$ are regular values. Then $M = \bigcup_i D_i$, $D_i \subseteq \operatorname{Int}E_i$, and the observation ``that will be useful later'':
\[
E_i \cap E_{i+2} = \varnothing ,
\]
since $E_i \subseteq f^{-1}\big((-\infty, a_{i+1}]\big)$ and $E_{i+2} \subseteq f^{-1}\big([b_{i+1}, \infty)\big)$ with $a_{i+1} < b_{i+1}$; more generally $E_i \cap E_j = \varnothing$ when $|i - j| \ge 2$.

Left: a sublevel set of an exhaustion function on a surface with holes, as on the board. \textit{(Not from lecture: the surface is plotted, not drawn.)} Here $M$ is the boundary of a thickened ladder in $\mathbb{R}^3$, the zero set of a smooth function: a noncompact surface (it continues upward) with a hole between consecutive rungs, and $f$ is the height, an exhaustion function on $M$; the sublevel set $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big)$ (orange) is compact. Right: the slicing (``Lee doesn't have a figure''). $E_i$ runs from the regular value $b_{i-1}$, just below $i$, to $a_{i+1}$, just above $i + 1$, and contains the band $D_i$ (teal) between the integer levels $i$ and $i + 1$ in its interior. The height has critical points at the top and bottom of each rung, where the topology of the sublevel sets changes (the starting point of Morse theory); the levels $c$, $a_i$, $b_i$ are regular values, so they miss these heights, and each $E_i$ is a compact manifold with boundary --- here $E_i$ contains two of the holes.

\begin{propbox}[A Proper Embedding from the Slices]\thmlabel{prop:noncompact-embedding}
Let $f$ be an exhaustion function on $M$, $\dim M = m$, and $E_i, D_i$ as above. Suppose that each $E_i$ admits an embedding $F_i : E_i \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$, and let $\rho_i : M \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth with $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq \operatorname{Int}E_i$ and $\rho_i \equiv 1$ on a neighbourhood of $D_i$. Then
\[
F = \Big( \sum_{i \text{ even}} \rho_i F_i,\ \sum_{i \text{ odd}} \rho_i F_i,\ f \Big) : M \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2(2m+1)+1}
\]
is a proper injective immersion, hence an embedding.
\leeref{Theorem 6.15 (proof)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~22 gave the construction and the reason for properness; injectivity and the immersion property ``are completely analogous to the compact [case] \ldots\ you can read it in Lee,'' and are filled in from Lee. The two hypotheses are the lecture's ``credit'': that compact manifolds with boundary embed in $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ --- ``forgetting that we have manifolds with boundary, which we haven't discussed'' --- and that the cutoffs $\rho_i$ exist, which partitions of unity provide.)}

\emph{$F$ is smooth.} $\rho_iF_i$, ``in principle only defined on $E_i$, \ldots\ extends smoothly as zero outside'': it is smooth on the open set $\operatorname{Int}E_i$ and zero on the open set $M \setminus \operatorname{supp}\rho_i$, which together cover $M$. ``These sums that look very, very scary are actually locally finite'': the $E_i$ with $i$ of one parity are pairwise disjoint closed sets, and only finitely many of them meet a neighbourhood $f^{-1}\big((c - 1, c + 1)\big)$, since $E_i \subseteq f^{-1}([i - 1, i + 2])$. So near each point at most one term of each sum is nonzero.

\emph{$F$ is proper} --- ``properness comes from having $f$'' as a component. If $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{2(2m+1)+1}$ is compact, the last coordinate is bounded on $K$, say by $c$, so $F^{-1}(K)$ is a closed subset of the compact sublevel set $f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big)$, hence compact (Definition~\ref{def:proper-map}).

\emph{$F$ is injective.} Suppose $F(p) = F(q)$. Then $f(p) = f(q)$, so if $p \in D_j$ then $q \in D_j$, and $\rho_j(p) = \rho_j(q) = 1$. In the block of the parity of $j$, every other term vanishes at $p$ and $q$: for $i \neq j$ of that parity $|i - j| \ge 2$, so $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i \subseteq E_i$ misses $E_j \supseteq D_j$. So that block reads $F_j(p) = F_j(q)$, and $F_j$ is injective: $p = q$.

\emph{$F$ is an immersion.} Let $p \in D_j$, and $W \subseteq \operatorname{Int}E_j$ an open neighbourhood of $p$ on which $\rho_j \equiv 1$. On $W$ the block of the parity of $j$ is $F_j$, since the other terms of that block are supported in sets $E_i$ disjoint from $E_j$. So that block of $dF_p$ is $d(F_j)_p$, injective because $F_j$ is an embedding; hence $dF_p$ is injective.

\emph{An embedding.} A proper injective immersion is an embedding (Theorem~\ref{thm:proper-embedding}).
\end{proof}

A student asked whether the last coordinate is there for injectivity. ``This entry here makes it proper'': ``an exhaustion function is proper,'' and properness is what turns an injective immersion of a noncompact manifold into an embedding. ``That's a beautiful, clever idea.''

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} Why the noncompact embedding is made proper. The curve $\gamma(t) = \big(\sin 2s, \sin s\big)$, $s = \pi + 2\arctan t$, is an injective immersion $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2$, but both ends approach $\gamma(0)$: the preimage of a small closed disc $\overline{B}$ about $\gamma(0)$ contains two half-lines, so $\gamma$ is not proper, and its image is not an embedded submanifold near $\gamma(0)$. Adding an exhaustion function as an extra coordinate (``this entry here makes it proper'') pulls the ends apart in height, which is what Proposition~\ref{prop:noncompact-embedding} does with $f$.
%% <<< END ADDED


\textit{The projection step}, only indicated: ``since you now have a noncompact manifold, the thing can be all over the place.'' $\mathbb{R}^{2(2m+1)}$ is diffeomorphic to an open ball, so the first two blocks can be squeezed into a ball, and with $f$ as the last coordinate the image lies in a tube, ball $\times\ \mathbb{R}$; ``once you have it in a tube, you can start controlling the projections. The projections have to be proper.'' Reading: Lee, Lemma~6.14 and its figure; Uribe's email of Oct 26 assigns Lemmas~6.13 and~6.14 and Theorem~6.15 for the noncompact case.

\begin{thmbox}[The Whitney Embedding and Immersion Theorems]\thmlabel{thm:whitney}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $m$. Then there is an embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ and an immersion $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2m}$.
\leeref{Theorems 6.15 and 6.18}
\end{thmbox}

``In other words, any manifold is diffeomorphic to a submanifold of some Euclidean space'' (Theorem~\ref{thm:embedding-image}). The course proves the compact case in full (Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact}). The noncompact case, which first makes the embedding proper, is sketched above and assigned as reading in Lee (Lemma~6.14 and Theorem~6.15): ``he has a beautiful picture.''

\begin{rembox}[The Hard Version]\label{rem:strong-whitney}
In the ``hard'' version the dimensions are one less: an embedding into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ and an immersion into $\mathbb{R}^{2m-1}$ (for $m > 1$ in the second; Lee, Theorems 6.19 and 6.20). ``We will not discuss this at all. The proof is very specialized and really long \ldots\ The smaller the codimension, the tighter it is, and you have to wrestle the manifold more to get it in there. It's like packing your clothes in a suitcase.''
\end{rembox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (sketch; the details are reading in Lee)]
\textit{(Lecture~22 sketched the noncompact case; the rest is assigned reading.)} For $M$ compact this is Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact}. In general, take an exhaustion function $f$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:exhaustion-exists}) and slice $M$ into the compact pieces $E_i$ above. Each $E_i$, a compact manifold with boundary, embeds in $\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}$ by the method of Theorem~\ref{thm:whitney-compact} (manifolds with boundary are not treated in these notes), and the cutoffs $\rho_i$ come from partitions of unity (Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity}, \ref{sec:partitions-of-unity}); Proposition~\ref{prop:noncompact-embedding} then gives a proper embedding $M \to \mathbb{R}^{2(2m+1)+1}$. Lowering the dimension to $2m + 1$ needs projections that stay proper: squeeze the image into a tube, ball $\times\ \mathbb{R}$, and project as in Lemmas~\ref{lem:projection-injective}--\ref{lem:projection-immersion} (Lee, Lemma~6.14 and Theorem~6.15). The immersion into $\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ is Lee, Theorem~6.18; in the compact case it is part of the homework.
\end{proof}

\section{Partitions of Unity}\label{sec:partitions-of-unity}

\roadmark{Stage: analysis}{Writing $1$ as a locally finite sum of smooth functions subordinate to any open cover: the tool for gluing local constructions into global ones.}

\textit{Lecture 22. ``A key tool for constructing exhaustion functions, and many other things --- we're going to use it to integrate forms, for example --- is the notion of partition of unity. And Lee pays the bills up front. He deposits a lot of money'' (Lee, Chapter~2).}

\begin{defbox}[Partition of Unity]\deflabel{def:partition-of-unity}
A \textbf{partition of unity} on $M$ is an indexed family $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ of smooth functions on $M$, over an arbitrary index set $A$ (``could be uncountable''), such that
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $0 \le \chi_\alpha \le 1$ for every $\alpha$;
\item the family of supports $\{\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is \textbf{locally finite}: every $p \in M$ has a neighbourhood $U$ for which $\{ \alpha \in A : U \cap \operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \neq \varnothing \}$ is finite;
\item $\sum_{\alpha \in A} \chi_\alpha(p) = 1$ for every $p \in M$.
\end{enumerate}
By (2) the sum in (3) has only finitely many nonzero terms at each point. The partition is \textbf{subordinate} to an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ if $\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \subseteq U_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$.
\leeref{Ch.~2, \emph{Partitions of Unity}}
\end{defbox}

``This is where the name comes from. You take the number one, and you write it as a sum of smooth functions.'' ``These things allow us to localize''; the bump functions so far, and the cutoffs $\rho_i$ above, are made of the same material.

The simplest example, on $M = \mathbb{R}$: a function $\chi_1$ that is $1$ far to the left and $0$ far to the right, and $\chi_2 = 1 - \chi_1$.

\begin{thmbox}[Existence of Partitions of Unity]\thmlabel{thm:partition-of-unity}
If $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is any open cover of $M$, there is a partition of unity $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ subordinate to it.
\leeref{Theorem 2.23}
\end{thmbox}

The proof has two steps of different kinds: an analysis step in $\mathbb{R}^m$, and ``serious point set topology'' on $M$. \textit{Reading (Uribe's email of Oct 26): Lee, Chapter~2, from Lemma~2.20 to the beginning of the section on applications of partitions of unity (p.~44); for paracompactness, Theorem~1.15 (p.~9).}

\begin{lembox}[Plateau Functions]\thmlabel{lem:plateau}
For all $\varepsilon > \delta > 0$ there is $\rho \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with $0 \le \rho \le 1$, $\rho \equiv 1$ on $[-\delta, \delta]$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho \subseteq (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. Then $f(x) = \rho(|x|)$ is smooth on $\mathbb{R}^m$, $f \equiv 1$ on the closed ball $\overline{B}_\delta$, and $\operatorname{supp} f \subseteq B_\varepsilon = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^m : |x| < \varepsilon \}$.
\leeref{Lemmas 2.20--2.22}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~22: ``I'm not going to prove that \ldots\ you start with a function that is $e^{-1/x}$ for $x$ positive and zero for $x$ negative \ldots\ and then you do trickery with it --- reflect, divide, add. It's not complicated, but it takes 10 minutes to check.'' The trickery is step~2 of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence}.)} With $h$ as there and $\delta < r' < \varepsilon$, take $\rho(t) = h(r'^2 - t^2)\big/\big(h(r'^2 - t^2) + h(t^2 - \delta^2)\big)$: smooth, between $0$ and $1$, equal to $1$ for $|t| \le \delta$ and $0$ for $|t| \ge r'$, so $\operatorname{supp}\rho \subseteq [-r', r'] \subseteq (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. Then $f(x) = \rho(|x|)$ is the function $H$ of that proof (with $r = \delta$), smooth on $\mathbb{R}^m$ --- ``$|x|$ is not a $C^\infty$ function at the origin; however, $\rho$ is constant equal to one near $0$'', so $f$ is constant near $x = 0$ --- with $f \equiv 1$ on $\overline{B}_\delta$ and $\operatorname{supp} f = \overline{B}_{r'} \subseteq B_\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\textit{The topology.} ``We need some serious point set topology \ldots\ we're paying the bills. It's a little painful.''

\begin{defbox}[Paracompact Space]\deflabel{def:paracompact}
A space $X$ is \textbf{paracompact} if every open cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ has an open refinement $\{V_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ that covers and is locally finite:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $X = \bigcup_i V_i$, and for every $i$ there is $\alpha(i)$ with $V_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)}$;
\item every $p \in X$ has a neighbourhood $W$ such that $\{ i : W \cap V_i \neq \varnothing \}$ is finite.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Paracompactness}}
\end{defbox}

``Compactness would say that any cover has a finite subcover, and in this case we have [a] locally finite \ldots\ it's not a subcover; it's just a refinement.'' (The usual definition allows refinements indexed by any set; with the countable index set of the lecture it is what holds for manifolds, Theorem~\ref{thm:manifolds-paracompact} below.)

\begin{lembox}[Exhaustion by Compact Sets]\thmlabel{lem:compact-exhaustion}
A second-countable, locally compact Hausdorff space $X$ is the union of compact sets $K_1 \subseteq K_2 \subseteq \cdots$ with $K_j \subseteq \operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$ for every $j$.
\leeref{Proposition A.60}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; filled in, following Lee.)} \emph{A countable basis of precompact sets.} Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a countable basis, and $\mathcal{B}'$ the set of $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with compact closure. $\mathcal{B}'$ is still a basis: if $x \in W$ open, local compactness gives an open $V \ni x$ with $\overline V$ compact, and some $B \in \mathcal{B}$ has $x \in B \subseteq V \cap W$; then $\overline B$ is a closed subset of the compact $\overline V$ (closures computed in the Hausdorff space $X$), so compact. Enumerate $\mathcal{B}' = \{B_1, B_2, \ldots\}$ (if it is finite, $X$ is compact and $K_j = X$ works).
\emph{The exhaustion.} Put $K_1 = \overline{B_1}$. Given $K_j$ compact, it is covered by the $B_i$, hence by $B_1, \ldots, B_n$ for some $n$; take the least such $n$ with $n \ge j + 1$, and $K_{j+1} = \overline{B_1} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{B_n}$, compact as a finite union of compact sets. Then $K_j \subseteq B_1 \cup \cdots \cup B_n \subseteq \operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$, and $B_j \subseteq K_j$ for all $j$, so $\bigcup_j K_j = X$.
\end{proof}

\begin{thmbox}[Manifolds Are Paracompact]\thmlabel{thm:manifolds-paracompact}
Let $M$ be a topological manifold, $\{U_\alpha\}$ an open cover, and $\mathcal{B}$ any basis of the topology of $M$. Then $\{U_\alpha\}$ has a countable, locally finite open refinement that covers $M$ and consists of elements of $\mathcal{B}$. In particular $M$ is paracompact. More generally, every second-countable, locally compact Hausdorff space is paracompact, by the same proof.
\leeref{Theorem 1.15}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Stated in Lecture~22 --- ``manifolds are paracompact, and in fact the refinements can always be taken from a basis of the topology'' --- with the proof left to Lee; filled in, following Lee.)} $M$ is Hausdorff, second countable (Definition~\ref{def:second-countable}) and locally compact (Proposition~\ref{prop:locally-compact}); let $K_1 \subseteq K_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-exhaustion}, and $K_0 = K_{-1} = \varnothing$. For $j \ge 0$ put
\[
A_j = K_{j+1} \setminus \operatorname{Int}K_j \ \ \text{(compact)}, \qquad W_j = \operatorname{Int}K_{j+2} \setminus K_{j-1} \ \ \text{(open)}, \qquad A_j \subseteq W_j .
\]
For each $x \in A_j$ choose $\alpha$ with $x \in U_\alpha$, and $B_x \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B_x \subseteq U_\alpha \cap W_j$. Finitely many $B_x$ cover the compact set $A_j$. The union over $j$ of these finite families is a countable family of elements of $\mathcal{B}$; it covers $M$, because the $A_j$ do (each point lies in some $K_{j+1} \setminus \operatorname{Int}K_j$); and it refines $\{U_\alpha\}$. \emph{Locally finite:} the sets chosen for $j$ lie in $W_j$, and $W_j \cap W_k = \varnothing$ when $|j - k| \ge 3$; a point of $A_j$ has the neighbourhood $W_j$, which meets only the sets chosen for $j - 2, \ldots, j + 2$, finitely many.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Is Local Compactness Needed?]\label{rem:paracompact-hypotheses}
The board stated the theorem as ``if $X$ is $T_2$ and second countable, then it is paracompact'', and Uribe was unsure: ``I'm not sure \ldots\ whether you need local compactness \ldots\ Check your email. I'll clarify.'' The email (Oct 26) settled it: ``Indeed local compactness is needed: Hausdorff, 2nd countable and local compactness imply paracompactness. Lee proves directly what we need for manifolds in Theorem~1.15, page~9.'' So the theorem is stated with local compactness, as above. \textit{(Filled in.)} Why some hypothesis beyond Hausdorff and second countable is needed: A paracompact Hausdorff space is normal, in particular regular (Munkres, Theorem~41.1), and the \emph{$K$-topology} on $\mathbb{R}$ --- generated by the open intervals and the sets $(a, b) \setminus \{1/n : n \ge 1\}$ --- is Hausdorff and second countable but not regular (Munkres, \S31), so not paracompact. Local compactness, as above, suffices; so does regularity. For manifolds nothing changes: they are locally compact. Uribe on second countability: ``we haven't used [it] at all until this moment, when we're paying the bills'' --- it was used once before, for countable subcovers in measure zero (Lemma~\ref{lem:countable-subcover}).
\end{rembox}

\begin{defbox}[Regular Coordinate Ball]\deflabel{def:regular-coordinate-ball}
An open set $B \subseteq M$ is a \textbf{regular coordinate ball} if there are a chart $(U, \varphi)$ with $B \subseteq U$ and numbers $0 < \delta < \varepsilon$ such that $\varphi(B) = B_\delta(0)$, the $\delta$-ball centred at $0$, and $B_\varepsilon(0) \subseteq \varphi(U)$ --- an $\varepsilon$-ball centred at $0$ containing $\varphi(B)$, with room to spare.
\leeref{Ch.~1, \emph{Regular Coordinate Balls}}
\end{defbox}

``Why do you even need the second condition?'' asked a student. ``Because I want to pull back my function that I had before. You need a little room.''

\begin{lembox}[Regular Coordinate Balls Form a Basis]\thmlabel{lem:regular-balls-basis}
Let $\{U_\alpha\}$ be an open cover of $M$. The regular coordinate balls $B$ whose chart $(U, \varphi)$ can be chosen with $U$ inside some $U_\alpha$ form a basis of the topology of $M$.
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Filled in.)} Let $W$ be open and $x \in W$, say $x \in U_\alpha$. Take a chart $(V, \psi)$ at $x$, restrict it to $U = V \cap W \cap U_\alpha$, and translate so that $\varphi = \psi|_U - \psi(x)$ sends $x$ to $0$. $\varphi(U)$ is open, so it contains some $B_\varepsilon(0)$; for $0 < \delta < \varepsilon$, $B = \varphi^{-1}(B_\delta(0))$ is a regular coordinate ball with $x \in B \subseteq U \subseteq W$, and its chart domain $U$ lies in $U_\alpha$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity} (begun in Lecture~22; completed, following Lee)]
\textit{(The lecture's steps; Uribe stopped here: ``I will finish the proof next time.'')} By Theorem~\ref{thm:manifolds-paracompact} with the basis of Lemma~\ref{lem:regular-balls-basis}, there is a countable, locally finite refinement $\{B_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of $\{U_\alpha\}$ covering $M$, each $B_i$ a regular coordinate ball with chart $(U_i, \varphi_i)$, $\varphi_i(B_i) = B_{\delta_i}(0)$, $B_{\varepsilon_i}(0) \subseteq \varphi_i(U_i)$, and $U_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)}$. ``Pull back the function $f$ from the first part'' (Lemma~\ref{lem:plateau}, with $\delta_i < \varepsilon_i$) by $\varphi_i$, and extend it by zero: this gives a smooth $f_i : M \to \mathbb{R}$, as in step~3 of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence}, with
\[
f_i|_{B_i} \equiv 1, \qquad \operatorname{supp} f_i \subseteq U_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)} .
\]
``The $B_i$ form a cover, and $f_i$ is identically equal to one there,'' so $\sum_j f_j \ge 1$ at every point. Let
\[
g_i = \frac{f_i}{\sum_j f_j}, \qquad \text{so that} \qquad \sum_i g_i \equiv 1, \qquad
\chi_\alpha = \sum_{i \,:\, \alpha(i) = \alpha} g_i .
\]
``What we don't have [yet] is the index'': grouping the $g_i$ by $\alpha(i)$ re-indexes the partition by $A$.

\textit{(Lecture~23 went straight on to an application, \ref{sub:exhaustion-proof}; the rest is the assigned reading, Lee's proof of Theorem~2.23. Completed here, following Lee.)} What remains: the sums are locally finite, so that $\sum_j f_j$, the $g_i$ and the $\chi_\alpha$ are smooth, and $\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \subseteq U_\alpha$. One point needs care. Local finiteness of $\{B_i\}$ does not by itself make $\{\operatorname{supp} f_i\}$ locally finite, since $\operatorname{supp} f_i$ sits in the larger ball $\varphi_i^{-1}(B_{\varepsilon_i}(0))$, not in $\overline{B_i}$. Lee avoids this by choosing $f_i$ positive on $B_i$ and supported in $\overline{B_i}$. That is the only change to the lecture's construction: $f_i$ is no longer $\equiv 1$ on $B_i$, only positive there, which is all the division needs.

\emph{Two facts about a locally finite family $\{A_i\}$ of subsets.} (a) $\{\overline{A_i}\}$ is locally finite: an open set meeting $\overline{A_i}$ meets $A_i$. (b) If each $A_i$ is closed, then $\bigcup_i A_i$ is closed: for $p \notin \bigcup_i A_i$, take an open $W \ni p$ meeting only $A_{i_1}, \ldots, A_{i_k}$; then $W \setminus (A_{i_1} \cup \cdots \cup A_{i_k})$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$ missing every $A_i$.

\emph{The new $f_i$.} With $h$ as in step~1 of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence} ($h(t) = e^{-1/t}$ for $t > 0$, $h(t) = 0$ for $t \le 0$), put
\[
f_i = h\big(\delta_i^2 - |\varphi_i|^2\big) \ \text{ on } U_i, \qquad f_i = 0 \ \text{ on } M \setminus U_i .
\]
$f_i > 0$ exactly on $B_i = \varphi_i^{-1}(B_{\delta_i}(0))$. The set $K_i = \varphi_i^{-1}\big(\overline{B}_{\delta_i}(0)\big)$ is compact ($\overline{B}_{\delta_i}(0) \subseteq B_{\varepsilon_i}(0) \subseteq \varphi_i(U_i)$, and $\varphi_i^{-1}$ is continuous), hence closed in $M$. So $f_i$ is smooth, as it is smooth on the open set $U_i$ and zero on the open set $M \setminus K_i$, which together cover $M$ (as in step~3 of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:bump-existence}). Its support is $\overline{B_i} = K_i$: $K_i$ is closed and contains $B_i$, and every point of $K_i$ is a limit of points of $B_i$.

\emph{Smoothness.} By (a) the supports $\overline{B_i}$ form a locally finite family. Each $p$ has an open neighbourhood $W$ on which all but finitely many $f_j$ vanish, so on $W$ the sum $\sum_j f_j$ is a finite sum of smooth functions; hence $\sum_j f_j$ is smooth. It is positive everywhere, because the $B_i$ cover $M$ and $f_i > 0$ on $B_i$. So $g_i = f_i / \sum_j f_j$ is smooth, $0 \le g_i \le 1$, $\operatorname{supp} g_i = \overline{B_i} \subseteq U_i \subseteq U_{\alpha(i)}$, and $\sum_i g_i \equiv 1$.

\emph{Re-indexing.} For $\alpha \in A$ let $\chi_\alpha = \sum_{i : \alpha(i) = \alpha} g_i$, with the empty sum $0$. On $W$ as above, only finitely many terms are nonzero, so $\chi_\alpha$ is smooth; and $0 \le \chi_\alpha \le \sum_i g_i = 1$. Each $i$ has exactly one $\alpha(i)$, so $\sum_\alpha \chi_\alpha = \sum_i g_i \equiv 1$. The set $\{\chi_\alpha \neq 0\}$ lies in $\bigcup_{\alpha(i) = \alpha} \overline{B_i}$, which is closed by (b), so
\[
\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha \subseteq \bigcup_{i \,:\, \alpha(i) = \alpha} \overline{B_i} \subseteq U_\alpha .
\]
Finally, $W$ meets $\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha$ only if it meets some $\overline{B_i}$ with $\alpha(i) = \alpha$, and $W$ meets only finitely many $\overline{B_i}$. So $\{\operatorname{supp}\chi_\alpha\}$ is locally finite, and $\{\chi_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is a partition of unity subordinate to $\{U_\alpha\}$.
\end{proof}

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 22).} Page~58 of the handwritten notes states the theorem ``if $X$ is $T_2$ and 2nd countable, then it is paracompact (need locally compact?)''; as stated it is false in general, and local compactness, which manifolds have, is the missing hypothesis (Remark~\ref{rem:paracompact-hypotheses}).

% ============================================================================
% Lecture 23 (Wed Oct 28, 2026): exhaustion functions from partitions of unity
% ============================================================================

\subsection{An Application: Exhaustion Functions}\label{sub:exhaustion-proof}

\textit{Lecture 23. ``I do want to tell you about the application of partitions of unity that we need for the sketch of the Whitney embedding theorem, the noncompact case'': the existence of exhaustion functions (Definition~\ref{def:exhaustion-function}, Proposition~\ref{prop:exhaustion-exists}). ``The proof will be quick using partitions of unity.''}

The proof starts from a countable cover by open sets with compact closures, which was set as an exercise.

\begin{lembox}[Countable Precompact Covers]\thmlabel{lem:precompact-cover}
Every manifold $M$ has a countable open cover $\{V_i\}_{i \ge 1}$ such that $\overline{V_i}$ is compact for every $i$.
\leeref{Proposition 2.28 (proof)}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Set in Lecture~23 as an exercise: ``The argument that I have in mind uses paracompactness. Maybe you have another way of doing it.'' Filled in, by paracompactness.)} Every $p \in M$ has an open neighbourhood $W_p$ with $\overline{W_p}$ compact (Proposition~\ref{prop:locally-compact}). By Theorem~\ref{thm:manifolds-paracompact} the cover $\{W_p\}_{p \in M}$ has a countable open refinement $\{V_i\}$ covering $M$; if it is finite, repeat one of its sets to index it by $i \ge 1$. Each $V_i$ lies in some $W_{p(i)}$, so $\overline{V_i}$ is a closed subset of the compact set $\overline{W_{p(i)}}$, hence compact. (Another way: the countable basis of precompact sets built in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:compact-exhaustion} is already such a cover. Local finiteness of the refinement is not needed here.)
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:exhaustion-exists}]
\textit{(Lecture~23.)} Let $\{V_i\}_{i \ge 1}$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:precompact-cover}, and let $\{\chi_i\}_{i \ge 1}$ be a partition of unity subordinate to it (Theorem~\ref{thm:partition-of-unity}). Reviewing what this means (Definition~\ref{def:partition-of-unity}):
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $0 \le \chi_i \le 1$ for all $i$;
\item $\{\operatorname{supp}\chi_i\}$ is locally finite;
\item $\sum_i \chi_i(p) = 1$ for all $p \in M$ --- a finite sum at each point, by (2);
\item $\operatorname{supp}\chi_i \subseteq V_i$ for all $i$ --- ``that's the subordinate part.''
\end{enumerate}
``The clever construction'' is to define
\[
f = \sum_{j \ge 1} j\, \chi_j .
\]
``If you don't put the $j$, you get one. But the clever idea is to put $j$ in front.'' Again this is a locally finite sum of smooth functions, so $f$ is smooth; and $f \ge 0$ because the $\chi_j$ are nonnegative (in fact $f \ge \sum_j \chi_j = 1$). It remains to show that the sublevel sets are compact.

\emph{Claim.} For every $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and every integer $N \ge 0$ with $N \ge c$,
\[
f^{-1}\big((-\infty, c]\big) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^N V_i \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^N \overline{V_i} .
\]
\emph{The claim implies the proposition.} $\bigcup_{i=1}^N \overline{V_i}$ is a finite union of compact sets, so it is compact. $f^{-1}((-\infty, c])$ is closed, since $f$ is continuous, and a closed subset of a compact set is compact.

\emph{Proof of the claim.} We prove the contrapositive. Let $p \notin \bigcup_{i=1}^N V_i$. For $i = 1, \ldots, N$, $p \notin V_i \supseteq \operatorname{supp}\chi_i$, so $\chi_i(p) = 0$. Hence the sum defining $f(p)$ really starts at $N + 1$, and since every coefficient is at least $N + 1$ (``an $\ell^1$--$\ell^\infty$ estimate, or whatever''),
\[
f(p) = \sum_{j = N+1}^\infty j\, \chi_j(p) \ \ge\ (N + 1) \underbrace{\sum_{j = N+1}^\infty \chi_j(p)}_{=\, \sum_j \chi_j(p) \,=\, 1} = N + 1 > c .
\]
So $p \notin f^{-1}((-\infty, c])$.
\end{proof}

\begin{rembox}[Why the Closures]\label{rem:why-closures}
A student asked whether the contrapositive should use the union of the \emph{closures}. Uribe: the proof shows the inclusion in $\bigcup_{i \le N} V_i$, and that ``is contained in the union of the closures, so it doesn't make a difference.'' The open sets give the stronger statement; the closures are where compactness lives, since the $V_i$ were chosen so that the $\overline{V_i}$ are compact, and $\bigcup_{i \le N} V_i$ alone need not be compact. ``It is important that in the end I end up in here.'' Lee runs the contrapositive from $p \notin \bigcup_{j \le N} \overline{V_j}$ instead (Proposition~2.28); either way the sublevel set lands inside the compact set $\bigcup_{j \le N} \overline{V_j}$.
\end{rembox}
