\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added, computed.)} The construction on $M = \mathbb{R}$, with $V_1 = (-1, 1)$ and $V_j = \{ j - 1.6 < |x| < j \}$ for $j \ge 2$, and $\chi_j$ obtained by normalizing bumps positive exactly on $V_j$. Then $f = \sum_j j\chi_j$ climbs one step on each successive $V_j$, so it grows like $|x|$. The sublevel set $f^{-1}((-\infty, 2.5])$ (red) lies inside $\overline{V_1} \cup \overline{V_2} \cup \overline{V_3} = [-3, 3]$, as the claim with $N = 3$ says.

``This technique of using partitions of unity is a very common technique in this subject, and the best way to learn to use it is to use it in a homework problem with hints.'' The next assignment will have ``at least one, maybe a couple of applications of partitions of unity.''

\textbf{Transcription note (Lecture 23).} The board defined $f = \sum_{j \ge 0} j\chi_j$ but wrote the union in the claim from $i = 1$ (Uribe: ``wherever your index starts''). These notes index the cover and the partition from $1$, as Lee does. If the index starts at $0$, the union in the claim must start at $i = 0$ too. Otherwise a point of $V_0$ outside $V_1, \ldots, V_N$ can have $f(p) = \sum_{j > N} j\chi_j(p) < N + 1$, since then $\sum_{j > N}\chi_j(p) = 1 - \chi_0(p)$.
% ============================================================================
% CHAPTER: INTEGRAL CURVES AND FLOWS (Lecture 23, Wed Oct 28, 2026)
% ============================================================================
\chapter{Integral Curves and Flows}

\textit{Lecture 23. ``We get a little bit disorganized, I'm sorry \ldots\ It's actually a new chapter in Lee. We're in sync with Lee in a way. It's going to be Chapter~9.'' The chapter on vector fields (\ref{sec:fields}--\ref{sec:lie-morphisms}) treated vector fields \emph{as operators}: derivations, the commutator, the Lie algebra of a Lie group. ``But now we have this other side of vector fields \ldots\ as velocities'': vector fields as \emph{generators of dynamics}. Think of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ as a section of $TM \to M$ (Definition~\ref{def:vector-field}), a velocity vector attached to each point.}

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: INTEGRAL CURVES
% ============================================================================
\section{Integral Curves}\label{sec:integral-curves}

\roadmark{Stage: dynamics}{Curves whose velocity is prescribed by a vector field; in coordinates, a first-order system of ODEs.}

The velocity of a curve at a time $t$, from \ref{sec:velocities}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t} (Velocity at Time $t$).} Let $\gamma : J \to M$ be a smooth curve and $t_0 \in J$. The \textbf{velocity} of $\gamma$ at time $t_0$ is
\[
\dot\gamma(t_0) = \frac{d\gamma}{dt}(t_0) := \gamma_{*t_0}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t_0}\Big) \in T_{\gamma(t_0)}M, \qquad\text{explicitly}\qquad \dot\gamma(t_0)[f] = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=t_0} f\big(\gamma(t)\big)
\]
for a germ $f$ at $\gamma(t_0)$.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Recall: Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-at-t-coords} (Velocity at Time $t$ in Coordinates).} Let $\gamma : J \to M$ be smooth, $t_0 \in J$, and $(U, \varphi)$ a chart at $\gamma(t_0)$ with coordinate functions $x^1, \ldots, x^n$. Then
\[
\dot\gamma(t_0) = \sum_{j=1}^n \big(x^j \circ \gamma\big)'(t_0)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\Big|_{\gamma(t_0)} .
\]
Writing $x^j(t) = x^j(\gamma(t))$, this is $\dot\gamma = \sum_j \dot x^j\, \partial/\partial x^j$.
\end{quote}

In this chapter curves are mostly called $c : I \to M$, with velocity $\dot c(t)$; the corollary is the board's $\dot c = \langle \dot x^1, \ldots, \dot x^m \rangle$.



\begin{defbox}[Integral Curve]\deflabel{def:integral-curve}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. An \textbf{integral curve} of $\mathbf{X}$ is a smooth map $c : I \to M$, where $I = (a, b) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is an open interval (possibly $a = -\infty$ or $b = +\infty$), such that
\[
\dot c(t) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)} \qquad \text{for all } t \in I. \tag{$*$}
\]
The variable $t$ is called \textbf{time}. If $0 \in I$ and $c(0) = q$, the curve \textbf{starts at} $q$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Integral Curves}}
\end{defbox}

``This is the key notion. You might have seen this in your ordinary differential equations.''

\begin{propbox}[The Velocity Curve]\thmlabel{prop:velocity-curve}
Let $c : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Then $\dot c : I \to TM$, $t \mapsto \dot c(t)$, is a smooth curve in $TM$ lying over $c$, that is, $\pi \circ \dot c = c$. A smooth curve $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ if and only if $\dot c = \mathbf{X} \circ c$ as maps $I \to TM$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}; Ch.~9, \emph{Integral Curves}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture; added from a question: ``how is $\dot c$ defined, when $M$ is a general manifold?'')} \emph{Over $c$.} $\dot c(t) \in T_{c(t)}M$ by Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t}, so $\pi(\dot c(t)) = c(t)$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-projection}).

\emph{Smooth.} Let $t_0 \in I$ and $(U, \varphi = (x^1, \ldots, x^m))$ a chart at $c(t_0)$; on the open interval $I_0 = c^{-1}(U) \ni t_0$, $\dot c$ takes values in $TU$. In the chart $\tilde\varphi$ of $TM$ over $U$ (Definition~\ref{def:tb-chart}), whose last $m$ entries are the components in the coordinate basis, Corollary~\ref{cor:velocity-at-t-coords} gives
\[
\tilde\varphi\big(\dot c(t)\big) = \Big(x^1(c(t)), \ldots, x^m(c(t)),\ (x^1 \circ c)'(t), \ldots, (x^m \circ c)'(t)\Big), \qquad t \in I_0 ,
\]
smooth in $t$ because each $x^j \circ c$ is a smooth real function. So $\dot c$ is smooth near every $t_0$.

\emph{The integral-curve equation.} Both $\dot c(t)$ and $\mathbf{X}_{c(t)} = (\mathbf{X} \circ c)(t)$ lie in $T_{c(t)}M$, so $(\ast)$ compares two vectors in the same tangent space, for each $t$; and $(\ast)$ for all $t \in I$ says exactly that the maps $\dot c$ and $\mathbf{X} \circ c$ from $I$ to $TM$ are equal.
\end{proof}

So an integral curve is a curve whose velocity curve in $TM$ is the field read along the curve. For a curve in a regular level set $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^N$, the velocity $\dot c(t)$ is the ordinary derivative $c'(t)$, seen as the derivation $D_{c'(t)}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-at-t-level-set}).


\begin{propbox}[Integral Curves in Coordinates]\thmlabel{prop:integral-curve-coords}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open, with coordinates $x^1, \ldots, x^m$, and $\mathbf{X} = \sum_i f^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-coords}). Write a smooth curve as $c(t) = (x^1(t), \ldots, x^m(t))$, with velocity $\dot c(t) = \langle \dot x^1(t), \ldots, \dot x^m(t) \rangle$. Then $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if
\[
\dot x^i(t) = f^i\big(x^1(t), \ldots, x^m(t)\big) \qquad \text{for all } i = 1, \ldots, m \text{ and all } t \in I .
\]
The same holds on any manifold, in any chart, with the $x^i(t)$ the coordinates of $c(t)$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Integral Curves}, (9.1)}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-coords}, applied at each time $t$ to the shifted curve $s \mapsto c(t + s)$, $\dot c(t) = \sum_i \dot x^i(t)\, \partial/\partial x^i|_{c(t)}$, while $\mathbf{X}_{c(t)} = \sum_i f^i(c(t))\, \partial/\partial x^i|_{c(t)}$. The $\partial/\partial x^i|_{c(t)}$ form a basis of $T_{c(t)}M$, so $(*)$ holds at $t$ exactly when the components agree. The argument uses only a chart, so it applies on any manifold.
\end{proof}

The angle brackets mark $\dot c$ as a vector, not a point: ``I've been trained \ldots\ that you should distinguish vectors from points.'' What the proposition shows is that $(*)$ is a \emph{system of first-order ODEs}, usually nonlinear. All the derivatives are on the left-hand side, solved for: the right-hand side involves no derivatives. And it is a genuine \emph{system}, because the equation for $\dot x^i$ involves, in principle, all of the $x$'s. (Lee: solving a system of ODEs is called ``integrating'' it, hence the name \emph{integral} curve.)

\begin{rembox}[Why an Integral Curve Is an ODE]\label{rem:integral-curve-is-ode}
\textit{(Not from lecture; added from a question: ``how did integral curves suddenly connect to ODEs?'')} The definition is already an ODE, written without coordinates. In $(\ast)$ the unknown is the curve $c$; its derivative is set equal to something that depends on where $c$ currently is: ``the velocity at time $t$ is the arrow that $\mathbf{X}$ puts at the point where $c$ is at time $t$.'' The derivative of the unknown equals a known function of the unknown --- that is an ODE. Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords} only unpacks it into components.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \emph{The simplest example.} On $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbf{X} = x\, \frac{d}{dx}$: the equation is $\dot x = x$, so $x(t) = x_0 e^t$. The point runs away from $0$ faster and faster, because the arrows get longer further out.
    \item \emph{Conversely}, every autonomous system $\dot x^i = f^i(x)$ with smooth $f^i$ on an open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ is the system of the field $\sum_i f^i\, \partial/\partial x^i$: autonomous first-order systems on $U$ and vector fields on $U$ are the same thing. (``Autonomous'': the right-hand side does not depend on $t$, as the field does not change in time.)
    \item \emph{Higher order.} $\ddot x = -x$ becomes, with $y = \dot x$, the first-order system $\dot x = y$, $\dot y = -x$, the field $y\, \partial_x - x\, \partial_y$ --- minus the rotation field of Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}, whose integral curves it runs backwards in time. The harmonic oscillator is ``follow this field in the phase plane''; likewise Hamilton's equations, for a time-independent Hamiltonian, say that the motion follows the integral curves of one vector field on phase space.
    \item \emph{Local versus global.} On a manifold a chart turns $(\ast)$ into such a system, so the local questions --- existence, uniqueness, smooth dependence on the starting point --- reduce to ODE theory in $\mathbb{R}^m$; this is why Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local} is quoted in its Euclidean form. What one chart cannot settle is how far a solution continues: solutions in different charts must be patched together, and a solution may escape in finite time, which already happens in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape}). That is the content of Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}.
\end{itemize}
\end{rembox}

\textit{Lecture 24 recalled the definition with the velocity written ``in a fancy way'', $\dot c(t) = c_{*t}(d/dt)$, ``the derivation at $c(t)$ defined by $c$'' (Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t}), and gave the velocity curve a name: ``to any curve $c : I \to M$ one can naturally associate a lift'' to the tangent bundle.}

\begin{defbox}[Lift of a Curve]\deflabel{def:curve-lift}
Let $c : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Its \textbf{lift} to the tangent bundle is the curve
\[
\tilde c : I \to TM, \qquad \tilde c(t) = \big(c(t), \dot c(t)\big),
\]
the point $c(t)$ together with the velocity $\dot c(t) \in T_{c(t)}M$. It is the velocity curve $\dot c$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-curve}, so it is smooth and $\pi \circ \tilde c = c$.
\leeref{Ch.~3, \emph{Velocity Vectors of Curves}}
\end{defbox}

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 & TM \arrow[d, "\pi"] \\
I \arrow[ur, "\tilde c"] \arrow[r, "c"'] & M
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}

The lift exists for every smooth curve, injective or not. By Proposition~\ref{prop:velocity-curve}, $c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ exactly when $\tilde c = \mathbf{X} \circ c$: the lift is the field along the curve.

\begin{propbox}[An Integral Curve Returns with the Same Velocity]\thmlabel{prop:same-point-same-velocity}
Let $c : I \to M$ be an integral curve of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. If $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$ for some $t_1, t_2 \in I$, then $\dot c(t_1) = \dot c(t_2)$. Hence a smooth curve that passes through a point twice with different velocities is an integral curve of no vector field.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Integral Curves}}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: ``the field is single-valued at each point.'')} By $(\ast)$ at the times $t_1$ and $t_2$, and since $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$,
\[
\dot c(t_1) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t_1)} = \mathbf{X}_{c(t_2)} = \dot c(t_2) .
\]
The second sentence is the contrapositive: if $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$ but $\dot c(t_1) \neq \dot c(t_2)$, no vector field $\mathbf{X}$ satisfies $(\ast)$ at both times.
\end{proof}

\begin{exbox}[A Curve with a Loop]\exlabel{ex:loop-curve}
Let $c : I \to M$ pass through the same point at two times, $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$, with different velocities $\dot c(t_1) \neq \dot c(t_2)$, as in the figure. Its lift $\tilde c$ is still a well-defined map: it records the time, not just the point. ``But this cannot be an integral curve of anything'' (Proposition~\ref{prop:same-point-same-velocity}).
\end{exbox}

\emph{Simple and useful lemmas,} (Lecture~24) for any $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, ``completely general.''

\begin{lembox}[Translation and Rescaling]\thmlabel{lem:translation-rescaling}
Let $c : I \to M$ be an integral curve of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item \emph{(Translation lemma.)} For $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, the curve $\tilde c(t) = c(t + t_0)$, defined on $I - t_0 = \{ t - t_0 : t \in I \}$, is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$.
\item \emph{(Rescaling.)} For $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, the curve $\tilde c(t) = c(\lambda t)$, defined on $\{ t : \lambda t \in I \}$, is an integral curve of $\lambda\mathbf{X}$.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Lemmas 9.3 and 9.4}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: ``immediate by chain rule''; filled in.)} Both domains are open intervals (for $\lambda = 0$ the second is all of $\mathbb{R}$). Fix $t$ in the domain and a germ $f$ at $\tilde c(t)$; by Definition~\ref{def:velocity-at-t} and the chain rule for real functions of one variable:
\[
\dot{\tilde c}(t)[f] = \frac{d}{dt} f\big(c(t + t_0)\big) = (f \circ c)'(t + t_0) = \dot c(t + t_0)[f] = \mathbf{X}_{c(t + t_0)}[f] = \mathbf{X}_{\tilde c(t)}[f]
\]
for (1), and for (2)
\[
\dot{\tilde c}(t)[f] = \frac{d}{dt} f\big(c(\lambda t)\big) = \lambda\, (f \circ c)'(\lambda t) = \lambda\, \dot c(\lambda t)[f] = \lambda\, \mathbf{X}_{c(\lambda t)}[f] = (\lambda\mathbf{X})_{\tilde c(t)}[f] .
\]
Two tangent vectors at a point that agree on every germ are equal.
\end{proof}

``You can always translate time. We're going to use it a lot.'' Rescaling: ``you can rescale a field pointwise by a fixed factor, and the integral curves of that are easily related to the integral curves of the original.'' With $\lambda = -1$: the integral curves of $-\mathbf{X}$ are those of $\mathbf{X}$ run backwards.

\node[font=\scriptsize, align=center] at (1.7,-1.0) {rescaling with $\lambda = -1$: run backwards\\ black: times of $c$\\ \textcolor{red!70!black}{red: times of $\tilde c(t) = c(-t)$, a curve of $-\mathbf{X}$}};

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} Both operations keep the image of the curve and change only the clock. Translation relabels the times, so the point reached at time $t_0$ by $c$ is reached at time $0$ by $\tilde c$; the arrow (the velocity) is unchanged. Rescaling by $\lambda = -1$ reverses the arrow, which is why $\tilde c$ follows $-\mathbf{X}$. (A general $\lambda$ also changes the speed by the factor $|\lambda|$.)

\begin{lembox}[Integral Curves Under a Diffeomorphism]\thmlabel{lem:integral-curves-diffeo}
Let $F : M \to N$ be a diffeomorphism, $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, and $F_*\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(N)$ its pushforward (Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}, Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}). A smooth curve $c : I \to M$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if $F \circ c$ is an integral curve of $F_*\mathbf{X}$.
\leeref{Proposition 9.6}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: ``the check'' in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold}, there for a chart; written here for any diffeomorphism.)} $F \circ c$ is smooth, as a composite of smooth maps. Fix $t \in I$. By the chain rule (Theorem~\ref{prop:pushforward-functorial}), the velocity of $F \circ c$ at $t$ is
\[
(F \circ c)_{*t}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big) = dF_{c(t)}\Big(c_{*t}\Big(\frac{d}{dt}\Big)\Big) = dF_{c(t)}\big(\dot c(t)\big),
\]
and by Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward} at the point $F(c(t))$, whose preimage is $c(t)$,
\[
(F_*\mathbf{X})_{F(c(t))} = dF_{c(t)}\big(\mathbf{X}_{c(t)}\big) .
\]
The linear map $dF_{c(t)}$ is injective: by the chain rule, $d(F^{-1})_{F(c(t))} \circ dF_{c(t)} = d(F^{-1} \circ F)_{c(t)}$ is the identity. So the two vectors above agree exactly when $\dot c(t) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)}$: $F \circ c$ satisfies the integral-curve equation of $F_*\mathbf{X}$ at $t$ if and only if $c$ satisfies that of $\mathbf{X}$ at $t$.
\end{proof}

``This is a kind of naturality that I will come back to, because this is very general.'' (Lee, Proposition~9.6: a smooth $F$ takes integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ to integral curves of $\mathbf{Y}$ for all integral curves exactly when $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are $F$-related.)

% ============================================================================
% SECTION: LOCAL EXISTENCE AND UNIQUENESS
% ============================================================================
\section{Local Existence and Uniqueness}\label{sec:ode-existence}

\roadmark{Stage: dynamics}{Integral curves exist and are unique for short times: in $\mathbb{R}^m$ by ODE theory, on a manifold through a chart; two integral curves that meet agree on their whole common domain.}

``There's a fundamental theorem that, again, from --- we have moved from Calc~3 to Calc~4 --- ODEs.'' Uribe quoted it in the following form.

\begin{thmbox}[Local Existence and Uniqueness in Euclidean Space]\thmlabel{thm:ode-local}
Let $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ be open and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. Given any $p \in M$, there are $\varepsilon > 0$, an open neighbourhood $U \subseteq M$ of $p$, and a smooth map
\[
\varphi : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \longrightarrow M
\]
such that
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $\varphi(0, q) = q$ for every $q \in U$;
\item for every $q \in U$, the curve $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$, $t \mapsto \varphi(t, q)$, is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$;
\item \emph{(uniqueness)} if $q \in U$ and $c : I \to M$ is any integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ with $0 \in I$ and $c(0) = q$, then
\[
c|_{I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)} = \varphi(\cdot, q)|_{I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)} .
\]
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Theorem D.1}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (not given in this course)]
Taken from ODE theory, not proved in the course: ``a big, big theorem that takes forever to prove'', the theorem on existence, uniqueness and smooth dependence on initial conditions (Lee, Theorem~D.1, proved in Appendix~D). ``This theorem here packs everything that we will quote from the Euclidean case.''
\end{proof}

Items~(1) and~(2) together are \emph{existence}: every $q \in U$ has an integral curve $\varphi(\cdot, q)$ starting at $q$, all defined on the same interval $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$; the smoothness of $\varphi$ in the pair $(t, q)$ is \emph{smooth dependence on the initial condition}. Item~(3) is \emph{uniqueness}, on a par with existence; on the board it came as an addition, ``Furthermore (still the Euclidean theorem).''

``Imagine a Calc~3 plot of a field \ldots\ the vectors at every point.'' The theorem gives a time interval $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ and a neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ (drawn as a rectangle) such that from every point $q \in U$, $p$ included, there is an integral curve $t \mapsto \varphi(t, q)$ that starts at $q$ and is defined at least for $|t| < \varepsilon$.

\emph{What the theorem says beyond ``there is a path through $q$''} (a student's question). ``It says a lot of delicate things.'' The time interval is \emph{uniform}: as long as $q \in U$, the curve is defined at least for $|t| < \varepsilon$. And $\varphi$ is smooth as a function of the pair $(t, q)$ on the product $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U$: smooth in $t$, as an integral curve must be, but also, for fixed $t$, smooth in the initial condition $q$. Asked whether the image of $\varphi$ is ``just a slightly bigger open set around $U$'', Uribe answered: ``All of the above can happen.'' The examples below show some of the possibilities.

\begin{defbox}[Notation: $\varphi_t$ and $\varphi_q$]\deflabel{def:flow-notation}
In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}, and likewise of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold} below, for fixed $t \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ and fixed $q \in U$ write
\[
\varphi_t(q) := \varphi(t, q), \qquad \varphi_q(t) := \varphi(t, q).
\]
Then $\varphi_t : U \to M$ is a smooth map, and $\varphi_q : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$ is the integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ with $\varphi_q(0) = q$: it ``starts at $q$''.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Flows}}
\end{defbox}

``This notation is useful when you want to fix $t$.'' For the second one: ``we don't use it, but I suppose we could \ldots\ maybe we should use it. It sounds pedagogical. I actually like it.'' The board then used it. The two notations differ only in the letter in the subscript, so whether $\varphi_s$ means a map or a curve is read off from what $s$ is: a time or a point. Lee writes $\theta_t(p)$ and $\theta^{(p)}(t)$ for the two (Chapter~9). In these notes $\varphi$ also names charts $(U, \varphi)$; from here on it is the flow unless a chart is named.

\begin{exbox}[The Rotation Field]\exlabel{ex:rotation-flow}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $\mathbf{X} = -y\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} + x\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}$, ``the classical rotation.'' By Proposition~\ref{prop:integral-curve-coords} the integral curves solve
\[
\dot x = -y, \qquad \dot y = x .
\]
Then $\ddot x = -\dot y = -x$, so $x(t) = A\cos t + B\sin t$ and $y(t) = -\dot x(t) = A\sin t - B\cos t$. At $t = 0$, $(x_0, y_0) = (A, -B)$. So
\[
\varphi : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^2 \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2, \qquad \big(t, (x_0, y_0)\big) \longmapsto \big(x_0\cos t - y_0\sin t,\ x_0\sin t + y_0\cos t\big).
\]
$\varphi_t$ is the rotation by the angle $t$. The integral curves are the circles centred at the origin, traversed counterclockwise, and the constant curve at the origin. They exist for all time.
\leeref{Example 9.1}
\end{exbox}

``The harmonic oscillator, or rotation, whatever you want''; ``everybody has solved this some time, either in an ODE class or in a physics class.'' It is ``the benign case'': in Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local} one can take $U = \mathbb{R}^2$ and any $\varepsilon$, indeed $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Going back to the question about the image, $\varphi_t(U)$ is $U$ rotated about the origin, possibly far from $U$.

\textit{Lecture 24. The definition again, then the local theorem on a manifold, two ``simple and useful lemmas'', and uniqueness on the whole common domain: ``the deep --- meaning foundational --- theory of the subject.'' The definition and the lemmas are in \ref{sec:integral-curves}.}

The Euclidean theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}) is ``Theorem~D.1 in Lee, with proof. I will forever be amazed by how much [Lee] was able to put in his book.'' Its manifold version ``follows immediately from the Euclidean version.''

\begin{thmbox}[Local Existence and Uniqueness on a Manifold]\thmlabel{thm:ode-local-manifold}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$. There are $\varepsilon > 0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a map
\[
\varphi : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U \longrightarrow M
\]
such that
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item $\varphi(0, q) = q$ for every $q \in U$;
\item for every $q \in U$, the curve $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$, $t \mapsto \varphi_t(q)$, is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$;
\item \emph{(local uniqueness)} if $c : I \to M$ is any integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ on an open interval $I \ni 0$ with $c(0) = q$ for some $q \in U$, then $c(t) = \varphi_t(q)$ for all $t \in I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, $\varphi$ is smooth.
\leeref{Proposition 9.2; Theorem D.1}
\end{thmbox}

On the board, (3) was stated for $c : (-\delta, \delta) \to M$, with the conclusion on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \cap (-\delta, \delta)$; ``these domains don't have to be symmetric'', which is the form of~(3) above. By~(3), ``there's only one map like that.''

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: ``use a chart at $p$, and then push forward \ldots\ push this thing down here. Now we have the theorem at the level of open sets in Euclidean space, and we just push it up again.'' The chart is called $\psi$, since $\varphi$ is the flow --- ``which is why Lee uses $\theta$.'' The details are filled in.)} When $M$ is an open set in $\mathbb{R}^m$ this is Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}. In general, take a chart $\psi : W \to \psi(W) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ at $p$. It is a diffeomorphism of the open submanifold $W$ onto the open set $\psi(W)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:chart-diffeo}), so the field $\mathbf{X}|_W$ has a pushforward $\mathbf{Y} = \psi_*\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(\psi(W))$ (Definition~\ref{def:vf-pushforward}, Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-pushforward}).

\emph{The check.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-curves-diffeo}, applied to the diffeomorphism $\psi : W \to \psi(W)$, a curve $c : I \to W$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ if and only if $\psi \circ c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$.

\emph{Push down, solve, push up.} Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}, for $\mathbf{Y}$ on $\psi(W)$ at $\psi(p)$, gives $\varepsilon > 0$, an open $U' \ni \psi(p)$ and a smooth $\varphi' : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U' \to \psi(W)$. Put $U = \psi^{-1}(U')$ and
\[
\varphi(t, q) = \psi^{-1}\big(\varphi'(t, \psi(q))\big) \in W .
\]
$\varphi$ is smooth, as a composite of smooth maps, and $\varphi(0, q) = \psi^{-1}(\psi(q)) = q$. For $q \in U$ the curve $t \mapsto \varphi'(t, \psi(q))$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$ in $\psi(W)$, so by the check, applied to $c = \varphi(\cdot, q)$ (for which $\psi \circ c = \varphi'(\cdot, \psi(q))$), $t \mapsto \varphi_t(q)$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$. This gives~(1) and~(2).

\emph{Uniqueness.} The one point beyond pushing down is that an integral curve $c$ of $\mathbf{X}$ might leave $W$, where the chart says nothing. Let $c : I \to M$ be an integral curve, $I \ni 0$ an open interval, $c(0) = q \in U$, and let $J = I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. The set $c^{-1}(W) \cap J$ is open and contains $0$; let $J_0$ be the open interval that is its connected component containing $0$. On $J_0$, $\psi \circ c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{Y}$ starting at $\psi(q)$ (the check), so Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}(3) gives $\psi(c(t)) = \varphi'(t, \psi(q))$, that is, $c(t) = \varphi(t, q)$, for $t \in J_0$. Suppose $J_0 \neq J$, say $b = \sup J_0 < \sup J$ (the left end is handled the same way). Then $b \in J$, and by continuity $c(b) = \lim_{t \to b^-} \varphi(t, q) = \varphi(b, q)$, which lies in $W$. So $b \in c^{-1}(W) \cap J$, an open set; an interval around $b$ lies in it, and the component $J_0$ would contain $b$ and points beyond it, contradicting $b = \sup J_0$. Hence $J_0 = J$, and $c(t) = \varphi_t(q)$ on all of $I \cap (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$: this is~(3).
\end{proof}

``Now the core technical result that I want to prove today.''

\begin{propbox}[Uniqueness on the Common Domain]\thmlabel{prop:global-uniqueness}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, and let $c_i : I_i \to M$, $i = 1, 2$, be integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$. If there is $t_0 \in I_1 \cap I_2$ with $c_1(t_0) = c_2(t_0)$, then
\[
c_1|_{I_1 \cap I_2} = c_2|_{I_1 \cap I_2} .
\]
\leeref{Theorem 9.12 (proof)}
\end{propbox}

``Suppose you have two integral curves that agree at some time $t_0$ \ldots\ Then the conclusion is that they agree wherever they can.''

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24. Details from the discussion in class are added where noted.)} \emph{Reduction to $t_0 = 0$.} By the translation lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)), $t \mapsto c_i(t + t_0)$ are integral curves on $I_i - t_0$ that agree at $0$, and the conclusion for them is the conclusion for the $c_i$. So assume $t_0 = 0$, and let $q = c_1(0) = c_2(0)$.

\emph{Local uniqueness.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold}(3) at $q$, both $c_i$ equal $\varphi_\cdot(q)$ near $0$. So there is $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq I_1 \cap I_2$ and
\[
c_1|_{(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)} = c_2|_{(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)} .
\]
``The only thing is to extend this local uniqueness into global uniqueness.''

\emph{Argue by contradiction.} Introduce
\[
\mathcal{T}_+ = \{ t \in I_1 \cap I_2 \cap (0, \infty) : c_1(t) \neq c_2(t) \} .
\]
We want to show $\mathcal{T}_+ = \varnothing$. Assume $\mathcal{T}_+ \neq \varnothing$. It is bounded below by $\varepsilon$; let $\tau = \inf \mathcal{T}_+ \ge \varepsilon > 0$. \textit{(Filled in: $\tau$ is in the domain.)} $I_1 \cap I_2$ is an interval containing $\varepsilon/2$ and some point of $\mathcal{T}_+ \ge \tau$, and $\varepsilon/2 < \tau$, so $\tau \in I_1 \cap I_2$. By the definition of the infimum, $c_1 = c_2$ on $(0, \tau)$.

\emph{Claim: $c_1(\tau) = c_2(\tau)$.} Again by contradiction. If $c_1(\tau) \neq c_2(\tau)$, since $M$ is Hausdorff (Definition~\ref{def:hausdorff-t2}) there are neighbourhoods $U_i$ of $c_i(\tau)$ with $U_1 \cap U_2 = \varnothing$. By continuity of $c_1$ and $c_2$ there is an open interval $J \ni \tau$, inside $I_1 \cap I_2$ (which is open), with $c_i(J) \subseteq U_i$. So there is $\tau_1 \in J$ with $0 < \tau_1 < \tau$, and $c_1(\tau_1) \in U_1$, $c_2(\tau_1) \in U_2$, so $c_1(\tau_1) \neq c_2(\tau_1)$ and $\tau_1 \in \mathcal{T}_+$. This contradicts $\tau = \inf \mathcal{T}_+$. Hence $c_1(\tau) = c_2(\tau)$.

\emph{Local uniqueness at $\tau$.} ``By the translation lemma, local uniqueness at $t = 0$ is equivalent to local uniqueness at any $\tau$'': apply the local-uniqueness step to the integral curves $c_i(\cdot + \tau)$, which agree at $0$. So there is $\delta > 0$ such that the curves agree on $(\tau - \delta, \tau + \delta)$. Together with $c_1 = c_2$ on $(0, \tau]$, they agree on $(0, \tau + \delta) \cap I_1 \cap I_2$, so every point of $\mathcal{T}_+$ is $\ge \tau + \delta$, and $\inf \mathcal{T}_+ \ge \tau + \delta > \tau$: a contradiction. So $\mathcal{T}_+ = \varnothing$.

\emph{Negative times.} ``Of course you do the same thing for $\tau_-$ from the other side. You take the sup'': with $\mathcal{T}_- = \{ t \in I_1 \cap I_2 \cap (-\infty, 0) : c_1(t) \neq c_2(t) \}$ and $\sup \mathcal{T}_-$, or apply the above to $t \mapsto c_i(-t)$, integral curves of $-\mathbf{X}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(2)). With $c_1(0) = c_2(0)$, the curves agree on all of $I_1 \cap I_2$.
\end{proof}

\textit{(Figure after the board.)} The situation the claim rules out: the curves agree on $(0, \tau)$ and differ at $\tau$, with disjoint neighbourhoods $U_1, U_2$. ``When you do elementary Euclidean geometry and argue by contradiction, every picture that you draw doesn't look contradictory, because the thing is true.'' A student noted that the argument is ``very similar'' to the Euclidean one; Uribe agreed. Another student asked how $J$ stays inside $I_1 \cap I_2$; it does because the domains are open intervals.

\begin{rembox}[Where the Hausdorff Property Is Used]\label{rem:uniqueness-hausdorff}
\textit{(Filled in.)} The claim $c_1(\tau) = c_2(\tau)$ is the one step of the proof that uses that $M$ is Hausdorff (``since $M$ is $T_2$'' on the board): it says that the set of times where the two curves agree is closed in $I_1 \cap I_2$. Without the Hausdorff property the proposition fails. The line with two origins (\ref{sec:ex-two-origins}), two copies $\mathbb{R} \times \{1\}$ and $\mathbb{R} \times \{2\}$ glued along $x \neq 0$, has smooth charts (each copy) but is not Hausdorff. The field $d/dx$, in either chart, is well defined, and $c_i(t) = (t, i)$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$, $i = 1, 2$, are integral curves of it. They agree at every $t \neq 0$ and differ at $t = 0$, where they pass through the two different origins.
\end{rembox}

\begin{corbox}[Non-Injective Integral Curves Repeat]\thmlabel{cor:returning-curve-periodic}
Let $c : I \to M$ be an integral curve of $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, and suppose $c(t_1) = c(t_2)$ for some $t_1 < t_2$ in $I$. Put $T = t_2 - t_1 > 0$. Then
\[
c(t + T) = c(t) \qquad \text{for every } t \in I \text{ with } t + T \in I .
\]
\leeref{Problem 9-1}
\end{corbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Uribe, by email after Lecture~24: ``I realized that I did not really answer today's question of whether integral curves must be injective. The answer is that if an integral curve is not injective, then it must be periodic.'')} By the translation lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)), the curve $g(t) = c(t + T)$, defined on $I - T$, is an integral curve of the same field. Both $c$ and $g$ are defined at $t_1$: $t_1 \in I$, and $t_1 \in I - T$ because $t_1 + T = t_2 \in I$. There they agree:
\[
g(t_1) = c(t_1 + T) = c(t_2) = c(t_1) .
\]
Therefore, by uniqueness (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}), $g = c$ on $I \cap (I - T)$, that is, $c(t + T) = c(t)$ for every $t \in I$ with $t + T \in I$.
\end{proof}

``Note that $T$ may not be the smallest period.'' For the rotation field (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}), the integral curve $c(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$ has $c(0) = c(4\pi)$, so $T = 4\pi$ is a period, while the smallest period is $2\pi$. A constant curve, at a zero of $\mathbf{X}$, is periodic with every $T > 0$. \textit{(Filled in.)} The email says $c(t + T) = c(t)$ ``for all $t$''. For a curve on a bounded interval the corollary only covers the $t$ with both $t$ and $t + T$ in $I$; for the maximal integral curve the domain is then all of $\mathbb{R}$, and the identity holds for every $t$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:returning-maximal-periodic}).

\begin{rembox}[Must an Integral Curve Be Injective?]\label{rem:integral-curve-injective}
A student asked this in Lecture~24, after Example~\ref{ex:loop-curve}. ``We're about to prove something related \ldots\ except if it's constant'': at a zero of $\mathbf{X}$ the constant curve is an integral curve. The ``something related'' is Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}. \textit{(Filled in.)} Constant curves are not the only exception: the circles of the rotation field (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}) are integral curves that return to the same point with the same velocity, every $2\pi$. Uribe answered the question by email after the lecture: ``if an integral curve is not injective, then it must be periodic'' (Corollary~\ref{cor:returning-curve-periodic}; for the maximal curve, Proposition~\ref{prop:returning-maximal-periodic}). Lee shows that a maximal integral curve is exactly one of: constant, injective, or periodic and nonconstant (Lee, Problem~9-1).
\end{rembox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} The three kinds of maximal integral curve (Lee, Problem~9-1). An integral curve that comes back to a point comes back with the same velocity, the value of the field there; by Corollary~\ref{cor:returning-curve-periodic} it then repeats itself. The loop of the previous figure, which comes back with a different velocity, is none of the three: it is not an integral curve.

\begin{exbox}[The Euler Field]\exlabel{ex:euler-field}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $\mathbf{X} = x\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} + y\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}$. The integral curves solve $\dot x = x$, $\dot y = y$, so $\varphi_t(x_0, y_0) = e^t(x_0, y_0)$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$. For $(x_0, y_0) \neq 0$ the image is the open ray from the origin through $(x_0, y_0)$, since $e^t$ takes every value in $(0, \infty)$ and never $0$; at the origin the integral curve is constant.
\end{exbox}

``If you go to Desmos or whatever, you see the integral curves of the Euler field \ldots\ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ radial, like that, and they seem to intersect, but they don't.'' The rays are open, and the origin is its own integral curve. The images of the integral curves $t \mapsto e^t(x_0, y_0)$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$, partition $\mathbb{R}^2$, as Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} requires. \textit{(Filled in.)} If two of them pass through a common point, $c_1(t_1) = c_2(t_2)$, then $t \mapsto c_2(t + t_2 - t_1)$ is an integral curve (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1)) that agrees with $c_1$ at time $t_1$, so it equals $c_1$ on $\mathbb{R}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}), and the two images coincide.

% SECTION: MAXIMAL INTEGRAL CURVES AND FLOWS
% ============================================================================
\section{Maximal Integral Curves and Flows}\label{sec:flows}

\roadmark{Stage: dynamics}{The maximal integral curve through each point, complete vector fields, and the flow: all maximal curves assembled into one smooth map on an open domain in $\mathbb{R} \times M$.}

\textit{Lecture 24. ``What this allows us to do'' --- uniqueness on the common domain, Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} --- ``is to define the maximal domain of an integral curve, given an initial condition.''}

\begin{defbox}[Maximal Domain]\deflabel{def:maximal-domain}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$. Define
\[
\big(\alpha(p), \beta(p)\big) = \bigcup_{I} I ,
\]
the union over the domains $I$ of all integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$:
an open interval containing $0$, possibly infinite or semi-infinite. It is the \textbf{maximal domain} of integral curves of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$.
\leeref{Theorem 9.12}
\end{defbox}

The union is nonempty, since an integral curve starting at $p$ exists (Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local-manifold}). Each domain $I$ is an open interval containing $0$, ``because it starts at $p$'', so the union is an open interval containing $0$. ``So it's something that is very harmless to take.''

\begin{propbox}[The Maximal Integral Curve]\thmlabel{prop:maximal-curve}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ and $p \in M$. There is an integral curve $\varphi_p : (\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \to M$ of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$, and every integral curve $c : I \to M$ starting at $p$ satisfies $I \subseteq (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ and $c = \varphi_p|_I$. So $(\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ is the largest possible domain of such a curve, and $\varphi_p$ is the unique maximal integral curve starting at $p$. This proves Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(1).
\leeref{Theorem 9.12}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Lecture~24: ``How do you define it? Well, I take a point $t$ here. It's in some $I$, so there is some integral curve defined in the neighbourhood of that. I define it by that, and it doesn't matter which $I$ I chose, by the previous lemma.'' Details filled in.)} For $t \in (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, choose an integral curve $c : I \to M$ starting at $p$ with $t \in I$, and set $\varphi_p(t) = c(t)$. \emph{Well defined:} if $c' : I' \to M$ is another, then $c$ and $c'$ agree at time $0$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness} they agree on $I \cap I' \ni t$. \emph{An integral curve:} near each $t$, $\varphi_p$ equals the smooth curve $c$ on the open interval $I \ni t$, so $\varphi_p$ is smooth and $\dot\varphi_p(t) = \dot c(t) = \mathbf{X}_{c(t)} = \mathbf{X}_{\varphi_p(t)}$, since velocity at $t$ only depends on the curve near $t$. And $\varphi_p(0) = p$. \emph{Maximal:} if $c : I \to M$ starts at $p$, then $I$ is one of the domains in the union, so $I \subseteq (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, and $c = \varphi_p|_I$ by the definition of $\varphi_p$.
\end{proof}

``The uniqueness is absolutely fantastic for the theory.'' The maximal domains of the examples: $\mathbb{R}$ for the rotation and Euler fields (Examples~\ref{ex:rotation-flow} and~\ref{ex:euler-field}); $(-\infty, 1/(x_0y_0))$ and $(-\infty, -x_0)$ for the two examples that follow.

``Now I want to give you a problematic example. Problematic in the sense that because of examples like the one I'm about to give you, the theory becomes, well, necessarily elaborate.''

\begin{exbox}[Escape in Finite Time]\exlabel{ex:finite-escape}
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $\mathbf{X} = y x^2\, \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} + 0 \cdot \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}$. The integral curves solve
\[
\dot x = y(t)\, x(t)^2, \qquad \dot y = 0 .
\]
So $y(t) = y(0) = y_0$ for all $t$, and $dx/dt = y_0 x^2$ separates, for $x_0 \neq 0$, as $dx/x^2 = y_0\, dt$: $-1/x(t) = y_0 t + C$ with $C = -1/x_0$. Hence
\[
x(t) = \frac{x_0}{1 - x_0 y_0\, t}, \qquad y(t) = y_0 .
\]
\emph{Observation:} the denominator is zero at $t = 1/(x_0y_0)$. Take $M$ to be the open first quadrant $\{x > 0,\ y > 0\}$ (``otherwise there are sign issues; nothing interesting happens''). Fix $T > 0$, and let $q = (x_0, y_0)$ lie on the hyperbola $xy = 1/T$. Then
\[
\lim_{t \to T^-} x(t) = +\infty .
\]
For negative $t$ nothing goes wrong: the denominator only grows, and $x(t) \to 0$ as $t \to -\infty$. So the maximal domain of an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $(x_0, y_0)$ is
\[
\Big( -\infty,\ \frac{1}{x_0 y_0} \Big).
\]
\leeref{Example 9.10}
\end{exbox}

The integral curves lie on horizontal lines. Starting at $q$ the point moves to the right for $t > 0$, and the velocity $y_0x^2$ grows quadratically in $x$: ``the particle just gets to infinity in finite time, beating everybody else.'' Backwards in time the point moves against the arrows, towards the $y$-axis, where the field vanishes: ``it gets stuck,'' but there is no blowing up. The escape time $1/(x_0y_0)$ depends on the initial condition, through the hyperbola $xy = 1/T$ on which it lies. So, by inspection, not all integral curves are defined for all time --- ``and that makes life complicated.'' (The curve does not continue past $T$, even inside $\mathbb{R}^2$: its $x$-coordinate is unbounded. No other integral curve from $q$ does either, by uniqueness on the whole common domain: two integral curves starting at $q$ agree wherever both are defined (Proposition~\ref{prop:global-uniqueness}; Lee, Theorem~D.4). The uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local} alone gives this only for $|t| < \varepsilon$.)

\begin{exbox}[Running Off the Edge]\exlabel{ex:half-line}
Let $M = (-\infty, 0)$ and $\mathbf{X} = \dfrac{d}{dx}$. The integral curves solve $\dot c(t) = 1$, so the integral curve starting at $x_0$ is
\[
\varphi_t(x_0) = x_0 + t ,
\]
translation by time $t$, with $\varphi_t(x_0)|_{t=0} = x_0$. It stays in $M$ exactly while $x_0 + t < 0$. So for every $x_0 \in (-\infty, 0)$ the maximal domain in $t$ is
\[
\{ t : x_0 + t < 0 \} = (-\infty, -x_0) .
\]
\end{exbox}

\textit{(Not from lecture; figure added.)} The maximal domains of Example~\ref{ex:half-line}, assembled into the set $\mathcal{D} = \{ (t, x_0) : x_0 < 0,\ t < -x_0 \}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:maximal-flow}(2), an open set. Compare the flow domain of Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape} above: there $\beta(p) = 1/(x_0y_0)$ blows up as $x_0 \to 0$, here $\beta(x_0) = -x_0$ shrinks to $0$ at the end of $M$. Neither field is complete.

\begin{propbox}[Non-Injective Maximal Integral Curves Are Periodic]\thmlabel{prop:returning-maximal-periodic}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, $p \in M$, and let $\varphi_p : (\alpha(p), \beta(p)) \to M$ be the maximal integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$. If $\varphi_p$ is not injective, say $\varphi_p(t_1) = \varphi_p(t_2)$ with $T = t_2 - t_1 > 0$, then $(\alpha(p), \beta(p)) = \mathbb{R}$ and
\[
\varphi_p(t + T) = \varphi_p(t) \qquad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R} .
\]
\leeref{Problem 9-1}
\end{propbox}

\begin{proof}
\textit{(Not from lecture: Uribe's argument by email, Corollary~\ref{cor:returning-curve-periodic}, completed by maximality.)} Write $I = (\alpha, \beta) = (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ and $c = \varphi_p$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:returning-curve-periodic},
\[
c(s + T) = c(s) \qquad \text{whenever } s \in I \text{ and } s + T \in I . \tag{$\dagger$}
\]
Since $\alpha < t_1 < t_2 < \beta$, we have $T < \beta - \alpha$.

\emph{$\beta = +\infty$.} Suppose $\beta < +\infty$. The intervals $I = (\alpha, \beta)$ and $I + T = (\alpha + T, \beta + T)$ overlap, because $\alpha + T < \beta$, and their union is $(\alpha, \beta + T)$. Define $\tilde c$ on it by
\[
\tilde c(t) = c(t) \ \ (t \in I), \qquad \tilde c(t) = c(t - T) \ \ (t \in I + T) .
\]
This is well defined: if $t \in I \cap (I + T)$, then $s = t - T$ has $s \in I$ and $s + T = t \in I$, so $c(t - T) = c(t)$ by $(\dagger)$. On the open interval $I$, $\tilde c$ is the integral curve $c$; on the open interval $I + T$, it is the integral curve $t \mapsto c(t - T)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:translation-rescaling}(1) with $t_0 = -T$). Smoothness and the equation $\dot{\tilde c}(t) = \mathbf{X}_{\tilde c(t)}$ only involve $\tilde c$ near $t$, so $\tilde c$ is an integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$. It starts at $p$, as $0 \in I$ and $\tilde c(0) = c(0) = p$. Its domain $(\alpha, \beta + T)$ is not contained in $(\alpha, \beta)$, which contradicts Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}. So $\beta = +\infty$.

\emph{$\alpha = -\infty$.} In the same way, if $\alpha > -\infty$, then $\tilde c(t) = c(t)$ on $I$ and $\tilde c(t) = c(t + T)$ on $I - T = (\alpha - T, \beta - T)$ define an integral curve starting at $p$ on $(\alpha - T, \beta)$: on the overlap $I \cap (I - T)$ the two agree by $(\dagger)$ with $s = t$. This again contradicts Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve}.

\emph{Periodicity.} Now $I = \mathbb{R}$, so $(\dagger)$ holds for every $s \in \mathbb{R}$.
\end{proof}

So a maximal integral curve is either injective or periodic and defined for all time. Lee's Problem~9-1 separates out the constant curves, which are periodic with every period.

\begin{defbox}[Complete Vector Field]\deflabel{def:complete-field}
$\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ is \textbf{complete} if $(\alpha(p), \beta(p)) = \mathbb{R}$ for every $p \in M$.
\leeref{Ch.~9, \emph{Complete Vector Fields}}
\end{defbox}

``This is the case where there are no headaches \ldots\ you can go forever, and backwards in time as well, forever.'' (``The existential question is: the time domain of the universe --- is it complete?'') The rotation field and the Euler field are complete; the fields of Examples~\ref{ex:finite-escape} and~\ref{ex:half-line} are not.

``When you're doing theory, you wonder: are there results that have the conclusion `this vector field is complete'? It's hard to tell in general.'' ``A very powerful-seeming little result'':

\begin{lembox}[Uniform Time Lemma]\thmlabel{lem:uniform-time}
Let $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$. If there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \subseteq (\alpha(p), \beta(p))$ for every $p \in M$, then $\mathbf{X}$ is complete.
\leeref{Lemma 9.15}
\end{lembox}

\begin{proof}[Proof (to be filled)]
To be proved in Lecture~25 (``I'll prove this on Monday'').
\end{proof}

The lemma's hypothesis is that a uniform strip $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times M$ fits inside; its conclusion is that the whole of $\mathbb{R} \times M$ does. (``I always reverse the cartoon axes. Someday I'll learn.'')

Announced for Monday, as consequences of Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform-time}:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item every vector field on a compact manifold is complete: ``compactness will assure that there is a uniform time'' (Lee, Corollary~9.17);
\item every left-invariant vector field on a Lie group is complete, ``because you're going to be able to translate solutions'' (Lee, Theorem~9.18).
\end{itemize}

\textit{The flow. Lecture 23, the last minutes: ``Let me tell you the bigger picture of what actually is happening, and then we'll see how much of that we get to prove \ldots\ We'll prove a big chunk of this on Friday.''}

\begin{thmbox}[Maximal Integral Curves and the Flow]\thmlabel{thm:maximal-flow}
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $\mathbf{X} \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$.
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item For every $p \in M$ there is a unique \emph{maximal} integral curve of $\mathbf{X}$ starting at $p$, maximal with respect to its domain. Write it $\varphi_p$ and its domain $(\alpha(p), \beta(p))$, where $\alpha(p) \in [-\infty, 0)$ and $\beta(p) \in (0, +\infty]$: ``$\alpha$ or $\beta$ may be $\pm\infty$.''
\item Let
\[
\mathcal{D} = \bigcup_{p \in M} \big(\alpha(p), \beta(p)\big) \times \{p\} \ \subseteq\ \mathbb{R} \times M, \qquad \varphi : \mathcal{D} \longrightarrow M, \quad (t, p) \longmapsto \varphi_p(t).
\]
Then $\mathcal{D}$ is open in $\mathbb{R} \times M$, and $\varphi$ is smooth.
\end{enumerate}
\leeref{Theorem 9.12}
\end{thmbox}

\begin{proof}[Proof of (1) (Lecture~24); (2) to be filled]
Part~(1) is Proposition~\ref{prop:maximal-curve} above, proved in Lecture~24. Part~(2) is to be proved. Uribe's indication for (1), in Lecture~23: ``by uniqueness and something called the translation lemma, which is very easy to see,'' there is ``only one way to continue the curve forwards in time and then backwards in time until either you never stop or you run into the edge of the manifold.'' Openness of $\mathcal{D}$ ``is surprisingly long to prove.''
\end{proof}

$\varphi$ is ``just flowing, like we were doing before'', except that the domain of the time variable depends on the point, as in Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape}. The theorem is the local picture of Theorem~\ref{thm:ode-local}, with its rectangles $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times U$, put together on the whole manifold. In the two examples:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item Rotation (Example~\ref{ex:rotation-flow}): $\alpha \equiv -\infty$, $\beta \equiv +\infty$, $\mathcal{D} = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^2$.
\item Escape (Example~\ref{ex:finite-escape}): $\alpha \equiv -\infty$, $\beta(x, y) = 1/(xy)$, so $\mathcal{D} = \{ (t, (x, y)) : x, y > 0,\ t\,xy < 1 \}$, open, and $\varphi(t, (x, y)) = \big(x/(1 - xyt),\ y\big)$, smooth on $\mathcal{D}$.
\end{itemize}

\appendix
\chapter{Concordance with Lee}\label{app:lee}

These notes follow the course, and Lee's \emph{Introduction to Smooth Manifolds} (2nd ed.) is the course text. The two cover the same mathematics by different routes. The course is more algebraic --- germs, derivations of germs, the ideal $I_p$ --- and it builds tangent spaces from the geometric picture towards the abstract one, where Lee starts abstract. This appendix is for reading the two side by side. It records where the notation differs, where the routes diverge, which parts of Lee each section corresponds to, and, for every result of Lee's cited in these notes, where its counterpart is. Throughout the notes, the line \textsc{Lee}: at the foot of a box gives the same information locally.

\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A.1\quad Notation}

$\varphi_t(q) = \varphi_q(t) = \varphi(t, q)$; $\dot c(t)$ & $\theta_t(p) = \theta^{(p)}(t) = \theta(t, p)$; $\gamma'(t)$ & The flow and its integral curves (Definition~\ref{def:flow-notation}); the subscript is a time for $\varphi_t$, a point for $\varphi_q$. \\

\section*{A.2\quad Where the routes diverge}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A.2\quad Where the routes diverge}

Each row is expanded in a \textbf{Comparison with Lee} paragraph at the place indicated.

\begin{longtable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.2cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.9cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.7cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Topic} & \textbf{These notes} & \textbf{Lee} \\ \midrule \endhead
Hausdorff quotients & One criterion for all open quotients (Theorems~\ref{thm:hausdorff-criterion} and~\ref{thm:2c-quotient}), reused for orbit and coset spaces & Checked example by example (Example 1.5, Problem 1-9) \\
Regular level sets & Implicit function theorem, topological first (Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-value}), smooth afterwards (Proposition~\ref{prop:level-set-smooth}) & Example 1.32 for one function; Corollary 5.14 via the constant-rank theorem \\
Hausdorff orbit spaces & Compact group on a Hausdorff space, purely topological (Theorem~\ref{thm:orbit-T2-strong}) & Proper actions of Lie groups (Proposition 21.4, Corollary 21.6) \\
Homogeneous spaces & $G/H$ compact and $X$ Hausdorff (Theorem~\ref{thm:GH-homeo}); the hypothesis is needed (Example~\ref{ex:GH-not-homeo}) & Smooth version, no compactness (Theorem 21.18) \\
Tangent vectors & Derivations of germs; locality is built in, and no bump functions are needed & Derivations of $C^\infty(M)$; locality from bump functions (Proposition 3.8) \\
Order of ideas & Geometric first, $T^{\geo}_pM = \ker F'(p)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:tangent-kernel}), then derivations & Derivations first; $T_pS = \ker d\Phi_p$ later (Proposition 5.38) \\
Cotangent space & The dual, and also $I_p/I_p^2$ of germs, via a non-degenerate pairing (Theorem~\ref{thm:cotangent-ideal}) & The dual in the text (Chapter~11); $I_p/I_p^2$ of global functions, via $f \mapsto df_p$, as Problem 11-4 \\
Transversality & Level sets in Euclidean space (Theorem~\ref{thm:transverse-preimage}) & Embedded submanifolds (Theorem 6.30) \\
Linear algebra & The toolkit of \ref{sec:vector-spaces}, including the pairing theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:pairing}) & Appendix B; dual spaces in Chapter~11 \\
